articles.title: Amazon SageMaker Inference: 2026 launches in review, part 2 | Amazon Web Services
articles.text:
Artificial Intelligence
Amazon SageMaker Inference: 2026 launches in review, part 2
Once a model is in production, the questions change. Teams want to know which configuration the model should run on now that traffic is real, how to fit more models onto GPUs they already pay for, what to do when the next model is too large for one machine, why requests wait in one Region while GPUs sit idle in another, and why latency rose when nobody changed anything. This post takes those questions in the order teams usually meet them.
For HyperPod Inference, it listed additional routing strategies, broader support for model serving frameworks, and expanded multi-Region networking. The Inference Gateway delivers the routing, and managed NVIDIA Dynamo is a new serving framework. For managed endpoints, the roadmap pointed to deeper integration with the rest of the AWS AI landscape. Inference recommendations now run from Amazon SageMaker AI Studio, the SageMaker Python SDK, and the coding agents engineers already use, and endpoints can now route requests across Regions and accounts.
To keep each section concrete, we follow one hypothetical team through the blog post. In the spring, they launched a customer support assistant on a 70B-parameter model behind a single SageMaker AI endpoint, using the launches from part 1. By the fall, they need to support more product lines, adopt a larger reasoning model, serve customers in a second Region, and keep their GPU bill flat.
The launches at a glance
Choose the right configuration from wherever you work
The team picked its first configuration from a benchmark run in April. Since then, they have added four LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation) adapters, one for each product line, and the product team has set a target of 500 milliseconds for time to first token (TTFT) at peak load. The April configuration was never tested against either change. The engineers who will re-run the analysis work in notebooks and coding agents, and few of them use the console.
Inference recommendations launched in April as an API. Four updates since then make it available in more of the places teams work, and let it answer two harder questions: how many adapters an endpoint can carry, and how much concurrency it can take before it misses a latency target. A new agent skill brings the same expertise into coding agents.
Inference recommendations in SageMaker AI Studio (July 2026)
Blog: Launching UI for generative AI inference recommendations in Amazon SageMaker AI
The April launch automated instance, container, and optimization selection through APIs. Inference recommendations are now also available in SageMaker AI Studio as a guided, low-code workflow. In Studio, choose Jobs, then Inference optimization. Choose a use-case profile (Interact, Generate, Summarize, or Custom), an optimization goal (minimize latency, maximize throughput, or minimize cost), and a model from SageMaker JumpStart, Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3), the Model Registry, or an existing SageMaker model.
SageMaker AI benchmarks candidate configurations on real GPU infrastructure using NVIDIA AIPerf and applies techniques that match the goal, such as speculative decoding for throughput or kernel tuning for latency. You compare the ranked results by TTFT, inter-token latency, throughput, and cost, and then deploy the chosen configuration to a real-time endpoint from Studio.
Inference recommendations in the SageMaker Python SDK v3 (August 2026)
Blog: LLM optimization integration for Amazon SageMaker Python SDK
Benchmarking and recommendations previously required SageMaker AI Studio or direct Boto3 calls. They are now part of the SageMaker Python SDK v3 (version 3.17.0 and later), the same interface teams use for training and deployment, so the workflow fits into notebooks, CI pipelines, and MLOps workflows. You can benchmark a live endpoint against your workload traffic, generate ranked recommendations for a latency, throughput, or cost goal, and deploy the top-ranked configuration to a real-time endpoint in a single call.
The SDK also supports longer workflows. You can run recommendation jobs in parallel to compare serving frameworks such as LMI and vLLM, and you can resume from a completed job so that deployment happens in a different notebook or pipeline stage without re-running the benchmarks.
LoRA adapter support in inference recommendations (September 2026)
Developer guide: Get recommendations for models with LoRA adapters
Many teams use LoRA adapters to specialize one foundation model for several use cases. Each adapter kept in GPU memory reduces the number of concurrent requests the endpoint can serve, and the right balance depends on the instance type, the number of adapters, and the traffic profile.
Inference recommendations now accept adapters as Model Package Amazon Resource Names (ARNs), for adapters produced by SageMaker fine-tuning, or as S3 URIs, for adapters from external pipelines such as Hugging Face PEFT. SageMaker AI benchmarks combinations of adapter count and concurrency on real GPU infrastructure and returns ranked results for your workload. The output lists both formats for every adapter. The recommended deployment uses SageMaker Inference Components, with one component for the base model and one for each adapter, so you can add, update, or remove an adapter without disrupting the base model or the other adapters.
SLA-based concurrency search (September 2026)
Blog: Right-size generative AI endpoints with concurrency sweeps on Amazon SageMaker AI
Right-sizing an endpoint means finding the highest concurrency it can sustain without breaching latency or error targets. Until now, that meant picking concurrency levels by hand, running a sweep, checking the results against the service level agreement (SLA), and repeating with a narrower range whenever the model or instance changed.
Inference recommendations now include a search that finds that boundary directly. Set search_recipe to max-concurrency-under-sla and supply targets for any combination of maximum TTFT, maximum time per output token, maximum end-to-end latency, and maximum error rate. The benchmarking engine (AIPerf) starts from a broad range, narrows it based on which probes pass or fail, and converges in fewer iterations than a linear sweep. The result reports the largest passing concurrency (feasible_max) or, if no level qualifies, the smallest failing one (infeasible_min).
The search uses the same CreateAIWorkloadConfig and CreateAIBenchmarkJob APIs as concurrency sweeps. Optional parameters (concurrency_min, concurrency_max, search_max_iterations, and search_initial_points) bound the cost and speed up convergence.
Agent skill for optimized generative AI inference (October 2026)
Blog: New agent skill: Amazon SageMaker optimized generative AI inference for your coding agent
Engineers increasingly ask their coding agent which instance and container to use. Without grounded knowledge and access to real benchmarks, the agent can only guess, and a wrong instance choice shows up later as missed latency targets or wasted spend.
The aws-ai-ml skill, available through the Agent Toolkit for AWS, gives coding agents such as Kiro built-in SageMaker AI inference expertise. Engineers describe what they need in plain language, and the agent can do the following:
- Find the right instance. Ranked deployment options with measured throughput, latency, and TTFT for a model in Amazon S3, SageMaker JumpStart, or the Hugging Face Hub.
- Benchmark a live endpoint. A report from real load covering throughput, P50 and P99 latency, inter-token latency, and supported concurrency.
- Compare runs. The percentage change on every metric, which shows whether a configuration change helped.
Answers are grounded in measured performance and delivered as SageMaker Python SDK v3 code that engineers review and run under their own credentials. Setup takes about 10 minutes. The skill works with any agent that supports the Model Context Protocol (MCP) and in SageMaker AI Studio JupyterLab spaces.
For the support team, one recommendation job that includes all four adapters, followed by a concurrency search against the 500 millisecond TTFT target, replaces the manual sweeps they ran in April. The engineer who owns it can start the job from a notebook or ask a coding agent to run it.
Fit more models onto each GPU
The support assistant does not run alone. An embedding model, a reranker, and a small classifier that routes tickets live in the same account, and each uses a fraction of a GPU. On a standard endpoint, each model copy still held a whole accelerator, so the team ran out of placement slots while GPU memory sat unused.
Inference Components in the SageMaker AI console (October 2026)
With Inference Components, you can host several models on one endpoint and size and scale each model separately. Until now, they were available only through the SDK and the AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI). Every create, resize, and scaling policy had to be scripted, and there was no single view of what each model was using.
In the SageMaker AI console, you can now create, view, update, and delete inference components:
- Create and edit. Create an endpoint with inference components, add or delete components later, and change each component’s accelerators, CPU, memory, and copy count.
- Scale each model. Set an automatic scaling policy for each component, down to zero copies, so an idle model stops holding accelerators.
- Monitor. See alarms and per-component metrics on the same page.
The console calls the same SageMaker AI APIs as the SDK and CLI, so teams can start on the console and automate later, or manage scripted components visually.
GPU partitioning with NVIDIA Multi-Instance GPU (October 2026)
Blog: SageMaker Inference now supports Multi-Instance GPU to maximize GPU utilization for model endpoints
GPU partitioning uses NVIDIA Multi-Instance GPU (MIG) technology to divide one physical GPU into as many as seven partitions, depending on the accelerator. Each partition has dedicated GPU compute and memory, with complete hardware isolation. You define the partition layout when you create an endpoint for inference components and choose a partition type for each component. Applications keep invoking models by inference component name, so client code does not change.
MIG isolates GPU compute and memory between partitions. Models on the same instance still share host CPU, host memory, networking, storage, and endpoint routing. You pay the standard rate for the full instance-hour, so the saving comes from placing more models on each instance, not from a lower hourly price.
For the support team, the embedding model, the reranker, and the classifier now run in separate partitions of one GPU on a single endpoint, and the team manages every component, including the assistant and its adapters, from the console.
Serve models larger than one instance
The team’s next model is a reasoning model whose weights alone exceed the GPU memory of any single instance. They have also noticed that long, retrieval-heavy prompts slow token generation for every other user on the endpoint. For a model this size, they move the workload to HyperPod Inference, which gives them dedicated clusters and Kubernetes-native control. The support assistant stays on managed endpoints.
Managed NVIDIA Dynamo on HyperPod Inference (November 2026)
Blog: Managed NVIDIA Dynamo on Amazon SageMaker HyperPod Inference
Part 1 covered two building blocks for large models on HyperPod: disaggregated prefill and decode in Inference Operator v3.2, and KV-aware routing as part of the managed tiered KV cache. This launch adds multi-node serving and changes who operates the stack. NVIDIA Dynamo is an open source inference framework that provides multi-node sharded serving, disaggregated prefill and decode, and KV-aware routing. Teams could already run Dynamo on their own Kubernetes clusters, but they had to build and operate everything around it: placing all the nodes of a replica together, wiring Elastic Fabric Adapter (EFA) networking so prefill can hand its KV cache to decode at hardware speed, maintaining serving images, and recovering when one failed node takes down a multi-node replica.
With this launch, Dynamo runs as a managed serving engine on HyperPod. Dynamo makes the serving decisions: how the model is sharded, how prefill and decode are split, and where each request goes. HyperPod provides what those decisions depend on:
- Capacity and networking. GPU capacity and EFA networking, provisioned and wired automatically.
- Node recovery. Node health monitoring and replacement, with multi-node workers rescheduled automatically when a node fails.
- Endpoint operations. Autoscaling, endpoint registration, TLS, and observability.
- One install and upgrade path. The Inference Operator add-on installs Dynamo, the serving images, and the Grove and KAI schedulers as one unit and upgrades them together.
The capabilities Dynamo brings to HyperPod are:
- Multi-node (sharded) serving. One copy of the model spans several nodes, so you can serve models that do not fit on any single instance.
- Disaggregated prefill and decode. Prompt processing and token generation run on separate GPU pools, each on an instance type suited to its work, so a long prompt no longer slows responses for other users.
- KV-aware routing. Each request goes to the worker that already holds its KV cache, which reduces TTFT.
There are three ways to start. Teams running Dynamo on self-managed Kubernetes can bring their existing DynamoGraphDeployment (DGD) manifests largely unchanged. Teams already on HyperPod Inference can update the add-on and add a short dynamoSpec block to an existing InferenceEndpointConfig, which HyperPod converts into a DGD, while existing endpoints keep serving. Teams new to both can create a cluster with the add-on and Dynamo enabled from the console. In each case, clients call a standard OpenAI-compatible endpoint, so client code does not change.
Managed Dynamo supports vLLM, SGLang, and TensorRT-LLM, and is available in the Regions where Amazon SageMaker HyperPod is available.
For the support team, the reasoning model runs as one sharded replica across several nodes, with separate prefill and decode pools. When a node fails, HyperPod replaces it and reschedules the replica without a page to the on-call engineer.
Send each request to a GPU that can serve it
The support assistant now serves customers in North America and Europe, so the team runs endpoints and HyperPod clusters in two Regions. During the US morning peak, requests queue in the US Region while GPUs the team already pays for sit idle in Europe. Some European traffic must also stay in Europe.
Routing decides whether capacity a team owns does useful work. It happens at four levels, and the launches below cover one level each: which instance serves a request inside an endpoint, which pod inside a HyperPod cluster, which cluster across a fleet, and which Regional endpoint across Regions and accounts.
KV-cache-aware routing for endpoints (November 2026)
Blog: Amazon SageMaker AI real-time endpoints now support KV cache aware routing
Applications with long prompts or multi-turn conversations repeat a large prefix across requests. A model server can reuse the matching KV cache, but only if the next request reaches the instance that holds it. Prefix-aware routing, covered in part 1, fingerprints the start of each prompt and sends matching prompts to the same instance. Because it works from request history, its view of each instance’s cache becomes less accurate as the model server adds and evicts entries.
KV-cache-aware routing uses the cache state the model container reports. The container publishes cache creation and eviction events to a central cache index, and SageMaker AI routes each request to an eligible instance that holds the longest matching cached prefix. This raises cache reuse for long-context prompts, multi-turn conversations, and workloads that share dynamic prompt prefixes.
It works with single-model endpoints and endpoints that use inference components, including LoRA adapters. It supports InvokeEndpoint, InvokeEndpointWithResponseStream, and the OpenAI-compatible API for Completions and Chat Completions payloads. You turn it on in the endpoint configuration. The first release requires an AWS-verified model container that implements the cache-event, tokenization, metrics, and OpenAI-compatible interfaces. You can track KV cache hit rate in detailed inference observability.
Which one to use. Prefix-aware routing works with any container and needs no container changes. KV-cache-aware routing needs a verified container and tracks the actual cache, which helps most when prefixes vary or caches turn over quickly.
Inference Gateway for HyperPod (September 2026)
Blog: Introducing Amazon SageMaker HyperPod Inference Gateway
Inside a HyperPod cluster, capacity and demand rarely line up. One pod can be partway through a long-context request with its KV cache nearly full, while the next pod sits idle or already holds the prompt prefix or LoRA adapter the next request needs. Without visibility into that GPU state, new requests queue behind busy pods, and teams add GPUs to protect latency instead of using the ones they have. Each model also had its own endpoint, so clients had to track one endpoint per model.
The Inference Gateway is a GPU-aware router that installs with the HyperPod Inference Operator add-on and gives each cluster one OpenAI-compatible endpoint for all of its models. For each request, it reads live signals from every model pod and picks the best one, with weights you can tune per workload:
- KV cache utilization. Avoids pods whose cache is nearly full.
- Queue depth and running requests. Avoids pods with a backlog and balances active work.
- Prefix cache hit rate. Prefers pods likely to hold the prompt prefix.
- LoRA adapter residency. Prefers pods that already hold the requested adapter, which avoids swap latency.
Compared with round-robin routing, it reduced P99 TTFT by up to 97% on mixed GPU generations and by up to 98% under bursty traffic. It is available in all Regions where SageMaker HyperPod is available.
Cross-Region Inference Routing in Amazon SageMaker AI
On managed endpoints, the same idea takes the form of the Cross-Region Inference Routing, managed routing that sends real-time and asynchronous requests across Regional endpoints a team has already deployed, in the same account or in different accounts. You group endpoints that serve the same model under a routing target, and the application invokes the target instead of a specific Regional endpoint. The router does not add capacity, replicate models, or deploy endpoints, and the existing invocation path keeps working.
The router replaces the failover logic teams build themselves today:
- One invocation path. SageMaker tries the local endpoint first and moves traffic to another registered endpoint when the local one cannot serve a request.
- One routing policy. The policy combines endpoint metrics with service-side capacity signals, including insufficient capacity errors that customers cannot observe on their own.
- Private connectivity. Cross-Region traffic runs over AWS PrivateLink with a managed cross-account authorization model, so routing to another Region or account does not need internet or NAT gateways.
- Overflow and residency guardrails. The endpoint owner can cap how much cross-Region traffic a fallback endpoint accepts, and the application can restrict which Regions may serve a request.
Keep endpoints tuned after launch
Two months after the move, the team adds retrieval to the support assistant, and the average prompt length roughly doubles. TTFT is now higher than it was at launch, but nothing has failed, so every alarm stays green. When the team finds a better configuration, they will need to roll it out on large GPU instances that are hard to get more of.
Continuous performance monitoring (November 2026)
Amazon SageMaker AI now continuously monitors your generative AI inference endpoints and tells you when a change could improve performance or lower cost. Monitoring is on by default for SageMaker AI inference endpoints, with no setup required, and you can opt out of endpoints. SageMaker AI looks only at operational signals: latency, GPU utilization, and the endpoint’s serving configuration. It does not read your requests or responses. When a finding clears its confidence threshold, a notification appears on the AWS Management Console, and the same message arrives by email for teams that work in notebooks and the CLI. The recommended action opens the SageMaker AI agentic experience in SageMaker AI Studio with the finding already filled in, so the analysis, the comparison, and the deployment change happen in one conversation. Nothing deploys until you apply it, and you can turn monitoring off at any time.
There are three types of findings:
- Latency drift after a traffic change. When a change such as added retrieval lengthens prompts, TTFT rises. The finding quantifies the regression week over week and recommends re-running inference recommendations against recent traffic to find a configuration that brings TTFT back down.
- A configuration gap present since deployment. The endpoint was never well tuned for its workload, and the finding points to the change that would close the gap.
- Idle GPU capacity. When capacity stays unused week after week, the finding flags a chance to right-size the endpoint and reduce cost.
In-place rolling model updates (November 2026)
A standard rolling update replaces an endpoint one batch at a time, and every batch runs on newly provisioned instances. On a large GPU fleet, that means finding new capacity at every step, and an update can fail partway through when the next batch of instances is not available. Each released instance must also finish cleanup before it can be used again, which slows the rollout.
SageMaker AI now updates models in place. It provisions one small batch of additional instances at the start, shifts traffic to that batch, and then updates the instances it frees, reusing them to roll the change across the rest of the fleet. The update still rolls out in stages, but it needs new capacity only once. For a fleet of 20 instances with a batch size of 2, the update acquires 2 new instances instead of 20. Customers do not need to change anything. As with container caching in part 1, the improvement applies automatically to rolling model updates.
For the support team, a Drift Watch finding quantifies the TTFT regression and opens a new recommendation job against recent traffic. They roll out the updated model with one batch of extra instances, instead of finding new GPU capacity for every instance in the fleet.
Summary: 13 launches, continuing from part 1
The numbering continues from the 13 launches in part 1.
        14. Inference recommendations in SageMaker AI Studio (July 2026). A guided, low-code workflow for ranked, benchmarked configurations, with deployment from Studio.
15. Inference recommendations in the SageMaker Python SDK v3 (August 2026). Benchmark, recommend, and deploy from a notebook or pipeline, with parallel and resumable jobs.
16. LoRA adapter support in inference recommendations (September 2026). Benchmarks adapter count against concurrency and deploys adapters as inference components.
17. SLA-based concurrency search (September 2026). Finds the highest concurrency that meets TTFT, latency, and error-rate targets.
18. Agent skill for optimized generative AI inference (October 2026). Instance selection, benchmarking, and run comparison from MCP-compatible coding agents.
19. Inference Components in the SageMaker AI console (October 2026). Create, scale, and monitor each model on a multi-model endpoint without scripts.
20. GPU partitioning with NVIDIA MIG (October 2026). Up to seven isolated partitions per GPU, assigned per inference component.
21. Managed NVIDIA Dynamo on HyperPod Inference (November 2026). Multi-node and disaggregated serving, with HyperPod operating the platform underneath.
22. KV-cache-aware routing (November 2026). Routes each request to the instance that holds the longest cached prefix, based on cache events from the container.
23. Inference Gateway for HyperPod (September 2026). One endpoint per cluster with GPU-aware routing, and up to 97% lower P99 TTFT than round-robin.
24. Cross-Region Inference Router. Routes across Regional and cross-account endpoints over PrivateLink, with overflow and residency guardrails.
25. Continuous performance monitoring. Detects latency drift, configuration gaps, and idle capacity, with a guided fix in SageMaker AI Studio.
26. In-place rolling model updates (November 2026). Rolls out model updates with one batch of additional instances at the start, then reuses existing instances across the fleet.
By the end of the year, the support team serves four product lines from one base model, runs its small models on shared GPUs, serves a reasoning model that no single instance can hold, and routes traffic across two Regions with residency controls. It did not need to build its own benchmarking harness, failover logic, or drift monitoring to get there.
Part 1 argued that advantage in AI inference comes from operating an efficient inference stack. These 13 launches apply that argument to the months after launch day. The AWS Experience-Based Acceleration program can help your team put them to work by benchmarking your workloads and configuring your inference stack against your SLAs and cost targets.
What is next
On managed endpoints, we plan to extend in-place rolling updates in early 2027 with scale-in-first updates, which remove the need for any additional instances during a model update.
Documentation and getting-started guides for every capability in this post are in the Amazon SageMaker AI Developer Guide. Start with the section that matches your current problem. If your traffic has changed since you deployed, re-run inference recommendations. If you are short on placement slots, move small models onto partitioned GPUs. If requests queue while capacity you own sits idle, register your clusters and endpoints for cross-Region routing.
References
- Amazon SageMaker Inference: 2026 year-to-date launches in review
- New agent skill: Amazon SageMaker optimized generative AI inference for your coding agent
- Introducing Amazon SageMaker HyperPod Inference Gateway
- What’s New: GPU partitioning for SageMaker AI

articles.title: Ya jugamos GTA 6: así fueron las primeras horas del mundo de Jason, Lucía y Mandy
articles.text:
Recuerdo muy bien las primeras veces que jugué cada Grand Theft Auto en mi vida y con San Andreas fue una tarde especial junto a mi primo, en la que juntos nos dedicamos hacer caos en la ciudad como jamás lo habíamos imaginado en un juego. Casi 20 años después de aquel momento, aquellos niños, hoy convertidos en adultos por la vida, volvieron a juntarse para empezar juntos desde el primer segundo GTA 6, algo que estaban esperando desde hace mucho tiempo.
Unos 10 minutos antes de las 00:00 horas del 19 de noviembre de 2026, una llamada por Discord nos unió y cuando menos lo pensamos la cuenta llegó a cero, la espera de casi 10 años había terminado, se acabaron los rumores, los videos filtrados, las mil posibilidades. Era real, ibamos a jugar lo nuevo de Rockstar.
Los colores nos llenaron los ojos con una serie de imágenes de referencia a todo lo que seguramente veremos en las más de 50 horas que promete este nuevo GTA. Después el clásico menú de configuración de imagen y control, que ahora cambia la manera de correr para hacerlo con L3 y no con X, como habia sido desde hace mucho tiempo.
Después de eso la ansiedad de la espera se convirtió en nerviosimo por no saber cómo iba a arrancar este nuevo viaje. Apareció el logo que hemos tenido en la mente mientras llegaba la fecha y un fundido a negro dio comienzo a una aventura que cambiará la vida de muchas personas...
Así fueron las primeras horas con GTA 6
Todo arranca con una escena para presentarnos a Lucia y Jeison. El momento romántico en el que esta pareja se conoce: él robando un auto, que ella había robado previamente y la policía los atrapa. Luego logran salir de la situación con mentiras, diciendo que eran novios, y regresando al vehículo se presentan, dando inicio a una relación real viviendo juntos.
Durante los primeros 20 minutos de esta nueva experiencia vamos a estar viendo más que jugando, apenas moveremos a Lucia un poco. Pero en este arranque lo que el juego nos propone es mostrarnos los protagonsitas, su relación, el espectular estilo gráfico, la iluminación y sentar las bases de la historia: una pareja que se ve separada por el crimen y que está a punto de volverse a juntar, porque ella está en la carcel e ingresó a un programa de libertad condicional.
Esta primera parte también sirve como tutorial para entender los controles básicos: movernos, saltar, correr, apuntar, tomar objetos e incluso robar un auto, pero esto es opcional. Durante el recuerdo de por qué Lucia está en la carcel, yo logré escapar parcialmente robando un auto, mientras que mi primo me contaba que a él lo capturaron de inmediato.
Todo esto lo ibamos viviendo con algunos momentos de silencio, impactados ambos por lo que estabamos viendo y el nivel de detalle en cada imagen. Se nota el tiempo dedicado a cada aspecto que vemos y cómo reacciona el mundo a nuestras acciones. Por lo que los comentarios que haciamos no paraban de ser expresiones de lo increible que teníamos alfrente.
Luego de esa parte de Lucia es momento de controlar a Jeison. Aquí el juego se abre más y ya nos permite manejar una pequeña embarcación para relizar la primera misión recogiendo paquetes que nos arrojan desde un avión. La persona que iba en la aeronave finalmente llega a un puerto y allí es capturada. Siendo un segundo tutorial para que nosotros debamos rescatarla y entendamos mécanicas como disparar, ser sigilosos, cambiar de arma, arrojar objetos y pelear.
Al salir de allí tomamos el avión y damos por finalizada esa misión, luego de conducir a casa. Una media hora muy bien llevada, porque el juego logró condensar los elementos más importantes, mostrar los diferentes tipos de conducción, armas y mécnicas en un tutorial balanceado de cinemáticas, acción y la primera muestra del show de luces que nos espera.
Bienvenidos a Leonida
Estas primeras dos horas que pudimos disfurtar fueron cortadas por la madrugada y la necesidad de levantarnos temprano a tener la vida de adultos. Pero luego de esa introducción ambos tomamos caminos diferentes y ahí está la grandeza de GTA.
Mientras mi primo tomó la decisión de arreglar la casa y salir a la primera misión, yo preferí la libertad y explorar el mundo. Lo escuchaba al él decir que usaba el taladro y luego salir en un vehículo a buscar a un amigo para cobrar un dinero.
En mi caso salí a caminar al calle y me encontré con un mundo gigante. Jeison vive al sur del Leonida, por lo que es una zona casi rural, con calles amplias y un ambiente solitario. Visité algunas tiendas, donde el juego da la posibilidad de asaltarlas, compré ropa, algunas armas y de la nada me atacaron personajes que eran parte de la pantilla de la misión anterior del avión. Todo como un evento natural.
La policía luego identificó mi ropa y mi rostro cuando ataque una tienda, lo que tomó cierto tiempo en poder resolver.
Pero al final de este primer corto viaje, la sensación más recurrente es estar ante un juego inmenso. El mapa tiene muchas zonas por explorar, y cada calle que transitamos cuenta con detalles que nos obligan a mirar, las interacciones se siente naturales y la fluidez que nos propone corta con la locura que se sentía en títulos anteriores.
Lo mejor es que aún nos queda mucho por descrubrir en GTA 6.

articles.title: Civilization and XCOM developer Firaxis cuts a third of its workforce
articles.text:
Rumor mill: Firaxis Games, the studio behind the Civilization and XCOM strategy franchises, eliminated about 60 jobs on Tuesday, representing roughly a third of its workforce, according to people familiar with the cuts. The Maryland-based developer says the smaller team will focus on design, technology, and the player experience – areas that have defined its games for three decades.
Studio head Heather Hazen is also leaving as part of the restructuring. Meanwhile, people familiar with the matter say a new XCOM game, which is already behind schedule, could face further changes as a result of the overhaul.
Firaxis is owned by Take-Two Interactive Software Inc. and operates under 2K Games, one of Take-Two's publishing labels. A 2K Games spokesperson confirmed Hazen's departure. The people who provided details about the scale of the layoffs asked not to be identified because they were not authorized to speak to the press.
The spokesperson described the cuts as a restructuring intended to refocus Firaxis on what it does best: develop strategy games that have set the genre's standards for 30 years. The studio is being downsized so it can concentrate on design, technology, and the player experience, the spokesperson added. That means parting ways with talented colleagues who helped build the studio.
The rep acknowledged that the decisions were difficult but described them as "essential to build the next chapter of Firaxis."
By highlighting technology alongside design and player experience as areas of continued focus, Firaxis is signaling that its engine and systems development will remain central to the studio's work despite the downsizing. The company did not disclose which departments were affected by the layoffs. If the sources' figures are accurate, and 60 employees represent roughly a third of the workforce, Firaxis had approximately 180 employees before Tuesday's cuts and will continue operating with around 120.
That reduced workforce is responsible for two technically demanding franchises. Civilization VII, the studio's most recent release, launched last year to mixed reviews. Since then, Firaxis has released a steady stream of updates, requiring designers and engineers to continue working on the game well beyond its initial launch.
The new XCOM game has reportedly faced greater difficulties, according to people familiar with the project. They said development ran into problems and the game missed a significant milestone over the summer. Work on the project will continue, they added, but the layoffs could lead to further changes. Firaxis has not publicly commented on the game's status.
The timing puts the layoffs in sharp relief across Take-Two. They come right as Grand Theft Auto VI drops, which is expected to rank among the most lucrative entertainment launches of all time. Rockstar, another Take-Two publishing label, is responsible for developing and publishing the game.
The contrast highlights two very different sides of the same publisher. One label is preparing for a record-breaking open-world launch, while another is scaling back to a smaller core team that it says will continue developing the technology behind its strategy games. How effectively Firaxis's reduced workforce can support Civilization VII while getting the next XCOM game back on track will help determine whether the restructuring pays off.

articles.title: MSI Unveils the EdgeMesa N AI+ Series, Powering the Future of AI Teammates
articles.text:
Thursday, November 19th 2026
MSI Unveils the EdgeMesa N AI+ Series, Powering the Future of AI Teammates
MSI, a global leader in AI computing and innovative technology solutions, introduces the EdgeMesa N AI+ Series, a compact AI desktop designed to bring powerful local AI computing into everyday workspaces. Powered by NVIDIA RTX Spark, the new series combines advanced AI acceleration with MSI's thoughtful engineering, enabling developers, creators, and AI enthusiasts to build, run, and deploy AI applications locally. With Windows 11 and a space-saving design, it provides a practical platform for turning AI experimentation into real-world workflows while maintaining greater control over data and computing resources.
Designed for continuous AI workloads, the EdgeMesa N AI+ Series features a refined 1.3-liter aluminium chassis with a fingerprint-resistant finish. Its MSI AI Pulse Cooling System integrates Vapor Chamber technology and dual turbo fans to manage heat efficiently, helping sustain 140 W TDP performance and support reliable 24/7 AI agent operation. This combination brings demanding AI computing to desktops without occupying valuable workspace.As AI evolves from a simple tool that responds to commands into a more intelligent teammate capable of reasoning, planning, and taking action, the EdgeMesa N AI+ Series supports a new generation of autonomous AI applications. Developers can create coding assistants, build retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) applications using private knowledge bases, and deploy agents to automate repetitive tasks. These practical applications range from document processing and knowledge management to vision AI and voice-based interactions, bringing NVIDIA's vision of moving "From Tool to Teammate" closer to everyday users.
NVIDIA RTX Spark unites NVIDIA AI, RTX graphics, and unified memory in one slim, powerful Windows PC. Designed to run larger AI models locally—without cloud dependency—and move between creative work, development, and immersive gaming without missing a beat. Connect apps, tools, and workflows into one seamless experience. Private by default. RTX Spark brings NVIDIA's full-stack AI platform, ready for the AI workloads of today and whatever comes next. Delivered on the familiar, trusted Windows platform.
At its core, the NVIDIA RTX Spark N1X superchip combines a 6,144-core NVIDIA Blackwell RTX GPU with a 20-core NVIDIA Grace CPU, delivering up to 1 petaflop of FP4 AI performance. With up to 128 GB of LPDDR5X unified memory and native NVIDIA CUDA acceleration, the system enables developers to run larger AI models, prototype applications, and accelerate inference locally. Creators benefit from NVIDIA Studio acceleration for 3D rendering, video editing, and AI-assisted content generation, while gamers can enjoy NVIDIA RTX technologies, including ray tracing, DLSS, and Reflex.
High-speed connectivity extends these capabilities beyond a single desktop. With 10 Gb LAN and Wi-Fi 7, users can transfer large datasets and support connected AI workflows, while 20 Gbps USB-C and up to four displays enable flexible multitasking. NVIDIA Personal AI Router (PAIR) technology further enables compatible devices to form a personal AI inference cluster, intelligently routing independent inference requests across available local computing nodes to maximize resource utilization.
By combining NVIDIA RTX Spark performance with MSI's compact design, sustained cooling, and practical AI capabilities, the EdgeMesa N AI+ Series provides a versatile foundation for developing, creating, and working alongside intelligent AI agents.

articles.title: Anthropic rival says companies can (mostly) skip the pricey models | TechCrunch
articles.text:
On the same day that Anthropic went public in the largest IPO on record, with investor enthusiasm for the AI lab through the roof, far away at the Slush startup conference in Helsinki, the topic du jour was open source everything.
That’s the enormous opportunity being chased by companies like Fireworks AI, as enterprises seek ways to avoid paying frontier prices for their AI needs.
Fireworks runs AI models for other businesses. It specializes in open-weight models, which anyone can download, and helps customers tune them on their own data so they run faster and cheaper than the models of Anthropic, OpenAI, and other heavyweights, and are harder for rivals to copy. Customers have included Uber, Shopify, and Notion. Co-founder Chenyu Zhao and I spoke onstage toward the end of the day.
Zhao and many others believe companies are gravitating toward platforms like his because frontier models are pricey and, in most cases, he says, unnecessary unless you need the very latest and greatest generalized intelligence. There are also growing concerns that frontier labs absorb too much of their customers’ know-how, even if only through the prompts used to get answers, a worry Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella raised in July.
Fireworks has also gotten its first black eye, having disclosed two security incidents this fall. In one, hackers reached API keys and tokens stored as secrets for a limited number of accounts; in the other, attackers breached its cloud provider, made their way into a development system, and nabbed customer data, including billing records and some datasets.
Notion says AI chat transcripts from fewer than 1% of its workspaces were exposed, but it has disconnected from Fireworks. Uber says hackers stole the names, addresses, birth dates and driver’s license numbers of about 150,000 drivers through a vendor that TechCrunch identified as Fireworks. Fireworks will have to win back the confidence of customers like them.
Fireworks, assigned a $17.5 billion valuation by its investors in summer, is reportedly in “early talks” for yet another round, though Zhao declined to comment.
There’s money chasing everyone in the category, seems like. Rival companies Together AI and Baseten have announced massive rounds in recent months. On Wednesday, Palo Alto Networks said it will buy Applied Compute, which, like Fireworks, helps companies train and run custom AI models on their own data. The deal for the startup, founded just a year ago by former OpenAI researchers, is $4.5 billion, all of it in stock.
Here’s some of what Zhao had to say. This conversation has been edited for length and clarity.
You spent a decade at Google, including managing a 50-person engineering team on Google Cloud Vertex AI. Why leave when you did?
When you meet great co-founders, it’s obvious within five minutes that they’re really smart. I was sold after talking to Lin [Qiao] and Dima [Dzhulgakov]. It’s also important to find people who are genuinely nice, people you’ll enjoy working with.
How do you describe Fireworks to a CEO who has never heard of it?
I describe Fireworks as a specialized intelligence platform. OpenAI and Anthropic are building general intelligence. We use open models, which are often smaller, cheaper, and faster, and let companies add their own data to specialize them. That way you own your AI rather than being beholden to giant AI conglomerates. If you’re just using Opus or Sonnet, that’s not a differentiator.
How far behind are open models right now?
A few years ago I’d have said a year, a year and a half. Then came DeepSeek and a waterfall of fantastic open models. These days it’s at most six months behind, probably closer to three.
If the models are so close behind, why are businesses slow to switch?
Frontier models are a household brand, and before you find product-market fit, using the best model is low risk. But once you pass 10,000 or 100,000 users and you’re spending $10,000 to $100,000 a month on tokens, it’s time to think about open source.
In July, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella warned that companies using proprietary AI models pay twice, once in money and again in know-how. Do you think that warning had a material effect?
We think we’ll live in a two-model world, with frontier and open models in parallel. You want the best intelligence for high-level planning, but you don’t need a frontier model for basic arithmetic. That’s why there’s so much interest in routing, and why people now think about cost per task, not just cost per token.
Anthropic went public today. What do you think of its valuation? There’s one scenario in which it just continues to cement its place in this sort of oligopoly; there’s another where it starts to lose traction.
On the record: I’ll probably call my broker tonight and buy a few shares. This is a long-term bet. In 10 years AI usage will be at a completely different scale, and that takes an incredible amount of capital, which is why these companies are going public.
Fireworks has had a couple of security breaches recently. What do you tell customers?
Every company is probably seeing an unprecedented frequency of attacks. For our incident, a lot of the motivation was LLM jacking: hunting through providers for API keys and secrets to sell tokens on illicit marketplaces. Our promise is zero data retention for inference traffic, and there’s no indication that has been compromised.
Notion has disconnected from Fireworks. Did you lose other customers?
I don’t think I can publicly name the specific customers that were impacted. Some, such as Notion and Cursor, have gone public already. It was a small subset of our customers that had this data impact.
How did that customer data get exposed, given your zero-retention promise?
Notion was using batch prediction, where you upload a dataset that’s stored at rest, so it’s not a zero-retention product by nature. We’re moving those services to an online flow so we keep data only as long as we need it.
Jensen Huang left Nvidia last week, and Nvidia has backed Fireworks since 2024. Does that affect you?
It’s been a blow to the industry, and we feel for Jensen and his family. But Nvidia has always been a strong supporter of open source, and I don’t see that changing. We expect it to keep investing in Nemotron, and we’re excited to keep partnering with them.

articles.title: Já há mais satélites visíveis a olho nu do que estrelas em várias regiões • Tecnoblog
articles.text:
Já há mais satélites visíveis a olho nu do que estrelas em várias regiões
Rastros de satélites já são muito visíveis em grande parte da Europa e nos Estados Unidos.
Um estudo realizado pela empresa de engenharia Accu acende um alerta para um fenômeno cada vez mais perceptível: em muitos pontos do planeta, já há mais satélites artificiais cruzando o céu do que estrelas visíveis a olho nu. A causa é um tanto óbvia: o número crescente de satélites de órbita baixa direcionados a serviços de internet, com destaque para as unidades da Starlink.
A pesquisa foi baseada em dados levantados entre 12 e 18 de outubro deste ano. Esses dados fazem parte de um sistema de monitoramento de satélites disponibilizados pela Força Espacial dos Estados Unidos no site CelesTrak.
No período em questão, os pesquisadores da Accu analisaram as trajetórias de 15.833 satélites artificiais que operam em órbita baixa — em linhas gerais, aqueles que estão a até 2.000 km de altitude.
O estudo constatou que, em média, 710 satélites atravessavam o céu de uma cidade britânica de latitude intermediária à noite, considerando o horizonte completamente desobstruído. Destes, uma média de 105 satélites poderiam ser vistos a olho nu porque estavam refletindo a luz do Sol, brilhando tanto ou mais do que as estrelas.
Este é, de fato, um ponto de atenção, pois satélites artificiais não emitem luz própria. Eles podem ser notados à noite, ao entardecer ou ao amanhecer porque refletem a luz solar.
Note, porém, que os satélites não ficam todos visíveis ao mesmo tempo. A visibilidade depende de fatores como posição do satélite em relação ao Sol, sombra projetada pela Terra, condições atmosféricas (“céu limpo”) e a localização geográfica do observador.
Ao site Space, um representante da Accu explicou o seguinte:
Em uma cidade típica do Reino Unido, cerca de 300 satélites captam a luz solar na primeira hora após o anoitecer. Esse número cai para menos de 20 por volta da meia-noite e volta a subir para cerca de 300 antes do amanhecer.
Accu Components
Embora o estudo tenha sido baseado no território do Reino Unido, os pesquisadores afirmam que o tráfego intenso de satélites já é perceptível em grande parte da Europa, nos Estados Unidos e em regiões localizadas em latitude norte e sul na faixa de 40 a 50 graus.
Digamos que o Brasil é privilegiado nesse aspecto, pois grande parte do território do país está em latitudes próximas ao Equador, onde o tráfego de satélites tende a ser menos intenso.
O vídeo a seguir, de 2019, mostra um rastro de satélites Starlink visíveis a olho nu:
Por uma série de motivos. Para começar, o problema gera um efeito de poluição luminosa que não só tira a “naturalidade” do céu noturno, como também pode atrapalhar atividades de observação astronômica.
Leve em conta, como exemplo, que o rastro luminoso de um satélite artificial pode interferir no campo de visão de um telescópio, prejudicando análises ou coletas de dados.
Existe também uma preocupação sobre um número elevado de satélites refletindo a luz solar causar um efeito de aumento do brilho do céu, dificultando a observação de objetos astronômicos muito distantes, por exemplo.
O estudo completo está disponível no site da Accu.

articles.title: MAHA PAC spent more on steak, luxury club than candidates, report shows
articles.text:
In the wake of the Make America Healthy Again movement’s midterm wipeout, a top leader suggested the heavy losses came down to being outspent by wealthier, more powerful rivals. But a Stat report on MAHA’s own spending in the run-up to the election raises questions about whether the group’s priority was ever winning elections in the first place.
The dive into the financial documents reveals that the MAHA PAC, led by Tony Lyons, spent more on allies, boosters, meals, luxuries, and its affiliated nonprofit than it did on political candidates.
The findings are in stark contrast to an announcement from Lyons in the spring that he was heading a $100 million fundraiser to boost MAHA’s clout in the midterms. In reality, MAHA PAC took in $3.2 million. During the election cycle, the PAC spent more than $10.5 million, with over $7 million coming from money it had collected previously.
According to Stat’s findings, of the $10.5 million the MAHA PAC spent on the midterms, less than a tenth—roughly $1 million—went to messaging on political candidates, which are expenses called “independent expenditures.”
Andrew Mayersohn, a committees researcher at OpenSecrets, called the spending “pretty unusual,” explaining that “Major super PACs spend most of their money on independent expenditures.”
MAHA perks
In some cases, the scant political spending was dwarfed by spending on luxuries. For instance, in a key House race in Northern California, MAHA supported Kevin Kiley over his political rival, pediatrician Richard Pan. Despite calling the race “the most direct ideological confrontation” between MAHA and its opposition “anywhere on the 2026 ballot,” the PAC only spent $49,900 to back Kiley. That’s a little less than the $50,100 it spent at Mastro’s Steakhouse, an upscale restaurant that offers $110 porterhouse steaks in Washington, DC. Further, it’s less than a third of the $155,900 the PAC spent at Ned’s Club, a luxury club near the White House that has become a popular gathering spot among Trump officials.

articles.title: Developer vibe codes Windows 11 alternative operating system for amd64, arm64, and riscv64 hardware — LiberNT is a free 64-bit clone promising reliable, stable, and efficient performance
articles.text:
Developer vibe codes Windows 11 alternative operating system for amd64, arm64, and riscv64 hardware — LiberNT is a free 64-bit clone promising reliable, stable, and efficient performance
New OS is ‘Built out of love for the NT architecture’ and released under GPL3.0.
There’s a new vibe-coded OS in town going by the name of LiberNT. Its name provides a big clue to its nature: Liber (free), NT (New Technology architecture, as in Windows NT). As it has been released under GNU’s GPL3.0 license, LiberNT also provides a free new way to run apps designed for Microsoft’s Windows 11.
LiberNT has been under development for some time, but on Wednesday it made a big leap. Reading the intro, you might have wondered if this work had a ReactOS connection, and indeed there is. But what started as a fork of ReactOS has already got a new boot loader, graphics stack, memory manager – and yesterday a new kernel. “LiberNT is not affiliated with or endorsed by the ReactOS project or Microsoft,” insist the devs behind this OS.
This still fledgling operating system is designed (mostly) for modern hardware and focuses on 64-bit platforms: amd64, arm64 and riscv64. Ambitiously, the goal is to develop this OS to deliver a free Windows alternative that is “stable, reliable and efficient.” On that latter point, yesterday’s blog update relays some impressive efficiency and performance stats.
The LiberNT team has benchmarked their eponymous OS against Microsoft’s Windows NT, and it beats it hands-down in 112 of 132 system tests. The testing assessed performance in the following areas: file caching, memory handling, threads and locks, plus FAT32 and NTFS storage. Interestingly, both the free and commercial OS were benchmarked on a Mac with an Apple M3 Pro chip. We scanned through the results, and the worst loss for LiberNT was a 28% performance deficit vs Win11, but it claims some astounding relative performance wins showing the free OS being over 2000% faster.
The devs are entirely clear about the fact that the operating system was vibe coded. “AI is part of how LiberNT is built. It helps us review and write code, and everything it writes is then reviewed by a human,” explains a section of the GitHub page for the project. “Before anything reaches the main branch, a person runs and validates the end-to-end tests. We care about this project too much to let a regression slip through.”
If the above highlights about this new OS's scope, mission, compatibility, and performance have whetted your appetite, there is the full code available via the GitHub link (top), and even some ready-made builds as bootable disk images. Indeed, I’m quite eager to give this new OS a spin. Hopefully, it works as well as the ambitious developers suggest, and I won’t be disappointed by any stability issues using my daily productivity apps like Firefox, Word, and an old release of Photoshop.

articles.title: Eazeebox co-founder Srinivas Shanbhogue passes away
articles.text:
Eazeebox co-founder Srinivas Shanbhogue passes away
Shanbhogue spent two decades at Schneider Electric before building Eazeebox, a Bengaluru startup that helps neighbourhood electrical shops restock from multiple brands through a single app.
Srinivas Shanbhogue, co-founder and CEO of Eazeebox, has died, his former Schneider Electric colleague Bidisha Nagaraj said in a LinkedIn tribute.
Shanbhogue worked at Schneider Electric for 20 years, serving as vice president of home and distribution in India.
In a farewell post in 2023, he recalled coming from a small town and credited Schneider with giving him the opportunity to grow into a business leader. As he left to become an entrepreneur, he told colleagues he hoped to keep contributing to Schneider’s growth from outside the company.
At Eazeebox, Shanbhogue stayed close to the trade he knew from Schneider Electric. A shopkeeper who needs to restock wires, switches and circuit breakers may have to call several distributors. Eazeebox lets retailers order across brands through one app. The startup stocks products in local warehouses and says it can deliver within two hours, with no minimum order size. Shopkeepers can order a few items as they run out.
Nagaraj remembered Shanbhogue as someone who went out of his way to help people and could go several rounds over a campaign idea. Colleagues called them “Tom and Jerry,” she wrote, recalling how they pushed each other while working on campaigns for Schneider Electric India’s home business.
One of those campaigns was Ghar Zindagi Se Roshan. Its words landed differently after his death, Nagaraj wrote. “I think they’ll always bring me back to the joy of working with him.”

articles.title: Mauvaise nouvelle si vous attendez l'iMac OLED : Apple bloque sur ces deux points
articles.text:
Après l’Apple Watch, l’iPhone et le récent lancement du MacBook Pro avec écran tactile, l’iMac devait logiquement suivre le cours de l’histoire en adoptant un écran OLED d’ici 2029. Mais sous l’impulsion de John Ternus, le nouveau PDG d’Apple en poste depuis septembre, la firme de Cupertino réévalue de fond en comble la viabilité commerciale de certains de ses projets.
Des coûts de production trop lourds face aux ventes de l’iMac
Apple se heurte d’abord à une équation tarifaire particulièrement défavorable pour son ordinateur de bureau. Contrairement aux smartphones ou aux PC portables de la marque qui s’écoulent à des dizaines de millions d’exemplaires, l’iMac représente un volume de ventes moins important, ce qui empêche d’amortir facilement le surcoût de fabrication des panneaux OLED par rapport aux LCD. Ajoutez à cela la hausse récente du prix des puces mémoire et la facture globale des composants pèse de plus en plus lourd, pour Apple comme pour le consommateur final.
Cette prudence de la part d’Apple s’explique également par le ralentissement des ventes des appareils équipés de cette technologie. Les expéditions globales de panneaux OLED pour l’iPad Pro devraient ainsi chuter de 18 % cette année, passant de 6 millions à 4,9 millions d’unités. Dans le détail, Samsung Display verrait ses livraisons s’effondrer de 2,1 à 1,5 million d’unités, tandis que LG Display reculerait de 3,9 à 3,4 millions. Malgré l’utilisation d’une structure « tandem » à deux couches émettrices, le prix de vente élevé de la tablette a freiné les ardeurs des acheteurs, incitant Apple à réfléchir à deux fois avant de changer la technologie d’affichage de son iMac.
Un retour pragmatique à la technologie LCD à l’horizon 2029
Apple avait pourtant initié des démarches auprès des industriels du secteur. Des demandes d’information avaient été envoyées l’an dernier pour concevoir un écran de 24 pouces affichant une luminosité de 600 cd/m2 et une densité de 218 ppi. Samsung Display développait pour l’occasion une dalle QD-OLED à cinq couches afin de garantir une brillance optimale et une excellente durée de vie. De son côté, LG Display étudiait des dalles WOLED et le procédé FLiPP pour 2030. Mais les développements chez LG Display pour ce premier iMac OLED seraient désormais suspendus.
À lire : Test iMac 24 M3 (2023) : un boost de puissance bienvenu, et quelques regrets
Pour éviter de faire grimper en flèche le prix payé par les consommateurs, Apple choisit donc de revoir ses priorités et de prolonger la vie du LCD sur l’iMac. Le constructeur a récemment sollicité BOE et d’autres fournisseurs afin d’étudier la création de nouveaux panneaux LCD prévus pour un lancement autour de 2029. Ce choix pragmatique permettrait ainsi de préserver un prix d’entrée accessible pour les familles et les professionnels, qui sont les deux principales cibles de l’iMac.

articles.title: Apache Iceberg and intelligent storage help AI reach production - SiliconANGLE
articles.text:
Hitachi Vantara bets smarter storage can close AI’s pilot-to-production gap
Enterprises pushing AI from pilot to production are learning that data, not GPUs, is the hardest part, and open table formats such as Apache Iceberg are part of the answer. Demand for AI infrastructure shows few signs of slowing, but much of the information companies need is still scattered, ungoverned and out of reach.
That pressure is turning storage into an active layer that classifies, governs and serves data to models. Unstructured files such as logs and medical images hold intelligence AI can now extract, according to Arun Prasad Raman (pictured, left), vice president of hybrid cloud and AI infrastructure at Hitachi Vantara Corp.
“Storage is not seen as just storing the data,” Raman said. “You need to bring in more intelligence natively rather than moving the data to another replication and bringing it back for, say, indexing. If it can do it natively, that’s where the value add is.”
Raman and Jeff Lundberg (right), principal product and solutions manager at Hitachi Vantara, spoke with theCUBE Research’s John Furrier and Gemma Allen at SC26, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed AI’s pilot-to-production gap, Apache Iceberg and how Hitachi Vantara is adding intelligence to storage. (* Disclosure below.)
Apache Iceberg and the push for intelligent storage
Reference architectures for AI factories and data platforms are largely settled. Most projects stall because data is spread across on-premises systems, software-as-a-service applications and the cloud, while access control, governance and shifting regulations add friction, according to Lundberg. Hitachi Vantara is responding with industry-specific solutions built on its Hitachi iQ stack and its sister businesses’ rail and energy experience, he explained.
“It’s about the outcome more so than the technology that we’re trying to put into place,” Lundberg said. “That’s an enabler to get you to the solution you’re trying to get to.”
Much of that work now happens in storage. Last week, Hitachi Vantara expanded its VSP One platform with new object storage and data lakehouse capabilities. A service in its object store flags files containing personal information, such as Social Security numbers. Data scientists can then keep that data out of specific models or block its replication to another country, Raman explained.
“That’s the intelligence we are adding into the storage itself,” Raman said. “So that’s where the evolution of storage is making it more intelligent.”
Analytics follow the same logic. CT scan metadata can be stored in Apache Iceberg format on the company’s object store and queried directly. An application could list every abdominal scan from the past year without a separate extract, transform and load or ETL process or database, Raman noted.
“Whether it’s a backup or it’s 10 years old, it still carries some intelligence,” Raman said. “As long as it carries intelligence, it becomes important to AI.”

articles.title: 'COLD RELIC remains an active threat': Google warns Russian hackers are hitting public sector firms with sophisticated phishing and malware campaigns
articles.text:
'COLD RELIC remains an active threat': Google warns Russian hackers are hitting public sector firms with sophisticated phishing and malware campaigns
There is more than one way to make use of stolen information
- Google says Russian-linked espionage group COLD RELIC uses stolen accounts and internal data to fuel follow-on phishing attacks
- Attackers harvest emails, contact lists, and organizational details to impersonate trusted contacts and compromise new targets
- Researchers recommend phishing-resistant MFA, session monitoring, and stronger cloud-access controls to disrupt the campaign
Google has sounded the alarm on a Russian state-sponsored threat actor known as COLD RELIC, claiming it continues to target high-value individuals and organizations with sophisticated phishing and malware campaigns.
In its report, Google’s Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) shared new details about the group’s espionage methods, and how it hops from one victim to another using stolen identities.
COLD RELIC
Google said it saw COLD RELIC steal a single cloud account from one company, pull a significant amount of sensitive data from the victim’s environment, and then use it to launch a separate attack - against other firms connected to the original victim. The group is also called COLDRIVER, UNC4057, Star Blizzard, Callisto, and Gossamer Bear, Google says, stressing that the US Department of Justice (DoJ) placed it well within Russia’s Federal Security Service (FSB) - essentially Russia’s FBI.
The threat actor has been active for more than a decade, taking aim primarily at individuals and organizations with information of strategic or political interest to the Russian governments. Its victims include government officials, defense contractors, and non-government organizations (NGOs) in the West.
"The group is known for implementing sophisticated phishing and malware campaigns with the aim to gain access to information of strategic or political relevance to the Russian government," Google said.
The report focuses on COLD RELIC’s ability to use information stolen during one intrusion to make subsequent attacks more convincing. Instead of just grabbing sensitive data from a compromised company’s environment and calling it a day, the threat actors use stolen emails and identities to impersonate legitimate contacts and approach new targets.
Google detailed two intrusions that Mandiant investigated, both of which were against US-based organizations. The first one happened last year, when COLD RELIC stole the login credentials of a Super Admin and used them to waltz into an organization’s cloud productivity environment. The account had multi-factor authentication (MFA) enabled, so the attackers spammed the target with hundreds of approval requests until they just approved one to make the notifications stop.
Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed!
They then downloaded everything they found in the cloud storage, exported employee lists, and launched a domain-wide data export. They also deleted security investigation and email audit logs to cover their tracks.
Bunny hopping to other targets
The information found there eventually helped them launch a separate attack against an entirely different US-based organization. A year later, they impersonated an employee of the previously compromised company, contacted a new victim, and shared phishing links designed to steal login credentials and authentication tokens for Microsoft Entra ID.
It worked, and the technique is now something COLD RELIC frequently uses in its attacks. "Once COLD RELIC compromises a target, it uses stolen emails and data to establish authentic pretexts and impersonate contacts when reaching out to subsequent targets," the report explains.
The threat actors collect organizational rosters, contact lists, resumes, and event schedules - pretty much anything that would help them build convincing pretexts for future phishing attacks. Google warns that COLD RELIC remains active, and that GTIG observed evidence of new phishing attacks earlier this month.
To defend against pesky Russian spies (and all other, for that matter), Google recommends organizations strengthen their authentication security and enforce phishing-resistant MFA (Hardware security keys such as Google Titan, FIDO2/WebAuthn authentication, and passkeys). It also advises organizations monitor suspicious passkey and device registrations, and revoke existing sessions and OAuth permissions when responding to suspected account compromises.
Finally, businesses should monitor logins coming from residential proxy networks, since this seems to be the stable of COLD RELIC attacks. Google said it will continue tracking and disrupting the group's infrastructure to protect cloud users.
