articles.title: Una pistola fabricada en Argentina apareció en GTA VI: qué dijo el CEO de la empresa sobre la referencia
articles.text:
Una pistola que remite a un modelo producido en Argentina apareció entre las armas de GTA VI, el último lanzamiento de una de las sagas más populares de la industria de los videojuegos. La referencia no lleva el nombre ni la marca de la empresa, pero una pieza similar a la Bersa Thunder 380 quedó asociada a la Scorpio Nipper .38 dentro del juego, a partir de los mensajes que recibió la compañía.
Para Manuel Pizarro, CEO de Bersa, el hallazgo fue inesperado. La fábrica argentina no había sido consultada ni había intervenido en la inclusión del arma, ya que el videojuego no identifica al modelo con su denominación comercial. “Nos sorprendimos ayer con esto porque no lo sabíamos”, afirmó el directivo en Infobae Al Mediodía.
La asociación surgió por la apariencia del arma y no por un acuerdo entre la empresa y los desarrolladores de GTA VI, explicó Pizarro. Dentro de la trama, el arma se llama Scorpio Nipper .38, una denominación ficticia que, según señalaron los conductores del programa, reúne rasgos de la Thunder 380 fabricada por Bersa.
Pizarro remarcó que la ausencia de la marca explica por qué no hubo un pedido de autorización. La compañía no recibió consultas previas sobre su presencia en el juego ni confirmó si buscará comunicarse con los responsables del título después de conocer la referencia visual.
La conversación se dio tras el lanzamiento de GTA VI, una nueva entrega de la saga ambientada en una ciudad ficticia. Durante la entrevista también surgieron otras alusiones argentinas dentro del videojuego, entre ellas música y una parrilla, mientras el CEO de Bersa se detenía en el caso del arma vinculada con su producción.
Bersa exporta desde 1974 y Estados Unidos es su principal mercado
La aparición en el videojuego llevó la charla hacia la trayectoria de la fábrica. Pizarro contó que Bersa tiene 68 años de actividad, que fue fundada por tres inmigrantes italianos y que inició sus exportaciones en 1974, un recorrido que la vinculó con mercados externos desde sus primeras décadas.
El ejecutivo precisó que las ventas regulares a Estados Unidos comenzaron en 1979 y que ese país se mantiene como el principal destino de las exportaciones. Según Pizarro, entre 60% y 70% de la producción de Bersa se destina al exterior, además de las operaciones que la firma sostiene en cerca de 30 países.
La planta fabrica entre 10 mil y 12 mil pistolas por mes, de acuerdo con el CEO. Pizarro señaló que la empresa debió ajustar costos para sostener su competitividad fuera de Argentina, en un contexto que describió como marcado por la inflación en dólares.
Al repasar la historia del sector, el directivo sostuvo que hace 40 o 50 años funcionaban más de 40 fábricas de armas en Argentina. Atribuyó la continuidad de Bersa a las inversiones en tecnología, procesos y recursos humanos, tres áreas que, según explicó, permitieron sostener la actividad industrial.
La estructura de la compañía reúne entre 170 y 180 empleados directos. Pizarro estimó, además, que cerca de mil trabajadores indirectos dependen de proveedores que elaboran piezas para la empresa, una red que acompaña la fabricación de cada arma.
Para esa producción, Bersa importa acero y aluminio, indicó el empresario. El resto de su cadena de abastecimiento se apoya en proveedores locales, según explicó, con componentes que llegan desde distintos puntos del país hasta la fábrica.
El mercado civil representa hasta 10% de las ventas de la empresa
En el mercado interno, el segmento civil representa entre 5% y 10% de las ventas, según Pizarro. El CEO lo definió como un mercado pequeño en relación con la cantidad de habitantes de Argentina, aunque señaló que mantiene una dinámica estable.
La firma comercializa alrededor de 2.500 armas por mes a usuarios civiles argentinos, afirmó el directivo. El resto de la producción tiene como destinos centrales la exportación y las fuerzas de seguridad, dos canales que explican el volumen de actividad de la compañía.
Pizarro sostuvo que la mayoría de las fuerzas de seguridad del país utiliza armas de Bersa. La empresa participa en licitaciones y, en esos procesos, compite con fabricantes extranjeros para proveer equipamiento a los distintos organismos.
Esas compras incluyen pruebas de exigencia, relató el CEO. Entre los ensayos que mencionó figuran cinco mil disparos consecutivos, caídas y exposiciones a arena y barro, procedimientos con los que las fuerzas evalúan el desempeño del armamento antes de una eventual adquisición.
Además de esas condiciones, las evaluaciones alcanzan la seguridad y el funcionamiento de cada arma, según Pizarro. El empresario dijo que la firma busca combinar sus productos con capacitaciones y adaptarlos a los requerimientos de cada organismo que participa de las licitaciones.
Bersa también abrió una fábrica de armas no letales, explicó su CEO. Pizarro sostuvo que las fuerzas deben recurrir al arma como último recurso y disponer antes de otras herramientas para intervenir en diferentes situaciones.
El empresario agregó que la compañía trabaja con las fuerzas de seguridad en programas de capacitación. Las provincias, indicó, aplican protocolos y entrenamientos distintos, por lo que la formación puede variar de acuerdo con cada jurisdicción.
Tenencia de la portación y capacitación
Sobre la discusión por la portación civil, Pizarro afirmó que Bersa no promueve que más personas lleven armas. A la vez, sostuvo que quienes cumplen las normas, reciben instrucción y actúan de manera responsable no deberían enfrentar restricciones.
El CEO consideró que la portación tiene requisitos estrictos en Argentina. Según su planteo, el sistema podría revisar las condiciones aplicables a las personas que acrediten el cumplimiento de las normas vigentes.
Pizarro diferenció la tenencia de la portación y afirmó, ante una consulta, que una persona puede manipular un arma si respeta la normativa y recibe entrenamiento. “El entrenamiento es todo”, dijo al comparar esa formación con la que requiere conducir un automóvil.
El directivo también señaló que un arma puede durar toda la vida si recibe mantenimiento. En ese sentido, reiteró que Bersa no incentiva la compra de armas, aunque defendió el acceso de quienes cumplan los requisitos establecidos.
–

articles.title: Google will force Android developers to make their apps work properly on foldables
articles.text:
Looking ahead: Foldables aren't exactly taking the world by storm, but mobile ecosystem incumbents are still going to try to improve foldable-focused software experiences. Meet Google's latest quality criteria, which will essentially force developers to better support foldables even if they did not plan to.
Google recently published the new "adaptive quality standards" Android developers will be required to adopt over the next few months. The change will affect apps published on the Google Play Store, with a specific focus on improving support for the latest foldable devices coming to Android.
Google said that customers are paying a premium for their cracking new foldable devices, and are consequently going to expect a similarly premium app experience. Developers will just have to adapt, or they are going to risk being demoted in Google Play's app promotion programs.
The main requirement is that apps will need to meet the "Tier 3" baseline in Android's official adaptive quality guidelines. Tier 3 apps are "adaptive ready" experiences, which means they will have to completely fill a foldable's display area without letterboxing effects or compatibility modes. Furthermore, Tier 3 apps will have to preserve text or playback state during rotation or folding, while supporting multi-window environments at the same time.
Android's foldable guidelines also refer to "adaptive optimized" (Tier 2) and "adaptive differentiated" (Tier 1) apps, which should provide an even better experience on foldables. Starting April 2027, the Tier 3 baseline will be required for all new app releases. Developers will also have to provide at least three screenshots showing their apps on foldable devices in addition to the standard phone screenshots.
According to Google's official timeline, Tier 3 enforcement is already live today. Developers can add their foldable screenshots through the Google Play Console, while Tier 2 and Tier 1 apps can access "enhanced merchandising" options on the store. In April 2027, all "standard" apps will need to support the new adaptive baseline. Older apps that haven't been updated will remain available for download, although they will likely be much lower in Google Play's app promotion plans.
Google said that developers can review the new design requirements and guidelines on Android's official online documentation. The Mountain View giant is going to enforce the additional foldable requirements for gaming apps starting August 2027. Updated apps will also need to target Android 17's API level 37. Finally, the company is already working on its future plans for improving app adaptability on tablets, Chromebooks, and other large-screen devices.

articles.title: China-based AI robotics biotech firm MegaRobo raises $200M to accelerate scientific discovery - SiliconANGLE
articles.text:
China-based AI robotics biotech firm MegaRobo raises $200M to accelerate scientific discovery
Chinese biotech robotics firm MegaRobo Co. Ltd. today announced it has raised $200 million in new funding to invest in its core technology and expand its automated life sciences infrastructure for increasingly complex physical systems.
Founded in 2016, MegaRobo builds robotic systems that let artificial intelligence software run physical experiments, alongside precision measurement and inspection tools for manufacturers.
Investors joining the round included Oman Investment Authority, Asia Investment Capital, Granite Asia, Sinovation Ventures and CMB International. The company raised $600 million to date across multiple funding rounds, including nearly $300 million in Series C during 2022.
“The first generation of AI learned from humanity’s accumulated knowledge. The next generation will increasingly learn by acting in the physical world — through experiments, production and continuous feedback,” said founder and Chief Executive Daniel Huang. “That shift changes AI from a system that interprets the world into one that can help create new knowledge, materials, processes and products.”
The company’s two most prominently marketed offerings are Megalaxy Lab, an AI-connected experimental platform and CellVue T2000, its automated cell-imaging instrument. Both appear on the company’s English-language homepage. MegaRobo also sells more specialized lab equipment, including the Auflo sample-preparation workstation and the Seloris cell culturing automation system.
The key distinction is that Megalaxy Lab is the public face for the company’s AI-for-science strategy, while CellVue and other systems represent concrete examples of the instruments it builds for the industry.
The company said through Megalaxy it is making real-world experimentation programmable and accessible. Researchers and AI agents can configure experiments, route them through automated laboratory systems, track execution, receive structured, machine-readable results, and feed them directly into the next cycle of scientific reasoning. This includes virtual large data readouts that can be amplified as digital twins representing the scientific data, protein design, biochemistry and other properties.
MegaRobo said it’s working together with industry partners, including Tencent Cloud and Twist Bioscience, to expand its capability in the AI Science community with the launch of Poreva Open, a global AI protein design challenge open to all models and technical approaches. Megalaxy will provide wet-lab validation for more than 10,000 protein design sequences, creating an opportunity to test models against real experimental data.
The company is also developing the One Intelligence Stack as a common technology foundation for instruments, machines, materials processes and real-world feedback. It’s not just a collection of isolated AI applications and products, but a chain infrastructure that enables AI to act, learn and observe across complex physical environments.

articles.title: Want to see your live AI usage on your Mac's icons? This clever new app lets you | TechCrunch
articles.text:
There’s a new way to keep an eye on your AI usage and when your limits reset: by using your Mac’s app icons. Yes, really!
Designer Michael Flarup has just launched a new Mac utility called IconSwapper, which lets you replace any app’s official icon with one of your own creation. While you can use this tool to change your icons’ appearance, design, shading, and more, one of the more interesting ways to use it is to swap the icons for AI apps like ChatGPT or Claude with versions that can display your live AI usage.
Doing so is fairly simple, and you don’t have to be technically minded to get this to work. After installing the app on your Mac, you simply choose which application you want to create a “live” icon for — meaning one that responds to a particular app.
Besides tracking AI usage in ChatGPT, Claude, and Cursor, you can also create live icons for a number of the built-in Mac apps like Messages, Mail, Safari, Finder, Music, and others like Chrome and Spotify, but these configurations tend to be more fun than they are practical. For instance, you can configure Safari’s compass to follow things like page loads and downloads, or you can make it so that the Finder guy’s eyes follow your cursor around the screen. (That one is hilarious!)
Of course, there are plenty of other ways to track your AI usage — you don’t need an icon to do that. You can track usage from your account or your harness, even from a fun little gadget. But tracking it from the icon adds a certain whimsy to your Mac desktop setup. (If your dock is crowded, note that you can also see your icon customizations from your tab bar as you switch apps.)
Beyond live icons, you can also change what an icon looks like using IconSwapper’s built-in tools.
There are a surprising number of built-in customizations that are as easy to use as clicking a few buttons or toggling a switch. IconSwapper also comes with a large library of alternative icons for every app that are already ready to use, or you can upload your own.
Flarup is based in Copenhagen, where he runs a design studio, and he has been drawn to icon design and customization for years. He’s been making his own Mac icons since the early 2000s and even wrote a book about app icons that celebrates the work of designers.
He had been working on a solution that would allow him to customize Mac icons, which had proven tricky because macOS has no official support for theming and protects its system icons. To work around this, he came up with a different technique that involves drawing directly on the icons without replacing them, allowing him to use shaders, motion, and display real data.
Flarup tells TechCrunch that his renderer runs the icon artwork through custom Metal shaders in real time.
“The breakthrough was figuring out how to send the Dock a bitmap for another running app and have it draw that frame itself,” he explained. “I spent a lot of time getting the artwork to follow the icon through all the little ways macOS moves it, from Dock magnification to the Command-Tab switcher. Once I had that working, I could make the icon react to whatever’s happening,” Flarup said.
That lets users configure icons to do all kinds of fun, new things they never could before, like make light move across a gold icon as you drag your cursor over it, or animate an app’s icon while it’s thinking.
“That opens up a lot of fun ways to make your Mac feel like yours. I’ve always felt the software we use every day could be a little more fun and a lot more personal,” he added.
The app itself is a one-time purchase of $19 as a launch promo but will later sell for $29, its website says.

articles.title: Traumatized teens sue school, cops after Doritos bag triggers AI gun alert
articles.text:
In October 2025, four Black high school students were sharing Cool Ranch Doritos after football practice, winding down and waiting for their rides home. It was then, in the lull of a moment any teen with after-school activities knows well, that the school’s AI gun detection system suddenly flagged one teen holding a bag of chips as a potential gunman.
Within two minutes, Baltimore County Public Schools officials who reviewed security camera footage linked to the alert determined there was no actual threat. They recognized the Doritos bag and canceled the alert, which notified not only other school officials but also the Baltimore County Police Department that no response was needed.
The false alert could have ended there—before a traumatizing campus clash with police—but it didn’t.
According to a lawsuit filed by the current and former students, Taki Allen, Yui-Osa Ogbeide, Devon Thompson Jr., and Keith Winfield III, due to “both technological and human errors,” school officials called police to the scene anyway, and the cops responded with force.
At least six patrol cars arrived with lights flashing, and some cops emerged with guns drawn. The teens froze and cooperated, confused and scared for their lives, their lawsuit said.
“No one told the students what they were suspected of,” the lawsuit said. “Officers separated the students, ordered them to their knees on the concrete, handcuffed them, and searched their persons and property.”
Only after the cops failed to find a gun did students learn that it was the school’s AI gun detection system, Omnilert, that triggered the police response. Allegedly, one of the responding officers muttered, “stupid AI cameras” and “fucking Omnilerts,” while another told the students that “AI is not the best.” Finally releasing the students, one officer seemed to acknowledge that they had put the teens in danger.
“Hey, thanks for not running away, that would have been a real problem,” the officer allegedly said. Walking away, another joked that the boys should remember to “be careful with your chip bags.”
Teens traumatized
The cops did not just target the suspected gunman but apparently told the other teens that they were guilty “by association” when they asked why they were searched.
Suing to stop any other teens from facing allegedly life-or-death situations due to officials’ blind trust of AI, the teens have asked for an injunction barring BCPS from using Omnilert until they can effectively establish protocols to prevent police responses to false alerts.
The lawsuit alleged that students’ constitutional rights were violated, as students were unlawfully searched and detained.
Damon Hewitt, president and executive director of the Lawyers’ Committee for Civil Rights Under Law—a nonpartisan nonprofit that’s representing the teens in the suit—said that “overreliance on artificial intelligence technology mixed with inept communication and coordination among key officials is a toxic mix.”
The complaint noted that BCPS was among the earliest adopters of Omnilert, and officials have touted it as “the largest deployment of AI visual gun detection” as a means to supposedly protect students. Instead, they alleged that Omnilert is marketing a defective product as triggering “near-zero false positives” without effectively requiring the adequate human review that claim depends on.
“We need a reckoning on how AI is being used, especially concerning public safety and kids,” Hewitt said. “We are fighting to deliver justice in this case, but it also holds lessons for educators and police officials across the country who should think twice before putting our children’s fate in the hands of AI.”
All the teens feel less safe on campus and less trusting of police following the incident. They also suffered from physical pain—including ”deep red marks” on their wrists from handcuffs—as well as “acute and lasting emotional distress, fear, anxiety,” and “humiliation.” Further, the teens report that rumors follow them around, falsely claiming that there was a gun and damaging their reputations.
Car pick-up will never be the same. The student falsely flagged as the gunman, Taki Allen, “no longer feels safe waiting for rides or spending time outside the school after hours” and “frequently pays for rides home from private car services to avoid waiting for rides from friends or family.” Keith Winfield’s house was very close to the school, but his mother, Frieda Winfield, said his anxiety was so bad that he would call her “multiple times after football practice ended to confirm that she was on her way to pick him up.”
Frieda Winfield called for change following her son Keith’s chilling interaction.
“The police told my son this could have been a real problem,” Frieda Winfield said. “No child in Baltimore County should face this kind of danger while waiting outside his own school for a ride home from his mother.”
What went wrong?
The teens’ lawsuit targets Omnilert and responding Baltimore County Police Department officers. It also challenges Baltimore County Public Schools and individual school officials who allegedly failed to establish proper protocols to prevent a police response to a canceled alert.
In a later investigation, the Office of the Inspector General (OIG) for Education concluded that Omnilert’s system had no “bias.” But OIG acknowledged that the “delegation of authority” process that Kenwood High School set up didn’t stop its principal, Kate Smith, from noticing the alert, failing to see it was canceled, and texting a school resource officer to deploy police 15 minutes later—all while acknowledging in that text that the object in the alert was “maybe not” a gun. Smith apparently was never trained on the Omnilert system, OIG’s report indicated.
The OIG agreed with teens that things should change. Immediately after the incident, an internal Omnilert training link was shared with BCPS staff, and OIG recommended that schools conduct biannual trainings moving forward.
They also recommended that the BCPS Department of School Safety “review its protocol” and reduce the number of individuals who receive campus gun alerts. That could help ensure “internal notification controls are followed” and police “are fully informed of a verified threat,” the OIG said.
Without changes, the OIG acknowledged that “the loss of alert notification controls could place not only BCPS staff and students at risk but could also place responding law enforcement in a potentially tragic situation.”
Another change offered a technical solution that may have prevented the tragic event. The OIG recommended that school officials switch to using the Omnilert app. Since Smith opened the alert in a text message window on her phone, they suggested that she could easily have overlooked the cancellation text message if her first instinct were to enlarge the image or review the camera footage.
These recommendations aren’t enough for current and former students suing, one of whom remains an active student who claims the principal never apologized and instead made light of the incidents using cry-laughing emojis in texts with other school officials. Teens alleged that Smith should have known that more than “99 percent of OGD Alerts in Baltimore County Public Schools were false positives that required no police response,” as the OIG’s report said, and she should have prioritized students’ safety and verified the threat before calling in police.
“BCPS’s failures amounted to deliberate indifference to the constitutional rights of its students,” their lawsuit alleged.
The teens asked a court for an injunction barring the use of Omnilert until BCPS staff and police are adequately trained. In their complaint, they alleged that none of the officers on the scene had reviewed the camera footage before responding, and none of the officers informed of the alert cancellation intervened.
BCPS silent; Omnilert defends tech
BCPS declined to comment on the lawsuit, pointing Ars to a statement issued to parents following the incident. That statement did not directly apologize to students but did say the school would provide “ongoing counseling and emotional support” to them while promising to take steps to prevent future incidents.
Blake Mitchell, Omnilert’s vice president of marketing, told Ars that Omnilert is reviewing the complaint.
“What these four students went through on October 20, 2025 should not have happened, and we are truly sorry for the fear they and their families experienced,” Mitchell said. “We understand why they want answers.”
Mitchell said that Omnilert is “built to send anything that could be a firearm to trained people for review, because missing a real gun is the worst possible outcome.” He also reiterated that the OIG investigation found no bias in Omnilert’s system and seemed to agree that it was the school’s authority delegation that failed the students, not necessarily the technology.
“In this case, the school’s designated safety staff reviewed the alert and canceled it within about two minutes, and everyone who received it was notified,” Mitchell said. “That is exactly why human review matters, and why a canceled alert must stay canceled.”
Len Kamdang of the Lawyers’ Committee representing the teens told The New York Times that teens want BCPS and Omnilert to acknowledge that “what happened to them was unacceptable.”
“This case is ultimately about how human beings allowed AI to substitute for their judgment,” Kamdang said.
As a mother, Frieda Winfield told a local news outlet that she was shocked by the incident, despite deliberately teaching her son to be cautious around police. The boys’ caution “saved their lives in my opinion,” she said.
“I was angry. I was fearful,” Frieda Winfield said. “The biggest part was fear, because they’re young men. Young Black men, and they were at school, and they didn’t understand why what was happening, happened to them.”
Kamdang told NYT that “for anyone with children, that is a scary, scary situation. For a Black student, especially a young Black man in America, that is a life-or-death situation.”
As AI tools are increasingly positioned as public safety solutions, the Lawyers Committee is pushing for police reform when cops or officials appear to be blindly trusting AI, their press release said. They noted that “this injustice also raises a broader concern regarding the use and reliability of AI-powered technology in public safety where accuracy is essential in life-and-death situations.”
Ashley is a senior policy reporter for Ars Technica, dedicated to tracking social impacts of emerging policies and new technologies. She is a Chicago-based journalist with 20 years of experience.

articles.title: Grok Bot tentou acessar contas sem autorização e depois mentiu • Tecnoblog
articles.text:
Grok Bot tentou acessar contas sem autorização e depois mentiu
Pesquisadores registraram 31 tentativas de acesso da IA a serviços como e-mail, Slack, calendário e GitHub, inclusive durante a madrugada.
O Grok Bot, agente de IA da SpaceX, tentou acessar contas corporativas de usuários sem receber nenhum comando. Pesquisadores registraram 31 requisições em cinco dias, algumas durante a madrugada e até quando os notebooks usados no experimento estavam fechados.
As solicitações foram bloqueadas por uma ferramenta da própria NewCore, segundo o Ars Technica. A princípio, o Grok Bot parecia apenas exercer a autonomia esperada de uma IA agêntica, mas continuou agindo após receber ordens para parar e, depois, “mentiu” ao negar a atividade.
A empresa de segurança NewCore instalou o Grok Bot em dois notebooks de funcionários e monitorou as interações do agente com serviços corporativos conectados. Durante cinco dias, o sistema tentou consultar informações de calendário, email, além de serviços como Slack e GitHub, sem que os usuários tivesse iniciado uma tarefa.
As requisições só foram percebidas percebida porque a empresa usa uma ferramenta que registra as solicitações feitas pelos bots e pode impedir que elas cheguem aos serviços de destino. As operações também não apareciam nos registros internos do Grok Bot. Sem a ferramenta da NewCore, o usuário não teria no histórico do agente uma indicação de que aquelas consultas haviam sido iniciadas.
Depois de identificar o comportamento, um dos funcionários pediu ao agente que não realizasse mais verificações por conta própria. A instrução foi repetida em quatro ocasiões diferentes e, em uma delas, o Grok Bot respondeu que pararia.
A NewCore enviou os registros ao suporte do Grok Bot em 4 de novembro, que disse que as consultas automáticas fazem parte de um recurso criado para tornar o agente mais proativo. A funcionalidade teria sido herdada do Cursor, serviço de programação de IA adquirido recentemente pela empresa de Elon Musk.
Na avaliação da empresa de segurança, falta clareza sobre a existência das verificações automáticas. Durante a configuração inicial, o agente informa que pode continuar trabalhando enquanto o usuário está ausente. Porém, para o pesquisador de segurança da NewCore, Ido Hoorvitch, o aviso é breve e não pede consentimento para consultas periódicas às contas vinculadas.
“Não há um bug para corrigir, e é exatamente por isso que isso é pior do que um bug. Uma vulnerabilidade pode ser consertada. Este é o produto funcionando conforme foi projetado”, afirmou Ido Hoorvitch, pesquisador de segurança da NewCore.
Ainda assim, a SpaceX parece ter verificado a situação. Quando a companhia procurou o suporte, disse não haver uma opção para desativar esse comportamento. Oito dias depois, as configurações do Grok Bot passaram a incluir uma chave chamada “mensagens proativas, que permite impedir esse tipo de atividade.
A opção, no entanto, permanece ativada por padrão e precisa ser desligada manualmente por um administrador.

articles.title: Amazon vows to fight warehouse union at BC warehouse
articles.text:
Amazon workers at a British Columbia warehouse have officially signed a union contract, marking the first North American site under a collective bargaining agreement. However, Amazon isn’t very happy about this arrangement.
The contract, which was signed for the YVR2 fulfillment center in Delta, BC, had its terms set by an independent arbitrator between union company Unifor and Amazon. Unifor said in a statement that it is a first for Amazon workers anywhere in North America.
According to Unifor’s statement, the agreement includes wage increases that bring hourly rates to $29 by the end of the agreement, enhanced severance protections of up to 18 weeks, and an additional week of vacation for employees with 10 years of service.
For context, the organizing drive was started in 2024, and the B.C. Labour Relations Board certified Unifor Local 114 as the workers’ union in July, 2025, after finding that the logistics company started an “unnecessary hiring spree” designed to stop the certification process. The board said in its decision that the company pursued a “lengthy and pervasive anti-union campaign.”
In August, the board ordered binding arbitration, finding that Amazon’s conduct had affected the parties’ ability to reach an agreement.
“Amazon tried to convince workers that they were too big to organize and used their power and money to deter workers while making billions in profits. They have fought every decision and tried to rewrite reality at every step, but they have failed,” says Western Regional Director Gavon McGarrigle. “These Amazon workers now have the binding union contract they deserve, and we intend to support them and thousands more, improving their lives in BC and elsewhere.”
However, Amazon argues that the agreement sets terms for wages, scheduling, layoffs, and benefits similar to what it already has. Adding to that, Amazon said the contract requires every employee in the unit to join the union whether they want to or not, and that union dues of up to C$1,604 are deducted from their pay in the first year, implying they take home less money.
The statement also reads that “Our associates weren’t allowed to vote on whether to accept it, which has become an unfortunate pattern with the British Columbia Labour Relations Board.” The company also added that “we believe that this process was improper, unfair, and defies common sense. If a group of people vote on issues that are important to them, their votes should be opened, counted, and respected.”
“We believe that it’s important to understand the facts and that associates should get to decide for themselves, at Amazon or anywhere else.”
Source: Unifor, Amazon via the Associated Press

articles.title: ‘My firm is more interested in what AI can do to radically change gameplay’: The former boss behind GTA IV thinks gamers are about to fall in love with generative AI — but I’m not fully convinced
articles.text:
‘My firm is more interested in what AI can do to radically change gameplay’: The former boss behind GTA IV thinks gamers are about to fall in love with generative AI — but I’m not fully convinced
AI in gaming is still waiting for a Toy Story moment
With the long-awaited release of Grand Theft Auto VI finally having arrived after a 13-year wait — and receiving stunning preliminary reviews in the process — the former CEO of Take-Two Interactive has said he believes that attitudes towards the use of generative AI in game development could be set to change.
Ben Feder presided over the release of hits such as Grand Theft Auto IV, Red Dead Redemption, Borderlands, and BioShock during his tenure, but believes that the negative sentiment surrounding AI mirrors the switch that animators made from hand-drawn frames to computer-generated images.
Feder argues that the gaming industry is waiting for a singular, groundbreaking moment where AI will prove its worth to gamers, similar to Toy Story’s demonstration of how computer-generated imagery revolutionized the animation industry, and allowed for deeper storytelling rather than detracting from it.
GTA VI untouched by AI, but Take-Two’s approach is changing
"A lot of incumbents think about AI as a way of reducing costs, which it is," Feder said in an interview with The Game Business. "Will it actually reduce costs or just kind of make the games bigger for the same cost? I don't know. But I personally, and my firm, is more interested in what AI can do to radically change gameplay."
There is a somewhat glaring contradiction in Feder’s beliefs. Toy Story was 100% human-authored with animators painstakingly shaping every individual frame, just with the assistance of a new digital tool. On the other hand, AI condenses existing human work into a probabilistic representation of what it is asked to create, removing the originality of human intent.
Feder’s perspectives may be somewhat skewed in favor of AI given his current work heading TIRTA Ventures, a venture capital fund investing in AI-native projects.
He argues that AI could instead give companies a way to add value by fundamentally reshaping gameplay and introducing a new generation of gaming experiences.
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
Well, GTA VI appears to have done exactly that without any AI assistance at all. Take-Two’s current CEO Strauss Zelnick assured fans before release that generative AI played “zero part” in the creation of GTA VI, and that the State of Leonida — where the latest release is set — was meticulously crafted by humans.
On the other hand, Zelnick said Take-Two is “actively embracing generative AI” across “hundreds of pilots” to test the worthiness of the technology in helping the company become the “most efficient company in the entertainment business.”
‘Efficient’ is an interesting choice of words, and follows a similar vein of vocabulary used by big tech companies in brutal waves of layoffs following the adoption of AI.
Zelnick is also heavily protective of the highly valuable intellectual property Take-Two has created in GTA VI, and recently called out companies like OpenAI and Anthropic for allowing their users to clone the IP of game developers through AI platforms, especially as multiple AI companies have accused China of ‘distilling’ their models — effectively stealing their own IP. Ironic.
Anthropic has since updated the backend of its Claude model to prevent users from making direct copies of existing games, but OpenAI is yet to make the same changes to ChatGPT.
Does AI really fit into games development?
Zelnick insists his pledge to increase efficiency isn’t about replacing human work, but instead reducing the burdensome load of repetitive tasks that currently cause production cycles of AAA games to run into the decades.
But those same burdensome loads — such as basic coding, quality assurance, and concept art design — have traditionally been entry-level workloads. If you cut out the work of junior positions, who replaces the seniors when they retire? AI adoption in this sense could cause a talent vacuum that leads game design to regress, rather than birth a new golden age of entertainment.
There is also the glaring issue of charging premium prices for a game that has been in part created using AI. Many gamers’ views on the technology have significantly hardened, with even the slightest suggestion of AI use in a trailer or artwork leading to outcry and review-bombing. Those handing over $80+ for a game expect their purchase to go towards rewarding human craftsmanship.
Given that GTA fans waited 13 years for a new game — and that Skyrim has just celebrated its 15th anniversary with only a title teaser to tide fans over for a new Elder Scrolls installment — there could be a balance to be struck.
Should humans remain in control of the full creative direction and AI only play an assistive role, it is entirely possible that fans would endure the use of generative AI if it leads to better games, shorter wait times, and reasonable pricing.
Whether that will actually happen remains to be seen.

articles.title: Chips, Geheimdienst, Anleger-Täuschung: Das steckt hinter der neuen Nvidia-Untersuchung
articles.text:
Gingen Nvidia-Chips heimlich nach China? Kalifornien nimmt Chip-Riesen nach Huang-Rücktritt ins Visier
Der Chip-Riese Nvidia gerät mit einer neuen Untersuchung in Kalifornien zu den angeblichen China-Verstrickungen von Ex-Chef Jensen Huang stärker unter Druck. Der Generalstaatsanwalt des US-Bundesstaats, Rob Bonta, ließ dem Konzern einen Fragenkatalog zustellen. Dabei gehe es unter anderem um die Frage, ob leistungsstarke Nvidia-Chips oder vertrauliche Informationen nach China gegangen seien, teilte Bonta mit. Die Ermittlungsbehörden versenden solche offiziellen Dokumente mit Fragen, um festzustellen, ob möglicherweise gegen Gesetze verstoßen wurde.
Bonta will laut seiner Ankündigung auch klären, ob Nvidia seine Anleger und die Öffentlichkeit falsch informiert habe. Das Verhalten von Nvidia lasse die Alarmglocken schrillen, erklärte er bereits jetzt. Von dem Konzern gab es zunächst keine Reaktion auf Bontas Vorstoß.
Nvidia-Chips sind für den Ausbau Künstlicher Intelligenz entscheidend. Das Unternehmen hat seinen Sitz im kalifornischen Silicon Valley.
Nvidia: Chiplieferungen nach China im Fokus
Huang trat vergangene Woche zurück, nachdem mindestens zwei außereheliche Affären bekanntgeworden waren. Bei einer der Geliebten, einer Managerin des damaligen Nvidia-Kunden Megaspeed, haben US-Sicherheitsbehörden den Verdacht, dass sie vom chinesischen Geheimdienst angeworben worden war. Die andere ist Berichten zufolge eine Top-Managerin von Nvidia, die Huang unterstellt war.
Inzwischen stehen aber auch immer mehr Fragen zu möglichen Lieferungen leistungsstarker Nvidia-Chips nach China in Umgehung von US-Verboten im Raum. Auch Megaspeed wird von US-Behörden verdächtigt, da mitgemischt zu haben. US-Finanzminister Scott Bessent forderte Nvidia auf, schnell aufzuklären, wer im Unternehmen wann was wusste. Für Dezember wurde Huang auch in Kongressausschüssen vorgeladen.

articles.title: Memory R&D Is a High-Stakes Game - EE Times
articles.text:
The need for significant investment in R&D is nothing new for memory makers, but Micron Technology’s creation of a dedicated facility that looks beyond the next node illustrates why the industry cannot afford to skimp on R&D, especially in the AI era.
Micron Research Labs, announced in the summer of 2026, gives the DRAM maker a long-term research home of its own. Based in Boise, Idaho, and backed by a planned $10 billion investment over the next decade, the facility will focus on critical memory technologies, advanced memory and compute architectures, packaging, and future semiconductor manufacturing. The investment also covers university collaborations, satellite labs, and ecosystem partnerships.
Micron expects to break ground in 2027 on a facility capable of hosting hundreds of researchers. It has already appointed Deirdre Hanford, who spent 37 years at Synopsys, as corporate VP and president of the new lab. Hanford will lead the establishment of the lab’s research infrastructure, operating model, and partnerships.
The lab’s first notable outreach came earlier this fall, when Micron said it intends to invest up to $50 million over five years to support the U.S. Department of Energy’s Genesis Mission Graduate Fellowship Pilot Program and related national laboratory research.
For Scott DeBoer, Micron’s recently appointed president and chief technology and products officer, the lab represents a change in how the company participates in semiconductor research. The need for R&D has always been pressing, but efforts have mainly focused on relatively near-term challenges and goals, he said in an interview with EE Times. “I couldn’t have imagined the R&D investment level that we’re at today.”
DeBoer said the lab’s funding is an addition to previously announced or forecasted investments, which have increased significantly every year over the past four years.
Looking beyond the roadmap
Micron has always had to look ahead, DeBoer said, but mostly within the bounds of the company’s technology roadmaps, which usually chart the next five to seven years. “We have to have a pretty good view of what we’re investing in and what we’re going to bring to market through that period of time.”
He said the company has had less influence on research that looks a decade ahead or beyond, in part because there was more government funding flowing into U.S. universities. “We actually didn’t have to be the leader of that kind of research effort.” Now that memory has become much more important, Micron is taking more of a leadership role in longer-term research with universities and national labs, DeBoer said.
Micron’s approach in recent years emphasized supporting professors and students in building workforce capacity. Longer-horizon partnerships allow it to pursue foundational research outcomes while mitigating some of the intellectual property complications associated with projects nearing commercialization. “This is a pivot, where we go out farther, where we actually can have research outcomes in mind,” DeBoer said.
AI adds to the R&D burden
Much of the memory industry’s R&D has historically focused on immediate process and manufacturing improvements—shrinking DRAM from one node to the next and getting yields up. AI makes that longer view more urgent while complicating nearer-term development.
DeBoer said memory is the engine driving AI, whether in the data center or at the edge, in cars and robots, all of which depend heavily on memory performance, memory bandwidth, and power.
He said the diversity of applications is a huge multiplier of R&D requirements. In the data center, for example, the capacity and performance specifications for LPDDR have changed drastically, while robotics and automotive bring in advanced packaging and 3D implementations. Nearly all of these involve specific engagements with key customers, rather than simply delivering another scaled DRAM node, DeBoer said. “You can’t optimize the system without optimizing how the memory works in it.”
R&D is the price of staying competitive
Dan Hutcheson, vice chair of research firm TechInsights, has studied semiconductor R&D since the 1980s, and told EE Times in an interview that Micron’s move makes complete sense—the new lab is a way to bring in external funding and outside ideas.
Hutcheson estimated that R&D costs rise by roughly 30% with each node transition and that, in the 1980s and 1990s, costs had often increased faster than the revenues available to support them. This became less of a problem as organizations such as Sematech and imec took on shared research. Rising costs nevertheless contributed to vendor consolidation, as companies found they could no longer keep up with the investment required for the next generation.
Hutcheson distinguished between “little r, big R, little d, big D,” noting that companies are usually “big D and very little r,” especially when it comes to basic research. “It doesn’t make sense for the companies to invest in Big R because it takes 10 to 20 years for these things to mature,” he said. That’s where universities and national labs come in—and where imec has excelled. “What imec has done is a great job of bridging that gap between the university, between suppliers, and between end customers.”
AI has transformed memory from being cost-driven to being value-driven, Hutcheson said.
Research must still reach the fab
There are two key cost centers at play for memory R&D: One is developing the technology; the other is financing the manufacturing capacity needed to exploit it.
Jim Handy, principal analyst at Objective Analysis, said in an interview with EE Times that vendor consolidation is being driven by the costs of building a competitive fab, which have been rising faster than DRAM revenues.
Regardless, R&D gets its own line in a memory maker’s business model, Handy said. A DRAM manufacturer typically allocates about 20% of revenue to capital spending and about 10% to R&D. “And generally, very few layoffs happen in the R&D team,” he added.
Handy said he sees the Micron announcement partly as a repackaging of spending that would happen anyway into a 10-year commitment. “They’re pretty darn sure that they’re going to be spending that much anyway.”
The budget is also available when big AI players don’t see price as an object, Handy said. This is giving DRAM makers gross margins of 80% versus the 30% or below they are used to. More R&D should also help manufacturers advance nodes faster and squeeze more bits from existing capacity. “That will help lower the price, and that’ll be good for the buyers,” he said.
Handy stressed the value of research organizations such as imec and CEA-Leti, where companies pool their efforts to do “precompetitive” research. DRAM rivals such as Samsung, SK Hynix, and Micron might jointly fund a project to evaluate a new material, for example. If it pans out, they will all go off and develop their own recipes, he said. “That speaks to the incredible cost of doing this R&D.”
That model matters even more for emerging memories such as MRAM, ReRAM, and FRAM, which have spent years—sometimes decades—finding their niches rather than displacing DRAM or flash outright.
Partnerships keep emerging memories in the game
ReRAM maker Weebit Nano has relied heavily on research partnerships to bring its technology to market. CEA-Leti has been a partner from very early on, said Eran Briman, the company’s VP of marketing and business development. Weebit benefited from approximately a decade of research already undertaken by the institute before the two organizations joined forces, he said in an interview with EE Times.
Weebit Nano began working with universities and research institutes in 2018 on neuromorphic computing. In 2019, it demonstrated spiking neural networks running on its ReRAM in collaboration with CEA-Leti. In-memory compute is a nearer-term opportunity, Briman said. Compared with GPUs, CPUs, and accelerators, running AI in memory could theoretically be 10× to 100× more power-efficient, he said.
The company recently launched its Weebit Matrix In-Memory Compute (IMC) Research Program to accelerate the exploration of next-generation computing architectures. The program provides industry and academic researchers with a ReRAM-based hardware development kit to explore and prototype IMC algorithms and systems.
Through the program, researchers can use Weebit Nano’s ReRAM-based platform to develop and test AI algorithms, investigate innovative programming methods, explore new AI and neuromorphic architectures, and assess potential gains in power efficiency and performance. Participating researchers will share their ReRAM-related findings and feedback with the company to help improve the technology and contribute to the broader research community.
Research is where problems get solved, and development is implementation, Briman said. “It took a couple of decades to actually get where we are today,” he said of ReRAM’s maturity.
Commercial availability does not end that work. Customers keep requesting higher densities, greater endurance, and better performance at elevated temperatures. Briman said demands have progressed from 10,000 programming cycles to 100,000 and, for some applications, a million. AI updates, code changes, and data logging are among the drivers.
Briman said semiconductors remain a very expensive industry to play in, noting that some ReRAM vendors have tried and failed multiple times. He sees Micron’s investment as a rising tide. “There’s a ripple effect for the entire industry where we sit, and we’re going to see this coming in the next couple of years.”
Learning from failure
Memory R&D doesn’t always pay off. Micron spent billions on 3D XPoint before DeBoer killed the program earlier than its partner, Intel. “We made a decision that we had learned what we could from it.”
Bringing a new memory to market requires the technology, manufacturability, and customer acceptance, DeBoer said. “If you don’t have all three of those things worked out, it’s just not happening.”
Ultimately, Micron Research Labs reflects the company’s changing role in the semiconductor research ecosystem, DeBoer said, as memory and logic become more tightly integrated. “We intend to transform what Micron is in 10 years,” he said. “Today and going forward, this combination of memory and logic is going to be really the enabler across AI.”

articles.title: Anthropic entre en Bourse et bat le record historique de SpaceX
articles.text:
Ce jeudi 19 novembre, Anthropic fait officiellement son entrée en Bourse. Les échanges débutent sur le Nasdaq sous le symbole « ANT ». Cette entrée en Bourse est tout simplement historique : avec 81,34 milliards de dollars, l’offre initiale d’Anthropic dépasse les 75 milliards de dollars levés par SpaceX lors de sa propre introduction en Bourse.
Anthropic entre officiellement en Bourse
Ça y est, nous y sommes : Anthropic fait officiellement son entrée en Bourse ce jeudi 19 novembre. L’entreprise derrière Claude a fixé le prix de son introduction en Bourse à 83 dollars par action. Au total, l’opération porte sur pas moins de 81,34 milliards de dollars, un montant qui dépasse celui de l’offre initiale de SpaceX. Pour rappel, SpaceX, dont l’entrée en Bourse avait été qualifiée d’historique, avait initialement levé 75 milliards de dollars lors de son introduction en Bourse, avec un prix par action fixé à 135 dollars.
Pour être plus précis, sur ces 81,34 milliards de dollars, Anthropic doit en percevoir 79,38 milliards avant déduction des commissions et des frais, tandis que les 1,96 milliard restants reviennent aux actionnaires qui vendent une partie de leurs titres. Par ailleurs, Anthropic espérait initialement proposer 825 millions d’actions à un prix compris entre 70 et 78 dollars. En fin de compte, l’entreprise spécialisée dans l’intelligence artificielle est parvenue à porter le nombre de titres proposés à 980 millions, grâce à une forte demande.
À noter qu’Anthropic affiche actuellement une capitalisation boursière d’environ 1 100 milliards de dollars. Ce montant grimpe même à 1 500 milliards de dollars si l’on prend en compte les actions qui pourraient être distribuées aux salariés dans le cadre de leur rémunération.
Des revenus en forte hausse, mais des pertes notables
Au niveau de ses résultats financiers, Anthropic affiche une croissance impressionnante. Son chiffre d’affaires annualisé est passé de 71 milliards de dollars fin septembre à 81 milliards fin octobre. Entre juillet et septembre, l’entreprise a ainsi réalisé 16,96 milliards de dollars de chiffre d’affaires, soit une hausse de 47 % par rapport au trimestre précédent.
En revanche, il faut aussi noter que son bénéfice d’exploitation de 974 millions de dollars au deuxième trimestre s’est transformé en une perte de 567 millions au troisième trimestre. Sa perte nette atteint même 23,3 milliards de dollars (dont 21,9 milliards correspondent toutefois à des charges comptables sans sortie de trésorerie).
Précisons enfin qu’Anthropic investit une grande partie de son budget dans la puissance de calcul pour faire fonctionner Claude. Au cours des six premiers mois de l’année, Anthropic a dépensé près de 9 milliards de dollars pour financer ses capacités de calcul et ses infrastructures, soit presque quatre fois plus que sur la même période l’année précédente. À cela s’ajoute les folles dépenses de l’entreprise pour payer ses salariés. Quoi qu’il en soit, la Bourse s’apprête à vivre une journée historique.

articles.title: Vembu flags possible US immigration reversal, says it could revive housing demand
articles.text:
Vembu flags possible US immigration reversal, says it could revive housing demand
Sridhar Vembu warns that a possible US immigration policy reversal could restore population-driven demand in housing and other sectors.
Zoho Co-founder Sridhar Vembu says a political shift in Washington could revive immigration-driven demand in the US economy, including in housing.
In a post on X, he argues that tighter immigration controls reduced a source of demand supporting asset prices, and that a change of course could restore it.
“Given the scale of MAGA losses, it is likely that immigration policy will make a sharp reversal in America, both legal and illegal immigration,” Vembu wrote. He added, “The unsustainable financial and economic bubble had long been sustained with demographic fuel. A good example is housing.”
Vembu said, “The demographic fuel tap for the bubble was shut for a period and now it may be turned back on.” He described this as a possible scenario rather than a firm prediction.
His reference is to the November 3 midterm elections, in which Democrats won control of both chambers of Congress, dealing U.S. President Donald Trump a major political setback. The result could constrain his agenda but does not guarantee an immigration policy reversal. The administration retains control of federal enforcement, while Congress can shape funding and legislation.
The demographic shift is measurable. US Census Bureau estimates show net international migration fell 53.8%, from 2.7 million in the year to June 2024 to 1.3 million in the year to June 2025. Net migration measures arrivals minus departures, rather than unauthorised border crossings alone.
There is evidence for Vembu’s housing argument, although it does not establish that immigration alone inflated property prices. Harvard University’s Joint Center for Housing Studies found immigrants accounted for 55% of US household growth in 2023, adding more than 800,000 households. A subsequent Harvard analysis expects the effects of lower immigration on household formation to deepen in 2026 and 2027, potentially resulting in nearly 500,000 fewer immigrant households annually by 2027 than in 2024.
Mortgage costs, limited supply and local conditions also shape housing markets. The Congressional Budget Office says slower immigration reduces labour-force growth and consumer demand, and could slow housing construction and long-term economic output.

articles.title: Vous n'avez pas de boite de jeu GTA 6 ? Voici l'astuce qui vous permet d'en avoir une sans bouger de chez soi
articles.text:
GTA 6 est enfin disponible, et beaucoup ont préféré opter pour l'unique code à télécharger. Pour ceux qui s'imaginent avoir une boîte du jeu sans que cela ne leur coûte grand-chose, il existe une astuce très simple.
Cette fois, c'est palpable, puisque depuis minuit ce jeudi 19 novembre 2026, GTA 6 est bel et bien accessible pour tout le monde, que vous soyez sur Xbox Series X ou S, ou sur PlayStation 5. Et avec les stocks un peu éclatés ou la malchance, beaucoup ont dû acheter le jeu en ligne, en ne récupérant qu'un unique code pour profiter du titre de Rockstar Games. Mais même si la boîte physique est vendue sans disque, un vrai crève-cœur pour certains, des joueurs aimeraient bien en avoir une flaguée du logo de GTA VI. Sachez que sans trop réfléchir, il est possible de se réconcilier avec ça. Clubic vous explique comment.
Vous pouvez, sans la recevoir, faire vous-même votre boîte GTA 6
Pour avoir votre propre boîte de jeu GTA 6, il vous faut une connexion internet (je pense que là, il n'y a pas de souci), quelques minutes de votre temps, une imprimante (avec de l'encre, si possible) pour imprimer la jaquette des aventures de Jason et Lucia, et une ancienne boîte de jeu PS5 ou Xbox Series S|X, voire Xbox One, ça peut faire l'affaire.
La première chose que vous devez faire, c'est vous rendre sur le site Leonida Verse, qui vous propose de créer gratuitement et presque sur mesure votre jaquette GTA 6, en choisissant la langue de votre choix, la console, la version (Ultimate ou Standard) et même de quoi imprimer une pochette à coller sur un ancien disque.
Une fois cela fait, rendez-vous dans ChatGPT. Voici ce que j'ai demandé au robot conversationnel d'OpenAI, en utilisant sa fonctionnalité Créer une image : « Est-ce que tu penses que tu peux me préparer sur un format A4 la jaquette de GTA 6 à imprimer que je pourrai imprimer et ensuite la mettre dans une boîte que j'ai déjà de jeu Xbox One ? Est-ce que tu peux faire ça ? Aux parfaites dimensions ». En quelques dizaines de seconde, ChatGPT a généré trois versions de la jaquette, dont une en PDF, l'autre au format PNG haute résolution.
C'est l'affaire de quelques minutes pour créer l'illusion
Après, vient l'étape la plus périlleuse, celle de l'impression. Ce qu'on vous conseille, c'est d'imprimer la jaquette en passant par votre PC, qui vous propose plus d'options d'ajustement que votre téléphone. Au moment de paramétrer l'opération, pensez bien à ajuter l'impression à 100 % de votre feuille A4, sinon vous risquez d'avoir une mauvaise surprise.
Si tout va bien, et que vous avez suffisamment d'encre dans votre cartouche couleur, vous devriez avoir une jaquette qui tient la route. ChatGPT a pensé à tout, puisqu'il a bien dessiné le patron, avec des petits traits des quatre côtés de la jaquette, pour vous aider à découper comme il faut cette dernière.
Une fois votre jaquette découpée, vous n'avez plus qu'à récupérer une ancienne boîte de jeu. À titre personnel, j'ai sacrifié Top Spin 2K25 pour Xbox, paix à son âme, puisque j'ai une Xbox Series S, pour mettre à l'intérieur, en quelques secondes également, mon morceau de papier si bien découpé. Si je compare avec une vraie boîte GTA 6, le rendu n'est pas si dégueulasse, vous en conviendrez.
N'hésitez pas à nous dire en commentaire si vous aviez pensé à cette petite astuce des familles, ou si elle a pu vous aider.

articles.title: Unos científicos de la Universidad de Pensilvania quieren usar mantas de emergencia para construir edificaciones lunares
articles.text:
La tecnología ha dado muchas vueltas desde que se escribió el cuento de “Los tres cerditos”. Ahora las mejores casas no llevan solo ladrillo, sino que también están recubiertas de plástico. Al menos, es así si vas a vivir en la Luna. Y es que en los futuros asentamientos lunares no se valorará únicamente la resistencia de los materiales. También se buscarán aquellos que aíslen mejor de las temperaturas extremas, tanto altas como bajas. Existen algunas opciones que aíslan muy bien, como los aerogeles o los recubrimientos multicapa clásicos. Sin embargo, son demasiado frágiles para un ambiente tan extremo. Por eso, unos ingenieros han estado buscando alternativas hasta dar con una propuesta interesante: usar el material de las mantas de emergencia.
Capas apiladas de Mylar. Las mantas de emergencia están hechas con BoPET (tereftalato de polietileno orientado biaxialmente), un material conocido comercialmente como Mylar, que se obtiene estirando el PET clásico en dos direcciones. Así, se consigue una lámina mucho más fina y resistente. Pero no solo es resistente. Si se le añade aluminio, refleja muy bien la radiación infrarroja, por lo que se convierte en un aislante térmico ideal. Esa es justamente la razón por la que esta combinación se usa para fabricar mantas de emergencia, como las que se emplean para tapar a corredores de maratón tras un ejercicio extremo o a las víctimas de un accidente o desastre natural.
Los ingenieros de la Escuela de Ingeniería y Ciencias Aplicadas de la Universidad de Pensilvania quisieron usar esta misma combinación de materiales para ver si sería útil en la Luna. Pero no necesitaban solo que fuera un buen aislante. También requerían un material resistente. Por eso, probaron a apilar capas muy finas de Mylar, una sobre otra, añadiendo óxido de aluminio para no perder su efecto aislante.
Difícil, pero útil. El procedimiento no fue coser y cantar. Las capas eran tan finas que, según explicaron estos científicos, solo con respirar cerca de ellas podían salir volando. Las manipularon con ayuda de unas pinzas y lograron un prototipo de un centímetro cuadrado. De ahí a las construcciones lunares hay un camino larguísimo, pero al menos sirvió para comprobar en el laboratorio si este material, al que han bautizado como HyLIFS, tiene las cualidades esperadas.
Vaya si las tiene. En ese centímetro cuadrado encontraron un material con una conductividad térmica extremadamente baja, de unos 2,2 mW/m·K. Eso significa que aísla muy bien, tanto de altas como de bajas temperaturas. Para hacernos más o menos una idea. Para hacernos una idea, la conductividad térmica de los ladrillos puede ser de más de 1.000 mW/m·K. Por otro lado, la muestra resistió una presión de 20 megapascales, comparable a concentrar unos 200 kilogramos en un área del tamaño de la punta de un dedo. Esta prueba de resistencia se repitió 10 veces seguidas con idénticos resultados, así que la estructura del material sigue resistiendo después de soportar presiones altas muchas veces seguidas.
Partículas microscópicas. Al analizar mediante microscopía este nuevo material, los científicos vieron que gran parte del calor pasa de una lámina a otra por los puntos de contacto de unas partículas microscópicas ‘antiadherentes’ que los fabricantes añaden al Mylar para que las capas no se peguen. Es decir, estas partículas, necesarias para separar las capas, son también el principal camino por el que se cuela el calor, lo que abre la puerta a mejorar el aislamiento optimizándolas.
Un largo viaje y una estancia inhóspita. Los materiales que se usen en las construcciones lunares deben poder doblarse, golpearse y someterse a altas presiones, tanto durante el viaje a la Luna como durante la construcción y una vez en su destino. Por eso es tan importante combinar resistencia y aislamiento. Estos científicos lo han conseguido, pero en un tamaño muy reducido. Ahora habrá que comprobar que, efectivamente, las propiedades se mantienen en fragmentos más grandes de materiales.
Además, es importante encontrar un método de producción más rápido, ya que hacerlo manualmente con unas pinzas no es viable si se van a fabricar grandes rollos. Y, para terminar, será necesario seguir investigando para comprobar que resiste bien a golpes, arañazos y flexiones repetidas. Esto es solo el principio, pero parece que las mantas de emergencia podrían tener una aplicación inesperada en la Luna.
