articles.title: How the BMW Group governs hundreds of agents across thousands of developers | Amazon Web Services
articles.text:
Artificial Intelligence
How the BMW Group governs hundreds of agents across thousands of developers
When hundreds of agents serve thousands of developers, enterprise governance can’t be an afterthought.
At the BMW Group’s R&D, more than 12,500 developers work on approximately 500 million lines of vehicle software code. This software is augmented by the BMW Connected Vehicle backend, a cloud-based system of more than 1,300 microservices providing digital services for 24 million vehicles in the field. In regulated industry, the bar for (software) quality, stability, and governance compliance is exceptionally high.
While research, frameworks, and guidelines now facilitate building agents, industrializing and operating high-quality agents in an efficient, scalable manner remains a significant challenge.
Scaling agentic AI across a large organization cannot be achieved by isolated teams. It requires collective effort, locally driven experimentation, and active knowledge sharing across the enterprise. This creates a fundamental governance dichotomy: Development teams need the freedom to innovate rapidly, while the enterprise must enforce standards for safety, security, composability, and cost-efficiency. Without that balance, organizations risk a fragmented landscape of AI islands and costly duplicate work. This presents a real challenge given hundreds of globally distributed teams building agents across the BMW Group.
In this post, we detail the practices and patterns that support BMW’s R&D teams in building, governing and operating agents at scale without sacrificing speed, quality or compliance.
Solution
Our premise is straightforward: build agents that can cooperate from the start. This requires an architecture that makes diversity composable, governable, and automatable, without requiring a single framework or toolchain.
Central to this architecture is the agent harness, a runtime layer wrapped around a large language model (LLM). It provides the execution loop, tool dispatch, memory management, and observability hooks for autonomous operation.
Just as the AWS Well-Architected Framework standardized cloud infrastructure design, agentic systems need equivalent patterns, reusable blueprints encoding governance, composability, and operational best practices from the start.
We organize our solution around five interlocking practices, drawn from hands-on experience building and operating agentic systems at enterprise scale since 2023. Each practice is codified as infrastructure as code (IaC), making adoption repeatable, auditable, and enforceable across teams without blocking DevOps velocity.
Govern proactively, not retroactively
Governance must be structural from the start and maintained across the full lifecycle. We advocate for three properties of effective agentic governance:
Framework-agnostic and externalized: Governance rules such as authentication, authorization, rate limiting and content filtering are enforced at the integration layer. This includes a Model Context Protocol (MCP) gateway, a central agent registry and orchestration boundary, rather than within individual agent codebases. This means governance survives framework migrations, model swaps, and team reorganizations.
Domain-sensitive and graduated: Not every agent action carries the same risk: drafting documentation, updating customer records, and production database writes demand very different levels of oversight. We implement graduated trust through per-step autonomy levels:
- Level 0 (Human-in-the-loop): Every action requires explicit human approval. This is the starting point for new agents and high-risk operations.
- Level 1 (Human-on-the-loop): The agent executes autonomously but surfaces decisions for asynchronous human review. Suitable for medium-risk tasks with defined inputs, outputs, and rollback options.
- Level 2 (Autonomous within guardrails): The agent operates independently within strictly defined policy boundaries, enforced deterministically rather than through prompt instructions (see below). Reserved for low-risk, well-understood operations with verified track records.
Assign trust levels per step, not per agent. A single workflow can include steps at all three levels, so teams can start conservatively and incrementally increase autonomy as confidence builds, grounded in measurable evaluation data, not assumptions.
Deterministically enforced: Governance runs as deterministic code outside the agent’s reasoning loop. In practice, this happens mainly in the CI/CD pipeline. Permission checks, policy-as-code rules, and compliance validations gate every deployment there, before an agent reaches production. Because these checks run separately from the agent, neither the agent nor its prompts are in a position to override them. Egress controls (recipient allowlisting, outbound secret scanning) help prevent an agent holding confidential data from disclosing it through an otherwise legitimate call.
Instrument, verify, and evaluate continuously
Observability in agentic systems goes beyond traditional application monitoring. The real question is no longer whether a service returned an HTTP 200 status, but whether an agent produced a faithful, policy-compliant output, and how this can be demonstrated through observable execution traces. Answering that requires a ground-truth dataset covering common queries and edge cases. This dataset is used for evaluation from day one, so quality is measured against representative and appropriately governed evaluation datasets for evaluation, not synthetic prompts.
This infrastructure cannot be retrofitted and must be part of the initial design. The continuous integration and continuous delivery (CI/CD) pipeline enforces this, so agents lacking instrumentation fail validation before evaluation runs.
We recommend instrumenting three dimensions:
- Intent tracing: Capture the observable agent trajectory (reasoning steps, tool invocations, and context retrievals) for each execution. OpenTelemetry spans create a queryable lineage from user request to final output.
- Verification and evaluation as CI: Any change to the agent (prompt edits, tool additions, model swaps) triggers the pipeline. Verification runs first with automated regression tests covering agent components and then their interactions. As most harness components are deterministic, these tests are fast and fully automatable. Evaluation runs second, scoring non-deterministic output against the ground-truth dataset, gated on quality thresholds. This sequencing is deliberate: Verification acts as a gate, so evaluations only run on a passing build.
- Model tiering and routing telemetry: When agents route between models, capture the routing decision and its justification, not just the outcome. Tier assignments are derived from evaluation results per task type and poor outcomes flow back as new evaluation cases.
Start focused, design for composition
For distributed cloud systems, the industry solved the complexity of end-to-end workflows by adopting architectural patterns such as microservices or service meshes. The evolution of agentic systems needs to follow a similar trajectory, moving from monolithic, generalist agents toward multiple collaborating specialized agents.
Teams should define the problem before considering agents’ functionality. Before writing any orchestration logic, they should produce five concrete artifacts:
- Clear scope definition: what the agent should and shouldn’t do.
- Interaction model: how users and other agents will invoke it.
- Unambiguous tool definitions: each tool and parameter precisely defined.
- Ground-truth dataset: the evaluation reference described above, established before any implementation begins.
- Evaluation criteria: quality thresholds and benchmarks the agent will be measured against.
This discipline prevents the most common failure modes we observe: agents that take on too many responsibilities accumulate bloated prompts, reducing accuracy and increasing latency.
Once a single agent is well-scoped, it must be designed as a composable building block. Therefore, we define a three-tier composition hierarchy:
- MCP tools are atomic integration contracts. Each tool wraps a single capability (for example, an API call or a database query) without encoding workflow assumptions. This is the stable, reusable layer.
- Skills are bundled, domain-specific compositions of MCP tools. A code review skill, for example, might chain a static analysis tool, a style-check tool, and an LLM-based reasoning step. Skills encode domain logic but remain portable across workflows.
- Flows are end-to-end orchestrations of skills, representing complete business processes (for example, an entire PR review pipeline or a requirements-to-deployment cycle).
Each tier is validated independently in the CI/CD pipeline. Component tests cover tools and skills, interaction tests cover their composition into flows.
These tiers are connected through open standards: MCP and Agent Skills for tool integration, the protocol for agent-to-agent communication, and OpenTelemetry for observability across the resulting interactions.
Figure 1 shows how the three tiers build on each other, from individual MCP tools at the base to complete flows at the top.
Specialize as you learn
In production, even well-scoped agents can break down as real-world usage diverges from what was anticipated at design time: query patterns shift, tool-selection logic struggles, and performance degrades unpredictably.
The right response is to decompose complex agents into multiple specialized ones, each with clearer instructions, simpler tool sets, and more focused reasoning. The benefits are concrete:
- Evolve independently: updating a requirements engineering agent does not require touching the coding agent.
- Scale individually: when scope and interfaces are well-defined, individual agents can be scaled independently without redeploying or resizing the broader system.
- Minimized scope: a failure or hallucination of one agent does not cascade across the entire workflow.
- Cost savings: A narrowly scoped agent can often run on a smaller model, which cuts inference and hosting costs.
Complexity can be reduced along two axes:
- Within an agent: decompose capabilities into skills since tools and few-shot examples consume context on every invocation while degrading accuracy and increasing cost. Determine granularity empirically: merge skills the agent rarely selects and split skills that produce different behavior depending on the input.
- Across agents: delegate work outside an agent’s domain to a specialized peer over the A2A protocol rather than extending the current agent. An agent should grow in capability, not in context.
Critically, since each specialized agent only accesses the data and tools required for its role, this architecture helps to enforce least-privilege by design, a compliance requirement in regulated industries.
Realizing these benefits, however, requires that agents can find and interoperate with each other. To prevent the emergence of AI islands, we maintain a centralized registry of agents, tools, and skills. This registry serves as:
- Discovery mechanism: cataloging available agents, tools, and skills based on metadata stored during build.
- Governance checkpoint: confirming approval of the asset types for production use and maintaining an audit trail.
- Security checkpoint: automated security checks are applied before approval, such as prompt injection and similar issues.
- Deduplication safeguard: identifying equivalent capabilities already maintained by other teams to avoid duplicate work. This check runs automatically at registration, flagging duplicates before approval.
Scale through codification
The shift from managing individual agents to governing an agent fleet requires agent architectures to be codified. Using Infrastructure-as-code frameworks such as Terraform or AWS CloudFormation, teams provision and manage agent infrastructure with the same rigor applied to any production system:
- Fine-grained least-privilege roles: scoped per agent or tool.
- CI/CD pipelines: consistent, validated deployments across accounts and regions, with automated deployment stops on failed tests or metric deterioration.
- Policy-as-code: rules (for example, AWS Config, Open Policy Agent) scanning deployed agents for compliance with organizational standards.
All three are enforced as pipeline gates, validated before registration, not audited after the fact.
The adoption model is deliberately bottom-up with central curation. Individual teams build skills and MCP tools to solve their immediate problems. All teams can contribute by sharing their assets through the registry. A central team builds automatic governance checks as part of the CI pipeline to uphold standards. To support development teams and foster shift-left, the central team additionally provides building blocks as governance-as-code modules.
This balance avoids both centrally mandated architectures and unmanaged experimentation. As a result, when new operational concerns arise, teams can extend existing patterns rather than redesign their architectures.
Operationalizing best practices across the agent lifecycle
Architectural patterns and governance standards are only effective if they are embedded into the workflows teams use to build and operate agents before and at runtime.
Before deployment
Governance begins before a single line of orchestration logic is written. Teams are provided with reference architecture patterns and examples drawn from the registry. These pre-validated blueprints cover common agent configurations, tool integration patterns, and composition structures, which accelerate development while encoding proven defaults. Before anything reaches production, standardized CI/CD controls enforce these practices. Figure 2 shows the four phases of a reference pipeline, which run in order from left to right.
Phase 1 from Figure 2 runs fast, deterministic checks: supply chain security (approved registries only), component and interaction testing, evaluation library references, and observability instrumentation.
Phase 2 runs security and governance checks in parallel. Static analysis scans the code for issues, and security tests probe the agent in an isolated staging environment. The pipeline also validates egress controls and least-privilege permissions. Two more checks confirm that the agent’s declared autonomy level matches its actual permissions and that its configuration passes the policy-as-code rules. A governance agent accelerates audits by checking the agent against established standards and flagging findings for human review, such as:
- Scope creep: operating beyond originally defined purpose or permissions.
- Prompt bloat: unnecessary complexity in instructions.
- Tool misuse: calling tools outside their intended use case.
- Performance degradation: declining accuracy, latency, or cost-efficiency.
Figure 3: Example governance agent workflow
This assessment surfaces concrete, actionable measures that teams can apply immediately, rather than abstract recommendations. Figure 3 shows the governance agent’s dashboard for an agent maturity assessment. The governance agent provides evidence and actionable recommendations, while accountable humans own governance decisions. Recommendations require human confirmation before being applied, maintaining a four-eyes principle for accountability. Findings update the agent’s governance status in the registry, while full details are logged separately in a central knowledge base for audit and traceability.
Phase 3 evaluates the agent as a running system: the ground-truth evaluation gate (scores outputs against benchmarks established at design time) and agent performance (latency, token consumption). Figure 4 details the metrics, scoring criteria and the relationships between them.
Phase 4 checks for duplicates before registering the agent, its sub-agents, tools, and skills. The following table shows the metadata fields stored per agent in the registry.
| Agent metadata | 
| Core data: | 
| Service level agreement data: | 
| Data governance flags: | 
Table 1: Example agent metadata stored in the registry
If any step fails or metrics deteriorate, the deployment stops with logs for root cause analysis. If all checks pass, the agent is packaged and deployed as a containerized workload, producing consistent, reproducible deployments. This prevents ungoverned agents from reaching production, automates compliance checks, and keeps the registry accurate.
At runtime
At runtime, observability has to catch two kinds of drift. Data drift shows up as new or shifting user query patterns, or changes in upstream APIs. Model drift shows as rising error rates or falling tool-selection accuracy. When a customer flags a response, that also triggers an investigation. Alerts for drift, distribution shifts, declining evaluation scores, or direct customer flags prompt a staged response. These events are logged and forwarded to human review. Additionally, teams can run the governance agent continuously to flag drift and operational issues for the responsible team to investigate.
Summary
Building and operating agents at scale is an engineering discipline, not an experimentation exercise.
Effective governance must be structural from the start, externalized, domain-sensitive, and deterministically enforced. We introduced a three-tier composition hierarchy (MCP tools, skills, and flows) as the architectural foundation for reusable, composable, and interoperable agents, decomposed into specialized agents to contain complexity and scope. We showed how verification and evaluation in every CI/CD run make quality assurance part of everyday development, and how defining agent infrastructure as code lets teams apply the same governance rules to every agent in the fleet. Finally, we operationalized these patterns across the agent lifecycle, from pre-validated reference architectures and structured pipelines to a runtime governance agent that continuously evaluates deployed agents.
Our experience has shown these practices pay off in a few ways. Reusable templates and shared infrastructure reduced development costs. Teams also got agents to production faster, thanks to standard interaction models and automated deployment. Quality improved too, because the pipeline enforces proven patterns at every stage of the lifecycle.
Scaling agentic governance is an industry-wide imperative. The shift toward AI and generative-AI-supported workflow automation is already reshaping how engineering organizations operate. The winners will be those who move beyond experimentation and establish the discipline to govern autonomous agent networks at scale. With these practices in place, BMW engineers can focus on solving the problems that matter: Building the ultimate driving machine.
To apply these ideas to your own agents, start with the AWS Well-Architected Framework. This post used it as the model for reusable agent blueprints. To see how BMW codifies governance across its AWS environment, read How BMW Group uses automation to achieve end-to-end compliance at scale on AWS.
Outlook and next steps
The patterns and practices described in this post are a foundation, not a finish line. We are actively extending them across several fronts:
- Improve architectural guidance: publishing best practice guides on architectural trade-offs, composition patterns, and anti-patterns for teams building agents.
- Expand infrastructure-as-code templates: providing agent blueprints as usable IaC modules with built-in security and governance standards by default.
- Deepen governance compliance testing: adding CI/CD test cases verifying governance compliance.
- Automate standards enforcement: expanding automated checks and managed compliance-scanning rules across pre-deployment and runtime stages.
- Extend agentic FinOps: Govern the right-sizing of models and tool calls.
- Agentic user guidance: integrating described patterns into Archimedes, BMW’s architectural guidance agent, to provide contextual architectural recommendations.
Acknowledgements
The authors would like to thank (in alphabetical order) Alexander Stark, Alexander Zimmer, Dr. Céline Laurent-Winter, Dominik Segl, Florian Seidel, Hugo Lerias, Dr. Lars Lewerenz, Mark Neumann, Ralf Bottesch, Ramona Weber, Satish Vasireddy, Samuel Voss, Xagarey-Louis Meyer.

articles.title: Intel says its graphics-free D270 GPU beats Nvidia's RTX Pro 6000 by up to 5.9x in benchmarks
articles.text:
In context: Intel first teased Crescent Island over a year ago as a data center GPU that can't even render graphics. It has none of the 3D or ray-tracing hardware you'd find on a regular graphics card; instead, the chip – now sold as the GPU D270 – spends that space on AI and scientific work. Until this week, though, Intel hadn't really shown how fast it is. That changed at the SC26 supercomputing show in Chicago.
In a post, Intel put the D270 up against Nvidia's RTX Pro 6000 Blackwell Server Edition. Instead of games or AI models, Intel went with something a little more niche. It picked four workloads that banks rely on to put a price on financial contracts.
Across those four, the D270 delivered between 1.92 and 5.9 times the performance of Nvidia's card. Its biggest win showed up in a European Monte Carlo simulation. Intel's card also did all of this at just 350W, compared to the 600W that Nvidia's card is rated for.
All four tests rely on double-precision, or FP64, calculations. Intel's Xe3P architecture handles those calculations at full speed, so the D270 barely slows down when a task needs that extra accuracy. That full-speed FP64 support is where most of the D270's lead over Nvidia's card comes from.
The RTX Pro 6000, on the other hand, uses the same chip as the GeForce RTX 5090. That silicon only handles FP64 at a tiny fraction of its usual speed, so by sticking to FP64-heavy workloads, Intel chose the kind of tests where Nvidia's card was likely to fall behind.
Of course, these are Intel's own numbers from pre-production chips. On top of that, the two cards didn't even run in matching systems, since Intel put the D270 in a single-socket server but gave Nvidia's card a bigger dual-socket machine.
Intel only claims modest gains in its AI tests, though, such as a 12% throughput edge on one language model. That's a little surprising, since AI is what the D270 was designed for in the first place.
Picking FP64 workloads also lets Intel poke at a sore spot for its rival. Nvidia's newest Blackwell Ultra chips offer only about a teraflop of double-precision compute, as HPCwire pointed out last December. So Nvidia has been nudging scientists toward software that emulates FP64 on its Tensor Cores, though it has promised more FP64 muscle in future chips.
As for the D270, customers are already testing it ahead of a 2027 launch, but Intel still hasn't said a word about how much it will cost.

articles.title: TSMC Reportedly Reviews Customer Finances, Asks Some Chip Buyers to Pay Upfront
articles.text:
Thursday, November 19th 2026
TSMC Reportedly Reviews Customer Finances, Asks Some Chip Buyers to Pay Upfront
TSMC is reportedly seeking to audit its customers' ability to finance chip allocations, as the company aims to secure funding for its production runs. The report states that TSMC is going as far as obtaining data on customers' financial situations, data center construction stages, and other factors that influence demand assessments. These assessments are then used to propose credit lines based on each company's balance sheet. This evaluation includes collecting information on past debt defaults, the company's position in the industry, and its liquidity. For any orders that exceed the TSMC-imposed credit limit, TSMC requires cash payments for its production runs, with some customers even needing to make upfront payments to secure production capacity. Those who cannot secure a good credit line may pre-pay their production runs to ensure allocation.
With NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang now out of the loop, TSMC is conducting checks with customers to ensure that, in the event of a broader industry shakeup, its production remains well-funded. The reported AI circular financing scheme that the entire industry has been engaging in is net positive for valuations, but TSMC wants to ensure it gets paid first, regardless of the situation. Many chipmakers and startups have been raising capital to access more cash to fund operations, and a significant portion of that will go to TSMC for its production lines. It is important to note that TSMC isn't changing the way it allocates supply. The company is simply protecting the way that allocation is settled, and the old rule of "first come, first served" remains in practice for securing allocation on any node, including leading-edge and upcoming ones.For example, TSMC has been making demand projection estimates based on data center buildouts, so it knows how many wafers its facilities need to produce. For instance, NVIDIA's supply chain commitments include $390 billion in spending through Fiscal Year 2030, and a large portion of that will go to TSMC. This way, TSMC knows that its biggest customer will pay for orders in the years to come, but it also needs reassurance from smaller customers.

articles.title: Un mystérieux boîtier repéré sur le bureau d’un DJ dévoile le premier appareil IA de Nothing
articles.text:
Un petit boîtier sans écran apparaît sur une photo publiée par le DJ Sebastian Ingrosso. Plusieurs détails rappellent les images déjà diffusées par Nothing, qui prévoit un lancement en décembre.
Pour apercevoir le premier appareil de Nothing conçu autour de l’IA, il fallait regarder entre un MacBook et un casque, sur le bureau d’un DJ de Swedish House Mafia, un groupe de musique électronique. Le Suédois Sebastian Ingrosso a en effet publié la photo sur X le 19 novembre en mentionnant simplement la marque. À côté du casque Nothing Headphone (1), l’objet paraît assez petit pour tenir dans la paume. Le média Android Authority dit avoir confirmé auprès de ses sources qu’il s’agit bien du futur produit de Nothing.
Le point rouge est familier, la touche Talk intrigue
La photo laisse distinguer une touche marquée d’un point rouge, comme sur un enregistreur, et une autre qui porte l’inscription Talk. Les deux voyants oblongs, l’un rouge et l’autre vert, figuraient déjà dans le court aperçu diffusé le 10 novembre par Carl Pei, le patron de Nothing. Une petite ouverture à une extrémité pourrait servir au microphone. Android Authority envisage que le cliché montre deux exemplaires superposés, ce qui laisse un doute sur la disposition exacte des commandes.
Pei avait annoncé le 4 novembre l’arrivée, en décembre, d’un appareil pensé pour l’IA et dépourvu d’écran. La photo en dit davantage sur sa forme. Son nom, son prix, sa fiche technique et les pays où il sera vendu restent inconnus.
Nothing a déjà un bouton pour prendre des notes à la voix
Le boîtier des écouteurs Ear (3) possède lui aussi une touche Talk. Associée à un téléphone équipé de son appli maison Essential Space, elle permet d’y envoyer une note vocale. Sur le Nothing Phone (3a), un appui long sur l’Essential Key sert à enregistrer une idée ou un rappel. Essential Space se charge ensuite de classer les captures et peut en tirer des résumés ou des actions à suivre.
« Le contexte ne vit pas dans une fenêtre de chat », écrit Carl Pei en légende de sa vidéo sur X. La formule cadre avec l’idée d’un appareil auquel on pourrait dicter une note au fil de la journée.
Un boîtier de plus à glisser dans sa poche
Si Nothing prépare bien un dictaphone, le NotePin S de Plaud donne une idée de ce qui existe déjà. Cet enregistreur IA sans écran, vendu 179€ hors promotion, se pilote avec un bouton et s’appuie sur une application pour transcrire et résumer avec précision les échanges vocaux. Comme le Soundcore Work, il inclut 300 minutes de transcription par mois. Pour aller au-delà, il faut toutefois payer un abonnement mensuel ou créditer son compte, c'est d'ailleurs le business modèle de ces marques.
- Des retranscriptions très fidèles
- Une captation irréprochable
- Son design et l'accroche magnétique
Un appareil dédié à l’IA doit aussi donner une raison de le garder sur soi. Humane a coupé les services en ligne de son AI Pin en février 2025, moins d’un an après sa sortie. Le Rabbit r1, dévoilé en janvier 2024, a déçu lors des premiers essais, où plusieurs fonctions promises manquaient à l’appel. Carl Pei assure pour sa part que son produit n’aurait pas pu prendre la forme d’une simple application à installer sur un smartphone.
Si Nothing prépare bien un enregistreur IA, s’adressera-t-il surtout aux utilisateurs de ses smartphones ou cherchera-t-il, comme Plaud, à toucher un public plus large ?
- Puissance sonore
- Assez bonne isolation des basses
- Boitier luxueux et très pratique (Super Mic)
- Bonne qualité sonore, beaucoup de polyvalence
- Excellente autonomie
- Bonne isolation passive
- Un Phone (2a) en mieux, et toujours aussi peu cher
- Une autonomie impressionnante
- Un bon téléobjectif

articles.title: "Be ready for change": AAIF’s CTO on why the agent stack won’t settle
articles.text:
“Be ready for change”: AAIF’s CTO on why the agent stack won’t settle
If you’ve spent any time over the past year trying to get AI agents to talk to each other without tearing your architecture apart, you know the struggle: vendor lock-in, fragmented protocols, and context that definitely vanishes the second you attempt to make a cross-framework handoff.
It’s astounding how fast developers’ needs have changed just in 10 months since the Agentic AI Foundation (AAIF) was formed to help solve those problems.
The Linux Foundation-backed AAIF gives shared agent infrastructure a home outside any one vendor’s control. It launched in December 2025 with three projects, including the Model Context Protocol (MCP), which connects AI applications to external tools and data.
On October 22, Anthropic contributed Agent Skills, and OpenAI contributed Open Responses to the foundation, alongside projects from Hugging Face and Alibaba. The additions brought AAIF to 10 hosted projects.
The New Stack Editor-in-Chief Nick Lucchesi sat down with Manik Surtani, AAIF’s co-founder and CTO, for The New Stack podcast at AGNTCon + MCPCon in San Jose, shortly after Surtani announced the additions in his October 22 keynote. The news was still fresh — the problems behind it, though, were all too familiar.
“I think that’s always been there,” Surtani said of the needs these projects address. “We’ve always known that sandboxes are really important.” Agent Skills, too, was already in use before joining the foundation. What had changed was where these projects would be governed.
“…having a standardized way to speak to a model is super important.”
“I’m really happy [Agent Skills] is here. And Open Responses as well. I mean, having a standardized way to speak to a model is super important. And I’m glad to see that it’s now happening in a way that is vendor-neutral, in a neutral governance and everything else.”
Four giant projects join the foundation
The big news from Surtani was this: Four heavy-hitting projects had joined the AAIF. Here’s what each brings to the table:
- Agent Skills (Anthropic): An open format for bundling instructions, scripts, and reference materials that an agent can load when it needs to perform a particular task. Write those instructions once, and use them across agents that support the format.
- Open Responses (OpenAI): An open specification, based on OpenAI’s Responses API, for how applications send requests to language models and receive results. A shared format means less translation work when developers switch between compatible model providers.
- OpenEnv (Hugging Face): A framework for building and sharing reinforcement learning environments, where agents practice tasks and receive feedback that can be used to train them.
- OpenSandbox (Alibaba): A platform for running agent-generated code and other work in isolated environments, separating that execution from the surrounding system.
While Anthropic, OpenAI, Hugging Face, and Alibaba rallying around a neutral foundation sounds like an AI miracle, Surtani noted that developer demand for open governance has existed from Day 1.
“More than faster, I think people are going to be able to build on top of things that they can trust more.”
“More than faster, I think people are going to be able to build on top of things that they can trust more,” Surtani said. “It’s not like you couldn’t trust open responses before. Of course you could. But now everyone has a say in how it’s going to grow and how it’s going to get shaped.”
Developers learned this lesson the hard way during the early cloud-native boom. Nobody wants to build core enterprise infrastructure on tech they can’t help steer.
Tackling the real pain points: Agent memory and portability
What problem keeps Surtani up at night? In the near term, it’s agent memory and context management — the information an agent needs to keep working on a task, including what’s already happened. A harness is the software around a model that manages its tools and workflow. Carrying that context from one model or harness to another remains difficult, Surtani said; he wants teams to be able to share it across the agents and people working on the same problem.
Beyond context portability, Surtani emphasized that software engineering teams should design for model independence right now using abstractions, proxies, and standardized interfaces. In practical terms, that means keeping the application from being tied too tightly to one model provider: A proxy or router sits between the application and the model, letting a team switch the model behind the scenes. It doesn’t solve everything, he cautioned, but it handles much of the heavy lifting.
Unlike the cloud stack associated with the Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF) — which Surtani described as already well-defined — the agentic AI stack is inherently fluid.
“My advice to people is just be ready for change. Change is going to happen.”
“My advice to people is just be ready for change. Change is going to happen,” Surtani told The New Stack. “Now, the good thing in all of this is that change is actually easy as well. With agents actually building themselves and writing code, it’s not going to be that expensive or that hard to migrate from one thing to the other.”
A sandbox for early-stage projects
With more than 300 member organizations signing on in just 10 months (ranging from fintechs to non-tech giants such as the Gates Foundation), AAIF realized its initial high barrier to entry — borrowed from the mature CNCF template — was ill-suited for a space evolving at warp speed.
To adapt, the foundation launched a new Sandbox lifecycle phase on September 1 to bring in early-stage, high-momentum community tools before they hit massive enterprise scale.
This Sandbox phase is a project maturity category, separate from the isolated execution environments provided by OpenSandbox. It gives promising young projects a place to develop under neutral governance, even before they have widespread production use.
Surtani’s main call-to-action for developers? Push your vendors for open standards, transparent specs, and true longevity.
Watch the full interview
Watch our full interview with Surtani to get his take on agentic commerce, agent permissions, advertising without human eyes, and why an AI stack might never fully solidify. Subscribe to The New Stack‘s YouTube channel to keep up with our new episodes as they are released.

articles.title: Meet the innovators exhibiting at Bengaluru Tech Summit 2026
articles.text:
Meet the innovators exhibiting at Bengaluru Tech Summit 2026
In our photo essay from BTS at the Bangalore International Exhibition Centre, we showcase highlights from the exhibition halls.
Launched in 2014, PhotoSparks is a weekly feature from YourStory, with photographs that celebrate the spirit of creativity and innovation. In the earlier 1,030 posts, we featured an art festival, cartoon gallery. world music festival, telecom expo, millets fair, climate change expo, wildlife conference, startup festival, Diwali rangoli, and jazz festival.
With the theme AI & Beyond, Bengaluru Tech Summit (BTS) celebrated its 29th annual edition this week, at the Bangalore International Exhibition Centre (BIEC). In conference tracks, exhibitions and workshops, it brought together startups, tech firms, business incubators, R&D labs, and government agencies.
In this photo essay, we feature startups such as Nife, Gnani, Data Caffe, Valamm.AI, Faveo, Trip Gain, and others. We also feature incubators and accelerators such as C-CAMP, Art Park, Foundation for Quantum Computing, Manipal BioIncubator, and Ramaiah Technology Business Incubator.
The pavilions also included other states of India such as Bihar, and overseas exhibitors from countries like South Korea. See our BTS showcases from earlier editions as well in 2025 and 2024, and YourStory’s TechSparks exhibitors from 2026 and 2025.
Nife is a deeptech company specialising in cloud infrastructure management, multi-cloud orchestration and edge computing. Its offerings include application deployment, infrastructure automation, cloud cost management (FinOps), and AI-driven site reliability engineering.
Gnani AI offers conversational AI, voice technologies and intelligent enterprise agents. Its solutions enable businesses to automate customer interactions across voice calls, messaging platforms and other communication channels, with support for multiple Indian languages and regional accents.
DataCaffe is a Bengaluru-based AI product engineering company that integrates AI into enterprise workflows, helping organisations improve productivity, automate processes and make better use of their data. At BTS 2026, the company showcased its CommandIQ control-plane solution designed to provide governance and oversight of AI agents, applications and models.
Valamm.AI is a strategic market-entry and business acceleration platform that helps global AI, SaaS and technology companies expand their presence in India. It offers an Incubate–Accelerate–Transfer model that supports market validation, customer acquisition, business development, and eventual expansion.
Faveo Helpdesk is a customer support and service management software product with a ticket-based support system that captures, tracks, assigns, and resolves customer queries. Its product suite includes Faveo Helpdesk Community and Enterprise editions, as well as Faveo Service Desk Enterprise.
TripGain offers an integrated platform for corporate travel and expense management. It helps businesses manage employee travel bookings, hotel reservations, expense claims, approvals, and travel-policy compliance through a unified digital platform.
C-CAMP (Centre for Cellular and Molecular Platforms) is a leading life-sciences innovation and biotechnology incubator based in Bengaluru. Established with support from the Department of Biotechnology, Government of India, it facilitates the translation of scientific research into commercially viable products and technologies, particularly in healthcare, agriculture and environmental sustainability.
ART PARK (AI & Robotics Technology Park) is an innovation and entrepreneurship initiative hosted at the Indian Institute of Science (IISc), Bengaluru. It supports the development and commercialisation of solutions in areas such as healthcare, agriculture, mobility, smart manufacturing, logistics, and infrastructure.
The Foundation for Quantum Computing Innovation at IISc has been formed under the Government of India's National Quantum Mission, and supported by the Department of Science and Technology. It aims to develop quantum computing infrastructure, provide cloud-based access to quantum resources, and encourage collaboration between academia, industry and startups.
Manipal–Government of Karnataka BioIncubator is a technology business incubation initiative of Manipal Academy of Higher Education (MAHE), in collaboration with the Government of Karnataka. It provides researchers, students, faculty members, and entrepreneurs with access to specialised bio-incubation infrastructure, technical expertise, mentorship, and industry connections.
Ramaiah Technology Business Incubator (Ramaiah-TBI) is hosted at Ramaiah University of Applied Sciences (RUAS). Its incubation support includes product development and prototyping assistance, business mentoring, intellectual property guidance, and business connects.
With pavilions across five large exhibition halls of BIEC, innovators at BTS gained a broader perspective of how technologies like AI are being developed and are transforming the world around us. For cross-border innovation, numerous opportunities were explored for market entry and expansion.
Karnataka is home to 1,088 Global Capability Centres (GCCs), accounting for over half of India's total. Such developments and trend were highlighted in the report, GCCs in Karnataka: Shaping the Future of Enterprise AI, released at BTS by Zinnov and the Karnataka Digital Economy Mission (KDEM).
As part of the Government First Initiative, the state government selected eight startups for deployment of their technology within government departments to address public sector challenges. This initiative, launched by the Department of Electronics, Information Technology and Biotechnology (IT & BT), aims to make government departments potential customers for startups.
Bengaluru accounts for 36.3% of India's native AI startup funding. It is also home to 71% of India's AI and deep tech unicorns created since 2023, as described in a number of reports released at BTS.
The Bengaluru Innovation Report 2026, prepared by KDEM and 3one4 Capital and data from Tracxn, profiles the growth and scope of Bengaluru's startup ecosystem. It spans capital, talent, unicorns, policy, and six frontier technology sectors.
Bengaluru reportedly ranks eighth among the world's startup ecosystems and second in Asia for AI-native startups. Through its ELEVATE initiative, the state has supported nearly 1,500 startups with equity-free grants worth $41 million over the past decade.
At BTS, 24 venture capital firms announced investments worth approximately ₹1,050 crore in deeptech startups at the Future Makers Conclave. The startups are in aerospace, AI, robotics, semiconductors, biotechnology and others.
The exhibition also featured Innoverse, a deeptech accelerator that will support 35 growth-stage ventures over the next five years. It helps startups move beyond product development and scale up to industrial-level operations.
Now what have you done today to pause in your busy schedule and harness your creative side for a better world?

articles.title: El plan de Microsoft ya suma 50 millones de agentes IA para empresas
articles.text:
Microsoft presentó durante Ignite 2026 una nueva generación de herramientas de inteligencia artificial y anunció que su plataforma Agent 365 ya reúne a más de 50 millones de agentes autónomos para organizaciones.
La compañía planteó una estrategia denominada Frontier, presentada por su presidente y CEO, Satya Nadella, que busca combinar ambición humana, control sobre la inteligencia organizacional y confianza. El objetivo declarado fue que las empresas incorporen estas capacidades a sus operaciones y las traduzcan en resultados de negocio.
La expansión de los agentes autónomos llevó a Microsoft a reforzar los mecanismos de identidad, seguridad y gobernanza para administrarlos. También anunció Agent 365 Business Analytics, una función para identificar qué factores impulsan el gasto en inteligencia artificial, vincular las inversiones con resultados empresariales y optimizar el retorno.
“A medida que las organizaciones amplían el uso de agentes autónomos, Microsoft fortalece las herramientas para administrarlos y mantener el control sobre su identidad, seguridad y gobernanza. La compañía destacó que ya cuenta con más de 50 millones de agentes en Agent 365 y anunció Agent 365 Business Analytics, una nueva capacidad que permite identificar los factores que impulsan el gasto en inteligencia artificial, relacionar las inversiones con los resultados empresariales y optimizar su retorno en diferentes escenarios”, indicó Microsoft en el evento.
Copilot como sistema operativo del trabajo
Copilot reunirá Chat, Cowork, Code y Autopilot en una experiencia integrada para responder consultas, desarrollar aplicaciones personalizadas y delegar tareas complejas a agentes que pueden avanzar de forma continua.
La plataforma se apoyará en Work IQ, una herramienta que incorpora información sobre documentos, reuniones, comunicaciones, relaciones y proyectos de cada organización. Microsoft también anunció conectores para aplicaciones empresariales y una colaboración con Salesforce para integrar sus capacidades en Copilot.
Microsoft IQ concentrará datos y conocimientos de Fabric, Foundry, Microsoft 365 y aplicaciones de terceros. La plataforma sumará cientos de conectores para que los agentes accedan a un contexto empresarial más amplio y ejecuten tareas con mayor precisión.
Modelos especializados y seguridad agéntica
Microsoft incorporará GPT-6.2 a Microsoft Foundry y prevé sumar los modelos más recientes de Meta. La compañía presentó además Microsoft-Decision-1.1, un modelo multimodal para acelerar y mejorar decisiones empresariales que ya utilizaron más de 4.000 clientes.
Las herramientas Code 2 y Code 2 Flash se orientarán a programación y desarrollo de software, mientras que Cyber 2 Flash buscará elevar el rendimiento de las tareas de seguridad a una menor fracción del costo por operación. En paralelo, Perception quedó disponible de forma general como un sistema que simula ataques, detecta amenazas y ejecuta acciones de remediación mediante equipos de agentes especializados, con supervisión humana.
Microsoft anunció Maia 300, un desarrollo de infraestructura que ofrecerá 40 % más de tokens por vatio frente a sistemas líderes basados en GPU, y confirmó la disponibilidad general de las máquinas virtuales Cobalt 200 de próxima generación.
La Iniciativa de Transparencia en IA incorporará una colaboración más amplia con el NIST y la participación de 40 organizaciones para definir y aplicar estándares abiertos de sistemas seguros, responsables y verificables de manera independiente.

articles.title: Run your whole selling business in AWS Quick | Amazon Web Services
articles.text:
Artificial Intelligence
Run your whole selling business in AWS Quick
Most sellers do not need another AI product to learn. They need the tools and information they already use brought together, so they can see what is happening in their business and act on it.
AWS Quick and the Amazon Selling Partner plugin do that together. Quick brings an Amazon seller’s sales data, inventory signals, and marketplace intelligence into one place, where questions become answers and answers become actions. It understands the seller’s full business context, so the seller does not need to re-explain their catalog, their margins, or their competitive landscape in every conversation. It is built on AWS, the same infrastructure Amazon uses to run its own marketplace.
At Amazon Accelerate on September 23, 2026, Amazon announced the Selling Partner plugin and launched it in beta in AWS Quick. This post covers what launched, how to claim the free AWS Quick offer, and what the experience looks like day to day. It also covers how the skills and connectors work when a seller puts them to use.
Limited-time offer: 12 months of AWS Quick Plus, free. Every primary selling account holder worldwide can claim a free 12-month subscription, plus access for 10 additional users you delegate. Sign up by December 31, 2026. Claim your free AWS Quick Plus offer.
1. Why Quick is right for Amazon sellers
Four things make Quick a fit for how Amazon sellers already work: it learns the business, it reaches beyond the Amazon store, it turns data into decisions, and it protects seller data on infrastructure sellers already trust.
Quick knows your business, not only your prompts
Quick and the Selling Partner plugin connect to a seller’s inventory feeds, sales data, and operational documents. From these, Quick builds a living understanding of the catalog structure, margin thresholds, seasonality, and competitive position. Ask Quick to audit your ASINs for Q4, and it returns a ranked recommendation built on the seller’s real margin data, historical conversion, and inventory availability. Its recommendations get sharper the more the seller works with it.
Quick does not stop at your Amazon store
A seller’s business runs across many tools: a storefront on another channel, an email inbox, an accounting system, spreadsheets, a supplier portal. Quick connects to where the seller already works and pulls context from across the whole operation. It is a business assistant that happens to know Amazon deeply, so the seller grows overall, not on one channel alone.
It turns data into decisions you can act on
Sellers are not short on data. They have Brand Analytics, Search Query Performance, advertising reports, inventory health, and listing quality data. The problem is turning those signals into one clear action. Quick does the synthesis. It watches for change, flags what matters, builds the analysis, and presents the decision with the evidence behind it.
Your data stays protected on the infrastructure you already sell on
Quick runs on AWS and does not use seller data to train models, not for general improvement and not for anything else. Seller data stays in the seller’s environment and never informs anyone else’s models. For a seller already operating on the Amazon marketplace, there is no new security posture to evaluate. The infrastructure is the same one protecting the seller account today, and the seller’s chosen AWS Region governs where data stays.
The Amazon Selling Partner plugin
The Selling Partner plugin connects AWS Quick directly to live Seller Central data. After one sign-in with a Seller Central account, the plugin gives conversational access to product listings, inventory, and sales data, pulled live rather than exported and reassembled by hand. It installs like an app, with no coding required. It ships with curated Amazon skills, and it pairs with Amazon Ads MCP so campaign performance and spend sit next to the selling data. The plugin is in beta for US stores.
Figure 1: The Selling Partner plugin consent screen, where the seller grants None, View, or Edit access per data category
The permission screen is worth a pause. The seller grants access per data category, choosing None, View, or Edit for each, and reviews an agreement before authorizing. Nothing is all-or-nothing, and access can be narrowed or revoked later.
2. How to redeem the Quick Plus offer
- Claim your free AWS Quick Plus subscription (12 months free plus 10 delegated users, by December 31, 2026).
- Connect the Selling Partner plugin with one sign-in to your Seller Central account. It installs like an app.
- Ask your first question, something you would normally build a spreadsheet for.
Figure 2: Connecting the Selling Partner plugin from the AWS Quick sign-up flow
3. What the experience looks like
After the plugin is connected, the work happens in a conversation. You ask in plain language, Quick pulls the relevant live data, and it comes back with an answer and a recommended next step. Instead of checking a dashboard, exporting a report, and reconciling it in a spreadsheet, you move from a question to an answer to an action in one place. You review what Quick proposes before anything is sent.
Figure 3: Quick diagnosing whether a sales dip comes from traffic or conversion, using live selling data
4. Two use cases a seller can build
At the Accelerate workshop we had sellers build real agents live, from a plain-language description, in a few minutes. Quick turns the description into a working agent, which the seller then refines in conversation.
Use case A: Inventory Launch Prep
The seller is staging a new product into Amazon and wants the lowest total landed cost. The agent reads supplier data and weighs the fulfillment options per SKU on inbound cost, storage, and speed to sellable. It walks through placement choices and returns the output the seller picks: a shipping plan, a cost comparison, or a combined packet. It explains its reasoning and confirms before it creates anything.
Figure 4: The Inventory Launch Prep agent comparing FBA and AWD fulfillment per factor and recommending a hybrid approach
Use case B: Post-Launch Product Health
After the launch, the agent reads four signal families through the Selling Partner plugin: listing health, inventory, sales, and traffic. It connects them to find the cause rather than just reporting numbers. Flat sales with healthy traffic points to a conversion problem. Flat sales with falling traffic points to discoverability. Good conversion with falling units points to supply. It returns a health summary per ASIN, the diagnosis with evidence, and a ranked fix list, labeling any low-confidence call.
Figure 5: The Post-Launch Product Health agent’s weekly summary, with week-over-week sales evidence
One honest limit, handled honestly: the selling data does not include cost of goods, so the agent reports margin after Amazon fees and labels it that way. When the seller wants true gross margin, the agent asks them to bring their cost numbers into the conversation. It never presents after-fees margin as if it were gross margin.
5. Skills and connectors in action
The Selling Partner plugin and Amazon Ads MCP bring the Amazon selling and advertising data into Quick. Other connectors in AWS Quick bring in the rest of how the business runs, organized by role. These include a second storefront (orders and products from another channel), email and calendar (draft a supplier note, track what is due), team messaging (share an update), and accounting and inventory systems (cost and stock context the selling data does not carry). Because the pieces sit together, the seller can ask one question that reaches across Amazon data and the tools around it.
6. A seller’s morning, start to finish
At Accelerate, Richard Brown, who runs the sneaker care brand Proof Culture and sells across five stores including Amazon, showed what this looks like. He had built his own AI assistant over time, and the hard part was never the AI. It was getting his selling data connected in real time.
        “The hard part was never the AI. The hard part was getting my selling data into it, and that is the part that is now simple with the plugin. With Quick and the Selling Partner plugin, just connect your account and start asking questions.”
— Richard Brown, Proof Culture, at Amazon Accelerate 2026
In his demo, Richard asked Quick about upcoming sneaker drops and checked whether he had enough FBA stock to cover a major release. He had Quick model how far his current inventory would carry him. Then he asked it to draft a reorder purchase order and a message to his team. A morning of research across different tools took a few minutes.
7. Getting started
- Claim your free year of AWS Quick Plus (by December 31, 2026).
- Connect the Selling Partner plugin.
- Follow the setup instructions to connect the Ads MCP within AWS Quick so you can manage campaigns conversationally alongside your selling data.
- Connect the rest of your business by role: your other storefront, email and calendar, accounting and inventory systems, team messaging.
- Start with one real question you would normally handle in a spreadsheet.
Next steps:
Claim your free year of AWS Quick Plus
Read the AWS Quick documentation
Media captured from the Amazon Accelerate 2026 workshop ‘Build It Live: Automate New Product Launch in AWS Quick.’ Non-Amazon tools referred to by role, not brand.

articles.title: Memory pooling helps Liqid fix AI inference tokenomics - SiliconANGLE
articles.text:
AI’s next build-out: Inference racks that resize themselves for every new model
Memory pooling is fast becoming one of the sharpest tools in AI inference economics, with companies racing to wring more output from every graphics processing unit.
Most AI servers still ship with a fixed GPU-to-memory ratio that holds for the life of the machine. But that is a poor fit when nobody knows what model they will deploy six months from now, according to Sumit Puri (pictured), co-founder and chief technical officer of Liqid Inc.
“Our core fundamental technology is around pooling and sharing the most critical resources in the data center, which are now GPU and memory,” Puri said. “Rather than statically deploying these things inside of a server, our vision is simple. Let’s put pools of resources in the rack, GPUs and memory, and dynamically assign them to any server that needs it based upon the model or the workload that we are looking to deploy.”
Puri spoke with theCUBE Research’s John Furrier and Gemma Allen at SC26, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed pooling GPUs and memory, the tokenomics of AI inference and Liqid as a Service. (* Disclosure below.)
Memory pooling meets the tokenomics test
Liqid measures payoff in tokenomics, with the yardsticks being tokens per second, tokens per watt and, above all, tokens per dollar. Supply is another pressure point in the AI infrastructure build-out, with memory among its most constrained components. But delivering only the memory each application needs stretches scarce supply further, Puri explained.
“Supply chain is a massive constraint for all of us — memory being a giantly massive constrained thing,” he said. “If we can do things like pool memory, share memory, optimally deliver memory to the server in the right amount of memory as required by the application, we can directly address some of those supply chain issues.”
Liqid is also widening how customers buy memory pooling. At SC26, the company announced Liqid as a Service, a fully managed, single-tenant offering, and it is moving toward preconfigured appliances. The bet is that most enterprises will deploy models rather than build them and therefore require their own capacity, according to Puri.
“The world went to unlimited consumption of minutes, and that’s where we believe tokens are headed,” Puri said. “Everybody’s going to own their own token machine so they can consume these tokens at will.”

articles.title: "You’re right"—LLMs will get climate info wrong if you ask
articles.text:
Many studies over the years have examined how people encounter climate science information. Some focused on the top results that Google surfaced (back when Google was still in the business of serving links), while others examined social media content or newspaper and TV news coverage. With large language models (LLMs) now forming a share of the public information diet, it’s worth looking at how they handle climate change.
But there’s no direct way for researchers to look at the information people have seen. It is served ephemerally to individual users, confined to their chat session. A study led by researchers from University College London and the United Nations Educational, Scientific, and Cultural Organization (UNESCO) tried to tackle this question from multiple angles, testing LLMs with different prompts and evaluating their output. They started with benchmarks of simple factual questions (benchmarks that might even be in models’ training data at this point) but also analyzed more complex interactions—including when users think they’re right to push back on an answer.
CO2 Q&A
LLM research often faces (no-true-Scotsman-tinged) criticism for focusing on a particular model rather than some other frontier model that may have been released after the experiment concluded. In this case, the study used 33 models, including multiple versions of the major frontier and open-weight models. The flagship frontier models used were Claude Fable 5, Claude Opus 5, Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview, Gemini 3.6 Flash, and GPT-5.6 Sol. (You can find the full list in the report.)
All the models were scored for correct answers to 600 questions from several benchmark sets. This included multiple-choice textbook questions, “reading comprehension” questions based on text snippets from scientific papers, and questions about how confident climate scientists are in different conclusions drawn from IPCC reports.
That last one was the most difficult, with the flagship models answering around 78 percent correctly and the smallest open-weight models coming in at around 47 percent. For the other benchmarks, frontier models and large open-weight models generally scored around 90 percent, while small open-weight models scored in the 70s.

articles.title: These tech outages are giving Y2K, AI agent style | TechCrunch
articles.text:
It’s going down, as the American rapper Yung Joc might say: the airline booking systems, banking platforms, and productivity platforms. In the past two weeks, the U.S.’s top businesses have faced technical outages that have disrupted the systems that run everyday life.
Apple Pay went down. NASA’s internal communication network went down. The FAA had to ground all flights for hours (only the third time in history since 9/11), and Microsoft was hit with an outage that took down Outlook, Teams, and Copilot for nearly two days.
The first thought, naturally, is an AI hacker invasion of some sort, especially after hackers managed to attack fridges in a grocery store and a blood bank in France a few weeks ago. Here in the U.S., the director of National Intelligence said these outages don’t seem related to state-sponsored terrorism, while President Trump called the issues “individual events.” Many of the companies themselves have said the outages were not caused by cyberattacks or AI attacks, but tech issues.
Only, there’s the fact that they all struck within a short timespan of each other, and just a few weeks after Cybersecurity’s so-called “Black October,” when a slew of also-unrelated cybersecurity incidents occurred on October 21, striking PHP, Node.js, LiteLLM, more.
While there’s no reason to view these outages as cyberattacks, there may be more than coincidence going on: It’s giving AI-native Y2K, frankly.
Dave DeWalt, an investor who worked in cybersecurity for more than three decades (including as president and CEO of McAfee and as vice chairman of the CISA Advisory Council for the Department of Homeland Security), also thinks it’s probably AI-related.
The technical outages are most likely the “growing pains of a security system that’s getting stronger, not weaker,” and that “AI is surfacing vulnerabilities at a speed and scale we’ve never had before through AI tools like Mythos and others,” he told TechCrunch.
The thing is, many of these technical flaws have always existed, but because AI is surfacing them so fast, enterprises are rushing to fix them before bad actors can exploit them. “That surge in patching is disrupting things in the short term,” he said.
This was, perhaps, the first moment when legacy meets modern, Anusha Iyer, a software engineer and founder of the security startup Corsha, told TechCrunch. “These industrial systems were never designed to be connected, let alone securely connected in the way we are pushing them to be today,” she said.
Virginia Senator Mark Warner, vice chair of the Senate Intel Committee, came to a similar conclusion (although investigations are still underway as to what could be happening). “These disruptions should serve as a wake-up call. It feels like every day brings another reminder that AI is moving faster than our ability to manage its consequences,” the senator wrote on X.
AI is reshaping how software is built, deployed, and operated, on a scale where everyone feels the sharp learning curve. Iyer cited the FAA outage as an example of legacy tech that is not as sophisticated or advanced as the technologies companies are trying to merge it with.
In less technical terms, she said the outage may have been caused (and preliminary findings point to this) when the FAA was trying to modernize its telecommunications infrastructure and the transition overwhelmed parts of its legacy hardware, where the new tech likely operated at a normal modern capacity while the legacy hardware couldn’t keep up.
When looked at this way, she said, AI is actually getting the bad rep. “It’s not rapid adoption of AI yet causing these outages,” she said. “The fault is the rushed mix of the legacy and modern systems without a clear understanding of operational and cyber risk or the ability to gatekeep and protect the legacy systems.”
Organizations need a more steadfast approach to AI adoption, including more testing and prioritizing what needs to be fixed and when, DeWalt said.
Iyer added, “These industrial systems need to be segmented more tightly and more access controlled, so as modern systems are introduced, it can be phased in and risk mitigated.”
Actually, there might be a silver lining to all of this for companies (and for venture investors). DeWalt said he’d rather see these U.S. enterprises find and patch their flaws, even in this messy way, than have bad actors find and exploit those vulnerabilities in AI warfare that could cause even more national security issues.
And maybe some aspiring founders were inspired by them. DeWalt expects a rise in companies focused on “AI-driven vulnerability management, autonomous remediation, safe patch testing and deployment, and resilience for the systems that keep critical infrastructure running,” he said.
“There’s real pain in this transition as we’ve seen in the past week,” DeWalt said. “But there’s also enormous opportunity for the companies that help organizations move at AI speed without breaking things.”

articles.title: Intel Diamond Rapids shows signs of life in SC26 demo running live server
articles.text:
Intel Diamond Rapids shows signs of life in SC26 demo running live server — next-gen Xeon 7 CPU breaks cover at partner booths, no showcase from Intel
Diamonds Rapids is set to launch next year.
Intel’s next-gen Xeon Diamond Rapids CPUs appeared at Supercomputing 2026 (SC26) in two separate booths, but neither was from Intel directly. Most interesting was a running server at the CXL booth, showcasing a demo with a Diamond Rapids CPU. The server ran for the first day of the show, and upon returning to the booth, we were informed that it had been shut down due to noise complaints (it’s hard to mistake a running server). Elsewhere at Bull’s booth, a Diamond Rapids CPU was shown installed in a server behind a glass case. Notably, Intel didn’t have a Diamond Rapids demo, instead focusing most of its booth on Xeon 6+ and its new D270 GPU, otherwise known as Crescent Island.
The demo in question is for Montage’s CXL MXC, or Memory eXpander Controller. If you’re unfamiliar, memory expansion via CXL is an increasingly common tactic to give multi-host environments access to a large pool of memory, breaking free of an individual server’s capacity via CXL. In the demo, Montage is showing off its memory expansion controller running across a Xeon 6 and a Diamond Rapids server, each sharing a pool of memory over CXL. CXL is an open standard, built atop PCIe.
Of course, the demo doesn’t say much about Diamond Rapids performance, but it’s the first time we’ve seen a chip running in the wild. The 256 GB memory capacity shown doesn’t provide any hints, either. Intel has announced that Diamond Rapids will support 16-channel memory, with RDIMM support up to 8,000 MT/s and MRDIMM support up to 12,800 MT/s, matching AMD’s recent EPYC Venice CPUs. However, Intel hasn’t revealed capacity, though we anticipate the maximum capacity will be far above 256 GB – for context, last-gen Granite Rapids-AP supports up to 3 TB per socket.
Bull is a French server designer focused on HPC and AI infrastructure, and it showed off two Xeon 7 Diamond Rapids chips installed in the Bullsquana XH31600 server. As expected for a 2P Diamond Rapids server, it supports 32 channels of DDR5 memory, and it’s designed for a liquid-cooled deployment.
As you can see from the image, these aren’t production chips. They’re labeled with “Intel confidential,” and the code starts with “Q,” revealing that this is a sample. Originally, we expected to see Diamond Rapids in the second half of this year, perhaps around this time. However, in August, Intel revealed that Xeon 7 chips would launch in 2027.
Based on the various servers we saw and the live demo, it seems Intel is targeting a launch earlier in the year, likely in Q2; we expect a larger consumer focus in Q1. It could slip later into the year, though that seems very unlikely given that Diamond Rapids was already pushed back, and the insatiable demand for CPUs in AI data centers doesn’t appear to be drying up.
Also pointing to a relatively quick release are the various servers we saw on the floor at SC26. Several partners showed off their next-gen servers built for Diamond Rapids CPU, sporting the LGA 9324 socket, including Dell and Asus (pictured above). However, Bull was the only vendor we could find that had an actual chip on display.
Diamond Rapids is Intel’s true next-gen CPU, following up on the E-core-only Xeon 6+ range that launched earlier this year. Diamond Rapids packs up to 256 P-cores, and it’s built on Intel’s performance-enhanced 18A-P node. The most interesting aspect of the chip is its topology, with Intel breaking from its previous layout and building something much similar to an EPYC CPU. The package features centralized memory and I/O, which were pushed out to the edges of the package with Granite Rapids. You can read more about the design of the chip in our Diamond Rapids recap from Hot Chips on Tom’s Hardware Premium.
Jake Roach is the Senior CPU Analyst at Tom’s Hardware, writing reviews, news, and features about the latest consumer and workstation processors.

articles.title: Disappointed that GTA 6 feels a bit choppy for frame rates — even on a PS5 Pro? Here's why motion blur could be key to smoother gaming on an OLED TV
articles.text:
Don't overlook this GTA 6 graphics setting on your OLED TV — gamers report that 'motion blur' could be the key to solving 30fps frame rate choppiness for some
To blur, or not to blur? There isn't a straightforward answer here
- GTA 6 has provoked a lot of discussion about console frame rates, particularly around the PS5
- The PS5 Pro offers a rock-solid 30fps, leveraging PSSR2 to great effect
- As well as the controversy about base PS5 performance, another topic of debate is whether to use motion blur with OLED TVs
GTA 6 is out, and everyone is playing it – well, a vast army of console gamers are, anyway – and there's been a lot of chatter about PS5 performance in particular, one aspect of which I feel bears closer examination: motion blur.
Before I come back to that, let's talk about overall performance. Digital Foundry (DF) conducted a deep dive into the frame rates and smoothness of GTA 6 across consoles, and its conclusion was that the PS5 Pro is the best way to play, followed by the base PS5 and Xbox Series X, which are roughly even. Both the latter still "play well" according to DF, with the caveat of "occasional minor frame-rate drops during regular play and a softer 1440p image".
What makes the PS5 Pro the clear winner is PSSR2 upscaling that produces a "4K-like image quality", and there's also a "noticeable visual upgrade thanks to ray-traced shadows".
Perhaps more crucially, PS5 Pro gamers get a smoother and more stable frame rate, with GTA 6 remaining steadfastly at 30fps – as DF observes, it's an "unwavering 30fps lock with perfect frame pacing".
What's crucial here is that 1% lows – where the game dips to its very slowest frame rates – are much better with the PS5 Pro, which combats any big judders and leads to a smoother gaming experience.
As we've previously been told, this is why Rockstar made the decision to stick with 30fps even on the PS5 Pro, and not try to force a 40fps mode – because that more robust feel for the frame rate was more important. Particularly when it comes to high-speed street races, for example, which is a slight weak point that some gamers are concerned about if they're playing on the base PS5.
Motion blur: should you enable it, and if so, at what level?
There's an interesting wrinkle here, though, and that's the topic of motion blur as mentioned at the outset. The issues therein are neatly encapsulated by a discussion I stumbled across on the PS5 Pro subreddit, one that urges owners of that console to "Disable Motion Blur" (in all-caps just to make the point very clearly).
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
The Redditor advises that turning off motion blur "significantly improves the image quality and blurriness when looking at objects far away", adding that: "At first I was like why is there so much blurriness on my [PS5] Pro? Disabled it and woah looked insane."
Before you start heading for the graphics options (Settings > Display) on GTA 6, there's a bit more to this than simply turning off motion blur (by setting it to zero) and you're good.
As another gamer immediately argues back, this isn't necessarily good advice for those with an OLED TV, where motion blur helps 30fps games. Why? OLED screens work differently to LCDs, with much faster (almost instant) response times, but this can actually be a drawback at a lower frame rate (like 30fps). It creates a touch of choppiness, and motion blur actually helps to smooth out that very slight stuttering. (Note that with 60fps gaming, this isn't an issue – it's just with lower frame rates).
That said, your mileage may vary, and other GTA 6 players with OLED TVs have chipped in to this thread to state that they aren't seeing any such stuttering without motion blur.
One Redditor notes: "I would usually agree [that motion blur is needed for OLED] but I'm loving the 0 motion blur on my LG CX right now. Feels way more responsive, and with the stable frame pacing, the stutters are not nearly as noticeable as opposed to most other games where my eyes hurt."
So, it seems that the rock-solid stability of the frame rate of GTA 6 on the PS5 Pro means that at least for some, the countermeasure of motion blur for OLED isn't needed – at least subjectively.
In the end, there's a simple way to proceed: try GTA 6 with motion blur, and without the setting (preferably in fast-action scenes), and see how you feel about it. Note that there are different levels of motion blur if it's enabled, and there's quite a bit of disagreement as to how high you should go. Some suggest higher values for an OLED, others feel a middling level of motion blur (4 to 6) is about right.
Again, this is likely subjective, but the key takeaway is to try different levels of motion blur, and turning it off (to zero), and see which you feel strikes the best balance between smoother gaming and better image clarity.
Meanwhile, as these console performance discussions unfurl, some PC gamers on Reddit are quite happily gloating that the PC port is going to be the best way to play GTA 6 when it arrives, particularly due to the observations about the frame rate on the base PS5 console and Xbox. That's caused quite some controversy, as you might imagine – DF is far from saying that the base PS5 version of the game provides a subpar frame rate.
That said, the way that GTA 6 runs on the PS5 Pro certainly indicates that the PC version is going to be spectacular, especially for those with beefier rigs – you'll just have to be patient for it (although perhaps the wait won't be as long as you might think).
