articles.title: Amazon Bedrock AgentCore harness adds Strands harness defaults, built-in tools, and lifecycle hooks | Amazon Web Services
articles.text:
Artificial Intelligence
Amazon Bedrock AgentCore harness adds Strands harness defaults, built-in tools, and lifecycle hooks
When building an AI agent, selecting a model is only the first step. The agent still needs tools, instructions for finishing the job, a way to manage context growth in long sessions, and guardrails before it executes any consequential actions, like issuing a refund.
We are upgrading Amazon Bedrock AgentCore harness to use Strands harness, our open-source agent harness, released earlier this year, available under an Apache 2.0 license. AgentCore harness also introduces lifecycle hooks, so you can apply your own deterministic checks and notifications at defined points in the agent loop.
With this upgrade, agents that rely on the managed defaults get a recommended model, a task-oriented system prompt, automatic prompt caching (initially for Anthropic models on Amazon Bedrock), and proactive context management. They also get additional built-in tools for planning, web retrieval, filesystem access, context offloading, and task delegation. This gives agents greater capabilities during long tasks, allowing them to keep track of subtasks, reduce context window usage, and delegate work. With hooks, you can transform non-deterministic AI behavior into predictable, safe, and governed workflows by running deterministic code at specific lifecycle checkpoints.
There’s no new resource type or integration to adopt. You automatically get both updates in the AgentCore harness you already use.
Strands capabilities, on AWS
Strands harness provides an assembled agent foundation with recommended instructions, tools, and context management. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore harness operates that foundation as a managed AWS service. The result is a production-grade default agent that doesn’t require you to assemble and operate the harness or its infrastructure yourself.
You do not need to provision compute, bundle and host the agent loop, manage session scaling, or operate tool-execution infrastructure. Each session runs in a secure, kernel-isolated microVM in AgentCore runtime, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, with managed compute, scaling, and high availability.
AgentCore achieves this by connecting the harness to the services required for production agents, including session persistence, streaming responses, usage metadata, observability, AgentCore memory, Identity, Gateway, Browser, Code Interpreter, and customer-provided containers. You retain control over the model, instructions, tools, permissions, and lifecycle policies while AgentCore manages the underlying execution environment.
A more capable managed harness
Harness now provides a stronger experience when you use its managed defaults:
- A current recommended model. When you omit the model, Harness uses a recommended default model that evolves as new models are released, always keeping your harnesses up to date. Explicit harness-level and per-invocation model configurations continue to take precedence.
- Task-oriented instructions. The managed system prompt encourages the agent to gather relevant context, use appropriate tools, continue until the task is resolved, adapt to failures or denied actions, and verify its work before reporting completion. The default system prompt improves over time to support the latest harness behavior.
- Automatic prompt caching. For supported models using Converse on Amazon Bedrock, Harness caches the system prompt, tool definitions, and conversation history. Repeated calls with the same prompt and tool surface can use lower-priced cache-read tokens, reducing input processing latency and cost.
- Proactive context management. By default, Harness summarizes older conversation turns while retaining recent context once the context window reaches a configurable threshold. Keeping the context lean this way helps Harness run at about 34% lower token cost than other leading harnesses.
- Context offloading. Large tool results can be moved out of the immediate model context. The agent receives a preview and can retrieve the complete result when needed, reducing repeated context usage without losing access to the data.
- Planning across invocations. The todo_write tool maintains a structured task plan that can be restored in later invocations within the same session, including after conversation summarization.
- Focused delegation. The subagent tool delegates a self-contained task to a fresh worker and returns the result to the parent agent. The worker is internal to the invocation, not a separately managed harness resource, and shares invocation limits and your tool-call lifecycle hooks.
- Web retrieval. The web_fetch tool retrieves content from a specified webpage to give your harness up-to-date external context.
- Granular filesystem access. With separate read, write, and edit tools, you can grant only the granular filesystem capabilities an agent needs.
Customer-provided Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers, AgentCore Gateway (a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore), Browser, Code Interpreter, inline functions, skills, memory, and customer-provided containers continue to work through the existing harness interfaces.
Recommended by default, configurable when needed
Harness manages its defaults so that agents using them receive the current AgentCore recommended experience as models, instructions, context management, and built-in capabilities improve.
Explicit configuration always takes precedence:
- Configure a model ID to keep using a specific model.
- Configure systemPrompt to completely replace the managed system prompt.
- Configure truncation to keep a specific context-management policy.
- List individual allowedTools selectors to maintain a fixed tool surface.
When allowedTools is omitted or set to ["*"], Harness provides the current recommended built-in tool set. Because this set can gain capabilities over time, applications with a fixed security or capability boundary should list only the tools they need.
For example, the following configuration permits read-only filesystem access and web retrieval without granting shell access or file modification:
Govern consequential actions with lifecycle hooks
With lifecycle hooks, you can run your own deterministic code at defined points in the agent loop. For example, an AWS Lambda function can allow or deny a request or a tool call, and an Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) topic or Amazon EventBridge event bus can receive a notification to record activity or start an asynchronous workflow.
Harness supports four lifecycle events:
| Event | When it runs | Effect of a Lambda denial | 
| before_invocation | Before the agent processes the request | Stops the invocation with hook_stopped | 
| before_tool_call | After the model proposes a tool call and before execution | Skips the tool call. The agent loop continues | 
| after_tool_call | After a tool result exists | Retains the result and stops before further inference | 
| after_invocation | After the invocation completes | Reports the decision. Output already streamed cannot be retracted | 
Only Lambda hooks can change the agent loop. They run synchronously and return allow or deny, with an optional reason. SNS and Amazon EventBridge hooks are notifications and don’t block the agent loop.
For example, a customer-support agent can investigate an order on its own while a before_tool_call hook checks each refund against an approval limit before the refund tool runs. The following configuration attaches that Lambda function to the harness:
The function receives the proposed tool call in the hook payload and returns a decision:
When the function denies the call, the harness skips the refund and the agent continues, so it can tell the customer that the request was escalated. Each decision also appears in the InvokeHarness response stream as a hookEvent:
Hooks also apply to subagents. When the agent delegates a task, each tool call the subagent makes runs through the same beforeToolCall and afterToolCall hooks, so delegation can’t bypass your refund policy. The invocation-level hooks (beforeInvocation, afterInvocation) run once for the whole invocation.
You configure hooks with CreateHarness or UpdateHarness. If a Lambda function times out or returns an error, the hook applies its failureMode, which defaults to deny. For timeouts, payload fields, and context limits, see Lifecycle hooks in the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Developer Guide.
To see every event and target type working together, try the Refund Desk sample in the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore samples repository on GitHub. A six-step guided tour shows all four lifecycle events and the AWS Lambda, Amazon SNS, and Amazon EventBridge targets. It also shows validation of client-supplied inline function results and the difference between failureMode deny and allow.
Run a multi-agent research coordinator with the AgentCore CLI
Creating a harness takes a single command. You name it and set up the instructions, context policy, and limits you want. This example creates a Research Coordinator: a harness with a task-oriented system prompt and summarization-based truncation. In a single invocation, it runs a researcher, a synthesizer, and a reviewer as subagents and returns one consolidated report. You get multi-agent orchestration and context management without provisioning infrastructure or wiring the delegation yourself.
The agentcore harness commands call the harness APIs directly, so you don’t need a CLI project or a deployment step. Install the AgentCore CLI, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, with npm:
The CLI uses your default AWS credentials. It has no --profile flag, so set the AWS_PROFILE environment variable if you want a specific profile. Save the coordinator’s instructions from the sample as system_prompt.md in your working directory.
Create the harness
This command passes the coordinator’s system prompt, a summarization policy that keeps the 30 most recent messages intact as the conversation grows, and limits high enough for the full workflow. Because it omits the model, memory, and execution role, the harness uses the current AgentCore recommended model and managed memory, and the CLI creates an execution role in IAM for you.
Creation is asynchronous. Wait for creation to finish. The last command should print READY:
Send the prompts
Invoke your harness with a new session ID. Start with a basic question. The coordinator answers it directly, without calling its subagents:
Then ask for a full research report in the same session. The coordinator plans the work and delegates to the researcher, synthesizer, and reviewer in order. It runs at most one revision cycle if the reviewer asks for it, and delivers the final report. Reusing the session ID continues the conversation in the same environment.
With --prompt, the CLI prints the completed transcript as JSON when the turn finishes. The research run takes about 10 to 15 minutes. To follow along as it works, leave out --prompt, and the CLI opens an interactive chat.
The same example in Python (boto3), including the full system prompt, is available in the AgentCore samples repository on GitHub.
Clean up
Delete the harness when you’re done. This also deletes its managed memory unless you pass --delete-managed-memory false. The execution role that the CLI created stays in your account, so delete it in the IAM console if you no longer need it.
Rollout and compatibility
On November 11, AgentCore harness began rolling out the Strands harness-backed experience to new and existing harnesses. No customer action is required.
Configuration you explicitly provide remains unchanged. Harnesses that omit the model, system prompt, or truncation configuration, or use allowedTools: ["*"], receive the upgraded managed defaults.
If your application requires fixed behavior or a fixed capability boundary, configure those settings explicitly.
Learn more
Create and invoke an AgentCore harness as you do today. Use the managed defaults for the complete current recommended experience, or configure individual settings when your application requires fixed behavior.

- Lifecycle hooks.
- Refund Desk lifecycle hooks code sample.
We look forward to seeing what you build with the upgraded AgentCore harness.

articles.title: Groundcover launches Agent Investigations, a shared workspace for AI agents and engineers - SiliconANGLE
articles.text:
Groundcover launches Agent Investigations, a shared workspace for AI agents and engineers
Observability company groundcover Inc. today announced the launch of Agent Investigations, a shared workspace designed to allow groundcover’s artificial intelligence agents, a team’s own coding agents and on-call engineers to work production incidents together.
Agent Investigations is aimed at the problem of scattered findings as AI agents take on a bigger role in incident response. When production goes down, several engineers often point their own agents at the same issue, with each agent working in isolation, according to the company. What those agents conclude, it says, is end up in private chats, tickets or Slack messages out of view of the rest of the team.
Investigations in the new workspace are started automatically by groundcover once a monitor issue opens. Engineers also have the option to launch one manually from the groundcover interface or from a button in Slack.
On groundcover’s side, the work is split between two agents. The first, known as the Investigator agent, is said to build a graph of questions and hypotheses before testing each one against groundcover’s logs, metrics, traces and Kubernetes data. Supporting graphs are attached to each of its findings.
Reviewing every proposed conclusion is the job of the second, a Moderator agent. The Moderator, which is the only agent allowed to close a hypothesis, sends back any claim that lacks supporting findings. Doing so is said to separate generating a possible explanation from validating whether the evidence actually supports it.
Ending each hypothesis is a structured assessment that either supports or refutes it. The company claims teams get a set of tested answers to read through instead of pages of generated text.
Agent Investigations also offers access for outside agents, including Anthropic PBC’s Claude Code and OpenAI Group PBC’s Codex, through groundcover’s Model Context Protocol server. Connected agents can read from and contribute to the same investigation, with agents used for business intelligence and product roadmapping also able to take part. In October, groundcover launched agent-to-agent observability tools that let outside coding agents hand production investigations to its own agent.
Hypothesis status and assessments post to the Slack thread tied to the original alert. With replies posted in that thread also fed back into the investigation, engineers are able to steer the work from inside the incident conversation.
“Every engineer now has an agent, but each of those agents investigates on its own and findings end up in a chat window,” said co-founder and Chief Executive Shahar Azulay, who started groundcover in 2021 with Yechezkel Rabinovich. “Agent Investigations gives humans and agents one place to work an incident, where every hypothesis is tested against production data and every conclusion has to be backed by evidence.”
Omer Mayer, senior product manager at groundcover, said the wait while agents are working and the on-call engineer has nothing to look at is often “the hardest stretch of an incident.” Engineers using Agent Investigations instead get to watch, he said, as each hypothesis is supported or ruled out in real time.
The graph the Investigator builds also serves as the record, said to show how a team reached the root cause, including the hypotheses that were ruled out along the way. According to the company, keeping the monitor, Slack thread, investigation and conclusion linked means nobody has to piece the history back together from separate tools after an incident closes.
Powering the investigations is the full-fidelity telemetry collected by groundcover’s sensor. Because groundcover uses a bring-your-own-cloud architecture, the data remains in the customer’s own cloud account even while agents are querying it.
Agent Investigations is available to groundcover customers whose backends have AI enabled. The company will demonstrate it at Amazon Web Services Inc.’s re:Invent conference in Las Vegas Nov. 30-Dec. 4.
Groundcover has raised $160 million to date, including a $100 million Series C round led by One Peak in July.

articles.title: NASA's new Moon plans have a problem: Orion wasn't designed to fly this way
articles.text:
NASA recently announced a significant shakeup to the Artemis program that will land humans on the Moon.
The moves were designed to give the agency’s lunar lander providers—SpaceX with its Starship vehicle, and Blue Origin with Blue Moon—more flexibility in reaching the Moon. For Starship, this means docking with Orion in Earth orbit, and then traveling to the Moon in tandem. For Blue Moon, it shifts the rendezvous with Orion all the way to low-lunar orbit.
These changes benefit the lunar landers, but in turn impose more of a burden on the Orion spacecraft, which is built for NASA by Lockheed Martin. To understand the implications for the spacecraft, Ars spoke with Kirk Shireman, Human Spaceflight Exploration and Orion program manager at Lockheed.
Starship challenges
For Starship, the evolved plan has SpaceX fueling a Starship lunar lander in low-Earth orbit before docking with Orion in high-Earth orbit. The crew will fly to the Moon on board Orion before two of the four astronauts transfer into Starship for a landing on the Moon.
Due to the docking configuration with Starship, Orion must now fly backward to the Moon, with its Service Module at the top of the stack. This is a fundamentally different flying posture than Orion was designed for, Shireman said, and creates issues for Orion’s propulsion system.
As a result, the Service Module, which is provided by the European Space Agency, will require modifications to its propellant tanks. This is because liquid propellant would move toward the gas inlet side of the tanks, rather than settling in the direction expected during normal operation.
“When you push it the other way, the liquid goes to the gas end of the tank, and you don’t want the liquid in the gas part,” Shireman said. “Bad things can happen to you.” To address this, he said, the European Space Agency and its main contractor, Airbus, are modifying the vehicle’s tanks for Starship lunar missions.

articles.title: SA’s SEQFLO launches to take risk out of buying from strangers - Disrupt Africa
articles.text:
South African startup SEQFLO has launched a digital trust platform that adds identity verification, protected payments and dispute resolution to private transactions between strangers.
Founded in Cape Town by Jarrett Booysen, SEQFLO is not a marketplace, but rather acts as a trust and transaction layer for deals that start elsewhere, whether on Facebook Marketplace, Gumtree, WhatsApp, Instagram or a seller’s own website.
Sellers create a transaction on SEQFLO and then advertise through their usual channels. Both parties are verified and agree on the terms before any money changes hands. The buyer then pays through SEQFLO, and the funds are held within the platform’s approved banking and payment structure.
Delivery or collection can be documented with photographs, and the seller is paid once the agreed conditions have been met. If something goes wrong, a structured evidence and dispute-resolution process kicks in.
“We’re not asking people to trust strangers more. We’re building SEQFLO so they don’t have to rely on trust alone,” said Booysen, who built the platform after being scammed himself.
“We constantly tell people to check a profile, ask for ID, look at proof of payment and trust their gut. But sophisticated scammers know exactly how to create those signals of legitimacy,” he said.
SEQFLO is designed to protect both sides of a deal. Buyers are covered against paying for goods that never arrive. Sellers are covered against fake proofs of payment and fraudulent buyers.
There is no subscription for private users. Instead, buyers pay a protection fee on successful transactions. This structure positions the platform for everything from second-hand purchases to high-value private and business deals.
“We won’t eliminate dishonesty,” Booysen said. “But we can make it much harder for dishonest people to exploit trust and much safer for honest people to transact with one another.”

articles.title: Starting with Rs 30 lakh and a salon-focused haircare brand in 2016, Mumbai-based Ccigmaa Lifestyle has expanded into men’s grooming, children’s perso
articles.text:
How Dhruv Sayani built Ccigmaa Lifestyles into a five-brand personal care business
Starting with Rs 30 lakh and a salon-focused haircare brand in 2018, Mumbai-based Ccigmaa Lifestyles has expanded into men’s grooming, children’s personal care and skincare, with a network of over 27,000 salons across 86 cities.
Hair and water composition can change significantly every 100 kilometres across India, affecting how haircare products perform. It was this observation, made while researching premature greying in his 20s, that led Dhruv Sayani to build Ccigmaa Lifestyles, a Mumbai-based personal care company.
Sayani found that keratin, the protein that makes up most of human hair, responds differently to these regional variations, something he believed conventional haircare formulations did not adequately address.
In 2018, he launched KT Professional, a salon-focused haircare brand developed specifically for stylists. Since then, Ccigmaa Lifestyles has expanded its portfolio with three more brands, KT Men, KT Kids and KT Derma, each focused on specific personal care needs.
The company, founded in 2018, aims to inspire “millions of minds” through Indian-made personal care products, according to Sayani.
Build credibility before distribution
Proving the regional-formulation premise required evidence a lab alone could not generate.
Rather than build retail distribution first and let salons discover the brand afterward, Ccigmaa Lifestyles went the other way around, giving hairstylists across Indian cities access to formulations, and letting their feedback, not a marketing brief, decide what shipped outside the production.
KT Professional was launched with Rs 30 lakh of the founder’s personal savings in 2018, exactly that route. Nearly a decade later, the company works with more than 27,000 salons across 86 cities, a distribution footprint built one stylist and salon relationship at a time rather than through a single national launch mode.
Turn specialization into a growth engine
Once KT Professional’s salon-first model was validated, the more conventional path was to push that single brand harder, deeper into more cities, more product lines, more advertising.
Sayani chose a different growth mechanism instead: apply the same underlying logic, that a mass-market, one-size-fits-all product underserves a large share of its actual buyers, to categories beyond haircare.
That decision produced KT Men and KT Kids as standalone brands rather than product extensions, a materially harder path since each requires its own credibility, its own distribution relationships, and its own reason to exist, rather than borrowing KT Professional's. It is also, by most available market evidence, the better-timed one.
Redseer projects India’s beauty and personal care market reaching $40 billion by 2030, positioning India as the fourth largest such market globally, with Gen Z and Alpha consumers becoming the largest beauty-spending cohort in that growth. A market moving toward younger, more specific buyers rewards brands built around a defined need far more than it rewards a single brand trying to serve everyone.
Position KT Men around performance, not vanity
Sayani says most Indian grooming brands have built their positioning around attraction or plain cosmetic vanity rather than performance, a framing he believed increasingly out of step with younger, fitness-oriented male consumers.
KT Men was built to compete on the second premise instead of the first, launching at an accessible Rs 399 entry point before extending into a higher Rs 699 to Rs 999 band through its G.O.A.T Edition range, a licensing partnership with the Argentina Football Association built around Lionel Messi, Julian Alvarez and Enzo Fernandez.
The brand has since disclosed a Rs 36 Crore marketing investment behind that range, against a Rs 200 crore revenue target over 18 to 24 months, sitting on top of KT Men’s original Rs 100 crore first-year ambition. Whether that specific target lands on schedule matters less to the decision itself than the positioning bet underneath it, that performance, not image, was the underused argument in Indian men's grooming.
Design for two customers at once
Children’s personal care carries a structural complication most categories do not: the person buying the product and the person using it are rarely evaluating it the same way.
A parent checks an ingredient list and asks whether a formulation is genuinely mild enough for a child's skin. A child has no interest in either question and decides on nothing more sophisticated than whether the experience of using it was enjoyable.
Rather than let KT Professional’s existing haircare range absorb a children's line as a smaller variant, Ccigmaa built KT Kids as its own brand, formulated specifically for children rather than adapted from adult products, and has run two entertainment-licensing partnerships in 15 months, first with SpongeBob SquarePants, then with Peppa Pig, timed separately rather than bundled, each aimed at a distinct age band.
The decision to treat that dual-audience problem as its own category, rather than a footnote inside an existing one, is the same underlying instinct that produced KT Men, applied to a harder version of the same question.
The company created five brands with one method to connect them: identify a specific need a generalist product is failing to serve, validate the idea against real, direct feedback before scaling it, and build a dedicated brand around it rather than stretch an existing one to cover it.
Ccigmaa's next test is whether that method holds as a repeatable business engine rather than a run of good individual calls, since a Rs 40 billion market moving toward specificity will reward the companies that can keep making this decision correctly, not just the ones that made it once.

articles.title: Youtube Premium pour moins cher : Google lance une nouvelle façon de s’abonner
articles.text:
Alors que le prix de YouTube Premium n’en finit plus de grimper, voilà un possible bon plan qui se profile à l’horizon. Pour peu que vous ayez besoin de l’abonnement le plus cher de Google pour son IA Gemini et le stockage en cloud, vous pourrez alors faire d’une pierre deux coups et obtenir la plateforme de streaming musicale non seulement pour vous, mais aussi pour votre famille.
Dans le détail, cette nouveauté s’applique à l’abonnement Google AI Ultra à 99,99 euros par mois. Auparavant, cette offre permettait d’obtenir un compte Youtube Premium individuel. Désormais, elle débloque un compte famille, ce qui permet de partager l’abonnement avec jusqu’à cinq personnes supplémentaires.
Une montée en gamme plus cohérente
Ce changement permet de mieux appuyer la montée en gamme entre le tiers Google AI Pro et AI Ultra. Le premier, coûtant tout de même 49,99 euros par mois, offre 10 To de stockage et Youtube Premium Lite en individuel. L’abonnement Ultra à 99,99 euros, en plus de ses 20 To de stockage des limites d’utilisations de Gemini cinq fois plus élevé, permet donc de passer deux tiers sur son abonnement Youtube Premium.
Pour une fois, le changement n’est pas disponible uniquement aux États-Unis. La page Google One qui résumes les différents tiers des abonnements à Google Cloud a été mise à jour pour affiche le changement.
Google revendique 150 millions d’abonnés à YouTube Music et Premium. En comptant les essais gratuits, on tombe autour des 116,6 millions d’abonnés. À titre de comparaison, Spotify possédait en septembre dernier 306 millions d’abonnés payants et 788 millions d’utilisateurs actifs.

articles.title: Madrid tiene una carretera por la que no ha pasado ningún coche en 20 años
articles.text:
Madrid, 2005. Un puñado de operarios tienen una misión. Dos años después, esa misión se trunca. Desaparece. Llega el abandono. Hace casi dos décadas que ni un sólo trabajador pisa el suelo de la M-203, una carretera asfaltada en parte pero conectada a ninguna parte. Ahora, la Comunidad de Madrid parece haberse tomado en serio su resurrección.
¿Qué ha pasado? La Comunidad de Madrid invertirá 61 millones de euros para culminar la carretera M-203, una vía que quedó abandonada en 2007, apenas dos años después de que dieran inicio las obras. Este anuncio ya se esperaba después de que en el verano del año pasado se pusiera sobre la mesa revivir esta carretera.
Ahora, la Comunidad de Madrid tiene precio a la vuelta de los operarios a la M-203. La intención es que con 61 millones de euros se culmine una vía alternativa para el corredor del Henares, una zona con graves problemas de tráfico. De salir adelante, sus vecinos tendrán una conexión directa entre la A-2 y la R-3.
¿M-203? Sí, así se llamó el proyecto que en 2005 arrancó de la mano de Cintra. En aquellos años se aseguró que la construcción de la vía sería posible gracias a una inversión de 78,5 millones de euros por parte de la empresa concesionaria y, a cambio, la Comunidad de Madrid le otorgaba un plazo de explotación durante 30 años.
La intención era que los conductores pagaran algo más de un euro (en precios de 2005) por hacer uso de la carretera que debía descongestionar parte del tránsito de entrada y salida de la capital en el entorno de la A-2 a la altura de Alcalá de Henares.
¿Y qué pasó? Que Cintra abandonó por completo su construcción. El proyecto contemplaba que para construir poco más de 12 kilómetros de carretera apenas bastaba un año para iniciar las obras y otro para abrirlas al público. En 2008 la carretera debía estar en servicio.
18 años después seguimos esperando que se remate. Hasta el día de hoy, lo único que tienen los madrileños son unos pocos kilómetros asfaltados que empiezan y terminan en un tramo de tierra.
Un culebrón. Con el abandono de la carretera, comienza un culebrón del que, todo indica, estamos viendo sus últimos capítulos. Entonces, la Comunidad de Madrid (PP) echaron en cara al Gobierno (entonces PSOE) que habían hecho lo posible para torpedear el proyecto. Más tarde, ya con el PP dirigiendo el Gobierno nacional, el problema se estancó con Adif y un paso complicado bajo la línea de alta velocidad Madrid-Barcelona.
En El País tienen un repaso completo de aquellos años en los que Ignacio González, entonces presidente de la Comunidad de Madrid, llegó a asegurar que "esta infraestructura no va a costar ni un solo euro a las arcas públicas”. Aquellos años, Ferrovial (dueña de Cintra) y el gobierno regional se enzarzaron en una disputa en la que los primeros reclamaban más de 200 millones de euros de compensación pese a no haber cumplido con la construcción de la carretera.
Finalmente, la Comunidad de Madrid tuvo que pagar 71,3 millones de euros a Ferrovial pero el TSJM desestimó la reclamación de 248 millones de euros de la constructora. Y es que, explicaba el año pasado el Economista, cuando la concesión se otorgó a Ferrovial no se tuvo en cuenta un problema: la Comunidad de Madrid no había obtenido los permisos ni de Adif ni de la Confederación Hidrográfica del Tajo ni del Ministerio de Fomento por cuyos terrenos pasaba la nueva carretera.
¿Y ahora? Para tratar de desatascar el asunto, desde la Comunidad de Madrid se intentó llegar a todo tipo de acuerdos con Cintra, incluido ampliar el periodo de concesión de 30 a 60 años. Sin embargo, nada de esto resultó y el Henares se quedó con una carretera que va y viene a ninguna parte.
El año pasado, sin embargo, el gobierno regional ya lo incluyó en su plan regional de carreteras para el periodo 2025-2032. En septiembre, se confirmó que se invertirán 61 millones de euros para culminar de una vez por todas el enlace entre la A-2 y la R-3 a través de la M-203, el nuevo nombre que obtuvo al perder la categoría de carretera de peaje ya que empezó llamándose MP-203.

articles.title: Hackers steal data of 1.6 million SBC Medical Group customers
articles.text:
SBC Medical Group has warned in a filing with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) that two cybersecurity incidents exposed sensitive customer and employee information, including personal data belonging to 1.6 million people.
SBC Medical Group is a clinic management company whose main business is in Japan, but it also has a limited presence in the U.S., is traded on Nasdaq as SBC, and holds a minority stake in the medical spa chain OrangeTwist. Its clinics receive 7 million patient visits annually.
The first compromise concerns the SBC databases, while the second involves unauthorized access to clinic administrator accounts on Tribeau, a third-party booking platform.
The company discovered the database breach on November 16 and was notified of the Tribeau compromise the same day. Both incidents affected its Japan-based businesses.
"On November 16, 2026, unauthorized access occurred to certain databases within a website system managed and operated by SBC Medical Group, Ltd., the Company’s, Japanese subsidiary, in connection with its management services in Japan," reads a FORM 8-K filing with the SEC.
"The Company confirmed that an unauthorized third party accessed and extracted customer information. The method of intrusion and full scope remain under investigation."
The incident impacting SBC databases exposed basic personal information belonging to 1,624,000 people, including:
- Full names
- Contact details
- Dates of birth
- Patient card numbers
- Member IDs
- Passwords
- Survey responses
Not all of the above data types were exposed for all 1.6 million people.
Additionally, the incident exposed 255,416 reservation requests, 217,769 inquiries submitted to SBC websites, and thousands of treatment description records, image filenames, and customer reviews.
The company said the attackers also stole approximately 20,000 employee account records, including names, IDs, and passwords. For a small subset of 459 employees, the affected data also included bank account and tax information.
The second incident involved administrator accounts on the Tribeau booking platform, a service used by 56 clinics.
The operator reported access to reservation information for 12,641 people, as well as access to treatment names, dates, and fees for 6,804 people who received treatment.
SBC noted that it has not confirmed unauthorized access to electronic medical records or information from its mySBC reservation site in the database breach.
As of November 18, when the Form 8-K was submitted, the company has not seen any evidence of misuse of the exposed data.
SBC said the investigation remains ongoing, and at this time, it could not estimate the financial impact of these cybersecurity incidents.

Le casque sans fil Sony WH-1000XM5 bénéficie d’une réduction de 43 % chez Amazon pendant le Black Friday : son prix passe de 419 € à 237,83 €, et sa livraison est offerte à tous les clients du site.
Qu’il s’agisse d’atténuer les bruits dans les transports en commun ou de limiter l’impact des conversations de bureau au travail, l’usage d’un casque doté d’une réduction active du bruit efficace peut tout changer. Si vous ne savez pas vers quel modèle vous tourner, sachez qu’en ce moment, Amazon propose le Sony WH-1000XM5 à 237,83 €. Il s’agit d’un casque Bluetooth qui a déjà largement fait ses preuves, et qui peut convenir pour un usage régulier en déplacement ou en télétravail.
Le casque Sony WH-1000XM5 à réduction de bruit est disponible à 237,83 € chez Amazon durant le Black Friday.
Pourquoi choisir le Sony WH-1000XM5 ?
- Pour sa réduction active du bruit : elle atténue les sons environnants pour mieux profiter de sa musique ou se concentrer.
- Pour sa connexion multipoint : le casque peut rester connecté à un ordinateur et à un smartphone en même temps afin de passer facilement de l’un à l’autre.
- Pour son autonomie : Sony annonce jusqu’à 30 heures d’écoute avec la réduction de bruit activée.
Un casque pratique au bureau comme à l’extérieur
Si vous prenez les transports en commun pour vous rendre au travail, il est possible que vous ayez besoin de passer de votre smartphone à votre ordinateur une fois arrivé au bureau. Le Sony WH-1000XM5 vous évite d’avoir à jongler entre vos appareils grâce à sa connexion multipoint, qui lui permet de rester connecté à deux appareils en même temps. Ses commandes tactiles permettent de gérer la lecture et le volume directement sur l’écouteur, tandis qu’un mode ambiant laisse passer les sons extérieurs si vous avez besoin de garder le contact avec votre entourage.
Notre test du Sony WH-1000XM5 a accordé la note de 9 sur 10 au casque, en saluant notamment ses qualités d’isolation et ses nombreux réglages. Son autonomie peut monter jusqu’à 30 heures, ce qui permet d’espacer les recharges.
Un casque sans fil qui aurait pu être plus compact
Le casque WH-1000XM5 de Sony est confortable à porter, mais il faut tenir compte du fait que ses oreillettes ne se replient pas vers l’intérieur de l’arceau. Il occupe donc davantage de place dans un sac qu’un casque pliable, et sa housse de transport s’avère assez volumineuse.
✅ Les points forts
- Réduction active du bruit et mode ambiant.
- Connexion Bluetooth à deux appareils.
- Jusqu’à 30 heures d’autonomie annoncées avec réduction de bruit.
❌ Les limites
- Arceau non pliable pour le transport.
- Port USB-C qui ne prend pas en charge l’audio USB.
Disponible pour 237,83 € au lieu de 419 €, le casque Sony WH-1000XM5 bénéficie de 43 % de remise chez Amazon.
Le casque sans fil Sony WH-1000XM5 convient aux personnes qui ne peuvent pas se passer de musique au quotidien, ou encore à celles qui ont tendance à travailler dans un environnement bruyant. Sa réduction de bruit très efficace et sa connexion multipoint sont de vrais atouts.
Par contre, si vous cherchez un casque pliable qui prend peu de place quand vous ne le portez pas, ce n’est peut-être pas le modèle auquel vous devez vous intéresser en priorité.

articles.title: Paie, congés, soins : la Commission européenne piratée avec un outil IA en accès libre — Frandroid
articles.text:
Le porte-parole de la Commission européenne, Thomas Regnier, a confirmé le 19 novembre une cyberattaque « assistée par l’IA » de l’organe exécutif, quelques heures après les révélations de Politico reprises par Reuters. Pendant plus de dix jours, les agents de l’institution n’ont pas pu utiliser normalement plusieurs de leurs outils internes, et on ne sait toujours pas si leurs données personnelles ont fuité.
Dans sa déclaration à Politico, Thomas Regnier indique que « la Commission européenne a pris les mesures nécessaires suite à la détection d’une cyberattaque […] Des systèmes individuels ont été ciblés et, conformément à notre procédure habituelle, nous avons informé les personnes concernées. »
Devant la presse, le porte-parole a aussi indiqué que la Commission n’avait reçu aucune demande de rançon. Il a en revanche refusé de dire qui se cache derrière l’attaque et quel outil d’IA a été utilisé.
Politico a sorti l’affaire dans sa newsletter Brussels Playbook, en s’appuyant sur un responsable européen resté anonyme. D’après ce dernier, le service chargé de la cybersécurité des institutions de l’Union (CERT-EU) a repéré début novembre que des « hackers internationaux » utilisaient un outil IA contre la Commission. Par précaution, plusieurs applications ont été coupées.
Du 19 au 30 novembre, le Plaud Note Pro passe à 149 € au lieu de 189 € ! Il enregistre vos réunions, les transcrit et les synthétise pour vous, il suffit d’appuyer sur un bouton. Les Plaud Note, NotePin et NotePin S sont aussi à -20 %. Bref, c’est le moment d’arrêter de perdre du temps au travail !
Sysper, la plateforme RH qui gère les fiches de paie, les congés et les feuilles de temps, et MyPMO, qui rembourse les frais médicaux des agents, n’ont été rétablies qu’en début de semaine. Sysper a encore planté mercredi dernier et les services de traduction ont aussi été touchés mardi. Les salaires sont tout de même tombés à l’heure, mais certains agents n’ont pas pu poser de congés ni remplir leurs feuilles de temps.
ARTEX, un outil de test devenu arme de piratage
La Commission européenne n’a pas indiqué l’outil utilisé par les pirates ni la porte utilisée.
D’après les sources de Politico, il s’agirait d’ARTEX, un outil de test d’intrusion piloté par IA. Publié sur GitHub en juillet 2026 par Li Puhua, un chercheur chinois en cybersécurité, il a rapidement été détourné de son objectif premier par des pirates. Son auteur a bien supprimé le dépôt le 8 octobre, mais des copies, des versions modifiées et même une édition commerciale, baptisée ARTEX PRO, circulent toujours.
ARTEX se branche sur un grand modèle de langage et pilote plusieurs agents IA qui enchaînent seuls le repérage des cibles, la recherche de failles et leur exploitation. Selon le FBI, qui a lancé une alerte à son sujet début novembre, certaines intrusions passent ainsi du premier ciblage à un accès privilégié, avec des droits d’administrateur, en moins de trois heures. ARTEX permet également à des attaquants sans grande expertise technique de viser plusieurs cibles simultanément.
La Commission est loin d’être la seule victime. D’après le FBI, des pirates utilisent ARTEX depuis le mois d’août contre des organisations du monde entier dans des secteurs critiques : finance, administrations, défense, énergie, santé ou encore télécoms. Des institutions financières sud-coréennes en ont notamment fait les frais récemment.
Des données personnelles toujours dans le flou
Sur la question des données qui auraient pu fuiter, la Commission reste prudente. Thomas Regnier a précisé que l’intrusion avait été repérée fin octobre et que le rôle de l’IA avait été confirmé quatre jours plus tard.
Une enquête a été immédiatement ouverte, et le porte-parole assure n’avoir, à ce stade, aucun élément montrant une fuite de données touchant l’ensemble du personnel.
En interne, le responsable cité par Politico se montre moins affirmatif. Il explique que les enquêteurs cherchent encore à savoir si des données du personnel ont été compromises, et dans quelle proportion.
Selon lui, la Commission n’en sait pas assez pour informer clairement ses agents, d’où une communication au compte-gouttes. Trois fonctionnaires se sont d’ailleurs plaints du manque d’information auprès de Politico. Une réponse du service informatique à un incident sur Sysper parlait ainsi d’un simple « problème général », sans un mot sur une cyberattaque. Les outils touchés contiennent pourtant des informations sensibles sur les agents, de la paie aux remboursements de soins, et la piste de données personnelles potentiellement compromises n’est toujours pas écartée.
La Commission a déjà été visée deux fois cette année. En janvier, une attaque contre son infrastructure de gestion des terminaux mobiles a pu exposer les noms et numéros de téléphone d’agents. En mars, l’infrastructure cloud qui héberge les sites Europa.eu a été compromise, et environ 91,7 Go de données ont été dérobés, dont des informations personnelles et le contenu de courriels, rappelle Euronews.

articles.title: Voici le guide officiel ultime de GTA 6
articles.text:
GTA 6 est sorti ce jeudi 19 novembre sur PS5, Xbox Series S et Xbox Series X, et son guide officiel est en ligne depuis le même jour. En prime, il est gratuit, alors que le guide papier officiel de GTA 5, édité par BradyGames, coûtait 24,99 dollars (environ 22 €) à sa sortie en 2013. Conçu avec IGN, il se consulte gratuitement sur le site du média.
« Bienvenue dans le guide stratégique et la carte officiels de Grand Theft Auto VI. Vous y trouverez des solutions étape par étape pour chaque mission, une immense carte interactive recensant des milliers de lieux à explorer et à cocher, ainsi qu’un guide complet à 100 % pour vos collections et objets à récupérer. GTA 6 raconte l’histoire de Jason et Lucia : chacune de vos décisions peut affecter non seulement le monde vivant de Leonida qui vous entoure, mais aussi votre relation, et nous vous expliquerons comment vos choix mènent à différents dénouements », écrit IGN en présentation du guide, en précisant l’avoir conçu avec Rockstar Games.
Carte interactive, missions, objets : ce que contient le guide
La promesse de solutions « pour chaque mission » n’est pas encore tenue. Le guide d’IGN démarre avec les solutions des deux premiers chapitres, la carte interactive de Leonida et quelques autres rubriques. Rockstar Games et le média ne donnent pas de calendrier pour la suite de l’histoire, découpée en cinq chapitres et quelques 91 missions.
Le guide, entièrement écrit par des humains selon IGN, se divise en plusieurs onglets thématiques. Il y a d’abord une carte interactive avec tous les points d’intérêt et les filtres qui vont bien pour s’y retrouver. Il y a ensuite le déroulé des missions de l’histoire, avec le nombre de chapitres et les récompenses obtenues.
À cela s’ajoutent les objets à collectionner, les activités secondaires, les missions annexes, les opérations illégales, les variantes d’armes uniques, des astuces utiles… Autant d’éléments qui vous aideront à vous rapprocher des 100 % de complétion en cas de besoin.
Le guide dispose d’un moteur de recherche. On peut même y créer sa propre liste de tâches, à cocher au fil de la partie. Il se consulte aussi sur mobile, avec une navigation un peu moins pratique.
Rockstar Games Grand Theft Auto VI
+ rapide, + pratique, + exclusif

articles.title: Ein unsichtbarer Begleiter: Forscher finden Himmelskörper, den es nicht geben dürfte
articles.text:
Das „unmögliche“ Objekt: Forscher entdecken mysteriösen Begleiter im All
Ein Team von Wissenschaftler:innen hat im Sternbild Fische ein Doppelsternsystem mit einem Roten Riesen als Hauptstern entdeckt. So weit, so unspektakulär. Schließlich sind etwa 50 bis 70 Prozent aller Sterne der Milchstraße Teil eines Doppel- oder Mehrfachsystems.
Klein, unsichtbar und ungewöhnlich massereich
Doch der Begleiter des Roten Riesen gibt den Forschenden Rätsel auf. Er ist sehr klein und außergewöhnlich massereich.
Das mysteriöse Objekt ist außerdem unsichtbar. Es lässt sich also nicht direkt optisch wahrnehmen, sondern nur durch die Auswirkungen seiner Schwerkraft auf die Umlaufbahn des Roten Riesen.
Ist das unsichtbare Objekt ein Neutronenstern?
Um welche Art von Himmelskörper handelt es sich bei dem seltsamen Begleiter? Die Autor:innen der Studie, die in der Zeitschrift Science Advances erschienen ist, tippten zunächst auf einen Neutronenstern.
Da Neutronensterne sehr klein sind, ist ihr Licht mit gängigen Instrumenten meist nicht messbar. Diese extrem dichten Objekte entstehen, wenn ein massiver Stern als Supernova explodiert.
Neutronensterne besitzen typischerweise eine Sonnenmasse von 1,4. Sie sind also 1,4 Mal so massereich wie unsere Sonne.
Zu schwer für einen Neutronenstern – zu leicht für Schwarzes Loch
Der mutmaßliche Neutronenstern im neuentdeckten Doppelsystem weist laut den Forschenden jedoch eine Sonnenmasse zwischen 1,8 und 2,8 auf. Die wahrscheinlichste Schätzung liegt bei 2,2 Sonnenmassen.
Für einen Neutronenstern ist das Objekt also zu massiv. Für ein Schwarzes Loch ist es aber wiederum nicht massereich genug. Dieser Typ entsteht, wenn noch massereichere Sterne als bei den Neutronensternen explodieren.
Leichte Schwarze Löcher sind mindestens drei Mal so massig wie unsere Sonne. Supermassive Schwarze Löcher können bis zu mehreren Milliarden Sonnenmassen entsprechen. Schwarze Löcher sind unsichtbar, da das Licht ihrer starken Anziehungskraft nicht entkommen kann.
Gigantischer Neutronenstern oder schwaches Schwarzes Loch?
„Damit befindet sich der unsichtbare Begleiter potenziell in der Masselücke zwischen Neutronensternen und Schwarzen Löchern“, heißt es in der Studie. Es handelt sich also entweder um einen besonders massiven Neutronenstern oder ein extrem massearmes Schwarzes Loch.
Am wahrscheinlichsten ist es laut der Studie, dass der mysteriöse Kompagnon ein supermassiver Neutronenstern ist. Diese Objekte sind ziemlich selten, da sie sich von ihrer Masse her an der Grenze bewegen, an der ein Stern normalerweise zu einem Schwarzen Loch kollabiert.
So könnte der supermassive Neutronenstern entstanden sein
Auf die Frage, wie dieser mutmaßliche supermassive Neutronenstern entstanden ist, haben die Forschenden noch keine Antwort. Supermassive Neutronensterne können in Doppelsystemen entstehen, wenn Neutronensterne Materie vom anderen Stern absorbieren.
Doch in diesem Fall liegen die Umlaufbahnen des Roten Riesen und seines Begleiters so weit auseinander, dass ein direkter Austausch von Materie unmöglich scheint.
Entdeckung stellt Stand der Forschung infrage
Stattdessen könnte das System ursprünglich aus drei Sternen bestanden haben. Aus zwei Neutronensternen oder einem Neutronen- und einem normalen Stern könnte sich ein einziges, supermassives Exemplar geformt haben.
Die Forschenden schließen auch nicht die Möglichkeit aus, dass supermassive Neutronensterne aus ganz normalen Supernovae entstehen können. Und unser bisheriges Wissen über extrem massive Himmelskörper noch große Lücken aufweist.

articles.title: Amazon Polly launches voice cloning: A unique voice for your brand | Amazon Web Services
articles.text:
Artificial Intelligence
Amazon Polly launches voice cloning: A unique voice for your brand
Voice cloning in Amazon Polly is now generally available as a gated release. Give Amazon Polly a few minutes of audio recordings from a speaker who has agreed to have their voice cloned, and Amazon Polly builds your own cloned voice in that speaker’s voice. The cloned voices run on the Amazon Polly generative engine, which delivers similar naturalness and accuracy as the rest of the generative voices. Amazon Polly voice cloning launches with seven languages: English, Spanish, German, French, Italian, Portuguese, and Hindi. Each cloned voice speaks the language it was recorded in. The cloned voices are automatically encrypted and access-controlled: only you can access your cloned voices.
Amazon Polly voice cloning is available in all the AWS Regions supported by the Amazon Polly generative engine, including the AWS GovCloud (US) Region. Access is already enabled for select Amazon Polly customers. Others can reach out to their AWS account team or apply for access to get access.
With this new feature addition, you can build the cloning lifecycle into AWS applications. Building a cloned voice is free for Amazon Polly customers, and Amazon Polly charges for cloned voice usage on a pay-as-you-go basis, see Amazon Polly Pricing page for details.
Hear it for yourself
Press play: the first few seconds are a real recording of the speaker, and then their cloned voice takes over with words they never recorded.
- From recordings to TTS voice. A few minutes of our science lead Trevor’s source audio, and the resulting generative voice. 
         
  - Recorded: “Hello, I’m Trevor, from Science.” Cloned voice: “That first sentence was my real voice. This is my cloned voice, created from a few minutes of my recordings. It can read any text you give it.”
- Supports seven languages. Hear Jonas, one of the authors, speaking German in his recording and then in his cloned voice: 
         
  - Recorded: “Hallo, ich bin Jonas. Das ist meine echte Stimme.” (Hi, I’m Jonas. This is my real voice.) Cloned voice: “Und das ist meine geklonte Stimme! Gleiche Stimme, neue Worte: Diesen Satz habe ich geschrieben, aber nie aufgenommen.” (And this is my cloned voice! Same voice, new words: I wrote this sentence, but never recorded it.)
- Use in a variety of applications. Here’s Trevor in a new job he hasn’t had: a non-player character in a game. 
         
  - “Who’s that crossing my bridge? Oh, it’s you again. Same deal as last time: answer my riddle, or hand over the sandwich.”
- Expand your voice library with voice cloning. Hear this audio sample from AWS Chief Evangelist Jeff Barr: a real recording, then his cloned voice.
         
  - Recorded: “Hi, I’m Jeff, and this is how I really sound.” Cloned voice: “And this is how my cloned voice sounds, reading a sentence I never recorded.”
- Hannah: a real recording, then her cloned voice on a support line.
         
  - Recorded: “Hello, I’m Hannah. This is my real voice.” Cloned voice: “Thanks for calling AnyCompany. Your order 4471 9902 ships today and should arrive on Thursday between 9 AM and 1 PM. Your confirmation code is K-7-Q-2-X-9.”
- Joely: a real recording, then her cloned voice narrating a lesson.
         
  - Recorded: “Hi, I’m Joely, and this is how I really sound.” Cloned voice: “In this module, we’ll look at how a neural network learns. First, it makes a guess. Then it measures how far off that guess was, and adjusts, a little at a time.”
What you can build
A consistent brand voice across channels
Establish one recognizable voice and use it across your interactive voice response (IVR) system, cascaded voice agents, mobile app, in-store announcements, advertising, and connected devices. Rather than relying on a generic stock voice or re-booking a recording session each time a script changes, you can generate on-brand audio on demand, with a consistent sound in every channel.
Contact centers
Deliver a distinctive, on-brand voice across self-service flows, and update prompts as offers and policies change without a new studio session. You can create prompts from source text, test them before rollout, and use the same voice across greeting, routing, and notification experiences.
Media and content at scale
Creators, publishers, and studios can create audiobooks, courses, podcasts, game characters, and videos in multiple custom voices to enhance the listening experience, and produce subsequent chapters or updates quickly.
Localization with a consistent persona
Maintain a recognizable voice identity across a content library, so narration remains coherent across titles and updates. Each cloned voice speaks only the language it was recorded in. For multilingual experiences, create and review approved voices per supported language.
Accessibility and personalization
Offer a natural, human-sounding voice for reading experiences, assistive tools, and personalized interactions. You confirm the speaker’s consent each time you create a voice.
How voice cloning works
With voice cloning, you can build a custom Amazon Polly voice from recordings of a single speaker and then synthesize speech in that voice through the Amazon Polly generative engine. The voice moves through four steps, from recording the speaker to using the finished voice:
A cloned voice goes through four steps:
- Record. You record one speaker (see the following recording tips). You can send the recordings directly in the CreateVoice request or upload them on the console. You can also store them in an Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) bucket in the AWS Region where you want the voice and point Amazon Polly to them.
- Create. You call CreateVoice with 1-10 recordings, the language they are spoken in, and TermsAccepted=True, your confirmation that you have the speaker’s consent. Amazon Polly returns a voice ID (vc-…) right away and builds the voice in the background.
- Wait. Creation is asynchronous and typically takes 5-10 minutes. During that time, Amazon Polly also checks the quality of your text-to-speech (TTS) voice for speaker similarity. You call GetVoice until the status changes from pending to active or failed.
- Use. You pass the voice ID to SynthesizeSpeech for real-time audio or to StartSpeechSynthesisTask for long-form audio written to S3, with Engine="generative", the same way you call the other generative voices in Amazon Polly. When you no longer need the voice, you call DeleteVoice.
Consent and control
A cloned voice is made from one person’s recordings. You confirm that you have the speaker’s consent for all recordings and that you control who can use the voice and when it’s deleted.
- You confirm consent for each voice you create. When you create a voice, on the console or with TermsAccepted=True in the API, you confirm that you have obtained all rights and consents necessary to create and use the cloned voice. Your use of voice cloning is subject to the AWS Service Terms, the Biometric Notice and Consent Terms, the AWS Responsible AI Policy, and the AWS Acceptable Use Policy.
- Generated speech carries a watermark. Amazon Polly adds a watermark to text-to-speech audio generated with the cloned voice.
- Only your account can use it. A cloned voice is scoped to the AWS account that created it, and you control access with AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM). You can encrypt voices with your own AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) key and tag them.
- You decide when it goes away. Delete a voice with one DeleteVoice call or on the console, once it’s active or its creation has failed.
- Amazon Polly does not retain a copy of your voice recordings once the voice is created and doesn’t use them to train Amazon Polly models. It keeps only the voice data it needs to synthesize speech, and stores it encrypted. You can use your own AWS KMS key for that encryption, and DeleteVoice removes the data immediately.
We recommend that you:
- Keep a record of each speaker’s consent.
- Delete the voice if the speaker withdraws consent.
- Tell listeners when they’re hearing a synthetic voice where that’s appropriate.
- Grant voice permissions only to the people and systems that need them.
For details on intended uses and limitations, see the Amazon Polly AI Service Card and the AWS Responsible Use of AI guidance.
Best practices for recordings
Your cloned voice learns from the recording, including the parts you’d rather it didn’t: the laptop fan, the room echo, the meeting app’s noise filter.
- Record two to ten minutes of natural speech, split into takes of up to a minute. You can send up to 10 recordings per voice, and up to 15 minutes of audio in total. Quality matters more than length: more audio might not change how the voice sounds.
- One speaker, a quiet room, the same distance from the mic. Use a USB microphone, or a phone app that can record WAV. Record in mono WAV, 16-bit, at 24 kHz from the start, so there’s nothing to convert later. Amazon Polly accepts other audio formats, but we recommend WAV. See the Amazon Polly Developer Guide for supported formats and limits.
- Avoid using meeting apps and browser recorders. Their echo cancellation and noise suppression change the voice, and the clone learns those changes too.
- Record every take in the style you want the voice to have. The cloned voice takes its style from the recordings and can’t blend several, so upbeat, sad, and angry takes won’t give you a voice that can do all three.
- Record in the language the voice should speak. Voice cloning is tested with recordings in US English, German, US Spanish, French, Italian, Brazilian Portuguese, and Hindi. Recordings in other accents of these languages, such as British English or Canadian French, also work but are less tested, so check the voice with your own content.
Getting started
On the console: once voice cloning is enabled for your account (see Availability), expand the left panel and choose Voice cloning, upload up to 10 recordings or select them from Amazon S3, confirm the terms, and choose Create. Each upload can be up to 5 MB. When the voice is ready, try it out on its details page.
In code, you need:
- The latest version of boto3 (pip install --upgrade boto3).
- IAM permissions for polly:CreateVoice, polly:GetVoice, polly:DescribeVoices, polly:SynthesizeSpeech and polly:DeleteVoice. For long-form audio, also polly:StartSpeechSynthesisTask, polly:GetSpeechSynthesisTask and s3:PutObject on the output bucket.
- For the following Amazon S3 example: your recordings in a bucket in the Region where you create the voice, with s3:GetObject permission for the IAM role or user that calls CreateVoice.
If Python reports that the Polly object has no attribute create_voice, upgrade boto3.
For long texts such as audiobook chapters or course modules, use an asynchronous synthesis task that writes the audio to S3:
For additional end-to-end Speech AI applications you can build with Amazon Polly, including the voice cloning feature, such as cascaded voice agents and live speech translators, go to the Amazon Polly GitHub repo.
Production considerations
Create voices ahead of time
Voice creation takes minutes, so treat it as a provisioning step, not part of a user request. A small workflow (for example, AWS Step Functions or a job queue) can call CreateVoice, check GetVoice every 30 seconds until the voice is active, and then store the voice ID in your configuration. CreateVoice and DeleteVoice share a limit of 1 request per second, so queue bulk creations and deletions.
Keep an inventory
DescribeVoices lists your cloned voices alongside the voices built into Amazon Polly. Cloned voices have Origin set to customer. Store the voice ID, Region, language, consent reference, and owner for each voice, and give each voice a unique Name. If a CreateVoice call times out or returns a server error, the voice might already exist, and the SDK’s automatic retries can create a second one. Check DescribeVoices for that name before you try again.
Plan for errors
CreateVoice returns ThrottlingException when you exceed the 1-request-per-second limit it shares with DeleteVoice, and ServiceQuotaExceededException when the account has reached its cloned-voice quota in that Region. Synthesizing with, or deleting, a voice that is still being created returns ConflictException. If a voice uses your own KMS key, callers without access to the key get an access-denied error. When creation fails, StatusReason gives only a general message, so check the recordings against the preceding recording best practices, then delete the failed voice and create a new one.
Scope permissions to voices
Cloned voices are IAM resources, so you can give the role that serves traffic permission to synthesize with one voice of choice. If the voice uses your own KMS key, that role also needs access to the key. Keep polly:CreateVoice and polly:DeleteVoice for a separate provisioning role. Here’s an example policy for the serving role:
With tags, you can write the same rule once for a whole group of voices using aws:ResourceTag conditions. Review your existing policies too: a statement that allows polly:SynthesizeSpeech on all resources ("Resource": "*") also covers every cloned voice in the account.
Plan for quotas and Regions
Each account has an initial quota of 10 cloned voices per Region. To request an increase, contact your account team or AWS Support. A voice exists only in the account and Region where you created it. To serve another Region or account, create the voice again in that Region from the same recordings, and make sure the speaker’s consent covers every copy.
Test with your real scripts
Before a voice goes live, listen to it reading your own content: product names, numbers, addresses, and the longest sentences you have. The same text can come out slightly differently from one request to the next. For fixed prompts such as phone-line greetings, generate the audio once, approve it with the speaker and your brand team, and serve the stored file. If a name or term comes out wrong, spell it differently in the text or use a Speech Synthesis Markup Language (SSML) <phoneme> tag. Phoneme tags work with cloned voices in English, French, Italian, German, and Spanish. See Supported SSML tags.
Things to know
| Availability | Access is enabled per AWS account. If you see Voice cloning in the Amazon Polly console (expand the left panel and see if Voice cloning is listed), it’s enabled for your account. If not, you can reach out to your AWS account team or apply for access to request access. Supported AWS Regions are the same as the generative engine: US East (N. Virginia), US West (Oregon), Europe (Frankfurt), Europe (Zurich), Europe (London), Asia Pacific (Sydney), Asia Pacific (Seoul), Asia Pacific (Singapore), Asia Pacific (Tokyo), Canada (Central), and AWS GovCloud (US-West). A cloned voice lives in the AWS Region where you created it. | 
| Languages | English, German, Spanish, French, Italian, Portuguese, and Hindi. Tested recording locales: US English ( en-US), German (de-DE), US Spanish (es-US), French (fr-FR), Italian (it-IT), Brazilian Portuguese (pt-BR), and Hindi (hi-IN). Other accents of these languages also work but are less tested. Each voice speaks the language it was recorded in. | 
| Recordings | 1-10 recordings per voice, up to 15 minutes in total. WAV is recommended: mono, 16-bit, at 24 kHz or 44.1/48 kHz. Amazon Polly accepts other audio formats too. Console uploads are limited to 5 MB per file. For larger files, use Amazon S3. | 
| Data handling | Amazon Polly deletes its copy of your recordings once the voice is created and doesn’t use them to train Amazon Polly models. It keeps only the voice data needed for synthesis, stored encrypted (you can use your own AWS KMS key), until you call DeleteVoice. | 
| Creation time | Typically takes 5-10 minutes to build a TTS voice, asynchronous. | 
| Synthesis latency | Same as Generative voices in Amazon Polly. | 
| Quotas | 10 cloned voices per account per AWS Region initially. To request an increase, contact AWS Support. CreateVoice and DeleteVoice share a limit of 1 request per second. | 
| Synthesis | Cloned voices follow the Amazon Polly quotas for generative voices, including the text limits per request and per synthesis task. See Amazon Polly quotas. | 
| Pricing | Creating a cloned voice is free. Amazon Polly charges for cloned voice usage on a pay-as-you-go basis. See Amazon Polly pricing. | 
| APIs | CreateVoice, GetVoice, DeleteVoice and DescribeVoices to manage voices. SynthesizeSpeech and StartSpeechSynthesisTask with Engine="generative" to use them. See the Amazon Polly API reference. | 
Conclusion
Voice cloning in Amazon Polly gives your application a voice people recognize: recorded once, with the speaker’s consent, and ready to use through the Amazon Polly APIs. To get started on the console, make sure Voice cloning is enabled for your account, prepare a recording and the required consent, open the Amazon Polly console, and create your first cloned voice. If you are a new customer and would like to enable voice cloning, reach out to your AWS account team or apply for access to get access.
For the developer guide, refer to the Amazon Polly documentation. For pricing, see the Amazon Polly Pricing Page. For additional speech AI use cases you can build with Amazon Polly, including voice cloning, check out the GitHub repo.
We can’t wait to hear what you build.
Thanks to Trevor Wood, Jonas Rohnke, Suyin Wang, Hannah Barrett, Nikie Xiong, Jeff Barr, and Joely Huang for lending us their voices.

articles.title: Los nacidos entre 1960 y 1970 pueden cobrar el 100% de la pensión, pero necesitan haber cotizado estos años
articles.text:
Quienes han nacido entre 1960 y 1970 ya no tienen tan lejos la jubilación, y por eso es un buen momento para repasar cuánto aspiran a cobrar y los años cotizados que necesitan para llegar al 100% de la pensión. El número de años cotizados es uno de los factores que más pesan, porque marca tanto la edad a la que puedes retirarte como el porcentaje de la base reguladora que te corresponde.
Si vemos los datos de la edad de jubilación, durante 2026 hacen falta 36 años y seis meses de cotización para cobrar ese 100%, y a partir de 2027 el listón sube a 37 años. Pero cobrar la pensión máxima también depende de las bases por las que hayas cotizado a lo largo de tu vida laboral.
Cuántos años hacen falta para el 100% y para jubilarse a los 65
La pensión se calcula combinando los años cotizados con la base reguladora, que a su vez se obtiene a partir de las bases de cotización del trabajador durante un periodo concreto. Según las tablas de la Ley General de la Seguridad Social, los primeros 15 años cotizados dan derecho al 50% de la base reguladora, y a partir de ahí cada mes adicional va sumando un pequeño porcentaje hasta completar el 100%.
Otra cosa que cuenta es la edad ordinaria de jubilación, que el calendario de la reforma de las pensiones va subiendo poco a poco hasta llegar a los 67 años en 2027 para quienes no acrediten suficiente cotización. Durante 2026 pueden jubilarse a los 65 años los trabajadores que hayan cotizado al menos 38 años y tres meses, mientras que para el resto la edad ordinaria es de 66 años y diez meses.
A partir de 2027 los requisitos quedan así: 65 años para quien acredite al menos 38 años y seis meses cotizados, y 67 años para quien no llegue a ese periodo. Vamos, que hay que distinguir entre los años que te dan el 100% de la base reguladora y los que te permiten jubilarte a los 65, porque son dos requisitos diferentes y cumplir uno no garantiza cumplir el otro.
El nuevo cálculo de la base reguladora y las otras formas de jubilarse
Lo que acabes cobrando depende también de las bases de cotización que hayas ido acumulando. Hasta 2025, el cálculo tenía en cuenta los últimos 25 años de cotización, pero desde 2026 tenemos un sistema dual: la Seguridad Social calcula la base reguladora con las dos fórmulas y aplica de oficio la que resulte más favorable para el trabajador.
¿Y cómo es la fórmula nueva? En 2026 toma las 302 bases más altas de los últimos 304 meses, y ese periodo se va ampliando poco a poco hasta 2037, cuando ya se contarán las 324 mejores bases dentro de un periodo de 29 años, de manera que se podrán descartar los dos años con las cotizaciones más bajas.
Este cambio puede beneficiar a las personas que han tenido etapas con ingresos más bajos o interrupciones a lo largo de su trayectoria laboral, porque esos meses peores pueden acabar quedándose fuera del cálculo.
Otra cosa a tener en cuenta es que llegar al 100% de la base reguladora significa que tienes derecho a cobrar todo el porcentaje que te corresponde según el cálculo de la Seguridad Social, pero no garantiza que vayas a recibir la pensión máxima. Esta depende de las bases de cotización y está sujeta a un límite legal que se actualiza cada año. Por eso dos personas que hayan cotizado exactamente los mismos años pueden acabar cobrando cantidades diferentes.
También hay distintas modalidades de jubilación. Por una parte tienesla jubilación anticipada que te permite dejar de trabajar antes a cambio de reducir permanentemente tu pensión final. Y luego tienes la jubilación parcial, que combina una reducción de la jornada laboral con el cobro de una parte de la prestación.
Existe también la jubilación activa, que permite seguir trabajando mientras se cobra una parte de la pensión, y la jubilación demorada, pensada para quienes deciden alargar su vida laboral más allá de la edad ordinaria y que, según la guía del CSIF, da derecho a incentivos económicos. Para los nacidos entre 1960 y 1970, revisar el historial laboral y las bases de cotización es especialmente importante a la hora de planificar esta etapa, porque de esos años y de esas bases depende tanto cuándo podrán jubilarse como cuánto van a cobrar.
