articles.title: El MIT crea el primer microrobot volador con sensores y computadora propios capaz de operar fuera del laboratorio
articles.text:
Investigadores del Instituto de Tecnología de Massachusetts (MIT) diseñaron un microrrobot aéreo de alas batientes con sensores y computación a bordo, capaz de seguir una trayectoria compleja y aterrizar con precisión sobre un girasol sin depender del sistema externo de cámaras usado hasta ahora en el laboratorio. Aunque todavía recibe energía desde una fuente externa, el avance abre la puerta a usos prácticos en entornos que los robots de mayor tamaño no pueden alcanzar, informó MIT News, el portal de noticias del instituto.
El vehículo pesa menos que un clip y tiene un tamaño y una forma similares a los de un microcasete. Sus cuatro alas se mueven mediante actuadores blandos, músculos artificiales que baten con rapidez y le permiten realizar maniobras detalladas.
Los investigadores rediseñaron esos actuadores para que el robot pudiera cargar la electrónica necesaria y volar de forma autónoma. Los agrandaron un 50%, lo que se tradujo en un 46% más de fuerza de sustentación —es decir, mayor capacidad para levantar peso y mantenerse en el aire—. Con esa mejora, el robot alcanzó una relación sustentación-peso de 1,9, suficiente para transportar un paquete electrónico de apenas 244 miligramos.
El sistema incorpora, además, una unidad de medición inercial para estimar su orientación, un sensor de flujo óptico que calcula la velocidad lateral y la posición, y un sensor de tiempo de vuelo que mide la altura. Esos componentes permiten que el aparato perciba su movimiento y ejecute cálculos durante el vuelo.
“Este es un hito muy importante para la comunidad de investigación. Es la primera demostración de un microrrobot aéreo autónomo en percepción y computación”, afirmó Kevin Chen, profesor asociado del Departamento de Ingeniería Eléctrica y Ciencias de la Computación del MIT y director del Laboratorio de Robótica Blanda y Micro dentro del Laboratorio de Investigación en Electrónica.
Chen señaló que existen tareas, como la polinización o la vigilancia industrial, para las que no puede utilizarse un robot de mayor tamaño. “Los robots a pequeña escala están especialmente indicados para este tipo de trabajos y, si esta línea tecnológica tiene éxito en el futuro, podría ser muy prometedora”, sostuvo.
Sensores para volar sin cámaras externas
Los microrrobots aéreos desarrollados durante la última década por el MIT podían moverse con una velocidad, agilidad y resistencia comparables a las de un abejorro. Sin embargo, dependían de un sistema de captura de movimiento instalado en el laboratorio, lo que los restringía a operar únicamente en ese entorno controlado y limitaba su aplicabilidad en situaciones reales.
Al prescindir de ese sistema para poder operar en entornos reales, surgió un nuevo obstáculo: los sensores a bordo no replican su precisión, por lo que el robot puede desviarse de su recorrido aunque mida el movimiento, la orientación y la altura.
El equipo diseñó entonces un algoritmo que procesa los datos de esos sensores y estima la orientación, la velocidad angular y la posición del robot de forma extremadamente rápida, lo que simplifica los cálculos para reducir el costo computacional, y prioriza estimaciones continuas y veloces, que ofrecieron mejores resultados que mediciones más precisas pero lentas.
“Dedicamos mucho tiempo a optimizar la selección de sensores y estimadores de posición para que el robot tuviera una desviación muy baja”, explicó Yi-Hsuan Hsiao, estudiante de posgrado del MIT y uno de los autores principales. “Ahora puede volar con una precisión posicional comparable a la que logra con cámaras externas”.
Los sensores y los componentes de cómputo fueron montados sobre un sustrato de fibra de vidrio, una decisión destinada a evitar que las vibraciones del robot alteraran el funcionamiento de la electrónica.
Jonathan P. How, profesor Ford de Aeronáutica y Astronáutica del MIT e investigador principal del Laboratorio de Sistemas de Información y Decisión y del Laboratorio de Control Aeroespacial, remarcó las restricciones de diseño: “Cuando se trata de una computadora tan pequeña, hay que pensar cuidadosamente cada detalle. Debe encargarse tanto de la percepción como del control, caber en el robot y operar con la velocidad necesaria para que el vehículo se mantenga estable durante el vuelo”, indicó How.
El objetivo de polinizar cultivos y evitar obstáculos
Las pruebas incluyeron vuelos estacionarios a distintas alturas y recorridos entre puntos determinados. El aparato se desplazó con rapidez y precisión, con errores de posición de apenas unos centímetros.
Los investigadores también usaron un joystick para enviar indicaciones generales de posición y guiar al vehículo alrededor de varias plantas antes de que aterrizara cuidadosamente sobre un girasol. La demostración buscó mostrar su potencial para la polinización artificial.
En el futuro, estos robots podrían desplazarse entre almendros o arbustos de arándanos para polinizar flores delicadas en regiones donde las poblaciones naturales de polinizadores fueron diezmadas por la pérdida de hábitat. También podrían mantenerse suspendidos cerca de las plantas sin dañarlas, controlar el estado de los cultivos e identificar plagas antes de que se extiendan.
El análisis del consumo energético determinó que la electrónica utiliza cerca del 6% de la potencia total. El resto alimenta los músculos artificiales y las alas del robot.
La reducción adicional de ese consumo permitiría sumar componentes como una cámara para reconocer objetos. El grupo trabaja ahora en integrar ese dispositivo para que el vehículo identifique objetos y evite obstáculos de forma autónoma, además de incorporar electrónica de potencia y baterías que hagan posible el vuelo sin conexión externa en ambientes al aire libre.
La investigación, publicada en Science Robotics, fue realizada por Hsiao, Quang Phuc Kieu y Zhongtao Guan como autores principales, junto con Chen, How, Elizabeth Farrell Helbling, profesora asistente de la Universidad de Cornell, y otros integrantes del MIT.

articles.title: Nvidia's latest drivers may be wearing out your SSD with tens of gigabytes of unnecessary writes
articles.text:
TL;DR: Users who have recently updated their Nvidia display drivers should check the Resource Monitor's Disk tab to see whether an executable called NVDisplay.Container.exe is writing excessively to the disk. Nvidia had not acknowledged the issue at the time of writing, but reports claim that it now writes tens of gigabytes per day, which might shorten an SSD's lifespan. Until Nvidia provides a fix, rolling back to driver version 621.01 is the only foolproof remedy.
TroubleGrid recently published a summary of the issue, which impacts driver versions 621.14 and 621.24, both released in November. Besides rolling back drivers, users can restart the affected service or change the display container settings, but neither solution is perfect.
The problem occurs because the display container service now rewrites its log instead of appending to it, exponentially increasing the amount of data written to the SSD. Users can confirm whether they are experiencing the issue by opening the Resource Monitor app, clicking the Disk tab, and searching for a process called "NVDisplay.Container.exe" to see how much data it is writing in bytes.
While some users report the figure holding steady at around 20 MB, others report it writing dozens of gigabytes each day, even while idle. SSDs start breaking down after writing a certain amount of data, usually measured in hundreds of terabytes, so it's best to monitor how much each program writes.
The simplest countermeasure is to stop the service, delete the log, and restart it. To do this, press Windows + R, type "services.msc," press Enter, find "NVIDIA Display Container LS," and select Stop from the right-click menu. Then, delete the file at "C:\ProgramData\NVIDIA Corporation\nvtopps\nct\nvlog.nvlgstg," return to the display container service, and click Start. While this might reduce data usage by up to 91%, the solution is only temporary, as the file will grow back.
A more permanent but still problematic solution is to set the service to manual. Find it in services.msc again, double-click it, change "Startup type" from Automatic to Manual, click Stop, and click OK. Unfortunately, this prevents the Nvidia Control Panel and Nvidia App from working properly, so users should only try this if they don't need to change resolution or graphics settings via those menus.
Finally, as the issue has not been reported in driver version 621.01, users can safely revert to it. It is available via the Nvidia app, on the company's website, or on third-party sites like TechSpot.
AMD recently fixed a similar problem that caused the External Events Utility service to create a process that could write more than 400GB per day. To resolve the issue, install AMD Radeon Adrenalin hotfix version 26.11.1.

articles.title: Where should AI workloads run? Probably next to the data.
articles.text:
Where should AI workloads run? Probably next to the data.
AWS raised prices on EC2 Capacity Blocks, its reserved GPU capacity, by about 15% in January and about 20% in July. Picture a platform team watching a training job’s bill climb after copying a few hundred terabytes of sensor data across regions just to reach the GPUs, then realizing the data never had to move.
For AI workloads, the real question is whether the workload goes to the data or the data goes to the workload. Data gravity usually answers it.
Data gravity hits AI workloads harder than it ever hit analytics
Data gravity is the tendency of compute, applications, and services to be pulled toward large concentrations of data, because moving the data costs more than moving the logic that processes it. The larger a dataset grows, the more expensive every copy becomes, and the more everything that needs that data ends up living next to it.
Scheduled BI often tolerates periodic queries against sampled or aggregated data. Large training runs can require repeated reads of a much larger dataset, while agents retrieve fresh context throughout a workflow. When those reads cross regions or environments, transfer costs and latency add up. Each agent output also becomes new data that feeds the next round of retrieval, which compounds the pull over time.
A January 2026 analysis in BigDATAwire argued that AI workloads removed the cushion that let enterprises leave data gravity unmanaged for a decade. The year’s pricing moves make the same point from the cost side. Combined, the two increases add up to roughly 38% on the H200 instances that took both.
Moving data to the compute stops working at AI scale
Centralizing compute can require copying data into its environment before a job starts, and that transfer may carry charges.
For illustration, assume a transfer rate of $0.02 per GB and a 300 TB dataset (300,000 GB). The transfer alone would cost $6,000 per copy. That’s a hypothetical, not an AWS quote. Real charges depend on source, destination, route, service, and terms, so cross-region and cloud-to-premises movement needs explicit costing. Remote reads also add network latency, which matters when a workload has a tight response-time target.
“Transfer bills, duplicate pipelines and the engineering hours spent maintaining them belong in the placement calculation alongside compute charges.”
Two more costs rarely show up next to the GPU rate:
- Interoperability overhead: cross-environment pipelines need their own translation layers when engines, query languages, connectors, and software development kits (SDKs) differ.
- Lock-in: transfer charges and the engineering work of moving data and pipelines can make leaving an environment expensive.
Transfer bills, duplicate pipelines and the engineering hours spent maintaining them belong in the placement calculation alongside compute charges.
Moving compute to the data instead
A scheduling and placement layer can send a job to an environment that already holds its data, avoiding repeated full-dataset transfers. The job still needs compatible accelerators, enough memory, a supported runtime, and adequate storage throughput. Model weights, container images and checkpoints may also need to move.
Making that decision well means evaluating four inputs together, every time a job is scheduled:
| Input | What to evaluate | 
|---|---|
| Cost | The total cost of this job in each candidate environment, including compute, transfer, storage, and queueing, at current prices. | 
| Data gravity | How much data the job needs, where it sits, and what it would cost to move. | 
| Residency | Which jurisdictions the data and the job are allowed to touch. | 
| Policy | Which access rules, classifications and quality gates apply wherever the job lands. | 
A placement layer first excludes environments that violate residency or access rules, then compares feasible options by capacity, performance, and total cost. It dispatches the job with its runtime policies and revisits placement when those conditions change.
Where a specific workload belongs depends on the workload
There’s no universal rule. It’s a workload-by-workload decision.
Bursty training: public cloud can suit elastic demand, provided suitable GPU capacity is available, and transfer costs don’t erase the benefit.
Residency-restricted work: applicable law or contract determines the permitted jurisdiction and environment. An approved in-region cloud can qualify where an out-of-region on-premises cluster cannot. Large data volume adds an economic constraint, not a legal one.
Transaction-near inference: place execution close enough to the transaction to meet its latency target, whether in cloud, on-premises or at the edge.
Back to the platform team. Their training job reads a large dataset from an on-premises store, and policy excludes processing outside an approved region. A local cluster has the required GPU memory and runtime. An approved cloud region offers suitable GPUs but requires copying the dataset. So they compare completion time and total cost, including transfer, storage, and queueing. If local execution meets the deadline at lower total cost, the job runs there with the same access controls. If not, they assess the approved cloud option.
If neither environment meets policy and capacity requirements, the job is queued or rejected rather than sent to an unapproved region with restricted data. They record the choice and its assumptions so a price change, a growing dataset, or a missed deadline triggers a new review.
Formal policy on all this is uneven. In BARC’s State of Data and AI Governance study, which Acceldata sponsored, 56% of North American respondents report formal sovereignty policies for AI processing and storage, against 30% in Europe, the Middle East and Africa (EMEA). That runs against expectations, since Europe is known for strict data rules. EMEA respondents also name siloed data as a top governance obstacle more than twice as often as their North American peers, 35% versus 17%.
Hybrid architecture matters more than picking a cloud
Hybrid can be a lasting architecture, not merely a stop on the way to the cloud. Data-heavy, latency-sensitive, or sovereignty-bound work can stay on-premises, while the cloud handles demand where elasticity is worth the cost.
It needs common operational controls across both environments: identity, runtime compatibility, observability, and policy enforcement. An all-cloud estate incurs transfer and lock-in costs when data must leave a region or provider. An all-on-premises estate leaves bursty work waiting for fixed capacity.
“Hybrid can be a lasting architecture, not merely a stop on the way to the cloud.”
Job portability helps only where the target environment supports the required engines, dependencies, and hardware. Open table formats such as Apache Iceberg, Delta Lake, and Apache Hudi help here, because several engines can read the same tables in place. Moving the job doesn’t have to mean converting or copying the data first.
This is the problem Acceldata built its xLake platform around: keep data where it lives, in open formats, and bring governed compute to it across cloud and on-premises environments.
Sovereign AI requires more than GPU power
The sovereign AI conversation usually starts with GPUs, but GPU compute alone is an incomplete architecture. Owning or reserving GPU capacity says nothing about whether the data feeding those GPUs, or the retrieval and orchestration layers around them, stays inside infrastructure the organization controls. Sovereignty is a property of the whole data and AI stack. Compute is one layer of it.
For a strict customer-controlled boundary, Acceldata’s May 2026 analysis of sovereign GPU infrastructure identifies four controls:
- Route tool calls through internally hosted endpoints so operational data, prompts, and workflow context never leave the organization’s network.
- Retrieval infrastructure (embedding indexes and vector search) running on infrastructure the organization controls rather than a provider-managed vector service.
- Orchestration of prompts, memory, and intermediate agent state inside the organization’s own environment.
- Access policies for permissions and retrieval scope enforced within that same governed boundary.
“A workload can run on the most expensive reserved GPUs available and still fail a sovereignty review if its prompts, embeddings, or agent state cross a boundary they were never cleared to cross.”
Placement decisions inherit all four. A workload can run on the most expensive reserved GPUs available and still fail a sovereignty review if its prompts, embeddings, or agent state cross a boundary they were never cleared to cross.
The workload goes where the data already lives
Changes in compute prices are a reason to revisit placement, not proof that one environment is always cheaper. Transfer charges, storage, engineering effort, and completion time belong in the same comparison. That makes the cost of reaching the data a first-order input to any placement call, not a footnote to the GPU rate.
Keep the assumptions with each decision: dataset location, permitted destinations, compatible capacity, expected completion time, and total cost. When one changes, review the affected workload. Where running beside the data wins, move the job instead of the dataset.
Teams that revisit placement now, while their datasets are still manageable, will spend less fighting data gravity later than teams that keep copying data to wherever the GPUs happen to be.
That’s the lesson the platform team learned the hard way at the start of this piece. The data never had to move. The job did.

articles.title: Superhuman unveils personal AI assistant and expands Go across entire suite - SiliconANGLE
articles.text:
Superhuman unveils personal AI assistant and expands Go across entire suite
Superhuman Inc., formerly known as Grammarly, today announced the expansion of Go, its proactive artificial intelligence assistant and multi-agent platform, along with updated features across its entire suite.
Among the updates, the company added a new personalized AI assistant in Go that users can name, give work to and ask to watch projects and to-do lists in the background. The new assistant will work across connected tools, suggest next steps, draft content in the user’s voice, and manage a team of other AI agents, with the user always in the loop.
Superhuman also brought agents into Docs and Mail and updated Fathom, the company’s note-taking app, to act as a collaborative, bot-free app that connects natively to every application across the Superhuman suite and captures video, screen sharing, and audio.
“Superhuman is solving for the last mile of AI: the gap between deployment and adoption,” said Chief Executive Shishir Mehrotra. “The best AI shows up for your whole team, not just the power users who go looking for it. It’s embedded in the tools you already use, it works ahead of you, and it collaborates alongside you.”
A personal agent for everyone
Superhuman Go is growing with a personal agent that works ahead of a user on their behalf, with their approval. The company said the new Go assistant acts like an extra set of eyes and ears, watching out for users throughout their day, finding tasks they need to do, and keeping up with their “need to know.” It tries to stay ahead of their task list, offers to complete things it can, picks up slack, summarizes meeting notes, and answers important emails or preps for important meetings.
It also writes like the user and gets better over time with direction. It learns from past responses to draft content that sounds like them, refines writing before they hit send, and keeps learning their style to improve over time.
Superhuman said that it added more than 20 new partner agents, which can help pull in expert knowledge and capabilities from enterprise services. For example, a user can connect to Legora AB’s agent for legal intelligence, Databricks Inc.’s Live Metrics agent for metrics and relevant numbers, Amplitude Inc.’s Product check agent to verify product usage claims, and Blackboard Inc.’s Assignment Coach agent to help students improve coursework.
With the rise of personal AI agents such as OpenClaw and Meta Platform Inc.’s Muse, the open-source community, startups and enterprises have begun offering personalized agents that autonomously assist users with day-to-day tasks and work. Anthropic PBC also recently launched Claude Duet, a similar proactive AI agent for professionals and small businesses in private preview, that completes tasks when asked and keeps working in the background.
Agentic collaboration throughout the entire suite
Superhuman Go agents are now native in Docs, the company’s AI-native collaborative workspace that combines documents, spreadsheets and automated workflows. Users can share a doc with any agent, just mentioning it with @ to hand off work, and it will show up as another collaborator.
Users can add agents with triggers for when to run, and they will interact with the document whether it’s open or not, updating it whenever something changes. This will allow agents to collaborate by adding to the document and changing it by checking email, watching connected apps or checking connected tables, so that the information in the doc stays fresh.
Similarly, agents connect to Mail and every other tool. This means that when drafting an email, agents can suggest content as users type. Superhuman Mail can use agents to pull in information from Slack, meeting notes or internal documents. The company said auto drafts already saves users an average of nine minutes per draft. For a user who replies to four emails a day, that can save about three hours a week.
In addition to these changes, Superhuman said the Go platform software development kit is generally available to partners and customers with new agent-building capabilities. Partners can now easily build and connect their own agents that show up anywhere within Go. The company plans to add more specialized partner agents.

articles.title: How to tell a cyberattack from a plain old outage
articles.text:
Yet there’s still no evidence that any one of these clustered technological failures were related, much less caused by hackers. Their improbable, sequential timing left Americans anxiously doomscrolling for signs of foul play. But in cases like these, it’s the job of cybersecurity analysts (and reporters at WIRED) to determine—vibes aside—whether the latest tech outage was actually an accident or the result of a cyberattack.
The baseline for that fact-finding, as anyone tasked with investigating these incidents will tell you, is that the vast majority of these digital breakdowns are not the result of malicious intent but rather casualties of IT admins’ constant war to keep computer systems from collapsing under the weight of their own complexity.
“I’ve just seen enough times where we thought maybe it’s a cyberattack and it turns out it’s not. Sometimes it will be, but typically not,” says Matthew Prince, CEO of the Internet infrastructure company Cloudflare. “Right now, most of what we’re seeing is the standard background noise. Stuff breaks, and that’s just the nature of complex systems.”
So in the interest of soothing the country’s rattled nerves and helping us all find ground truth amid seemingly endless tech catastrophes, we at WIRED present our general guide to determining whether a tech outage is the result of a cyberattack. So take a breath—maybe open the bunker door to let in some fresh air—and read on.
1. Start with a presumption of innocence–or negligence
The process of determining the cause of an IT service outage should begin with the assumption that it was an accident, says cybersecurity researcher Doug Madory.
As the head of Internet analysis at the network security firm Infoblox, Madory says he monitors as many as a dozen network outages a day. Only around “one in a thousand,” he says, turns out to have been caused by hackers. “One’s default position should be that it isn’t a cyberattack,” he says, “unless there is some concrete evidence to the contrary.”
Given the rarity of cyberattacks compared to outages as a whole, it’s wise to look at other potential causes first. “Most big outages that look like attacks are self-inflicted,” says João Tomé, the Internet research editor at network data company IPinfo. (In response to WIRED’s questions, Tomé also wrote his own guide for distinguishing outages from cyberattacks.) The usual suspects, he says, include “a bad update, a configuration change, a cable cut, or a power failure.”
2. Look at status updates from organizations that might be involved
In the scramble to understand what’s really happening with a given outage, it can sometimes be difficult to tell which sites and services are actually down. And there can be a few reasons for this muddled picture. Sometimes, an outage occurs within a foundational service like a big cloud provider. Major downtime within Amazon Web Services, for example, can cause a cascade of other failures among the company’s customers, who are all dependent on that infrastructure.
In other cases, multiple services can seem to be having outages and producing errors but are functioning normally and only having problems when they interact with an entity that’s down. This appears to have been the case in this week’s bank outage: Multiple banks appeared to be having issues, but they all seem to have been linked to certain inter-institutional transactions that involved JPMorgan Chase. Another good example of this scenario is situations where it may appear that multiple wireless carriers are struggling, but all of the failed calls actually involve one network that’s having an outage.
On top of these, there are also scenarios where one or more large services are down, and false (typically accidental or anecdotal) reports of additional outages create further confusion and opacity.
It can all feel overwhelming, even impossible, to attempt to parse these situations yourself—but there is a concrete place to start. If you think a website or service from a major tech company may be down, look for acknowledgment of the situation on their verified social media accounts or in the “newsroom” press release section of their websites. And keep in mind that you can find these pages and social media accounts through search engines, so you definitely don’t need to be familiar with every company’s communications strategy. Use this same approach for government agencies and other institutions.
Another concrete and vital source of information that you can find through search engines is what’s often known as “status dashboard” pages. Large digital platforms specifically offer these informational pages to provide transparency into whether different components of their service are functioning normally or dealing with issues. In a major incident, companies often thread incremental updates about system restoration on the status dashboard. AWS, Google Cloud Platform, and Microsoft Azure all offer these landing pages, and there are similar ones for other services like Meta business products, Google Workspace, telecom companies, AI companies, and so on.
3. Check trusted sources of network data
When a cascading tech failure causes outages across many services at once, and the point of failure isn’t clear, sources of network data that monitor the Internet at a broad scale can also help determine the underlying issue. Amanda Meng, a research scientist at Georgia Tech who helps run its Internet Outage Detection and Analysis service, or IODA, points to not only IODA’s own data—and its social media accounts on BlueSky and Mastodon—but also tools like Cloudflare Radar and Watch the Net. Infoblox’s Madory also posts his own findings about network outages on his socialmediaaccounts.
When IODA sees evidence of a network disruption, “we’ll look at the timing of it, the start, the end, the network affected, anything we can find out about it, and then try and connect it with what we see from reporting,” Meng says. That scope, location, and timing of an outage can help determine a suspected cause, whether it’s a single network that might be the victim of a buggy update, a region cut off by damage to a fiber optic cable or, in rarer instances, a cyberattack or even a government purposefully cutting off Internet access to its citizens to stifle protests.
Even with those network clues, however, Meng advises returning to step two: Once an affected service is identified, its actual owners are often the best source to monitor for updates. “Usually the operators have the most information about what’s actually going on,” she says.
4. Look for claims of responsibility
Most often, mea culpa updates from companies or government agencies confirm an outage is caused by a tech mishap. In the rarer cases when that downtime results from an actual cyberattack or hacker breach, however, the hackers responsible often claim responsibility in some form.
Ransomware gangs, perhaps the most common source of serious malicious Internet disruption, publicize their breaches on dark web pages that list their targets for the purposes of extortion, sometimes with a countdown timer designed to pressure victims to pay before they leak stolen information. In other cases, like the NotPetya or WannaCry worms—two of the worst cyberattacks in history—the hackers’ self-perpetuating code left behind ransom messages on machines that quickly spread on social media as the attacks unfolded. Ideological “hacktivist” groups—or state-sponsored hackers working for military or intelligence agencies but posing as hacktivists—also often take credit for their cyberattacks on platforms like X, Telegram, or their own websites. These messages then quickly spread to social media and through news reports.
Even these statements, however, should be taken as just another significant data point: Hacker groups exaggerate, misdirect, or lie when it serves their purposes. And some significant mass hacking incidents—such as the Mirai attack on the Internet infrastructure company Dyn in 2016 that took down thousands of websites—have been accompanied by no public message at all from the hackers responsible.
In cases where neither the perpetrator of a hacking incident nor its target has confirmed the attack, confirmation can sometimes come first from a government agency—such as the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency—or even from threat intelligence researchers at private cybersecurity firms. Government and industry investigators sometimes post their findings to their websites or share them with media, but it often takes days, weeks, or even months to come to confirmed conclusions. Hence, step five.
5. Sit tight and reserve judgment
If all these other measures of determining the cause of an outage don’t offer a clear understanding of the situation, the best approach may be patience. “It’s going to get a little conclusive at some point,” Madory says. “Sometimes you just have to just sit and wait.”
Aside from the time it takes for companies to admit to their screwups—or hackers to claim a win—the length of an outage can also sometimes offer a clue to its cause. A faulty update, power outage, or cascading bug can often be resolved quickly. Determined hackers who have maximized their damage, who shift tactics to outsmart defenders, or who may still be in a network they’ve breached can cause far longer and more severe outages. “A rollback takes minutes or hours,” Tomé says, referring to reverting to older code as a fix for a faulty update that introduces a bug. “Ransomware takes days or sometimes even weeks.”
In other words, as with all breaking news, when facts are in short supply, it’s better to maintain skepticism about early rumors or conspiracy theories and wait for more concrete evidence.
In the information vacuum that precedes that evidence, it can be easy to see connections between events that may just be coincidences. What are the odds, you may ask, that five major IT outages occurred on a sequential Thursday, Friday, Monday, and Tuesday?
For Doug Madory, who tracks those network outages every day of the week, that string of failures may just be a sign of the increasing complexity of technology—and how fundamentally our civilization has come to depend on it. “For better or worse, modern society is completely mediated through Internet-based services. They have outages from time to time. And that’s a reality I don’t think we’ll ever completely eliminate,” Madory says.
“If you’re immersed in that world of looking at outages for years on end, then they don’t really surprise you,” he adds. “You just try to understand what’s different about each one. And maybe what we can learn from it.”

articles.title: Anthropic's IPO could deliver $156B to charity | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Anthropic’s blockbuster IPO has made quite a few people generationally wealthy, but it will also be an enormous windfall for the causes backed by the frontier lab and its employees.
As you might expect from a company whose leadership emerged from the world of effective altruism (EA), Anthropic has multiple different avenues for cash raised in its market debut to be directed to philanthropy.
First, the company’s Public Benefit Fund, or PBF (analogous to OpenAI’s foundation), was allotted 5% of the company’s shares, almost 850 million. At the current trading price of about $95, that will leave it with an endowment of $80 billion. And if the company continues its astonishing growth rate, Anthropic could add further 2% increases every time the company’s valuation grows more than 50% over the IPO price of $83, or about $124.50 per share for the next threshold.
The PBF’s money will be focused on research and activities related to increasing the benefit of artificial intelligence to humanity. The first commitment of the PBF was $200 million to study the impact of AI on workers; Anthropic has said it will consider donations to philanthropic organizations or “direct distributions to specific populations” — perhaps a hint of future UBI plans.
Anthropic also donated $50 million to the city of San Francisco last week. A company spokesperson tells TechCrunch the donation did not come from the PBF.
Next, Anthropic’s employees have pledged shares to philanthropic causes of their choice, and the company will match those donations 3-to-1 for longer tenured employees and 1-to-1 for newer ones. In its S-1 filing, the company said that it had reserved more than 550 million shares to fulfill pledges made before September 30.
Working backwards from that figure, and based on the disclosure that 84% of the shares were reserved for early employee matches, we can estimate that employees have pledged $23 billion of donations; the company’s match on those would be roughly $53 billion, depending on the stock price when those matches are delivered.
All told, it adds up to $156 billion — a huge amount of potential philanthropy. For context, Americans donated $617 billion to charity in 2025; if all of the pledged funds resulting from today’s transactions get to do-gooders, that will be equal to about a quarter of all U.S. donations made last year.
Employees will need to make good on their pledges for this to work out, and the value of the match will ultimately depend on when Anthropic makes its donation. The shares could also go to donor-advised funds, which would likely limit their initial impact.
Interviews with employees and institutions suggest that donors are most likely to support EA-inflected charities like Longview Philanthropy, GiveWell, Coefficient Giving, Foresight Institute, and Giving What We Can. And it seems likely that significant funding will be allocated to AI safety research, given the concerns expressed about that subject by many Anthropic employees.

articles.title: Desativou o histórico do Gemini? O Google salva mesmo assim • Tecnoblog
articles.text:
Desativou o histórico do Gemini? O Google salva mesmo assim
Empresa atualizou tempo que suas conversas na IA ficam registradas de três dias para dois meses, independente da configuração de histórico.
O Gemini agora “lembra” seus últimos dois meses de consultas na plataforma, mesmo que você tenha desativado completamente seu histórico. O Google atualizou suas políticas de privacidade para a inteligência artificial na terça-feira (17/11) e aumentou o tempo que suas interações ficam salvas: de 72 horas para dois meses.
Você ainda pode ajustar por quanto tempo deseja reter as trocas. A configuração dá a opção padrão de 18 meses, além de opções de três ou 36 meses, além de deixar esse limite indefinido ou totalmente zerado (mas nem tanto). Independente da sua escolha, a nova política garante pelo menos dois meses de mensagens salvas.
Segundo o Google, a mudança tem como objetivo usar as interações para “proteger o Google, seus usuários e o público”. Ao avisar sobre a novidade, a empresa fala ainda em “ajuda de revisores humanos”, dando a entender que pessoas reais teriam acesso ao que você pergunta ao Gemini.
O acesso às informações trocadas com a IA não é uma novidade. Uma recomendação comumente dada por especialistas na área, inclusive, é não fornecer dados sensíveis nessas consultas à IA, como números de cartão de crédito, documentos, entre outros exemplos.
A revisão dessas mensagens por humanos também é algo padrão das IAs, e está previsto na política de privacidade do Google. Empresas como a Anthropic publicam relatórios frequentes trazendo exemplos de mau uso a partir de revisões do tipo. O próprio Gemini assume que algumas interações são checadas por pessoas reais, mas sem identificação dos usuários.
A retenção de mensagens também é algo comum no mercado. Segundo o Gizmodo, Anthropic e OpenAI falam em 30 dias, por exemplo, mas afirmam que podem manter as interações salvas por mais tempo se necessário. O Google cita motivos de segurança para manter esses logs, mas não explica como isso pode significar uma proteção maior ao usuário.
Mesmo com a retenção obrigatória pelo Google, você pode eliminar seu histórico e desativar o salvamento automático. Apesar de ficar disponível internamente para fins de “segurança” e funcionamento da IA, não será possível acessar as conversas anteriores na sua conta. Para apagar e interromper o salvamento desses chats, siga o passo a passo:
Você também pode configurar a exclusão automática de mensagens de até 3 anos atrás. A opção fica disponível em “Excluir atividades com mais de…”, logo abaixo da configuração de desativar o salvamento. Basta selecionar o período desejado e confirmar a ação para finalizar.

articles.title: Before you judge Sandpapergate, watch these 3 documentaries
articles.text:
Before you judge Sandpapergate, watch these 3 documentaries
Three documentaries you need to watch before judging sandpapergate
It just won't go away for Cricket Australia.
Eight years after Cameron Bancroft was caught using sandpaper to tamper with the ball during the 2018 Test series in South Africa, fresh allegations have emerged suggesting that more people knew about the plan than just Bancroft, captain Steve Smith and vice-captain David Warner.
Much of the renewed controversy stems from Usman Khawaja's recently released autobiography, Sabr, in which he claims that knowledge of the ball-tampering extended throughout the Australian team, including players and staff. His account has since received support from Warner, Bancroft and former Australia bowler Chadd Sayers, who was part of the 2018 squad.
However, current Australian Test captain Pat Cummins has strongly rejected Khawaja's claims, describing them as "complete and utter nonsense" during an extraordinary 70-minute press conference last week.
Cricket Australia has now announced a voluntary forum, giving former and current players and staff an opportunity to share their recollections of the scandal. But with no new investigation, sanctions or guaranteed public findings, will it really uncover anything new?
Before making up your mind, we recommend watching these three documentaries to gain a deeper perspective on one of cricket's biggest scandals.
Read More: How to watch New Zealand vs India 1st Test
Crossing The Line - 2018
Produced by South Africa's Supersport, Crossing The Line is perhaps the most insightful of all the documentaries exploring Sandpapergate. Featuring perspectives from Shaun Pollock, Graeme Smith, Shane Warne, Allan Border, Michael Holding and Michael Haysman, it offers a fascinating range of viewpoints on the controversy.
Rather than focusing solely on the ball-tampering incident, the documentary examines the Test series as a whole, providing valuable context on the long-standing rivalry and animosity between Australia and South Africa, both before and after the scandal.
At just 56 minutes long, it's an ideal watch if you have an hour to spare.
The Test - 2020
While The Test is by no means a documentary dedicated solely to Sandpapergate, it's arguably the best choice if you want to understand the scandal's impact on Australian cricket culture.
The opening episode explores the background and fallout of the controversy before following Justin Langer and Tim Paine as they attempt to rebuild the team's reputation, restore public trust and steer Australian cricket into a new era.
The Cause, The Crime, The Impacts - 2023
Although an independent three-part series available on SB Media's YouTube channel, this documentary neatly pieces together the Sandpapergate scandal across three carefully structured episodes: The Cause, The Crime and The Impacts.
While it doesn't necessarily uncover anything new, it's an excellent way to get a comprehensive understanding of what happened, why it happened and the lasting impact the scandal has had on Australian cricket culture.

articles.title: Telus Buy One, Give One promo returns for Black Friday
articles.text:
Telus is bringing back its Buy One, Give One promo for Black Friday.
The Vancouver-based national carrier will give a phone through its Mobility for Good program for every phone purchase between Nov. 27 and 29, helping connect youth aging out of government care and others in need.
To qualify, phones must be purchased on a two-year Telus financing plan with a postpaid activation. Like last year, Telus pledged to give up to a maximum of 5,000 phones through the Buy One, Give One program.
In its sixth year, Telus says the Buy One, Give One initiative helps Canadians “shop with purpose,” adding that people can know their purchase helps “bridge digital divides” and keep vulnerable youth, low-income seniors, and families in need connected through free or subsidized rate plans and devices.
To add some context, Mobility for Good is part of Telus’ larger Connecting for Good programs, a series of initiatives launched in 2016. They’re designed to provide connectivity and technology for “those who need it most” by supplying used phones (Mobility For Good), internet (Internet For Good), tablets and computers (Tech For Good), and access to health services (Health for Good) to individuals like in-need families, low-income seniors, and the previously-mentioned youth aging out of care.

articles.title: Three 'e-waste' Nvidia V100s hit 100 tokens per second on Qwen 3.6 35B in a $1,042 homelab rig — decommissioned GPUs outpace a $5,399 M5 Max Mac Studio at long contexts
articles.text:
Three 'e-waste' Nvidia V100s hit 100 tokens per second on Qwen 3.6 35B in a $1,042 homelab rig — decommissioned GPUs outpace a $5,399 M5 Max Mac Studio at long contexts
An M5 Max Mac Studio is slightly faster at short context, but the V100s pull ahead at 64K and longer.
A homelab builder benchmarked three used Nvidia V100s on Qwen 3.6 35B, achieving about 100 tokens per second in a custom setup costing $1,042 with just “e-waste” GPUs. The smaller, dense Qwen 3.6 27B manages about 24 tokens per second on the same platform, and the V100s use about half the energy of the same number of P100s for a given job.
The blog post, “Scaling ‘E-Waste’: LLMs on Multiple Decommissioned GPUs,” compares nine different builds — one to three K80s, P100s, or V100-16GB cards — on a single Supermicro dual-Xeon board. The test uses llama.cpp and covers more than 130 LLM tests, including Qwen 2.5, Gemma 4, and, of course, Qwen 3.6, at Q4/Q8/F16 precisions and from 4K to 128K context sizes. GPU energy per run is also recorded. The builder is “daily driving Qwen 3.6 35B” on the V100s and notes that scaling decommissioned GPUs will only get you so far.
“E-waste,” in this case, refers to decommissioned enterprise GPUs, which are a popular but somewhat underpowered option when compared to very expensive modern alternatives. The Nvidia Tesla V100s in question are tested as a follow-up to a July round which tested 15 “e-waste” GPUs, and this time the board and CPUs stay the same for every build — the Supermicro X10DRG-Q with two Intel Xeon E5-2687W 12-core CPUs, powered by the Corsair HX1500i PSU.
Performance is judged based on what is considered “realtime interaction” which, here, is 70 tokens per second. As to why the number of GPUs is three: Qwen 3.6 35B, the primary tested model, fails on just one or two at Q8, or 8-bit quantization.
Here are the given prices, with the note that they aren’t “100% reflective of what you could find on eBay today,” although the totals count only one of the two CPUs and omit RAM, storage, the case, and any cooling.
| What the builder paid for each three-card build |  |  |  | 
|---|---|---|---|
| Part | 3x K80 | 3x P100 | 3x V100-16GB | 
| Three GPUs | $270 ($90 each) | $403.50 ($134.50 each) | $655.16 ($436.77 per pair) | 
| Board | $211 | $211 | $211 | 
| PSU | $147.70 | $147.70 | $147.70 | 
| One CPU | $28.20 | $28.20 | $28.20 | 
| Builder’s total | $657 | $790 | $1,042 | 
| With 2nd CPU | $685 | $819 | $1,070 | 
The older cards are relatively inexpensive because they “run hot and ship without cooling,” which required the builder to 3D print one blower duct per card and has led to the development of a standalone cooler.
The bench itself involves 10 runs of 512 generated tokens per test with context pre-filled to 4K, 32K, 64K, or 128K. Qwen 3.6 35B is a mixture-of-experts (MoE) model, which only activates about 3 billion out of its 35 billion total parameters per token. The numbers that immediately follow are at Q8.
Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.
The token goal was easily reached…when the context window was small, or 4K. The 100.8 tokens per second there fell to 72.7 at 128K, still usable by the 70 tokens per second goal. The 27B model, which is not MoE, fared much worse, at 24.3 at 4K, 21.6 at 32K, 18.7 at 64K, and just 14.2 at 128K. The MoE ends up about four to five times faster, depending on the context size.
| Qwen 3.6 35B generation speed by context length (tokens per second) |  |  |  |  | 
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Setup | 4K | 32K | 64K | 128K | 
| 3x V100, Q8 | 100.8 | 89.4 | 83.5 | 72.7 | 
| 2x V100, Q4 | 105.4 | 96.2 | 89.5 | 77.1 | 
| 3x P100, Q8 | 55.2 | 50.9 | 47.5 | 40.2 | 
| M5 Max Mac, 8-bit | 105.5 | 91.1 | 78.5 | 61.3 | 
Also tested were other dense models of about 30B parameters. At 4K, Gemma 4 31B achieved 20.9 and Qwen 2.5 32B 21.0, while the MoE Gemma 4 26B cleared the 70 tokens per second bar with just two V100s at Q8. If you move down to Q4, or 4-bit quantization, two V100s can run Qwen 3.6 35B at 77.1 to 105.4 tokens per second, between 128K and 4K context size. This is where it’s claimed that adding more cards gives you more memory, which enables larger models to be run, but not speed.
The P100s, for comparison, only hit 40.2–55.2 tokens per second in the same context range with Q8 Qwen 3.6 35B, and the target 70 only with Qwen 2.5 3B. If we compare to more modern hardware — the Nvidia DGX Spark, MSRP $4,700, and the M5 Max Mac Studio, which starts at $2,499 but costs $5,399 with the tested 40-core GPU, 128GB of memory, and a 1TB SSD — the 3x V100 build holds its own, using sourced data.
The Mac comparison comes from the oMLX benchmark page for the M5 Max with 40 GPU cores and 128GB of unified memory, and that hits 43.9 tokens per second with a ~195K-token prompt on the Qwen 3.6 35B model. The Mac is slightly ahead at 4K and 32K, while the V100s pull ahead at 64K and 128K, by 19% at the longest context. These numbers have to be taken loosely, as the machines use different runtimes.
The Spark run came from Kleybrink’s dgx-spark-bench, using Ollama in thinking mode with short prompts. Its 45.8 tokens per second is less than half the V100s’ 4K figure.
Going further to modern GPUs, which “destroy our decommissioned equivalents,” as the builder puts it, you get about 315 tokens per second on two H100s and about 455 on one B200 at 128K, the B200 roughly six times the V100 box, even though the hosted cards ran the full 16-bit model against the V100s’ 8-bit. Parasail, an inference provider, sponsored that comparison with dedicated H100 and B200 deployments.
As for energy, the V100 setup came out to about 0.02 kWh for a 128K 35B run, with the P100s taking twice that much and two or three K80s as much as 0.35 to 0.45 kWh. The V100-16GB simply “[puts] up better scores while consuming less energy,” in comparison to the P100s. These numbers are for the GPUs and not from the wall.
There’s more to come. The builder wants a benchmark that “maps to ‘software factory’ performance,” a term for models being prompted constantly, around the clock, where instant speed matters less. Then there’s the cooler, which is “almost ready for release,” with beta testers to be recruited from the mailing list, although no date has been given. From the Reddit thread, the builder mentions the intention to compare inference backends and use speculative decoding to improve performance.

articles.title: Filtrado el Razr Flex, la respuesta de Motorola al Galaxy Z Fold 8 y el iPhone Duo
articles.text:
El segmento de plegables con formato wide está pronto a sumar un nuevo contrincante a modelos como el Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8, el iPhone Duo y el Xiaomi 18 Fold. Se trata del Motorola Razr Flex, cuyas imágenes se han filtrado para revelar las principales características de su diseño.
Que Motorola está preparando un plegable de las citadas características no es una novedad. La compañía ya había dejado ver su silueta en un primer teaser, luego de que Apple diera el salto al mercado de móviles con pantallas flexibles. No obstante, ahora sí podemos verlo en todo su esplendor y con sus opciones de colores.
El material filtrado revela que el Motorola Razr Flex tiene un formato de libro como el del Razr Fold, pero con un diseño más ancho y retacón. Este dispositivo expandirá el catálogo de la marca posicionándose como una alterativa más compacta y que busca sacar provecho del concepto de "tablet de bolsillo".
Los móviles plegables con relación de aspecto 4:3 destacan por permitir mayor maniobrabilidad al usar la pantalla exterior con una sola mano. Asimismo, la pantalla interior suele destacar por brindar un formato optimizado para el consumo multimedia y la productividad; esto último, gracias a que permite una mejor ejecución de dos apps lado a lado.
Así es el Motorola Razr Flex
Las imágenes filtradas por SammyGuru presentan al Motorola Razr Flex en dos colores: verde y marrón. Los nombres oficiales de los dispositivos estarían vinculados con referencias oficiales de PANTONE, como ya es costumbre de la marca. En el caso de la versión verde, la parte trasera presentaría un acabado tipo tela, mientras que en la marrón sería similar al cuero. En ambos casos, los marcos metálicos estarían pintados con tonos acordes.
El material de marketing también permite apreciar al Motorola Razr Flex abierto en posiciones intermedias. Esto permitiría darle funcionalidades adicionales, más allá de lo que se puede hacer con el equipo totalmente abierto o cerrado. En la parte trasera también se observa que el fabricante abandonaría el módulo de cámaras que caracteriza a sus demás smartphones y que incorporaría un bloque tipo píldora, centrado y en horizontal.
Las especificaciones técnicas definitivas del Motorola Razr Flex son todavía un misterio. Sin embargo, filtraciones previas indican que será más pequeño que el Galaxy Z Fold 8. La pantalla exterior podría ser de 4,97 pulgadas, mientras que la interior alcanzaría las 6,92 pulgadas. Ambas medidas son bastante inferiores a las del plegable de Samsung, que cuenta con paneles de 5,5 y 7,6 pulgadas.
Sobre precio y fecha de lanzamiento, todavía no hay novedades. Se especula con que Motorola podría presentar el Razr Flex a comienzos de 2027, durante el CES. Aunque también se rumora un posible anuncio antes de finales del corriente año, con miras a lanzarlo el que viene.

articles.title: Chip Industry Week In Review
articles.text:
Intel Foundry signed its first external customer for its advanced 18A-P semiconductor manufacturing process, according to Intel executives. The customer has not been identified, and Intel has not disclosed a production timetable.
Siemens plans to acquireBreker Verification Systems, a developer of AI-driven test suite synthesis and system-level verification technologies. The acquisition is expected to close in December.
Microsoft selected Intel Foundry‘s EMIB advanced-packaging technology for custom silicon used in Azure’s infrastructure. The multiyear agreement also expands cooperation on Xeon processors, memory, and security technologies.
GlobalFoundries and Boston Dynamicsexpanded their robotics collaboration to deploy autonomous Spot inspection robots across fabs in the U.S., Germany, and Singapore. GF also plans to begin evaluating Boston Dynamics’ Atlas humanoid robots for semiconductor manufacturing tasks in early 2027.
AMD completed acquisitions of AI inference chip developer Taalas and AI model research company World Labs.
Funding
The European Commission said more than 20 semiconductor projects have been approved under the EU Chips Act, representing over €33B in public and private investment.
General Flash raised $128M to scale production of critical metals used in semiconductor and other industries.
Atom Computingfinalized an up to $100M CHIPS Act R&D award for neutral-atom quantum computers.
Science Corporation raised $400M for its retinal implant chip that aims to restore form vision for certain types of macular degeneration.
Chip trade and export controls
The U.S. Department of Commerceintroduced new restrictions addressing remote access to advanced U.S. AI computing through overseas data centers, along with new semiconductor licensing requirements affecting Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia, and Brazil.
The U.S. received license requests covering 3.4 million advanced Nvidia and AMD AI chips for China and approved more than 879,000, according to U.S. government data. It is unclear how many were actually shipped.
The U.S. government released new details of an ongoing investigation into Megaspeed over suspected semiconductor export-control violations. Nvidia placed Megaspeed on its no-sell list in June 2025, but its Malaysian subsidiary, Speedmatrix, later received more than $800M in Nvidia AI technology, mostly through third-party manufacturers, per the NYT. Nvidia says it blocked new orders and obtained government authorization for certain repair-parts shipments. An investigation is underway.
The Trump administration is moving toward restrictions on Chinese optical transceiver imports, despite opposition from major U.S. cloud companies, reported Reuters.
Manufacturing capacity
Nvidiaexpanded its manufacturing agreements with Amkor, Samsung Electro-Mechanics, SPIL, TSMC, and others. The commitments cover additional substrate manufacturing, advanced packaging, and wafer capacity. As part of the expansion, ASE subsidiary SPIL signed a multibillion-dollar agreement with Nvidia to triple its advanced semiconductor packaging capacity in Taiwan by mid-2029, including new production lines for wafer bumping, assembly, and testing.
ASE Technology inaugurated the first phase and began construction of the second phase of its Lujhu advanced-packaging facility in Kaohsiung, Taiwan.
Lam Research broke ground on a technology center in Zhunan, Taiwan, as part of its five-year, $3B global R&D expansion.
GlobalFoundries broke ground on a new 300mm semiconductor fab in Malta, New York, under a U.S.-Japan investment initiative providing up to $21B for two fabs. The first 300mm fab is expected to begin production in 2029.
ADEKA and Entegrisagreed to collaborate on advanced semiconductor materials production in Japan.
Silicon Box advanced its proposed semiconductor packaging and test facility in Novara, Italy, into the basic design stage. The project is intended to establish additional European advanced-packaging capacity for chiplet-based semiconductor devices.
SC26
The annual supercomputing conference kicked off this week in Chicago.
Nvidia announced a Rubin HPC GPU with more than 50,000 CUDA cores on a single GPU, along with sparse data acceleration capabilities. It also announced a 192-CPU Vera rack-scale platform for HPC with more than 200TB/s of aggregate peak memory bandwidth.
Lambda is deploying Nvidia’s CPO switches to connect GB300 NVL72 racks with more than 10,000 GPUs. Nvidia claims up to 5× better power efficiency and 15× higher reliability than conventional pluggable optics.
AMD announced that its Lux supercomputer at ORNL, powered by EPYC CPUs and Instinct MI355X GPUs, is now open to scientific users.
NAND flash contract prices are expected to decline in 2027 as Chinese cloud providers cut enterprise SSD orders amid GPU shortages and high inventories, reports TrendForce. Global NAND capital spending is projected to rise ~27% to ~US$30B.
CSIS examined the risks of using Chinese memory chips, including CXMT DRAM, citing security and supply-chain concerns. The report recommends restricting their use in sensitive government systems and expanding independent chip testing.
JEDEC previewed the DDR6 specification. While still subject to change, the current plan includes higher data rates and a wider bus, a pseudo-channel architecture, optimizations for die stacking and high-capacity modules, and data-center-focused low-power modes.
JEDEC also started a System Level Reliability Testing subcommittee to develop qualification methodologies, reliability practices, and evaluation approaches for emerging system applications.
Earnings and chip stocks
Year-over-year revenue change: Keysight Q4 up 40%; Kulicke & Soffa Q4 up 131%;Nvidia Q3 up 103%; and Soitec Q2 up 50% (at constant currency).
Cirrus Logic President/CEO John Forsyth was elected chair of the Semiconductor Industry Association, succeeding AMD CEO Lisa Su. GlobalFoundries Executive Chairman Tom Caulfield was elected vice chair.
Quick Links To More News
In-Depth— Manufacturing, Packaging and Materials newsletter; AI agents the new semi IP?; can AI agents shift chip design left.
Global— U.S. equipment expansion in Oregon; photonics R&D in Finland and Japan; SK hynix adds test capacity.
New Technologies— AI-assisted chip design; high-power test; panel-level bonding; cloud-based engineering simulation; secure auto Ethernet.
Security— AMD PSP flaw; DDR5 rowhammer; GPU side channels; memory DoS attacks.
Trending Video— Physics vs. data in simulation; process variability; memory and packaging optimization.
Workforce | Education— Student HPC competition in Chicago; New York training deal; new talent hub in Arizona.
Events and Webinars— Boston materials conference; AI data-center cooling; UCIe chiplets; GAA NSFET design.
Global
Americas
ACM Research opened a new research and manufacturing facility in Hillsboro, Oregon, as part of a U.S. expansion. The facility supports development and production activities associated with the company’s semiconductor wet-cleaning and electroplating equipment.
Europe
imec opened a photonics R&D center in Espoo, Finland, expanding its capabilities in optical design, simulation, testing, and system development.
Asia
imec established an R&D presence in Hokkaido, Japan, focused on photonic ICs, electronic-photonic integration, and CPO for AI and HPC.
SK hynix detailed plans for a jointly funded ₩874.6B (US$655M) semiconductor testing facility at its Yongin complex in South Korea. The cleanroom is scheduled to open in May 2027.
OpenAI reported advances in AI-assisted chip design, including RTL generation and design optimization for AMD processors and RISC-V cores. It is also working with Synopsys to train AI models to use EDA tools.
Advantestexpanded its V93000 EXA Scale test platform with the new EXA Scale QX test head for high-power, high-pin-count AI and HPC devices. The four-card-cage architecture provides 36 instrument slots, increasing test capacity while maintaining compatibility with existing V93000 instruments, wafer probers, and test handlers. The system is expected to become available in Q1 FY2027.
Siemens and Microsoft are planning to bring Simcenter X to Microsoft Azure, enabling engineering teams in automotive and other industries to run multi-domain simulations and scale HPC workloads in the cloud.
Keysight expanded its 6G sensing and communications testing capabilities with Cohere Technologies’ Zak-OTFS technology to simulate multiple drones and their wireless communications under realistic radio conditions.
Infineon introduced a TMR-based magnetic switch, combining ultra-low current consumption with direct load switching in a single component. Applications include glucose monitoring, smart glasses, AR/VR devices and medical disposables.
A KAIST team created a clock distribution network with backside clock mesh in BSPDN architecture, with experiments demonstrating “26% lower maximum local clock latency, 40% smaller global skew, and 29% less mesh switching power on average than the frontside baseline.”
AMD disclosed a critical Platform Security Processor boot ROM vulnerability affecting Zen/Zen+ processors that can let attacker-controlled firmware bypass secure-boot authentication and execute unsigned code with full PSP privileges. AMD does not plan to release a mitigation because the vulnerable boot ROM cannot be modified.
Intel issued a security announcement on a DDR5 rowhammer attack that researchers used to bypass certain protections, induce bit flips on systems with 12th- and 13th-gen Core processors, and escalate privileges. Intel recommends keeping platform firmware, BIOS, and operating systems current.
Security Research
A University of Luxembourg team identified new security risks in Nvidia GPU load/store units. Two timing side channels enabled full AES-128 key recovery and covert communication between processes under Nvidia’s Multi-Process Service (MPS).
University of Kansas and Cornell researchers demonstrated a practical low-bandwidth memory denial-of-service attack that caused more than 1,000× slowdowns on DDR5- and HBM2E-based systems while consuming less than 1 GB/s of memory bandwidth.
TU Berlin researchers demonstrated a physical attack on firmware TPM protections that can reset failed-login counters and bypass PIN lockout protections used by Windows Hello and BitLocker.
Government security news
Global government cybersecurity agencies in several countries warned about a Java/OpenJDK flaw that can allow remote code execution on affected x86-64 systems. CISA urged immediate patching.
Physics Vs. Data: Lam Research‘s David Fried talks about different approaches to speed up simulations, how to account for process variability with angstrom-level accuracy, and how to optimize systems for different memories and packaging options.
Quantum Hardware
Altera, OQC, and Nvidia demonstrated an FPGA-based quantum controller that uses an Agilex 9 Direct RF FPGA to connect a superconducting QPU to Nvidia GPUs for real-time control and readout. The reference design reduces the need for external RF conversion hardware.
Quantum Machines demonstrated real-time quantum error-correction processing using its OPX1000 quantum controller and Nvidia CUDA-Q over NVQLink. Tests using simulated error data achieved 2.4 microseconds of round-trip latency with a CPU-based decoder. GPU-based decoding is planned.
IBM, Nvidia, and Fermi National Accelerator Laboratory announced plans for a quantum-classical co-design platform, combining IBM quantum computers with Nvidia DGX B200 systems to research modular quantum architectures, scientific applications, and supercomputing integration.
Workforce, Education
A live 48-hour Student Cluster Competition was held at the SC26 supercomputing conference in Chicago, where teams of six undergraduate students built and ran their own high performance computing clusters. And the winner is….
University at Albany and Swagelok Albany launched a semiconductor workforce training partnership for lithography, advanced patterning, vacuum and plasma technologies, etch/deposition, metrology and cleanroom operations.
University of Arizona, Pima County, and Taiwan’s NYCU opened a new semiconductor talent and innovation hub in Tucson for hands-on training, academic programs and exchanges, and networking with semiconductor employers.
Lam Research and ASE expansions; data center shifts; CPO system architecture initiative; 2D-transistor interface solution; USENIX HW security; patent suits; image sensors; programmable AI memtransistor; Nvidia's new plan; earnings; Tier IV's L4 auto chip.
