articles.title: Optimize AI economics on Amazon Bedrock with Accenture’s sequenced approach | Amazon Web Services
articles.text:
Artificial Intelligence
Optimize AI economics on Amazon Bedrock with Accenture’s sequenced approach
As enterprises scale AI on Amazon Bedrock, token spend often grows even as per-token prices fall. Without cost allocation tags in place, your cloud invoice shows AI spend as a single line item rather than by team, workload, agent, or model. Cheaper tokens expand adoption, and agentic workloads multiply invocations. As successful AI use cases scale, consumption can rise faster than unit prices drop. The economic question is whether the business value generated grows faster than the cost of the intelligence required to produce it. The Linux Foundation has launched the Tokenomics Foundation to develop open standards for AI cost economics, a sign that managing the economics of AI is now an industry discipline.
In this post, you will learn about six levers for optimizing token spend, how Accenture applied them in production, and how to apply them using Amazon Bedrock.
Accenture applied these levers in four client engagements across telecom, insurance, mining, and a large enterprise deployment. The same levers are available natively on Amazon Bedrock as described in this post. Where savings were measured, token spend fell by about 40–85 percent. Results are specific to each client’s workload and may vary. Client names are withheld by Accenture to protect client confidentiality.
Attribution first: Measuring cost at the business level
Before you optimize anything, you need to see where consumption is occurring, who owns it, and what business value it produces. Cost allocation tags at the team, workload, and agent level are the prerequisite for connecting consumption to accountable owners and, ultimately, to business outcomes. You apply them through Amazon Bedrock application inference profiles, one profile per application or workload, tagged by team, cost center, and environment. After you activate them as cost allocation tags in the AWS Billing and Cost Management console, you can use these tags to trace which teams, applications, and agents are driving spend. They also make it possible to measure the impact of each change you introduce.
Three AWS services provide the underlying telemetry. AWS Cost and Usage Reports (CUR 2.0), delivered through AWS Data Exports, handle financial attribution, breaking down billed inference cost by workload and team after your cost allocation tags are active. Amazon CloudWatch captures operational signals such as invocation counts and latency. Amazon Bedrock model invocation logging records request-level detail, including the model used and the input and output token counts for each call.
Telemetry alone isn’t enough. Engineers can read cost per invocation on a dashboard, but product owners and program leaders need a metric expressed in business terms. Accenture’s Cost per Business Transaction (CpBT) framework bridges this gap. CpBT aggregates all the model invocations, retries, tool calls, and agent handoffs that contribute to one successful business output into a single fully loaded cost figure. It surfaces the true cost of producing a result, including the failed attempts that raw token pricing hides. Tracked against the business value each workflow delivers, CpBT distinguishes a growing bill that reflects scaling success from one that reflects waste.
The six optimization levers
The goal of these six levers isn’t to minimize tokens at all costs. It’s to use the right amount and level of intelligence to deliver each business outcome at the appropriate cost, quality, and risk. The levers are organized into three phases based on the complexity of the change and the investment it requires. AWS and Accenture recommend working through the phases in order, and you can apply each phase independently to the workloads where it will have the most impact.
Phase 1: Configuration only, no infrastructure change
With Amazon Bedrock prompt caching, the model reuses the parts of a prompt that repeat across requests, such as system instructions, tool definitions, and reference documents, so you stop paying full price to process the same content again. Amazon Bedrock stores the key-value state of previously computed prompt prefixes and is designed to skip recomputation on later requests. This is designed to reduce cached input token costs by up to 90 percent for supported models (see Amazon Bedrock Prompt Caching).
Amazon Bedrock batch inference processes non-urgent workloads asynchronously as a group at 50 percent lower cost than on-demand pricing for select models (see Amazon Bedrock Pricing). You submit inference requests as a batch job, and results are written to Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) when processing completes. Batch inference suits nightly reports, document processing pipelines, and evaluation runs that don’t need an immediate response.
Both levers add configuration to your existing setup. Prompt caching requires cache checkpoint markers in your prompts, and batch inference requires submitting eligible requests as a batch job instead of calling the on-demand API. Apply caching to interactive, on-demand traffic and batch inference to asynchronous work. Neither requires new infrastructure or architecture changes.
Phase 2: Architectural changes
Amazon Bedrock intelligent prompt routing directs requests across models within the same family, matching each task to the level of intelligence its business value, complexity, and risk require, rather than defaulting every request to the most powerful model. Intelligent prompt routing can reduce costs by up to 30 percent without compromising accuracy (see Amazon Bedrock intelligent prompt routing). Check Amazon Bedrock Pricing for any routing charges. In the following engagements, Accenture’s model tiering and triage routing apply this same routing lever.
Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) optimization tunes the retrieval step in the RAG process so that fewer unnecessary context tokens reach the model. Techniques such as hierarchical chunking, metadata-based filtering, and reranking narrow the retrieved context to the most relevant chunks, so you pay primarily for content that improves the answer.
Two complementary Accenture patterns work alongside these AWS native levers. Context scoping limits the data each agent receives to the document slice relevant to its step of the workflow, rather than passing the full case context at every handoff. Context compression summarizes or filters documents before they reach the model. Both reduce input token volume, especially across multi-agent chains.
Phase 3: Infrastructure and training investment
Semantic caching stores responses and reuses them when a new request is semantically similar to one already answered, even if the wording differs. This avoids redundant model invocations and reduces both cost and latency. On AWS, you can implement it with a vector store such as Amazon ElastiCache in front of the model. In an AWS benchmark on 63,796 real chatbot queries, a 0.90 similarity threshold produced a 74.5 percent cache hit rate, 92.3 percent accuracy, and 72.5 percent cost savings (see ElastiCache semantic caching benchmarks). As you apply routing and semantic caching, keep Amazon Bedrock Guardrails on every route, and set semantic cache expiry so that users don’t receive outdated answers.
Model distillation transfers knowledge from a large teacher model to a smaller, faster student model. Distilled models in Amazon Bedrock are up to 500 percent faster and up to 75 percent less expensive than original models, with less than 2 percent accuracy loss for use cases such as RAG. Distillation is best suited to stable, high-volume workloads where the transaction volume justifies the training investment.
In production: Four client engagements
Accenture applied these levers in four client engagements. Each engagement targeted a different cost pattern. In two of them, Accenture applied several changes together, so those results reflect the combined effect rather than any single lever.
The first engagement was a large enterprise deployment where every request went to a frontier model, with no caching, model tiering, or batching. Accenture applied three changes together: model tiering to match each task to the smallest model that could handle it well, prompt caching for repeated context, and batch processing for overnight and non-urgent jobs. Together they cut monthly token cost by 85 percent, and the saving was not separated by change. About 15 percent of tasks still needed the top model for hard, open-ended reasoning, and the rest ran on lighter models. Your split will depend on your workload composition.
The second engagement was a telecom operator with $12 million in annual token spend. Most of that spend came from agents fanning out requests without limits and from every request going to a frontier model regardless of complexity. Accenture applied triage routing, semantic caching, and context compression together. Input tokens fell by 70 percent, and annual token spend fell from $12 million to $3.8 million, a 68 percent reduction. Accenture validated output quality against the operator’s pre-change performance benchmarks.
The third and fourth engagements each applied a single cache layer. An insurer used model-layer prefix caching, reusing the static portions of its prompts across invocations. A mining operator used an application-layer semantic cache, returning stored responses for repeated queries before they reached the model. Across the two engagements, token spend fell by about 40 percent combined, without model routing changes or training investment.
Results
Outcomes ranged from about 40 percent to about 85 percent, reflecting each client’s starting point. The large enterprise deployment began with no optimization in place and reached 85 percent. The telecom operator reached 68 percent on $12 million in annual token spend, and the insurer and mining operator reached about 40 percent combined with one caching lever each. Results are specific to each client’s workload and may vary.
These savings aren’t the end goal. They create capacity to scale AI workloads, reinvest in higher-value use cases, and improve the return generated by each dollar of AI consumption. Two of these engagements applied several changes at once. When you apply one lever at a time, you can attribute each result to a specific change. AWS and Accenture recommend this sequence for your own workloads: connect consumption to owners and outcomes, apply one lever at a time, measure cost, quality, and business value, and build on what works.
Production governance: Four operating tenets
Optimizing AI economics in production requires an ongoing governance cycle spanning cost, quality, risk, and business value, not a one-time technical change. Before you apply any lever, establish a quantitative baseline for both cost and quality so that you can measure the impact of each change against a known starting point. When you validate output quality, use held-out evaluation sets drawn from your actual production traffic rather than synthetic benchmarks. Apply one lever at a time per workload so that you can attribute results to a specific change and roll back cleanly if quality drops below your acceptable thresholds. If you operate in a regulated industry such as financial services, insurance, or healthcare, document your quality test results and rollback procedures as part of your standard change management record.
These four tenets apply regardless of which levers you are using or what phase of the sequencing you are in. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore is an environment where you can build, connect, and optimize agents at scale with any framework or model. It includes AgentCore Evaluations, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore that provides batch evaluation to support your quality validation cycle as you progress through more advanced levers.
Getting started
You can begin with three steps. First, turn on cost attribution for Amazon Bedrock by applying cost allocation tags at the team and workload level so that your spend is traceable from day one. Second, activate those tags in the AWS Billing and Cost Management console. Then use CUR 2.0 and model invocation logging to identify high-consumption workloads, and assess each one based on spend, business value, quality requirements, risk, volume, and optimization potential. Third, apply Amazon Bedrock prompt caching to that workload’s interactive traffic and Amazon Bedrock batch inference to its asynchronous jobs as configuration-only changes, and measure the result before you move to architectural changes in Phase 2.
The AWS Well-Architected Agentic AI Lens includes model invocation and token cost optimization (AGENTCOST02), a focus area within the cost optimization pillar for agentic workloads. This focus area provides a structured framework you can use to apply these levers at scale across your organization.

articles.title: Samsung Galaxy : vous pourrez bientôt prêter votre téléphone sans donner accès à toutes vos applis
articles.text:
Avec la bêta de One UI 9.5, Samsung permet enfin de verrouiller ses applications une par une sans passer par le Dossier sécurisé. Vous pourrez ainsi prêter votre Galaxy déjà déverrouillé tout en gardant vos messages ou votre appli bancaire derrière une empreinte ou un code.
On tend son téléphone à quelqu’un pour lui montrer une photo et, d’un coup, toute la maison est ouverte. Sur les Galaxy, Samsung propose depuis longtemps un Dossier sécurisé pour isoler des applications et des fichiers. C’est pratique quand on veut séparer des contenus, un peu moins quand on veut simplement ajouter un verrou à la messagerie qu’on utilise tous les jours. On avait déjà repéré ce verrouillage dans une version interne de One UI 9.5 en août. Il est désormais accessible aux bêta-testeurs.
Un verrou pour chaque appli, même quand le Galaxy est déverrouillé
Vous choisissez les applications à protéger et elles restent à leur place sur le téléphone. Quand quelqu’un essaie d’en ouvrir une, One UI demande une authentification, même si l’écran est déjà déverrouillé. On peut utiliser la biométrie ou la méthode de déverrouillage du téléphone, qu’il s’agisse d’un code PIN, d’un schéma ou d’un mot de passe.
Le verrou sert aussi quand l’appli est fermée. Le contenu de ses notifications est masqué et ses widgets disparaissent de l’écran d’accueil. C’est un détail qui compte pour une messagerie. Quel intérêt de protéger l’ouverture de l’appli si le début du dernier message s’affiche encore pendant que quelqu’un d’autre tient le téléphone ? Xiaomi propose le verrouillage individuel depuis des années et Apple l’a ajouté avec iOS 18. Samsung comble enfin ce retard.
Le Galaxy S26 Ultra peut aussi activer son filtre d’écran
Sur le S26 Ultra, Samsung pousse l’idée un cran plus loin. Le filtre de confidentialité intégré à la dalle, que nous avions essayé lors de notre test, rend l’écran plus difficile à lire de côté. Comme le détaille SamMobile, une seule option permet désormais de le déclencher à l’ouverture de n’importe quelle appli verrouillée. Il reste actif si vous déployez le volet de notifications ou les réglages rapides pendant que vous utilisez l’appli. Pratique pour lire ses messages dans un métro bondé.
Ce réglage d’affichage est propre au S26 Ultra. Le verrouillage des applis, lui, fait partie de la bêta proposée à toute la série Galaxy S26. Samsung a annoncé son ouverture le 18 novembre dans plusieurs pays, dont l’Allemagne, le Royaume-Uni et les États-Unis, avec une inscription via Samsung Members. La France ne figure pas parmi les marchés cités et Samsung n’a pas encore donné de date pour la version finale.
On pourra donc tendre son Galaxy pour montrer une photo sans surveiller la prochaine notification. Pour le doigt qui fait défiler les trois photos suivantes, il faudra encore négocier.

articles.title: Dos turistas alquilan un Airbnb en San Sebastián para un mes, pero se van a los diez días: “Sentíamos que no quedaba nada por hacer”
articles.text:
Mar Yvette y su marido habían venido a San Sebastián para desconectar tras sus paradas en Londres y París. Habían alquilado un apartamento en Airbnb por un mes. Estaban seguros de que en Donosti iban a encontrar el suficiente motivo para quedarse. Yvette contaba que a los 4 días ya sentían que se les acababan las cosas que hacer. A los 10 días se fueron del alojamiento.
El alquiler en este apartamento en el Airbnb estaba previsto por 31 días. Además, estaba muy bien ubicado (a 2 minutos andando de la playa de La Concha) y cerca del casco viejo.
Después de varios días, habían hecho casi todo lo que querían. Fueron a hacer una excursión a Bilbao, donde esperaban encontrar nuevas razones para quedarse más días.
Más turistas de los que pensaban. Pintxos que no eran los suyos.
En principio, pensaron que, al ser una ciudad más pequeña que otras de España, iba a estar menos saturada de turistas, y se equivocaron. Era difícil entrar en las iglesias y también tenían problemas para encontrar sitio en la playa.
Por otro lado, había un problema con la gastronomía. Sabían que era conocida por sus pintxos. Sin embargo, no sabían hasta qué punto podían entrar en su alimentación, que era básicamente vegetal (con algún pescado y marisco). Hay muchos platos que llevan carne, huevos o productos lácteos que no entraban en sus preferencias.
Dentro de toda esta decepción, había dos sitios que les habían gustado. Por un lado, había una cafetería llamada Gogoan Kafetegia donde había bebidas vegetales y un restaurante llamado Mapa Verde donde daban comida vegana.

articles.title: First Circle Capital completes $26m final close of fund to build next generation of African fintech infrastructure - Disrupt Africa
articles.text:
First Circle Capital, a pan-African, female-led venture capital firm specialising in African fintech, has announced its final close at $26 million for First Circle Africa Fund I, its specialist early-stage fund backing companies developing the next generation of financial products, services, and technology infrastructure across the continent. 
First Circle Capital, which has offices in Kampala, Nairobi, Casablanca, and Cape Town, was founded by Selma Ribica, a former M-Pesa executive and fintech investor; Agnes Aistleitner, a serial entrepreneur with extensive experience in emerging markets; and Robert Smith, former strategy professional with a deep track record in technology entrepreneurship in East Africa.
Africa Fund I invests at the pre-seed and seed stages in companies driving the next generation of African financial services, across six core fintech verticals: insurtech, alternative lending models, interoperability and infrastructure, climate fintech, fintech SaaS, and regtech.
First Circle Capital’s “FinTech 2.0” investment thesis builds on the growth of Africa’s first generation of payments and lending businesses, targeting the next wave of innovation in financial services, from expanding access to credit and insurance to improving financial infrastructure, digital operations, and regulatory compliance.
Across these investment verticals, First Circle is placing a growing emphasis on AI-native fintech: companies using artificial intelligence, automation, and data-driven operations from inception to lower the cost of delivering financial services, build more efficient products, and reach customers at greater scale.
First Circle follows a thesis-led investment approach, identifying opportunities based on their potential to address structural gaps in African financial services. The fund has a pan-African mandate, investing across established and emerging fintech ecosystems including Kenya, Nigeria, South Africa, Egypt, Morocco, Uganda, Ghana, and Francophone Africa.
Investors in First Circle Africa Fund I include IFC, Bpifrance, MSMEDA, Axian, the Dutch Good Growth Fund, Stellar Foundation, and FSD Africa, bringing together international development finance institutions and other institutional and strategic investors around First Circle’s specialist fintech strategy.
“Africa Fund I is built around a clear thesis: the next generation of African fintech leaders will be those addressing the structural challenges that continue to limit access to financial services across the continent,” Ribica said.
“We are particularly excited by the emergence of AI-native fintech companies. Founders now have the opportunity to build financial businesses around automation, intelligence, and software from day one, fundamentally changing the economics of delivering financial services across African markets. We want to identify those businesses at the earliest stages and work closely with their founders as they scale.”
First Circle Capital has already invested in 18 companies across African markets, creating a diversified portfolio spanning payments, financial wellness, alternative lending, insurtech, climate finance, fintech SaaS, commerce enablement, card infrastructure, and fraud prevention.
Its existing investments reflect the firm’s focus on backing technology companies addressing structural inefficiencies in Africa’s financial services ecosystem while expanding access to financial products and services for underserved individuals and businesses.
Portfolio companies include TurnStay, the South African travel fintech building cross-border payment infrastructure for global travel merchants; Morocco-based WafR, digitising transactions and payments through neighbourhood retailers; Scale, a Card-as-a-Service infrastructure company enabling businesses and fintechs to launch card products; and Orca Fraud, AI-native fraud prevention for financial institutions.
Other investments include Opareta, which provides SaaS and data solutions for the management of mobile money agent networks; Balad, first regulated remittance infrastructure in Egypt facilitating international money transfers; and Power, which provides earned wage access solutions to major African banks.
“Despite the extraordinary growth of fintech across Africa over the past decade, significant gaps remain in key verticals such as financial access, interoperability, digital infrastructure, and the availability of specialised financial products,” said Agnes Aistleitner, co-founder and partner at First Circle Capital.
“We see a significant opportunity to back the founders addressing these challenges: making payments cheaper, expanding access to credit and insurance, strengthening fraud and risk management, improving financial operations through software, and developing innovative financial solutions for sectors such as agriculture and energy. Africa Fund I gives us the capacity to identify those companies early and support them as they develop into market-leading businesses across Africa’s financial services ecosystem.”
The strategy builds on the First Circle team’s experience investing in and supporting early-stage technology companies across the continent, with a focus on identifying specialist founders early and remaining closely involved as their businesses develop.

articles.title: Black Friday Roborock : jusqu’à 500 € de réduction et des robots laveurs dès 299,99 €
articles.text:
Un robot qui aspire, lave le sol, vide son bac et nettoie lui-même ses serpillières change vraiment le quotidien, mais on hésite souvent à l’acheter au prix fort. Pour le Black Friday, Roborock rend ses modèles les plus aboutis à prix bien plus accessibles : certains appareils voient leur prix carrément divisé par deux.
- Le Roborock Saros 10R, robot aspirateur laveur ultra-fin, passe de 989,99 € à 499,99 € sur Amazon, mais aussi sur le site officiel.
- Le Roborock Saros 20 Set, robot aspirateur laveur qui franchit les seuils, livré avec ses consommables de rechange, passe de 1 299 € à 799 € sur Amazon, mais aussi sur le site officiel.
- Le Roborock Saros 20X, le même robot dans sa version vendue avec des serpillières de rechange et une solution de nettoyage, passe de 1 289 € à 799 €
- Le Roborock Qrevo S Pro Set, robot aspirateur laveur avec station complète, passe de 599 € à 299,99 €, mais ausi sur le site officiel.
Roborock Saros 10R : le haut de gamme de 2025 passe sous les 500 euros
C’est l’une des offres les plus marquantes de cette sélection : le Roborock Saros 10R tombe à 499,99 euros au lieu de 989,99 euros, soit 490 euros de réduction. Lancé en 2025 parmi les modèles les plus haut de gamme de la marque, il conserve un équipement très complet, désormais à un prix bien plus abordable.
Son premier atout est sa finesse : avec seulement 7,98 centimètres de hauteur et aucun dôme LiDAR sur le dessus, il peut nettoyer sous de nombreux lits, canapés et meubles bas. Pour se repérer, son système StarSight 2.0 associe des capteurs 3D et une caméra afin de cartographier le logement et de détecter les obstacles du quotidien. Le dispositif latéral VertiBeam complète cette détection le long des meubles.
Dans son test, Frandroid lui attribue la note de 8/10 et souligne ses performances de nettoyage, son design premium et son entretien facilité. Sa brosse principale DuoDivide utilise deux demi-rouleaux pour diriger les cheveux et les poils vers le centre de l’aspiration et limiter leur enroulement. Un équipement particulièrement utile dans les foyers avec des animaux.
Pour nettoyer les sols durs, le Saros 10R dispose de deux serpillières rotatives. L’une d’elles s’étend sur le côté, tout comme sa brosse latérale, pour mieux atteindre les bordures et les coins. Sa station prend ensuite le relais : elle vide le bac à poussière, lave les serpillières à l’eau chaude et les sèche à l’air chaud, ce qui réduit les interventions manuelles.
Le Roborock Saros 10R est proposé à 499,99 euros pour le Black Friday, au lieu de 989,99 euros.
Roborock Saros 20 Set et Saros 20X : le robot qui ne s’arrête plus aux seuils de porte
Présenté en début d’année, le Saros 20 est le successeur direct du Saros 10R, et il corrige précisément ce qui arrêtait encore son aîné. Son châssis monté sur petites pattes se soulève pour franchir des seuils doubles jusqu’à 8,8 centimètres (une première marche de 4,5 centimètres, puis une seconde de 4,3), là où la plupart des robots renoncent au-delà de 2 ou 3. Dans un appartement ancien ou une maison où chaque pièce a sa barre de seuil, c’est la fin des robots coincés à l’entrée du salon.
Ce même châssis le relève sur les tapis pour garder la brosse au contact des poils, jusqu’à 3 centimètres d’épaisseur, et il conserve la silhouette ultra-fine du 10R pour passer sous les meubles bas.
Côté aspiration, Roborock annonce 36 000 Pa pour le Saros 20, qui reprend aussi la brosse anti-enchevêtrement DuoDivide pour limiter les cheveux et les poils enroulés.
« Il place la barre (de seuil) très haut », résume Frandroid, qui lui attribue la note de 8/10 dans son test et salue ses performances de nettoyage comme son intelligence face aux liquides. Le Saros 20 sait en effet reconnaître une flaque : il relève alors sa brosse pour ne pas aspirer de liquide et repasse la serpillière jusqu’à ce que la tache disparaisse, café et ketchup séchés compris.
Sa station de recharge automatise une grande partie de l’entretien : elle vide le bac à poussière, lave les serpillières à l’eau chaude, jusqu’à 100 °C annoncés contre 80 °C sur le Saros 10R, puis les sèche à l’air chaud. Ce lavage aide à déloger les résidus gras et à limiter les mauvaises odeurs.
Deux packs permettent de profiter du même robot avec des accessoires différents. Le Saros 20 Set, proposé sur Amazon, comprend deux sacs à poussière et deux serpillières supplémentaires. Le Saros 20X, distribué notamment chez Boulanger, à la Fnac et chez Darty, est accompagné de deux serpillières supplémentaires et d’une solution de nettoyage.
Pour le Black Friday, le Saros 20 Set est proposé à 799 euros sur Amazon au lieu de 1 299 euros, tandis que le Saros 20X est disponible à 799 euros chez Boulanger.
Roborock Qrevo S Pro Set : un aspirateur laveur complet pour moins de 300 euros
Pas besoin de casser sa tirelire pour confier le ménage à un robot. Le Qrevo S Pro Set offre ce qu’on trouvait il y a peu sur des modèles deux fois plus chers : un robot qui aspire et lave, et une station qui s’occupe de presque tout le reste.
Ses deux serpillières rotatives frottent les sols durs pour venir à bout des taches tenaces, et se relèvent automatiquement quand le robot passe sur un tapis, pour ne pas le mouiller. Ses 18 500 Pa d’aspiration suffisent largement pour la poussière, les miettes et les poils du quotidien, et ses brosses tout caoutchouc limitent l’enchevêtrement des cheveux. Un câble qui traîne, des chaussons au pied du lit, la gamelle du chat : le robot repère ce qui encombre le sol et le contourne au lieu de le pousser ou de s’y emmêler.
C’est surtout sa station qui fait la différence à ce prix. Elle lave les serpillières à 75 °C, les sèche à l’air chaud pour éviter les mauvaises odeurs, remplit le réservoir d’eau du robot et vide sa poussière : son sac tient jusqu’à 65 jours selon Roborock, soit un peu plus de deux mois sans y toucher.
Le robot est aussi compatible Matter, le standard commun de la maison connectée. On peut ainsi lancer le ménage depuis l’application Maison d’Apple, Google Home ou Alexa, et pas seulement depuis l’application Roborock, ou l’intégrer à une routine, par exemple pour qu’il démarre quand tout le monde a quitté la maison.
Pour un appareil qu’on achète pour plusieurs années, un dernier détail a son importance : Roborock arrive en tête du baromètre SAV 2026 de Fnac-Darty, qui classe les marques d’aspirateurs robots selon la fiabilité et la réparabilité constatées par ses techniciens.
Affiché à 599 euros en prix de référence, le Qrevo S Pro Set voit son prix divisé par deux pour le Black Friday. Comptez 299,99 euros seulement sur Amazon pendant les prochains jours.

articles.title: Galaxy Studio : batterie de 870 mAh et prise jack pour le futur casque de Samsung — Frandroid
articles.text:
Ce lundi 16 novembre, le site SamMobile a publié des graphismes qui dessinent l’allure probable du Galaxy Studio. Ces illustrations semblent tirées de l’application compagnon du casque, et le produit final pourrait en différer. Le leaker @evowizz avait avancé le nom Galaxy Studio pour la première fois le 8 octobre.
    Pour aller plus loin
Quels sont les meilleurs casques audio de 2026 ? Notre sélection
            
Samsung avait en outre déposé le 14 septembre une demande de marque aux États-Unis, pour des casques et des écouteurs. Cette demande est toujours en cours d’examen, ce qui ne garantit pas l’emploi de ce nom. Dès le mois d’août, des lignes de code de l’application Galaxy Wearable mentionnaient un casque désigné en interne sous le nom Galaxy H1.
Le dossier déposé à la FCC sous la référence SM-U700 montre aussi des oreillettes pivotantes, qui permettent de ranger le casque à plat dans un sac. Il mentionne deux coloris, noir et beige.
Ce que révèle la bêta de One UI 9.5
Selon SammyGuru, qui a publié ses trouvailles ce mercredi 18 novembre, la bêta de One UI 9.5 contient de nombreuses références au casque, qui y apparaît sous les noms Galaxy H1 et Galaxy Studio. Le site y a relevé une batterie de 870 mAh en capacité typique et de 850 mAh en capacité nominale. Les fichiers n’indiquent pas l’autonomie en heures.
Côté connectique, le casque permettrait l’écoute filaire en USB-C, ce même port servant à la recharge. Une connexion jack 3,5 mm est aussi mentionnée, sans que l’on sache s’il s’agit d’une prise dédiée ou d’un adaptateur USB-C. Le multipoint figure également dans la liste. La réduction de bruit est associée à un mode Son ambiant, qui peut s’activer automatiquement. Une option permet en outre de le garder pendant les appels.
La détection du port met la lecture en pause lorsque l’on retire le casque et la relance quand on le remet. Si on l’enlève pendant un appel, la conversation peut ainsi passer sur le haut-parleur du téléphone ou de la tablette.
Les commandes tactiles se trouvent sur l’oreillette droite. Un appui lance ou met en pause la lecture, un double appui passe au titre suivant ou décroche et raccroche, et un triple appui revient au titre précédent. Un appui prolongé appelle l’assistant IA. Les commandes vocales et les gestes de la tête des Galaxy Buds n’apparaissent pas dans les fichiers.
Le casque ne se pilote pas qu’au toucher. Selon SammyGuru, l’oreillette droite accueille aussi un bouton physique qui fait défiler les modes de réduction de bruit, et les boutons de volume + et, sont placés sur l’oreillette gauche. Une action permet d’activer le Son ambiant tout en baissant le volume, pour entendre quelqu’un sans retirer le casque.
Fonctions logicielles et homologations
Le logiciel mentionne aussi le support du format 360 Audio avec suivi des mouvements de la tête, Buds Auto Switch, Auracast et Samsung Find. SamMobile mentionne aussi les codecs SSC UHQ et LC3, que le site anticipait depuis octobre, mais SammyGuru ne les relève pas dans les fichiers. Côté réglages, on trouve un égaliseur, l’amplification des dialogues, la normalisation du volume et un mode jeu. Ces réglages seraient reliés à Modes et routines. L’extinction automatique peut se programmer après 30, 60 ou 120 minutes sans lecture.
En revanche, le Galaxy Studio est explicitement exclu du menu des options de qualité avancées, qui propose l’audio Haute Résolution jusqu’à 96 kHz sur d’autres futurs écouteurs de la marque. Or ce mode repose justement sur le codec SSC UHQ, dont la prise en charge par le casque reste donc incertaine.
Le casque a déjà franchi plusieurs étapes d’homologation. TÜV Rheinland l’a certifié en premier, avec une entrée de charge de 5 W. L’agence sud-coréenne des radiocommunications (RRA) a suivi le 23 octobre, puis la FCC aux États-Unis le 4 novembre. Le Galaxy Studio marquerait ainsi le retour de Samsung sur ce segment, plus de dix ans après le Level Over de 2014, son dernier modèle circum-auriculaire.
Le Galaxy Studio viserait le haut du marché, face aux Sony WH-1000XM6, AirPods Max 2, Sennheiser Momentum 5 Wireless et Bose QuietComfort Ultra Headphones 2e génération. Sa connectique pourrait faire la différence.

articles.title: EPFO approves systematic withdrawal plan for retiring members
articles.text:
EPFO approves systematic withdrawal plan for retiring members
Retiring members can now opt for receiving their retirement savings in periodic installments instead of a lump sum amount.
The retirement fund body Employees’ Provident Fund Organisation (EPFO) on Thursday approved a Systematic Withdrawal Plan (SWP) for its retiring members to receive their accumulated provident fund savings in periodic instalments instead of withdrawing the entire corpus at once.
Under the SWP, retiring members of the EPFO will receive their accumulated provident fund savings in periodic installments instead of withdrawing the entire amount at once, a Labour Ministry release said.
The decision was taken at the 240th meeting of the Central Board of Trustees (CBT) of the Employees’ Provident Fund (EPF), chaired by Union Minister for Labour & Employment and Youth Affairs & Sports, Mansukh Mandaviya.
The Board approved a proposal to introduce a Systematic Withdrawal Plan, enabling retiring EPF members to receive their accumulated provident fund savings in periodic installments instead of withdrawing the entire amount at once.
This reform will enable retiring members to withdraw their accumulated provident fund savings at regular intervals, such as monthly, quarterly or half-yearly, based on their preference.
This facility would provide members with a structured source of periodic income while allowing the remaining corpus to continue generating returns, thereby helping augment their retirement income and supplement their pension benefits.
The facility would be entirely voluntary, with no compulsion on members to opt for withdrawals.
The option may also be extended to eligible family members/beneficiaries, ensuring greater flexibility and financial security for the family. This aims to ensure stable post-retirement income, reduce reinvestment risks, strengthen fund sustainability, and extend social security coverage to gig and platform workers.
SWP will enable members to convert their retirement savings into a stable and predictable stream of systematic withdrawals post-retirement, while preserving ownership of the underlying corpus.
Approximately 6.32 lakh EPF members aged above 55 years with provident fund accumulations exceeding Rs 5 lakh are expected to be the primary beneficiaries of the proposed SWP framework during the initial phase.

articles.title: Fuite de données chez Chargemap : des millions de conducteurs sont touchés par une cyberattaque
articles.text:
Chargemap prévient tous les conducteurs concernés par mail. Consulté par 01net, le courriel révèle que l’application a été « la cible d’une attaque informatique » le 8 novembre 2026. Une personne non autorisée « a pu accéder à certaines données de comptes utilisateurs ». Pour ceux qui ne connaissent pas, Chargemap est une application française très utilisée par les conducteurs de véhicules électriques. Elle permet de localiser les bornes de recharge, de préparer ses trajets et de payer toutes ses recharges grâce au badge Chargemap Pass. La plateforme revendique plus de 3,5 millions d’utilisateurs. Le nombre de comptes touchés n’a pas été communiqué par l’entreprise originaire de Strasbourg.
À lire aussi : Fuite de données géante à La Poste – « 22 millions de personnes sont concernées » par une cyberattaque massive
Une faille sur une ancienne interface
D’après Chargemap, le pirate a exploité « une faille de sécurité sur une ancienne interface technique de Chargemap pour extraire certaines données de comptes utilisateurs ». Les équipes de l’entreprise ont repéré « une activité anormale » le 10 novembre, soit deux jours après le début de l’attaque. La faille a ensuite été corrigée dès le 12 novembre, quatre jours après la cyberattaque.
Conformément à la loi, Chargemap a ensuite prévenu la CNIL, le gendarme français des données personnelles. L’entreprise a aussi « engagé une procédure de dépôt de plainte » et « déploie des ressources et des mesures de sécurité supplémentaires pour se prémunir contre toute nouvelle attaque de ce type ».
Quelles données ont été volées ?
Pour tous les comptes concernés, le pirate a mis la main sur « votre adresse email, votre nom d’utilisateur et la langue de votre application ». D’autres informations sont touchées, mais « uniquement si vous les aviez renseignées lors de votre inscription », comme le prénom et le nom, le numéro de téléphone, la date de naissance, la ville et le pays, la photo de profil et la date de dernière connexion.
Pour les comptes créés avec un mot de passe, le pirate a pu récupérer « une empreinte ou une version chiffrée de votre mot de passe, et non le mot de passe lui-même ». Concrètement, le mot de passe a été transformé en une suite de caractères illisibles, par mesure de sécurité. Avec l’aide d’algorithmes, les pirates peuvent ensuite récupérer le mot de passe, même si l’opération est incertaine, fastidieuse, et prend du temps. : si votre mot de passe était retrouvé, « son décryptage pourrait aussi permettre à des tiers malveillants de se connecter à vos autres comptes ».
Chargemap reconnaît par ailleurs que les mots de passe des personnes qui ne se sont pas connectées depuis avril 2019 étaient conservés « dans un ancien format, moins robuste ». Même les anciens utilisateurs, qui ont supprimé leur compte, peuvent être concernés par la fuite de données.
L’entreprise se veut toutefois rassurante. L’incident « ne concerne ni vos moyens de paiement, ni votre adresse postale, ni vos recharges (historique, lieux, montants), ni vos factures, ni le numéro (RFID) de votre badge Chargemap Pass ». Néanmoins, Chargemap précise qu’une vingtaine de badges ont bien été touchés. Les détenteurs de ceux-ci seront prévenus individuellement dans les plus brefs délais.
« Quelqu’un pourrait utiliser ces données pour vous envoyer des messages frauduleux qui paraissent crédibles », prévient Chargemap.
Chargemap vient rejoindre la liste des entreprises piratées en France cet automne. Début novembre, le spécialiste de l’entretien automobile Auto Planning a confirmé le piratage de 14 millions de plaques d’immatriculation. Quelques jours plus tard, une filiale de La Poste a été frappée par une cyberattaque massive, touchant 22 millions de personnes.
À lire aussi : Cyberattaque contre Engie – une fuite de données touche les clients en France
Que faire si vous utilisez Chargemap ?
Chargemap recommande de modifier immédiatement votre mot de passe, surtout si vous recyclez celui-ci sur d’autres services. Profitez-en pour choisir un bon mot de passe, composé d’une suite aléatoire de chiffres, de lettres et de caractères spéciaux. Si vous vous connectez uniquement avec Google, Facebook ou Apple, vous n’avez rien à changer.
Restez aussi très « vigilant face aux emails, SMS ou appels se présentant comme Chargemap ». L’entreprise rappelle qu’elle ne vous demandera « jamais votre mot de passe ou vos coordonnées bancaires par email, SMS ou téléphone ». Par ailleurs, les messages émis par l’application proviennent toujours d’une adresse en « @chargemap.com ». Enfin, on vous recommande de consulter régulièrement votre historique de recharges à la recherche de la moindre session recharge inconnue.
 👉🏻 Suivez l’actualité tech en temps réel : ajoutez 01net à vos sources sur Google, et abonnez-vous à notre canal WhatsApp.

articles.title: ASUS warns of critical hard-coded key flaw in Control Center Express
articles.text:
ASUS released Control Center Express v1.7.29 to fix three critical vulnerabilities that could let remote attackers gain administrative control of the management console and the devices it manages.
Of the three, one is a maximum-severity vulnerability (CVSS score: 10.0) tracked under CVE-2026-114202, arising from a hard-coded cryptographic key used in the product.
The flaw lets an unauthenticated remote attacker forge an authentication token and gain administrator privileges, without requiring any privileges or user interaction.
The second flaw is CVE-2026-114204, also a hard-coded key problem, which lets a remote attacker with low privileges forge a session token for a recently logged-in account.
The third is CVE-2026-114205, an authorization flaw that lets a low-privileged user create an administrator account.
ASUS Control Center Express is a central dashboard that IT administrators use to monitor and remotely manage fleets of PCs.
ASUS markets it to businesses and IT service providers and lists support for more than 200 of its business, workstation, and Corporate Stable Model motherboards.
While all three vulnerabilities are rated critical, CVE-2026-114204 has a recent-session prerequisite, and CVE-2026-114205 requires a low-privileged account, whereas CVE-2026-114202 enables remote administrative access with no prerequisites.
ASUS’s security bulletin says versions earlier than v1.7.29 are affected. However, the CVE records only list affected versions through v1.7.27, leaving the status of v1.7.28 unclear.
Impacted users are advised to install v1.7.29, then update the agents on managed devices through Select Function → Client Agent Updater, and verify their versions.
Also yesterday, ASUS released security updates for Control Center Enterprise, its centralized IT management platform, and Armoury Crate, a hardware configuration utility.
Specifically, ASUS patched CVE-2026-126574, a critical authorization flaw that lets a remote user with the low-privileged Viewer role change an administrator’s password and take over the account.
The flaw affects Control Center Datacenter 4.0.0.2 and earlier and Control Center Enterprise 3.1.0.8 and earlier.
The Armoury Crate update addressed CVE-2026-112115, a high-severity privilege escalation flaw.
The flaw affects all versions up to and including 6.7.2 and could allow a low-privileged local user to trick an elevated process into loading a malicious library.

articles.title: From learning to leaderboard: How Cisco upskilled 1,200 engineers in agentic AI with AWS AI League | Amazon Web Services
articles.text:
Artificial Intelligence
From learning to leaderboard: How Cisco upskilled 1,200 engineers in agentic AI with AWS AI League
Cisco, like many large engineering organizations, is adopting generative and agentic AI to change how its engineers build software. The hard part is no longer access to the technology. It’s helping thousands of engineers move from watching a demo to confidently building with it. Recorded sessions and slide decks rarely close that gap. Engineers learn fastest when they build something real, see it fail, fix it, and try again.
AWS designed AWS AI League for exactly that. It turns hands-on AI learning into a gamified competition, where participants customize models and build agents on AWS, get instant feedback on a live leaderboard, and compete in a game-show-style finale.
Cisco is one of the clearest examples of what this looks like at scale. In 2025, Hemanth V, a Cisco software engineer, went from an internal Cisco event to being crowned the first AWS AI League Champion at AWS re:Invent 2025. In 2026, 1,200 Cisco engineers competed in an AWS AI League tournament at Cisco Transformation Fest 4.0. The winner, Nishanth Aluhonnu, earned a full event pass to AWS re:Invent 2026 in Las Vegas.
In this post, we share how Cisco and AWS used Cisco Transformation Fest and AWS AI League to build a lasting culture of learning by doing. We previously covered this program in From theory to delivery: How Atos upskilled 400 engineers in agentic AI, and here we look at Cisco’s experience. We walk through Cisco’s journey, share technical lessons from the 2026 winning agent, and explain how your organization can host its own AWS AI League.
What is AWS AI League?
AWS AI League helps organizations build advanced AI skills through competition. Each league follows three steps:
- Learn – A hands-on, 2-hour workshop led by AWS experts introduces the tools and the challenge.
- Build – Participants experiment at their own pace and submit to a live leaderboard, with an automated evaluator giving real-time feedback after each submission.
- Compete – Top finalists take the stage in a live, game-show-style grand finale.
Although AWS AI League offers multiple use cases, at Cisco it offered the following two challenges:
- Agentic AI challenge – Participants build agents with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, a platform to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale with any framework or model. The agents move through a maze-like grid, solving challenges on the way to a treasure chest. The challenges map to real-world tasks such as handling inappropriate content, running code, retrieving information from the web, and extracting structured data. Builders can choose models for supervisor and sub-agents and add tools such as AgentCore memory, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, and AWS Lambda Event Functions. Builders use Amazon Bedrock Guardrails to apply safety controls to their agents.
- Model customization challenge – Participants fine-tune models in Amazon SageMaker Studio using the latest training recipes. The challenge awards points when an automated evaluator rates a participant’s customized model as more accurate and comprehensive than a reference model on the specific tasks in the competition.
Finalists are scored on time efficiency, accuracy, agent planning, and token consumption efficiency.
The Cisco and AWS partnership
The AWS AI League story at Cisco grows out of a deep engineering partnership. Cisco and AWS bring together networking, cloud, security, and observability for shared customers including:
- Cisco SD-WAN, whose controller architecture runs on AWS and serves customers globally as a software as a service (SaaS) application.
- Cisco Meraki, Cisco Spaces, and Cisco’s IoT and smart buildings group.
- Cisco Cloud Control, a cloud-native, AI-powered application integrated with AWS services that brings together security, networking, observability, and collaboration.
- Cisco AI Defense, where Cisco’s security team uses Amazon Bedrock and Amazon SageMaker AI to embed AI governance and guardrails across the Cisco portfolio.
The two companies have also published joint deployment guides and Cisco Validated Designs across networking and AWS. A recent example of co-innovation is SD-WAN fabric on demand across the AWS backbone, built to deliver the resilience and uptime customers expect.
        “When you see that many business units independently choosing to build their next-generation platforms natively on AWS, that’s not a vendor relationship anymore. It’s a true engineering partnership.”
— Kumaril Kapoor, VP of Engineering, Cisco
Cisco’s VP of Engineering Kumaril Kapoor and AWS Industries India leader Chandra Balani sit down to discuss the AWS and Cisco partnership story, from co-innovation across networking, cloud, and AI to enabling thousands of engineers through the annual Cisco AWS Transformation Fest.
Cisco Transformation Fest: Enablement at scale
As the partnership grew, it extended beyond technology to people. Working closely with Cisco teams in India, AWS saw a strong appetite for learning and experimenting among Cisco engineers across many business units. The question was how to scale that impact beyond the day-to-day touchpoints of the partnership.
The answer was Cisco Transformation Fest, first held in 2022. The program is built on five tenets the team summarized as SCALE:
| Tenet | What it means for Cisco engineers | 
| Share | Share what you know with peers across teams. | 
| Connect | Connect with engineers across business units. | 
| Adopt | Adopt new skills and AWS services. | 
| Learn | Learn by building, not by watching. | 
| Experiment / Engage | Experiment hands-on and stay engaged with the technology and each other. | 
Transformation Fest brings together several formats: AWS GameDays, AWS AI League, sessions where Cisco leaders share best practices and success stories with peers, and sessions on Amazon and AWS culture. What began as a single event is now an annual, three-day program that has completed its fourth edition and reached around 2,000 engineers. AWS continues to engage Cisco teams with hands-on workshops and experience-based accelerations.
        “It has been genuinely valuable for us, and it’s really a journey, but I appreciate most is the intent behind it. It’s built around our people. It gives our engineers the time, the space, and the hands-on support to grow real skills on AWS. For us, it has turned into a lasting culture of learning by doing. It’s not a one-off event.”
— Kumaril Kapoor, VP of Engineering, Cisco
Where enablement becomes execution: AWS AI League at Cisco
Of all the Transformation Fest formats, AWS AI League has had the most visible impact. Its gamified, hands-on structure puts engineers to work with Amazon SageMaker on fine-tuning, model customization and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore for agent building, against a clock and in front of their peers. Participants leave with practical experience and genuine confidence in their AI skills.
        “This is where enablement actually turns into real execution.”
— Kumaril Kapoor, VP of Engineering, Cisco
2025: From the Cisco campus to global champion
Hemanth V, a software engineer in Cisco’s switching core platform team, had an inspiring journey that set the benchmark for Cisco.
His journey had two stages:
- AWS AI League at Cisco AWS Transformation Fest 3.0. He competed against more than 600 participants from Cisco in a model customization challenge, fine-tuning a small model in Amazon SageMaker, and won the title.
- Global grand finale at AWS re:Invent 2025. In Las Vegas he faced a completely different challenge: the agentic AI track, where he built an agent to navigate a dynamic, game-style maze. He took first place and was recognized during the re:Invent keynote.
Hemanth finished ahead of Ross Williams from Aqfer (second place) and Deepesh Khanna from Capital One (third place).
        “You don’t need to know everything beforehand. You will learn a lot of things on the way. The only thing that matters is your curiosity and willingness to learn.”
— Hemanth V, Software Engineer, Cisco, and 2025 AWS AI League Champion
2026: 1,200 engineers, one champion
In 2026, Cisco Transformation Fest 4.0 hosted a full AWS AI League agentic AI tournament. The AWS account team ran pre-event training so that engineers with no prior agentic AI experience could compete from day one. The format was designed to narrow a large field down to a single winner:
| Stage | Format | Winning result | 
| Qualifier | 1,200 participants across four cohorts. Top 5 per cohort advance to semifinal | 1st in cohort 3 with 15,906 points (98 submissions) | 
| Semifinal | 20 participants compete for 3 finalist spots | 1st with 16,321 points | 
| Finale | 3 live rounds on stage in front of Cisco and AWS leadership | 1st with 27,008 cumulative points | 
Nishanth Aluhonnu, a software engineer at Cisco, finished first at every stage and earned a full conference pass to AWS re:Invent 2026.
The finale itself showed why the format works. Participants could not change code, tools, or prompts during the finale, only a short steering instruction before each round. Success depended on how well each agent made decisions on maps it had never seen before. Nishanth lost the first round, then won the second by a wide margin by ignoring a board full of low-value coins in favor of a single high-value challenge.
Examining what it takes to win an agentic AI challenge
The 2026 winning agent offers lessons that go well beyond the game. Each design choice maps to a decision teams face when they run agents in production.
Output tokens are the real cost
The agentic AI challenge scores agents on challenge points, a treasure bonus, remaining lives, and a token bonus, computed as tokenBonus = 1000 - (totalOutputTokens / challengesVisited).
In the qualifier, the top four agents all solved the map. The first-place agent emitted 1,220 output tokens and the second-place agent emitted 1,430, and the final margin was only 16 points out of nearly 16,000. After every agent can solve the problem, efficiency decides the winner.
To understand which tokens mattered, Nishanth built nine variants of the same agent, changing one thing at a time. The result was clear: tool results and the system prompt didn’t count against the score, but everything the agent wrote, including tool call arguments, did. Each tool call carried roughly 52 tokens of fixed overhead on top of its arguments.
This mirrors real-world cost. Generating output is sequential and is typically priced several times higher than input, and in an agent loop that cost compounds across every step. A long, well-structured system prompt (which you can also cache) is cheap. A chatty agent isn’t.
One agent, not five
A common architecture for this challenge is a supervisor agent on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore that delegates to specialist sub-agents for navigation, computation, and web retrieval. It’s a sound pattern for many production systems. The winning design used a single agent with no sub-agents. Instead, the prompt began with a short dispatch table that matched each challenge type to the right approach in a single turn.
The reasoning was simple: every handoff between agents is a message the model has to write, and in this challenge every written token is scored. The lesson isn’t that sub-agents are bad. It’s to choose your architecture based on what coordination costs you. When coordination is expensive, a flatter design can win.
The following diagram shows the AWS reference architecture for the agentic AI challenge: a supervisor agent with specialist sub-agents. The winning design deliberately didn’t use this multi-agent pattern.
In this reference architecture, a supervisor agent runs in Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, and coordinates three sub-agents, with Amazon Bedrock Guardrails and AgentCore memory connected to the runtime. The supervisor and sub-agents route through the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, to four tools: a navigation tool, browser tool, code execution tool, and custom tools using AWS Lambda functions.
Put deterministic logic in tools
Route planning was not left to the model. It ran in an AWS Lambda function that treated the board as an optimization problem. Each tile carried an expected value: the points it paid, minus the lives it could cost, minus the tokens the agent would spend to solve it. The planner respected constraints, such as collecting a key before its door, and refined the route within a time budget.
This is a useful pattern for most agents: let the model handle language and judgment, and move search, math, and rules into tools where they are faster, cheaper, and repeatable.
Make decisions on value, not habit
The second finale round was designed as a trap. A seven-by-seven board was almost entirely covered in coins worth 25 points each, while a single scheduling challenge tile was worth 1,500 points. Habit said to collect the coins. The planner’s value table said the coins were noise. The agent went for the high-value challenge and scored 7,537 points in that round, compared with 5,953 for the next finalist. That round built the lead that carried the agent to the overall win.
Impact for Cisco
Across two years of AWS AI League at Cisco, the impact shows up in skills, culture, and recognition:
- Hands-on AI skills at scale. 1,200 engineers took part in the 2026 tournament, building agents on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, many of them with no prior agentic AI experience.
- Connections across business units. Engineers who would otherwise never have met competed in the same tournament, shared approaches, and learned from each other.
- A lasting culture of learning. Now in its fourth year, Transformation Fest has become an annual commitment rather than a one-off hackathon.
- Recognition, two years in a row. A Cisco engineer won the 2025 AWS AI League global title, and the 2026 Cisco champion will attend AWS re:Invent 2026.
- Leadership visibility. The 2026 finale took place in front of Cisco and AWS senior leadership, giving engineers a real stage for their work.
For Hemanth, the biggest takeaway was confidence. You do not need to master everything before you start. You learn by getting hands-on.
        “Technology alone isn’t enough. You need people who are empowered to experiment with it. Transformation Fest created that enablement environment, and AWS AI League created the opportunity for execution.”
— Kumaril Kapoor, VP of Engineering, Cisco
Conclusion
In this post, we showed how Cisco and AWS turned enablement into execution. Cisco Transformation Fest created a space for engineers to learn by doing, and AWS AI League gave them a real challenge, a scoreboard, and a stage. The result is a culture of hands-on AI building that reaches thousands of engineers.
To get started:
- Learn how to host a tournament in your organization on the AWS AI League page.
- Build your agentic AI and model customization skills with the AWS AI training catalog on AWS Skill Builder.
- Follow the AWS AI League 2026 global finale at AWS re:Invent 2026 in Las Vegas.
We look forward to seeing what your teams build.

articles.title: How Amazon ECS handles blue/green, canary, and linear deployments
articles.text:
How Amazon ECS handles blue/green, canary, and linear deployments
Deploying containers safely at scale can mean assembling your own system: traffic-splitting logic, alarm evaluation, rollback automation, approval gates. It’s infrastructure that exists solely to protect the deployment itself. AWS has built all of those capabilities directly into Amazon Elastic Container Service (ECS), so you don’t have to.
“Deploying containers safely at scale can mean assembling your own system: traffic-splitting logic, alarm evaluation, rollback automation, approval gates. It’s infrastructure that exists solely to protect the deployment itself.”
You can access all these tools through a single API endpoint. AWS built them to work out of the box when you use Amazon ECS as your container orchestration platform with the Amazon ECS deployment controller. As a result, you don’t have to build your own abstractions or learn a new framework to get the deployment behavior you want. Instead, you pick and choose the features you want through a service deployment configuration and update it as your needs change.
How the building blocks map to ECS
If you’ve run progressive delivery on Kubernetes with Argo Rollouts or Flagger, you know the shape of the stack: a controller you install and keep current, analysis wired to your metrics backend, and a traffic provider for weighted canaries. Argo Rollouts approximates canary weights with replica counts and uses an ingress controller, service mesh, or Gateway API for precise percentages. Flagger uses a service mesh or ingress controller for weighted canaries, and plain Kubernetes Services for blue/green. Both are mature open-source projects and a great fit when you want to own and tune every layer. ECS takes a different approach and builds the same capabilities into the service. Here’s a comparison of the different deployment controllers:
| What you need | With Argo Rollouts or Flagger (Kubernetes) | Built into ECS | 
| Deployment strategies | Rolling updates come with Kubernetes Deployments; blue/green and canary come from a controller you install and keep current | Rolling, blue/green, linear, and canary, set in the service’s deployment configuration | 
| Traffic shifting | Argo Rollouts: replica-count weighting by default, or an ingress controller, service mesh, or Gateway API for precise percentages. Flagger: a service mesh or ingress controller for weighted canaries | ECS shifts traffic through your ALB, NLB, ECS Service Connect, or VPC Lattice, or calls your own logic through lifecycle hooks | 
| Health and metric analysis | Analysis templates or built-in checks against your metrics provider (Prometheus, Datadog, CloudWatch, and others) | Deployment circuit breaker plus CloudWatch alarm monitoring | 
| Automatic rollback | The controller aborts and shifts traffic back to the stable version when analysis fails | ECS rolls back on circuit breaker or alarm, and you can pull the cord yourself with the StopServiceDeployment API | 
| Custom checks and approval gates | Webhooks, custom analysis steps, or manual promotion | Lifecycle hooks with Lambda or pause targets, resumed with the ContinueServiceDeployment API | 
When are rolling deployments not enough?
Rolling deployments are where ECS started, and they’re still the right default for most customers. In a rolling deployment, ECS replaces tasks running the old version with tasks running the new one, a batch at a time. New tasks start receiving production traffic as soon as they pass health checks, and ECS stops old tasks as the new ones take over. Two settings, minimumHealthyPercent and maximumPercent, control how many tasks can be replaced at once and how much extra capacity the deployment can use. Rolling deployments work with both the deployment circuit breaker and CloudWatch alarm-based automatic rollback, which we’ll cover below.
So, where’s the gap? Let’s say you have an API service running on ECS behind an ALB. You ship a large refactor. A bug surfaces, but it takes time because of metric emission and alarm-processing delays. By the time your alarm fires, a large share of your tasks (maybe all of them) are already running the new version and serving production traffic. ECS rolls back for you, but in a rolling deployment, rollback means another rollout of the previous task definition: ECS must launch new tasks, pass health checks, and replace the bad ones. Your application’s availability will be exposed for some time.
“There’s a limit to how fast a rolling deployment can roll back, which increases customer impact (measured by failed requests per unit of time) from the new, bad application version.”
So, there’s a limit to how fast a rolling deployment can roll back, which increases customer impact (measured by failed requests per unit of time) from the new, bad application version. Blue/green deployments can shorten the duration of the impact. With ECS’s built-in blue/green strategy, the old version stays running alongside the new one for a configurable bake period (up to 24 hours). All production traffic routes to the new version, but the old version’s tasks remain registered and ready to take traffic with a flip of a switch. If something goes wrong, rollback is a simple traffic shift, and not a complete redeploy.
The tradeoff is that you’re doubling compute capacity during the deployment window. For services where a bad release serving 100% of traffic for even a few minutes is costly, that tradeoff is worth it.
How does ECS know something went wrong?
How would Amazon ECS know when to flip traffic back? There are several ways to perform a service deployment rollback, and they’re all configurable through an ECS service’s deployment configuration:
- Task launch and health state monitoring during a deployment through circuit breaker
- Amazon CloudWatch alarm(s) monitoring and auto-rollback
- Controls to roll back an ongoing service deployment through the StopServiceDeployment API
- Service deployment lifecycle hooks (Lambda or pause target type)
For API server failures, you can set up Amazon CloudWatch alarms to monitor server response codes and trigger a rollback when a high volume of 4xx or 5xx codes is detected. But what if your application monitoring constructs are outside of Amazon CloudWatch and stored on another service like Datadog, Splunk, or Grafana? With service deployment lifecycle hooks, you can implement your own automation that polls these data sources for alarm data by implementing that logic in a Lambda function and configuring a Lambda target type. The primary consideration is configuring the lifecycle hook for the POST_PRODUCTION_TRAFFIC_SHIFT stage.
If you can’t use Lambda functions, then implement an Amazon EventBridge trigger with a pause hook target type instead. Amazon ECS will send an Amazon EventBridge event when the service deployment reaches the lifecycle stage configured for the lifecycle hook. The trigger should fire a process you own that runs the same polling loop to monitor an alarm or metric. Once the monitoring condition succeeds, call the ContinueServiceDeployment API to allow the service deployment to progress.
In addition to alarms and lifecycle hooks, the service deployment circuit breaker monitor can stop a bad deployment from progressing. This deployment monitor looks for failed or unhealthy tasks during a service deployment and compares the sum against a threshold. With configurable circuit breaker settings, you can customize the counter algorithm to ignore intermittent task launch or health failures. You can also customize the failure threshold based on your application’s needs.
Advanced deployment strategies
The example above is just one way to use built-in ECS features to customize your service deployment. If a one-step traffic shift isn’t suitable for your application, linear and canary deployments are also alternatives.
Linear and canary deployments are like blue/green deployments in that they use well-defined traffic-shift steps to isolate application traffic between versions. Linear deployments move traffic in equal increments based on your configuration. Canaries are a little different in that there is a two-step migration in application traffic as opposed to n number of incremental shifts.
Not advanced enough? There’s more!
All the deployment tools we talked about today apply to all deployment strategies that ECS supports. Similarly, all deployment strategies are compatible with ECS Service Connect and VPC Lattice network integrations. The only caveat is that lifecycle hooks can be applied to only two stages for a rolling deployment, since that lifecycle is inherently simpler than blue/green, linear, or canary deployments.
“All deployment strategies also work without a load balancer, ECS Service Connect, or VPC Lattice integration! That’s right, even blue/green, linear, and canary deployments.”
All deployment strategies also work without a load balancer, ECS Service Connect, or VPC Lattice integration! That’s right, even blue/green, linear, and canary deployments. We developed these service deployment lifecycle hooks with customization in mind, so we created specific integration points to shift your application traffic. You can control the behavior by writing your own logic, and Amazon ECS invokes a lifecycle hook at the production traffic-shift stage. Just note that this stage takes a Lambda target, since pause hooks can’t be configured there.
Which strategy should you pick?
Here’s the short version of everything above:
| Your situation | Reach for | What you get | What it costs | 
| Most everyday changes, or cost-sensitive services | Rolling with circuit breaker and alarms | Automatic rollback on failed tasks or alarms, and you can tune minimumHealthyPercent and maximumPercent so you’re not paying for a second copy of your service | Rollback is a redeploy, so the bad version serves traffic until it’s replaced | 
| A bad release is expensive, and you need an instant way back | Blue/green | Old version stays warm through the bake period; rollback is a traffic shift | Double compute capacity during the deployment window | 
| You want production signal from a small slice before full exposure | Canary | A small share of traffic hits the new version first, then the rest moves in a second step | Same capacity tradeoff as blue/green, and a slower rollout | 
| You want exposure to grow steadily and catch load-dependent issues | Linear | Traffic moves in equal increments, with a chance to roll back at each step | Same capacity tradeoff, and the longest rollout | 
| Your monitoring lives outside CloudWatch (Datadog, Splunk, Grafana) | Blue/green, linear, or canary, plus lifecycle hooks at the post-production traffic shift stage (rolling supports hooks too, at fewer stages) | Your own checks gate the deployment through Lambda or pause targets | Code you write and own | 
| You don’t use a load balancer, Service Connect, or VPC Lattice | Blue/green, linear, or canary, plus a Lambda lifecycle hook at the production traffic shift stage | ECS calls your logic to shift your own traffic | Code you write and own | 
Pick a strategy
Whichever deployment strategy you choose, the guardrails (alarms, circuit breaker, lifecycle hooks, and rollback) come with the service. Configure them once, and spend your engineering time on your product, not your pipeline.
Pick one service, turn on blue/green with a CloudWatch alarm, and see for yourself. The Amazon ECS lifecycle hooks guide is a good next step once you want custom checks.

articles.title: On a débridé GTA 6 à 60 FPS : Vice City n’a jamais été aussi fluide
articles.text:
À quoi ressemblerait Vice City à 60 images par seconde ? On a sorti le boîtier de capture pour vous en donner un aperçu, à partir de notre propre partie sur PS5 Pro.
Pour se faire une idée de la fluidité d’un jeu, rien de tel qu’un bon coup de stick. La caméra pivote, les façades défilent et, pour peu qu’on ait l’habitude de jouer à 60 images par seconde, on se prend à chercher le mode Performance dans les réglages. Dans GTA VI, on peut chercher longtemps. Rockstar a choisi de viser les 30 images par seconde, y compris sur PS5 Pro. Alors on a tenté une petite expérience avec les moyens du bord. Voici ce que donne notre partie une fois les images passées entre les mains d’un PC.
Pour en profiter, ouvrez la vidéo en plein écran et vérifiez que la qualité sélectionnée porte bien la mention « 60 ». Le bon réflexe, c’est de regarder le décor quand la caméra tourne. Sur une image fixe, vous pourriez compter les feuilles des palmiers, vous n’y verriez aucune différence. Ce qui change, c’est la façon dont l’œil suit un détail d’une image à la suivante.
Comment on a fabriqué ces trois minutes de GTA VI à 60 FPS
Tout commence avec une PS5 Pro et un boîtier de capture Elgato 4K. La console envoie une nouvelle vue du jeu une trentaine de fois par seconde et le boîtier enregistre aussi les répétitions. Ce sont elles qui nous intéressent.
La suite s’est jouée sur un mini-PC RTX Spark, sous Windows 11. On est partis d’un outil disponible dans ComfyUI, RTX Video Frame Generation, puis on a écrit un petit script avec l'intelligence artificielle pour lui confier toute la séquence. Imaginez une voiture qui passe devant une vitrine. À partir de deux images successives, l’outil de NVIDIA estime où la voiture devrait se trouver à mi-chemin et dessine l’image correspondante. Notre script la glisse à la place de la répétition. Il laisse tranquilles les plans immobiles et évite de mêler deux scènes au moment d’une coupe.
BenQ iScreenBar : la barre lumineuse qui s’accorde avec l’iMac
Des lignes en harmonie avec celles de l’ordinateur d’Apple, une conception rigoureuse, des matériaux sélectionnés, rien n’a été laissé au hasard, tout comme le service qu’elle rend une fois allumée !
Sur ces trois minutes et vingt-neuf secondes, on a ainsi remplacé 5 528 répétitions. Les images ont été calculées directement en 4K, puis FFmpeg a réassemblé la vidéo en reprenant la piste son d’origine. Vous pouvez donc écouter la piste audio défiler à sa vitesse habituelle.
Pour jouer à GTA VI à 60 images par seconde, il faudra sans doute attendre la version PC. Et on ne va pas se mentir, à force de tester les plus grosses cartes graphiques du moment chez Clubic, le retour aux 30 FPS pique un peu, surtout au premier coup de caméra. Seulement voilà, on a vite trouvé mieux à faire… GTA VI est déjà extraordinaire sur PS5, et si on reprendra volontiers le volant sur PC le moment venu, d’ici là, on a bien l’intention d’user quelques pneus sur console.

articles.title: Réunion au bureau ou cours au tableau : OBSBOT a une webcam pour chaque cadrage, dès 59 € pour le Black Friday — Frandroid
articles.text:
Une réunion depuis votre bureau et un cours donné debout devant un tableau ne posent pas le même problème de cadrage. Dans le premier cas, la webcam doit surtout vous garder au centre de l’image. Meet SE à 59 € : -40 %, la plus forte remise du Black Friday chez OBSBOT
Si vous cherchez avant tout à remplacer la webcam de votre ordinateur pour vos réunions ou vos cours en ligne, la Meet SE est le produit qu’il vous faut. À 59 € au lieu de 99 €, elle profite de la plus forte remise en pourcentage de cette sélection (-40 %, soit 40 € d’économie).
Son cadrage automatique s’adapte aussi bien à une personne seule qu’à un petit groupe. OBSBOT Tiny : deux webcams 4K qui vous suivent quand vous bougez

Vous passez de votre bureau à un tableau pendant un cours ou vous présentez un produit debout face à la caméra ? La nacelle de la Tiny 3 Lite peut pivoter pour vous garder dans le cadre, même lorsque vous vous déplacez. Ses trois microphones intégrés permettent également à la webcam de localiser la personne qui parle et d’orienter le cadre vers elle grâce au suivi vocal.
Les cinq modes audio permettent par ailleurs d’adapter la captation du son à chaque situation : une voix isolée pour une prise de parole, plusieurs interlocuteurs autour d’une table, une ambiance en stéréo immersive ou un enregistrement brut, sans aucun traitement.
Côté vidéo, elle filme en 4K à 30 images par seconde ou en Full HD jusqu’à 120 images par seconde. Elle passe de 229 € à 159 € pour le Black Friday, soit 70 € d’économie (-31 %), la plus forte remise de la gamme Tiny en pourcentage.

La Tiny 2 Lite a déjà tout ce qu’il faut pour une présentation ou un direct en streaming. Proposée à 144 € au lieu de 199 €, elle filme en 4K à 30 images par seconde ou en Full HD à 60 images par seconde. articles.title: « Pas assez puissante » : Rockstar explique pourquoi GTA 6 ne tournera jamais à 60 i/s sur PS5 Pro
articles.text:
C’est la douche froide pour de nombreux joueurs qui espéraient l’annonce d’un mode performance sur PS5 Pro. Alors que la plus puissante des consoles haut de gamme de Sony promet des graphismes de pointe, Rockstar Games a tranché : GTA 6 restera à 30 i/s sur PS5, PS5 Pro. Même chose pour la Xbox Series X et Xbox Series S. Aucun mode 60 i/s ni même 40 i/s n’est prévu, car les consoles actuelles ne sont tout simplement « pas assez puissantes ».
Le processeur des PS5 et PS5 Pro montre ses limites
C’est Marc Chambers, directeur technique de la production chez Rockstar Games, qui a évoqué les contraintes matérielles de la console de Sony. GTA 6 propose des effets de lumière particulièrement gourmands en ressources pour le processeur, qui est également très sollicité pour afficher tous les éléments « vivants » à l’écran. Sur PS5 Pro, le titre va encore plus loin en ajoutant des ombres en ray-tracing et un meilleur rendu visuel grâce à la technologie de suréchantillonnage PlayStation Spectral Super Resolution (PSSR). Le processeur graphique (GPU) de la PS5 Pro a beau être plus puissant que celui de la PS5, le goulot d’étranglement se situe au niveau du processeur (CPU).
À lire : GTA 6 va voler des millions d’heures aux autres jeux, à Netflix… et même à votre travail
En effet, Marc Chambers précise que si le CPU de la PS5 Pro s’avère légèrement supérieur à celui de la PS5 classique, il n’est tout simplement pas assez puissant pour gérer les calculs complexes demandés par GTA VI à des fréquences d’affichage plus élevées. Contrairement aux idées reçues, le verrouillage à 30 i/s ne provient donc pas du rendu graphique, mais bien de la charge qui pèse sur le processeur pour orchestrer la physique, l’intelligence artificielle et tout l’univers du jeu. Même si les développeurs faisaient le choix d’alléger ou de désactiver le ray-tracing, cela ne suffirait probablement pas à atteindre la barre des 60 images par seconde.
GTA 6 privilégie la fidélité visuelle à la fluidité
Le jeu repose sur une densité de population importante et les milliers de choses à faire dans Vice City. Les éléments visuels comme le ray-tracing viennent renforcer l’immersion. C’est notamment le cas des feux de camp qui viennent projeter des lueurs sur les visages, la carrosserie d’une voiture qui reflète le soleil sur les véhicules voisins, ou encore les voyants du tableau de bord que l’on voit sur le pare-brise la nuit. Retirer ces effets dénaturerait le travail qu’ont accompli les développeurs de chez Rockstar. Ajoutez à cela les avions qui sillonnent le ciel en permanence, le trafic routier et les PNJ, et le processeur est constamment sollicité au maximum de ses capacités.
À lire : GTA 6 : « chef-d’œuvre », 10/10 historique… ce que disent les premiers tests
La fidélité visuelle qui pousse les consoles actuelles au maximum de leurs capacités explique donc le choix du 30 i/s. Pour les adeptes du 60 i/s, il faudra attendre la version PC de GTA 6 ou les consoles de prochaine génération comme la PS6 et la Xbox Helix. En attendant, la version PS5 Pro est pour l’instant la meilleure expérience que vous puissiez avoir de GTA VI dans votre salon, même à 30 i/s. On vous laisse avec l’analyse technique complète de GTA 6 par Digital Foundry.
