Las freidoras de aire de doble cesta se han convertido en una de las opciones más prácticas para cocinar un menú completo de una sola vez sin mezclar sabores. Ahora, Lidl tiene una propuesta muy competitiva bajo su propia marca Silvercrest. Se trata de la freidora de aire de doble zona Silvercrest, que ya está disponible en su tienda online y llega mañana, viernes 20 de noviembre, a sus supermercados por 59,99 euros.
Freidora de aire de doble zona, 9,5 l
Si no llegas a tiempo a conseguir este chollo de Lidl, en el Black Friday de Amazon puedes comprar una alternativa también a buen precio. Se trata de esta Cecotec Cecofry Advance 9000 Window Total, que está rebajada a 65,90 euros. Tiene una potencia de 2.200 W, una capacidad de 9 litros (que puedes dividir en dos cestas de 4,5 litros gracias a su panel divisor) y una ventana transparente que te permite ver el estado de los alimentos.
Cecotec Freidora de Aire 9 L Cecofry Advance 9000 Window Total 2200W
Dos cestas independientes, 2.600 W y sincronización inteligente
Esta freidora de aire doble de Lidl divide sus 9,5 litros de capacidad total en dos cajones independientes de 4,75 litros cada uno (con capacidad óptima para unos 580 gramos de patatas fritas por cesta y hasta 880 gramos como máximo). Esto permite preparar dos recetas distintas al mismo tiempo (por ejemplo, una carne o pescado en un lado y la guarnición en el otro) con tiempos y temperaturas totalmente separados.
Para evitar que un plato se enfríe mientras termina el otro, integra dos funciones muy útiles desde su panel digital con pantalla LED y dial giratorio. Una de ellas es Sync-Finish, que sincroniza el final de la cocción para que ambas cestas terminen exactamente a la vez y Sync-Cook, que replica automáticamente los mismos ajustes de tiempo y temperatura en ambos compartimentos. Aunque también puedes controlar cada una de las cestas de forma independiente.
Ofrece un rango de temperatura muy amplio, desde 40 °C hasta 240 °C, funcionando con una potencia de 2.600 W, e incluye siete programas preestablecidos, incluyendo uno para conseguir acabados extra crujientes y otro para deshidratar. Por último, destacar que tanto los dos cajones como las rejillas interiores cuentan con revestimiento antiadherente ILAG y son aptos para el lavavajillas.

articles.title: South Korea uses nationwide emergency alert to catch exam cheats, exposes 22 students with hidden phones
articles.text:
Facepalm: South Korea has resorted to extreme measures to catch students sneaking phones into their university entrance exam: authorities sounded the country's highest-level emergency alert on handsets nationwide. The plan worked, too. The first alarm caught 22 students who hadn't handed over their devices.
Half a million people took South Korea's annual College Scholastic Ability Test (CSAT), known as the suneung, at 1,312 centers across the country on Thursday. The five exams take place over eight hours in a single day, and the results can determine which university a candidate gets into and what they can study.
There's been a lot of focus on cheating this year after the top scorer in South Korea's professional tax accountancy exam got a suspicious 159 out of 160 questions right. He later admitted to using a microcamera and generative AI to cheat.
At 8:30 am, just before the first exam began, authorities triggered the Extreme Emergency Alert, a 10.5-second alarm designed to sound at full volume even on phones set to silent. Officials say it caught 22 people across nine cities and provinces who had failed to surrender their smartphones. A second alert went off at 2:21 pm, while proctors were collecting the test papers and answer sheets after the third exam.
Given the tensions between North and South Korea, it's understandable that a nationwide emergency alert gave some people a fright. One Seoul resident said their first thought was that war had broken out. Two Japanese visitors at a café in central Seoul had to translate the message before they realized what had interrupted their morning coffee.
The alarm may also have caught a few people its organizers hadn't intended. According to the Korea JoongAng Daily, posts appeared online claiming that several soldiers had their second phones confiscated after the alert gave them away.
Then there was the civil servant who finished a night shift at around 8 am and was trying to get some sleep. A third alarm at 2:57 p.m. brought the day's total to three, prompting the understandably tired worker to complain that he "couldn't get a wink of sleep."
Authorities had originally planned to keep the timing of the afternoon alerts a surprise, but decided to give the public a heads-up. So at 2:45 pm, people received a message warning them that in 12 minutes they'd get another message telling them there was nothing to worry about.

articles.title: Hackers accedieron a datos financieros y médicos de empleados jubilados del gobierno de Nueva York
articles.text:
Hackers lograron acceder a los datos financieros y médicos de cerca de 4.000 empleados municipales jubilados de Nueva York, tras infiltrarse en la base de datos creada por una firma administradora. El sistema gestiona los pagos de un acuerdo judicial de USD 53 millones destinado a retirados del gobierno de la ciudad, según una exclusiva de Politico.
La plataforma comprometida pertenece a Atticus Administration, empresa encargada de procesar pagos derivados de acuerdos judiciales. La firma fue contratada a principios de este año por la administración del alcalde Zohran Mamdani y la aseguradora EmblemHealth para reembolsar a jubilados municipales copagos que les fueron cobrados de forma indebida en consultas médicas.
Esos fondos provienen de un acuerdo alcanzado en 2025 en el marco de una demanda colectiva presentada en 2022 por una organización de exempleados del gobierno de la ciudad.
Acceso desconocido a la plataforma y solicitudes sospechosas
Según una carta del 14 de octubre obtenida por Politico y marcada como “confidencial”, el co-CEO de Atticus, Thomas Logan, informó a ejecutivos de Emblem que “un usuario desconocido” penetró en la base de datos de reclamos el 20 de septiembre y luego de forma periódica entre el 5 y el 8 de octubre.
El intruso accedió a información de los reclamantes que incluía nombres, datos de salud, información financiera, montos de copagos y nombres de prestadores médicos, además de números de identificación internos asignados a cada jubilado.
Apenas dos días antes, la plataforma había registrado envíos de solicitudes de reembolso que fueron catalogados como “inválidos”. Alex Gomez, vocero de EmblemHealth, señaló que la compañía sospecha que esas presentaciones constituyeron intentos de los atacantes de obtener pagos fraudulentos del fondo del acuerdo judicial.
Sin embargo, Gomez aclaró que hasta la fecha no se ha desembolsado ningún monto, ya que el acuerdo aún aguarda la aprobación de un juez.
“Emblem Health considera que Atticus detectó cualquier reclamo fraudulento y que no hubo impacto en el cronograma de revisión y pago de los reclamos”, afirmó Gomez en declaraciones difundidas por Politico.
La investigación sigue mientras crecen las preocupaciones por ciberataques
En su carta, Logan precisó que Atticus confirmó con la entidad contratada para distribuir los fondos del acuerdo que “ningún pago a reclamantes fue creado, modificado ni redirigido” como resultado del hackeo.
De igual modo, la investigación interna de la empresa sigue abierta, según confirmó Gomez. La identidad de los atacantes permanece desconocida y no hay indicios de que el incidente esté vinculado a otros ataques informáticos que salieron a la luz esta semana.
Por otra parte, la intrusión se reveló en un contexto de creciente inquietud internacional por la seguridad digital, luego de que se revelara que piratas informáticos accedieron a los sistemas de decenas de grandes empresas, entre ellas bancos, plataformas financieras y compañías tecnológicas.
En declaraciones realizadas el lunes sobre las preocupaciones tecnológicas, el alcalde Mamdani afirmó que la respuesta del gobierno federal “no generó en muchos neoyorquinos una mayor sensación de confianza en nuestras capacidades nacionales en caso de que esto vuelva a ocurrir”.
Funcionarios de la administración del presidente Donald Trump indicaron esta semana que no tienen motivos para atribuir esas disrupciones a actividades hostiles de gobiernos extranjeros.
Consultado sobre las defensas de Nueva York ante este tipo de amenazas, según Politico, Mamdani declaró: “Estamos preparados y sabemos que cada día es una oportunidad para hacer más, especialmente en materia tecnológica”.

articles.title: AWS Releases a Free Local Emulator of AWS Built Entirely by Agents
articles.text:
AWS has released AWS Emulator, a free local implementation of more than 200 of its services dedicated to the public domain under CC0, and says that "thousands of autonomous AI agents wrote every line of code" in it. As InfoQ reported at launch, it ships as a single Rust binary generated from AWS's 438 public API models and listens on port 9297. The week since has brought the first independent fidelity numbers and a divided practitioner reaction.
Pointing an existing SDK, CLI, or coding agent at the emulator is a matter of environment variables, after which the launch post by Daniel Abib says, "your existing tests, CLI scripts, and coding agents keep working the way they already do":
export AWS_ENDPOINT_URL=https://127.0.0.1:9297
export AWS_SHARED_CREDENTIALS_FILE=~/.aws/emulator/9297/emulator_credentials
export AWS_CONFIG_FILE=~/.aws/emulator/9297/config
export AWS_EC2_METADATA_DISABLED=true
export AWS_REGION=us-east-1
unset AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY AWS_SESSION_TOKEN AWS_PROFILE
The same shell serves an agent. In the post, Kiro is asked to create and read back a DynamoDB table and issues the ordinary CLI calls against the local endpoint:
kiro> Using the local AWS Emulator (the environment variables
      are already set in this shell), create a DynamoDB table
      "kiro-demo" with a string key "id", put an item
      {id: "item-1", msg: "hello from kiro"}, then read it
      back with get-item.
$ aws dynamodb create-table --table-name kiro-demo \
    --attribute-definitions AttributeName=id,AttributeType=S \
    --key-schema AttributeName=id,KeyType=HASH \
    --billing-mode PAY_PER_REQUEST
$ aws dynamodb put-item --table-name kiro-demo \
    --item '{"id": {"S": "item-1"}, "msg": {"S": "hello from kiro"}}'
$ aws dynamodb get-item --table-name kiro-demo --key '{"id": {"S": "item-1"}}'
Matt Wood, AWS's chief AI and technology officer, argues that the loop matters because of what an agent does while a check is slow: "A coding agent can build a lot of software around an incorrect assumption." He also names the failure mode an emulator introduces:
An agent learns from the environment it experiences. If the emulator accepts behavior that AWS rejects, training can reinforce a mistake. An agent might also discover a shortcut that succeeds only because of an emulator defect.
The fidelity scores exist to expose that gap: each release publishes per service how many tests pass out of how many were verified against real AWS, with the failing tests public too, and Abib asks readers to "read a score as a snapshot of a product that's improving."
Senior principal engineer Matthew Goldberg traces the project to a three-line prompt given to Kiro, "the simplest prompt that I could think of without any expectation that this would work":
Write tests based on the AWS Command Line Interface (CLI)
Iterate on those tests until they pass against real AWS
Build an in-memory implementation that those same tests pass against
Kiro came back after 15 minutes with a passable first version of an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS). I refined my prompt and had Kiro build me the rest of AWS over the weekend. And it did. It obviously had gaps, but it was compelling enough that my team started using it to test our software that Monday.
The production version is built by three agent teams: "One team manages a test suite; one team finds issues in the emulator; and one team fixes those issues." Each fix must pass a gate that compiles the change and runs agent reviews for coding standards, security, and fidelity regression. "Our team hasn't written or reviewed any of the code," Goldberg writes, and describes what the gate carries:
If any of those checks fail, the change is sent back to the agent for rework; if they all pass, it is merged to mainline. We've seen thousands of issues fixed every day as hundreds of agents concurrently work on the codebase. Without this merge gate, we wouldn't trust what our agents are building.
Swami Sivasubramanian, in a guest post on Werner Vogels' blog, recalls rebuilding a replication engine with Kiro that had taken his team four months by hand:
I supervised the agent for four nights before I saw that it had no way to check its results. Once it had a spec and a test environment, the rebuild took about two hours
In his telling, the engineer's job becomes "to build the specs, tests, and merge gates that decide when that work is correct."
The first measurements from outside AWS come from Kento Ikeda, an AWS Community Builder, who ran version 1.0.322 in GitHub Actions the day after launch. DynamoDB, S3 and SQS passed roughly 60 to 70 percent of their fidelity tests at service level and 80 to 100 percent on the operations its code called, while CloudFormation sat near 20 percent. The emulator matched AWS's error wording, but a new DynamoDB table stayed in CREATING for three seconds and rejected writes until then. "Being generated from API models only means the shape of requests and responses matches AWS," he writes, and places the tool between mocks and a real sandbox as a third layer rather than a replacement for either.
The launch post draws its hardest line at security:
Don't use the emulator to test whether your application is secure. It doesn't evaluate AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) policies and resource-based policies the way AWS does, so a request that AWS denies might succeed in the emulator. Keep real credentials out of the environment of your test jobs, and test your security settings and your whole application on AWS before you go to production.
Unimplemented operations return HTTP 501, telemetry is on by default, throttling, outages and regional differences are not simulated, and the repository does not accept pull requests. On Hacker News, one reader quoted the line on the security page that the emulator "never denies a request signed with its own key" and asked why IAM was left out:
I think because the agents were only building on the public API surface, it's hard to build this part. But they should've tried and let the agents read whatever policy engines AWS has. Or maybe it's a way to prevent someone from trivially running aws-emulator as AWSaaS?
The thread's first question was whether this was "just an exercise or a real product they are going to ship and maintain," answered by a commenter identifying as AWS staff with "It's a real product that we plan to maintain." Another counted "29,684 commits in a repository less than a month old" and said it "does not instill confidence." On r/aws, the most-upvoted comment turned Amazon's own line around, calling agents that fix code "without human review" a terrible idea for a tool used to test before production. The reply was that the API specifications already exist and the SDKs are generated from them, so a server derived from a fixed contract is where agents can iterate until the tests pass.
The timing matters to the people in those threads. LocalStack's free Hobby plan now requires an account and prohibits commercial use, with paid seats from $39 a month, and several commenters had already moved to Floci. One of them put the AWS release in that context:
But in the wake of Localstack's changes, the landscape has been full of slopware and low trust anyway. I don't think this is worse, for now at least.
AWS's version costs nothing and can be forked by either project. Sivasubramanian says AWS "will share more about this work at re:Invent" in December.

articles.title: Transport for London breach exposes 265,000 Oyster card users' data
articles.text:
Transport for London (TfL) has announced that around 265,000 Oyster photocard customers may have had their account details exposed in a data breach.
TfL is London's public transport authority, operating the Underground, Overground, buses, trams, and the Elizabeth line. It recorded 3.53 billion passenger journeys in 2025/26, including 1.78 billion bus journeys and 1.20 billion Tube journeys.
Oyster photocards are travel smartcards with the holder's photo that give eligible passengers free or discounted travel.
The organization discovered the security incident on November 16, 2026, after receiving customer reports about emails requesting them to create an account, which came directly from TfL's mail systems as a result of a compromise.
The Oyster photocard website has now been taken offline and the organization is sending impacted individuals data breach notifications.
Oyster photocards remain valid for travel, and customers who need to renew their cards or check their journey history can still do so by contacting TfL's Customer Services.
These notifications, with one shared on Reddit, state that the following customer data may have been exposed:
- Full names
- Phone numbers
- Email addresses
- Home addresses
- Dates of birth
- Security questions and answers
TfL's current assessment is that passwords, bank and payment card details, journey information, and the names and dates of birth of children with Zip Oyster cards were not compromised.
The transportation organization also said it has found no evidence so far that the affected data has been misused.
TfL estimates that around 265,000 photocard customers may have been impacted, up from an estimated 250k previously, but the investigation is not yet complete and the figure may increase further.
TfL says it has now contained the incident and contacted affected customers. It has also notified the UK's Information Commissioner's Office (ICO).
Those who received the previous email urging them to create an account on the platform should ignore it.
The leak of security questions and answers is particularly concerning, as those may be used in account access restoration, so customers should remain vigilant for suspicious activity and report it to the organization as soon as possible.
Once the Oyster photocard portal is restored, all photocard customers will be prompted to change their password, security question, and answer.
However, if those same security questions are used at other sites, they should be rotated to new questions and answers.
It is also recommended to change passwords on other services where the same information was used.
In 2024, Scattered Spider members breached TfL's network and stole customer data and disrupted online services, including Oyster refunds.
The attack cost the agency £29 million in losses and recovery costs, while two of the hackers pleaded guilty in June 2026 and were sentenced to five years and six months in prison.

articles.title: Natural Products Canada to open $25-million food systems scale-up fund |
articles.text:
A new fund is looking to cut $1-million to $5-million cheques to companies contributing to Canada’s food production and supply chain capacity.
The news: Spearheaded by Natural Products Canada (NPC), the Capacity Building Fund is a $25-million fund launching next month. Announced on Thursday, the fund will back Canadian companies as they scale production capacity with non-dilutive funding. Intake opens on Dec. 9, with companies considered on a continuous basis.
From the source: The capacity-building fund is offering $1 million to $5 million in funding, up to 50 percent of eligible project costs. Projects can be up to three years in length and must be a minimum of $2 million in overall size. Applicants also need to match 50 percent of funds from private financing or non-dilutive government funding.
The context: The Capacity Building Fund was announced in conjunction with NPC’s second economic impact assessment report. The report, which outlines the more than $1 billion in GDP contributions generated from NPC’s portfolio over five years, affirmed continued growth among the portfolio since its last assessment in January. It also outlined a renewed $50-million investment from the federal government’s Strategic Response Fund, a portion of which is being used to supply capital to NPC’s new fund.
The fund is looking for early-stage companies that are majority Canadian-owned, have 150 employees or less, and less than $15 million in annual revenue. A full list of criteria is available here.
RELATED: Canadian companies are generating massive returns in the “bioeconomy”
Final thought: NPC’s portfolio companies generated a whopping $294 million in GDP contributions in 2026, according to the impact assessment. That’s nearly a third of the nearly $900 million in GDP generated by the portfolio between 2021 and 2025. NPC’s assessment cites growth among existing portfolio companies, more pre-commercial companies reaching market, and a robust set of new innovators entering the commercialization pipeline as reasons for the returns, underscoring the value of scale-up supports like the Capacity Building Fund.

articles.title: Los expertos en limpieza coinciden: "Para que la calefacción dé más calor y gaste menos, nosotros colocamos las láminas reflectantes detrás de los radiadores"
articles.text:
Cuando empieza a hacer frío y enciendes la calefacción, lo haces pensando en más calorcito sin que la factura sufra mucho. Para conseguirlo hay un par de trucos que te pueden venir muy bien, y uno de ellos es colocar láminas reflectantes detrás de los radiadores. ¿Por qué? Es una solución súper sencilla que es todavía más interesante cuando están instalados en paredes que dan al exterior.
Es probable que no lo sepas, pero cuando enciendes un radiador una parte termina calentando la pared que tiene detrás y, si esta da a la fachada del edificio o a una zona sin calefacción, parte de esa energía se puede perder. Justo ahí entran en juego estas láminas (fabricadas con aluminio u otros materiales metalizados) y, en algunos casos, incorporan una capa de espuma aislante.
Cómo aprovechar mejor el calor de tus radiadores
Lo que consigues con estos paneles es reflejar parte del calor hacia el interior de la habitación, reduciendo así las pérdidas que se producen a través de la pared. Según explica Energy Saving Trust, este recurso puede ayudarte a ahorrar energía, sobre todo si tu vivienda tiene paredes exteriores poco aisladas. Eso sí, el resultado dependerá del aislamiento de tu casa y de dónde estén colocados los radiadores.
A todo esto debes sumar otra cuestión que seguramente hayas visto alguna vez en casa: las manchas oscuras que aparecen encima de algunos radiadores. El aire caliente mueve partículas de polvo que pueden terminar acumulándose en la pared y, aunque las láminas no eliminan por completo este problema, sí pueden proteger la superficie que queda detrás del aparato. Además, dependiendo del material, puedes limpiarlas pasando una bayeta de microfibra ligeramente humedecida.
Y lo mejor es que colocarlas tampoco exige grandes complicaciones. Lo primero que debes hacer es medir el radiador y cortar la lámina para que no sobresalga por los lados. Después, con el aparato apagado y frío, conviene que retires el polvo de la zona antes de instalarla. Algunos modelos se fijan con adhesivos o clips, mientras que otros se pueden deslizar directamente detrás del radiador, así que lo más recomendable es que sigas las instrucciones del fabricante para que el panel quede bien colocado.
De esta forma, puedes reducir parte del calor que se pierde por las paredes exteriores sin necesidad de hacer obras. Eso sí, no debes olvidarte del mantenimiento habitual: revisar los radiadores, purgarlos cuando sea necesario y mantener sus rendijas libres de polvo también ayuda a que el aire caliente circule correctamente por la habitación.

articles.title: Google gives Gemini the ability to use your Mac for you | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Google on Thursday announced that it is bringing computer use to its Gemini desktop application on macOS, allowing its AI to complete tasks on users’ behalf, navigating native Mac apps, and browsing websites in the background.
The tech giant is a little late to the game with this launch, as other leading AI model makers like OpenAI, Anthropic, and Meta have already been offering agentic features in their desktop applications for some time. Meanwhile, Google only this week announced the broader rollout of Gemini’s “Tasks,” the in-app feature that allows the AI to work more as an agent, helping users sign into websites, make online purchases, or book appointments.
Google also only recently began admitting early testers to try its revamped “CC” AI agent, announced in September, which is designed to help families stay organized across email, calendars, chats, and tasks.
Computer use is another type of agentic offering that allows an AI agent to take actions directly on the user’s computer — in Gemini’s case, a Mac. This allows the AI to complete multistep tasks that involve getting things done across local files, apps, and the web. After the user instructs the AI what they want to do, they’ll see the agent working in a live preview in their chat, while still keeping their screen and cursor free to continue working on other things.
As with other AI agents offering computer use, users can pause, stop, and approve Gemini’s actions before they happen.
Google suggests the feature could be useful for tedious tasks and other workflows, like filling out forms, repeating the same task over and over across a batch of files, organizing files into folders based on specific criteria, creating slideshows from files or information in online dashboards, and more.
The feature is initially available in English in the U.S. and requires the Gemini app for Mac and a Google AI Plus, Pro, or Ultra subscription. The company didn’t say when it would expand to other markets or platforms.

articles.title: Nodal Networks raises $11.3M to solve global shipping bottlenecks - SiliconANGLE
articles.text:
Nodal Networks raises $11.3M to solve global shipping bottlenecks
Nodal Networks Inc., a company that builds artificial intelligence decision networks to manage the world’s shipping container terminals, announced today that it has raised $11.3 million in seed funding to help port and rail hubs reduce congestion and move more cargo.
Freight networks move more than a billion shipping containers per year. They carry everything from clothing, electronics, furniture, raw materials for construction and perishable goods – the things that people rely on every day.
However, according to Sea-Intelligence Pte. Ltd., a Copenhagen-based shipping consulting and data analytics company, in September only half of the world’s container ships arrived on time and the late ones were a week behind. Oftentimes, ships can spend nearly half their time at port not working cargo.
Nodal Networks believes the solution is better management, not new infrastructure, which will be key to providing better terminal capacity.
“Watching ports through Earth-observation satellites, I started to see transport as a physical internet: Containers are the data packets, ports and rail yards are the routers, and congestion is the lag,” said co-founder and Chief Executive Paul Albert-Lebrun. “So, we went looking for the routers. We spent eight months in ports, terminals and rail yards, and even sailed the North Sea aboard a container ship, learning the work from the people who do it.”
Albert-Lebrun worked in satellite operations and later led product at Kepler Communications Inc., a space telecom company. Co-founder and Chief Commercial Officer Nic Westgate, by contrast, comes from mining engineering, approaching the problem from the opposite end.
Together, they combined their expertise in Malcom, the company’s AI-powered platform for improving terminal operations, named after Malcom McLean, a North Carolina truck driver turned entrepreneur who pioneered modern container shipping.
The AI platform combines agents with specialized forecasting models that can see, understand and predict incoming shipments, timing and offloading metrics to follow congestion, track lost productivity and make better-informed decisions about container placement, equipment allocation and loading operations. The company said it’s already deployed in terminals across three continents but did not provide details on which locations.
“There’s a lot of noise about AI in our industry right now, and I see a new company pitching terminals almost every week,” said Peter Levesque, an adviser to Nodal and former president of Ports America Inc. and CEO of CMA CGM North America LLC. “Most bring a general-purpose tool and look for somewhere to apply it, and few can answer the question every operator asks: what’s the return? Nodal got into the details, surrounded itself with the right people and kept the customer’s bottom line at the center of everything.”
Levesque added that Nodal has proven itself in terminal after terminal by showing measurable results.
According to Nodal, Malcom has already reduced truck time by one-half in one terminal after operators reassigned yard equipment. At another terminal, ship loading and unloading speeded up by 5% after the team pinpointed what kept cranes waiting for containers. In both cases, the company said Malcom helped operators identify which decisions would have the greatest impact.
The company said it would use the new funding to expand Malcom’s reach to more terminals within the groups Nodal already works with, support new customers and advance product development. It also intends to extend Malcom beyond the terminal, adding planning for shipping lines, railroads and trucking companies, becoming support for transportation networks where operators work together to exchange information.

articles.title: Microsoft's official Agent Framework Python package on PyPI hijacked to push login-stealing malware
articles.text:
Microsoft's official Agent Framework Python package on PyPI hijacked to push login-stealing malware
Attackers push two versions in roughly half an hour
- Attackers compromised Microsoft’s Agent Framework package on PyPI and inserted malware designed to steal credentials and cloud tokens
- Malicious versions targeted Azure, AWS, GitHub, OpenAI, Docker, and other developer platforms before being removed
- Developers who installed the affected releases should rotate secrets, investigate environments, and treat systems as compromised
Threat actors broke into Microsoft’s official Agent Framework Python package on PyPI and used it to disseminate infostealing malware to hundreds of thousands of developers that rely on it daily. Fortunately, the attack was spotted and stopped rather quickly - although that doesn’t mean there were no victims.
The Microsoft Agent Framework Python package is an open source toolkit that helps developers build AI agents and applications where multiple AI agents can work together to complete different tasks.
It provides the building blocks for creating AI assistants that can use tools and follow instructions, as well as to interact with other agents and handle more complex tasks.
Gone in 31 minutes
For a relatively new tool, Agent Framework is gaining plenty of traction, with monthly downloads reaching almost 200,000 these days.
On November 17, 2026, someone released version 1.26.1 containing an infostealer that executed automatically when Python boots up, even in environments where the Agent Framework package was not imported. It kept its dependency on the earlier package (1.26.0), meaning the framework would function properly while the malware would do its work in the background.
The tool was designed to steal login credentials and other secrets from environment variables, as well as to nab local configuration files and other running processes. It targeted Azure, AWS, GitHub, Docker, Hugging Face, OpenAI, and numerous other services. What’s more, it tried to steal Azure managed identity access tokens, as well as Azure DevOps OIDC tokens.
PyPI took exactly 31 minutes to spot the intrusion and quarantine the malicious version. However, two minutes later, a second attack took place. Version 1.26.2 added GitHub Actions OIDC token requests, as well as searches of GitHub runner directories. The interesting thing about the second attack is that the threat actors somehow maintained access to Microsoft’s PyPI account even after the first cleansing. PyPI removed the second version approximately eight minutes after upload.
Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed!
We don’t know if the attack was successful and if any developers lost their secrets as a result. According to PyPIStats.org, the tool has approximately 6,900 downloads a day, or around 287 an hour. Therefore, the malicious versions were potentially downloaded around 150 times.
If you were among those who downloaded versions 1.26.1 or 1.26.2, remove it immediately and treat the system it was installed on as potentially compromised. It’s also worth mentioning that simply downgrading to a clean version is not enough, since the secrets were probably already exfiltrated. Therefore, make sure to check the environment for suspicious files, particularly the .pth files associated with the attack, and consider rebuilding affected environments from the ground up.
What to do in case of an infection
Also, all passwords should be considered exposed, including API keys, access tokens, and other secrets - make sure to revoke and replace them. Furthermore, make sure to review your Azure, AWS, GitHub, and other service accounts for suspicious activity, including unexpected logins or access requests. Finally, anyone using the package in automated build systems, particularly GitHub Actions, should investigate those environments as well.
The attack was spotted and documented by a number of security researchers, including Wiz, Aikido Security, Socket, and others. According to some researchers, the first malicious release used agent_framework_meta.pth to execute the credential stealer in agent_framework_meta/_telemetry.py during Python startup, while the second restored the original package initializer and moved the malicious code to af_runtime_diag.pth and af_runtime_diag.py.
Both versions were sending harvested information to the same server, located at https://webhook[.]site/d381fd80-ec62-42ad-8f5c-d1b15103c9bb.
No threat actors claimed responsibility for the attack and we don’t know how they gained access to Microsoft’s official PyPI project. The Windows maker has not issued a comment or a statement.
Via BleepingComputer
