articles.title: Keep inference running through regional capacity shortfalls with cross-Region inference routing in Amazon SageMaker AI | Amazon Web Services
articles.text:
Artificial Intelligence
Keep inference running through regional capacity shortfalls with cross-Region inference routing in Amazon SageMaker AI
Serving a model from more than one AWS Region is a well-established pattern for highly available inference: when one Region runs short of GPU capacity, requests move to another. The pattern is simple to describe and hard to operate. Until now, if you served models on Amazon SageMaker AI managed endpoints, cross-Region routing was a piece you still had to build yourself.
Today, we’re introducing cross-Region inference routing in Amazon SageMaker AI. It uses a new resource, the inference router, that gives your application one invocation path across the endpoints and inference components you already run, in one or more AWS Regions and AWS accounts. You register the destinations that serve a model, and your application invokes the router instead of a specific endpoint. The router keeps requests in its own Region while the local destination is healthy, shifts new requests to another registered destination when it isn’t, and returns traffic gradually after recovery.
In this post, we explain how cross-Region inference routing decides where each request runs, walk through an example with one model in two Regions, and cover monitoring, limits, and what you pay. For a cross-account deployment that serves several models, see How Salesforce is advancing global-scale model serving with cross-Region inference routing in Amazon SageMaker AI.
When one Region runs short of capacity
A SageMaker AI endpoint runs in one AWS Region and one account. When autoscaling can’t add instances of the type your endpoint needs, requests throttle and time out, even when the same model has spare capacity in another Region. To use that capacity, your application must detect a struggling endpoint and switch Regions, decide which errors are safe to retry without running the model twice, move traffic back after recovery without flapping, and manage access to endpoints in other accounts. That code sits on the critical path of every request, and every team serving models across Regions maintains its own version of it.
How cross-Region inference routing works
Cross-Region inference routing is based on a few core ideas:
- You decide where your model might run – For each model, you choose which endpoints and inference components the router might use.
- SageMaker AI decides which destination serves each request – The router prefers its own Region and shifts new requests to another destination only when the local one can’t serve reliably.
- Your endpoints stay the same – You deploy endpoints as you do today, with the same models, configurations, instance pools, and autoscaling. Direct InvokeEndpoint calls keep working, and the router passes InferenceId and CustomAttributes through, as InvokeEndpoint does.
- You can see every decision – Each real-time response tells you which destination served the request and why.
A few terms describe the pieces:
- Inference router – A Regional SageMaker AI resource in your account that your application invokes.
- Routing target – A name for one logical model on a router, such as fraud-model. A router can hold many routing targets, and each fails over independently of the others.
- Destination – A real-time endpoint, inference component, or asynchronous endpoint registered under a routing target, identified by its full Amazon Resource Name (ARN), which tells the router its Region and account. A routing target holds either real-time destinations, which can mix endpoints and inference components across Regions and accounts, or asynchronous endpoints only.
- Local destination – A destination in the router’s Region, preferred while it’s healthy.
- Routing reason – A value returned with each real-time response that explains where the request went and why.
The Region you create the router in is its local Region. To prefer a different Region, create a router there. The router doesn’t create capacity, scale your endpoints, deploy models, or copy model artifacts and container images. Each destination must already be running in its Region.
How routing decisions are made
The router considers only destinations that are registered on the routing target and that it’s authorized to invoke. Among those, it prefers destinations in its own Region, and when more than one local destination is healthy, it spreads requests across them evenly. Requests leave the Region only when local destinations can’t serve reliably. To detect that, SageMaker AI calculates a health score for each destination from its recent requests, measured in the destination’s own Region. Server errors (5xx), throttles, and timeouts lower the score. Errors from the SageMaker AI platform (for example, failed health check) lower it the most. Errors caused by the request itself, such as invalid input, don’t lower it, because the same request would fail in any Region. Model latency isn’t an input, so an endpoint that keeps returning successful responses keeps its traffic. Signals such as failed instance launches or an endpoint running fewer instances than its autoscaling target make the router react faster, but only after the destination starts failing requests.
The router evaluates each destination’s health and publishes it to Amazon CloudWatch as one of three states. A healthy destination serves normally. An overloaded destination still serves, and the router moves part of its traffic away. A degraded destination is failing or can’t serve, so the router moves most of its traffic away and keeps a small share to detect recovery.
SageMaker AI manages failover thresholds and timing, so you don’t need to tune any thresholds. If health information for remote destinations goes stale, the router keeps traffic in its own Region, so a gap in monitoring never moves traffic on its own.
When traffic moves, and when it comes back
The more requests fail, the more traffic moves, so a destination need not fail outright first. Traffic starts to move within about a minute of sustained errors, or longer for a destination with little traffic. Traffic that leaves the local Region is spread across the healthy remote destinations in proportion to their health. You can’t set weights or a fallback order. After recovery, traffic returns over several minutes, more slowly than it left. Requests in progress aren’t interrupted.
When a destination fails a real-time request without running the model, the router retries that request once on a different destination. This covers, for example, a throttle, a 503 error, a model that isn’t ready, a rejection by a cross-Region traffic cap, or access denied by the destination. The router never retries timeouts, 500 errors, or model errors.
For asynchronous requests, the router tries each eligible destination once, local destinations first, until one accepts the request.
Figure 4 shows where requests were served in one of our tests with a test model.
What you can route
The following use cases show common ways to use cross-Region inference routing in Amazon SageMaker AI.
- Keep serving when one Region runs short of GPU capacity. When your G-series instance type runs short in US East (Ohio) during peak traffic and requests start to throttle, the router shifts new requests to the same model in US West (Oregon), where autoscaling absorbs the overflow, and moves traffic back gradually after US East (Ohio) recovers.
- Route across endpoints owned by separate AWS accounts. When a central platform account owns the router and other accounts own the endpoints, each endpoint owner grants access to one named router, and requests reach those endpoints only through that router. We cover the setup after this list.
- Serve many models from one router. Create one router with one routing target per model, each listing that model’s destinations, and pass the routing target name on each request. Each model fails over independently.
- Put the router behind your own gateway. If you operate an API or model gateway, you can point its SageMaker AI integration at the router, so SageMaker AI handles Region selection for SageMaker-hosted models while your gateway decides when to use a different provider. For example, see the Salesforce post.
- Route asynchronous requests. Asynchronous endpoints, in the router’s account or in other accounts, can be destinations. Your application calls InvokeInferenceRouterAsync with the routing target name and the Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) input location, and gets back an InferenceId and the output and failure locations, as with InvokeEndpointAsync.
- Protect a receiving endpoint from other Regions’ overflow. On a real-time endpoint, you can set an optional cross-Region traffic cap so that requests from other Regions can use only part of its capacity. Your endpoint’s local callers keep the rest. We cover the details later in this section.
When a destination belongs to a different account than the router, both accounts must allow each request. On the endpoint side, the owner attaches a resource-based policy that allows the router account to invoke the endpoint, and the sagemaker:SourceInferenceRouterArn condition key limits that access to one named router. The following policy allows only my-router in account 444455556666 to invoke the endpoint. Its second statement has no router condition and lets the router account read the endpoint’s status. Without that statement, the destination shows its status as unknown.
In the router account, callers need sagemaker:InvokeInferenceRouter (or sagemaker:InvokeInferenceRouterAsync) on the router and sagemaker:InvokeEndpoint (or sagemaker:InvokeEndpointAsync) on every destination, because the router invokes each destination on the caller’s behalf. A router never gives a caller access to an endpoint they couldn’t call directly. For DescribeInferenceRouter to report each destination’s status, callers also need sagemaker:DescribeEndpoint on endpoints and sagemaker:DescribeInferenceComponent on inference components. Applications in other accounts call the router by assuming a role in the router account. For a walkthrough, see How Salesforce is advancing global-scale model serving with cross-Region inference routing in Amazon SageMaker AI and User Guide on cross-account destinations.
Protect a receiving endpoint with a cross-Region traffic cap
When the router moves requests away from a Region that’s short on capacity, those requests land on endpoints that already serve their own Region’s callers. By default, a receiving endpoint accepts any amount of cross-Region traffic, so a surge of overflow can push it into throttling. With a cross-Region traffic cap, the endpoint owner decides how much of the endpoint’s capacity other Regions might use.
You set the cap in CreateEndpointConfig with CrossRegionTrafficConfig, which takes two required values. MaxInvocationsPerSecondPerInstance is the number of invocations per second that one instance can take, which you measure with a load test of your model, instance type, and typical payload. MaxCrossRegionPercentPerEndpoint is the share of that capacity that other Regions might use. SageMaker AI multiplies the per-instance rate by the instances in service and applies the percentage, so the cap follows autoscaling. For example, with 50 invocations per second per instance, a 20 percent cap, and 4 instances in service, the endpoint accepts up to 40 requests per second from other Regions. When autoscaling adds 2 instances, the cap rises to 60 requests per second.
Only requests from other Regions count against the cap. Requests from the endpoint’s own Region, including direct InvokeEndpoint calls and calls from a router in the same Region, are never throttled by it. When cross-Region requests exceed the cap, the endpoint rejects the extra requests before your model runs, and the router retries each one once on a different destination. If no other destination can take the request, your application gets a throttling error.
The cap applies to real-time endpoints, and all inference components on an endpoint share it. For an endpoint that hosts inference components, load test one instance with its usual mix of inference components and payloads to measure MaxInvocationsPerSecondPerInstance, and run the test again when that mix or your payloads change. If you leave out CrossRegionTrafficConfig, the endpoint accepts any amount of cross-Region traffic.
Get started: One model in two Regions
In this example, we deploy Qwen3-4B with the vLLM container as an inference component in US East (Ohio) and US West (Oregon), in one account. Because the inference router doesn’t support response streaming, the application sends non-streaming requests, and each request must complete within about a minute, the same limit as InvokeEndpoint. We then create a router in US East (Ohio) with one routing target that lists both:
Run DescribeInferenceRouter and confirm that each destination’s RoutingStatus is Routable before you send traffic.
The application invokes the router with the routing target name and the same payload it would send to InvokeEndpoint, and reads the serving destination and routing reason from the response:
What we observed
| Step | RoutingStatus in DescribeInferenceRouter (us-east-2 / us-west-2) | Served by | Routing reason | 
| Both inference components running | Routable / Routable | us-east-2 | local-preferred | 
| us-east-2 inference component removed | Unroutable / Routable | us-west-2 | only-healthy | 
| us-east-2 inference component restored | Routable / Routable | us-west-2 | only-healthy | 
| Traffic back in us-east-2 | Routable / Routable | us-east-2 | local-preferred | 
Traffic stayed in US East (Ohio) while its inference component ran, moved to US West (Oregon) with no change to the application when we removed it, and came back after we restored it.
The complete notebook for this example is available on GitHub.
Tip: Use instance pools and cross-Region inference routing together. With a capacity-aware instance pool, SageMaker AI can use another instance type in the same Region at creation and during scale-out. The router moves new requests to another Region when the local endpoint as a whole can’t serve. For details, see Capacity-aware inference: Automatic instance fallback for SageMaker AI endpoints.
See where each request went
The inference router gives you two views of routing: a record on every real-time response and metrics in CloudWatch.
Per-request routing record
Every real-time response includes the ARN of the destination that served the request in InvokedRoutedResourceArn, and the routing reason in RoutingReason. The routing reason is one of the following:
- local-preferred – Served by a healthy destination in the router’s Region.
- capacity-available – Served by a destination with available capacity.
- failover – Moved away from a destination that couldn’t serve reliably.
- only-healthy – Served by the only eligible destination that was healthy.
We recommend logging both values with your application’s own request logs.
Asynchronous responses don’t include the serving destination. Router metrics in CloudWatch show where asynchronous requests were placed.
Router metrics in CloudWatch
The router publishes OpenTelemetry metrics to CloudWatch in its own account and Region, labeled with the router, routing target, and destination:
- aws.sagemaker.inference_router.invocations – Requests per destination, with an error.type label on failures (invocation_4xx, invocation_5xx, or invocation_model_error).
- aws.sagemaker.inference_router.destination.duration – Time at the destination, including your model.
- aws.sagemaker.inference_router.overhead.duration – The router’s own work plus network time to and from another Region.
- aws.sagemaker.inference_router.destination.status – Each destination as healthy, overloaded, or degraded.
Alarm on destinations that aren’t healthy and on the error rate across all error types. See Monitor an inference routers with Amazon CloudWatch and AWS CloudTrail.
Each destination endpoint keeps publishing its existing SageMaker AI metrics in its own account and Region. To view them in one place, use CloudWatch cross-account observability and cross-account cross-Region dashboards.
AWS CloudTrail records the router’s API calls (create, update, delete, describe, and list) as management events and router invocations as data events. You enable data events on your trail as you do for other SageMaker AI data events.
Plan your deployment
Keep the following in mind when you design with the inference router:
- Put the router in the Region where most of your traffic originates. The router always prefers destinations in its own Region.
- Size each Region for its own traffic plus the overflow you want it to absorb. By default, a receiving endpoint accepts any amount of cross-Region traffic, so configure autoscaling with headroom for the overflow you expect. To protect an endpoint’s local callers, set a cross-Region traffic cap, as described in Protect a receiving endpoint with a cross-Region traffic cap. If every remote destination reaches its cap, requests beyond the combined caps return throttling errors.
- Keep a low-cost standby Region. You can register an inference component in another Region and keep its cost low, but plan for how it gets capacity. A remote inference component with zero copies receives only a small share of traffic during failover, and those requests fail until it has copies. Keep at least one copy running, or configure autoscaling on copies and confirm that it scales out before you rely on the standby Region.
- Plan for resilience at the entry point. A router is regional, so if its Region is impaired, calls to it fail. Create routers in two Regions and switch between them on the client side.
- Register only destinations where your data might be processed. A request can be processed in the router’s Region or in any Region where you’ve registered a destination. For data that must stay in one geography, use a separate router, for example one for US data and one for EU data. You are responsible for configuring your routers to align with your data residency and compliance obligations.
- Keep your own retries modest. A throttling error means every destination was busy, and a service-unavailable error means no destination could take the request. A service-unavailable error after about a minute means the request timed out and the model might have run, so don’t retry it automatically.
- Remove deleted destinations from the router. Traffic already avoids a deleted endpoint, but the router never removes a destination on its own.
- Call the router privately. Applications in a virtual private cloud (VPC) can call the router through an interface VPC endpoint (AWS PrivateLink), which supports IPv4 (IPv6/dual-stack not supported).
Also note the following limitations:
- Response streaming isn’t supported.
- A real-time request that the destination doesn’t respond to within about a minute fails with a service-unavailable error.
- Each router holds up to 20 routing targets, each routing target holds up to 10 destinations, and real-time payloads can be up to 6 MB. For default quotas, such as routers per account and request rates, and how to request an increase, see Service Quotas in the Amazon SageMaker AI documentation.
Conclusion
Cross-Region inference routing in Amazon SageMaker AI gives your application one invocation path across the endpoints and inference components you already run, in multiple AWS Regions and AWS accounts. The router prefers its own Region, shifts new requests when a destination can’t serve reliably, returns traffic gradually after recovery, and shows you where each request ran and why. Your endpoints, models, containers, and autoscaling policies don’t change.
Cross-Region inference routing is generally available starting today in most commercial AWS Regions (except me-south-1 and me-central-1), for real-time and asynchronous inference.
There is no additional charge for cross-Region inference routing in Amazon SageMaker AI. You pay for the SageMaker AI endpoints and inference components that serve your requests at standard SageMaker AI pricing, whether a request reaches them directly or through an inference router. The inference router publishes metrics to Amazon CloudWatch in the router’s account, and you pay standard CloudWatch rates for those metrics and any queries you run on them. For details, see Amazon SageMaker AI pricing.
To get started, see the Amazon SageMaker AI documentation on cross-Region inference routing and explore the sample notebook on GitHub.

articles.title: Meta’s AI agent Muse is mixing up conversations and could be exposing private data, report says | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Meta employees have raised concerns that the company’s AI agent Muse has been mixing up conversations across different accounts and exposing private user data, according to a new Reuters report that looked at internal company posts.
In some of these instances, employees said Muse surfaced messages about childcare requests they never made, career advice they never asked for, product orders they never placed, and bank account balances that didn’t belong to them.
One employee told colleagues that Muse had randomly sent an extra message in a chat about weather and tide information, saying: “BTW, two bank updates, your Capital One balance is $2722.58, your Charles Schwab balance is $5899.57.”
In another example, an employee using the AI agent on her personal phone received a reminder from Muse to respond to a message from her sister on Signal, the popular end-to-end encrypted messaging app.
“This seems like an extreme privacy violation. I definitely did not grant it access to other apps, or recall being asked about this,” the employee said in her post, according to the report.
“Employee testing is core to the product development process and the entire point is to get feedback, so we can implement safety and privacy protections and improve products,” a Meta spokesperson said in an email to TechCrunch. “Importantly, employees have access to different versions of Muse than the public, so they’re often reviewing features, functionality, and behavior not available elsewhere.”
Launched in September, Muse is one of the fastest-growing apps on record, with more than 10 million downloads.
Update 11/19/2026 12:05 PM PT: The article was updated to include Meta’s comment.

articles.title: GTCO wants to revive its iconic 737 brand with new app
articles.text:
Ten years ago, Guaranty Trust Bank Plc, one of Nigeria’s largest banks, launched *737#, a USSD banking service that helped redefine how Nigerians accessed financial services beyond the brick-and-mortar of traditional bank branches.
At the time, the promise was to make banking as simple as ABC’s and 123’s. “Well, in this case, GTBank has made it as simple as 737,” the bank said in its 2016 announcement.
A decade later, GTB is now betting on the same 737 brand, now in the form of a mobile app, to win over a new generation of Nigerians who increasingly favour fintechs for their faster transactions and ease of use.
This comes as the original *737# loses influence. Between June 2021 and June 2026, USSD transactions fell by 80.79%, from ₦2.15 trillion ($1.58 billion) to ₦412.85 billion ($302.85 million). Transaction values declined every year during the period, reflecting the gradual shift in how customers interact with their banks.
Half-Year Transaction Value (2021–2026)
A visual breakdown of USSD market volumes shrinking from trillions to billions.
For a generation of Nigerians, 737 was more than a banking service. Its catchy jingle became a familiar part of everyday life, helping GTBank build one of the most recognisable brands in Nigerian banking. But the banking habits that made the service popular are changing.
Rather than abandon the brand, GTB is giving it a second life. On November 11, Guaranty Trust Holding Company Plc (GTCO), through its banking subsidiary GTB, launched a new 737 mobile application that turns customers’ phone numbers into account numbers and combines payments, savings, lending, and virtual cards in a single interface. The product is designed to operate more like a standalone fintech platform than a conventional banking app.
GTCO described the launch as a response to younger customers who are increasingly mobile-driven, digitally connected, and accustomed to managing different aspects of their lives from their phones. But the move also reflects how traditional banks are trying to defend their position in a payments market where fintechs have built customer loyalty around convenience and transaction speed.
The 737 app joins GTCO’s other consumer-facing application, GTWorld, its established mobile banking platform. Running two consumer-facing apps suggests that the group is pursuing a multi-product digital strategy: retaining GTWorld for its existing banking customers while using 737 to attract customers who may be more comfortable with the simplified, payments-led experience offered by fintechs.
The new app also lets GTCO retain the equity of its iconic 737 brand as it attempts to revive some of the buzz that made it synonymous with everyday banking.
Which app actually fits your wallet?
Select your profile below to cut through the marketing.
The Under-the-Hood Reality Matrix
The death of *737#
USSD was one of the most important ways Nigerian banks brought financial services closer to customers. It allowed people to transfer money, buy airtime, and check account balances without an internet connection or a smartphone.
First Bank, Nigeria’s oldest lender, introduced its USSD banking service, *894#, in 2015, and by 2020, it said more than 9.5 million of its 20 million customers were using the channel.
But it was GTBank that popularised USSD banking with *737# in 2016. Through radio jingles, branded clothing and caps, its marketing strategy turned the code into a recognisable banking brand.
The conditions that made USSD attractive, however, are changing. The spread of smartphones, relatively cheaper mobile data packages and the growing popularity of fintech applications have given customers more ways to access financial services without dialling a banking code.
Nigeria’s 2G connections, which typically indicate the prevalence of feature phones on a network, fell from 60.85% of total mobile connections in July 2023 to 36.42% in September 2026. Meanwhile, 4G connections, which indicate smartphone usage, rose from 24.16% to 54.37% over the same period.
USSD has also become a more expensive and sometimes frustrating channel. Failed sessions, network interruptions, and transaction costs have weakened some of its convenience advantage. The channel has also become a source of conflict between commercial banks and telecom operators, which provide the underlying infrastructure, particularly over its billing structure.
“USSD is a clumsy technology. It’s not state-of-the-art…,” Segun Agbaje, the group chief executive officer of GTCO, said in 2023. “The whole fight about USSD has been a fantastic distraction by the telcos.”
As *737# usage declined, however, GTCO’s mobile app channel grew. Transaction value through this channel increased from ₦11 trillion ($8.07 billion) in H1 2021 to ₦26.70 trillion ($19.59 billion) in H1 2026.
Why GTCO has another app
GTCO already has a customer-facing app, GTWorld, which crossed three million active users in October 2025 and was growing at a month-on-month rate of 12%. In H1 2026, it processed 337.4 million transactions, up 15.82% year-on-year.
GTWorld has become an important bridge between GTCO’s banking business and its broader payments ambitions, but 737 takes a slightly different approach.
When GTBank launched *737#, it targeted customers who wanted to avoid banking queues and access financial services from their phones. Many of these early adopters were university undergraduates and younger Nigerians who were becoming more comfortable with digital banking.
Today, GTCO is pursuing a similar customer base, but the competitive landscape has changed. Those customers have increasingly turned to fintechs, which have popularised phone-number-based account numbers and built their appeal around a focused experience: making payments, moving money and completing everyday financial transactions with as little friction as possible.
The new 737 app borrows from that approach, turning a customer’s phone number into an account number and bringing payments, savings, lending, and virtual cards into one interface.
The phone-number-as-account-number feature reduces the friction associated with sharing and remembering bank account numbers, while giving the product a familiar identity that customers can use in everyday transactions.
The app also adopts some of the features that fintechs have made popular, including facial verification, which companies such as OPay have helped mainstream. But one of its more interesting additions is betting.
Nigeria’s betting market, estimated at approximately $2 billion in 2023, represents a sizeable opportunity for platforms seeking to attract younger, digitally active customers. Fintechs have recognised this by integrating betting services into their apps, not necessarily as operators themselves but as gateways through which customers can fund betting accounts while continuing to use the same platforms for payments and transfers.
For a traditional commercial bank, incorporating betting into its consumer-facing products may be a more complicated decision because of its broader positioning and internal considerations. 737 gives GTCO room to experiment with features that might not sit as comfortably within its established banking app.
The feature is also a part of the broader goal among fintechs to turn their applications into everyday destinations where customers can access multiple services without switching platforms.
737 Growth Simulator
Does the new app grow GTCO or just shift users?
The race for everyday payments
Commercial banks in Nigeria control much of the country’s deposit base, but fintechs have built a significant presence in everyday payments and merchant transactions. In 2025, Nigeria processed more than ₦1.2 quadrillion ($880.51 billion) in electronic transactions. Fintech giants Moniepoint and OPay accounted for a significant share of this activity, processing a combined $644.85 billion.
The Everyday Payments Battle
Simulate the race for Nigeria’s digital transactions.
In 2020, Agbaje described OPay’s potential as scary while speaking about how banks could lose a significant portion of their revenue to emerging startups.
“Those models are the reason why I’m very encouraged that Guaranty Trust Bank going into the payment space will do very well, because we will pilot at scale and we will be very aggressive,” he said.
GTCO subsequently launched Habari Pay Ltd in 2022, its payments business, which has developed into a payments infrastructure business spanning switching and processing. Through GTWorld and Pay-with-Transfer, the group is processing increasingly large volumes of customer transactions. But its consumer-facing products still have to contend with fintechs that have built extensive distribution networks and captured a significant share of everyday payments.
Companies such as OPay have built their businesses around frequent payments, transfers, and other everyday financial services. Their appeal is partly rooted in the convenience of completing transactions without navigating the more traditional structures of banking.
The 737 app wants to close some of this gap by embedding itself in everyday transactions. Its scan-to-pay feature, for instance, is designed to make payments faster by eliminating the need to enter account details manually.
GTCO has already seen some success in this direction through its core banking app, GTWorld. Its Pay-with-Transfer feature recorded a 1,587.39% increase in transaction volume between H1 2025 and H1 2026.
But payment convenience alone may not be enough to win customers who already have established relationships with fintech applications. Lending could be another important battleground.
Commercial banks have traditionally been more cautious about unsecured retail lending, leaving room for fintechs to build credit businesses around transaction data and alternative credit assessment models. In H1 2026, OPay disbursed $927.6 million in loans in Nigeria, while GTCO’s retail lending stood at ₦381.27 billion ($279.68 million) over the same period.
OPay uses transaction data to assess borrowers who may lack conventional credit records. GTCO, like many traditional banks, relies more heavily on established indicators of creditworthiness, including regular income flows and account history.
On the 737 app, eligible customers can access its Quick Credit service, which is typically tied to salary or income accounts, with eligibility requiring at least six months of account ownership. The app also offers airtime and data loans.
Although its 2.95% interest rate could make the product attractive, its eligibility requirements may limit its appeal among the younger and more financially diverse customer base GTCO hopes to attract.
Fintechs have built lending products around customers’ transaction behaviour, while traditional banks still depend heavily on established banking relationships and documented income. If 737 is to compete for the same customers, GTCO may need to rethink how accessible its credit products are.
GTCO is not starting from zero. The 737 brand was an early disruptor in Nigerian banking in the mid-2010s. GTCO must now prove that it can disrupt the market a second time.

articles.title: Astronom:innen erwischen Supernova vor dem Höhepunkt – doch ihre Umgebung wirft Fragen auf
articles.text:
Kosmischer Schnellstart: Supernova SN 2026ahvu bringt Zeitpläne der Astrophysik ins Wanken
Am 2. November 2026 registrierte das automatische Himmelsüberwachungssystem ATLAS in der rund 50 Millionen Lichtjahre entfernten Balkenspiralgalaxie NGC 1433 eine neue Sternexplosion, die seither die Kennung SN 2026ahvu trägt. Wie aus der Entdeckungsmeldung hervorgeht, erwischten die Instrumente das Phänomen noch während des Helligkeitsanstiegs, dessen Scheitelpunkt Astronom:innen für den Zeitraum zwischen dem 18. und 23. November 2026 erwarten.
Spektralmessungen eines Teams um den Astrophysiker Wynn Jacobson-Galán vom US-amerikanischen California Institute of Technology am W.-M.-Keck-Observatorium im Bundesstaat Hawaii stuften den Ausbruch bereits einen Tag nach der Sichtung in einem Klassifikationsbericht als junge Supernova des Typs Ia ein. Bei dieser Unterart zieht ein ausgebrannter, dicht gepackter Sternenrest, ein sogenannter Weißer Zwerg, in einem Doppelsternsystem so lange Materie von seinem Nachbarstern ab, bis eine thermonukleare Kettenreaktion den Zwergstern zerreißt.
Automatische Reaktionskette von ATLAS bis zu den Teleskopen von Noirlab
Ursprünglich dient das Asteroid Terrestrial-impact Last Alert System (ATLAS) mit Teleskopen auf der Nord- und Südhalbkugel als Frühwarnsystem für erdnahe Asteroiden, erfasst beim Absuchen des Nachthimmels aber auch kurzzeitig aufleuchtende Himmelserscheinungen, die in der Fachsprache transiente Ereignisse genannt werden. Im Fall von SN 2026ahvu wertete eine an der britischen Universität Oxford von der Astrophysikerin Héloïse Stevance entwickelte Software namens Virtual Research Assistant den Datenstrom automatisiert aus und stieß Folgebeobachtungen am südafrikanischen Forschungsinstitut South African Astronomical Observatory an.
Inzwischen bündelt das Forschungszentrum Noirlab mit Sitz in Tucson im US-Bundesstaat Arizona laut einer Mitteilung des Instituts die Beobachtungen mehrerer Sternwarten in Chile. Darunter befinden sich die Dark-Energy-Camera am Cerro Tololo Inter-American Observatory und das Großteleskop Gemini South auf dem Berg Cerro Pachón. Solche automatisierten Warnketten verkürzen zwar die Reaktionszeit nach dem ersten Lichtsignal, liefern zunächst aber nur grobe Helligkeitswerte und bleiben für eine belastbare Einordnung auf knappe Beobachtungszeit an Großteleskopen mit Spektrografen angewiesen, die das Sternenlicht in seine einzelnen Wellenlängen zerlegen.
Archivdaten von Hubble und James Webb zeigen junge Sternhaufen neben dem Explosionsort
Um die Vorgeschichte des explodierten Sterns zu rekonstruieren, hat eine Gruppe von 33 Forscher:innen um den Astrophysiker Sumit K. Sarbadhicary von der Johns Hopkins University in Baltimore im US-Bundesstaat Maryland ältere Aufnahmen der Weltraumteleskope Hubble und James Webb ausgewertet. Auf 50 Millionen Lichtjahre Entfernung ist ein einzelner Weißer Zwerg vor seinem Ausbruch zwar selbst für diese Teleskope zu lichtschwach, doch laut einer Vorab-Studie auf der Forschungsplattform Arxiv liegen zwei Sternhaufen unmittelbar neben dem Explosionsort.
Alle Sterne eines solchen Haufens entstehen zur selben Zeit aus einer gemeinsamen Gaswolke, weshalb sich das Alter der gesamten Gruppe an Farbe und Helligkeit ihres Lichts ablesen lässt. Der näher gelegene Sternhaufen existiert demnach seit rund 37 Millionen Jahren, der zweite Nachbarhaufen seit etwa 95 Millionen Jahren. Gehörte der zerstörte Stern zu einer dieser beiden Gruppen, vergingen von seiner Entstehung über das Ausbrennen zum Weißen Zwerg bis zur Supernova weniger als 100 Millionen Jahre – gängige Modelle veranschlagen für diesen Ablauf meist Hunderte Millionen bis mehrere Milliarden Jahre.
„Sollte die Supernova tatsächlich mit dem jüngeren Sternhaufen zusammenhängen, würde das bedeuten, dass Typ-Ia-Supernovae fast unmittelbar nach der Entstehung eines Weißen Zwergs auftreten können“, schreiben Sarbadhicary und seine Kolleg:innen in dem Manuskript, das noch kein unabhängiges Fachgutachten durchlaufen hat. Weil das explodierte Doppelsternsystem auf den Archivbildern nicht selbst zu sehen ist, lässt sich bislang allerdings nicht sicher klären, ob und aus welchem der beiden Haufen der Stern tatsächlich stammte.
Warum SN 2026ahvu den Entfernungsstreit um die Galaxie NGC 1433 klären soll
Neben der Spurensuche nach dem Ursprungsstern soll der Ausbruch auch ein altes Messproblem rund um die Heimatgalaxie NGC 1433 lösen. Je nach Berechnungsverfahren kamen bisherige Studien für deren Entfernung auf widersprüchliche Werte zwischen rund 30 Millionen und 62 Millionen Lichtjahren.
Typ-Ia-Supernovae helfen bei solchen Abweichungen weiter, weil die Weißen Zwerge stets bei einer ähnlichen kritischen Masse explodieren und am Höhepunkt nahezu gleich hell strahlen. Astronom:innen nutzen sie deshalb als sogenannte Standardkerzen: Ähnlich wie bei einer Glühbirne mit bekannter Wattzahl lässt sich aus der auf der Erde gemessenen Helligkeit ableiten, wie weit die Lichtquelle entfernt ist.
Damit diese Rechnung aufgeht, müssen Teleskope allerdings den hellsten Moment des Ausbruchs erfassen. Wäre SN 2026ahvu erst beim Verblassen aufgefallen, hätten Forscher:innen den verpassten Spitzenwert nachträglich schätzen müssen. Selbst mit Messdaten vom Höhepunkt bleibt zudem eine Fehlerquelle, weil Staubwolken in der fernen Galaxie Licht schlucken und die Explosion dadurch dunkler und weiter entfernt wirken lassen können.
Archivbilder des Dark Energy Survey und Beobachtung von SN 2026ahvu am Südhimmel
Wie sich das Aufleuchten im Vergleich zum früheren Zustand der Galaxie abhebt, zeigen Vorher-Nachher-Aufnahmen von Noirlab. Für das Bild vor dem Ausbruch griffen die Forscher:innen auf Archivdaten des Projekts Dark Energy Survey zurück. Das Fermi National Accelerator Laboratory in Batavia im US-Bundesstaat Illinois hatte diese Himmelsdurchmusterung von 2013 bis 2019 geleitet, um die Dunkle Energie als Treiber der beschleunigten Ausdehnung des Universums zu erforschen.
Weil NGC 1433 im Sternbild Pendeluhr rund 47 Grad südlich des Himmelsäquators steht, bleibt die Galaxie in mittleren und höheren nördlichen Breiten dauerhaft unter dem Horizont. Abgesehen von südlich gelegenen Sternwarten der Nordhalbkugel wie auf Hawaii lässt sich der weitere Verlauf von SN 2026ahvu daher nur von Standorten in Südamerika, im südlichen Afrika oder in Australien verfolgen.

articles.title: Agent security is product security, and your marketing site counts
articles.text:
Agent security is product security, and your marketing site counts
A marketing site used to have two kinds of visitors: people and search crawlers. Now an agent can build a page, a second agent can scrape it, a third can summarize it for a potential customer, and a fourth can optimize it overnight after studying yesterday’s traffic.
“The ones that you do not control make the marketing site a product with agent users, and products need product security.”
You control some of these agents but not all the data they ingest and train on. The ones that you do not control make the marketing site a product with agent users, and products need product security. A marketing site is usually public with no login required to view or break. Adversaries go after whether the site still says what you wrote, serves what you built, and reports what real visitors did. This article calls those content integrity, delivery integrity, and signal integrity, and looks at where each kind of agent touches them.
Five agents, three kinds of integrity
Five agent roles show up on a marketing site today, agents that:
- build,
- read or scrape,
- analyze its visitor data,
- optimize the site from that data,
- adversarial agents that attack
Each role touches at least one of three things worth protecting the integrity of:
- Content – what the site says and links to.
- Delivery – how that content reaches a browser, including DNS, redirects, third-party scripts, hosting, and the publish pipeline.
- Signal – the visitor and behavior data the site produces, plus every decision made from it.
Because the content is public, the checks that matter are integrity checks. An agent with write access can be talked into making unapproved changes, so you need governance over what it may touch and logs that show what it did.
Agents that build sites
Builders are usually the first agents a team adopts, so they set the pattern for every agent that follows. A builder agent writes pages, config, scripts, and redirects. The risk sits in what it reads before it writes. A doc, a ticket, a scraped competitor page, or a CMS field can carry instructions, and an agent can follow them.
Recent incidents show the shape of this. In July 2025, someone slipped a destructive prompt into a pull request for the Amazon Q Developer extension for VS Code, and it shipped in a production version. AWS removed it and said no customer resources were affected, and reports indicate a formatting error kept the prompt from running. The same month, a Replit coding agent reportedly deleted a production database during a code freeze, despite instructions not to change anything. Replit’s response was to separate development and production databases automatically. The causes differ from provenance checks to agents stepping outside their boundaries.
The incidents above failed at different stages of Figure 2. Amazon Q failed at the input and review stages, where untrusted text in a pull request reached a trusted release. Replit failed at the harness, where an instruction to freeze changes was the only barrier between the agent and a production database. A marketing site has the same exposure, and three layers around the agent carry those controls.
- The agentic SDLC is the process – where agents act across plan, draft, review, and publish, and which stages need a human decision.
- The agent harness is the control layer – the code around the model that decides which tools the agent can call, with which credentials, and what gets logged or approved.
- The sandbox is the containment layer – an isolated runtime with no standing credentials, restricted network egress, and no path to production data.
For a marketing site, that translates into a few working rules.
- Give builder agents draft access and keep publishing behind a person.
- Review a diff of content, scripts, and redirects. A summary written by the agent describes what it believes it did.
- Treat every input as untrusted, including your own docs and tickets, because anyone who can edit them can steer the agent.
- Add provenance records – which agent changed which page, from which inputs.
Webflow’s AI site builder drafts a multi-page site and design system from a prompt. The Webflow MCP server connects AI tools like Claude to a site, so an agent can design, build, and manage it through natural conversation or agentic workflows.
“Treat every input as untrusted, including your own docs and tickets, because anyone who can edit them can steer the agent.”
Webflow’s controls map to the rules above. Agent Instructions give an agent your design system, voice, CMS, and policies as skills and rules stored with your site, and agents should read them before they act. They guide an agent but don’t enforce anything, and an agent follows them as an input, so edit access matters: only Site managers and Designers can change them, and new ones stay off until someone reviews and turns them on. To see what an agent is doing, agent presence shows where any agent connected through the Webflow MCP server is working on the canvas, the same way you’d see a teammate. For the record afterward, the Site Activity Log for enterprise labels each change as Human, Webflow AI, or MCP.
Site roles do the enforcing. They let a team give a builder a narrow role, such as a Marketer with publishing switched off. That role can build pages from components but can’t publish, create API tokens, or open custom code. On Enterprise plans, design approvals go further. A role without the “Edit main site without approval” permission works in page branches, and its changes reach the main site only after required reviewers approve them.
Source by Webflow, now in research preview, is a new platform purpose-built for teams and agents to drive growth on the web, together. Source’s site-building agents work directly on your codebase. It’s designed to let teams decide how much autonomy those agents have, from requiring human approval for every change to giving agents more freedom for lower-risk work, and to hold agent actions to the same roles, permissions, and review systems as human work, with a record of what changed and which agent changed it.
Agents that read and scrape the site
Search is turning into answers, and answers are built from your pages. Agents read page text as context, and a page can contain text no visitor sees. In August 2025, Brave researchers hid instructions behind a spoiler tag in a Reddit comment. When a user asked Perplexity’s Comet browser to summarize the page, Comet followed them and exfiltrated a one-time password. Perplexity patched the issue. Any field attackers can write to on your site, such as comments, reviews, form-fed content, or CMS entries, can carry the same kind of payload to every agent that reads it.
The agent also might not see the same page you do. Researchers at SPLX showed that a site can check the user agent and serve AI crawlers different content than it serves browsers. The same technique works against you if an attacker gains write access to your site: they can change what AI systems say about you while every human check looks clean. Monitor what agents see, not only what browsers see.
Before you can control which agents read your site, you need to see them. AI bots don’t show up in standard visitor analytics, so most teams have no record of which ones visit or what they request. Webflow’s LLM bot insights fills that gap with data from your site’s server logs, so it covers the bots it tracks whether or not visitor tracking is on. It groups each bot by purpose: agentic bots that fetch pages live to answer a user’s question, training bots that collect content for model development, indexing bots that map pages for retrieval, and bots with more than one purpose. You can view activity for the whole site or a single page, filter by provider or category, and export the data as a CSV.
That gives you a baseline. Bots often focus on different pages than human visitors do, and a jump or drop after you publish is easy to spot. A page that agents fetch heavily is also a page where tampered content or injected text reaches the most readers, which makes it a good place to start the integrity checks below. The view covers named LLM bots. It doesn’t flag traffic as hostile, and it doesn’t show a user’s original query or whether a page was cited.
Visibility tells you who is there. What to do about them is a separate decision, because scrapers differ in intent. An indexer that maps your pages for retrieval and a collector that copies them for training both read public content, and you may want to allow one and not the other. Scrapers that hit your endpoints at volume add hosting cost and can slow the site for real visitors, and they count as traffic in your analytics unless something classifies them. A robots.txt file states your preference but doesn’t enforce it. Set a policy for each purpose, enforce it with rate limits and bot rules, and carry the classification into analytics so scraper traffic is reported separately from human visitors.
Agents that analyze visitor data
Analysis agents work with the most sensitive data on the site: behavior tied to real people. Webflow shows what this looks like in practice. Webflow Analyze records click events, sessions, bounce rate, time on page, and audience attributes such as traffic source, region, and device. Teams can connect an AI tool to the Webflow MCP server and ask about their site’s traffic and engagement, including page-level data, goals, and filtered results, without opening Analyze. That connected tool is an analysis agent.
The shape of the data limits what the agent can expose. Analyze uses anonymous identifiers and, according to Webflow, collects no personally identifiable information, and it relies on local storage instead of cookies. This is the setup the controls below call for: an agent that reads an anonymized dataset, not raw visitor records. If you build your own analysis agents, keep sensitive identifiers out of their context, run them in a sandbox, and give them read-only access.
Two things still need your attention. The first is consent. Analyze lets you choose always-on, opt-in, or opt-out tracking, and the opt-in and opt-out methods need a consent management solution to work properly. The tracking method decides which visitors are in the data, so the consent choices you apply belong in the dataset before an agent reads it. The second is signal quality. An analysis agent reports what the site counted, and it learns from the same signal that attackers can pollute. Label automated traffic before it reaches the agent, so it can report human and agent traffic separately. Blended answers describe bots as much as people.
Optimization agents close the loop
Optimization agents turn signal into action. They rewrite headlines, reorder sections, and adjust audiences from traffic data. That makes signal integrity a content integrity problem. If an agent learns from poisoned traffic, it ships a confident change based on bad data, and the changed page produces more skewed data for the next round.
A person who sees a conversion spike from a country you don’t sell in asks questions. An agent ships the variant. The fix is to make the loop checkable: validate the signal before an agent acts on it, hold out traffic the agent can’t tune, and require approval and rollback for changes to live pages.
“If an agent learns from poisoned traffic, it ships a confident change based on bad data, and the changed page produces more skewed data for the next round.”
Webflow Optimize shows where this loop exists in a product. An optimization has a target goal, and its variations can be tested with a traditional A/B/n split, shown by personalization rules, or handled by an AI-optimized mode that uses machine learning to serve the best-performing variation and adapt as visitor behavior shifts. That last mode is the loop in Figure 3: whatever counts as a conversion becomes the signal the system learns from, so automated traffic that completes the goal action can push a weaker variation forward. A variation can also redirect a visitor to a different page, which puts redirect destinations in scope for the delivery checks above. For teams using these features, treat the target goal as a security decision. Pick goals that bots find hard to fake, separate automated traffic from human results, and have a person review results before an AI-optimized variation becomes the default.
Agents that attack the site
A marketing site does not require a login to view its public content. Attackers go after integrity: they attempt to change what the site says, hijack what it serves, or corrupt what it reports. Automation already does this at scale, and agents lower the cost further. In testing by hCaptcha’s threat group, browser agents run against 20 common abuse scenarios attempted nearly every malicious request without any jailbreaking. Most block attempts failed because the tool lacked the capability.
Content
Content attacks change what visitors read, or send them to a copy of your site. In July 2025, Okta reported that attackers were using Vercel’s v0, a tool that builds web pages from natural-language prompts, to clone sign-in pages for brands including Microsoft 365 and cryptocurrency companies. Okta’s researchers reproduced the attack with a single prompt asking for a copy of their own login page, and Axios reported it can take as little as 30 seconds. Vercel restricted access to the sites Okta identified. The same approach can reproduce a marketing site.
Agents that run on your site raise a related problem, and the attacker doesn’t have to be an agent. In December 2023, a visitor talked the chatbot on a Chevrolet dealership’s site into agreeing to buy a new Tahoe for $1 and calling it a legally binding offer. In February 2024, a Canadian tribunal ordered Air Canada to pay $812.02 after its chatbot gave a customer wrong bereavement fare information. The tribunal wrote that “it makes no difference whether the information comes from a static page or a chatbot.” It treated the chatbot’s words as the company’s words.
Platforms carry part of the response. Webflow’s Acceptable Use Policy prohibits using the platform for impersonation, fraud, malware, and content altered to mislead people, and Webflow’s Trust and Safety team removes sites that break it. Removals come from automated detection and from reports, and ~1000 sites are taken down each day. If you find a site impersonating yours on Webflow, you can report it through the form linked in the policy or at abuse@webflow.com.
Delivery
Delivery attacks hijack the path between your content and the visitor’s browser, and they don’t need to touch your page. In 2024, a company acquired the polyfill.io domain and changed the script it served, which redirected mobile visitors on more than 100,000 sites to scam pages. The site owners hadn’t changed a line of code, and Google began warning advertisers whose landing pages loaded the script. A week after the disclosure, Censys still counted nearly 385,000 hosts referencing the domain, including 182 government sites.
DNS follows the same pattern. Guardio Labs found more than 8,000 domains and 13,000 subdomains tied to well-known brands hijacked through dangling CNAME and SPF records, then used to send about five million emails a day under those brands’ names. Open redirects borrow a trusted domain’s reputation the same way. Cofense found that every US .gov domain abused in phishing campaigns between November 2022 and November 2024 was used for an open redirect, and KnowBe4 documented a 2025 campaign against finance and healthcare organizations that relied on open redirects in legitimate services.
Agents make the search for these cheaper. Finding a dangling record or a redirect parameter is a scanning problem, and agent tooling can follow a hit through to a tailored phishing page faster than a script could.
Signal
Signal attacks corrupt what the site reports. Fake form fills, synthetic sessions, and scripted browsing pollute analytics, attribution, and audiences. The scale is real: Imperva’s 2025 Bad Bot Report found that automated traffic reached 51% of web traffic in 2024, and bad bots accounted for 37%. Forms are the most direct path from a bot into a marketing team’s CRM, so they are a good place to start. Webflow’s form spam protection offers four methods that you can combine. The reCAPTCHA field asks visitors to identify themselves as human before they submit, although Webflow notes that it can hurt user experience and that more advanced bots can get around it. A site-level bot blocking setting uses AI to analyze mouse movements, inputs, and other signals, and blocks submissions from bots on every form on the site. A second site-level setting, spam filtering, checks all the form data sent on your site and filters out spam submissions. The honeypot technique adds a hidden field that real visitors never fill in, so a filled field marks the submission as spam. Because the CAPTCHA can be circumvented, none of these should carry the load alone.
The damage reaches visitors too. A visitor’s history is the record that drives what they see next. When synthetic sessions merge into real audiences, or identities get stitched together wrongly, retargeting and personalization act on the wrong history, and real visitors get irrelevant offers.
How to secure your marketing site against agents
The controls differ by layer, but the first step is the same for all three: list every agent that touches your site, including the ones you don’t operate. You can’t protect a layer from an agent you haven’t counted.
Content. Review agent-authored changes like code. Keep a record of which agent changed what and from which inputs, and alert on diffs nobody requested. Fetch key pages with common AI crawler user agents and compare the result to what a browser gets.
Delivery. Allowlist redirect destinations, and remove any endpoint that redirects to an arbitrary URL. Audit DNS for dangling CNAME records and SPF includes that point at services you no longer use. Keep an inventory of third-party scripts, and apply Subresource Integrity or serve them from your own origin where you can. The polyfill.io incident is the case for it.
Signal. Classify automated traffic before it reaches analytics. Rate-limit and validate form submissions, and layer the protections your platform offers, such as bot blocking, spam filtering, and a honeypot field. Tag agent-originated sessions so they stay out of human audiences and human-focused tests, and report on them as their own segment.
Across all of it. Apply least privilege to every agent, keep logs you can query, and put a person in front of the publish step.
Your marketing site now has more kinds of visitors, and some of them can edit it.
If an agent changed what your site says tonight, would you know which one it was, what it read first, and who approved the change?
This article was originally published on November 10, 2026, on webflow.com.

articles.title: Robots can do backflips but can't hold a gaze or press piano keys, and scientists think they've fixed that
articles.text:
What just happened? Engineers at the University of Pennsylvania have built an artificial muscle fiber that tracks its own temperature and corrects itself, so it can hold a precise position instead of slowly drifting back to its resting shape. The fiber pairs a rubber-like liquid crystal elastomer with graphene and an ultrathin copper coil that works as both a heater and a sensor. In lab tests, the muscles let a robot hand strike piano keys with different amounts of force and let a pair of robotic eyes hold a steady gaze.
The work, published in Advanced Functional Materials, is modeled on the small muscles that move human fingers and eyes. Those muscles make fine, controlled movements, and that kind of control has been hard to get from the hardware inside most robots today.
Large humanoid robots usually run on bulky, rigid motors and mechanical parts. That setup is good enough for walking and lifting, but not for small, careful motions. It's a familiar problem in robotics. Machines that can dance or do acrobatic flips still struggle with jobs people find easy, like folding laundry or keeping their eyes fixed on one spot.
Moving to soft materials brings its own trade-off. "Soft robotic muscles need to be both strong and flexible to mimic human movements, but these properties are rarely found in the same material," said Shu Yang, a University of Pennsylvania engineer and co-author of the study, in a statement.
The team's answer was a composite fiber in which each material has its own job. The liquid crystal elastomer, or LCE, is the part that moves. It contracts and stretches when heated, much like a muscle. Graphene mixed into the elastomer makes it softer and tougher, so the fiber holds up when an opposing muscle pulls the other way. That's important in any system where muscles work in pairs.
Even so, the elastomer and graphene alone couldn't hold a position. Heat makes the fiber move, but the fiber cools quickly and creeps back toward its original length. For a steady gaze or a light, constant press on a piano key, that drift is a serious problem, because the muscle has to stay in one place over time.
A copper coil fixed the drift. The researchers built it into the fiber so it would act as a temperature gauge, showing when the muscle was losing heat and starting to move back. With that reading, the system could add heat little by little to keep the fiber where it was supposed to be.
"We used the resistance of the embedded copper coil as a feedback signal and adjusted the heating power in real time to keep the resistance near a target value," said Xuelin Wu, a University of Pennsylvania Ph.D. student and co-author of the study. "Because the coil served as both a heater and a sensor, we did not need a separate sensor for feedback."
Because one part does both jobs, the design stays simple. There's no separate sensor to add or wire up, which helps as the muscles get smaller and are packed closer together.
The team tested the fibers in two setups. In the first, the muscles were fitted into a 3D-printed robot hand built to mimic how fingers move. The fingers pressed piano keys with varying amounts of force and at different speeds, and sensors under the keys measured how hard each note was struck. The hand isn't a skilled pianist, but it varied its touch on command.
In the second setup, the researchers put two robotic eyeballs on freely rotating ball joints inside 3D-printed shells. They attached the fibers in opposing pairs around the edges of each eye, much like the muscles that turn a human eye. The eyes shifted their gaze when commanded, and the movements were controlled and repeatable.
The Penn project is one of several efforts by labs and companies to replace standard motors with muscle-like actuators. Other researchers have stretched lab-grown human skin over robot faces and built synthetic hydrogel skin that lets robots sense burns and cuts. In 2025, the Polish startup Clone Robotics released a video of a faceless, human-sized robot hanging from a ceiling and twisting. The company said the robot was driven by synthetic muscles and a hydraulic system designed to copy human muscles and blood vessels, and it called the machine the world's first "musculoskeletal android." The video looked more like an early proof of concept than a finished prototype.
The Penn team's next step is to combine many of its fibers into larger systems, where dozens of small muscles have to work together to produce natural-looking expressions. Further out, the researchers want to explore using AI computer vision to coordinate those muscle groups. Their long-term goal is robots that look and move more like people.
"I'm excited about the possibility of using this approach to create robots that move with the same subtlety and expressiveness we see in human faces," said Ziyun Zhang, a University of Pennsylvania engineer and co-author of the paper.

articles.title: Scientists tracked kids for 8 years. What they found about screen time was surprising
articles.text:
Scientists tracked kids for 8 years. What they found about screen time was surprising
- Date:
- November 17, 2026
- Source:
- University of Jyväskylä - Jyväskylän yliopisto
- Summary:
- A surprising Finnish study found that children who spent more time using screens tended to have better cognitive processing abilities as teenagers, challenging the assumption that screen time is always harmful. Researchers suggest that what children do on screens may matter more than how much time they spend using them.
- Share:
An eight-year study of children in Finland has revealed a surprising connection between screen time and brain function. Researchers found that children who spent more time using screens tended to have better cognitive processing abilities as teenagers, challenging the widespread assumption that screen time is necessarily harmful to developing brains.
The findings suggest that the amount of time children spend in front of screens may be less important than how they use that time. Activities that encourage learning, creativity, and problem-solving could be particularly valuable. Researchers emphasize that the goal should not be to eliminate screen time, but to balance it with physical activity and mentally stimulating experiences.
The discovery comes amid growing concerns about insufficient physical activity among teenagers. A sedentary lifestyle has been linked to poorer academic performance, while regular exercise is known to support brain function, particularly in adults. However, scientists still have much to learn about how physical activity, sitting, and screen use during childhood influence thinking abilities later in adolescence.
These questions are especially important because childhood and adolescence are critical periods of brain development. Changes in attention, memory, and learning during these years can have lasting consequences, potentially influencing educational opportunities and career paths well into adulthood.
To investigate these relationships, Finnish researchers examined how screen time, physical activity, and sedentary behavior from childhood through adolescence were associated with cognitive performance in teenagers. They also explored whether the connections differed between boys and girls and whether the intensity of physical activity made a difference.
More Screen Time Linked to Better Thinking Skills
One of the study's most unexpected findings was that greater screen time throughout childhood was associated with better cognitive processing in adolescence.
Cognitive processing refers to the mental abilities people use to take in information, pay attention, remember details, learn new things, and solve problems. These abilities play an important role in school performance and everyday decision-making.
The findings challenge the idea that all screen time should be viewed as harmful. However, the researchers caution that the relationship may depend on what children are actually doing while using digital devices. Watching videos, playing games that require strategic thinking, and engaging in educational activities may involve very different levels of mental effort.
"The findings suggest that screen time can support children's and adolescents' cognitive processing. Presumably, the essential point here is what kind of things they do in their screen time. Teachers and parents should encourage children to use devices and screens in such ways that promote active thinking, problem-solving, creativity, and learning," states Doctoral Researcher Petri Jalanko from the University of Jyväskylä.
"We should not regard screen time solely as harmful but seek balance between physical activity and screen time that promotes active thinking," Jalanko summarizes.
Exercise Affects Boys' and Girls' Brains Differently
The researchers also uncovered a more complicated picture of how physical activity relates to thinking and memory.
Among girls, spending more time engaged in light-intensity physical activity since childhood was associated with better working memory during adolescence. For boys, greater participation in guided physical activity over the same period was linked to stronger working memory.
Working memory is the brain's ability to temporarily hold and use information. It allows someone to remember instructions while completing a task, keep track of numbers during mental calculations, or follow a conversation while processing new information.
Light-intensity physical activity generally includes relatively gentle movements that do not substantially increase breathing or heart rate. Guided physical activity refers to exercise carried out with some form of instruction or supervision, such as organized sports or structured exercise sessions.
The differences between boys and girls suggest that the relationship between exercise and brain health may depend on more than simply how much a person moves. The type of activity, how it is organized, and the individual's sex could all play a role.
Another Surprising Finding About Physical Activity
The study produced another counterintuitive result. Teenagers who reported spending less time in unsupervised physical activity tended to perform better on measures of cognitive processing.
Yet when researchers used wearable sensors to objectively measure movement and heart rate, they found no association between overall physical activity or sedentary time and cognitive performance.
One possible explanation is that wearable devices measure movement without revealing what a person is actually doing. For example, a sensor may record periods of sitting or physical activity, but it cannot determine whether someone is solving a difficult problem, studying, participating in an organized activity, or simply resting.
This distinction could help explain why questionnaire responses revealed relationships that were not apparent in the sensor measurements.
"Our study indicates that the connections of physical activity and sedentary behavior to cognitive processing are complex and depend on the sex, the type and assessment method of physical activity and sedentary time. Moreover, boys and girls may benefit from different types of physical activity in view of brain health," Jalanko adds.
"However, we need more intervention studies to find out causal relations and sex differences in this respect. Moreover, it is important to examine more specifically the effects of the intensity of physical activity on changes taking place in cognitive processing."
What the Eight-Year Study Revealed
The findings come from an eight-year follow-up conducted as part of the PANIC study, a long-running Finnish research project investigating children's physical activity and nutrition.
The current analysis included 260 participants, consisting of 124 girls and 136 boys. Their average age at the adolescent assessment was 15.8 years.
Researchers collected information about physical activity and sedentary behavior using both questionnaires and wearable devices that combined heart rate monitoring with movement measurements. This approach allowed them to compare participants' reported activities with data collected by sensors.
To evaluate cognitive abilities, the researchers used the CogState test battery, a collection of computerized assessments designed to measure aspects of mental performance. The tests examined learning, attention, and working memory.
Importantly, the findings show associations rather than cause and effect. They do not establish that increasing screen time will improve a child's thinking abilities or that reducing certain types of exercise will produce cognitive benefits. Intervention studies, in which researchers deliberately change participants' activities and measure the results, are needed to determine whether these relationships are causal.
Nevertheless, the results offer an important perspective on the continuing debate over children's screen use. Rather than treating all time spent with digital devices as equally harmful, the researchers suggest paying closer attention to whether those activities encourage active thinking and learning.
The research also highlights the importance of considering different forms of physical activity rather than focusing exclusively on the total amount of exercise children receive.
Together, the findings suggest that supporting healthy brain development may require a more nuanced approach, one that combines physical activity with opportunities for learning, creativity, and mental engagement, including those that take place on screens.
The study was published in the scientific journal Pediatric Exercise Science.
Story Source:
Materials provided by University of Jyväskylä - Jyväskylän yliopisto. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Petri Jalanko, Marja H. Leppänen, Bert Bond, Jari A. Laukkanen, Timo A. Lakka, Eero A. Haapala. Associations of Physical Activity and Sedentary Time From Childhood to Adolescence With Cognition in Adolescence: The PANIC Study. Pediatric Exercise Science, 2026; 38 (3): 268 DOI: 10.1123/pes.2025-0083

articles.title: From voice cloning to “digital eugenics”: disability leaders unpack how AI is improving and damaging accessibility | BetaKit
articles.text:
In many ways, AI has made things better for people living with disabilities. In others, the technology has exacerbated existing problems.
Speakers at Access to Success’ inaugural Canadian Disability Tech Summit in Toronto on Wednesday afternoon unpacked some of the most interesting ways that AI is improving accessibility, how its underlying nature is deepening existing divides, and how we ought to leverage this tech to build a more inclusive world.
“Disability has always been a driver of innovation.”
Pete Horsley, Remarkable
Panellist Max Lemmens, general manager of Canada at the UK-founded, US-based voice AI firm ElevenLabs, noted that AI has made it easier to not only create but restore things. Some of ElevenLabs’ work has focused on giving a voice to people living with permanent voice loss.
“Historically, people who’ve lost their voice have been stuck with what I’ll call the Stephen Hawking effect, where it’s a very robotic voice that’s not really theirs,” Lemmens said. “For many people, their voice is their identity.”
To help address this problem, Lemmens claimed that, to date, ElevenLabs has helped more than 11,000 people regain access to their voice by applying AI to old recordings.
Fellow panellist Pete Horsley, founder of Australian disability tech accelerator Remarkable, highlighted some of the capabilities that Calgary-based brain-computer interface startup Possibility Neurotechnologies has demonstrated in his country as another helpful use-case. Possibility aims to allow users to control devices using their thoughts.
RELATED: Accessibility isn’t “a niche problem,” says organizer of inaugural assistive tech conference
“For one child that we tested the technology [on] within Australia, they only [previously] had a signal for yes … [Possibility was] able to give this child the ability to say no, and they actually said no a whole lot more after that,” Horsley said to audience laughter.
Tom Butcher is a senior advisor and ambassador at Austrian disability research organization Zero Project. He said the World Institute on Disability’s work using AI to compile resources on where to find wheelchairs, interpreters, and accessible shelters during times of crisis is an example of how AI can break down barriers.
However, as panellist Jutta Treviranus pointed out, one of the biggest underlying challenges is that AI is “statistically representative.” Modern AI and large language models rely on statistical pattern recognition, often amplifying the biases and trends present in their training data.
Treviranus, professor at OCAD University and director of the Inclusive Design Research Centre, said that since AI chooses “the average, the middle, the majority, [of] the most popular … many of [its] determinations regarding people with disabilities are wrong right from the get-go.”
“What we’re creating is this almost digital eugenics.”
Jutta Treviranus,
OCAD and IDRC
“Disability is a universal condition,” Treviranus added. “We will all experience it, and we all know that within this room. But, for whatever reason, we haven’t considered that. What we’re creating is this almost digital eugenics where we’re removing difference, we’re removing comfort with difference, and we’re not addressing that diversity that is the key to our human survival.”
Treviranus is particularly frustrated that “we are now going into what is the disruption of our lifetime, or this generation, but we’re not disrupting; we are basically automating, accelerating, and amplifying past patterns.”
People in the disability community are often told to just use these AI tools. But in practice, they can “work the worst for people [who] need them the most” due to their algorithms and often limited data on users with disabilities, Treviranus said.
Treviranus believes the solution involves re-engineering those algorithms and enabling on-device AI that can make use of individual data to better serve members of the disability community. Lemmens thinks that AI trained on synthetic data based on disability-focused datasets like the one Treviranus has spent years collecting could also help fill this need.
RELATED: Toronto gets a new hub for accessibility innovation
Lemmens does not see avoiding AI as an option. He believes the best approach involves pushing things forward, recognizing the tech’s shortcomings, and addressing them “head on.”
Horsley stressed that “disability is not about some of us; it’s about all of us,” and encouraged people living with disabilities to play an active role in building the world they’d like to inhabit. “Disability has always been a driver of innovation,” he said. “When you don’t have a world that’s creative for your needs, you’re always thinking about, what is the solution for that?”
Given where we now sit in the AI era, Horsley sees a unique chance to build better systems “from the bottom up,” rather than retrofit for accessibility, which is typically costlier. Horsley said Remarkable has seen “a massive, massive uptick” in the number of founders with disabilities launching businesses using AI tools, and urged attendees to follow suit. “There are huge opportunities here to create your future in [this] space, so go ahead and do it.”
