articles.title: 98,3 % de victoires : la puce quantique de Google pulvérise un plafond logique classique
articles.text:
La mécanique quantique a une centaine d’années, et son interprétation continue de diviser les physiciens, tandis que ses propriétés restent difficiles à comprendre. Albert Einstein, lui, se demandait si la Lune est bien là quand personne ne la regarde : c’était sa façon de défendre l’idée que les propriétés physiques existent avant qu’on les mesure.
Google Quantum AI, la division de recherche quantique de Google, s’est justement penchée sur l’une de ces propriétés. L’étude est cosignée par l’un de ses membres, le Français Michel Devoret, prix Nobel de physique 2025. Cette propriété, la « contextualité quantique », est moins connue que l’intrication quantique, même si l’expérience de Google s’appuie aussi sur des qubits intriqués.
Qu’est-ce que la contextualité ? En termes simples, le résultat d’une mesure dépend des autres mesures compatibles faites en même temps, c’est-à-dire de son « contexte ». On ne peut donc pas supposer que les valeurs étaient fixées à l’avance. L’équipe publie ses résultats dans la revue Science, après les avoir mis en ligne en prépublication sur arXiv en décembre 2025.
Google a mené ses expériences sur ses puces quantiques Willow. L’entreprise dit avoir mesuré cette contextualité jusqu’à 105 qubits (les unités de calcul d’un ordinateur quantique). Or, jusqu’ici, on ne l’avait guère observée que sur des systèmes plus petits, ne mobilisant que quelques particules.
Pour le montrer, Google a utilisé le jeu du carré magique. Il s’agit de remplir une grille de 3 cases sur 3 avec des +1 et des −1, de sorte que le produit de chaque ligne fasse +1 et celui de chaque colonne −1. C’est impossible : pour satisfaire les lignes, la grille doit contenir au total un nombre pair de −1, et pour satisfaire les colonnes, un nombre impair.
Dans ce jeu, on compte deux personnes : Alice et Bob. Alice se voit attribuer une ligne et Bob une colonne. Sans se parler, Alice remplit sa ligne selon la règle de la ligne et Bob remplit sa colonne selon la règle de la colonne. Ils gagnent s’ils inscrivent le même nombre dans la case où leur ligne et leur colonne se croisent.
Or, explique Google, toute stratégie convenue avant la partie revient à remplir une grille fixe (un tableau pré-rempli, en somme), qui échoue forcément sur au moins une des neuf combinaisons ligne-colonne et plafonne donc à 8 victoires sur 9 (88,9 %). Mais la donne change avec le quantique, selon la firme de Mountain View.
Avec deux paires de qubits intriqués, c’est-à-dire liés de sorte que leurs mesures restent corrélées, la théorie promet en revanche de gagner à tous les coups. Sur Willow, Google a joué chacune des neuf versions du jeu 100 000 fois. Il en a gagné 98,3 % en moyenne, soit environ une défaite sur 60, que l’équipe attribue au bruit de la puce.
Ce carré magique ne mobilise que quatre qubits, deux par joueur. Pour passer à plus grande échelle, Google s’appuie sur d’autres épreuves : un jeu à plusieurs joueurs (dit « jeu GHZ »), mené jusqu’à 71 qubits, et un problème mathématique de « fonction linéaire cachée », résolu jusqu’à 105 qubits.
L’avantage sur le classique y est moins net. Dans le jeu GHZ, la marge se réduit à mesure que le nombre de joueurs augmente. Pour la fonction linéaire cachée, la comparaison repose sur une limite classique que l’équipe présente elle-même comme une conjecture.
Un banc d’essai dont la limite ne bouge pas
L’équipe a ensuite chiffré cette contextualité avec un test dit de Bell-Kochen-Specker, qui résume un ensemble de corrélations en un seul score. Si les résultats étaient écrits d’avance, ce score ne pourrait pas dépasser 4, alors que la mécanique quantique autorise jusqu’à 6. Willow a obtenu 5,59, soit environ 7 % sous le maximum.
Le test de Bell-Kochen-Specker ne dépend pas de la manière dont on prépare les qubits : il évalue donc la machine elle-même.
Pourquoi un tel test ? Les tests habituels comparent les puces quantiques aux superordinateurs, et la barre monte à chaque progrès des machines classiques (la « suprématie quantique » revendiquée par Google en 2019 avait ainsi été rattrapée par des ordinateurs classiques quelques années plus tard).
Dans le cadre du test mené par Google, au contraire, le plafond (un score de 6, 100 % de victoires) est fixé par les lois de la physique. L’écart avec ce plafond donne donc une note qui ne bouge pas avec les progrès des ordinateurs classiques, ce qui facilite les comparaisons entre machines. Par ailleurs, selon Google, cette approche a un autre avantage : déceler certains types d’erreurs.
Ainsi, selon l’équipe de recherche, il a été possible de révéler des dérives subtiles qui décalent l’état d’un qubit et que les tests à circuits aléatoires (des suites d’opérations tirées au hasard, le banc d’essai habituel de Google) ont tendance à noyer dans la moyenne. Google propose d’utiliser ce type de test pour évaluer ses futures puces quantiques.
Google reconnaît lui-même que ces travaux n’ont pas encore d’application immédiate.
Quid, alors, de la Lune d’Einstein ? L’anecdote, rapportée par le physicien Abraham Pais en 1979, résume le pari du père de la relativité : une mesure ne ferait que lire une valeur déjà fixée, comme on découvre une carte posée face cachée.
Les expériences menées dans les années 1970 et 1980 par John Clauser puis Alain Aspect sur des paires de photons, récompensées par le prix Nobel de physique 2022, avaient déjà mis à mal cette idée.
Willow va dans le même sens, cette fois sur une puce de calcul : si les réponses de ses qubits avaient été écrites d’avance, la puce n’aurait jamais dépassé 88,9 % de victoires au carré magique, ni un score de 4 au test de Bell-Kochen-Specker. En somme, pour les qubits de Willow, la réponse à la question d’Einstein ne va pas dans son sens.

articles.title: Quantum computers are getting too powerful to check. Scientists have a solution
articles.text:
Quantum computers are getting too powerful to check. Scientists have a solution
- Date:
- November 16, 2026
- Source:
- University of Innsbruck
- Summary:
- Scientists have developed a new way to determine whether quantum simulations can be trusted, solving a growing problem as quantum computers become too powerful for conventional machines to check. Demonstrated on a 51-qubit system, the technique measures uncertainty and provides verifiable error margins that could help unlock the full potential of quantum computing.
- Share:
As quantum computers grow more powerful, researchers face a troubling question: How can they know whether the results are correct when conventional computers can no longer verify them? Scientists have now developed a promising new method that could help overcome this challenge by measuring the accuracy of quantum simulations and identifying how much uncertainty their predictions contain.
The technique uses experimental measurements to reconstruct how a quantum system behaves, then calculates how uncertainties in that reconstruction affect the results. Researchers successfully demonstrated the approach using a quantum simulator with up to 51 qubits in Innsbruck, Austria.
Quantum systems are expected to become capable of solving increasingly complex problems that traditional computers struggle with or cannot handle at all. However, this progress creates a verification problem. When a simulation is small enough, scientists can compare its results with calculations performed on a conventional computer. As quantum systems grow beyond those limits, that direct comparison becomes impractical, making alternative ways to assess their reliability essential.
A New Way to Measure Quantum Computing Accuracy
The breakthrough comes from an international research team led by Tristan Kraft at the Technical University of Munich and Peter Zoller at the University of Innsbruck and the Institute for Quantum Optics and Quantum Information of the Austrian Academy of Sciences, working alongside Barbara Kraus of the Technical University of Munich. The researchers developed a method for experimentally determining how a quantum simulator operates and translating uncertainties in its behavior into measurable limits on the accuracy of its results.
Quantum simulators are specialized physical systems designed to reproduce the behavior of other quantum systems. They are especially useful for investigating situations involving large numbers of interacting particles, where the calculations required can quickly overwhelm even powerful conventional computers.
But quantum experiments are never entirely free from errors. "But no real experiment is perfect," says Tristan Kraft. "Interactions may turn out differently than expected, the system is influenced by its environment, and measurements are also subject to uncertainties."
Rather than assuming a quantum simulator behaves exactly as intended, the new approach examines experimental data to determine what is actually happening inside the system. This allows researchers to identify important interactions and account for disturbances such as fluctuations and noise.
"From this data, we determine the relevant interactions as well as key influences from fluctuations and noise. We then calculate how the uncertainties in this model affect the simulation results," explains Tristan Kraft. "The quantum simulator thus provides not just a single value, but a result with error margins that quantify its accuracy."
Successfully Tested on a 51 Qubit Quantum Simulator
To evaluate the method, the researchers began with a relatively small quantum system containing ten trapped ions. Because conventional computers can still calculate the behavior of a system of this size, the team could test its reconstructed models and calculated error limits against independent measurements.
After this initial validation, the researchers expanded their experiments to a chain of 51 trapped ions. The larger demonstration, carried out by a team led by Manoj Joshi and Christian Roos using an ion trap quantum simulator, showed that the technique could also work with substantially more complex quantum systems.
This represents an important step toward establishing how trustworthy quantum simulation results are, particularly as quantum devices advance into territory where direct verification with traditional computing methods becomes increasingly difficult.
Extending the Breakthrough to More Complex Quantum Systems
The next challenge is to bring the technique to two-dimensional quantum simulators. These systems can model more complicated interactions among particles, making them valuable for exploring quantum physics. At the same time, their growing complexity makes their results particularly difficult to confirm using conventional calculations.
"This is particularly important because classical calculations for such systems become significantly more difficult as the number of particles increases," explains quantum computing pioneer Peter Zoller. "This also makes independent verification of the results increasingly complex, making the question of experimentally determined error limits all the more important."
The researchers are now adapting their method for the newest generation of two-dimensional quantum simulators, which offer improved precision and can investigate systems containing larger numbers of particles.
Looking further ahead, the approach could help scientists establish a more meaningful way to measure quantum advantage, the ability of quantum systems to outperform conventional computers. Instead of comparing machines based only on their processing speed or the size of the problems they can handle, researchers could also examine how accurately each system produces its answers.
"After all, when a classical computer and a quantum simulator tackle the same problem, it's not just a matter of which one delivers a result faster. What's also crucial is which one can solve the problem with a smaller, verifiable margin of error," says Peter Zoller.
This shift could change how progress in quantum computing is evaluated. Future breakthroughs may be judged not simply by how many particles a simulator can model or how quickly it performs calculations, but by its ability to solve increasingly difficult problems with demonstrably reliable results.
The findings were published in Physical Review X. The research received support from the Austrian Science Fund (FWF), the German Ministry of Research, Technology and Space, the European Union, BMW, and other funding organizations.

articles.title: En 2008, Steve Jobs sacó el primer MacBook Air de un sobre: Richard Yu, de Huawei, sube la apuesta metiendo dos ordenadores
articles.text:
El 15 de enero de 2008, Steve Jobs subió al escenario de la Macworld, abrió un sobre de oficina normal y corriente y sacó de él un MacBook Air. El truco dejó claro que podían construir un portátil lo bastante fino y ligero para que el usuario pudiera llevárselo cómodamente a cualquier lugar. Casi dos décadas después, Richard Yu, director ejecutivo de Huawei, quiso tomar prestado el chiste para presentar el MateBook Fold S.
Lo que ha cambiado todo. En 2008 el remate era un portátil fino. Ahora el remate son dos PC plegables, uno sacado del otro. El perfecto ejemplo de cómo la tecnología y las pantallas han evolucionado a lo largo de estas últimas dos décadas. Ahora los ordenadores, tablets y dispositivos móviles se presentan en múltiples formatos, con pantallas plegables, y con hardware sobrado para nuestras tareas del día a día.
Qué ha pasado. Yu publicó un teaser en redes el pasado 10 de noviembre en el que aparece metiendo en un sobre el MateBook Fold Ultimate Design de 18 pulgadas, dobla el sobre por la mitad y saca una máquina más pequeña, en este caso el nuevo MateBook Fold S. El modelo original de 18 pulgadas se pliega hasta ocupar el espacio de 13 pulgadas, mientras que el Fold S se despliega hasta las 14,7 pulgadas. Cerrado tiene aproximadamente el tamaño de un cuaderno.
Los detalles. El Fold S tiene una pantalla exterior en la tapa que Huawei llama “Live display”, situada junto a su sistema de triple cámara. Esto permite mostrar información de todo tipo como, por ejemplo, la hora mientras el PC está cerrado. Una vez abierto, el dispositivo se parece a las tabletas MatePad Pro de la compañía y funciona con un lápiz óptico, un teclado magnético o un teclado dividido en pantalla.
Viene en colores azul, blanco y negro y las reservas anticipadas en China se abrieron el pasado 14 de noviembre. Todavía no hay información sobre si llegaremos a ver este producto en España, así que tendremos que esperar para conocer más detalles al respecto.
Entre líneas. Huawei aún no ha confirmado precio ni muchas de sus especificaciones técnicas, como chip, batería o peso, aunque se espera un dispositivo de unos 600 gramos. Desde Huawei Central apuntan a HarmonyOS PC como sistema operativo en lugar de Windows o Linux. Sería un paso en la estrategia para adaptarse a las restricciones impuestas por EEUU, con chips Kirin propios y software independiente de firmas estadounidenses.
¿Y el precio? Como referencia, el MateBook Fold de 18 pulgadas se puso a la venta en China desde 24.999 yuanes (unos 3.410 euros al cambio). Incluso si el Fold S es más barato, es poco probable que sea una ganga. Tampoco lo fue el MacBook Air de primera generación con los 1.649 euros de la época.

articles.title: Cette alternative open source à Google Maps passe à la 3D avec plein de nouveautés
articles.text:
Organic Maps publie sa mise à jour de novembre 2026. L’application de navigation open source affiche le relief en 3D et les profondeurs des océans, importe des zones colorées et permet d’inverser un itinéraire en un geste.
L’application s’appuie sur les données d’OpenStreetMap et reçoit cette version sur iOS, Android et ordinateur. Elle change l’affichage de la carte, le calcul des trajets et, sur Android, la navigation en transports en commun.
Quoi de neuf en novembre ?
La carte gagne du relief. Elle affiche le terrain en 3D, donne l’altitude en n’importe quel point et trace des courbes de niveau reliant les points situés à la même hauteur. Notons aussi l’affichage des profondeurs pour les océans. Les données OpenStreetMap datent du 10 novembre et les articles Wikipedia du 1er novembre.
Organic Maps sait maintenant importer des polygones aux formats KML, KMZ et GeoJSON. Ces fichiers décrivent une zone par son contour, par exemple une région que l’on veut repérer sur la carte. L’application les affiche avec des contours colorés, des remplissages et des « trous », c’est-à-dire des parties exclues à l’intérieur de la zone. Les développeurs présentaient déjà l’import de traces GPX et KML (des parcours enregistrés par GPS) dans une mise à jour tournée vers la randonnée et le vélo. Les traces reçoivent des flèches de direction. Celles en cours d’enregistrement sont sauvegardées chaque minute, pour les récupérer en cas de plantage.
Pour les trajets, les réglages d’évitement (péages, routes non revêtues, ferries) sont séparés selon le moyen de déplacement (en voiture, à vélo ou à pied). Sur iOS et Android, un bouton inverse un itinéraire avec tous ses arrêts en un seul geste, et n’importe quel point peut être supprimé, départ et destination compris. Les itinéraires KML enregistrés gardent leurs étapes et leur mode de déplacement, et les exports GPX et GeoJSON reprennent les arrêts comme points de passage. Le calcul et le recalcul des itinéraires ont également été améliorés.
De son côté Android reçoit des nouveautés en plus. Notons par exemple un nouvel affichage de la vitesse et des limitations, y compris dans Android Auto. Les instructions de transports en commun passent en plein écran, avec les arrêts où monter, les correspondances, les sorties et les stops intermédiaires. Un widget d’écran d’accueil lance l’enregistrement d’une trace et indique le temps écoulé, la distance et l’altitude, désormais mesurée et enregistrée par rapport au niveau moyen de la mer.
- Respect de votre vie privée
- Cartes détaillées, même hors ligne
- Améliorations continues avec OpenStreetMap

articles.title: Facebook n’est pas « gratuit » si l’on paye avec nos données, estime l’avocate générale de la Cour de Justice Européenne — Frandroid
articles.text:
« C’est gratuit et ça le restera toujours ». Si vous faites partie des quelques milliards d’internautes qui utilisent Facebook chaque mois, vous avez probablement croisé ce fier slogan affiché en gros sur la page d’accueil du site jusqu’en 2019. Malheureusement pour Meta, l’avocate générale de la Cour de justice de l’Union européenne (CJUE) estime que cette affirmation est trompeuse et contraire au droit européen.
Dans un avis rendu ce 19 novembre 2026, Laila Medina a effectivement estimé que « un réseau social n’est pas gratuit lorsque vous payez avec vos données pour l’utiliser ». Une conclusion qui pourrait avoir d’importantes répercussions pour Facebook et pour le web plus largement.
Du 19 au 30 novembre, le Plaud Note Pro passe à 149 € au lieu de 189 € ! Il enregistre vos réunions, les transcrit et les synthétise pour vous, il suffit d’appuyer sur un bouton. Les Plaud Note, NotePin et NotePin S sont aussi à -20 %. Bref, c’est le moment d’arrêter de perdre du temps au travail !
Nos données ont une valeur économique
S’appuyant sur la directive concernant les pratiques commerciales déloyales, l’avocate générale estime que « la fourniture de données à caractère personnel à des fins commerciales peut constituer une forme de paiement, même lorsque le consommateur n’est pas tenu de verser une somme d’argent ». Facebook ne peut donc pas se vanter d’être « gratuit », puisque la cession de ces données et leur utilisation « ont une valeur économique pour l’exploitant d’un réseau social », détaille l’avis.
« Limiter le paiement à de l’argent porterait atteinte à la protection des consommateurs, en particulier dans l’économie numérique, où les utilisateurs peuvent ne pas avoir connaissance de la valeur économique de leurs données ou de l’étendue de l’exploitation de celles-ci à des fins publicitaires », ajoute l’avocate générale.
Et même si ces données sont traitées en accord avec le RGPD, « cela n’empêche pas l’application de la directive sur les pratiques commerciales déloyales » qui régit ce genre d’affirmations marketing. Seul un traitement des données destiné à « fournir le service ou remplir des obligations légales » peut échapper à cette règle.
La fin de la « gratuité » sur le web européen ?
Ces conclusions n’empêchent pas une plateforme numérique de fournir un service sans contrepartie monétaire brute, mais simplement de qualifier ce service comme « gratuit » et d’en faire un argument commercial. « Les entreprises demeurent libres de proposer des services en échange de données à caractère personnel, mais ne peuvent pas les décrire comme étant “gratuits” lorsqu’une telle contrepartie est exigée », argue Laila Medina. « Le fait que les utilisateurs conservent leurs données n’empêche pas que l’utilisation de celles-ci à des fins commerciales constitue un paiement », continue l’avocate.
    Pour aller plus loin
Instagram et Facebook : pourquoi l’UFC-Que Choisir s’attaque à l’abonnement anti-pub
            
Les conclusions de l’avocate générale ne lient pas obligatoirement la CJUE et l’institution pourrait rendre un autre avis à une date ultérieure, mais généralement les deux décisions sont alignées. La « gratuité » du web en Europe pourrait donc prendre un sacré coup si la justice européenne venait à faire appliquer cette interprétation des règles.

articles.title: Open-Source-KI verliert ihren mächtigsten Fürsprecher – und das hat Gründe
articles.text:
Nvidia: Warum gerade die Open-Source-Szene Jensen Huangs Rücktritt bedauert
Inzwischen scheint klar, dass der Verwaltungsrat von Nvidia eine Rückkehr von Jensen Huang an die Konzernspitze ausschließt. Dies bestätigte die Interimschefin Colette Kress dem Sender CNBC. Die Petition, die in den vergangenen Tagen in den sozialen Medien die Runde machte, und mehr als 115.000 Unterzeichner:innen einsammeln konnte, konnte an diesem Schritt somit nicht rütteln.
Dennoch lohnt ein genauerer Blick auf diese Liste, denn ein bedeutender Teil von Huangs Unterstützer:innen stammt aus einem bestimmten Bereich der Tech-Welt. Die Personen, darunter Führungskräfte von Hugging Face, einer Plattform zum Austausch von Sprachmodellen, die mittlerweile Nvidia gehört, sowie der Risikokapitalfirmen Andreessen Horowitz und Sequoia Capital sind Verfechter einer bestimmten Art von KI.
Jensen Huang galt als eine Art Anführer der Open-Source-Bewegung
Der Personenkreis interessiert sich für die Weiterentwicklung quelloffener Modelle, also solcher, die im Gegensatz zu ChatGPT oder Claude von Nutzer:innen heruntergeladen und unabhängig von großen Tech-Unternehmen ausgeführt werden können. Befürworter:innen solcher KI-Systeme argumentieren, dass eine Konzentration von KI in den Händen einiger weniger mächtiger Unternehmen für alle anderen Nachteile mit sich bringt. Das klingt erst einmal nach grundsätzlicher KI‑Kritik. Doch viele Open-Source-Befürworter:innen sind gleichzeitig Risikokapitalgeber, die davon profitieren, wenn Startups auf kostengünstigere KI zurückgreifen können, ohne „Big Tech“ bezahlen zu müssen, also etwa OpenAI oder Anthropic.
Huang war zuletzt zu einer Art Anführer derjenigen geworden, die gegenüber politischen Entscheidungsträger:innen in den USA Open Source verteidigten. Dabei sollte Bedenken entgegengewirkt werden, dass solche Modelle keine Sicherheitsvorkehrungen bieten und sie dazu führen könnten, die Führungsposition im KI-Bereich an China abzutreten, wo die leistungsstärksten und beliebtesten Open-Source-Modelle entwickelt werden. Diese Gruppe will nun, dass Huang mit seiner einflussreichen Stimme wieder Gehör findet.
Doch es sind nicht nur Huangs außereheliche Affären, die seine (und Nvidias) Glaubwürdigkeit als Verfechter von Open-Source-KI gefährden. Neue Untersuchungen zu chinesischen Startups, die Nvidias Chips nutzen, sowie eine am 16.11.26 angekündigte neue Regelung des US-Handelsministeriums könnten sowohl dem Ruf der Bewegung als auch ihrem weiteren Voranschreiten einen Schlag versetzen.
Mehr fortschrittliche Chips in China
Als Huang in der vergangenen Woche zurücktrat, veröffentlichte der ehemalige OpenAI-Forscher Will DePue online Erkenntnisse, die darauf hindeuten, dass Chinas KI-Unternehmen weitaus mehr Zugang zu Nvidias fortschrittlichen Blackwell-Chips hatten als bisher angenommen. China ist der Zugang zu Nvidias modernsten Chips eigentlich untersagt, um Amerikas Vorsprung im Bereich der KI zu sichern.
Es ist unklar, wie die chinesischen Firmen Zugang zu den Chips erlangt haben könnten. DePue behauptet, die Ergebnisse seien von leitenden Forschern bei OpenAI und Anthropic verifiziert worden, doch eine unabhängige Analyse hat die Ergebnisse bislang nicht bestätigt. (DePue reagierte nicht auf eine Anfrage für ein Interview der US-Ausgabe von MIT Technology Review. Nvidia meldete sich ebenfalls nicht mit einer Stellungnahme zurück.) Die neuen Erkenntnisse belegen zwar nicht, dass Nvidia chinesischen Unternehmen dabei half, an die Chips zu gelangen. Allerdings zeigen sie, wie umfassend der Chipschmuggel war – und Nvidia offenbar zu wenig dagegen tat.

articles.text:
Good morning. ☀️️
By now, you’ve heard us mention TC Mzansi. Once or twice. Fine, a few times.
But Southern Africa’s tech ecosystem keeps giving us reasons to talk. Telecom giants are eyeing rivals, satellite companies are fighting for a foothold, and billion-rand deals are keeping things interesting.
Starting Monday, November 23, we’ll follow the money, the big moves, and the people shaping technology across the region. Join the waitlist—your Mondays are about to get more interesting.
TC Mzansi, our newsletter covering South African tech is coming on November 23.
companies
Kuda cuts 40 jobs as it chases group profitability by 2027
What do you do when you want to make more money but running your business keeps getting expensive? For Kuda, the Nigerian digital bank, the answer involves a smaller workforce.
What happened? Kuda is cutting about 40 jobs, representing 7.5% of its roughly 500 employees across Nigeria, the UK, South Africa, Canada, Tanzania, Uganda and Ghana. CEO Babs Ogundeyi says the latest redundancies will help the company reach group profitability and meet the capital requirements attached to its Nigerian banking licence.
Explain like I’m new here: This is Kuda’s second major restructuring exercise in 2026. In March, the company laid off hundreds of employees across several teams following a company-wide review. At the time, Kuda said the cuts were not driven by its financial performance but were part of an effort to focus on its core products and customers. Ogundeyi noted that Kuda’s Nigerian operation is already profitable; the challenge is achieving group profitability by 2027.
Is the profitability plan working? There are signs of progress. Kuda’s group losses narrowed to $5.83 million in 2024, from $35.11 million in 2023. Staff costs also dropped 46% to $6.31 million. However, revenue fell 15% to $18.34 million, partly because of naira depreciation.
In January, the Central Bank of Nigeria upgraded Kuda’s microfinance bank to a national licence, which requires at least ₦5 billion ($3.7 million) in paid-up capital. The bank must keep that money available to meet regulatory requirements, limiting how freely it can deploy it elsewhere.
Upgrade your business today
Pay with OPay is live on Fincra. Customers approve payments straight from their OPay wallet, and you get confirmation back on your site. Available now for NGN collections! Upgrade your business today with Fincra pay with OPay.
companies
terra Industries invests in South African safety startup
Terra Industries, the Nigerian defence-tech startup, has invested in South African public safety startup Community Wolf, leading its seed round. The deal marks Terra’s entry into the public safety market and extends its security technology into a new sector.
Explain like I’m new here: Since Terra captured the continent’s attention with its large funding rounds, it has been expanding quickly. In August, it closed Africa’s largest seed round and is building a 34,000-square-foot drone factory in Accra, Ghana, to complement its existing 15,000-square-foot facility in Abuja.
In September, Terra led a $1 million investment in Nigerian startup Aeon, which builds tools to protect networks, cloud systems, and other digital infrastructure. The companies formed a joint venture to pursue government and corporate contracts.
What does Terra get out of this? Terra’s existing business focuses on protecting assets such as mines, pipelines, and power plants, but these facilities do not exist in isolation. They sit within or near communities, and nearby residents may notice suspicious activity before a drone does.
Community Wolf gives Terra access to an existing network of residents and security operators who can feed information into its security operations. The companies will explore connecting Community Wolf to Terra’s command centres, allowing verified community reports to appear alongside information collected by drones and sensors.
crypto
Nigeria’s taxman gives crypto companies a compliance deadline
Nigeria is tightening oversight of cryptocurrency businesses, and the tax authority has given them less than two weeks to comply with its latest requirements.
The Nigerian Revenue Service (NRS), the country’s taxman, has directed cryptocurrency exchanges and other virtual asset service providers to register on its new tax portal by November 30. Companies must also connect their systems to the platform by December 31. Missing either deadline could attract penalties.
Explain like I’m new here: Nigeria has spent the past few years trying to bring cryptocurrency trading under clearer regulations. New tax laws passed in 2025 introduced reporting obligations for virtual asset businesses, while guidelines released in August 2026 set out how certain crypto transactions should be taxed.
The latest directive gives the NRS a system for putting those requirements into practice.
How it works: Companies must first submit their business details, Tax Identification Numbers (TINs), and information about their crypto activities. They will then connect their systems to the portal to support transaction reporting, tax assessments, and the payment of applicable taxes.
The rules cover Nigerian and foreign crypto exchanges serving residents, peer-to-peer (P2P) platforms, brokers, and custodial wallet providers. Individual crypto users are not required to register.
There’s an important distinction: Registration with the NRS is not permission to operate a crypto business. Companies must still obtain the necessary approvals from regulators such as the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) and the Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN).
Zoom out: The NRS’s latest move is to give the government a more direct way to monitor transactions and enforce existing obligations, including those involving companies based outside Nigeria.
Crypto firms have spent years building businesses around digital assets. Nigeria is now building the infrastructure to tax those businesses and hold them accountable.

articles.title: .NET 11 : ASP.NET Core: Union Type Support, OpenAPI 3.2 by Default and Blazor AI Components
articles.text:
Last week, Microsoft shipped ASP.NET Core in .NET 11 as part of the wider .NET 11 release. The update spans Minimal APIs, OpenAPI, SignalR, Blazor, authentication, and the Kestrel server. As stated in the announcement, .NET 11 is a Standard Term Support release with two years of support.
On the API side, developers can now use C# 15 union types in JSON request and response bodies across Minimal APIs and MVC. The release notes limit the feature to JSON bodies, so route, query, header, and form values cannot bind to a union.
Minimal API validation also runs asynchronous validators, which keeps threads free while a rule waits on a database lookup or a remote call. The framework can now localize validation messages and display names itself, and endpoints can skip the remaining middleware pipeline through a new [ShortCircuit] attribute.
Developers who generate OpenAPI documents now get version 3.2 unless they select an earlier one for tooling that has not caught up. As described in the release notes, the framework depends on Microsoft.OpenApi 3.3.1 for this, and the notes label that update a breaking change.
With 3.2, endpoints that stream server-sent events are documented with a schema for each event's payload, and the generator emits an anyOf schema for unions. Generated documents can also describe endpoints that use the HTTP QUERY method, and APIs that carry the [Obsolete] attribute show up as deprecated.
SignalR adds authentication refresh, so a long-lived connection no longer has to close when its access token expires. As reported, server developers enable it per hub, while the .NET client refreshes automatically by default and the TypeScript client can do the same. Blazor passes the refreshed identity on to Interactive Server components while the circuit stays connected.
Blazor receives the longest list of changes, and many of them target static server-side rendering. With the new CacheView component, developers can cache the rendered markup of a component subtree, and the child components do not run when a cached copy is served. Blazor now ships client-side validation for static SSR forms, enabled by default.
Developers can also carry data between requests with TempData or session values. According to the release notes, the Blazor Web App template drops its app.UseAntiforgery() call, because a middleware for CSRF protection is now added by default.
For Interactive Server apps, an opt-in package pauses the circuit of a hidden browser tab after a delay, two minutes by default, to free server memory. Lists built with Virtualize may now mix items of different heights, and Microsoft raised the default OverscanCount from 3 to 15. Page and sort state in QuickGrid now lives in the URL query string, with sortable headers and pager controls rendered as links instead of buttons.
The release notes flag this as a CSS breaking change, because custom styles written for the buttons also have to target the links. The release also includes Microsoft.AspNetCore.Components.AI, a set of components for chat and agent interfaces. According to the announcement, Microsoft treats that package as experimental and will keep it in prerelease throughout .NET 11.
On the security and server side, an experimental package adds Device Bound Session Credentials, a protocol that ties session refresh to a private key held by the browser. Response compression and request decompression gain Zstandard support, which is on by default.
Kestrel's HTTP/1.1 parser no longer throws exceptions on malformed requests, a change that is reported to raise throughput by up to 20 to 40 percent under heavy invalid traffic. The shared framework libraries of ASP.NET Core are now compiled with runtime-async, described in the release notes as an internal change with no public API impact.
Two older APIs are on the way out. The Microsoft.AspNetCore.Grpc.Swagger package is now deprecated, and Kestrel's TlsClientHelloBytesCallback option is obsolete in favor of the new UseTlsClientHelloListener extension.
Other changes in this release are native OpenTelemetry tracing attributes, client-side cancellation of SignalR hub invocations, scrolling to a specific item in Virtualize and QuickGrid, passkey display names inferred from the authenticator, and TimeProvider support in ASP.NET Core Identity.
For interested readers and developers, the full release notes are available in the What's new in ASP.NET Core in .NET 11 article on Microsoft Learn.

articles.title: Groundcover Investigations lets engineers steer AI SRE agents
articles.text:
Groundcover Investigations lets engineers steer AI SRE agents
Groundcover, the eBPF-based observability startup, has introduced Investigations, giving agents and engineers one place to collaborate on incident response in real time.
In the shared workspace, groundcover’s investigator and moderator agents work with on-call engineers and their preferred coding agents to investigate production incidents together, analyzing behavior across applications and infrastructure to create a shared record of evidence.
Rather than handing full control to agents, the idea is to help engineers and agents work together on incident investigations.
“Most AI SRE tools ask engineers to step back and let the agent take over. We built Investigations for engineers to step in.”
Shahar Azulay, CEO and co-founder at groundcover, tells The New Stack that “Most AI SRE tools ask engineers to step back and let the agent take over. We built Investigations for engineers to step in.”
Everyone has their favorite agent. That’s a problem
AI agents are flooding daily software engineering workflows. Already, Salesforce reports that organizations use an average of 12 agents — a number that’s expected to grow by 67% within two years. But half of those agents are working in silos.
This presents a particular problem in incident response. Individual agents, like Claude Code or Codex, may be able to troubleshoot on their own, but how can engineers aggregate their findings? They don’t — or at least, it’s very tricky. More often than not, Azulay says agents’ varying conclusions are spread across chats and tickets.
As he describes it: “Every engineer now has an agent, but each of those agents investigates on its own and findings end up in a chat window.”
How groundcover wants engineers and agents to work together
With its Investigations, groundcover aims to eliminate fragmented incident response and create a single source of truth for every engineer and agent. Here, agents can lead collaborative, evidence-driven investigations, testing hypotheses against production data, validating findings, and backing every conclusion with evidence. Engineers, for their part, get real-time visibility into the investigation and can step in to steer it as they see fit.
It all starts when a monitor issue fires and an engineer opens an investigation from groundcover or Slack. groundcover says automatically opening an investigation when a monitor fires is coming next.
The investigator agent builds a graph with a question (e.g., Why is checkout latency spiking in the US?) and then opens several hypotheses to explain it. From there, it turns to production telemetry to query the traces, logs, metrics, and Kubernetes events the groundcover eBPF sensor is already collecting, testing each one and recording what it finds as evidence.
Importantly, Azulay tells The New Stack, “the investigator can’t mark its own work as correct. When it thinks a hypothesis is supported, it submits a proposal that cites specific findings, and a separate agent, the moderator, acts as an LLM-as-a-judge and checks whether that evidence backs up the claim. No findings, no closure.”
“Separating the agent that does the work from the agent that judges it gives you a conclusion you can trust without redoing every step.”
Given the speed at which agents reach conclusions — and the risk that they act beyond scope — Azulay says this separation of hypothesis and conclusion is crucial to arriving at a trustworthy conclusion: “Separating the agent that does the work from the agent that judges it gives you a conclusion you can trust without redoing every step.”
According to groundcover, the investigator agent also learns from each investigation so it can understand which hypotheses tend to hold up and where to look first when similar problems arise.
External coding agents are invited to the party, too
While groundcover’s investigator and moderator agents lead investigations, the startup recognizes that most engineers already bring a slew of third-party agents to the table, whether for business intelligence, coding, product roadmapping, etc. Those agents are welcome in Investigations, too.
Using groundcover’s MCP server, engineers can connect Claude Code, Codex, and other agents to the shared workspace to read and add to the same investigation. That builds on groundcover’s October launch, which let outside coding agents query its telemetry over MCP and hand off investigations to groundcover’s own agent.
For Azulay, this lets each agent shine in what it does best. As he tells The New Stack:
“Coding agents and groundcover’s agents are good at different things. Our agents know your telemetry and how to query it fast. Your coding agents know your code. Neither has the full picture.”
Working together, then, via Investigations, the different agents can lean on each other depending on the task at hand. If a hypothesis points to a code problem, for example, the investigator agent may bring in Claude Code or Codex to check it. When engineers’ coding agent needs telemetry, groundcover’s agent fetches the data.
“Our agents know your telemetry and how to query it fast. Your coding agents know your code. Neither has the full picture.”
What matters is that every agent publishes its findings in the same investigation tree, preventing engineers from going on a wild goose chase trying to connect the dots across five different private chat sessions.
“Everyone can see what’s been checked, what’s still open, and why anyone believes what they believe,” says Azulay. “Every contribution is attributed, so you know a finding came from a specific engineer’s Claude session at a specific time.”
Does this mean agents and engineers are on even footing?
Not quite. Per Omer Mayer, senior product manager, groundcover, engineers can “watch each hypothesis get supported or ruled out in real time” — and they can “step in and steer it” at any time.
In other words, engineers can immediately see what groundcover agents are investigating. If they think the agents are off the mark, they can easily take over.
Azulay offers The New Stack an example: Suppose a checkout latency monitor fires, and an automated investigation kicks off, generating three hypotheses, one of which is a slow query from a recent deploy.
But the on-call engineer knows something the investigator agent doesn’t: The deploy was rolled back 10 minutes earlier and latency didn’t recover. Easy — they can stop that hypothesis, which closes everything under it and tells the agent to stop spending time and tokens there.
“The engineer might also add context the agents don’t have, like ‘the payments team changed their retry policy this morning,’” adds Azulay. “That opens a new line of inquiry nobody would have found in the telemetry alone.”
What’s also important is engineers’ right to override where agents can’t. Remember, the investigator agent is forbidden from closing anything without the moderator agent’s okay. But engineers don’t need the moderator’s permission to steer the investigation, Azulay says.
“The moderator is there to keep the agents honest, not to slow down the people responsible for the incident,” says Azulay.
More agents are teaming up
Earlier this year, more vendors made moves to bring individual agents out of isolated workflows and into a shared space.
On the coding side, Cognition, Microsoft, and Augment Code all launched team-layer coding agent platforms, pushing coding agents past the single-developer loop.
Last month, Harness acquired select Augment Code assets, including Cosmos, to link AI coding agents to its delivery platform. This way, teams writing code in Cosmos will have context from across the software development lifecycle available to the agent as it works.
Now, groundcover’s Investigations brings a similar shared-space principle to incident response. More work is happening elsewhere, too. Slack Code has given coding agents their own temporary channels for plans, diffs, and live previews, which Katie Steigman, vice president of product at Slack, told The New Stack is already being used for incident response.
Other companies are also building tools for collaborative incident investigations, including shared workspaces for engineers and agents and handoffs to coding agents over MCP.
So far, conversations have focused on agents’ individual prowess and what they can do. But as agents move deeper into software engineering workflows, agent-engineer teamwork looks like what will make incident response work best.

articles.title: Guía de GTA 6: cómo conseguir más vehículos y ampliar los espacios disponibles
articles.text:
En GTA 6, encontrar un auto y hacerlo tuyo son cosas distintas. Puedes robar vehículos para desplazarte, pero para incorporarlos a tu colección personal tendrás que registrarlos. Ese proceso se desbloquea al avanzar en la historia y tiene un límite de espacios que podrás ampliar con garajes o mediante ciertas misiones.
Una guía indica que durante el primer capítulo no podrás cambiar el vehículo personal de Jason, aunque sí podrás conducir autos robados. Para desbloquear el registro, tendrás que avanzar hasta el capítulo 2 y completar la misión “Moses (Take A Vehicle to Moses)”. Allí conocerás a Moses y accederás a su taller en Port Gellhorn, donde podrás revisar tus espacios, reparar vehículos y registrarlos.
Cómo registrar un auto y sumarlo a tu colección
Antes de llevar un vehículo al taller de Moses, tendrás que revisar si cumple los requisitos para ser registrado. Según la guía, al principio solo podrás registrar autos sin rastreador. Para comprobarlo, usarás la aplicación Waink del teléfono del personaje. Que un auto sea caro o llamativo no significa que puedas incorporarlo de inmediato a tu colección.
Si el vehículo es apto, condúcelo hasta el taller y revisa cuántos espacios tienes disponibles en la pantalla de registro. Si queda lugar, podrás completar el proceso. Si tu colección ya está llena, tendrás que liberar un espacio vendiendo un auto o aumentar tu capacidad antes de registrar otro.
Guardar un vehículo en un garaje también puede servir para conservarlo mientras esperas desbloquear su registro. Pero estacionarlo no lo convierte en un vehículo personal: para que aparezca entre los autos que puedes solicitar, tendrás que completar el registro.
Al comienzo del capítulo 3 se ampliarán las opciones. La guía señala que podrás vender autos robados en cualquier Pay ’n’ Spray y registrar vehículos que tengan rastreadores estándar. Esto facilitará el proceso, aunque no eliminará el límite de espacios: aun con más opciones de registro, necesitarás tener capacidad disponible.
Garajes para ampliar el espacio
Una forma de conservar más vehículos registrados será comprar garajes adicionales. Más adelante en el capítulo 2 recibirás la aplicación Vice City Real Estate, con la que podrás adquirir propiedades en distintas zonas de Leonida. Los garajes sumarán espacios para guardar vehículos y ampliar tu colección.
El precio dependerá de la propiedad, así que convendrá revisar cuánto cuesta antes de comprarla. Si necesitas espacio pronto y tienes dinero suficiente, podrás adquirir un garaje. Si puedes esperar, también tendrás una opción ligada a la historia: hacia la mitad del juego, Valentina te dará acceso a un garaje en Ocean Beach que añadirá dos espacios para vehículos personales.
Si no tienes lugar para un nuevo auto, vender uno de los que ya registraste liberará un espacio. Así podrás reemplazarlo sin comprar una propiedad. La decisión dependerá de si prefieres conservar los vehículos que ya tienes o ampliar la capacidad total.
Cómo encontrar los autos que ya tienes
Una vez que registres varios vehículos, podrás consultar cuáles están disponibles desde la aplicación Scooter Bros en el teléfono. Allí revisarás tu lista de vehículos personales y podrás elegir uno para que se lo lleven al personaje. También podrás visitar el taller de Moses o un Pay ’n’ Spray para ver los vehículos guardados.
En resumen, el proceso tendrá tres pasos: avanzar en la historia para desbloquear el registro, comprobar que el auto pueda registrarse y asegurarte de tener espacio. Los garajes comprados y el desbloqueo de Valentina permitirán ampliar el límite; vender un vehículo, en cambio, solo liberará un espacio ocupado. Así podrás decidir cuándo guardar un auto, cuándo sumarlo a tu colección y cuándo buscar más capacidad.

articles.title: Protect agent tool calls with Skyflow and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway | Amazon Web Services
articles.text:
Artificial Intelligence
Protect agent tool calls with Skyflow and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway
In this post, we show how Skyflow and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway keep sensitive data out of the tools your AI agents call, and out of the model context those tools feed. We add Skyflow Detect to Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway as a request and response interceptor. The Skyflow interceptor de-identifies data before it reaches a tool, restores it before the agent reads the result, and replaces documents with clean copies before the agent opens them. Your agents and tools don’t change.
Skyflow is available in AWS Marketplace, and the interceptor is open source on GitHub.
Agents act through tools, and tools move data
Agents have moved from answering questions to taking action, and they take action through tools: Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers, SaaS APIs, document stores, and web search. Every agent tool call is a data flow. Most enterprise controls cover what goes into and comes out of the model. Far fewer cover what an agent sends to its tools or what those tools send back.
That gap shows up in three ways:
- Sensitive data leaves through tool arguments. The model writes the arguments from everything in its context, including details the tool doesn’t need. Ask an agent about a customer, and the customer’s name, account number, or email goes straight into a query to a third-party server. That server sits outside your AWS account and your compliance scope.
- Sensitive data comes back in tool results. Scraped web pages, CRM records, and case notes land in the model’s context, memory, traces, and logs. This happens even when the task never needed them.
- Documents bypass text inspection. Document tools such as Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3), Box, and Google Drive return a signed URL, not text. A filter that inspects strings sees a link and lets it through, and the agent then opens the original file.
Patching each agent doesn’t scale across teams and frameworks, and it can’t reach third-party tools. The controls need to sit where every tool call passes, so authorization, content safety, and data protection apply the same way to every agent and tool.
AgentCore Gateway is that place. It fronts every tool an agent uses, whatever framework or model the agent runs on. It does more than route that traffic. With AgentCore Gateway interceptors, you can run your own code, as an AWS Lambda function, on every call that passes through it. A request interceptor sees each call before it reaches a tool, and a response interceptor sees each result before it reaches the agent. Either one can inspect the payload, rewrite it, or block the call. That makes the gateway a natural place to add data protection alongside Policy and Guardrails. This single control, attached once, covers every agent and every tool behind the gateway, without any change to agent or tool code.
Example: A dispute-resolution agent at a large European bank
Consider a large European bank with retail and corporate banking operations and strict data-residency obligations. Its operations teams are adopting agents to investigate card disputes.
An analyst asks the agent to look into a disputed transaction. The agent searches the web for the merchant, then pulls the dispute case note from Amazon S3 to summarize it. Without protection, three things happen:
- The model builds the search query from everything in context. The search provider receives ‘Mateo Jackson dispute AnyCompany Electronics London’. That’s the customer’s name, sent to a third party, for a search that only needed the merchant.
- Scraped merchant pages bring unrelated personal data into the model’s context.
- The agent reads the original case note, with the customer’s full name, email, phone number, and card details.
With the Skyflow interceptor on the gateway, the same workflow plays out differently:
- The search provider receives ‘[NAME_AJbrIud] dispute AnyCompany Electronics London’, where [NAME_AJbrIud] is a reversible vault token. The merchant results come back the same, the provider never learns who the customer is, and the analyst still sees the real name in the agent’s answer.
- Web content reaches the model already de-identified.
- The agent only ever receives a link to a de-identified copy of the case note.
Solution overview
The Skyflow interceptor is a single AWS Lambda function attached to both of the AgentCore Gateway interception points:
- REQUEST runs before the gateway calls a tool.
- RESPONSE runs after the tool answers and before the agent sees the result.
At each point, it calls Skyflow Detect to find sensitive entities such as names, email addresses, phone numbers, government IDs, card numbers, dates of birth, and locations. It replaces them with tokens, or restores the originals. Skyflow Vault stores the original values so authorized systems can reverse the tokens.
The Skyflow gateway configuration decides, for each tool, which of three protection modes applies: Shield the tool, Shield the model, and Shield the document.
| Mode | What happens | Who sees real data | How it works | Typical use | 
| Shield the tool | Sensitive values are stripped from arguments on the way out and restored in results on the way back | The agent and user, not the tool | Uses reversible vault tokens, so values the tool echoes back are restored before the agent reads them | Web search, enrichment, and third-party APIs that don’t need customer identity to do their job | 
| Shield the model | Prompts, history, files and tool results are de-identified before the model reads them. The answer is re-identified on the way back | Agent and user, not the model | Model calls go through the gateway’s inference endpoint. On the way back, only the tokens minted for that call are restored | Customer conversations, scraped web content, cross-Region or third-party models | 
| Shield the document | The file’s signed URL is swapped for one pointing to a de-identified copy | No one on the agent side | Skyflow Detect v2 (preview) fetches the file, cleans it and stores the copy in an approved Region. The file never passes through Lambda, so payload limits don’t cap file size | Case notes, statements, contracts in Amazon S3, Box, Google Drive | 
Four properties matter in production:
- No change to agents or tools. Agents discover the gateway and sign requests with their AWS Identity and Access Management (AWS IAM) role as before. To shield the model, the agent points its model client at the gateway’s inference endpoint. The interceptor is otherwise invisible to them.
- Configuration without redeploys. The policy sets the direction, entity types, and token type (reversible vault tokens or one-way tokens) per server and per tool. It lives in AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store, and changes take effect without redeploying.
- Fail closed. If de-identification can’t complete, the call is withheld rather than sent in the clear. The interceptor fetches files only from allowlisted locations, and it blocks traffic it can’t inspect rather than passing it silently.
- Operations built on AWS. The Skyflow API key lives in AWS Secrets Manager. Every decision is logged to Amazon CloudWatch, with metrics for alarms, and the interceptor never logs credentials or original values.
Architecture
The reference architecture shows where each component sits. The three walkthroughs after it follow a single tool call through the Shield the tool and Shield the document modes.
The following diagram shows how the interceptor sits between AgentCore Gateway and your tools.
The flow:
- The agent calls a tool through AgentCore Gateway, signed with its IAM role.
- The REQUEST interceptor matches the tool against the policy and, where required, de-identifies the arguments with Skyflow Detect.
- The gateway calls the tool, which receives tokens instead of sensitive values.
- The RESPONSE interceptor re-identifies the result, de-identifies it, or swaps a document URL, as the policy requires.
- The agent receives the result.
The agent runs on AgentCore runtime, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. Alongside that flow, the interceptor reads its policy from Parameter Store and its Skyflow API key from Secrets Manager, and it logs each decision to Amazon CloudWatch. It calls Skyflow Detect and Skyflow Vault in an approved Region to de-identify and re-identify data. The targets sit outside the gateway: a third-party web search MCP server, a case-note store in Amazon S3, and a model in Amazon Bedrock that the gateway reaches through an inference target. For model calls, the interceptor keeps a short-lived record in Amazon DynamoDB of which tokens each call minted, so it restores only those. The record holds no original values. For documents, Skyflow Detect fetches the file directly through a presigned URL, so the file bytes never pass through Lambda.
Walkthrough: Shield the tool
This is the web search from the dispute example, step by step. The customer’s name leaves as a token and comes back as the real value, so the search provider never sees it and the analyst still does.
Walkthrough: Shield the model
This is the analyst asking the agent to draft a reply to the customer. The customer’s name and email address reach the model as tokens, and the draft comes back with the real values in place.
Walkthrough: Shield the document
This is the case-note request. The interceptor never handles the file itself. It checks the presigned URL and hands it to Skyflow Detect, which returns a link to a clean copy.
Here is the case note as stored in Amazon S3, beside the copy the agent receives:
A token like [NAME_AJbrIud] is a vault token, which an authorized user can reverse through Skyflow. A token like [NAME_1] is a one-way counter that nothing can reverse.
The following video shows Shield the document end to end. The agent asks for the dispute case note and receives a link to a de-identified copy instead of the original.
Video 1: Shield the document in action. Without Skyflow, the agent reads the original case note. With Skyflow on the gateway, it reads a de-identified copy.
How it fits with the rest of AgentCore
The interceptor complements the controls AgentCore and Amazon Bedrock already provide:
- Policy in Amazon Bedrock AgentCore authorizes what agents can do, using Cedar and Dogwood. It goes beyond deciding whether a principal can call a tool. It can base decisions on earlier actions in the agent’s trajectory, control access to agents and models, stop specific arguments from being sent to specific tools, and check the data passing through the gateway using Amazon Bedrock Guardrails. Skyflow works alongside Policy. When Policy allows a call, Skyflow swaps the sensitive values in it for reversible tokens, so the call goes through without exposing real data to the tool or model. Policy decides what an agent may do, and Skyflow controls how sensitive data is handled when it does.
- Amazon Bedrock Guardrails handle content safety and sensitive information redaction for model interactions. Skyflow adds vault-backed tokenization and document de-identification to the same gateway. Use them together for layered protection across every model and tool call.
- AgentCore Identity, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, and AWS IAM stay as they are. The interceptor adds no credentials for agents to manage.
- AgentCore Observability, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, and Amazon CloudWatch record interceptor decisions alongside gateway traces.
Deploying the solution
The Skyflow interceptor is open source in the agentcore-skyflow repository on GitHub under the MIT license. Skyflow is available in AWS Marketplace. To add the interceptor to a gateway you already run:
- Subscribe to Skyflow in AWS Marketplace, create a vault, and store its API key in AWS Secrets Manager.
- Deploy the interceptor stack from the repository with the AWS Cloud Development Kit (AWS CDK). It creates the Lambda function, its policy parameter, a DynamoDB table for model-call records, and the Amazon CloudWatch metrics and alarms.
- Attach the interceptor to your gateway at both interception points. A script in the repository does this and grants the gateway role permission to invoke only that function. If you manage the gateway with AWS CloudFormation or the AWS CDK, declare the interceptor there instead, so later stack updates keep it.
- To shield the model, add an inference target to the gateway and point the agent’s model client at the gateway’s inference endpoint.
The repository also contains the complete reference deployment from this post, including the agent, the gateway, and its targets, which you can deploy with the AgentCore CLI, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore.
There are five ways in:
- Existing gateways. Attach the interceptor to a gateway you already run. Agents and tools stay as they are.
- New agents. Put tools behind AgentCore Gateway from day one.
- MCP servers outside AWS. Front them as gateway MCP server targets so their traffic passes through the interceptor.
- Document stores. Tools that return signed URLs are covered by adding their location to the policy’s allowlist.
- Model calls. Add an inference target and send the agent’s model calls through the gateway.
Skyflow offers several vault deployment models and Region choices to meet residency requirements. See Skyflow deployment models.
Considerations
- Formats. Text and Office formats (TXT, JSON, CSV, XML, JSONL, DOCX, XLSX, and PPTX) keep reversible vault tokens. PDFs and images are fully de-identified but receive one-way tokens, so the original values can’t be restored from those files.
- Availability. String de-identification and re-identification are generally available. Document de-identification through signed URLs uses Skyflow Detect v2, which is in preview. AgentCore Gateway availability varies by AWS Region. Before you deploy, check Supported AWS Regions in the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore documentation.
- Document size and latency. Document de-identification is bounded by design. The interceptor checks file size before submitting, so a file above your configured limit is refused immediately rather than timing out. Files within the limit complete within the connection window AgentCore Gateway allows. De-identification time scales with document size, so set the size limit to match your documents. Skyflow Detect v2 is in preview. Validate latency against your own workloads and Region during a pilot, before you widen the rollout.
Conclusion
Agents are only as trustworthy as the data they move. With AgentCore Gateway and the Skyflow interceptor, you can enforce a privacy control at the one place every tool call passes through. It works in both directions, covers documents and text, and needs no change to agent code.
Where to start
- Pick one agent workflow that touches customer data and calls at least one tool outside your account.
- List the entity types that must never leave, and the tools allowed to see them.
- Deploy the interceptor from the GitHub repository and attach it to that workflow’s gateway.
- Start with Shield the tool. Then add Shield the document for your document store, and Shield the model once the agent’s model calls go through the gateway.
- Watch the interceptor’s CloudWatch metrics for a week before widening the rollout.
- If you have further questions, see the Skyflow SDK documentation.

articles.title: Microsoft is experimenting with open-source AMD code to give Xbox up to 16% performance boost
articles.text:
Something to look forward to: Microsoft is testing an experimental open-source AMD shader compiler in the Xbox Game Development Kit, marking a major change in the way game consoles are optimized. Redmond believes that the update will improve game performance by 2% to 16% on current-gen Xbox consoles.
The open-source AMD compiler at the heart of the updated GDK is based on ACO, a shader compiler from the Mesa project that is used by the RADV Vulkan driver for AMD GPUs on Linux. It converts high-level shader instructions into machine code optimized for RDNA 2 GPUs powering Xbox Series X|S, Steam Deck, and other gaming handhelds.
Developed by the open-source Linux community in collaboration with Valve and independent developers, the compiler will replace the older LLVM-based architecture, enabling much faster shader compilation and yielding smoother runtime performance in Vulkan games on the Steam Deck and Linux PCs.
 – Xbox_Serious_X|S 🧬 🇺🇸 (@Xbox_Series_XS) November 15, 2026
By integrating technologies from multiple platforms, the new compiler is expected to eliminate existing shader bottlenecks and boost gaming performance. Microsoft noted that, following an initial evaluation, developers testing the updated GDK reported a performance improvement of between 2% and 16% depending on the game engine and graphics content.
The AMD compiler is an experimental addition that enables developers to optimize their upcoming games to perform better on Xbox consoles, but it does not automatically apply any optimization to existing games. Microsoft has yet to announce which titles will support the new compiler or when the changes will translate to tangible benefits for gamers.
The new compiler is part of Microsoft's latest Xbox GDK released in October. The updated kit also includes a new Xbox Test Account CLI that can be used to block player privileges based on account activity and a new command-line tool called ConvertPevt that converts .pevt offline timing captures from Xbox Series X|S consoles into .xpix captures without opening PIX.
The latest GDK also introduces AMD's machine learning-based FSR 4.1.2 upscaling to Xbox Series X|S, adding support for the existing Full INT8 model and a new Lite INT8 model, which is half the size and has a significantly lower computational cost. Developers will be able to pick between the two models to optimize either frame rates or visual quality, depending on the game.

articles.title: Newly Patched VMware vCenter Flaw Exploited as Zero-Day by Chinese APT
articles.text:
A China-linked espionage group exploited a VMware vCenter zero-day vulnerability for more than two months before Broadcom released a patch on Thursday, according to Google.
Tracked as CVE-2026-123890 (CVSS score of 9.8), the bug resides in the VMware Directory Service and could let remote, unauthenticated attackers obtain an authenticated session with administrator privileges.
Mandiant, which reported the bug to Broadcom, has linked its exploitation to Armory Castle, a suspected Chinese threat actor formerly tracked as UNC5221 and also known as Warp Panda.
According to Mandiant, the hackers gained initial access through CVE-2026-102764, a recently patched BeyondTrust Remote Support zero-day. They then pivoted to Linux appliances on the internal network and targeted vCenter in early September.
They used a custom tool called Bonesaw to exploit CVE-2026-123890, steal the Lightning Memory-Mapped Database (LMDB), extract SAML signing material, and create a single sign-on (SSO) administrator account.
Next, the attackers deployed a second tool to forge SAML tokens and installed backdoors. They also took the vCenter master encryption key and database credentials, then moved to an ESXi host and extracted additional information.
“Mandiant has evidence that Armory Castle had knowledge of CVE-2026-123890 prior to the disclosure of CVE-2026-59309 on July 29, 2026,” Google notes.
Bonesaw was used against a vCenter server already patched for CVE-2026-59309, a separate vCenter authentication bypass disclosed in July.
Charles Carmakal, CTO at Mandiant, said on LinkedIn that the company investigated multiple incidents involving Armory Castle’s exploitation of CVE-2026-123890.
Broadcom has released fixes in vCenter versions 9.1.1.0200, 9.0.2.0200, and 8.0 U3m. According to Mandiant, Bonesaw works against vCenter 7.x and 8.x. However, there is no public patch for version 7.0, which reached end of general support in October 2025.
Broadcom’s advisory, which also resolves four SDDC Manager and VMware Tools flaws, does not mention in-the-wild exploitation.
“Organizations should both apply the patches and examine their systems for evidence of compromise,” Carmakal said.
Related: Hackers Exploit Cisco Expressway Vulnerability Soon After PoC Release
Related: Critical Apache Roller, Axis Vulnerabilities Exploited in Attacks

articles.title: AI infrastructure economics favor Vultr's global footprint - SiliconANGLE
articles.text:
Sovereignty is the AI story everyone mentions and few have planned for ahead of 2027
AI infrastructure economics are entering a more sober phase as enterprises move past standing up AI factories and start asking how to run them profitably. Durability, real demand and long-term value are now the tests separating lasting providers from the froth.
That shift rewards cloud providers with an operating track record rather than a single speculative wager. Vultr has extended its global cloud to AI with chips from Nvidia Corp. and Advanced Micro Devices Inc. Enterprises are now making a flight to quality toward stable, cost-efficient platforms, according to Kevin Cochrane (pictured), chief marketing officer of Vultr.
“We’re seeing now not speculative bets in the buildout of AI infrastructure. We’re seeing real bets based on proven economics, proven ROI that people are looking to achieve,” Cochrane said. “What I think is going to wind up happening is a maturation of our industry leveraging this open stack.”
Cochrane spoke with theCUBE Research’s John Furrier and Rebecca Knight at SC26, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed how AI infrastructure economics favor a global footprint and why sovereignty requirements reach well beyond national governments. (* Disclosure below.)
AI infrastructure economics favor a global footprint
Vultr now operates 34 cloud data center regions, the latest a new region in Chennai, India. That footprint was built to keep cloud-native applications close to users, and inference follows the same logic, Cochrane explained. Agents make fast turns back to reasoning models, so CPUs and GPUs must sit together near the edge, he noted.
“This is kind of what Vultr was built for, which is one global platform, not isolated islands of data centers that are serving a bespoke customer. It is a true global cloud platform,” Cochrane said.
Sovereignty adds another constraint, and it reaches well beyond national governments. A global insurer tuning an open-source model for credit risk needs training clusters in each country because the underlying data cannot cross borders, Cochrane noted. Regulators are already tightening the rules, as the U.S. Commerce Department’s new curbs on remote chip access show.
“The way you have to post-train a model for credit risk in the U.K. versus Germany versus Singapore versus the United States, it’s going to be different,” Cochrane said. “It uses different data.”
