articles.title: Karnataka emerges as India's GCC powerhouse with 1,088 centres, says Kharge
articles.text:
Karnataka emerges as India's GCC powerhouse with 1,088 centres, says Kharge
Karnataka hosts 51% of India's GCCs and 43% of its GCC AI talent. Minister Priyank Kharge unveiled a new Zinnov-KDEM report at the Bengaluru Tech Summit 2026.
Global companies are increasingly looking to their India offices to do more than support business operations. In Karnataka, these centres are taking on a larger role in building and deploying artificial intelligence for their global businesses.
The State is home to 1,088 Global Capability Centres (GCCs), accounting for 51% of India's total. It also hosts 111,000 AI and machine learning professionals, representing 43% of the country's GCC AI/ML talent.
These findings are part of a new report, GCCs in Karnataka: Shaping the Future of Enterprise AI, released by Karnataka IT and BT Minister Priyank M. Kharge on November 19 at the Bengaluru Tech Summit 2026.
Prepared by Zinnov in collaboration with the Karnataka Digital Economy Mission (KDEM), the report examines how GCCs in the State are building AI capabilities, hiring specialised talent and taking on larger technology mandates.
Karnataka leads in AI maturity
The report finds that surveyed Karnataka GCCs score 1.12 times the national average in overall AI maturity. Around 66% have reached the Portfolio Hub stage, compared with approximately 43% across India.
The findings also point to stronger AI adoption within these centres. Around 69% of surveyed Karnataka GCCs have dedicated AI budgets, against 57% nationally. Similarly, 69% conduct role-specific AI training, compared with 53% across the country.
Around 83% reuse in-house AI platforms across business units, while 66% follow Responsible AI practices. The corresponding national figures are 57% and 49%, respectively.
Karnataka's position is also reflected in its AI infrastructure. More than 660 GCCs in the State have AI and machine learning capabilities, while over 120 dedicated AI and ML Centres of Excellence operate in the region. This represents around 48% of India's total.
Bengaluru attracts AI leadership talent
Beyond infrastructure and adoption, Bengaluru has emerged as a major destination for senior AI talent.
The city accounts for 44% of India's senior AI leadership job postings within GCCs, 6.4 times the average of other tier-I cities. It also accounts for up to 63% of Distinguished and Principal AI Engineer openings.
In 2026, AI skills featured in 13.6% of GCC job postings in Bengaluru, compared with 9.8% at the same companies' offices outside Karnataka.
The State's wider technology ecosystem supports this demand. Karnataka hosts more than 29% of India's AI startups and has over 5,000 active technology investors. It also produces more than 130,000 STEM graduates annually.
GCCs move beyond support roles
The report outlines five priorities for Karnataka's GCC ecosystem through 2030. These include attracting advanced GCC mandates, increasing global ownership of AI development, building AI leadership talent, scaling AI with measurable business outcomes and moving research into enterprise adoption.
The State currently hosts 1,088 GCCs, including 320 centres belonging to Global 2000 companies. Between FY2021 and FY2026, it attracted 217 of India's 510 new GCCs.
Launching the report, Kharge said Karnataka's GCCs were becoming key drivers of the State's technology leadership.
"With 1,088 GCCs and 111,000 AI and machine learning professionals, Karnataka is where global enterprises come to build AI," he said.
He added that the State would continue strengthening AI capabilities, research and skills through its dedicated GCC Policy and IT Policy 2025-30, while extending opportunities to other regions through the Beyond Bengaluru initiative.
Dr Manjula N, Secretary of the Department of Electronics, IT and BT, said Karnataka had embedded AI and deep technology across six State technology policies. She pointed to the higher adoption of role-specific AI training and Responsible AI practices among surveyed GCCs as evidence of this progress.
Nitika Goel, CMO and Managing Partner at Zinnov, said GCCs were entering a new phase in which their value would be measured by AI deployed in production rather than pilots and proofs of concept.
"The contest now is for talent, and Karnataka holds a rare advantage, with over a thousand GCCs, tier-1 academic institutions and the country's largest cohort of start-ups," she said.
The report also points to the State's efforts to build its talent pipeline through Nipuna Karnataka, a Rs 300 crore industry-driven programme focused on AI, deep tech and cybersecurity.
The report, GCCs in Karnataka: Shaping the Future of Enterprise AI, is available on the KDEM website.

articles.title: Nigeria’s Payaza secures Central Bank of Kenya licence - Disrupt Africa
articles.text:
Nigerian payments infrastructure company Payaza has been authorised by the Central Bank of Kenya (CBK) to provide payment gateway services, just weeks after getting regulatory approval in Zambia.
Payaza offers payment collection, payout and merchant tools to businesses in Africa and international markets. It handles card, mobile money and bank payments in more than 40 currencies and operates in more than 27 countries.
The CBK approval allows Payaza to operate as a licensed payment service provider in Kenya. It can now serve local merchants directly with online checkout and payment acceptance. The licence does not cover deposit-taking or customer wallets.
It comes after the Bank of Zambia gave Payaza a Certificate of Designation of a Payment System. The company has also recently picked up payment licensing milestones in China, Pakistan and Bangladesh.
“Kenya is the heartbeat of East Africa’s digital economy, and we are entering it the right way: fully licensed,” said Seyi Ebenezer, Payaza’s group CEO. “Coming so soon after our Bank of Zambia approval, this licence from the Central Bank of Kenya connects East, West and Southern Africa on one regulated platform.”
Payaza says it will now speed up merchant onboarding, build closer ties with banks and mobile money operators, and seek more licences across Africa, especially in East Africa. Nigeria makes up about 35 per cent of its revenue.

articles.title: Drupal patches critical RCE flaw, warns exploits may surface quickly
articles.text:
The Drupal Security Team has patched a critical remote code execution vulnerability that can let attackers take over vulnerable sites.
This content management system (CMS) is commonly used by large organizations that manage multi-site installations and massive data structures, including government entities, educational organizations, major research universities, and high-profile enterprise and media organizations.
The security flaw (tracked as CVE-2026-132165) was discovered by Anthropic's OSS Scanner, and anonymous users can exploit it to reinstall the Drupal CMS.
"Drupal core ships with an install.php file for installing Drupal core. Under specific conditions, an attacker can use the installer to attempt to reinstall Drupal. This can lead to a site takeover or remote code execution," the Drupal Security Team warned in a Wednesday advisory. "Some exploit paths are mitigated if the web server cannot write to or change permissions on settings.php."
Admins whose websites use the paid Drupal Steward Web Application Firewall (WAF) service are already protected from known attack vectors, but should still upgrade to Drupal 10.6.22, 11.3.22, or 11.4.13 in case other attack vectors are discovered.
Those who can't immediately upgrade should secure the Drupal installer by blocking access to /core/install.php in the web server configuration or the .htaccess file in the web root.
On Wednesday, Drupal also addressed a moderately critical gadget chain vulnerability (CVE-2026-132166) that attackers with admin privileges can exploit to gain remote code execution on a targeted site if the application deserializes untrusted data due to another security flaw.
"The Drupal Security Team urges you to reserve time for core updates at that time because exploits might be developed within hours or days," the security team said in a Monday advance warning. "The vulnerabilities are currently rated as critical and at least one can be exploited by anonymous users."
In May, Drupal also confirmed that attackers were actively exploiting an SQL injection vulnerability (CVE-2026-9082) in the database abstraction API that could let them escalate privileges, access sensitive information, or achieve remote code execution on unpatched servers.
More recently, Drupal warned that a critical access bypass vulnerability (CVE-2026-118539) in the Commerce Core module is being abused in attacks.
The US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) has flagged 5 Drupal vulnerabilities as exploited in the wild since November 2021, two of which have also been abused in ransomware attacks.

articles.title: « Improbable et grave » : l’IA a découvert une faille planétaire dans un langage informatique « dont nous dépendons tous »
articles.text:
Une nouvelle faille critique fait trembler le monde de l’informatique. Ce 17 novembre, la start-up californienne Calif a dévoilé une brèche dans le cœur du code de Java, un langage de programmation omniprésent dans le monde entier. Baptisée Java4Shell, la faille permet à un pirate de prendre le contrôle de certains serveurs à distance. Elle touche surtout les serveurs des entreprises équipés de processeurs Intel ou AMD récents. Les puces ARM, présentes dans la plupart des smartphones, ne sont pas concernées.
À lire aussi : « Un faux sentiment de secret » – face à l’IA, Google prend une décision qui divise le monde de la cybersécurité
Une faille découverte par l’IA… en une heure
L’affaire a commencé il y a quelques semaines quand Quang Luong, chercheur chez Calif, a décidé de se pencher sur le code de Java. Conscient de la difficulté de la tâche, il s’est tourné vers Codex, l’assistant d’OpenAI propulsé par GPT-6 Cyber, un modèle d’IA spécialisé dans la recherche de failles.
 Since the vulnerability has leaked: Calif discovered and reported Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938).
We’re publishing technical details by 1 PM Pacific today, after Oracle releases a patch.
Stay tuned!
— Calif (@calif_io) November 17, 2026
Au début, l’IA n’a proposé que des pistes inutiles. Moins d’une heure après le début des recherches, l’intelligence artificielle a mis le doigt sur une vraie faille de sécurité, bien plus préoccupante que prévu. Selon Calif, il n’a fallu qu’une heure pour trouver la faille, puis deux heures pour mettre au point une attaque, le tout pour moins de 200 dollars de frais de calcul.
« Je suis venu chercher du cuivre et j’ai trouvé de l’or », résume le chercheur.
64 lettres « A » pour pirater un serveur
La faille se cache dans une fonction très banale de Java qui sert à décoder du texte au format Base64. Ce format sert à transformer des données en suites de lettres et de chiffres pour qu’elles circulent facilement sur Internet. La fonction est notamment utilisée pour envoyer des identifiants de connexion ou des fichiers. Sur les processeurs récents, Java utilise une version accélérée de cette fonction. C’est dans cette fonctionnalité que l’IA a déniché une faille de sécurité.
Pour déclencher la brèche, il suffit d’envoyer 64 lettres « A » suivies d’un signe « = » à la fonction. Celle-ci se met alors à déborder et à écraser certaines des données de sa mémoire. Un pirate peut alors en profiter pour lire des informations secrètes, comme des mots de passe ou des clés de chiffrement, explique Calif. C’est la porte ouverte à des vols de données sensibles, susceptibles de compromettre des comptes en banque. Un attaquant peut aussi en profiter pour envoyer ses propres commandes par le biais de la fonction. Lors de ses tests, Calif a piraté plusieurs logiciels très utilisés en entreprise, comme Jira, Confluence ou Jenkins.
« Corriger immédiatement » la faille Java4Shell
L’annonce devait rester secrète jusqu’à la publication du correctif, conformément aux meilleures pratiques du monde de la cybersécurité. Selon Calif, l’information a été divulguée quelques heures trop tôt, alors qu’aucun correctif n’avait encore été annoncé. Le 17 novembre, la start-up a donc publié le résultat de ses travaux.
Le jour même, le géant américain Oracle, propriétaire de Java ,et OpenJDK, la version libre de Java, mettent en ligne un correctif pour colmater la vulnérabilité dans l’urgence. Dans la foulée, la CISA, l’agence américaine de cybersécurité, a appelé toutes les organisations à « corriger immédiatement » la faille pour éviter une explosion des cyberattaques.
 🚨We urge orgs to immediately patch the recently disclosed Oracle Java vuln CVE-2026-114938. This critical memory-corruption vulnerability, known as “Java4Shell,” affects the Base64 decoder of the x86-64 HotSpot JVM, part of the Java Development Kit. 🔗https://t.co/SwrhdPFlZF pic.twitter.com/3QGldeAerV
— CISA Cyber (@CISACyber) November 17, 2026
L’alerte fait rapidement le tour du monde. En Allemagne, le BSI (Bundesamt für Sicherheit in der Informationstechnik), l’agence fédérale de cybersécurité, met lui aussi en garde contre les attaques exploitant la faille de Java, rapporte Reuters. Le Canada et l’Inde ont rapidement publié des avis similaires, exhortant toutes les entreprises à agir dans les plus brefs délais.
Une faille jugée « improbable et grave »
Interrogé par la BBC, le chercheur Toby Walsh juge la faille « improbable et grave ». Il rappelle que Java est justement conçu pour protéger la mémoire à l’encontre de ce genre d’erreur. Selon Walsh, « l’IA met désormais au jour davantage de failles, bien plus rapidement ». Le chercheur Pedram Hayati ne cache pas son inquiétude. Il estime que la brèche dans Java pourrait compromettre « des systèmes financiers critiques ».
Pour Fouad Matin, le responsable de la préparation aux cybermenaces chez OpenAI, les travaux de Calif montrent que l’IA peut aider les chercheurs à débusquer des failles graves « dans des logiciels dont nous dépendons tous », selon des propos rapportés par le New York Times.
Bonne nouvelle, aucune cyberattaque n’a encore été détectée. Dans une réaction envoyée à 01net, les chercheurs de Group-IB révèlent n’avoir « trouvé aucune preuve d’exploitation » pour le moment. Comme le souligne le Centre canadien pour la cybersécurité, « cela peut changer rapidement ». C’est également l’avis de Cisco Talos, qui s’attend à voir les tentatives d’attaque se multiplier prochainement.
Avant Java, le chaos PHP
L’histoire de Java4Shell rappelle celle de PHP2Shell. En octobre, Calif avait déjà utilisé l’IA pour dénicher deux failles critiques dans PHP, un autre langage très répandu, plongeant une partie d’Internet dans le chaos. La faille a aussi été divulguée un peu trop tôt, ouvrant la porte à des tentatives d’intrusion. Des pirates chinois se sont rapidement servis de la faille pour mener des attaques. Les versions touchées sont Java 17 (à partir de la 17.0.6), 21, 25 et 27. Comme pour PHP, le plus dur sera de retrouver toutes les copies de Java cachées dans les logiciels et les machines à travers le monde. De facto, des systèmes risquent de rester vulnérables pendant un long moment…

articles.text:
Black Friday 2026 : Le casque à conduction osseuse Shokz OpenRun Pro 2 "5 étoiles" à 149,00 € (-23%)
Le casque à conduction osseuse Shokz OpenRun Pro 2 passe sous les 150 € chez Son-Video.com et i-Run soit une baisse d'environ 23% sur le prix habituellement constaté. C'est actuellement le meilleur produit de notre comparatif.
Avec l’OpenRun Pro 2, Shokz ne tente pas de repousser les limitations sonores de la conduction osseuse, il les contourne. Par le biais d’une architecture hybride, la marque se donne les moyens de ses ambitions dans le bas du spectre. Une formule payante, malgré quelques compromis.

articles.title: PolyAI Dialog-RSN-1 is now on Amazon SageMaker JumpStart | Amazon Web Services
articles.text:
Artificial Intelligence
PolyAI Dialog-RSN-1 is now on Amazon SageMaker JumpStart
Dialog-RSN-1, a reasoning model built for real-time complex dialog, is available today on AWS Marketplace and Amazon SageMaker JumpStart. It powers frontier dialog: agents that hear a live call, reason about it, and act in real time.
As an AWS customer, you can subscribe to Dialog-RSN-1 through AWS Marketplace and deploy it as a SageMaker endpoint inside your own AWS environment. You can also deploy directly from Amazon SageMaker Studio following the steps in Deploy and evaluate models with Amazon SageMaker JumpStart. That means the model designed to handle your customer conversations can be deployed like other Amazon SageMaker models with an AWS Marketplace subscription.
Deploying Dialog-RSN-1 inside AWS
Dialog-RSN-1 is the first PolyAI model available through AWS Marketplace. It runs inside your own AWS environment on the same AWS cloud that powers PolyAI’s compute and model training and serving.
All in a single pass, Dialog-RSN-1 perceives a caller’s audio directly, reasons about what they need, and responds in real time. On SageMaker, it deploys as an endpoint like other models you run there. It is reachable from your own architecture, billed through your AWS account, and covered by the same virtual private cloud (VPC), AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) roles, and monitoring you already have in place.
You keep ownership of orchestration, telephony integration, and business logic. Dialog-RSN-1 takes off your plate the hardest part to build yourself: understanding a live call and responding to it in real time. The endpoint speaks the OpenAI Realtime protocol, so an existing Realtime client connects through PolyAI’s bridge by changing its base URL. Audio in is 16-bit PCM mono at 16 or 24 kHz (transcode G.711 or Opus first). Connections last up to 30 minutes, and the model is English-only today.
To get started, find Dialog-RSN-1 on AWS Marketplace, then deploy it straight into an Amazon SageMaker endpoint in your own account. Or you can deploy directly from Amazon SageMaker JumpStart.
With Dialog-RSN-1 now onboarded to SageMaker JumpStart, deploying Dialog-RSN-1 takes one click. From the Amazon SageMaker AI console, open the Model Hub, select Dialog-RSN-1 from the JumpStart catalog, and choose Deploy. SageMaker JumpStart then spins up a real-time inference endpoint on a serving stack it has already tuned for you. No containers to wrangle, no instance types to second-guess, and no manual benchmarking. For automated workflows, the same one-click deployment also runs in a few lines of the SageMaker Python SDK.
The Dialog-RSN-1 endpoint runs entirely within your own AWS account. It is deployed in your VPC, accessed through your IAM roles, and monitored with the same Amazon CloudWatch logging and metrics you use for every other workload. Because inference happens inside your account, your callers’ audio and transcripts stay within a boundary you control. For a model handling live customer conversation, this helps support your data residency and auditability requirements.
Built for speed and accuracy
Models built for live calls may make you choose between speed and understanding. And models built for speed may miss the meaning, and ones built for reasoning may lead to wait time for callers. Dialog-RSN-1 avoids the tradeoff.
With PolyAI, you can build dialog agents that hear and handle calls the way your human agents would. These agents catch hesitation, hear frustration before it escalates, and know when to speak.
Real-time customer conversation is the job PolyAI’s Dialog-RSN-1 is built for, and it is already handling live calls in production today. Because the model reasons directly over the caller’s audio, it picks up tone, hesitation, and timing, the signals a plain transcript loses, and decides for itself the right moment to respond.
A model that hears calls the way humans do
Dialog-RSN-1 is a model focused on real-time conversations. There is no separate speech-to-text step and no reasoning model on the appropriate moment to talk, so thereby no multiple handoffs.
In practice, that means the callers get responses faster:
- Barge-in keeps working even when call volume spikes, instead of getting switched off to protect performance.
- Responses keep pace, so the model is not lagging behind the conversation while it reasons through what to say.
- Transcription is produced from the audio itself, because Dialog-RSN-1 is reading the actual audio, not someone else’s best guess at it.
Dialog-RSN-1 on Amazon SageMaker JumpStart
Amazon SageMaker JumpStart is the machine learning hub inside Amazon SageMaker AI, and it exists to collapse the distance between choosing a model and running it in production. For Dialog-RSN-1, that means the frontier of real-time dialog is a few clicks away. You can discover it, prove it on your own data, and ship it to a secure endpoint, all in one place. Here is what you get.
The code path using the SageMaker Python SDK is explained in our GitHub repository: Deploy PolyAI Dialog-RSN-1 on Amazon SageMaker AI.
Discover and evaluate before you commit
Dialog-RSN-1 shows up in the SageMaker JumpStart catalog with overview and sample notebooks in one place, so your team can understand the model before spending a dollar on infrastructure. To try the model on your own calls, deploy the endpoint and run PolyAI’s sample notebook, which streams recorded caller audio and prints the model’s turn decisions, replies, and transcripts.
One-click deploy and optimizations for your workload
From the same model card you choose Deploy, and Amazon SageMaker JumpStart stands up a real-time inference endpoint with a pre-configured serving stack. There is no manual container selection or instance guesswork. The real convenience is the named optimization profiles: instead of hand-tuning infrastructure, you pick the target that matches how you run Dialog-RSN-1. Latency optimized minimizes Time to First Token for interactive, real-time calls. Throughput optimized maximizes tokens per second for high call volumes. Cost optimized minimizes infrastructure cost per request. Balanced is an even tradeoff for general-purpose use.
Because Dialog-RSN-1 is built to respond in real time, you can use the latency-optimized profile to carry that responsiveness straight to your own endpoint. Before you deploy, SageMaker JumpStart surfaces the key performance metrics: P50 latency, Time to First Token, and throughput. This lets you right-size the ml.* instance for your traffic instead of benchmarking dozens of combinations by hand. You can run the whole flow from the console, or script it through the SageMaker Python SDK to wire deployments into continuous integration and continuous delivery (CI/CD).
Deployed in your account, governed by your controls
The endpoint runs inside your own account boundary: in your VPC, under your IAM roles, with the CloudWatch logging and metrics you already have in place. For a model handling live customer conversations, that means your call audio and transcripts stay in an environment you control, which keeps data residency and auditability straightforward.
The result is a frontier voice model that deploys like the other workloads your machine learning team already runs, using the same hub, the same discovery and evaluation tools, and the same security posture. The hard part is the conversation Dialog-RSN-1 handles, not the infrastructure behind it.
For more detail on the architecture behind our frontier dialog model and the evaluation results behind our benchmarks, read our Dialog-RSN-1 launch post.
Get started today with Dialog-RSN-1 on AWS Marketplace or directly deploy from Amazon SageMaker JumpStart. Also explore SageMaker JumpStart pretrained models.

articles.title: Google's Gemini 4 Neon tripled its coding score without changing the model
articles.text:
Google’s Gemini 4 Neon tripled its coding score without changing the model
Google’s new Gemini 4 Neon resolved 12.8% of the SWE-sweep coding benchmark using the mini-SWE harness, but that score jumped to 39.0% when the same model ran inside Antigravity.
The more-than-threefold improvement raises questions about how much coding-agent performance comes from the underlying model and how much depends on the harness…
Both results were reported Wednesday as part of the Neon launch. The more-than-threefold improvement raises questions about how much coding-agent performance comes from the underlying model and how much depends on the harness managing its tools, context, and execution.
A day earlier, a FrontierHarness benchmark found that running the same open model could cost up to five times more depending on the harness
Same model, different scores
Google’s Gemini 4 Neon model card compares three frontier models on SWE-sweep using their respective provider harnesses and a shared mini-SWE baseline.
Neon and Opus performed substantially better with their providers’ harnesses, but Sol did not.
Claude Opus 5.5 climbed from 3.6% with mini-SWE to 10.1% with Claude Code, while GPT-6.2 Sol went the other way, falling from 11.6% with mini-SWE to 8.3% with Codex. Neon and Opus performed substantially better with their providers’ harnesses, but Sol did not.
Google tested each model in two harness configurations, though the comparison does not isolate which changes account for the differences or whether the results would hold up across other benchmarks and repositories.
The harness does the work
Antigravity’s harness was co-trained with Gemini, and Neon has been updated to make fewer unnecessary file reads and better manage context during long coding sessions. Antigravity can also run subagents in separate Git worktrees and verify their changes.
Google only tested Neon against mini-SWE, so there’s no data yet on how it performs with other harnesses.
It’s unclear which of those changes contributed most to the SWE-sweep improvement, since they weren’t tested separately. Google only tested Neon against mini-SWE, so there’s no data yet on how it performs with other harnesses.
Neon plans, Hydrogen builds
Neon is joining the model-switching system Google introduced with Gemini 4 Hydrogen. It handles planning and harder coding problems, leaving routine work to Hydrogen, and can run multiple Hydrogen subagents in parallel using the /swarm feature introduced with Carbon.
Google hasn’t said how much this setup affects Neon’s SWE-sweep results or what it means for the cost of completing a task.
Counting the cost per task
The company reports that Neon scored 65.2% on Terminal-Bench 4.1 and 46.2% on FrontierCode 2.0 at its default high reasoning setting. It also topped the Artificial Analysis Coding Agent Index with a score of 58.6.
At its default high thinking level, the model costs 32% less per task than Gemini 4 Carbon, according to Google’s comparison using the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index. API pricing is $3 per million input tokens and $15 per million output tokens, with cached input at $0.15 per million tokens and a 1 million-token context window.
Neon is available through the Gemini API, Google AI Studio, and Gemini for Business. Google AI Pro and Ultra subscribers can also access it through Antigravity.

articles.title: Son pedigree est déjà bien chargé : c’est quoi ARTEX, l’outil de piratage chinois utilisé contre la Commission européenne ?
articles.text:
Le voici sur le devant de la scène médiatique… européenne.
Le 19 novembre 2026, Politico a révélé que le service de cybersécurité des institutions européennes avait détecté l’utilisation d’ARTEX dans une campagne de cyberattaques visant la Commission européenne.
Depuis plus de dix jours, cette attaque perturbe plusieurs services internes de la Commission, de la plateforme RH aux services de traduction en passant par l’outil de remboursement des frais médicaux.
L’outil n’a pourtant rien d’un inconnu dans l’écosystème cyber. Le CERT-EU lui avait consacré une note technique dès le 5 novembre, le FBI a publié une alerte le 13, et les grands éditeurs de cybersécurité suivent sa diffusion depuis la fin de l’été.
Qu’est-ce qu’ARTEX ?
Sur le papier, l’intention était bonne. ARTEX a en effet été conçu comme un outil de test d’intrusion (pentest), qui simule des attaques pour qu’une organisation découvre ses failles avant les pirates. S’il est présenté comme un outil d’IA, ARTEX n’est pas un modèle en lui-même. C’est une surcouche qui se branche sur des modèles existants, de Claude à DeepSeek, ou sur n’importe quel service compatible avec l’interface d’OpenAI.
Il fait travailler ensemble plusieurs agents, entre lesquels un module de planification répartit les tâches de l’intrusion, et chacun consigne ses découvertes dans un journal commun. Un opérateur humain les dirige et reprend la main aux moments décisifs. Ces agents scannent le réseau visé, exploitent les failles trouvées, installent des portes dérobées et récupèrent des identifiants, en changeant de piste dès qu’une voie est bloquée.
Sur le fond, ARTEX n’invente donc aucune technique d’intrusion. Il passe toujours par des identifiants volés ou des systèmes non mis à jour ou mal protégés.
Reste qu’il crée une sérieuse bascule dans la vitesse d’exécution, et c’est l’une des principales sources d’inquiétudes lorsqu’il tombe entre de mauvaises mains.
Publié en open source en juillet 2026, ARTEX n’est resté que quelques mois sur GitHub. Le 8 octobre, son développeur chinois, un certain « Autumn-27 » a annoncé qu’il ne le mettrait plus à jour et le passerait en code fermé « compte tenu des abus ».
Un retrait qui n’a pas fait disparaître l’outil pour autant. Selon le FBI, des copies archivées, des versions dérivées et une édition commerciale baptisée ARTEX PRO circulent toujours, et début novembre la société Censys recensait près de 1 500 consoles ARTEX accessibles publiquement sur Internet.
La Commission européenne n’est pas la première victime d’ARTEX
C’est une affaire antérieure à celle de la Commission européenne qui a poussé son créateur à le retirer. Fin septembre, au moins neuf établissements financiers sud-coréens ont été visés par des cyberattaques destinées à voler les données personnelles de leurs clients. Selon l’entreprise de cybersécurité CrowdStrike, l’attaquant se serait appuyé sur ARTEX et sur Claude Code, l’outil de programmation d’Anthropic.
Réputé pour laisser de nombreuses traces sur son passage, les usages malveillants d’ARTEX avaient même été repérés avant l’affaire coréenne. D’après les équipes de sécurité de Google, des groupes d’extorsion l’utilisaient déjà à la fin du mois d’août, et en septembre, l’institut néerlandais DIVD a été piraté par un agent qui, selon lui, s’appuyait sur l’outil.
Depuis, des groupes liés à Pékin s’en seraient emparés. Toujours selon CrowdStrike, le groupe APT VAPOR PANDA a visé à partir du 17 octobre plus de 200 organisations dans 14 pays en moins de deux semaines, parmi lesquelles des ministères et des opérateurs télécoms, et en a compromis au moins neuf. Microsoft impute de son côté la compromission du service ConnectWise Cloud Backup à Storm-0940, un autre groupe aligné sur la Chine.
Dans le cas de la Commission européenne, le rôle exact d’ARTEX reste à déterminer. Les enquêteurs ne savent pas encore si l’outil a permis l’intrusion ou s’il a seulement servi à repérer des failles, ni si des données du personnel ont été consultées ou volées, et aucun attaquant n’a été nommé.

articles.title: Google va compliquer l’installation d’APK dès le mois de janvier prochain — Frandroid
articles.text:
Rien n’y fait. Les accusations, les lettres ouvertes et la grogne des utilisateurs et utilisatrices n’auront pas suffi à ralentir Google dans son ambition de verrouiller Android. Dans un communiqué publié ce jeudi 19 novembre et repéré par Ars Technica, l’entreprise a annoncé que le déploiement mondial de son système de validation des développeurs allait intervenir à partir de janvier 2027.
Annoncé depuis mi 2025, ce changement va obliger les créateurs et créatrices d’apps à s’enregistrer auprès de Google pour permettre l’installation aisée de leur logiciel sur Android. Celles et ceux qui ne le font pas devront composer avec un processus d’installation alambiqué.
Du 19 au 30 novembre, le Plaud Note Pro passe à 149 € au lieu de 189 € ! Il enregistre vos réunions, les transcrit et les synthétise pour vous, il suffit d’appuyer sur un bouton. Les Plaud Note, NotePin et NotePin S sont aussi à -20 %. Bref, c’est le moment d’arrêter de perdre du temps au travail !
En collaboration avec Samsung, Oppo, Xiaomi…
Selon l’entreprise, la grande campagne de vérification des développeurs menée depuis 2025 a permis à « plus de 99 % de toutes les installations d’applications Android dans le monde » d’être couverte par ce nouveau système. Ces dernières pourront être téléchargées sans aucune difficulté depuis le Play Store, mais aussi le Galaxy Store ou les solutions de Honor, Oppo ou Xiaomi et d’autres.
Pour les autres, en revanche, la situation va évoluer en pire. Une application provenant d’un développeur non certifié ne pourra être installée qu’après un passage dans les options développeurs, un redémarrage du téléphone et une période d’attente de 24 heures. Google justifie le déploiement de ce « flux avancé » par des impératifs de sécurité, tandis que le monde du logiciel libre y voit une tentative de prendre le contrôle sur une plateforme mobile « autrefois ouverte ».
Une application déjà là
L’architecture nécessaire à l’application de cette nouvelle restriction a d’ores et déjà commencé à être mise en place sur la plupart des téléphones Android avec le déploiement silencieux de l’Android Developer Verifier en août dernier. Tous les appareils Android certifiés sous Android 7 ou plus récent sont concernés. L’application ne peut être désinstallée, mais il sera possible de désactiver le mécanisme de protection une bonne fois pour toutes après un passage dans les options développeurs.
    Pour aller plus loin

articles.title: Samsung prépare un Horizontal Lock pour la caméra selfie, repéré dans la bêta de One UI 9.5
articles.text:
Samsung travaillerait sur une version selfie de son stabilisateur d’horizon, apparue dans les fichiers de la première bêta de One UI 9.5. Jusqu’ici, la fonction se limite aux caméras arrière des Galaxy récents.
Le Horizontal Lock de la caméra selfie s’appellerait « Horizontal Leveling » et resterait pour l’instant sans calendrier ni liste d’appareils confirmés. L’intérêt est évident pour les vidéastes qui se filment en marchant, mais plusieurs inconnues demeurent.
Horizontal Leveling : la stabilisation de l’horizon gagne la caméra frontale
Des références à cette fonction ont été repérées par AndroidAuthority dans la première bêta de One UI 9.5. Le code indique qu’elle ferait partie du mode Super Steady, au même titre que Horizontal Lock, et qu'elle garderait les vidéos selfie stables et à niveau même quand le téléphone est incliné.
Rappelons le principe de l’original, lancé avec les Galaxy S26 puis étendu à d’autres modèles haut de gamme : l’image reste horizontale même si l’on penche, voire si l'on fait pivoter complètement le téléphone. Samsung explique que le S26 Ultra repère la direction de la gravité grâce à ses capteurs gyroscopiques et à des angles optiques élargis, pour maintenir la ligne d’horizon, y compris sur une rotation à 360°. Cette fonction ne concerne aujourd’hui que les caméras arrière.
Les créateurs de contenu, premiers visés, et un Galaxy S27 en tête de liste
Côté usage, la fonction viserait les vidéos tournées en marchant ou en courant, sans tremblements, et serait pensée pour les créateurs qui filment avec un équipement de stabilisation comme un gimbal. Autrement dit, le vlog à bout de bras gagnerait enfin ce que la caméra arrière sait déjà faire.
Reste la question du matériel compatible. Samsung n’a rien confirmé, et il s’agit pour l’instant de références découvertes dans une bêta : rien ne garantit que la fonction sorte telle quelle. One UI 9.5 stable devrait arriver préinstallé sur les Galaxy S27, ce qui en ferait les candidats naturels pour l’étrenner, mais cette hypothèse n'a rien d’officiel. Les propriétaires de modèles plus anciens ont déjà vu des fonctions du S26 descendre vers eux, comme avec le Galaxy S25 et One UI 9, mais rien n’indique que ce sera le cas ici.
Reste à voir si la caméra frontale, aux capteurs bien plus modestes que ceux de l’arrière, saura tenir l’horizon aussi bien.

articles.title: Balance Theory acquires CISO decision intelligence platform VectorBlack - SiliconANGLE
articles.text:
Balance Theory acquires CISO decision intelligence platform VectorBlack
Cybersecurity investment management company Balance Theory Inc. today announced that it has acquired VectorBlack, a decision intelligence platform for chief information security officers developed by ThreatShare.ai, for an undisclosed sum.
Developed by Jason Lewis, Gerry Eaton and Wayne Schepens, VectorBlack is designed to provide CISOs with timely decision support on emerging threats, industry developments and market trends. The artificial intelligence-driven platform is aimed at anticipating the issues most likely to catch the attention of chief executives and boards, allowing security leaders to raise them before the questions are asked.
Rather than simply aggregating information, VectorBlack is said to show security leaders what has changed in the cybersecurity landscape and why it matters to their organization. Its focus as what the company calls a CISO Strategic Intelligence Platform was shaped by input from security executives, including Ryan Clarque, CISO at Black Rifle Coffee Co. Clarque said having a strategic view ahead of a renewal, budget decision or board discussion “can make all the difference.”
Lewis began developing the underlying technology before teaming up with Eaton, an industry analyst, and Schepens, a cybersecurity entrepreneur who founded public relations firm LaunchTech Communications in 2015.
As part of the deal, Schepens will join Balance Theory as chief cyber market analyst to help shape market strategy and product adoption. Lewis is taking on the role of principal data engineer, leading the continued development and integration of VectorBlack’s technology. Eaton will focus on applying the platform to targeted research and sector-specific intelligence for cybersecurity leaders.
At the core of Balance Theory’s offering is an AI-native platform for cybersecurity investment decisions and execution. Combining program context, proprietary market intelligence and AI agents, the platform is used by security teams to manage more than $1 billion in cybersecurity spending. It claims customers average a first-year return on investment of more than 300%.
VectorBlack’s technology will be integrated into the Balance Theory platform, adding to the market intelligence that already informs customer investment decisions. By tracking market developments, competitive dynamics, emerging technologies and real-world experience with security products, the combined teams are aiming to show CISOs how their own investments are performing, what others in the industry are seeing and where the market is headed.
“VectorBlack will take Balance Theory’s capabilities a step further by delivering tailored intelligence across the security product categories our customers invest in,” said Greg Baker, co-founder and chief executive of Balance Theory. “This creates a powerful new level of insight to inform smarter technology investments and long-term security strategy.”
The company said details on integration and availability will be announced at a later date.
Balance Theory is a venture capital-backed company that raised $19 million in a Series A round led by SYN Ventures in July, with existing investors DataTribe and the Maryland Technology Development Corp. also participating. The round coincided with Accuvant Inc. founder and former Optiv Security Inc. Chief Executive Dan Burns joining Balance Theory as executive chairman. Including a $3 million seed round in 2022, Balance Theory has raised $22 million to date.

articles.title: Kuda cuts jobs for the second time in 2026
articles.text:
Kuda, the Nigerian digital bank, will cut about 7.5% of its workforce across seven countries in its second round of job cuts this year as it restructures operations to reach group profitability in 2027.
In March, the company laid off hundreds of employees across several units after a company-wide review. The latest cuts will affect roles in Nigeria, the UK, South Africa, Canada, Tanzania, Uganda and Ghana, Kuda said in a statement shared with TechCabal on Thursday.
Affected employees will go through a consultation period before any final decisions, and Kuda said it would offer them “a comprehensive support package.” In March, employees expected up to seven months of pay.
The redundancies are part of Kuda’s push to cut costs as it pursues profitability. Kuda said its March job cuts were not linked to financial performance. This round, Babs Ogundeyi, Kuda’s co-founder and CEO, said, will help the company achieve group profitability by 2027 and meet the capital rules for its banking licence.
Kuda’s Nigerian branch is already profitable, Ogundeyi told TechCabal on a call on Thursday, though he declined to share figures. Investors are still backing the company, he said, but “they are not putting in money as charity. At some point they expect a return beyond valuations.”
In January, the Central Bank of Nigeria upgraded Kuda’s microfinance bank to a national licence, which requires at least ₦5 billion ($3.9 million) in paid-up capital. Ogundeyi described that money as “idle capital” and said Kuda now has to hold more of it as it grows.
“That requires us to be more efficient than we would need to be at the earliest stage of our journey,” he said. “For our 8 million customers, nothing changes. Their money is safe, and we’ll keep building products that help them do more with it,” Ogundeyi said in the statement.
Kuda joins a growing list of African tech companies that are cutting staff as AI and better software change how many people they need. African tech companies cut a record 2,574 jobs in the first half of 2026, according to TechCabal Insights, which named restructuring and AI adoption as leading causes.
In May, Jumia said it would cut about 200 jobs as it brings AI into operations, logistics, finance and marketing. In October, Moniepoint began reorganising its engineers and product managers into smaller teams, a setup it said “requires fewer roles in some areas.”
“You can see a few companies in the industry doing this, so I do not think it comes as a surprise in an era of better technology and better tools for managing companies,” Ogundeyi said.
Kuda’s statement did not say how many people would lose their jobs. On the call, Ogundeyi said the company has “about 500 people” and put the number at risk at “around 40.”
The company tied both rounds of 2026 job cuts to the same plan. The changes “build on the Kuda 2.0 programme the company began in March 2026, which focused the business on its core products and customers,” it said.
Kuda’s push for profitability follows a period of rapid customer growth that came with high operating costs. Kuda’s loss narrowed to $5.83 million in 2024, from $35.11 million the year before, and staff costs fell 46% to $6.31 million, according to its financials. Group revenue, reported in dollars, fell 15% to $18.34 million, which management blamed on the weaker naira. Measured in naira, revenue at the Nigerian bank nearly doubled to ₦21.2 billion ($13.8 million). Customer deposits fell to ₦83.2 billion ($54.2 million) from ₦96 billion ($105.8 million).
Kuda’s future
To reach profitability, Kuda said it is taking a bigger bet on lending.
This week, some Kuda customers posted on X that the amounts they owed on overdue loans had been reduced. Kuda said the reductions are part of a campaign by its credit team that gives customers with long-overdue loans “a brief window between now and December 23” to settle.
Today, Kuda’s main loan product is its overdraft, a short-term loan that Oyegun said suited users who were running low “in the last two weeks of the month.” Now Kuda wants to sell the kind of loans big banks offer, like GTBank’s QuickCredit, to customers whose needs have grown.
“As I have grown older, my needs have changed. I want to buy a car or a house,” Nosa Oyegun, Kuda’s chief operating officer, said, describing his time as a Kuda user. The overdraft and other current products will stay, but new loans will be built on top of them.
“We have just offered the overdraft and some other loans here and there, but we have not built the product around credit,” he said. “Kuda 1.0 is done and dusted. It worked. Kuda 2.0 is for us to go deeper into what it means to bank a customer beyond transactions.”

articles.title: Así es la casita autosuficiente de esta familia de Karrantza: “El techo está hecho de tierra y la hierba que va creciendo funciona como aislante y nos protege del sol en el verano y del frío en el invierno”
articles.text:
Erika decidió irse al campo, dejar atrás la ciudad y mudarse con su familia a Karrantza (Bizkaia). Han optado por construir en armonía con el entorno.
“El tejado de la casa es un tejado verde”. Construyeron la casa con materiales locales. De esta manera consiguieron que la mayor parte de su consumo estuviese relacionado con su propio espacio y los productores de la zona. Según explica Erika, son totalmente autónomos en electricidad, tienen su propia producción y son semiautónomos en alimentación.
Paredes de paja y un tejado con hierba
Los cerramientos están realizados con fardos de paja de centeno. Los fardos se hacen con la paja que queda tras la recolección de este cereal. “Lo que queda de cosechar el centeno es la paja. Con esos fardos es con lo que está construida la casa”, explica Erika.
En cuanto al tejado, eligieron una cubrición de tierra vegetal. Sobre esta capa va creciendo la hierba. “No tiene tejas ni nada que se le parezca”.
Erika explica que de esta manera consiguen que haya un aislamiento térmico respecto al exterior. En sus palabras, “Es una forma de construir para que haga de aislante y nos proteja del sol en el verano y del frío en invierno”.
Además, también utilizan el sol para calentar la casa. En una de las fachadas existe una superficie de cristal que deja pasar la radiación solar en invierno. Erika explica que permite que el sol entre y “haga de calefacción pasiva”.
En los meses más fríos también utilizan una chapa de leña. Esta sirve tanto para cocinar como para calefaccionar. “La chapa es con lo que cocinamos en invierno y con lo que calefactamos la casa”.
Electricidad propia, con una inversión inicial
Los paneles solares cubren el consumo de electricidad de la vivienda y de un obrador que tienen junto a ella. En este edificio elaboran parte de los productos que posteriormente comercializan.
Explican que no tienen que pagar la factura de la luz. Sin embargo, tuvieron que hacer una inversión inicial. “No tenemos factura de la luz, pero sí que hemos hecho una inversión grande para tener la instalación de placas fotovoltaicas”.
Esta inversión la consideran a largo plazo. Una vez amortizados los paneles y demás equipamiento, consideran que el sistema es más barato que tener que pagar a una compañía de luz.
Una huerta que exige planificar las compras
Por otra parte, tienen una huerta de subsistencia. En ella planifican qué es lo que tienen que sembrar para que tengan determinados productos durante el año. Por ejemplo, es el caso de las cebollas y puerros, así como de las verduras de temporada. Además, en la parcela tienen árboles frutales.
Los productos que no pueden obtener los buscan básicamente en los agricultores y ganaderos de la zona. En el caso de la carne, miel o lácteos, aprovechan los de productores de la zona. Para otros productos como lentejas o garbanzos, los adquieren a granel (en sacos que les duran muchos meses).
También tienen que recibir suministros externos en el caso del obrador. En este utilizan harina de trigo ecológica. Explican que en Euskadi no hay suficiente producción para cubrir todas sus necesidades. Por ello tienen que traer parte de la materia prima de otros territorios.

articles.title: AI discovers a hidden heart signal that could predict sudden death
articles.text:
AI discovers a hidden heart signal that could predict sudden death
- Date:
- November 14, 2026
- Source:
- University of California - Berkeley
- Summary:
- Scientists have uncovered a hidden warning sign in routine heart scans that could predict sudden cardiac death before it strikes. The AI-powered discovery outperformed conventional screening methods, potentially revealing thousands of people at risk of a fatal heart malfunction that doctors might otherwise miss.
- Share:
More than 300,000 people in the United States die from sudden cardiac arrest each year. This deadly emergency occurs when the heart's electrical system suddenly fails, causing the heart to stop pumping blood. It can strike older adults with known heart conditions as well as seemingly healthy young athletes. Although implanted defibrillators can prevent some of these deaths, doctors have long struggled to determine which patients need them most.
Now, researchers at UC Berkeley have identified a previously overlooked warning signal in routine heart scans that could make it easier to recognize people at risk before a fatal event occurs.
The discovery was made using artificial intelligence trained on more than 440,000 electrocardiograms, or EKGs, collected in Sweden. By comparing the electrical patterns recorded in these scans with information from death certificates, the researchers taught an AI system to recognize subtle differences between healthy individuals, patients with known heart risks, and people who eventually died from sudden cardiac causes.
The team then evaluated the technology using thousands of additional patient records from the United States and Taiwan, testing whether the patterns could reliably identify people at heightened risk in different populations.
AI Detects Hidden Heart Risks That Standard Tests Miss
The results suggest that AI can identify vulnerable patients more effectively than the conventional tests doctors typically rely on. Current screening methods largely focus on how much blood the heart pumps with each contraction, a measurement used to assess whether someone might benefit from an implanted defibrillator.
Using these traditional measurements, doctors can identify a group of patients with an annual sudden cardiac death rate of 4.6%. The AI system, however, identified a group with an annual death rate of 7%, demonstrating a greater ability to distinguish patients facing serious danger.
Importantly, the algorithm also recognized a broader population of people at elevated risk, including thousands who would not normally raise concerns under existing medical guidelines. Most of these individuals would have been classified as relatively low risk using conventional methods.
Another major advantage is that the AI system works with ordinary EKG images, which are already routinely collected in hospitals and medical centers around the world. This means the technology could potentially improve screening without requiring an entirely new type of medical test.
The findings, published in Nature, could eventually help physicians make more informed decisions about who should receive an implanted defibrillator. They also raise an intriguing scientific question about what changes inside the heart produce the electrical patterns that AI has learned to recognize.
"Medical decisions are really hard, and I think that's why AI is so exciting for me," said Ziad Obermeyer, an associate professor at UC Berkeley's School of Public Health and the study's lead author. "We can not only make better decisions, but also start to understand what's actually going on with these patients before their heart stops."
Why Sudden Cardiac Death Is So Difficult to Predict
Sudden cardiac arrest is different from a heart attack. A heart attack happens when blood flow to part of the heart becomes blocked or severely restricted. Cardiac arrest, by contrast, results from a failure of the electrical signals that coordinate the heartbeat.
Immediate CPR and an electrical shock from an automated external defibrillator can sometimes restore the heart's rhythm. However, roughly 90% of people who experience sudden cardiac arrest outside a hospital die within minutes, making early recognition of those at risk especially important.
For Obermeyer, an emergency physician whose research combines artificial intelligence, medicine, and health policy, sudden cardiac death remains one of medicine's most frustrating unsolved problems.
Because victims often die without warning, researchers have limited opportunities to observe what happens inside the heart immediately before it stops. An autopsy may uncover blocked blood vessels, hardened tissue, or other structural abnormalities, but it cannot fully reveal how the heart was functioning in the moments leading up to death.
"One thing that makes the problem very tragic, but also very well suited for AI, is that we have the cure for this problem," Obermeyer said. "If you knew you were one of the people who was going to drop dead, you would go to a cardiologist and you'd get a defibrillator implanted. The problem is that doctors can't figure out who needs one before it's too late."
The Problem With Current Heart Risk Screening
Doctors currently rely heavily on a measurement of how effectively the heart pushes blood out with each beat. Patients whose hearts pump below a specified threshold may be considered candidates for an implantable cardioverter defibrillator, a device that can deliver an electrical shock when a dangerous heart rhythm develops.
But obtaining this measurement generally requires a more extensive medical evaluation. Many people who eventually experience sudden cardiac arrest never receive such testing because they have no obvious reason to suspect they are in danger.
The approach also has limitations for patients who are identified as high risk. About two-thirds of implanted defibrillators in these patients never need to deliver a shock. As a result, many individuals undergo expensive, invasive procedures for potentially fatal emergencies that may never occur.
At the same time, thousands of people who are not recognized as being at risk die unexpectedly each year.
"In some fraction of those people, we could have prevented those deaths if we had just known it in time," Obermeyer said. "There are a lot of lives being lost from people who are dropping dead of sudden cardiac death that are preventable if we just had better AI tools to find these things."
The researchers hope that identifying more accurate warning signs could help doctors direct preventive treatments toward the patients most likely to benefit.
How Researchers Trained AI to Recognize Deadly Heart Patterns
Developing the algorithm required three independent collections of medical data gathered from different parts of the world.
The researchers began with six years of EKG recordings from Sweden's unified healthcare system. By linking these scans to death certificates, they could examine the electrical patterns of patients who later experienced sudden cardiac death and compare them with those of other patients.
The AI learned to identify combinations of spikes, waves, and other characteristics in the recordings that appeared to be associated with increased risk. Once the system had been trained, the team tested it against two additional datasets: two years of anonymized EKG records from a San Diego hospital system and a separate collection of patient data from Taipei.
This international testing helped researchers evaluate whether the algorithm's predictive abilities extended beyond the Swedish population used to develop it.
"Good AI starts with good data," said Obermeyer, who is also part of the joint UCSF-UC Berkeley Computational Precision Health program. "Unfortunately, data like the ones we used for this study are incredibly hard to access. It's a big part of why there's so little clinical AI in use today."
Obtaining and organizing the information was itself a massive undertaking. According to Obermeyer, assembling the datasets took approximately 10 years and involved contributions from two organizations he helped establish, Dandelion Health and Nightingale Open Science. Both organizations work to advance medical research through better access to data and artificial intelligence.
"It's one of the tremendous luxuries of being at Berkeley," Obermeyer said. "You can pursue these projects that just are a slow burn and then have -- hopefully -- a big return when they get over the finish line."
From Hidden Heart Signals to Lifesaving Treatments
The researchers have already begun exploring how the system might be used in actual healthcare settings.
Obermeyer is collaborating with medical systems in Sweden, Taiwan, and the United States to introduce the algorithm into hospital EKG databases. The goal is to examine existing heart scans for signs of elevated risk and identify patients who may benefit from additional monitoring.
Under the proposed approach, physicians would contact patients whose EKGs receive a high-risk assessment and offer them the opportunity to wear a patch that continuously records their heart's electrical activity.
These longer recordings could provide valuable clues about the biological processes responsible for the warning signals detected by the AI. Understanding those processes could help researchers explain why certain hearts are more vulnerable to suddenly developing fatal electrical disturbances.
For some patients, the additional information might ultimately support a recommendation to receive an implanted defibrillator, potentially preventing a sudden and otherwise unexpected death.
Obermeyer has also created a website where people interested in learning about their own risk can provide basic personal information and an email address. The research team can then contact them about EKG analysis when the technology becomes more widely available.
Could AI Reveal New Secrets About the Human Heart?
Beyond its potential to improve the prevention of sudden cardiac death, the discovery highlights how artificial intelligence could help scientists investigate medical mysteries that have resisted conventional approaches.
Rather than simply identifying patients who might need treatment, the algorithm has uncovered patterns in heart activity that researchers do not yet fully understand. Studying those signals could lead to new insights into the electrical disturbances responsible for sudden cardiac death and potentially reveal additional opportunities for prevention.
Obermeyer believes this ability to uncover previously unrecognized biological patterns could become one of AI's most important contributions to medicine, opening new directions for research while helping physicians make better decisions.
"There is also going to be a new way of doing science that comes out of these tools," Obermeyer said, "and it's fun to think about how that starts happening."

articles.title: One UI 9.5 ya está disponible para actualizar términos de privacidad en celulares Samsung
articles.text:
Samsung puso en marcha la beta de One UI 9.5, la nueva versión de su capa de personalización para celulares y tabletas Galaxy. La actualización incorpora cambios en la cámara, nuevas herramientas de salud, funciones de accesibilidad y opciones adicionales para proteger la privacidad de los usuarios.
Por ahora, el programa de pruebas está disponible únicamente para los Galaxy S26, S26+ y S26 Ultra, y en un número limitado de mercados. La compañía surcoreana todavía no confirma una fecha de lanzamiento general ni la lista completa de dispositivos que recibirán la versión estable.
Qué celulares pueden instalar la beta de One UI 9.5
El acceso anticipado a One UI 9.5 está habilitado para los usuarios de la serie Galaxy S26 en Alemania, Corea del Sur, Estados Unidos, India, Polonia y Reino Unido. México no figura entre los países incluidos en el anuncio inicial, por lo que los usuarios de ese mercado deberán esperar una ampliación de la beta o el lanzamiento de la versión estable.
Para sumarse al programa, los propietarios de uno de estos modelos deben abrir la aplicación Samsung Members, ubicar el apartado del programa beta y registrarse en la convocatoria correspondiente. Si la inscripción es aceptada, la descarga queda disponible desde el apartado de actualizaciones del sistema.
Qué celulares podrían recibir la versión estable
Samsung no publicó todavía una lista definitiva de los teléfonos que recibirán la actualización estable. Un listado preliminar elaborado por SamMobile, basado en los ciclos de soporte previos de la marca, contempla modelos de distintas gamas. Ese listado no representa una confirmación oficial y la disponibilidad puede variar según el país y la variante del dispositivo.
Galaxy S:
- Galaxy S26, S26+ y S26 Ultra
- Galaxy S26 FE
- Galaxy S25, S25+ y S25 Ultra
- Galaxy S25 Edge y S25 FE
- Galaxy S24, S24+ y S24 Ultra
- Galaxy S24 FE
Galaxy Z:
- Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra y Z Fold 8
- Galaxy Z Flip 8
- Galaxy Z TriFold
- Galaxy Z Fold 7 y Z Flip 7
- Galaxy Z Flip 7 FE
- Galaxy Z Fold Edición Especial
- Galaxy Z Fold 6 y Z Flip 6
Galaxy A:
- Galaxy A57, A56 y A55
- Galaxy A54
- Galaxy A37, A36 y A35
- Galaxy A27 y A26
- Galaxy A25
- Galaxy A18
- Galaxy A17, A16 y A15 (versiones LTE y 5G)
- Galaxy A08 y A07 (versiones LTE y 5G)
Galaxy M:
- Galaxy M56 y M55
- Galaxy M54 5G
- Galaxy M16, M15 y M06
Galaxy F:
- Galaxy F56 y F55
- Galaxy F36
- Galaxy F16 y F15
- Galaxy F07 y F06
Galaxy XCover:
- Galaxy XCover 7
- Galaxy XCover 7 Pro
La previsión también contempla doce tabletas de las familias Galaxy Tab S y Galaxy Tab Active:
- Galaxy Tab S12 Ultra y Tab S12+
- Galaxy Tab S11 Ultra y Tab S11
- Galaxy Tab S10 Ultra y Tab S10+
- Galaxy Tab S10 FE+ y Tab S10 FE
