articles.title: 100 Millionen Euro: Telekom investiert in das wertvollste KI-Startup Europas
articles.text:
Telekom steigt bei Mistral ein: 100 Millionen Euro für Europas Antwort auf OpenAI
Die Deutsche Telekom steigt beim größten europäischen KI-Unternehmen Mistral AI ein. Die Konzerntochter T.Capital Tech Fund habe bei einer neuen Finanzierungsrunde 100 Millionen Euro in das französische Startup investiert. Das teilte die Telekom auf Nachfrage mit und sprach von einem ersten Schritt zu einer strategischen Partnerschaft. Zuerst hatte der Spiegel darüber berichtet.
Laut Mitteilung planen die Telekom und Mistral, gemeinsam Unternehmen und den öffentlichen Sektor in Deutschland bei der Einführung passgenauer KI zu unterstützen. Die Zusammenarbeit stütze sich auf Investitionen der Telekom in souveräne KI-Infrastruktur in Deutschland und die wachsende Präsenz von Mistral.
„Die europäische Wettbewerbsfähigkeit hängt davon ab, ob wir leistungsstarke KI entwickeln und einsetzen können“, sagte Telekom-Vorstandsmitglied Ferri Abolhassan. Unternehmen müssten dieser Technologie vertrauen und gleichzeitig die Kontrolle über ihre Daten behalten können.
Telekom verdoppelt KI-Rechenleistung in München
Die Telekom nahm im Februar in München eine KI-Fabrik in Betrieb. Wegen der hohen Nachfrage baut der Konzern den Standort aus. Die Telekom investiert knapp eine weitere Viertelmilliarde Euro in die Fabrik und verdoppelt so die Rechenleistung der Anlage.
Zu den Nutzern zählen namhafte Industrieunternehmen wie Siemens und Daimler Trucks. Die Infrastruktur dient unter anderem dem Training von KI-Sprachmodellen, der Robotik-Entwicklung und der Simulation komplexer Produktionsabläufe.
Mistral sammelte 3 Milliarden Euro für KI-Expansion ein
Erst im September hatte sich das französische KI-Startup Mistral in einer Finanzierungsrunde drei Milliarden Euro gesichert. Die Bewertung des 2023 gegründeten Unternehmens stieg auf über 21 Milliarden Euro – die bislang größte Eigenkapitalfinanzierung eines europäischen Technologieunternehmens überhaupt. Mistral positioniert sich als europäischer Gegenentwurf zu US-Unternehmen wie OpenAI, Google und Anthropic.
Das Startup ist nach eigenen Angaben mittlerweile in 20 Ländern aktiv und unterstützt mehr als 125 Großkunden bei unternehmenskritischen KI-Projekten, darunter Airbus, der niederländische Halbleiterausrüster ASML und die Großbank HSBC. ASML hatte im vergangenen Jahr rund 1,3 Milliarden Euro in Mistral investiert und wurde damit größter Anteilseigner.
Im Juli kündigten der US-Technologiekonzern Microsoft und Mistral an, ihre strategische Allianz auszubauen. Mit einer neuen Vereinbarung über mehrere Milliarden Euro wollen die Partner die europäischen Infrastrukturkapazitäten für Künstliche Intelligenz erweitern und hochmoderne KI-Modelle in sensiblen Unternehmen und Behörden verankern.
) Heiße Mädchen warten auf dich — Miss4.fun

articles.title: DDR6 RAM shrinks by 44% while delivering 4X DDR5's baseline bandwidth — JEDEC previews 12.8 GT/s modules with up to 1 terabyte of capacity per slot
articles.text:
DDR6 RAM shrinks by 44% while delivering 4 times more bandwidth than DDR5 — JEDEC previews 12.8 GT/s modules with up to 1 terabyte of capacity per slot
Today's best RAM will look huge compared to upcoming DDR6 memory. JEDEC has just released a preview of the DDR6 specification, confirming that next-generation memory modules will be 44% shorter than DDR5. That is only the physical aspect, though. From a performance perspective, DDR6 will debut at 12.8 GT/s, more than double DDR5's baseline transfer rate, while also quadrupling the memory bandwidth per memory module thanks to a new design.
JEDEC's DDR6 preview highlights improvements in various areas, including performance, capacity, reliability, and power efficiency. These advancements align with the upgrades DDR5 brought to the table when it launched.
One of the most notable differences is that DDR6 memory modules will measure just 74mm in length, 44% shorter than DDR5’s 133mm memory modules. This makes DDR6 only 6% longer than DDR5 SO-DIMM modules, which you commonly find in laptops and mini-PCs.
JEDEC has maintained the pin count for many years, sticking to 288 pins for DDR4 and DDR5. However, DDR6 may finally break that mould. Given the substantial reduction in length with DDR6 and the data bus width upgrade, it is reasonable to assume that DDR6 will have a completely different pinout and density. Sadly, JEDEC has not revealed the pin count for DDR6.
Early rumors suggested that DDR6 may be limited to CAMM form factors to feed the AI boom. However, JEDEC's announcement at least does not rule out other form factors. It appears JEDEC is still determining which form factors DDR6 will use. Potential options include RDIMM, UDIMM, and CAMM formats, just like DDR5.
DDR6 Specifications
| Header Cell - Column 0 | DDR6 | DDR5 | DDR4 | 
|---|---|---|---|
| Baseline JEDEC Transfer Rates (MT/s) | 12,800 | 4,800 | 1,600 | 
| Baseline JEDEC Bandwidth Per Module (GB/s) | 153.6 | 38.4 | 12.8 | 
| Peak JEDEC Transfer Rates (MT/s) | 14,400 | 9,200 | 3,200 | 
| Peak Baseline Bandwidth Per Module (GB/s) | 172.8 | 73.6 | 25.6 | 
| Channels | 4 x 24-bit | 2 x 32-bit | 1 x 64-bit | 
| Burst Length | ? | BL16 | BL8 | 
| Banks | 64 | 32 | 16 | 
| Nominal Operating Voltage (V) | ? | 1.2 | 1.1 | 
| Pins | ? | 288 | 288 | 
| Length (mm) | 74 | 133 | 133 | 
Notably, JEDEC has increased the data bus width in DDR6 to 96 bits, a 50% boost over DDR5's 64 bits. The channel architecture for DDR6 will also change substantially. While DDR4 and DDR5 leveraged a single 64-bit channel and two 32-bit sub-channels, DDR6 takes a different approach. JEDEC will implement a design with four 24-bit sub-channels.
Using the baseline for comparison, DDR6 offers up to 153.6 GB/s of total module bandwidth, compared to DDR5's 38.4 GB/s. That is a 4X uplift in bandwidth. If we compare DDR5-9200 RDIMMs, which max out at 73.6 GB/s per module, with DDR6-12800 RDIMMs, the uplift is a little more than double.
Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.
At least on the server side, DDR6 RDIMMs will start at DDR6-12800, whereas DDR5 RDIMMs topped out at DDR5-9200. JEDEC anticipates DDR6 reaching DDR6-14400 and beyond. This is for the server and enterprise market, though. It remains to be seen which DDR6 speed will launch in the consumer market. DDR5 commenced at DDR5-4800.
DDR6 may be shorter than DDR5, but it makes up for it by having 2X the bank count. This will help push higher data rates and capacities. DDR6 will support 128Gb (16GB) dies, which represents a massive leap. We are looking at 4X the density of early DDR5 memory modules. Instead of placing chips side by side on the PCB, DDR6 enables die stacking, allowing manufacturers to place multiple dies on top of each other via Through-Silicon Vias (TSVs).
Consumer DDR5 memory modules currently sit at 64GB per module, while server RDIMMs have reached 512GB. DDR6 could raise module capacity to 128GB or 256GB and potentially scale RDIMMs to 1TB or more per slot.
DDR6 has no official launch date. Many believe 2029 is a realistic target for commercialization. However, in the current state of things, it would be a miracle if DDR6 had no setbacks.
Download the Tom's Hardware app for up-to-the-minute updates on iOS and Android. Also follow Tom's Hardware on Google News, or add us as a preferred source, to get our latest news, analysis, & reviews in your feeds.
Zhiye Liu is a news editor, memory reviewer, and SSD tester at Tom’s Hardware. Although he loves everything that’s hardware, he has a soft spot for CPUs, GPUs, and RAM.

- thestryker If it doesn't change between now and the specification actually being published this should mean the death of SODIMMs. The last couple of generations have both been a bit under 70mm long so with this being 73mm I cannot see why it would be carried forward. On the UDIMM side of things I'm wondering if there will be any latency penalties having packages not all being next to each other. DDR5 SODIMMs of 16GB+ have two packages side by side and then two above, but all DDR5 UDIMMs have them side by side. On the topic of consumer products there's the potential that channels could be side by side length wise and not take up much more room than a single UDIMM does today.
I believe this is the first confirmation that DDR6 channels are going to be effectively 96-bit though it was expected given that LPDDR6 is. DDR6 is going to be the biggest fundamental change to socketed memory since the advent of dual channel. The base configuration, on paper, has a dual channel bandwidth of ~307GB/s which effectively doubles the best available today. This ought to mean a lot for integrated graphics and the amount of bandwidth per core as CPU core counts are increasing.
Typically we would see client products first (less validation required), but in the current market I just don't see that happening. DDR6 was also supposed to have the specification rolling out this year, but that obviously isn't happening either. I suspect next year is when it will be finalized and then it could be in enterprise as early as 2028 depending on demand and how well MRDIMMs are scaling. I'd like to see it pop up in client ASAP, but I wouldn't really bet on any earlier than end of 2029 to some time in 2030. LPDDR6 will likely hit client much earlier than DDR6 does so it will be interesting to see what sort of productization it sees.

articles.title: 700 euros por una ceremonia "dog-friendly": el negocio de las bodas ya no está en los novios, sino en las mascotas
articles.text:
En España hay 15,2 millones de mascotas, casi la mitad de ellas perros, según su primer censo oficial. Para hacernos una idea del alcance de esa cifra, superan en número a los niños. Y por goleada. Ante semejante panorama no sorprende que cada vez más parejas decidan que sus compañeros peludos estén presentes durante sus bodas o que (también) cada vez resulte más fácil encontrar negocios especializados en el cuidado de mascotas durante los enlaces. Incluso hay quien habla ya de la figura del ‘dog wedding planner’, profesionales que garantizan ceremonias dog-friendly.
Nuevos tiempos, nuevas bodas.
¿Qué hacemos con Toby? Ponte en situación. Tú y tu pareja os casáis dentro de un par de meses y ya tenéis escogido el lugar de la ceremonia, el menú del banquete, los trajes, las flores, la música, si habrá o no bus hasta el restaurante… Incluso tenéis reservada ya la luna de miel. Queda sin embargo un fleco pendiente: ¿Qué hacer con vuestro perro?
Teniendo en cuenta que ‘el día de autos’ vuestras familias y amigos más cercanos estarán en la boda, ¿quién podría cuidar de vuestra mascota? ¿Es buena idea llevarla a un hotel canino? ¿No sería bonito que estuviera presente en la boda y compartiese con vosotros un día tan especial? ¿Y si se encarga de llevar las alianzas? Pero en ese caso… ¿Quién cuidaría de ella durante el resto de la ceremonia y el banquete? ¿Y si el animal se estresa entre tanta gente?
“Nos lo pedían”. Preguntas parecidas a esas fueron las que hace un tiempo llevaron a Jenny y Jaime a poner en marcha Wedding Guau, un servicio de Zaragoza pensado para que los perros puedan participar en las bodas sin que eso suponga un quebradero de cabeza para los novios ni una experiencia estresante para el animal. Organizan el mejor plan para el perro, se encargan de cuidarlo el día del ‘si quiero’ y luego se encargan de devolverlo a su hogar para que descanse.
La idea, explica Jenny a Aragón Digital, “nació de escuchar las necesidades de las familias”. “Había muchas familias que querían que sus perros les acompañaran en un día tan especial, pero siempre surgía la misma pregunta: ¿Quién se encarga del perrete?” Ella ya tenía experiencia en el cuidado de mascotas, así que no le costó dar el paso. Ahora Wedding Guau aspira a darse a conocer dentro y fuera de Aragón.
¿Es un caso único? Para nada. Si buscas en la plataforma especializada Bodas.net o curioseas en Google te encontrarás con negocios parecidos en Cataluña, Madrid, Canarias o Galicia, entre otras regiones. La idea es más o menos la misma en todos los casos: no se trata solo de llevar el perro a la boda y vigilarlo mientras dura la ceremonia y el banquete. El servicio arranca mucho antes, con la planificación del evento, una entrevista para saber qué quieren los novios y un período para que el animal se adapte al cuidador que se encargará de cuidarlo el gran día.
Los protagonistas. “El objetivo es simple: que la pareja disfrute del día sin estrés y que la experiencia sea positiva también para su compañero de vida”, resume otra de las empresas que se encargan de velar por que los enlaces sean pet-friendly. Tampoco es raro que incluyan un hotel canino, servicio que permiten extender hasta la luna de miel.
“El perro se convierte en el protagonista total, los novios pasan a un segundo plano”, bromea Javier, responsable de un negocio con sede en Galicia que ofrece un servicio de acompañamiento similar, en una entrevista con Faro de Vigo. Sus tarifas oscilan entre 350 y 700 euros, aunque no se limitan a la jornada de la ceremonia. Más o menos un mes antes empieza a familiarizarse con la mascota y el día grande se encarga de recogerla en casa, pasearla, dejarla impoluta y velar por que esté cómoda y tranquila antes de llevarla a descansar.
¿Es tan extraño? No. Servicios como el que prestan Javier o Jenny conectan con un fenómeno mucho más amplio y que no es (ni mucho menos) exclusivo de España: a medida que ganan peso en nuestros hogares, las familias gastan cada vez más en servicios orientados al cuidado de las mascotas. Incluso planifican sus vacaciones y ocio pensando en ellas. Hay un dato que ayuda a entender el fenómeno: según cálculos de EAE Business School, el negocio de los animales de compañía mueve ya casi 5.800 millones de euros anuales en España y, en general, la economía pet-money crece a un ritmo del 8,3%.
“En la España actual, cuidar de una mascota se ha convertido en una decisión económica con retos y gastos que los dueños de los animales afrontan al considerarlos uno más de la familia. Y, como tal, apuestan por alimentos premium, cuidados de veterinarios o juguetes y accesorios”, reflexiona Paulo Sartorato, profesor del EAE Business School. Más allá de la cuestión cualitativa, está la cuantitativa. El censo de mascotas se ha disparado cerca de un 14% en cinco años, según datos oficiales del Gobierno.
Cambian los hogares… y las bodas. Esa es la otra clave. No solo está cambiando la configuración de los hogares, el peso que en ellos tienen las mascotas y nuestra disposición a gastarnos dinero en servicios orientados a su cuidado. También las bodas están transformándose. El patrón tradicional que se replicó durante décadas es cada vez más flexible y no cuesta encontrarse con ceremonias temáticas, adults-only o que se completan con “pre” y “post-bodas”. También con nuevos servicios, como los tatuajes nupciales.
Imágenes | Vasylyna Kucherepa (Unsplash), Desiray Green (Unsplash) y Ministerio de Derechos Sociales
En Xataka | En España ya hay tanatorios que permiten a las mascotas despedirse de sus dueños muertos

articles.title: What Canadian startups risk when they rely on a single AI provider | BetaKit
articles.text:
As Canadian startups race to integrate AI into their products and services, many are relying on third-party models and infrastructure to power their businesses.
These technologies can help companies develop products faster and with fewer upfront costs, but they also introduce risks that may become difficult to manage as those businesses grow.
“A lot of startups are wiring their entire product to one AI provider and treating that as a permanent decision.”
LSP, Zoho Canada
AI model providers can raise prices, change their terms of service, or introduce competing products of their own. For startups that have built their businesses around a particular provider, those decisions can threaten profit margins, undermine their competitive advantage, and leave them facing costly technical challenges.
Chandrashekar Lalapet Srinivas Prasanna, known as LSP, the managing director of Zoho Canada, worries that startups are becoming increasingly vulnerable to decisions made by their technology suppliers.
“You end up competing against the company that supplies a core part of your product,” LSP said. “That’s difficult if most of what you offer is an interface or a light workflow on top of their model, because they can often ship something similar with better economics.”
According to LSP, startups building products around third-party AI models risk losing control over their operating costs and product development. He believes founders need to consider those dependencies before they become too expensive to undo.
When the supplier calls the shots
A June report from RBC noted that three US tech companies now account for 85 percent of Canada’s cloud infrastructure spending. In its National Artificial Intelligence Strategy, Canada’s federal government warned that Canadian businesses building on technology largely controlled outside the country are “competing on infrastructure they do not own, govern, or meaningfully influence.”
“A lot of startups are wiring their entire product to one AI provider and treating that as a permanent decision,” LSP said. “It feels smart in the moment because you move faster and spend less on engineering. The problem shows up later.”
LSP’s concern is vendor lock-in, where a company becomes so dependent on one technology supplier that switching to another becomes difficult or expensive. As startups develop their products, their prompts, data retrieval systems, and methods for evaluating AI performance can become closely tied to the requirements of a particular model.
“If your context structures, evaluation tests, and tool abstractions are already locked to one provider’s formats, you will only discover how expensive it is to leave when you actually need to leave,” he said.
Vendor lock-in also carries financial risks. LSP warned that higher supplier costs could erode a startup’s profit margins, particularly if switching would be prohibitively expensive. He also questioned how startups can protect their competitive advantage when their core technology can be accessed by competitors.
“An interface that just calls the same model everyone else can call is hard to defend,” LSP added. “Investors notice when the core capability can be replicated by competitors or by the model provider itself.”
The price of true independence
Zoho has taken a relatively expensive route to technological independence. The company, which offers a suite of cloud software applications for businesses, operates data centres in multiple regions, including Canada, and has invested in developing its own AI models rather than relying entirely on third-party providers. The strategy gives Zoho greater control over its infrastructure and the direction of its products.
“Owning the relevant parts of the stack gives us the ability to adapt without being forced into someone else’s timeline or terms,” LSP said.
But operating data centres requires significant investment in physical infrastructure and technical staff. Zoho also accepts that competitors using external models can sometimes introduce new capabilities faster.
“The biggest trade-off is the sustained investment in capital, people, and time,” LSP explained.
What to own, what to outsource
Most startups don’t have the resources to build their own technology stacks, and LSP acknowledged that total independence is unrealistic even for established software companies. His advice is to identify which parts of a product are worth retaining control over, and which can be outsourced without creating an excessive dependence on a single supplier.
For Canadian startups, Zoho offers one way to reduce that dependence without having to build their own infrastructure. According to LSP, Zoho’s ownership of its AI models and underlying infrastructure makes customers less vulnerable to disruptions when outside providers change their pricing, policies, or access terms.
“The point isn’t to avoid external technology. It’s to make sure you still own the knowledge and the decision rights that let you adapt while the models keep changing.”
LSP, Zoho Canada
“Controlling where your data is stored is no longer enough,” LSP said. “Businesses also need to know who controls the models and infrastructure that process it. Zoho owns both layers and has never sold customer data.”
For startups developing their own products, LSP believes external AI models and infrastructure can still play an important role, provided their software is designed to accommodate another provider. Still, he encouraged founders to calculate the cost of switching while they still have the ability to do so.
LSP suggests starting by considering what would happen if their provider changed its terms tomorrow. Could they continue operating and improving their products? Could they move their data retrieval systems and AI performance tests to another provider, or would doing so require extensive engineering work?
He also encouraged startups to consider what information they’re sharing with their suppliers, including usage patterns and corrections that help improve AI systems. Retaining control over that knowledge, he argued, is essential to building a business that can adapt as the underlying technology changes.
“The point isn’t to avoid external technology,” LSP said. “It’s to make sure you still own the knowledge and the decision rights that let you adapt while the models keep changing.”
PRESENTED BY
Meet Zia, Zoho’s AI assistant built to automate tasks, deliver insights, and boost productivity in your everyday business operations
Feature image courtesy Unsplash. Photo by Immo Wegmann.

articles.title: Apple is hiring engineers to build its own AI agent
articles.text:
Apple is working on its own AI agent that can perform a range of tasks for you, including browsing the web, working across apps, writing code, and calling services. That’s according to a job listing spotted by Bloomberg, which says Apple is looking for an engineer to lead the creation of an agentic AI assistant.
Apple is hiring engineers to build its own AI agent
Apple’s job listing describes an AI agent that can browse the web, work across apps, and call services.
An AI agent from Apple would put the iPhone maker in the running to compete with the likes of Meta’s Muse, OpenAI’s Dots, Anthropic’s Duet, and Google’s Tasks. Muse, ChatGPT, and Perplexity can already take control of a computer through their Mac apps, while Google just started letting Gemini do the same.
Apple began rolling out its AI-upgraded Siri in September, which you can use to ask questions about what’s on your screen, as well as perform actions across apps. It looks like Apple is planning to give Siri more agentic capabilities, as a report from Bloomberg suggests the company could add the ability to rotate and crop images in Photos, or organize Safari tabs. This lines up with the company’s new job listing, which says the engineer will work closely with teams across its Siri, UI Frameworks, and Apple Foundation Models divisions.
“People already do their most valuable work by moving fluidly between tools: a browser, a document, a terminal, an editor, a service,” the job listing says. “We’re building AI agents that can do the same… These agents plan and carry out multi-step tasks across apps, browsers, command lines, code, and APIs, and they can coordinate specialized sub-agents along the way.”
With its upcoming iOS 27.3 update, Apple is also giving developers the ability to integrate Siri AI into “all apps.” This is rolling out as part of a Developer Preview and will eventually allow Siri to perform tasks across a wider range of apps.

articles.title: Using NVIDIA Run:ai GPU Fractioning on Amazon EKS | Amazon Web Services
articles.text:
Artificial Intelligence
Using NVIDIA Run:ai GPU Fractioning on Amazon EKS
GPU sharing is not new: Multi-Instance GPU (MIG), time-slicing, and Multi-Process Service (MPS) address different isolation and utilization needs. NVIDIA Run:ai GPU Fractioning builds on MPS with Kubernetes-integrated scheduling, per-Pod memory contracts, enforcement, and metrics.
NVIDIA Run:ai is AI workload orchestration software for Kubernetes. Its GPU Fractioning Operator can help several teams share one or two GPUs on Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS). Notebooks, model evaluations, and small inference services can leave teams waiting even when GPU memory remains available. In this walkthrough’s baseline, the NVIDIA device plugin exposes the single GPU as one nvidia.com/gpu resource, with GPU sharing disabled. Two Pods each requesting nvidia.com/gpu: 1 cannot run concurrently on that node, even when their combined GPU-memory demand fits.
NVIDIA Run:ai GPU Fractioning adds Kubernetes scheduling integration, enforced GPU-memory limits, and per-Pod metrics to software-based sharing. The approach applies to NVIDIA GPUs that meet the GPU Fractioning Operator’s hardware and software requirements, including GPUs without MIG. We use one Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) g5.xlarge instance with an NVIDIA A10G Tensor Core GPU as the validated example. Other configurations require compatibility checks and validation.
NVIDIA announced the open source release of NVIDIA Run:ai on October 13, 2026. This example uses two of its four modular components: KAI Scheduler and GPU Fractioning Operator. KAI Resource Management and Workload Map address organizational governance and additional workload types, outside this walkthrough’s scope.
In this post, we show how to build a custom Amazon Linux 2023 (AL2023) image and configure GPU-memory sharing on Amazon EKS. In the validated G5/A10G example, you establish a whole-GPU baseline, give each Pod an 8 GiB memory contract, and verify 6 GiB allocations. You then inspect per-Pod metrics, test rejection of a 9 GiB allocation, and clean up the disposable environment.
Choose a GPU sharing approach
MIG provides hardware partitions on supported GPUs. Device-plugin time-slicing shares a GPU without replica memory or fault isolation. MPS permits concurrent CUDA processes. Fault containment depends on configuration. NVIDIA Run:ai GPU Fractioning adds enforced per-container memory limits and supports time-slicing (default) or sm-sharing compute modes. NVIDIA documents separate workload error domains for its default mode and a shared error domain for sm-sharing. These are not security guarantees. This walkthrough tests memory limits, not fault containment or compute performance. A memory limit does not reserve proportional compute.
Amazon EKS documents several GPU sharing options: MIG, time-slicing with the NVIDIA device plugin, and time-slicing with the NVIDIA DRA driver and Karpenter. For guidance on choosing among them, see the GPU sharing guidance in the Amazon EKS Best Practices Guide. Choose GPU fractioning when you need enforced per-Pod GPU-memory limits on GPUs without MIG and can run fixed-size GPU node groups.
Dynamic Resource Allocation (DRA) provides Kubernetes APIs for requesting and allocating devices. GPU sharing and isolation depend on the device driver’s implementation and enabled features. KAI Scheduler and GPU Operator support DRA. This walkthrough uses NvFractions annotations, not DRA.
GPU fractioning can help interactive notebooks with idle periods, short evaluation jobs, GPU compatibility tests, and small inference services. Choose each GPU-memory request from measured peak usage plus overhead, then test latency under concurrent load. The demonstrated density improvement does not establish a throughput gain or a universal cost reduction.
Solution overview
The following diagram shows the validated single-GPU environment in the US East (Ohio) Region (us-east-2). You use the AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI), eksctl, Helm, and Packer to build and operate it. The Amazon EKS control plane runs Kubernetes version 1.36 in an AWS managed Amazon Virtual Private Cloud (Amazon VPC), separate from the customer VPC. It connects to EC2 workers in private subnets of the customer VPC.
An m7i.large system node hosts the operator controllers and KAI Scheduler. KAI Scheduler places both Pods on a tainted g5.xlarge with one A10G containing 23,028 MiB of GPU memory.
Each Pod has an 8 GiB GPU-memory limit and allocates 6 GiB of GPU memory. The GPU worker uses custom AL2023 with the NVIDIA R615 driver branch, NVIDIA Container Toolkit, and containerd. It runs fractiond with Node Resource Interface (NRI) integration and MPS for sharing. The metricsd daemon exports per-Pod GPU-memory metrics.
Implementation walkthrough
The walkthrough uses the AWS Samples repository. Confirm the prerequisites and validated component versions, then complete Steps 1 through 10.
Prerequisites
Use an AWS account with permissions for Amazon EKS, AWS CloudFormation, Amazon VPC, Amazon EC2, Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS), AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM), and AWS Systems Manager for Amazon Machine Image (AMI) discovery. Confirm quota and capacity for g5.xlarge, the system node, and a temporary m5.xlarge image builder. Install AWS CLI v2, eksctl, kubectl, Helm, Packer, Git, jq, and curl.
Use your normal AWS credential provider: a named profile, AWS IAM Identity Center, an assumed role, or access-key environment variables. Prefer temporary credentials. AWS_SESSION_TOKEN is required when using temporary access keys. The examples use us-east-2. Another Region must support the selected Amazon EKS version and instance types.
Before choosing another GPU, check NVIDIA’s GPU Operator hardware list, the selected driver’s hardware support, and the GPU Fractioning Operator prerequisites. Hardware support alone does not establish fractioning compatibility. This walkthrough validates the G5/A10G configuration only. The AMI build targets x86_64. Check CUDA compatibility and memory headroom: The two 8 GiB contracts require room for both contracts and runtime overhead. Smaller devices need smaller contracts and adjusted probes.
The walkthrough creates billable resources, including an Amazon EKS control plane, a NAT gateway, instances, volumes, and an AMI snapshot. Use a disposable environment and complete cleanup when validation finishes.
Use the validated AL2023 stack
At the time of validation, the EKS-optimized AL2023 NVIDIA image provided R580 and R595 driver branches. GPU Fractioning Operator v0.1.7 requires R615 or newer. R615 is short-lived and is not the GPU Operator default. This example builds a custom standard Amazon EKS 1.36 AL2023 image with AMI-owned driver and toolkit. It does not use an operator-managed driver container on another OS. The table records lab validation, not vendor support certification.
| Component | Validated version | 
| Amazon EKS | 1.36 | 
| GPU | NVIDIA A10G, 23,028 MiB | 
| NVIDIA driver / Container Toolkit | 615.71.10 / 1.20.1-1 | 
| containerd | 2.3.5 with NRI | 
| GPU Operator / device plugin | 26.7.1 / 0.20.1 | 
| KAI Scheduler / Fractioning Operator | 0.18.5 / 0.1.7 | 
We validated this walkthrough on October 22, 2026, using NVIDIA driver 615.71.10. On November 18, 2026, after updating the GPU node taint, we repeated every step except the Step 3 image build, using an image with the same driver. The results matched. The table lists the tested component versions, not a permanent support matrix. Recheck the Amazon EKS AMI documentation and NVIDIA prerequisites before changing any component.
Step 1: Clone and configure
Clone the repository, then create a local configuration file from the provided example and restrict its permissions:
After cloning, use walkthrough.env for configuration and run.sh for each stage. Generated files and kubeconfig stay in the ignored .state directory. GPU_INSTANCE_TYPE selects the instance type. Changing it alone does not establish compatibility.
Defaults and optional authentication settings in walkthrough.env
Never commit credentials. The local configuration file is ignored by Git. Confirm the active identity before provisioning:
Run stages separately to inspect results, or use ./run.sh walkthrough to run through the memory-limit test. Cleanup is always a separate action.
Step 2: Create the disposable cluster
Run the following command to create the disposable Amazon EKS cluster and its system node:
The command provisions an Amazon EKS cluster running Kubernetes version 1.36, a dedicated VPC with one NAT gateway, OpenID Connect (OIDC) integration, and a private m7i.large managed node.
Selected fields from config/eksctl-cluster.yaml.tpl
Step 3: Build the custom AL2023 image
Run the following command to build the custom AL2023 image with the R615 driver branch:
The script discovers a public builder subnet and the recommended standard Amazon EKS AMI for Kubernetes 1.36 on AL2023. Packer installs the current patch release from the R615 driver branch and the toolkit, configures the NVIDIA runtime, checks package state, and creates an encrypted image. The Region-specific AMI ID is stored in .state/ami-id.
NVIDIA_DRIVER_VERSION selects the R615 branch. It is not an exact patch pin. The workflow records the discovered driver version with the AMI ID and uses that version in AMI and node-group tags. Read .state/installed-driver-version for the version observed in your build. For production, pin exact packages and the base image in your own build and validate a supported driver-branch upgrade.
You need this step only because the EKS-optimized AL2023 NVIDIA AMI did not include the R615 driver branch at the time of validation. Prefer an EKS-optimized NVIDIA AMI once the driver that it selects for your GPU and the remaining host prerequisites meet the GPU Fractioning Operator requirements. Check the driver versions in the Amazon EKS AMI releases on GitHub. The sample’s scripts currently require the R615 driver and metadata from the image build, so using a stock AMI also requires script changes.
Relevant Packer settings from ami/eks-al2023-r615.pkr.hcl
SOURCE_AMI_ID and PACKER_SUBNET_ID are optional overrides for an approved base image or builder subnet. Rebuild and test images when the operating system or GPU stack changes.
Step 4: Add the GPU worker
Run the following command to add a GPU managed node group that uses the custom image:
By default, the managed node group uses the custom image and stays at one On-Demand g5.xlarge, the validated GPU worker. A GPU taint excludes ordinary workloads. The script disables eksctl’s NVIDIA device-plugin installation because GPU Operator manages that component.
Selected fields from config/eksctl-gpu-nodegroup.yaml.tpl
Step 5: Install GPU Operator and inspect the host
Run the following command to install GPU Operator and inspect the GPU worker’s host configuration:
GPU Operator 26.7.1 supplies the device plugin and Kubernetes integrations. Its configuration preserves the image-owned driver and toolkit:
The same command runs a temporary privileged inspection Pod on the GPU worker, prints the host configuration, and removes the Pod. The validated node reports:
Observed host configuration
On this AL2023 node, /var/run is a symbolic link to /run. Both paths identify the same socket. Limit privileged inspection to the disposable environment and confirm the Pod is removed.
Step 6: Establish the whole-GPU baseline
Run the following command to test whole-GPU scheduling before fractioning is installed:
Each baseline Pod requests and limits nvidia.com/gpu to 1. The test assumes one available physical GPU with sharing disabled: One Pod runs and the other remains Pending. This demonstrates the whole-device scheduling constraint before fractioning is installed. On multi-GPU nodes, adapt this baseline and verify that both fractional workloads use the same GPU.
Measured baseline result
The script checks this state and removes both baseline Pods.
Step 7: Install KAI Scheduler and GPU Fractioning Operator
Run the following command to install KAI Scheduler, which includes GPU Fractioning Operator:
The pinned KAI Scheduler 0.18.5 chart includes GPU Fractioning Operator 0.1.7. The values turn on NvFractions and per-Pod metrics while retaining GPU-stack version checks. The optional nvidia.com/container.<name>.gpu-compute.mode annotation selects compute mode. These workloads leave the default unchanged.
Relevant fields from helm/kai-values.yaml
In the validation, FractiondReady, MpsdReady, and Ready are True. DriverUpgradeInProgress is False with reason NoDriverUpgrade, consistent with the AMI retaining driver ownership.
Step 8: Run the positive sharing test
Run the following command to deploy two Pods with 8 GiB GPU-memory contracts:
Each Pod requests and limits memory to 8 GiB and selects kai-scheduler. Neither requests a whole nvidia.com/gpu resource. The repository applies these scheduling fields and runs a CUDA probe that allocates 6 GiB:
Essential fields from kubernetes/fraction-8gi-pods.yaml
Measured positive result
The script verifies matching node names and GPU UUIDs. In the validation, both Pods see 8,192 MiB and report allocation_succeeded_mib=6144. Those checks establish placement on one physical GPU, the bounded device view, and successful allocations within each contract.
Measured allocation output from each Pod
Observe memory while both Pods remain active
The gpu_fractioning_gpu_memory_used_bytes metric attributes memory by Pod and GPU UUID. The observed 6,394 MiB (about 6.24 GiB) per Pod exceeds the probe’s 6,144 MiB allocation by 250 MiB. Metrics can include CUDA context and runtime overhead. This experiment does not measure that breakdown. Retain workload identity and request, limit, and usage values together when monitoring the shared device.
Measured per-Pod metric series
Step 9: Verify rejection above the limit
Run the following command to test an allocation that exceeds the 8 GiB contract:
This command removes the positive-test Pods and creates one Pod with an 8 GiB contract that attempts a 9 GiB allocation. The probe reports:
Measured over-limit result
Measured negative-test Pod status
Here, cudaMalloc returns an out-of-memory error, which the probe handles before exiting with code 0. Completed is expected, not OOMKilled. This demonstrates allocation rejection, not container termination or general fault isolation.
Step 10: Clean up
Capture the VPC ID before deleting the cluster. The independent checks that follow use the default cluster name and Region. Substitute your configured values if you changed them.
Capture the VPC ID
Remove the disposable environment
Standard cleanup removes the test namespace, Helm releases, and disposable cluster while preserving the custom AMI and its Amazon EBS snapshot.
Verify resource deletion
Expect explicit resource-not-found responses for deleted resources. Authentication or permission errors do not establish deletion. Also inspect remaining node groups and cluster-tagged instances. If cleanup fails, inspect CloudFormation events and resolve owned dependencies before retrying. An absent Amazon EKS endpoint does not prove that its VPC is gone.
Use ./run.sh cleanup-all only when the custom AMI and its Amazon EBS snapshot are no longer needed. If image deletion is refused, confirm the AMI ID and sample ownership tag. Do not bypass the safeguard.
Production considerations
Treat this as a behavior validation. Use trusted workloads and apply least-privilege IAM, namespace controls, approved images, and admission rules for fraction requests. Choose whole GPUs or MIG on supported hardware when stronger isolation is required.
The pinned fractioning daemons use privileged containers, host PID access, and NRI/MPS host mounts. Restrict their deployment and configuration to trusted administrators.
Allow headroom for CUDA contexts, caches, batching, and runtime overhead. Measure latency and throughput under concurrent load. Monitor allocation failures, MPS health, NRI connectivity, and GPU errors. Pin the base AMI, driver, toolkit, device plugin, operator, scheduler, and workload images as one tested combination. Rebuild images and test rollback before rollout.
This walkthrough requires pre-provisioned GPU capacity. It does not configure or validate GPU-fraction-aware autoscaling. The fractional Pods select kai-scheduler, request no nvidia.com/gpu resource, and use a nodeSelector that targets a node group fixed at one node. Karpenter support for secondary schedulers is an open feature request (issue #742 on GitHub). The custom image cannot run on Amazon EKS Auto Mode-managed nodes, because Auto Mode selects and manages their AMI. A cluster can mix Auto Mode-managed nodes with managed node groups, but we did not validate this walkthrough in such a cluster.
Teams that use Karpenter can reference the same custom AMI by ID in an EC2NodeClass. The autoscaling limit still applies. We did not validate this path.
KAI Scheduler is a second scheduler. It handles queueing and placement for Pods that select it. If you already use Kueue, decide which component owns queueing for GPU workloads before you adopt KAI Scheduler.
We recommend running the Amazon EKS node monitoring agent on GPU nodes. In a November 18, 2026 regression run, the agent ran on the custom R615 image with MPS sharing active and reported healthy GPU conditions throughout the sharing and limit tests. That run did not test fault detection. Because GPU Operator already runs a Data Center GPU Manager (DCGM) host engine, configure the agent to use that host engine instead of its bundled one.
Conclusion
In this post, we showed how to configure GPU-memory fractioning on Amazon EKS with a custom AL2023 image, using G5/A10G as the validated example. The approach extends to compatible NVIDIA GPUs after checking prerequisites and validating the selected configuration. You established the whole-GPU baseline, ran two bounded workloads on the same GPU, inspected per-Pod memory usage, and verified rejection of an allocation above the limit. Fractioning can improve access to existing capacity when workload memory fits. Production adoption also requires isolation controls and performance testing.
To repeat the experiment, clone the AWS Samples repository and compare your results with its validated evidence. Explore the GPU Fractioning Operator documentation and the Amazon EKS accelerated AMI guidance before adapting the example to your workloads.

articles.title: Applications open for Kora Collective’s Spring 2027 founder cohort - Disrupt Africa
articles.text:
Applications are now open for the Spring 2027 cohort of the Kora Collective, a private network for seed-to-Series A founders building for emerging markets.
The Kora Collective is aimed at founders who are past day zero, have found traction, and are now focused on scaling, whether through bigger teams, new markets or better products. Its members are backed by investors including Coinbase, Digital Currency Group, Kraken, Hustle Fund, Jump and Cadenza.
The Spring 2027 cohort will bring together 15 founders, and will kick off in London in April. Members are placed in a small peer group of founders at a similar stage and in the same vertical across markets, and are paired with a coach.
They also take part in off-the-record sessions with operators who have built category-defining companies, reached US$1 billion-plus valuations and exited, and are connected one-on-one with senior venture capitalists matched to them based on fit.
For now, the collective is focused on two areas – payments and money movement, and credit, but an artificial intelligence (AI) track, covering agents, automation and intelligent infrastructure, is set to be added in future.
According to the Kora Collective, its existing members have processed more than US2.7 billion in combined volume, raised an average of US$6 million, and serve more than 10 countries across Africa, Asia and Latin America.
Founders have until December 18 to apply here.

articles.title: Welcome to GTA VI day!
articles.text:
Well, it's finally here. After 13 years, countless rumors, trailers, delays, and a level of anticipation few games have ever experienced, Grand Theft Auto VI is officially launched.
The hype has translated into extraordinary sales, too. GTA VI is estimated to have generated more than $1.5 billion in preorders. Early reviews have been overwhelmingly positive, with critics praising Rockstar's ridiculously detailed recreation of Vice City, its living, breathing open world, and the story of Jason and Lucia.
Of course, there's plenty to debate beyond the hype. GTA VI is launching exclusively on PS5 and Xbox, with no PC version in sight. And despite all the visual wizardry, Rockstar has settled on a 30 fps target across consoles, including the PS5 Pro. For some, that's a reasonable trade-off. For others, going back to 30 fps in 2026 is a tough sell.
So, who's jumping into Vice City today or over the weekend? Which console are you playing on? Did you buy new hardware just for GTA VI?
Anyone taking a day off work or skipping class for the occasion? And if you've already spent a few hours with it, what are your first impressions? If you're waiting for the PC release, a discount, or simply don't understand the hype, we'd like to hear from you, too.
Consider this our GTA VI launch-day hangout. Share your experiences, discoveries, and hot takes below. Just keep the story spoilers out of the comments for now.

articles.title: Meta quer colocar sua IA em chaveiro com internet 5G
articles.text:
A Meta estaria preparando um novo dispositivo vestível para ampliar o acesso ao seu agente de inteligência artificial (IA). Chamado Muse Charm, o aparelho tem formato de chaveiro e pode chegar ao mercado por US$ 300 (cerca de R$ 1.590), acompanhado de até 12 meses de conexão 5G gratuita da Verizon, segundo informações publicadas pelo The Information.
A proposta é permitir que usuários conversem com o Muse sem precisar pegar o celular. A Meta apresentou o dispositivo durante a edição de setembro do evento Meta Connect e afirmou, na ocasião, que ele seria lançado a tempo das festas de fim de ano.
O preço e o pacote de conectividade, no entanto, ainda não foram confirmados oficialmente pela empresa. A Meta não comentou o assunto.
Como deve funcionar o Muse Charm?
- O Muse Charm foi concebido para concentrar recursos do agente de IA da Meta em acessório pequeno, que pode ficar preso a um chaveiro e estar sempre disponível para interações por voz;
- Durante a apresentação do produto, Mark Zuckerberg afirmou que o dispositivo reuniria a experiência completa do Muse, incluindo os recursos de voz em tempo real e de avatar, em formato que cabe em chaveiro;
- O aparelho também deve contar com leitor de impressões digitais. O recurso serviria para verificar a identidade do usuário antes de executar comandos;
- De acordo com as informações divulgadas, o pacote de lançamento incluiria até um ano de dados móveis 5G da Verizon. Não há detalhes adicionais sobre eventuais limitações da conexão ou sobre as condições para utilizar o benefício.
Leia mais:
- Meta testa aplicativo de apostas em previsões entre funcionários
- Itália multa Meta em € 805 milhões por uso de fotos sem consentimento
- Meta lança Achados, app de compra e venda de usados no Brasil
Meta quer levar seu agente de IA para além do celular
O Muse Charm faz parte de estratégia mais ampla da Meta para tornar seu agente de inteligência artificial acessível em diferentes dispositivos. A empresa já disponibilizou aplicativo do Muse para relógios com Wear OS e watchOS.
Em outubro, a companhia também compartilhou guias de código aberto para que desenvolvedores criem seus próprios dispositivos compatíveis com o agente, chamados de Muse Gadgets.
A aposta acontece enquanto o Muse ganha usuários: o serviço já ultrapassou a marca de dez milhões de pessoas.
A Meta também trabalha em ferramentas de comércio eletrônico para permitir que usuários façam compras por meio do agente. Nesse modelo, a empresa pretende cobrar taxa dos estabelecimentos comerciais pelas transações realizadas.
Zuckerberg já afirmou que, no futuro, o Muse poderia gerar mais receita por usuário do que os aplicativos tradicionais da companhia.
A estratégia também ajudaria a Meta a ter mais controle sobre a relação com seus consumidores. Hoje, boa parte de seus serviços depende de aplicativos acessados por smartphones, plataformas sujeitas às regras de empresas, como Apple e Google.
Além do chaveiro, a companhia estaria desenvolvendo um dispositivo vestível semelhante a um smartwatch. Esse projeto, porém, teria sido adiado para 2027, de acordo com o The Information.
Rodrigo Mozelli é jornalista formado pela Universidade Metodista de São Paulo (UMESP) e, atualmente, é redator do Olhar Digital.

articles.title: Google lanza Gemini 4 Neon: más rápido, más barato y demoledor escribiendo código
articles.text:
Google ha presentado Gemini 4 Neon, su nueva IA diseñada para ejecutar tareas complejas a velocidades mucho más rápidas. A unos días de anunciar Hydrogen y Carbon, el gigante tecnológico vuelve al ruedo con un modelo que se sitúa entre los dos anteriores. Google señala que Gemini 4 Neon ofrece capacidades de nivel frontera en ingeniería de software, análisis empresarial e investigación científica, pero enfocándose en la velocidad y eficiencia.
Como ocurre en todos los lanzamientos, Google mostró un listado de cifras y benchmarks que ponen a prueba el poder de su nueva IA. En el índice de inteligencia de Artificial Analysis, Gemini 4 Neon alcanza los 61 puntos en su nivel de razonamiento más avanzado, lo que le permite colarse en el listado de los mejores modelos. La IA también ofrece buen rendimiento en pruebas enfocadas en agentes de IA y seguimiento de instrucciones.
Además de la rapidez, una de las características más top de Gemini 4 Neon es la capacidad de trabajar con grandes volúmenes de información. El modelo cuenta con una ventana de contexto de hasta un millón de tokens, lo que le permite analizar hojas de cálculo, documentos en PDF, gráficos, audio y vídeo de forma simultánea. Neon puede convertir estos datos en informes o entregables, lo cual podría ser útil para quien trabaja en una oficina y necesita preparar una presentación.
Según Google, Neon también fue optimizado para tareas analíticas y científicas de alta complejidad. En algunos benchmarks de análisis científico y razonamiento matemático, el nuevo modelo se acerca cada vez más a otras IA más potentes. La tecnológica añade que en algunas pruebas iguala o supera a Gemini 4 Carbon, aunque con una velocidad hasta tres veces más rápida y a menor coste.
Gemini 4 Neon es una bala en programación
El desarrollo de software es otro de los puntos fuertes de Gemini 4 Neon. Google optimizó el modelo para flujos de trabajo de larga duración y puede actuar como un agente que gestiona herramientas, repositorios y proyectos complejos. En el Artificial Analysis Coding Agent Index, una prueba que mide cómo se desempeñan los agentes en tareas de ingeniería, Neon lidera la lista superando a Claude 5.5 Opus y GPT-6.2 Sol.
El nuevo modelo de Google puede depurar código en múltiples archivos, refactorizar repositorios grandes y comprender arquitecturas complejas. En una publicación en su web, Google mostró algunos de los ejemplos que logró con Gemini 4 Neon, como programar desde cero un simulador de esquí en primera persona con física realista a 120 Hz.
Otro ejemplo muestra cómo un enjambre de agentes de Gemini 4 Neon convirtió una imagen en una hoja de cálculo de 100.000 celdas sin imágenes incrustadas.
Por último, Gemini 4 Neon es capaz de generar código más seguro que Carbon en pruebas de ciberseguridad. La IA encuentra vulnerabilidades de código más rápido y a la mitad del coste de sus competidores; puede validarlas mediante explotación y parchearlas mejor que el modelo más poderoso de Google. Neon también reduce las alucinaciones y mejora la resistencia frente a los ataques de prompt injection, usando protecciones comparables a las de Gemini 4 Carbon.
Google confirmó que Gemini 4 Neon estará disponible a partir de hoy a través de la API y dentro de la app de Gemini. Para usarlo es necesario contar con una suscripción a Google AI Pro o Ultra. El modelo ofrece cuatro niveles de razonamiento y también puede probarse en Google Antigravity y AI Studio. Lamentablemente para los usuarios con cuenta gratuita, la única opción disponible será Gemini 4 Hydrogen.

articles.title: What Is Driving Silicon Wafer Demand Recovery?
articles.text:
The high number of new and upcoming production lines is a unique factor influencing this particular cycle.
Global silicon wafer shipments are forecast to grow 11.8% in 2026, according to the Q3 2026 SEMI Silicon Wafer Market Monitor. This increase is primarily due to strong demand for AI, which is projected to drive shipments through 2029.
Alongside AI, rising process material sales are also supporting recovery. The positive correlation between material sales and silicon wafer demand not only reflects growth in manufacturing complexity, but it also points to greater material consumption per wafer.
Finally, increases in memory demand, precautionary inventory building, and global fab capacity expansions are boosting silicon wafer shipments as well.
To better understand today’s landscape, it’s helpful to revisit past silicon wafer demand curves. From 2018 to 2019 and from 2022 to 2023, silicon wafer shipments rose ahead of major increases in memory work-in-process (WIP) inventories, or unfinished memory chips undergoing fabrication. However, shipments lagged at the same time WIP inventory peaked. Because fabrication lines were already producing at full capacity, their need for silicon wafers slowed.
While this pattern provides historical context for today’s demand recovery, the high number of new and upcoming production lines is a unique factor influencing this particular cycle.
Silicon Wafer Shipments and Memory WIP: Historical Lead–Lag Pattern. Both series use four-quarter moving averages. Sources: SEMI SMG and financial disclosures from Samsung Electronics, SK hynix, and Micron. Data for 3Q26–2Q27 are forecasts.
SEMI’s fab investment outlook predicts continued growth in planned equipment spending beyond 2026. So long as investment plans remain broadly on track, ongoing equipment installation and capacity ramps are likely to support silicon wafer demand. The report also demonstrated a widening gap between YoY growth rates for semiconductor fab equipment spending and silicon wafer manufacturing equipment spending, suggesting that investment support for wafer demand may persist longer than initially expected.
This also helps explain why the historical relationship between wafer shipments and WIP does not necessarily imply an imminent slowdown. Wafer procurement momentum can moderate before WIP inventories peak, although investment support may slow if moderation becomes visible in wafer shipments.
Investment Spread: A Signal of a Later Wafer-Cycle Slowdown. Spread between the YoY growth rates of semiconductor fab equipment spending and silicon wafer manufacturers’ equipment spending, compared with silicon wafer shipment trends. Sources: SEMI Silicon Wafer Shipment Statistics and SEMI WWSEMS. Shipment data are updated through 2Q26, while equipment spending data are updated through August 2026.
SEMI projects continued wafer shipment growth in 2027, although growth will likely be more moderate than it was in 2026. As inventory stockpiles subside, ongoing production will be important for sustaining demand. If planned capacity expansions continue and customers buy the resulting chips, semiconductor companies can gradually reduce their wafer inventories while also maintaining their purchase rate. However, investment delays or weaker demand for semiconductors would slow this absorption and increase the risk of declining silicon wafer orders.
While AI-related investment is a critical source of support, broader semiconductor recovery is still uneven. Because of this, the key to maintaining demand growth will be how quickly fabs can use wafers purchased in advance. Doing so will help shape the duration of this recovery period and the depth of any subsequent wafer inventory adjustments.

articles.title: Reducing Rollout Bottlenecks in Reinforcement Learning with NVIDIA Dynamo | NVIDIA Technical Blog
articles.text:
Reinforcement learning (RL) uses rewards to train models to solve problems and complete tasks more successfully.
Inference drives this process. Workers generate rollouts: sequences of model outputs, actions, and environment interactions. The RL framework scores the results, updates model weights, and sends those weights back to the workers for the next round.
As RL training scales, redundant compute work, slow rollouts, weight updates, and worker failures can waste GPU capacity and delay training.
NVIDIA Dynamo provides the serving layer to address these constraints, helping teams generate more accepted training samples and complete training iterations faster.
This blog post explains the rollout bottlenecks that slow RL training and how Dynamo addresses them through routing, ModelExpress weight updates, and recovery.
1. Why RL needs distributed rollout infrastructure
A reasoning rollout may contain one response. A coding-agent rollout can involve repository exploration, edits, tool calls, and tests. These differences create an uneven workload across inference workers.
Three constraints determine how effectively that workload supports training.
Rollout completion time. When training requires a group of samples, the slowest required rollout can delay the next step. Distributing request counts evenly across GPUs does not necessarily distribute work evenly.
Repeated context. Multiple attempts often begin with identical instructions, task descriptions, or coding repository context. Recomputing those prefixes consumes GPU capacity before new output is generated.
Weight freshness. Training produces new model weights throughout the run. Workers must receive them according to the algorithm’s requirements for sampling and acceptable staleness.
Addressing these constraints can let teams complete more iterations within a fixed compute budget. The right optimization depends on which constraint limits the workload.
2. The Dynamo architecture for RL
Dynamo sits between rollout orchestration and inference workers. The RL framework submits generation requests; Dynamo routes them to eligible capacity; inference engines execute the model.
The responsibilities of each component remain explicit:
| Component | Role | 
|---|---|
| RL framework | Optimization, rewards, environments, checkpoints, and sample acceptance | 
| Dynamo | Routing, worker management, serving controls, and telemetry | 
| Inference engine | Generation and application of updated weights | 
| ModelExpress | Model-weight and artifact distribution through supported integrations | 
The generation and weight administration follow distinct paths. Requests use the shared serving frontend, while refresh operations target selected workers under framework control. This lets the framework determine when workers may generate samples and which results are eligible for training.
The separation allows teams to improve serving without transferring ownership of the learning process. Routing decisions determine where generation runs; the framework determines whether the resulting samples satisfy its training requirements. See the RL integration reference.
3. How Dynamo accelerates routing, weight distribution, and recovery
KV-aware routing: Reduce repeated prompt computation
RL often generates several solutions to the same task using a shared prompt. Sending these requests to a worker that has cached the prompt avoids repeated processing, saving GPU compute. But sending every request to that worker can create a queue, delaying rollouts and the next training step.
Dynamo’s router balances KV cache reuse and worker load to reduce redundant computation and waiting. The objective is earlier completion of the samples needed for training.
ModelExpress: Reduce recurring weight-distribution overhead
RL training repeatedly updates the model. Sending a full checkpoint to every rollout worker takes time and can interrupt generation.
ModelExpress reduces this overhead by reusing weights already available in the cluster instead of loading from remote storage. Compatible workers can copy weights directly from another GPU over NIXL.
Delta weight transfer reduces the data sent between updates. Instead of moving the full model, it sends a compressed representation of what changed. Workers reconstruct the new weights from the matching base version, reducing transfer time and network traffic.
This also helps recovery. A replacement worker can load a checkpoint and apply subsequent deltas to catch up with the training run. Healthy workers can continue generating rollouts while capacity is restored.
The RL framework coordinates when workers apply updates, handles cached state, and checks readiness before accepting new samples.
Recovery: Limit the impact of worker failures
Long training runs must accommodate worker failures without unnecessarily interrupting healthy capacity.
Dynamo detects worker loss, directs new requests toward eligible workers and adds replacement workers to routing once ready, keeping rollout generation moving when a worker fails.
Supported configurations also enable migration for eligible in-flight requests and graceful draining.
The RL framework handles interrupted samples and ensures replacements use the required weights.
Dynamo in RL workflows
Dynamo adoption in RL spans frontier-model development, managed infrastructure and open source frameworks:
- Microsoft AI used NVIDIA Dynamo to support RL rollout inference during post-training.
- CoreWeave uses Dynamo and ModelExpress to accelerate model weight updates by up to 15×.
- Cognition used Dynamo to manage inference workers and route rollouts during the post-training of SWE-1.7.
- Prime Intellect uses Dynamo for distributed inference orchestration.
- H Company used Dynamo and ModelExpress to reduce average training-step time by up to 20% and GPU-hours by up to 5%.
- Open-source integrations connect Dynamo to existing RL stacks, including verl, NeMo RL, Slime, and prime-rl.
Get started with Dynamo for RL
Efficient RL infrastructure keeps rollout generation, weight distribution, and worker recovery moving together. Dynamo brings these serving capabilities into the training loop, helping teams turn distributed GPU capacity into accepted training samples and faster iterations.
Explore the Dynamo RL documentation and start scaling the inference behind your next model.
Acknowledgments
Aichen Feng, Biswa Ranjan Panda, Elaine Hou, Hyunjae Woo, Jinyan Chen, John Thomson, Sean Choi, Sophia Yang, William Arnold, and Zhongdongming Dai contributed to this post.

articles.title: How Nigerian startup PeoplePulse is helping SMEs digitise HR with AI - Disrupt Africa
articles.text:
Nigerian startup PeoplePulse has developed an affordable, AI-powered workforce management platform designed to help African small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) manage their people and automate routine HR processes.
Founded in June 2025, PeoplePulse grew out of HR and business consultancy Bridgemead Consulting, which has worked with SMEs on recruitment, HR outsourcing, employee management and training.
The platform brings employee records, onboarding, leave and attendance management, payroll support, performance management, workforce analytics and compliance into one place.
“Many growing African businesses still manage their HR operations using spreadsheets, WhatsApp, paper records and disconnected tools. At the other end of the market, enterprise HR platforms can be too expensive or complicated for smaller organisations,” Adetola Abolarinwa, co-founder and chief product officer, told Disrupt Africa. “PeoplePulse is designed to bridge that gap: it is accessible enough for an SME but robust enough to support a growing workforce.”
The startup, which has an 11-strong team, competes with the likes of SeamlessHR and BambooHR, but believes its combination of affordability, simplicity, localisation and AI-powered automation sets it apart.
“We did not begin by making assumptions about what SMEs needed; we had already spent years working directly with them and understanding their operational problems,” Abolarinwa said.
Funded by its founders and a friends-and-family round, PeoplePulse piloted its platform with around 280 employees across eight companies between May and July 2026, with all eight converting into paying customers. It was also selected as one of the top 11 finalists for Cycle 7 of the Women in Tech Accelerator Nigeria.
The startup charges between NGN2,000 (US$1.5) and NGN3,500 (US$2.5) per employee per month across three subscription tiers.
“Our focus is not simply on acquiring registrations. We are concentrating on successful onboarding, active usage, retention and expanding adoption within each customer organisation,” Abolarinwa said.
PeoplePulse is focused on building a strong customer base in Nigeria, with Bridgemead’s network of more than 80 businesses providing a warm pipeline, before expanding into other African markets.
“We see PeoplePulse as a pan-African opportunity, but we intend to build a strong foundation in Nigeria before expanding aggressively,” said Abolarinwa.

articles.title: Gen Z’s guide to self-improvement: Build habits that pay off
articles.text:
Gen Z’s guide to self-improvement: Build habits that pay off
Explore practical self-improvement habits for Gen Z that improve focus, confidence, productivity and personal growth while delivering long-term results.
Self-improvement is everywhere, especially on social media. From morning routines and fitness challenges to productivity hacks and financial goals, Gen Z is constantly exposed to ways of becoming a better version of themselves. But with so much advice available, it can be difficult to know which habits are actually worth the effort.
The truth is that personal growth does not require a complete lifestyle makeover. It comes from small, consistent actions that create meaningful results over time. Instead of following every new trend, Gen Z can focus on habits that improve everyday life, strengthen skills and support long-term goals.
7 Practical self-improvement habits that offer a real return on effort
1. Set goals that have a clear purpose
Self-improvement becomes easier when you know what you are working towards. Rather than setting vague goals such as becoming successful or more productive, identify specific outcomes you want to achieve. It could be learning a professional skill, improving your fitness, saving money or reading more books.
Break larger goals into smaller steps and give yourself a realistic timeline. When you understand why a goal matters, it becomes easier to stay committed and measure your progress.
2. Learn skills that improve your future opportunities
In a competitive job market, learning beyond formal education can make a meaningful difference. Gen Z can invest time in practical skills such as communication, writing, digital marketing, financial literacy, data analysis or using AI tools responsibly.
You do not need to master everything at once. Choose one skill that supports your career or personal interests and practise it regularly. Free online courses, tutorials and hands-on projects can help you build knowledge without spending a fortune.
3. Build a routine that protects your focus
Constant notifications, social media and multitasking can make it difficult to concentrate. A simple daily routine can help you use your time more intentionally.
Start by identifying your most important tasks and completing them before getting distracted by less urgent activities. You can also set aside specific periods for studying, working, exercising and relaxing. The goal is not to follow a perfect schedule but to create a routine that makes your day easier to manage.
4. Develop better money habits early
Financial independence is an important part of personal growth. Developing healthy money habits early can help Gen Z make better decisions as their income and responsibilities increase.
Start by tracking your expenses, setting a monthly budget and saving a portion of your income whenever possible. Learn the basics of emergency funds, interest, debt and long-term investing before making financial decisions. Even small savings can build discipline and provide greater financial security over time.
5. Read and learn beyond social media
Social media can introduce you to new ideas, but meaningful learning requires more than scrolling through short videos and posts. Reading books, listening to educational podcasts and exploring reliable resources can help you develop a deeper understanding of different subjects.
You do not have to finish an entire book every week. Start with a few pages a day or spend 15 minutes learning something useful. Consistent learning can gradually improve your vocabulary, critical thinking and ability to make informed decisions.
6. Take care of your physical and mental well-being
Productivity should not come at the cost of your health. Regular movement, balanced meals, adequate sleep and time away from screens are essential parts of sustainable self-improvement.
Make realistic changes instead of following extreme fitness or wellness trends. Take a walk, maintain a consistent sleep schedule and make room for activities that help you relax. Taking care of yourself can support better concentration, energy and emotional well-being.
7. Track progress instead of chasing perfection
One reason people give up on self-improvement is that they expect immediate results. However, meaningful changes often take time. Missing a workout, delaying a task or breaking a routine does not mean you have failed.
Keep track of your progress through a journal, habit tracker or weekly review. Notice what is working, identify what needs improvement and adjust your approach when necessary. Focus on becoming more consistent rather than trying to achieve perfection every day.
Final thoughts
For Gen Z, self-improvement should be less about following every productivity trend and more about making choices that create lasting value. The best habits are not necessarily the most impressive ones; they are the ones that make everyday life better.
Whether it is learning a new skill, managing money, protecting your focus or prioritising health, every small effort can contribute to long-term growth. Instead of asking how quickly you can transform your life, ask which habits will continue to benefit you months or even years from now.
That is the real return on effort: building a life where today's small actions create tomorrow's opportunities.

articles.title: BMW dit non à Apple CarPlay Ultra, mais ouvre la porte à un autre retour très attendu dans ses voitures
articles.text:
Apple CarPlay et Android Auto ont révolutionné notre rapport à l’infodivertissement automobile. Les deux interfaces proposent en effet de répliquer en toute simplicité les écrans de nos smartphones afin d’utiliser nos applications préférées à bord. Une belle avancée qui va encore plus loin avec CarPlay Ultra faisant des combinés d’instrumentation de nouveaux territoires de conquête.
Mieux que cela, le système prend aussi la main sur certaines commandes du véhicule. C’est le cas de la ventilation et des aides à la conduite. Intéressant, mais encore rare : à ce jour, seul Aston Martin intègre le dispositif. BMW, de son côté, confirme que CarPlay Ultra n’arrivera pas de sitôt sur ses modèles. L’ensemble ne pourra d’ailleurs s’afficher sur aucun écran à bord du véhicule. La marque évoque des risques sur la confidentialité.
Le vrai motif du refus de la marque à l’hélice
Cela veut-il dire qu’aucun changement ne sera à prévoir pour les années futures ? Claudia Maier, responsable du numérique chez BMW, affirme que rien n’est fixé et que le constructeur pourrait éventuellement procéder à des ajustements sur l’interface des modèles Neue Klasse. Toujours pas de CarPlay Ultra, donc, mais les classiques connectivités Apple CarPlay et Android Auto. Et pourquoi donc ?
Maier explique que CarPlay Ultra ne correspond pas à la stratégie, ni à la philosophie portée par la marque à l’hélice. BMW souhaite conserver toutes ses données dans ses propres logiciels en interne afin de les sécuriser au maximum. Il faut dire que le constructeur a également investi du temps et de l’argent pour développer son Panoramic iDrive. Tout changer dans l’immédiat avec CarPlay Ultra serait un immense gâchis.
Ce revirement ergonomique que les conducteurs attendaient
En outre, un retour en grâce des boutons physiques pourrait être envisageable. Sur les i3 et iX3, les commandes de ventilation logées dans les écrans peuvent déjà déranger, même si elles sont constamment affichées en accès direct. Cependant, orienter le flux d’air impose aussi une manipulation sur l’écran tactile, ce qui commence à poser d’évidents problèmes d’ergonomie. Un revirement est donc plausible.
Plausible ne veut cependant pas dire certain. Maier a en effet indiqué que BMW est sûr que ses clients finiront par s’habituer au Panoramic iDrive utilisant massivement les commandes tactiles et vocales. La disparition de la mythique molette contrôlant l’infodivertissement au profit d’un environnement complètement numérique, est-ce vraiment une évidence pour tous ?
La fin de la mythique molette iDrive fait grincer des dents
Permettez-nous de douter, car une telle adaptation ne se fera pas sans douleur pour les habitués. Si changement il y a, il faudra ainsi attendre la prochaine génération de véhicules qui arrivera encore dans très longtemps. Heureusement que la Neue Klasse assure côté technique avec d’excellents scores d’autonomie et de recharge. De quoi faire avaler la pilule…

articles.title: Microsoft tests new Edge Lockdown Mode that disables GPU APIs
articles.text:
Microsoft is developing a new Edge security feature to reduce the attack surface by disabling the WebGL, WebGL2, and WebGPU APIs.
Inspired by Apple's Lockdown Mode, the new feature shares the same name and builds on Edge Enhanced Security Mode (also known internally as Super Duper Secure Mode), which disables Just-In-Time Compilation (JIT) from the V8 processing pipeline.
The new Edge Lockdown Mode offers optional, extreme protections for users facing highly targeted attacks who are willing to sacrifice website compatibility for stronger defenses.
"Lockdown Mode is designed for users who are at particular risk of being targeted in cybersecurity campaigns. This may include journalists, executives, security researchers, and administrators," said Partner Security Group Manager Gareth Evans.
"Individuals whose threat model justifies accepting reduced compatibility in exchange for stronger protection. It may also apply to devices operating within highly restricted environments."
Evans also warned that websites that use the disabled APIs (especially those with interactive graphics like games or maps) may not work as expected when this security feature is toggled on.
Edge users can test Lockdown Mode by switching to the Canary release channel, enabling the #edge-sdsm-plus flag, restarting the browser, then toggling on Strict mode for "Enhance your security on the web" and blocking WebGL graphics and WebGPU graphics.
After enabling it, users will see a new "Lockdown Enabled" indicator in the address bar when WebGL or WebGPU is blocked on a web page.
While the current Edge Canary Lockdown Mode blocks websites from using WebGL, WebGL2, and WebGPU APIs to stop attacks that try to escalate privileges and escape the sandbox, Microsoft plans to extend the feature in upcoming releases.
"The initial set of Lockdown Mode mitigations focus is the GPU process, a more privileged component that handles complex graphics workloads across browser code, third-party libraries, and device drivers," Evans added.
"Results from this experiment will inform the finished Lockdown Mode experience, including clearer descriptions of restricted capabilities and site-level exceptions that restore trusted sites without weakening protection everywhere else."
According to the company's estimates, this new security feature would have blocked around 60% of privilege escalation attacks targeting Edge users in the wild.
Last year, Microsoft also introduced a new Edge scareware sensor to ensure Defender SmartScreen blocks scam pages faster, and restricted access to Edge's Internet Explorer mode after learning that hackers were leveraging zero-day exploits in the Chakra JavaScript engine to access target devices.
