articles.title: Grand Theft Auto VI launches to rave reviews and will be the biggest entertainment release ever - Tech Guide
articles.text:
Grand Theft Auto VI has launched to rave reviews and is set to become the biggest entertainment release in history.
For gamers it’s a massive event with many die-hard GTA fans coordinating their annual leave so they can play the game for days on end without interruptions.
The game, which has been 13 years in the making, has launched to perfect reviews from gaming sites which are in awe of its scale and detail.
Grand Theft Auto VI is expected to generate more than $5 billion in revenue.
It will easily eclipse the highest-grossing films of all time including Avengers: Endgame ($2.94 billion), Avatar ($2.92 billion and Spider-Man: Brand New Day ($2.52 billion).
Those on the outside looking into this launch will be wondering what all the fuss about?
Firstly, most don’t appreciate the size of the gaming industry.
In Australia, revenues from computer gaming easily outstrips the box office.
In 2025, Australians spent more than $4.2 billion on video games. That’s up 12 per cent from the $3.8 billion spent in 2024.
In the same period the Australian box office totalled $970 million.
This year the Australian box office has already crossed the $1 billion mark in 2026, the first time it has done this since 2019, thanks to the success of The Odyssey and Spider-Man: Brand New Day.
This year Grand Theft Auto VI will beat all those totals in Australia on its own.
The game has been available for pre-order for some time before today’s release. Rockstar, the game’s developer, even allowed users to download the 212 GB game to their system early so it would be ready to play at the stroke of midnight.
In fact, it set a download record for the NBN with a 30 per cent increase above baseline traffic and almost 8Tbps of increased load in the busy hour.
Another thing to note for planning to go into a store to buy GTA VI – is a discless game.
When you buy the game cover over the counter, there’s no disc inside, just a download code.
One common misconception around gaming is that it’s only for kids.
The average age of an Australian gamer is 35 so it’s very much an adult pastime and a popular family activity.
Getting back to Grand Theft Auto VI, why is it so popular?
The main appeal of the game is its sheer scale and scope.
This is what’s called an open-world game, where players can follow the playable character’s story but also go off and explore the world on their own.
The game is set in the fictional town of Vice City and follows the story of Jason and Lucia who find themselves on the wrong side of the law and must use their guile and ingenuity to stay alive.
Is a single-player game. It does not have an online multiplayer option.
But unlike regular computer games, Grand Theft Auto VI is a much larger sandbox.
A recent release, which we quite enjoyed, was Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4.
The campaign was a remarkable mission-based story that had a beginning and end.
After completing the campaign if you decide to play the game again, it would be the same experience.
With Grand Theft Auto VI, there are tasks and missions to complete but the attraction to hardcore fans is the fact they can venture out into the world and create their own adventures.
Being called Grand Theft Auto, the earlier versions of the game were all about stealing cars, running away from the police and building your wealth.
Those elements are still at play in Grand Theft Auto VI but it is now much broader.
You can spend days and weeks in little pockets of the world, interacting with people, driving cars, steering boats, flying planes and getting you up to all sorts of mischief.
IGN has called the game precedented, unbelievable, and unmissable.
It’s review said: “As optimistic as I was about a new GTA built in the wake of everything Rockstar learnt from the majestic Red Dead Redemption 2, I was simply not ready for just how much richer, deeper, and more satisfying Grand Theft Auto VI has proven to be. After three weeks and over 120 hours playing it, I’m still hopelessly hooked, absorbing the world at walking speed like a tourist in a new town.”
GameSpot says Grand Theft Auto VI sets the bar for open worlds impossibly high.
It said: “This game is the culmination of everything the developer has previously achieved in the open-world space that pushes the genre to heights that, in all likelihood, no other developer will be able to reach. GTA VI is an astonishing open-world action game that I’d wager won’t be outdone until Grand Theft Auto VII.”
Kotaku says the game is overwhelming, exciting, and different than any past GTA game.
It said: “GTA VI is a truly remarkable game. A masterpiece of open-world design that brings forward the best parts of all of Rockstar’s past games into one billion-dollar adventure that is unlike anything I’ve played before. It’s a game I’ll be playing for years, and I can’t wait to talk about it with others.”
Grand Theft Auto VI is available now for PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X and S.

articles.title: Un grand écran pour les films, 144 Hz pour jouer : le TCL 55P89L passe à 499,99 € pour le Black Friday — Frandroid
articles.text:
Plus l’écran est grand, plus ses défauts se voient. Sur une dalle de 55 pouces, des noirs qui tirent sur le gris ou des mouvements qui saccadent suffisent à gâcher une soirée film comme une partie en ligne. La profondeur des noirs, la richesse des couleurs et la fluidité comptent donc autant que la diagonale.
Avec le 55P89L, TCL s’appuie sur un rétroéclairage Mini LED capable d’ajuster la lumière dans différentes zones de l’écran. Ce réglage fait ressortir les éléments lumineux tout en préservant les parties sombres de l’image. Les Quantum Dots complètent ce dispositif pour élargir la palette de couleurs, tandis que la dalle 144 Hz et les fonctions gaming répondent aux besoins des joueurs exigeants. Pour le Black Friday, ce modèle est proposé chez BUT à 499,99 €.
Mini LED : comment le rétroéclairage par zones améliore le contraste
Un téléviseur LCD utilise des LED pour éclairer sa dalle. Pour afficher du noir, les cristaux liquides doivent bloquer cette lumière. Mais ils ne la bloquent jamais complètement : lorsque le rétroéclairage reste puissant, les parties sombres peuvent paraître grisâtres.
Le Mini LED utilise des LED beaucoup plus petites. Sur le TCL 55P89L, elles sont réparties derrière la dalle et regroupées en zones dont la luminosité peut être réglée séparément. C’est ce qu’on appelle le local dimming.
Prenons une pleine lune dans un ciel nocturne : le téléviseur augmente la lumière derrière la Lune et la réduit derrière les grandes parties sombres du ciel. Il peut ainsi afficher une Lune brillante tout en conservant un ciel plus noir autour. Ce contrôle par zones améliore le contraste et contribue à limiter les halos lumineux.
Ce rétroéclairage s’appuie sur une dalle HVA, dont TCL annonce un contraste natif de 6 000:1 sur le modèle 55 pouces, contre 1 200:1 pour une dalle IPS classique. Les zones sombres partent ainsi d’un noir plus profond, avant même l’intervention du local dimming.
Pionnier du Mini LED, TCL associe dans son 55P89L ce rétroéclairage à une couche de points quantiques, les Quantum Dots. Ces matériaux élargissent la palette de couleurs que le téléviseur peut reproduire : TCL annonce une couverture de 93 % de l’espace colorimétrique DCI-P3, la référence utilisée au cinéma. Cette association, appelée QD-Mini LED, permet selon TCL d’afficher plus d’un milliard de nuances.
Les deux technologies se complètent : le Mini LED ajuste la lumière dans les différentes zones de l’image, tandis que les Quantum Dots enrichissent les couleurs. De quoi restituer aussi bien les teintes vives d’un film d’animation que les nuances plus discrètes d’un paysage ou d’un visage.
144 Hz et HDMI 2.1 : le bon cocktail pour jouer
Au-delà de sa qualité d’image, la dalle 4K du TCL 55P89L affiche un taux de rafraîchissement natif de 144 Hz, utile pour les retransmissions sportives comme pour le jeu vidéo. Ses quatre ports HDMI 2.1 acceptent un signal 4K à 144 Hz, de quoi tirer pleinement parti d’une console de dernière génération ou d’un PC puissant. Sur les ports HDMI 1 et 2, la fonction Game Accelerator pousse même la fréquence jusqu’à 288 Hz en VRR.
Le téléviseur embarque les principales technologies attendues par les joueurs :
- VRR (taux de rafraîchissement variable) : synchronise l’écran avec la console pour éviter les déchirures d’image (tearing) ;
- AMD FreeSync Premium : contribue à limiter les déchirures d’image et certaines saccades avec une source compatible ;
- ALLM : bascule automatiquement le téléviseur en mode jeu lorsqu’une source compatible signale qu’un jeu est lancé, réduisant ainsi le temps de latence.
Le 55P89L tourne sous Google TV, avec l’assistant Gemini. Les applications de SVOD, de replay et de streaming se téléchargent depuis le Google Play Store, et le téléviseur intègre Chromecast et AirPlay 2 pour diffuser une vidéo depuis un smartphone ou un ordinateur. L’un de ses ports HDMI est compatible eARC, pour relier une barre de son ou un ampli home cinéma.
Image HDR et son Dolby Atmos : l’immersion à la maison
Le traitement de l’image est confié au processeur AiPQ, développé par TCL, qui s’appuie sur des algorithmes d’apprentissage profond pour adapter le rendu à chaque contenu. Le téléviseur est compatible Dolby Vision et HDR10+, deux formats HDR dynamiques, ainsi que HLG. Les contrastes, les couleurs et les pics de luminosité sont ainsi optimisés scène par scène sur les contenus compatibles.
Côté son, le modèle 55 pouces s’appuie sur un système 2.0 de 20 watts, composé de deux haut-parleurs de 10 watts. L’ensemble est compatible Dolby Atmos et DTS Virtual:X.
Enfin, les bords très fins du 55P89L laissent toute la place à l’image, que le téléviseur soit posé sur ses pieds latéraux ou accroché au mur grâce à sa fixation VESA. TCL a opté pour un châssis métallique au design épuré, qui s’intègre discrètement dans le salon.

articles.title: How Takealot's e-commerce network could help SA SMEs grow
articles.text:
Takealot, part of Naspers-owned global technology group Prosus, wants to make its e-commerce infrastructure work for more than its own business.
South Africa’s largest online retailer believes its marketplace, logistics network and technology can help small businesses reach customers beyond their immediate markets without building their own digital retail operations.
For small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), sustainable sales depend on affordable fulfilment, reliable logistics and the ability to compete. Takealot has more than 16,000 independent marketplace sellers, giving businesses access to its platform and millions of potential customers across South Africa.
At Africa Tech Festival in Cape Town on Thursday, Takealot Group chief executive officer (CEO) Frederik Zietsman discussed digital commerce opportunities for SMEs. Tomiwa Aladekomo, CEO of Big Cabal Media, TechCabal’s parent company, moderated the session.
Takealot served more than six million active customers and processed over 60 million orders in its last financial year. It surpassed $1 billion in revenue and recorded its first profitable year. Its marketplace gives independent sellers access to this customer base without building their own e-commerce platforms.
The company has spent more than a decade developing the technology and operational capabilities to manage orders, coordinate deliveries and maintain customer trust.
“Ultimately, it starts with trust and ends with trust. If you don’t build trust, you eventually fail,” Zietsman said.
Takealot records about 2.5 million daily sessions across its apps and processes around 150,000 orders nationally, he said. Managing those volumes requires coordination across distribution centres, logistics networks and multiple points in the customer journey.
Zietsman said its operational data network tracks these processes, identifies problems at critical handover points and helps the company respond when something goes wrong. For smaller sellers, this infrastructure could reduce the burden of building an online retail operation, including customer acquisition and delivery capabilities.
Takealot built its own logistics operations after third-party providers struggled with its volumes. Zietsman recalled a difficult peak season around 2015, when three providers failed to meet the company’s requirements.
“We realised that, for us to build this business, we had to do it ourselves,” he said.
Takealot staff sometimes worked inside providers’ facilities, redesigning processes and effectively running operations on their behalf. The experience convinced the company that controlling the customer experience required greater investment in its own infrastructure.
Today, Zietsman said, Takealot operates Africa’s largest mid-mile electric vehicle fleet and generates solar power at its distribution centres. The investments form part of an effort to reduce operating costs and improve efficiency.
“The challenge isn’t simply executing at scale and velocity. It’s doing that while driving efficiency: reducing inventory holding, lowering our cost per unit and increasing the return on capital deployed,” he said.
Technology is another part of that strategy. Takealot applies artificial intelligence (AI) to demand prediction and software development. Zietsman said its adoption must produce measurable commercial benefits.
“If AI doesn’t save us costs, drive efficiency or make customers’ lives easier, why are we doing it?” he said.
The company’s ambitions also extend beyond online retail. In September 2025, Takealot partnered with the Department of Higher Education and Training to align technical and vocational education with skills required in e-commerce, logistics and digital entrepreneurship. The partnership included initiatives supporting township manufacturers and restaurants.
For Zietsman, building a business that can create these opportunities has itself been a long and demanding process of learning, adapting, taking risks and pushing through difficult periods.
“Sometimes, we could have stopped five years ago. But you need to push through those difficult times. Eventually, you reach a level of operational leverage, which is where we are today. That gives us the ability to generate a profit and reinvest in the business,” he said.

articles.title: Durante 17 horas, las webs de Ikea, la BBC y Zoom intentaron robar tarjetas a quien entraba. Ninguna de las tres lo sabía
articles.text:
Que alguien ataque una web cualquiera y logre inyectar código parece algo relativamente sencillo, que esto ocurra con webs como la de la BBC, Ikea o Zoom se antoja casi imposible. Pero no, ocurrió. Aunque con una estrategia distinta: en lugar de atacar las páginas principales, los atacantes han logrado hackear a un proveedor. Su nombre es Optimizely.
Qué ha ocurrido. El pasado lunes 16 de noviembre un proveedor de pruebas A/B, ese tipo de tests que las empresas utilizan para comprobar qué versión de un cambio funciona mejor, se vio comprometido. Los atacantes lograron inyectar código malicioso en ese proveedor aprovechando un fallo en el proceso de alta de cuentas, según la propia Optimizely. Y dicho código terminó en las webs que contrataron el servicio de pruebas.
El ataque tuvo lugar el lunes y se prolongó por espacio de unas 17 horas. Al principio nadie se dio cuenta de que el servicio que ofrecía Optimizely estaba comprometido: el código llegó a la BBC, Ikea, CNN, Fox News, Zoom, Air France-KLM... Y permitía robar datos de tarjetas bancarias, cargaba exploits para aprovecharse de iPhone y iPad sin actualizar y hasta cambiaba las direcciones de las carteras cripto. Todo sin que las empresas que servían las páginas se dieran cuenta.
La raíz del problema es que el código salía de cdn.optimizely.com, el servidor oficial de la empresa, con su certificado válido. Para el navegador era un script auténtico, así que las webs y sus visitantes se lo comieron sin sospechar. Lo detectó Scott Helme, de Report URI: tras analizar 1.611 scripts de Optimizely, encontró 188 infectados, de 178 organizaciones.
Quién es Optimizely. Es una empresa que casi nadie conoce y que, sin embargo, se encuentra en muchas webs que usamos a diario. Su especialidad son las pruebas A/B (A/B testing). Por ejemplo, una prueba de este tipo enseña a la mitad de los usuarios un botón verde y a la otra mitad uno azul: el que más clicks saque es el que mejor funciona. Así pueden descartar el menos efectivo.
Optimizely se ha especializado en ofrecer A/B testing a otras empresas para que ellas no tengan que hacer los desarrollos ni la implementación. Para obrar la magia, las webs cargan un pequeño programa (script) en cada visita con un campo que las empresas rellenan con su propio código. Para quienes contratan a Optimizely es muy cómodo, porque les permite cambiar la web sin tocar sus propios servidores. Es justo por donde entraron los atacantes.
El agujero de confianza. La cadena mantiene los eslabones unidos, pero no todos poseen la misma fuerza. Como usuarios, confiamos en las páginas web que aportan autoridad, porque resulta inconcebible que Ikea quiera robar nuestros datos bancarios. A su vez, estas páginas confían en otras empresas para aportar valor a sus propios servicios. Y la cadena de subcontratas va creciendo hasta que falla un eslabón.
Por mucho que confiemos en una página o app, siempre existe el riesgo de que un código que carguen de otro sitio pueda venir infectado. Y si las empresas no auditan todo aquello que contratan estamos vendidos: el incidente de Optimizely demuestra que nuestros datos privados nunca van a estar completamente asegurados.
El robo. El script malicioso estuvo sirviéndose a las webs de al menos 178 organizaciones de enorme relevancia hasta que se dieron cuenta de la inyección y Optimizely le puso remedio. Durante ese tiempo, y según los datos preliminares de Report URI, las carteras del atacante recibieron unos 7.000 dólares en cripto, aunque algunas ya tenían actividad antes del ataque. No hay constancia de que los iPhone y iPad resultaran vulnerados por el código malicioso ni tampoco de la cantidad de tarjetas o cookies que los atacantes pudieron llevarse. 
Optimizely todavía no explicó cómo funcionaba el fallo, cuántos visitantes recibieron el código ni quiénes son los atacantes que se encuentran por detrás. Y no es su primer susto del año: en febrero ya confirmó una intrusión tras un ataque de phishing por teléfono. Para una empresa cuyo producto vive dentro de las webs de sus clientes, son demasiadas preguntas abiertas.

articles.title: La reflexión del actor Maxi Iglesias sobre el trabajo: “Trabajamos para pagar cosas que no necesitamos”
articles.text:
Durante la promoción de una de sus películas ha habido una reflexión que me ha llamado la atención. Se trata de cuánto tiempo invertimos en nuestro trabajo y qué hacemos con el dinero obtenido. “Trabajamos para pagar cosas que no necesitamos”, dice Maxi Iglesias. Porque en este modo de gestionar nuestra vida siempre parece haber algo más que conseguir.
En la conversación, él mismo lo asocia a un problema de consumismo. Y para explicarlo utiliza la película “El club de la lucha” (David Fincher, 1999), protagonizada por Brad Pitt y Edward Norton.
Y en ella se asocia el hecho de ganar dinero con el de comprar cosas. De tal forma que si nuestras ambiciones materiales van en aumento, también tenemos que trabajar para ello. Es importante pararse a pensar en estas metas.
La obligación de sentirse productivo
Por otro lado, es relevante dejar claro que no hablamos de la vivienda. “Dejando el tema de la vivienda a un lado, somos muy autómatas en ese sentido, seguimos lo que el sistema nos ha dicho que hay que hacer: generar, producir, sentir que somos productivos, que hacemos y generamos”.
Hay que destacar esta idea de que tenemos que estar haciendo algo. Además de añadir metas a las anteriores. También es importante destacar que el problema está en que esperamos seguir creciendo sin saber dónde está el límite. “¿Hasta dónde se va a engordar la lista? ¿Hasta dónde se va a crecer?”, plantea.
Por otro lado, se puede reflexionar sobre el papel que tiene el trabajo en nuestra vida personal. Es importante repensar nuestras prioridades e incluso el tiempo que dedicamos a otras actividades sin recompensa económica inmediata.
Con el trabajo podemos satisfacer nuestras necesidades. Además, nuestro objetivo puede ser avanzar en nuestro ámbito profesional. Sin embargo, hay que tener cuidado con caer en el problema de ir añadiendo requisitos de manera inercial sin pararnos a pensar para qué sirven. “Lo llevo diciendo muchos años: esto en algún momento va a explotar”.

articles.title: AI-powered bionic eye breakthrough could help the blind see again
articles.text:
AI-powered bionic eye breakthrough could help the blind see again
Using AI to make bionic vision smarter and more precise, scientists are bringing the possibility of restoring sight to people with blindness one step closer to reality.
- Date:
- November 12, 2026
- Source:
- University of California - Santa Barbara
- Summary:
- Scientists have developed an AI-powered approach that makes experimental bionic vision technology more precise, helping predict the flashes and shapes of light perceived by a blind man with a brain implant. By learning how an individual's brain responds to electrical stimulation, the technology could bring researchers closer to restoring some degree of sight to people with blindness.
- Share:
Artificial intelligence could help overcome one of the biggest challenges in restoring vision to people who are blind: getting a brain implant to produce reliable visual experiences. Researchers from three institutions, including UC Santa Barbara, have demonstrated that AI can improve how precisely an experimental visual prosthesis stimulates the brain and predicts what a person perceives.
The team used a deep learning system to develop electrical stimulation patterns for electrodes temporarily implanted in the visual cortex, the region at the back of the brain responsible for processing visual information. By analyzing the brain's responses, the technology gave researchers greater control over neural activity and helped them better anticipate the visual sensations produced by the implant.
Published online in the journal Neuron, the proof-of-concept study represents progress toward more advanced visual prostheses, sometimes described as bionic eyes. These devices could eventually become more effective by learning how each person's brain responds to stimulation rather than relying on predetermined settings.
"Building a model in the abstract is one thing," said Michael Beyeler, an associate professor of computer science and psychological and brain sciences at UC Santa Barbara. "Seeing it shape an experiment with a person is something else entirely. That ability to go from theory to something that may one day help people is what drives much of the work in our lab."
How Bionic Vision Could Bypass Damaged Eyes
For decades, scientists have worked to develop technologies capable of restoring some vision to people who are blind, although the results have generally been limited. Some experimental devices stimulate the retina, the layer of tissue at the back of the eye that detects light. Others attempt to activate parts of the visual system farther along the pathway that carries visual information to the brain.
Visual cortical prostheses work differently. Instead of depending on the eyes or optic nerves, they deliver electrical signals directly to the visual cortex. This approach could offer a potential solution for people whose visual pathways have been damaged but whose visual cortex can still respond to stimulation. Possible candidates include individuals who lost their sight because of strokes, neurodegenerative diseases, or traumatic brain injuries.
The ability to regain even limited vision could be especially meaningful for people who remember what it was like to see.
Beyeler highlighted those "who have been able to see for part of their life, but then, because of an inherited eye disease or an accident, have lost their vision," adding, "For those people, the desire may be very strong to get some vision back."
The new findings build on earlier computational research supported by Beyeler's 2022 National Institutes of Health (NIH) Director's New Innovator Award. The five-year, $2 million grant has supported his efforts to make artificial vision systems more accurate, predictable, and effective.
Scientists Test AI With a Brain Implant in a Blind Man
An important opportunity to test the technology came in 2024, when researchers from Beyeler's Bionic Vision Lab traveled to Spain. Their goal was to determine whether their computer models could improve the performance of a brain implant already being used in an experimental study.
At Hospital IMED Elche, the team worked with a 27-year-old man who had become blind following a traumatic brain injury. He had received an implant containing 96 electrodes arranged in an array within his visual cortex. The device was intended to remain in place for six months before being removed.
When researchers activated the electrodes using electrical current, the participant experienced visual sensations known as phosphenes. These can appear as spots, flashes, or shapes of light, sometimes resembling stars or fireworks.
Producing these sensations is possible, but making them consistent and predictable is much more difficult. The same electrical stimulation does not always trigger an identical response, and activating particular electrodes does not guarantee that the person will perceive a specific visual pattern.
To address this problem, the researchers trained a deep neural network, a type of AI designed to recognize complex patterns, to predict how the visual cortex would respond to different electrical stimulation settings. The model also considered the brain's resting activity immediately before stimulation, giving it information about the participant's current neural state.
Using these predictions, the researchers identified combinations of electrical signals that were most likely to produce particular patterns of brain activity.
AI Makes Bionic Vision More Precise
When the scientists tested the stimulation patterns selected by AI, the results were encouraging. The new approach generated the intended patterns of neural activity more accurately than the comparison methods while requiring less electrical current.
Another important discovery emerged when the team examined the relationship between brain activity and the participant's visual experiences. The patterns recorded directly from his brain were better predictors of what he perceived than the stimulation settings themselves.
This distinction matters because activating the brain is not the same as knowing what a person will see. Even when researchers can produce a desired neural response, they still need to understand how the brain transforms that activity into a conscious visual experience.
"Engineers naturally want to treat phosphenes like pixels: stimulate more electrodes, and you should get a more complete image," Beyeler said. "But the brain does not work that way. Electrodes interact, neural responses fluctuate, and what we put into the brain is not necessarily what the person perceives. The challenge is to learn more about that transformation."
The findings suggest that future visual prostheses may need to do more than simply deliver electrical signals. They may also need to monitor how the brain reacts and use that feedback to continually improve stimulation.
Teaching Brain Implants to Adapt to Each Person
A key advantage of the implant used in the experiment was its ability to perform two tasks. It could stimulate the visual cortex with electrical current while simultaneously recording the resulting neural activity.
This allowed researchers to train their AI model using the brain's actual responses rather than relying exclusively on information about which electrodes were activated and how much current they delivered.
The participant also provided feedback about what he experienced. He reported whether he saw a phosphene and, during certain experiments, described its appearance, including its shape, size, brightness, and color.
Comparing these reports with the recorded brain activity revealed that neural responses contained more useful information about the perceived visual sensations than the electrical stimulation parameters alone.
The AI system also used measurements of resting brain activity to account for changes in the participant's neural state before each stimulation. This could be particularly valuable because the brain's response to electrical signals can vary over time, including from one day to the next.
By adapting stimulation to these changing conditions, future prostheses might provide more consistent visual experiences without requiring users to adjust to a rigid set of signals.
"A useful visual prosthesis cannot rely on a fixed recipe," Beyeler said. "It has to learn how an individual brain responds and adapt the stimulation accordingly. Ultimately, the device should adapt to the person, not the other way around."
A Collaborative Step Toward Restoring Sight
The research brought together scientists from UC Santa Barbara, ETH Zurich, and Miguel Hernández University (MHU). Beyeler described the effort as "a true collaboration."
The project was led by co-first authors Pehuén Moure of ETH Zurich, Jacob Granley of UC Santa Barbara, and Fabrizio Grani of MHU. The supervising researchers were Beyeler, Shih-Chii Liu of ETH Zurich, and Eduardo Fernández of MHU. Their work forms part of a larger feasibility trial taking place in Spain.
Although the technology remains experimental and the participant's visual experiences were limited to flashes and shapes of light, the results demonstrate how AI could improve communication between artificial vision devices and the brain.
Rather than treating every brain as if it responds the same way, future bionic vision systems could learn from each individual and adjust their signals accordingly. That personalized approach may prove essential to developing implants that can eventually restore useful vision to people who have lost their sight.
Story Source:
Materials provided by University of California - Santa Barbara. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Pehuén Moure, Jacob Granley, Fabrizio Grani, Leili Soo, Antonio Lozano, Rocío López-Peco, Adrián Villamarín-Ortiz, Cristina Soto-Sánchez, Shih-Chii Liu, Michael Beyeler, Eduardo Fernández. Deep learning-based control of electrically evoked activity in human visual cortex. Neuron, 2026; DOI: 10.1016/j.neuron.2026.07.006

articles.title: Una IA ya podría ayudar a detectar el cáncer de piel a partir de una fotografía: cómo funciona
articles.text:
La startup española Legit.Health, especializada en inteligencia artificial aplicada a la dermatología, logró la certificación europea de productos sanitarios (MDR) para su herramienta de diagnóstico cutáneo basado en IA. La compañía busca extender la tecnología a más centros sanitarios en España y Europa para reducir las demoras en dermatología, la especialidad con mayor tiempo de espera para una primera consulta en España.
Según informó Euronews, en España los pacientes aguardan un promedio de 127 días para acceder a una primera consulta dermatológica, de acuerdo con datos del Ministerio de Sanidad citados por la propia empresa. Esa cifra supera la media general de 102 días del conjunto de especialidades médicas y posiciona a dermatología como la especialidad con mayor demora para una primera consulta, por delante de neurología y traumatología. Para la compañía, esos números ilustran la urgencia de incorporar herramientas tecnológicas que agilicen la detección y derivación de pacientes.
La herramienta analiza lesiones cutáneas a partir de una fotografía
El funcionamiento del sistema es directo: el médico toma una fotografía de la zona de piel afectada y la carga en la plataforma. A partir de esa imagen, el algoritmo evalúa la lesión y asiste al profesional en la identificación de posibles patologías. Según la compañía, la herramienta puede reconocer indicios de más de 300 enfermedades de la piel, desde afecciones frecuentes como el acné hasta cuadros de mayor gravedad, como el melanoma, un tipo de cáncer cutáneo que requiere diagnóstico temprano.
La plataforma no se limita al diagnóstico inicial. También permite evaluar la gravedad del cuadro clínico y monitorear la evolución del paciente a lo largo del tratamiento, para determinar si la enfermedad responde o se agrava con el tiempo. Ante una lesión sospechosa, el sistema puede orientar al médico sobre si el caso requiere derivación urgente al especialista o si admite un seguimiento sin intervención inmediata.
La decisión clínica final recae siempre en el profesional sanitario. La inteligencia artificial cumple una función de apoyo y no reemplaza al médico. El propósito es que los casos más graves accedan antes a la atención especializada y que los dermatólogos concentren su tiempo en quienes más lo necesitan.
La certificación MDR acredita seguridad clínica y respaldo científico
La homologación obtenida por la firma tecnológica certifica que su tecnología cumple con el Reglamento Europeo de Productos Sanitarios (MDR), uno de los estándares más exigentes de la Unión Europea (UE) para dispositivos de uso médico. El proceso evalúa la seguridad, el rendimiento clínico y las pruebas científicas que respaldan el dispositivo antes de autorizar su aplicación en entornos reales.
Superar ese proceso otorga a la empresa respaldo regulatorio para operar en los mercados del bloque europeo y ofrecer su solución tanto a instituciones públicas como privadas. Para una startup del sector salud, la certificación MDR es un requisito indispensable para escalar el despliegue de la herramienta dentro del sistema sanitario europeo y acceder a nuevos contratos institucionales.
La certificación también implica auditorías continuas. Los dispositivos médicos que operan bajo este estándar deben mantener su cumplimiento a lo largo del tiempo, lo que obliga a las empresas a sostener niveles constantes de seguridad y eficacia clínica.
La startup ya opera con servicios de salud de Asturias y Aragón
Además de la certificación MDR, la startup obtuvo en 2026 el aval del Esquema Nacional de Seguridad (ENS), que establece los requisitos de ciberseguridad para sistemas que gestionan datos públicos en España. Ambas certificaciones en el mismo año consolidan el posicionamiento de la compañía dentro del sector de la salud digital.
La empresa ya colabora con los servicios públicos de salud de Asturias y Aragón, y mantiene acuerdos con aseguradoras en España y Polonia. Esa presencia en dos países distintos muestra una proyección internacional que la certificación europea busca ampliar hacia otros mercados del bloque.
Su objetivo declarado es agilizar los diagnósticos y contribuir a acortar las listas de espera en dermatología. Sin embargo, la empresa todavía no presentó datos que permitan medir el impacto concreto de la tecnología en los tiempos de atención. La expansión hacia nuevos centros sanitarios, habilitada por la certificación MDR, será determinante para evaluar esos resultados en los próximos meses.

articles.title: Hackers Exploit Cisco Expressway Vulnerability Soon After PoC Release
articles.text:
Hackers exploited a critical Cisco Expressway vulnerability to breach a Russian organization soon after proof-of-concept (PoC) exploit code was released publicly, according to cybersecurity firm F6.
Expressway gateways allow remote employees, partners, and third-party users to securely connect to an organization’s collaboration services, including video calls, voice calls, and instant messaging.
Tracked as CVE-2026-76466 (CVSS score of 9.8), the flaw can be exploited without authentication by remote attackers with network access to a device, allowing them to execute commands as root. It affects virtual and appliance versions of Expressway Core and Expressway Edge, but only when the devices are clustered.
Cisco, which disclosed the issue on October 21, said it resides in the Expressway database service feature and stems from persistent cookies.
An attacker possessing the persistent cookies could reach the database service and issue certain remote procedure call (RPC) commands, gaining the ability to run root-level commands on the underlying operating system.
Expressway X15.5.20 resolves the vulnerability. There are no workarounds, and customers on X14 or earlier releases need to move to a fixed release, Cisco says.
The advisory has not been revised since its initial release and still states that Cisco is unaware of public announcements or malicious use of the flaw. However, a PoC exploit has since been posted on GitHub, and F6 says the attack it investigated came shortly after.
According to F6, the attackers first breached two Expressway X15.5.3 devices exposed to the internet. They then pivoted from one of them to two other cluster nodes sitting on the organization’s internal network.
After securing root privileges, the attackers prepared tools for lateral movement. These included custom Python scripts designed to scan the network, locate SMB resources, interact with SQL Server and WinRM, and search GitLab repositories, aiming to exfiltrate credentials and other sensitive information.
F6 determined that the attackers modified the scripts on the fly, during the attack. “The source code contained characteristic comments and descriptions of fixes indicating the use of an AI assistant,” the company says.
F6 did not name the victim or attribute the attack to a known threat actor.
To detect exploitation, F6 points to the Erlang system log on Expressway devices. The security firm has also published IP addresses and file paths associated with the attack.
Although Cisco lists no workarounds, F6 recommends that organizations unable to patch immediately block connections to TCP ports 4371–4372 at the firewall, except from the IP addresses of trusted cluster nodes.
SecurityWeek has reached out to Cisco for comment on F6’s findings and will update this article if the company responds.

articles.title: Discord Rewrites Desktop and Mobile Clients in Rust Using Zed's GPU-Accelerated Rendering Framework
articles.text:
Discord’s CTO Stanislav Vishnevskiy recently announced rewriting its desktop and mobile clients in Rust, moving away from Electron and React Native. The project (codenamed Phoenix) eliminates layers of abstraction to directly leverage the device’s GPU, native mobile views, and a Rust core shared across platforms. Early results hint at a significant reduction in RAM usage and boot time for chat, voice, and streaming.
Vishnevskiy expanded on the rewrite on X:
We’ve been early adopters of Rust since 2018 and a lot of our infra, voice tech, and even some of the current client is already Rust, the holy grail was getting the whole client there. That means Electron goes away, and so does React Native, mobile keeps native UI but shares app code with desktop via Rust. We hope to get it into testing with users soon™. (And it’s not Tauri, it’s GPUI, so good guess everyone.)
The desktop app thus drops Chromium/Node.js for GPUI, the open-source, GPU-accelerated Rust UI framework built by the Zed team for the Zed editor. Zed is an open-source code editor written in Rust for macOS, Linux, and Windows by a team including the creators of GitHub’s Atom code editor, which was sunsetted in 2022, four years after Microsoft’s acquisition of GitHub. Zed touts a narrow focus on performance and user (i.e., developer) experience:
VS Code won by being good enough for everyone. Zed wins by being excellent for developers who refuse to compromise on speed.
Discord’s mobile app rewrite drops React Native, instead directly leveraging native iOS and Android views and reusing a common Rust core.
The browser client keeps rendering HTML with the application logic layer compiled to WebAssembly. Embedded web surfaces (e.g., YouTube videos and Activities), however, invoke an OS webview, with Electron’s built-in browser no longer available.
Vishnevskiy signals decreasing RAM usage, startup time, and latency as key motivations behind the rewrite:
The new Discord client using less RAM is just part of the story. Clicking around feels instant, I can’t go back. Check out the boot time.
Early internal builds for the desktop app reveal RAM usage at around 290 MB (measured with two accounts logged in simultaneously) and a near-instant cold start versus 5.5 s on Electron.
Vishnevskiy showcased similar improvements on mobile with a load time under 2 seconds for the rewrite versus approximately 5 seconds for the legacy app.
Elias Floreteng, in his master’s thesis at KTH this year (An Empirical Study of React Native’s New Architecture), reported performance gains across several metrics for native Swift and Kotlin over React Native, even with its new architecture. The controlled benchmark involves a 1,000-row scrollable image list using stock list and image components, with identical assets and row geometry across all binaries. Floreteng concludes that Swift beats React Native across every comparable runtime metric on iOS. On Android, the gap to native is small and runs in both directions, with native ahead on memory and CPU.
On desktop, Zed proved that leveraging GPUI could provide better performance over Electron and alternative frameworks reusing the device’s native webview (e.g., Tauri).
While Tauri also uses a Rust backend, it leverages the operating system’s native webview. This has the advantage of letting web developers reuse their knowledge of HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, while also avoiding the bundling of Chromium. Executable size is, as a result, generally smaller. Tauri apps’ RAM usage on Windows, however, tends to be similar to that of their Electron counterparts, as the same core, resource-hungry browser technology is used. Webview behavior may also be inconsistent across operating systems.
GPUI replaces the browser engine with a hybrid immediate and retained mode, GPU-accelerated UI framework that targets 120-frames-per-second rendering without garbage-collection pauses. In exchange for the reported performance gains, developers give up many rendering and accessibility features that come baked into the browser (e.g., text layout, input method integration, screen-reader accessibility hooks, right-to-left support). While miscellaneous Rust libraries exist to address some of these issues (e.g., Parley for text layout), developers still have to wire them into a consistent user experience.

articles.title: Enabling Real-Time AI for Scientific Instruments with GPU-Native Data Acquisition | NVIDIA Technical Blog
articles.text:
In science and industry, analyzing sensor measurements in real time can enable AI to adjust processes, guide experiments, and search for better operating conditions. Yet limits on how quickly the measured data can be moved and processed often shape how an instrument is designed, from readout electronics to acquisition timing. What could scientific instrument makers simplify—or make possible—if processing could keep pace with their sensors?
NVIDIA DAQIRI is a software-defined data acquisition library that moves high-bandwidth instrument and sensor data into GPU-ready workflows. It enables developers to process measurements during acquisition without first writing them to disk. An NVIDIA Holoscan platform library, DAQIRI bridges sensors optimized for measurement with programmable GPU platforms for scientific analysis, AI inference, and feedback applications.
For existing Ethernet-capable instruments, this opens opportunities to add processing and feedback capabilities, as described in the previous post, Enable Real-Time AI for High-Speed Data Acquisition with NVIDIA DAQIRI. For new instruments, it allows opportunities for reconsidering acquisition constraints from the start.
This post explores how a new electron microscopy camera and GPU processing enable analysis during acquisition. It then introduces new DAQIRI features, including hardware packet reordering, performance and throughput improvements in the library, and a low-latency NIC polling mode for time-sensitive packet processing.
Case study: Connecting high-dynamic-range imaging to GPU processing
A high-dynamic-range electron microscopy camera developed at Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory’s Molecular Foundry illustrates what becomes possible when advanced detectors and GPU processing are designed to work together.
Electron energy-loss spectroscopy (EELS) measures the energy electrons lose as they interact with a sample, helping scientists identify which elements are present and how they are bonded together. These measurements contain both strong and faint signals. To capture those differences in intensity, the conventional approach uses two separately optimized acquisition processes in rapid succession.
This requires precise coordination of the electron optics, exposure timing, and detector readout. The resulting measurements then need to be aligned and combined, adding complexity to both acquisition and processing. The new high-dynamic-range camera developed at the Molecular Foundry captures strong and faint signals together.
This advancement simplifies the experimental setup and microscope optics, but generates more than 500 gigabits of data per second (Gbps)—a stream that must be received and processed to make those measurements useful during acquisition. This is over 500x faster than conventional EELS data streams, which greatly enhances the raw detector information available for further processing and analysis.
Handling that stream requires an acquisition and processing pipeline designed to keep pace with the camera. This is where the collaboration between Berkeley Lab and NVIDIA brings together the camera, DAQIRI, and GPU-accelerated processing. FPGA readout electronics transmit detector data over Ethernet, DAQIRI receives the packets directly into GPU memory, and GPU processing assembles and corrects detector frames before reducing them to energy-loss spectra.
Computation also improves the spatial information recovered from the detector, enabling submicron spatial resolution from sensor pixels measuring 5 micrometers across. Through this pipeline, the team enables inspection of the data during the measurement and adjusting the acquisition parameters and regions of interest in real time, all while processing high bandwidth data incoming at more than 500 Gbps.
The benefits of this approach extend beyond electron microscopy. Connecting sensors to GPU processing can extract more information from measurements and give instrument makers greater flexibility in how they acquire, analyze, and act on data. Realizing those benefits requires efficient data movement, ordered payloads ready for processing, and low-latency communication for feedback.
Designing acquisition paths for intelligent instruments
The latest DAQIRI release adds hardware packet reordering, an optimized library backend for improved throughput, and direct polling for low-latency packet transmission and reception.
Reorder data as it arrives with NIC hardware
Most networks rely on protocol processing or receive-side buffering to handle out-of-order packets, which can add latency and memory overhead. DAQIRI can now offload packet reordering tasks to supported NVIDIA ConnectX-7 or newer NICs, preserving CPU and GPU resources for analysis. For compatible sequence formats, the NIC parses sequence fields and places each payload directly into its ordered position in memory. The application receives the assembled, ordered data without requiring a separate software reorder copy step.
Hardware-based reordering is defined here for a specific receive queue. The configuration dictates how to parse the sequence number from the packet header, which reordering method to use, and how missing packets should be handled.
- name: "rx_reorder_seq_1024"
  reorder_engine: "hw"          # NIC places payloads in order
  cyclic_sequence: true         # Confirm compatible cyclic numbering
  missing_action: “drop”        # Drop partial batches on RX timeout
  reorder_type: "gpu"           # Deliver packets to GPU memory
  memory_region: "Reorder_RX_GPU"
  payload_byte_offset: 42       # Skip 42-byte Ethernet/IPv4/UDP header
  packet_size: 8192             # Payload bytes per output slot
  flow_ids: [201]               # Apply reorder to RX flow 201
  method:
    seq_packets_per_batch:      # Reorder by one sequence field
      sequence_number:
        bit_offset: 336         # Sequence starts at bit 336
        bit_width: 32           # 32-bit sequence field
      packets_per_batch: 1024   # 1024 packets per output buffer
Use the ibverbs engine for efficient acquisition
DAQIRI introduces an ibverbs engine for high-rate receive and transmit of raw Ethernet packets. Built on libibverbs and NVIDIA DevX, the engine is selected by default for raw Ethernet streams. Developers can also select it explicitly by adding engine: “ibverbs” to their DAQIRI configuration, without changing how they use the application API. By reducing per-packet CPU overhead, the ibverbs engine delivers approximately twice the per-core throughput of the previous default DPDK backend at small packet sizes (up to 1024 bytes) and extreme data rates (greater than 200 Gbps), based on benchmark tests performed on the NVIDIA DGX Spark, NVIDIA IGX Thor, and NVIDIA RTX PRO server platforms.
Reduce feedback latency with direct polling
Intelligent instruments may require latency-sensitive feedback from GPU analysis to adjust acquisition or control settings. The DAQIRI direct polling mode reduces communication latency by letting the application thread receive and submit packets directly, eliminating the handoff to a separate I/O worker. In cabled loopback benchmark tests, application send-to-receive latency on the order of 2-4 µs has been demonstrated in direct polling mode. When using the ibverbs engine, developers can select direct polling for control queues while retaining batched processing for high-throughput data streams.
Set poll_mode: "direct" on the latency-sensitive TX and RX control queues so the application thread submits and receives packets directly.
# TX/RX queue settings in example configuration file
tx:
  queues:
  - name: "control_tx"
    id: 0
    poll_mode: "direct"         # App thread submits packets
    memory_regions: ["Control_TX"]
rx:
  queues:
  - name: "control_rx"
    id: 0
    poll_mode: "direct"         # App thread polls received packets
    memory_regions: ["Control_RX"]
Run the direct-polling latency benchmark using a cabled loopback between TX and RX ports on the same host.
First, replace the configuration’s hardware address placeholders and other system-specific settings with values for your system:
sudo ./build/examples/daqiri_bench_raw_latency 
examples/daqiri_bench_raw_latency_ibverbs.yaml --samples 
10000 --warmup 1000 --csv latency.csv
Get started with GPU-native data acquisition
During the process of making scientific instruments, GPU-native data acquisition enables you to design around what will be measured and your desired means of response. Advanced detectors and GPU processing can work together for reconsidering acquisition constraints.
The latest DAQIRI capabilities extend the options for moving and organizing measurements efficiently and connecting analysis to experimental control. That means more engineering effort can focus on measurement quality and scientific insight.
To explore these capabilities, start with the DAQIRI documentation and DAQIRI configuration examples. Then use the DAQIRI benchmarks to evaluate throughput and communication latency on your hardware.
To learn more, check out these related resources:
- Explore the NVIDIA/daqiri GitHub repo
- Browse the DAQIRI plus TensorRT Streaming Inference Reference Application
- Generate DAQIRI Configurations for your hardware

articles.title: Float to open Montréal office, invest $5 million in Québec expansion | BetaKit
articles.text:
Fresh off closing its Series C round, Float is expanding its presence in Québec with a new office.
The news: Toronto-based FinTech company Float Financial, which provides banking and AI-powered financial management services for small and medium-sized businesses, announced on Thursday that it’s committing $5 million to grow its Québec presence and open an office in Montréal, its first outside of Toronto. Float said it plans to hire a general manager for the region and expand its team in sales, product support, and customer success.
From the source: The news comes as a growing share of Float’s customer base leans into AI. An August study of its business customers found that monthly AI spending has increased by more than twelvefold over the past two years, while 47 percent of businesses buy at least one AI product, up from 27 percent.
The context: Founded in 2019, Float got its start offering Canadian small and medium-sized businesses corporate cards and expense management software to simplify their spending. It has since grown to serve more than 10,000 customers, including Cohere and Clutch. It has roughly 1,000 customers in Québec, including medtech company Puzzle Medical Devices.
The company recently released its AI intelligence layer, which can automate tasks for finance teams, like tracking down receipts, data entry, and payment reconciliation. It also just brought on Jack Fraser as its first CFO; Fraser invested in Float while he was at BDC Capital.
Final thought: Float is part of a cohort of FinTech companies that joined the non-profit national organization Payments Canada as members this year, setting the stage for it to build on top of national payment infrastructure like the new Real-Time Rail. This week, CEO Rob Khazzam said Float can now directly facilitate pre-authorized debit requests from third-party financial institutions without a “middleman,” which wouldn’t have been possible without its new Payments Canada designation.
Feature image courtesy Float.

articles.title: Nimble enters the item-tracking market with eco-friendly luggage tags and keychains | TechCrunch
articles.text:
As Google steps up its competition with Apple in the item-tracking market, smaller brands are also looking to carve out a piece of the category. The latest entrant is Nimble, the sustainable accessories brand best known for its charging products.
Founded in 2018 by former Mophie executives, the California-based company announced Thursday that it’s expanding into the category with “Trace,” a seven-product collection of item trackers designed to blend tracking technology into everyday accessories.
Nimble’s new collection arrives as competition in the Bluetooth tracking market continues to heat up. Apple’s AirTag helped popularize the category, while Google recently introduced its first-party tracker, the $29 Pixel Tag, powered by its Find Hub network. Meanwhile, established third-party players, such as Chipolo and Pebblebee, continue to expand their lineups.
Nimble is taking a slightly different approach. Rather than introducing another stand-alone tracker to attach to a set of keys or slip into a bag, the company has integrated tracking technology directly into practical accessories, including wallets, keychains, luggage tags, and passport covers.
The lineup includes seven products, ranging from the $14.95 Trace Tag, which features a replaceable coin-cell battery, to the $49.95 Trace Folio, a passport cover with built-in rechargeable tracking. Other options include the Trace Keyfob ($19.95), Trace Slim Wallet Card ($29.95), Trace Keychain ($29.95), Trace Luggage Tag ($39.95), and Trace Wallet ($39.95).
The entire collection is compatible with both Apple’s Find My and Google’s Find Hub networks.
Ross Howe, co-founder and CEO of Nimble, told us that the company’s approach is designed to differentiate its products from traditional trackers.
“Most locators are built as utility gadgets, not as things you want to own. Few were asking why the locator couldn’t just be the nice object itself. So, for example, we made a wallet findable instead of making a tracker that fits a wallet. We also thought more options should be rechargeable.”
The Trace Luggage Tag and Trace Folio are arguably the most interesting products in the collection. Dedicated luggage tags and passport covers with built-in tracking remain relatively uncommon, giving Nimble an opportunity to stand out in a market. There are only a few alternatives, including Spotminder’s $59 passport cover with Apple Find My support, which is $10 more than Nimble’s option. Knog Scout offers a luggage tag, although I find its design a little too bulky.
Rechargeability is another appealing aspect of Nimble’s new collection. Several models support USB-C or wireless charging, offering an alternative to the disposable batteries found in many traditional trackers. Howe says battery life lasts for “months,” with the Trace Keyfob, for example, rated for approximately six months on a charge.
Sustainability is another major part of Nimble’s pitch. Staying true to its roots, the company has incorporated eco-friendly materials throughout the collection, including recycled plastics and plant-based, vegan aloe leather. The products have also undergone third-party testing for chemicals of concern.
“We’ve spent the last two years going through the chemistry of our products line by line to remove or limit as many harmful ingredients as possible. Trace is the first collection designed specifically to meet these higher standards. We’re not 100% yet, but the independent labs checking our work will help us get there,” Howe said.
The collection is available now through its website and Amazon. All seven products come in five color options: Black, Stone, Tangerine, Plum, and Teal.

A cheap intro to a smart home setup
I don't know if I'd ever recommend buying an Echo Dot at full price, because you always know it will be cheaper at Prime Day and Black Friday. But I guess there's always the question of how much cheaper it will be.
This year, it's down to £32.99 in both its standard and Kids forms. Both have been cheaper before, and who knows, maybe they will be cheaper again in the next week. But for now, this remains a very good deal rather than a must-buy.
Echo Dot: was £79.99 now £32.99 at Amazon
Echo Dot Kids: was £79.99 now £32.99 at Amazon
An impressive soundbar under £150
Sticking with the soundbars theme, here's something a little cheaper…
Amazon's own-brand soundbar is really good, impressing us in our Amazon Fire TV Soundbar Plus review — it's maybe not the pinnacle of value at full price, but at nearly half price? Now we're talking. And we're talking in a way you can hear over the film score in the background, which may make a change if you've been relying on your TV's built-in speakers.
Amazon Fire TV Soundbar Plus: was £249.99 now £136.99 at Amazon
The best soundbar under £300
The Sony HT-2000 is the best budget soundbar in our view, if we view budget and meaning under £300 with this discount. (The Sonos Beam 2 is also excellent, but is slightly over this crucial price barrier.)
It's impactful, delivers clear dialogue, and immersive 3D elements to movie soundtracks — all from a compact body.
Sony HT-S2000 soundbar: was £399 now £269 at Amazon
The best kitchen purchase I ever made
I think somebody already posted about this Ninja air fryer below, but I'm going to share it again anyway — because it's awesome.
I'm talking about the five-star-rated Ninja AF300UK, which is a dual-basket air fryer, meaning you can cook two things at once. Chips in one and (veggie) sausages in the other? Yes please! It's revolutionised my cooking (on the days when I don't do actual cooking) and right now it's at a super-low £119.
Ninja AF300UK Air Fryer: was £199.99 now £119 at Amazon
Apple's mini marvel is on sale
I bought a Mac mini M4 a couple of years ago and it's one of the best tech purchases I've made — so dinky, so stylish and well crafted, but packing tons of power inside and available for a bargain price. That bargain price is unfortunately not a thing any longer — the RAM crisis has put paid to that — but it remains a great choice of desktop computer.
Amazon currently has it on sale for £804 in its 256GB guise, which is a mere £5 above the lowest price we've seen for it so far and a handy saving of £95.
Apple Mac mini M6, 256GB: was £899 now £804 at Amazon
An oldie but goldie espresso machine
I don't have a great record of buying my partner gifts, but she has described her Sage Bambino Plus as the best thing I ever bought her, and if pushed I think she would now choose it over me. I don't drink coffee, but she assures me that it makes a fantastic espresso, and to coffee lovers that's an important thing, I gather.
This is far from the lowest price we've ever seen for it — it was £224 soon after its launch in 2018 — but it hasn't been lower for a couple of years, and £40 is still £40.
Sage The Bambino Plus: was £399 now £359 at Amazon
That's no moon. It's a Lego Star Wars Death Star
This is simultaneously the best and worst deal I've ever written about.
Best because if my parents had bought me one of these as a kid then I would have known happiness beyond that which any human has ever experienced. Come on, look at it! It has 9023 bricks! It comes with 38 Minifigures! It enables you to recreate iconic scenes such as the trash compactor and hangar bay!
Worst because it's £808 and really, can anyone justify that? Still, it is currently £91 off at Amazon for Black Friday, so that's something.
Lego Star Wars Death Star: was £899 now £808 at Amazon
A child-friendly tablet for less
One thing I quickly discovered when my kids were young was that a good tablet can be a lifesaver. Don't worry, I wasn't one of those parents who used an iPad as a babysitter — screen time was controlled, as was the content they consumed. And I did that with the help of Amazon's excellent Fire Kids tablets.
Fire Tablets are no more, replaced by the Amazon Kids Tablet 8 and Tablet 11, and these devices offer several upgrades including — finally! — the fact that they run on full Android rather than Amazon's Fire OS. That means access to the riches of the Google Play Store, but you still get all of the parental controls you need, plus the much-needed colourful bumper case and a 1-year subscription to the Amazon Kids+ service. Oh, and both models are on sale for Black Friday — so what are you waiting for?
Amazon Kids Tablet 8: was £199 now £149 at Amazon
Amazon Kids Tablet 11: was £289 now £199 at Amazon
Start your stargazing journey here
One of my hobbies is taking photos of space, a pursuit I've enjoyed far more since the arrival of smart telescopes a few years ago. I've used and written about two of the best at the more affordable end of the spectrum — the Seestar S30 Plus and S30 Pro — and both are now available for less at Amazon. Seestar S30 Plus smart telescope: was £449 now £426 at Amazon
Seestar S30 Pro smart telescope: was £649 now £616.55 at Amazon

Good evening, Marc here to take on live blogging duties for a few hours.
Amazon's usual Fire TV Stick discounts have arrived, and I expect that this is the lowest price we'll see for these models — I don't expect a second drop on Black Friday itself. But when you look at the size of the discounts, that seems fair enough!

Amazon Amazon Fire TV Stick 4K Plus: was £79.99 now £34.99 at Amazon
Amazon Amazon Fire TV Stick 4K Max (newest Gen): was £99.99 now £46.99 at Amazon
The eco-friendly plaque-buster
See that picture? That's a look inside the box of the Suri Pro Sonic Toothbrush 2.0, the top model with a sustainable angle. Suri brush-heads — made of plant-based materials — can be sent back to the company to be recycled via freepost.
The brush itself has a magnetic mount, four-week battery life, a powerful motor behind a simple sonic movement, and a case packing a UV cleaning light. We gave it 4.5 stars in our review, and right now, you can save 22% on its sticker price.
Suri Pro Sonic Toothbrush 2.0: was £89 now £68.98 at Amazon
Save £50 on the Ninja Crispi 3.8L 4-in-1 Glass Air Fryer
As well as the Ninja Foodi Dual Zone, there's another stellar discount from Ninja — this time on the Ninja Crispi. This 4-in-1 air fryer clips onto the top of its glass case, which is dishwasher safe for easy cleaning.
Described as a 'portable cooking system', the Crispi allows you to simply click a lid on the glass container after frying for easy storage and transport. And it's glass, so you can see it cooking without stopping the process!

articles.title: Meta’s Muse Charm might cost $300
articles.text:
Meta is planning to price the Muse Charm, a little gadget with a screen that lets you chat with your Muse AI agent, at $300, according to The Information. CEO Mark Zuckerberg revealed the gadget earlier this year and said the company expected to ship the Charm “in time for the holidays in December,” but he didn’t provide a price at the time.
Meta’s Muse Charm might cost $300
The Information has reported a potential price for the Muse Charm, which is expected to ship in time for the holidays.
When he announced the Muse Charm, Zuckerberg said that the company had “packed the whole Muse experience,” including real-time voice and avatar technology, into the gadget. It has a fingerprint sensor, and you can tap it to be able to talk to a Muse AI agent without unlocking a phone or opening an app. The Information reports that the Muse Charm will come with a free 12-month 5G data plan from Verizon.
Spokesperson Tyler Yee wrote to The Information that “We’re charmed by the interest in our AI devices, and we’ll have more to share soon.” When reached for comment by The Verge, Yee provided the same statement.
The company is also working on a smartwatch, The Information says, but a launch for that has been pushed to 2027 as Meta tries to get Muse Charm out the door.
Meta also open sourced code to let users make their own Muse gadgets, which my colleague Sean Hollister used to make his own DIY Muse Charm.
Update, November 19th: Noted statement given by Meta spokesperson Tyler Yee.

articles.title: Black Friday MacBook : les 10 meilleures offres sur les PC d'Apple — Frandroid
articles.text:
Apple n’est pas la marque la plus sujette aux promotions dans les rayons tech, ce qui rend les baisses de prix du Black Friday d’autant plus notables. Nous avons retenu dix références qui couvrent l’essentiel de la gamme actuelle : des ordinateurs portables, des machines de bureau et quelques accessoires pour compléter un setup.
Les meilleurs bons plans du Black Friday sur les PC d’Apple
- Apple MacBook Air 13 M5 à 1 174 euros au lieu de 1 399 euros avec le code promo 25DES299
- Apple MacBook Neo à 717 euros au lieu de 799 euros avec le code promo 25DES299
- Apple Mac mini M6 à 924 euros au lieu de 1 049 euros avec le code promo 25DES299
- Apple Mac mini M5 Pro à 1 874 euros au lieu de 1 999 euros avec le code promo 25DES299
- Apple Mac Studio (2026) à 2 674 euros au lieu de 2 999 euros avec le code promo 25DES299
- Apple MacBook Pro 16 M5 Pro à 2 999 euros au lieu de 3 399 euros
- Apple MacBook Pro 14 M5 Max à 4 199 euros au lieu de 4 799 euros
- Apple Magic Trackpad à 98 euros au lieu de 139 euros
- Apple Magic Keyboard à 147 euros au lieu de 199 euros
- UGREEN Nexode 160W à 47,60 euros au lieu de 89,99 euros
Apple MacBook Air 13 M5
Le MacBook Air 13 M5 est l’ultraportable Apple de référence pour qui veut une machine silencieuse, légère et capable de tenir une journée complète sur batterie. La puce M5 apporte des gains de performance significatifs par rapport à la génération précédente, et Apple a enfin doté ce modèle d’un SSD à la hauteur de ses ambitions.
Notre test du MacBook Air 13 M5 lui a décerné la note de 9/10. La connectique reste limitée à deux ports Thunderbolt, et l’écran plafonne à 60 Hz en 2026 : ce sont les seuls points qui peuvent freiner les profils les plus exigeants. Pour les autres, c’est la référence dans notre guide des meilleurs ordinateurs d’Apple.
Les points forts du MacBook Air 13 M5
- Performances M5 en nette progression
- Autonomie exceptionnelle au quotidien
- SSD rapide inclus de série
Le MacBook Air 13 M5 est affiché à 1 174 euros chez Cdiscount au lieu de 1 399 euros, soit 225 euros d’économie, avec le code promo 25DES299.
Apple MacBook Neo
Avec le MacBook Neo, Apple relance l’idée d’un Mac abordable sous la barre des 800 euros, pensé pour les étudiants et les primo-accédants à l’écosystème macOS. Son écran Liquid Retina de 12,9 pouces affiche une calibration soignée, et ses performances s’avèrent étonnamment solides pour le segment, comme le rapporte notre test du MacBook Neo, noté 9/10.
Il faut toutefois composer avec 8 Go de RAM seulement, un clavier sans rétroéclairage et une connectique réduite, qui peuvent peser dans les usages intensifs. Pour qui cherche un point d’entrée sérieux dans l’univers Mac, il figure en bonne place dans notre guide des meilleurs PC portables de 2026.
Les points forts du MacBook Neo
- Tarif de lancement sous les 800 euros
- Écran 12,9 pouces bien calibré
- Fonctionnement silencieux en toutes circonstances
Le MacBook Neo est disponible à 717 euros chez Cdiscount au lieu de 799 euros, avec le code promo 25DES299.
Apple Mac mini M6
Compact au point de tenir dans la poche d’un manteau, le Mac mini M6 est un mini PC de bureau qui ne fait aucun compromis sur les performances. La puce M6 pousse encore les capacités de calcul vers le haut et intègre des fonctions d’inférence IA que les générations précédentes ne proposaient pas.
Le Black Friday est lancé sur l’univers Apple. Sur Back Market, profitez de promotions sur les iPhone, MacBook, iPad, AirPods et Apple Watch. Chaque appareil est soumis à jusqu’à 100 points de contrôle qualité et est livré avec une garantie de 12 mois. De quoi profiter de performances comparables à celles d’un produit neuf.
Notre test du Mac mini M6 lui attribue la note de 9/10 : il est notre recommandation principale dans notre comparatif des meilleurs mini PC. Le revers de la médaille est un tarif de base en hausse par rapport au M4, et un SSD désormais soudé à la carte mère, ce qui exclut toute mise à niveau ultérieure.
Les points forts du Mac mini M6
- Châssis de 12,7 cm de côté, 670 g
- Performances M6 parmi les meilleures du segment
- Wi-Fi 7 et Bluetooth 6.0 inclus
Le Mac mini M6 est proposé à 924 euros chez Cdiscount au lieu de 1 049 euros, soit 125 euros d’économie, grâce au code promo 25DES299.
Apple Mac mini M5 Pro
Au-dessus du Mac mini M6, Apple propose cette même forme ultra-compacte équipée d’une puce M5 Pro, pensée pour les usages qui demandent davantage de ressources CPU et GPU en continu : montage vidéo, compilation, modélisation 3D légère. La puce M5 Pro bénéficie d’un nombre de cœurs CPU et GPU supérieur à la M6, ce qui se traduit par des marges de manœuvre plus importantes sur les tâches longues et les projets multifichiers. Le prix de base reste élevé, et les options de mémoire ou de stockage supplémentaires creusent encore davantage l’addition.
Les points forts du Mac mini M5 Pro
- Puce M5 Pro, plus de cœurs CPU et GPU que le M6
- Châssis identique, encombrement minimal
- Jusqu’à 64 Go de RAM configurables
Le Mac mini M5 Pro est affiché à 1 874 euros chez Cdiscount au lieu de 1 999 euros, soit 125 euros d’économie, avec le code promo 25DES299.
Apple Mac Studio (2026)
Le Mac Studio occupe un territoire à part dans la gamme Apple : plus massif qu’un Mac mini, il embarque ici la puce M5 Max et accueille 512 Go de stockage et 36 Go de RAM. Sur le bureau, le châssis en aluminium de 19,7 cm de côté concentre une connectique complète, avec plusieurs ports Thunderbolt, des USB-A, un lecteur de carte SDXC, une sortie HDMI et un port Ethernet 10G.
C’est la machine que choisissent les créatifs dont les projets débordent les capacités d’un Mac mini : effets visuels, musique multipiste, traitement d’images en grand format.
Les points forts du Mac Studio
- Puces M5 Max ou M5 Ultra au choix
- 512 Go de stockage et 36 Go de RAM
- Connectique très complète
Le Mac Studio (2026) est disponible à 2 674 euros chez Cdiscount au lieu de 2 999 euros, soit 325 euros d’économie, avec le code promo 25DES299.
Apple MacBook Pro 16 M5 Pro
Le MacBook Pro 16 M5 Pro s’adresse aux créatifs et aux développeurs qui ont besoin d’un écran grand format sans renoncer à la mobilité. Sa puce M5 Pro embarque un CPU 18 cœurs et un GPU 20 cœurs, avec ici 24 Go de mémoire vive. L’écran Liquid Retina XDR de 16,2 pouces affiche jusqu’à 3456 × 2234 pixels à 120 Hz, ce qui en fait une référence pour le montage vidéo ou la retouche photo. Les performances sont à la hauteur du gabarit, et le tarif aussi.
Les points forts du MacBook Pro 16 M5 Pro
- CPU 18 cœurs, GPU 20 cœurs, 24 Go de RAM
- Écran Liquid Retina XDR 16,2 pouces, 120 Hz
- Batterie 100 Wh pour de longues sessions nomades
Le MacBook Pro 16 M5 Pro est disponible à 2 999 euros chez Amazon au lieu de 3 399 euros, soit 400 euros d’économie.
Par ailleurs, le MacBook Pro 14 M5 Max est lui aussi en promotion chez Amazon. La configuration avec un CPU 18 cœurs/GPU 32 cœurs, 36 Go de mémoire unifiée et un SSD de 2 To est disponible à 4 199 euros au lieu de 4 799 euros.
Apple Magic Trackpad
Pour qui utilise un Mac de bureau ou un Mac mini, le Magic Trackpad est une alternative sérieuse à la Magic Mouse. Sa grande surface en verre bord à bord accueille l’ensemble des gestes Multi-Touch de macOS et intègre la technologie Force Touch, qui détecte différents niveaux de pression pour étendre les actions disponibles. Bluetooth, rechargeable via USB-C, autonomie annoncée d’un mois entre deux charges : il s’intègre sans câble permanent sur un bureau.
Les points forts de l’Apple Magic Trackpad
- Grande surface en verre bord à bord avec Force Touch
- Connexion Bluetooth, charge USB-C, autonomie un mois
- Compatible avec tous les Mac récents
Le Magic Trackpad est affiché à 98 euros chez Amazon au lieu de 139 euros, soit 41 euros d’économie.
Apple Magic Keyboard
Le Magic Keyboard avec Touch ID est l’accessoire qui manque souvent aux possesseurs de Mac de bureau. Le capteur Touch ID intégré permet de se connecter, de valider un paiement Apple Pay ou de déverrouiller son trousseau sans saisir de mot de passe – exactement comme sur un MacBook. Le clavier est sans fil, rechargeable via USB-C et s’associe automatiquement au Mac dès la première connexion filaire. À noter : la fonction Touch ID est réservée aux Mac équipés d’une puce Apple silicon ; elle ne fonctionne pas sur les anciens Mac Intel.
Pour replacer cet accessoire parmi les meilleures options du marché, consultez notre guide pour choisir le meilleur clavier pour votre PC de bureau.
Les points forts de l’Apple Magic Keyboard
- Capteur Touch ID pour l’authentification sans mot de passe
- Sans fil Bluetooth, rechargeable USB-C, autonomie un mois
- Association automatique avec les Mac Apple silicon
Le Magic Keyboard avec Touch ID est disponible à 147 euros chez Amazon au lieu de 199 euros, soit 52 euros d’économie.
UGREEN Nexode 160W
Recharger un MacBook Pro et plusieurs autres appareils depuis une seule prise, c’est la promesse du UGREEN Nexode 160W. Ce chargeur GaN compact propose quatre ports – deux USB-C et deux USB-A – pour une puissance totale de 160 W, suffisante pour alimenter un MacBook Pro 16 pouces à pleine charge via son port USB-C principal tout en chargeant simultanément un iPhone et un iPad. Son format voyage reste raisonnable pour la puissance délivrée. C’est un accessoire qui prend tout son sens pour ceux qui veulent limiter les adaptateurs en déplacement.
Si vous hésitez, vous pouvez également jeter un œil à notre guide des meilleurs chargeurs pour MacBook Air et MacBook Pro.
Les points forts du UGREEN Nexode 160W
- 160 W au total, compatible MacBook Pro 16 pouces
- 4 ports simultanés : 2 USB-C, 2 USB-A

Le UGREEN Nexode 160W est proposé à 47,60 euros chez Amazon au lieu de 89,99 euros, soit 42,39 euros d’économie.

articles.title: Tesla n'est plus la seule lanterne rouge du contrôle technique allemand, une électrique chinoise l’y rejoint
