C’est devenu un marronnier dont les détracteurs de Tesla se régalent. Chaque fin d’année, le TÜV-Verband (la fédération des organismes TÜV, qui réalisent une grande partie des contrôles techniques outre-Rhin) dresse le bilan des véhicules les plus recalés (ainsi que les plus fiables). Comme les années précédentes, les Tesla Model 3 et Model Y figurent parmi les pires scores de la catégorie des véhicules récents.
Le rapport 2027, qui porte sur les contrôles réalisés du 1er juillet 2025 au 30 juin 2026, vient de paraître le 19 novembre 2026 sur le site de l’ADAC. Avec 18,5 % de contre-visites pour des défauts majeurs, le Tesla Model Y termine une nouvelle fois bon dernier, mais il est rejoint en bas de classement par la MG4 qui affiche 16 % de recalage à la première présentation du véhicule.
Comme souvent, des histoires de frein
Si ces voitures électriques échouent massivement, ce n’est pas parce que leur batterie flanche ou que leur moteur rend l’âme. Ce n’est de toute façon pas ce que vérifie le contrôle technique, qu’il soit allemand ou français. Le mal dont ces modèles souffrent est bien plus banal.
Dans le cas de la MG4, les inspecteurs allemands pointent un coupable majeur : les disques de frein. Sur plus d’une MG4 sur dix (10,3 %), les disques sont signalés comme défectueux ou piqués par la rouille, un chiffre dix fois supérieur à la moyenne des voitures de cet âge.
C’est le grand paradoxe de la voiture électrique : grâce au freinage régénératif, le conducteur ne sollicite plus assez le freinage mécanique. Sauf qu’à force de ne jamais pincer les disques, ces derniers rouillent, s’encrassent et finissent par perdre en efficacité, jusqu’à se faire recaler au contrôle. Un défaut qu’un simple freinage très appuyé sur une voie rapide de temps en temps suffirait souvent à éviter.
L’absence d’entretien régulier des Tesla les pénalise toujours
Pour les Tesla, le problème des freins sous-exploités s’ajoute à une usure prématurée des suspensions. Le Model Y et le Model 3 sont des véhicules particulièrement lourds et puissants, ce qui met les rotules et les triangles de suspension à rude épreuve sur les routes bosselées. En l’absence de révision par le constructeur qui constaterait ce défaut avant le passage au TÜV, beaucoup de propriétaires de Tesla se rendent directement au contrôle technique sans jamais être passés par un atelier de la marque depuis l’achat de la voiture.
Au contrôle technique, ces propriétaires se font alors recaler pour un phare mal réglé ou un triangle fatigué, obtiennent la liste exacte des défauts sur procès-verbal, et retournent chez Tesla pour réparer uniquement ce qui est nécessaire. Cette façon de faire gonfle mécaniquement le chiffre des véhicules recalés, l’ADAC le reconnaît lui-même, et maintient la marque en bas du classement.
Un chiffre joue en revanche en faveur de Tesla : les Model Y contrôlés affichaient 58 000 km en moyenne, soit 11 000 km de plus que la moyenne de leur classe d’âge. De quoi peser aussi sur l’usure des rotules et des triangles.
Le client y gagne, puisqu’il économise le prix des révisions. Sur le papier, en revanche, les statistiques de la marque virent au carnage. Les autres électriques du classement, choyées par des révisions annuelles chez leur concessionnaire (comme le Mazda MX-30 ou l’Audi Q8 e-tron), affichent d’excellents scores : 3,0 % de défauts importants pour le Mazda, troisième sur 109 modèles, et 3,2 % pour l’Audi, cinquième. Les révisions y sont sans doute pour quelque chose, une partie des défauts étant corrigée en amont par le garagiste.

Black Friday 2026 : L'aspirateur balai Dyson V8 Cyclone à 238,00 €
L'aspirateur balai Dyson V8 Cyclone est proposé à 238,00 € chez Amazon.
L'innovation peut-elle se nicher dans la réinterprétation ? Ce qui apparaît comme un sujet de bac de philo trouvera peut-être une réponse après notre test du Dyson V8 Cyclone, la vision 2025 d'un aspirateur-balai sorti en 2016.

Points forts
- Belles performances d'aspiration.
- Entretien facile.
- Relativement discret, aussi bien visuellement qu'acoustiquement.
Points faibles
- Autonomie trop faible à la puissance turbo.
- Extraction de la brosse pénible.
- Manque d'astuces pratiques (pas d'indicateur d'autonomie, de rampe de leds…).
Dans les grandes lignes, le Dyson V8 Cyclone reste le même que le V8 “normal”. Pour le meilleur et pour le pire, serait-on tenté d'ajouter. Certes, il existe quelques menues différences au niveau de la prise en main, une amélioration de la gestion du bruit, et on ne peut que féliciter Dyson d'avoir enfin pris le virage de la batterie amovible. On regrette d'autant plus que cet aspirateur-balai n'ait pas pris celui de l'indicateur d'autonomie précis, ou encore de la rampe de leds sur la tête d'aspiration. Ceci étant, malgré une durée de vie en mode turbo famélique, le V8 Cyclone est un modèle efficace et très simple à entretenir.

articles.title: Inside this quantum computer, memory vibrates like a guitar string
articles.text:
Inside this quantum computer, memory vibrates like a guitar string
- Date:
- November 11, 2026
- Source:
- ETH Zurich
- Summary:
- Researchers have created a quantum computer that stores information in microscopic vibrations, potentially making quantum machines smaller, more powerful, and better at preserving information. The breakthrough successfully demonstrated advanced quantum calculations and could help overcome major barriers to practical quantum computing.
- Share:
A quantum computer might seem to have little in common with a guitar, but researchers at ETH Zurich have found a surprising connection. Physicist Yiwen Chu and her team have developed a system that uses microscopic mechanical vibrations to store and manipulate quantum information, much like the vibrating strings of a guitar produce musical notes.
Unlike the sounds produced by a musical instrument, these vibrations occur at frequencies far beyond human hearing. They take place within a tiny quantum chip, where they serve as a new form of computer memory.
By harnessing these vibrations, the researchers have created a way for quantum computers to process information efficiently while accessing a flexible working memory. "The interaction between the quantum processor and the quantum memory provides a crucial foundation with a view to establishing quantum computers as a powerful and reliable way to perform computations that are not feasible with conventional computers," says Yiwen Chu.
The breakthrough, described in the journal Science, introduces a different approach to quantum computer design. Instead of closely integrating information processing and storage, as many existing systems do, Chu's team has developed an architecture that gives these functions more distinct roles.
Quantum Memory Inspired by Conventional Computers
The researchers drew inspiration from the basic design of everyday digital computers. In a conventional machine, the central processing unit (CPU) carries out calculations while information is held separately in working memory, commonly called random access memory (RAM). The arrangement of these components plays an important role in determining how efficiently a computer operates.
Chu's quantum system follows a similar principle. A superconducting qubit acts as the processing and control unit, performing a role comparable to that of the central processing unit (CPU). Meanwhile, a separate quantum memory temporarily holds the information needed during calculations, allowing the processor to retrieve and modify it as necessary.
The major difference lies in how that information is stored.
"In our quantum working memory, however, information is not stored electromagnetically -- as is usually the case today -- but rather in the form of mechanical vibrations," explains Chu.
Quantum computers take advantage of unusual properties of quantum physics, including superposition, which allows quantum systems to exist in combinations of different states, and entanglement, which creates powerful connections between quantum states. These effects could eventually enable quantum machines to tackle certain extremely complicated calculations much faster than conventional computers, including some problems that are currently beyond their practical capabilities.
Why Vibrating Quantum Memory Could Be Better
One of the greatest challenges in quantum computing is maintaining precise control over quantum information. The states used for calculations are delicate, and even small disturbances can cause information to be lost. To perform calculations reliably, the processor and memory must interact closely enough to transfer and manipulate quantum states with high precision.
In the new system, microscopic structures called mechanical resonators hold information in particular patterns of vibration. When the superconducting qubit needs that information, it accesses the stored vibrational state, performs the required operation, and returns the modified information to memory.
Many existing quantum computers instead use electromagnetic memory alongside superconducting qubits. Researchers understand these technologies well, and they can be combined to provide extremely accurate control over quantum states, including reading, changing, and manipulating stored information.
However, electromagnetic memory systems have a significant disadvantage. They can occupy considerable space, making it difficult to expand experimental quantum devices into the larger, more capable computers that researchers and industries ultimately need.
Mechanical resonators offer several potential advantages. They are substantially smaller, allowing more compact designs. They can also support numerous different patterns of vibration, providing opportunities to store more information simultaneously than conventional electromagnetic memory.
Another important benefit is that mechanical vibrations can preserve quantum states for longer periods before the stored information begins to fade. Longer storage times could make it easier to carry out complicated calculations that require information to remain available throughout multiple processing steps.
New Quantum Computer Passes Major Tests
The research published in Science provides the first experimental demonstration that mechanical resonators can work together with superconducting qubits to carry out quantum computations. The results establish that vibration-based memory is a feasible alternative to electromagnetic storage.
The achievement goes beyond simply storing information. Chu's team demonstrated that its architecture can handle both relatively straightforward calculations and more demanding quantum operations.
To evaluate the system, the researchers tested two important computational techniques: the quantum Fourier transform and period finding. Both are fundamental tools in quantum computing and require a computer to coordinate multiple quantum states with considerable precision.
"The Quantum Fourier Transform is a fundamental computational procedure required for many quantum algorithms. The period-finding algorithm we implemented served as a demonstration of how this procedure can be used," explains Igor Kladaric, doctoral student in Chu's team and co-author of the publication.
Successfully completing these tasks requires the system to store, control, and maintain coherent relationships among multiple quantum states at the same time. The experiments showed that the new architecture can meet these requirements, providing strong evidence that it can support genuine quantum computation rather than simply function as a memory device.
A Promising Step Toward Powerful Quantum Computers
One of the most significant findings is that the new system can, in principle, carry out all the fundamental operations needed for arbitrary quantum computations. This means the architecture has the essential capabilities required for a programmable, general-purpose quantum computer.
However, demonstrating those capabilities in an experimental chip is only the beginning. The next major challenge is scaling the technology to larger systems with greater processing power while preserving the precision and reliability demonstrated in the laboratory.
Chu and her colleagues are continuing to investigate how their approach can be developed further. Its long-term success will depend on whether mechanical quantum memory can remain effective as more components and increasingly complex computations are added.
Practical quantum computers powerful enough for widespread scientific and industrial applications are still some distance away. Nevertheless, by showing that tiny mechanical vibrations can serve as compact, capable quantum memory, the ETH Zurich team has demonstrated a promising new route toward making those machines a reality.

articles.title: App de enfermería envía trabajadores sin orientación: un caso terminó con la muerte de un usuario
articles.text:
Una investigación de WIRED y Proof News concluyó que ShiftKey, una aplicación que funciona como un Uber para el sector de enfermería, envía trabajadores independientes a hogares de ancianos de Estados Unidos con poca o ninguna orientación, lo que derivó en errores graves, según documentos judiciales e informes de inspección federales.
La plataforma, fundada en 2016 en Texas, reúne a más de 200.000 trabajadores de salud y a más de 10.000 centros. Los medios analizaron 108.706 turnos publicados en marzo, julio y agosto de 2026: el 89 por ciento correspondía a hogares de ancianos, y la mayoría pedía enfermeros auxiliares o prácticos.
El caso más grave es el de Emma Lewis, de 93 años. En mayo de 2022, la enfermera práctica Felicia Kaye le inyectó la insulina de su compañera de cuarto en el centro Peachtree. Lewis fue llevada a un hospital y murió 12 días después.
Kaye no era empleada del centro: había tomado el turno por la aplicación. Declaró en agosto que nunca recibió orientación y que solo le entregaron las llaves del carro de medicamentos. Era la única enfermera a cargo de un piso con 22 pacientes y había manejado más de 400 kilómetros para llegar.
ShiftKey sostuvo en el juicio que no es responsable porque Kaye nunca fue su empleada, y pagará USD 40.000 para llegar a un acuerdo con la familia. El centro Peachtree alegó que no responde por los actos de un contratista independiente y destacó que Lewis tenía otras enfermedades. Su certificado de defunción menciona una degeneración senil del cerebro.
Errores documentados por inspectores federales
Los informes de los Centros de Servicios de Medicare y Medicaid (CMS, el organismo federal que supervisa estos centros) describen otros episodios. En Ohio, una trabajadora de la app cometió un error al colocar un catéter hasta el corazón de un paciente y nadie había verificado que estuviera capacitada para esa tarea.
En Texas, un inspector vio a otra trabajadora intentar alimentar a la fuerza a un residente con una jeringa. Ella dijo que era su primera vez en el lugar. En Wisconsin, una enfermera contó que no le mostraron los planes de cuidado de los residentes el primer día.
También hay denuncias de abusos y robos. En Illinois, una trabajadora habría robado las tarjetas de débito de dos residentes en 2026. El centro la bloqueó en la aplicación y fue arrestada, según Tim Blythe, directivo de la empresa propietaria del hogar.
El director ejecutivo de ShiftKey, Mike Vitek, afirmó que la empresa verifica credenciales, antecedentes y registros de abuso. Según él, la capacitación que exige cada centro la da ese centro. “No empleamos enfermeros: solo facilitamos su acceso a turnos flexibles”, dijo.
Vitek rechazó que el modelo perjudique al sector. Citó una encuesta de ShiftKey según la cual más de un tercio de los trabajadores no podría seguir en el área de la salud sin una plataforma así.
Menos pago y un sistema de puntajes
Los trabajadores compiten por cada turno con ofertas. Kara Smith, auxiliar de enfermería de Virginia Occidental, contó que un centro le pagaba USD 32,50 por hora en el verano de 2025 y unos USD 26 un año después. “Las ofertas iniciales son vergonzosamente bajas”, dijo la mujer, de 47 años.
Vitek explicó que el sistema calcula tarifas “sugeridas” y que el precio dinámico solo se usa para subir el pago de turnos difíciles de cubrir. La aplicación también asigna un puntaje de confiabilidad que, según varios enfermeros, afecta su acceso a los turnos.
Constance Hicks, auxiliar de enfermería de Connecticut, dijo que encontró a un paciente con la cabeza atrapada en la baranda de la cama y llamó al 911. Según su relato, escribió a ShiftKey y nadie respondió; al día siguiente su cuenta fue desactivada. Su demanda fue enviada a arbitraje privado, según los registros judiciales.
Legisladores y expertos piden más control
Jasmine Travers Altizer, profesora de la Universidad de Nueva York, entrevistó este año a 22 administradores de hogares de ancianos. Ellos asociaron el uso de personal temporal con una atención menos uniforme, más traslados a hospitales y más caídas. “No debería ser el arreglo para la falta crónica de personal”, escribió.
Según el Departamento de Salud de Estados Unidos, entre 2019 y 2022 el personal contratado pasó de 4 a 12 por ciento de las horas de enfermería en estos centros y luego bajó, aunque sigue por encima de la prepandemia. En 2023, el entonces director de ShiftKey dijo a Axios que la empresa valía más de USD 2.000 millones.
La representante estatal de Minnesota Emma Greenman prepara un proyecto para frenar la clasificación errónea de estos trabajadores como contratistas, y acusó a estos modelos de querer “evadir, romper y distorsionar” la ley laboral. ShiftKey replicó que, como mercado tecnológico, no emplea a profesionales de salud y que cumple la ley.

articles.title: Microsoft stellt To Do ein – und lässt private Nutzer ohne Alternative zurück
articles.text:
Microsoft stellt To Do ein: Welche App den Wunderlist-Nachfolger künftig ersetzen soll
Microsoft übernahm im Jahr 2015 das Berliner Unternehmen 6Wunderkinder, das die Organisations-App Wunderlist entwickelt hat. Wie das Wall Street Journal damals berichtete, soll die Kaufsumme zwischen 100 und 200 Millionen Dollar gelegen haben. Microsoft stellte Wunderlist 2020 ein, stattdessen entwickelte das Team die App To Do. Jetzt soll aber auch damit bald Schluss sein. Wie der Tech-Konzern in einem Beitrag auf seiner Support-Seite mitteilt, wird die App zum 30. Juni 2027 eingestellt. Für private Nutzer:innen bietet Microsoft keine Alternative an. Sie sollen sich stattdessen „eine andere Aufgabenverwaltungsanwendung [suchen], die ihren Anforderungen entspricht“.
Wer jetzt auf den Planner umsteigen muss
Die Änderung betrifft alle, die To Do im Web, unter Windows, Mac, iOS und Android nutzen. Das gilt sowohl für den beruflichen und schulischen Einsatz als auch für private Microsoft-Konten. Der zugrundeliegende Dienst, die APIs und die Synchronisierung sollen zu separat festgelegten Zeitpunkten eingestellt werden. Diese Termine und die nötigen Vorbereitungsmaßnahmen will der Konzern später bekannt geben.
In dem Beitrag heißt es: „Für Arbeits- oder Schulkonten wird Microsoft Planner die Plattform sein, auf der persönliche Aufgaben neben zugewiesenen Arbeitsaufgaben verwaltet werden können.“ Eine entsprechende Funktion soll ab Dezember schrittweise eingeführt werden, in der Aufgaben dann übersichtlich als Liste erscheinen. Auf Daten aus To Do können Nutzer:innen dort noch bis zum 30. Juni 2027 zugreifen. Danach können sie diese im Planner nicht mehr anzeigen oder verwalten.
Nutzer:innen von To Do reagieren enttäuscht
To Do endet auch für private Microsoft-Konten, einschließlich Microsoft 365 Personal und Family. Für sie ist der Planner allerdings nicht verfügbar. Nutzer:innen mit entsprechenden Abonnements stehen damit künftig ohne App da. Microsoft rät ihnen, sich eine andere Anwendung zu suchen, mit der sie künftig ihre privaten Aufgaben verwalten möchten. Bei ihnen löst die Änderung entsprechend Frust aus. Einer dieser Nutzer:innen ist Abhijith M B, Redakteur bei Windows Latest. „Für jemanden wie mich, der To Do täglich nutzt, ist das verheerend“, schreibt er in einem Artikel. Über das Ende der App sei er „zutiefst enttäuscht“.
Auch für Nutzer:innen mit Arbeits- oder Schulkonto ändert sich mit dem Umstieg auf den Planner einiges. Microsoft weist selbst darauf hin, dass beide Apps unterschiedliche Aufgaben- und Kollaborationsmodelle verwenden. Der Konzern rät Kund:innen, die künftig statt To Do den Planner nutzen müssen, sich schon jetzt mit der neuen App vertraut zu machen und zu prüfen, wie das ihre Arbeitsabläufe ändert. Vor dem Ende von To Do will Microsoft außerdem eine Möglichkeit zum Datenexport bereitstellen. Weitere Informationen dazu sollen aber erst später folgen. Eine automatische Übertragung der Daten in den Planner ist nicht vorgesehen.
)))))) Heiße Mädchen warten auf dich — Miss4.fun

articles.title: La Ley de Propiedad Horizontal lo confirma: si un propietario aparca dos vehículos en una plaza de garaje, puedes apelar al artículo 9.1
articles.text:
Puede haber problemas entre vecinos por aparcar dos vehículos en una plaza de garaje. Esto puede ocurrir cuando uno de ellos sobresale y entorpece el acceso o maniobra de otros.
Hay algunas cosas que debemos tener en cuenta para reclamar.
En primer lugar, la Ley de Propiedad Horizontal (LPH) no prohíbe en general aparcar dos vehículos juntos. En el artículo 9.1 indica que deben respetarse los elementos comunes y su buen uso. Además, se debe actuar con diligencia con el resto de propietarios.
Por ello, el propietario ha de mantener sus vehículos en su plaza y no deben entorpecer los accesos o maniobras de los vecinos. Es importante también que sea consciente de las limitaciones que pueden existir en esta plaza. Por ejemplo, el tema de aparcar un coche y una moto juntos es un problema similar.
Qué puede hacer la comunidad si el problema continúa
En caso de que el vehículo invada el paso o entorpezca la utilización de la plaza contigua, es conveniente intentar hablar con el dueño. Si no es posible, podemos pasar la queja al presidente o administrador de fincas. Deberemos indicarle dónde está el problema y cómo nos afecta.
El artículo 7.2 habla de actividades que están prohibidas por los estatutos o que son dañosas para la finca. También incluye las que van en contra de las normas sobre actividades molestas, insalubres, nocivas, peligrosas o ilícitas.
En este procedimiento el presidente requerirá el cese de la actividad. En caso de que el infractor no cambie la situación, el presidente deberá obtener el permiso de la junta para llevar la demanda. Tendrá que adjuntar a la demanda la acreditación del requerimiento fehaciente y la certificación del acuerdo de la junta.
En caso de que la sentencia sea favorable, podrá disponer el cese definitivo y la correspondiente indemnización por daños y perjuicios. En el mismo artículo se habla de la posibilidad de privar de la utilización de la vivienda o local (como máximo 3 años), teniendo en cuenta la gravedad y el perjuicio que se cause a la comunidad.

articles.title: StepSecurity Secures $20 Million to Expand Supply Chain Protection
articles.text:
Supply chain security startup StepSecurity has raised $20 million in a Series A funding round, which brings the total raised by the company to $23 million.
The new investment round was led by Elephant, with additional support from Runtime Ventures, Inner Loop Capital, and SaaS Ventures.
Founded in 2021, Seattle-based StepSecurity has built a platform that combines developer-machine protection, repository checks, a hosted upstream proxy and policy gate, and a CI/CD security agent to identify and block malicious components.
According to the company, its platform can secure every stage of the software development process, including developers’ systems, AI coding agents, repositories, package registries, and CI/CD runners.
The startup offers a free community tier of its CI/CD runtime security agent Harden-Runner, already used by over 20,000 open source projects, which now also integrates a free Secure Registry proxy and policy gate tier to help open source maintainers block compromised packages.
StepSecurity will use the fresh funding to accelerate the development and distribution of its platform by growing its engineering team, enhancing the security research team’s capabilities, and expanding go-to-market efforts.
“We believe independent controls at all control points in agentic software pipelines are the strongest defense for agentic software development,” said StepSecurity co-founder and CTO Ashish Kurmi.
“We have seen our customers adopt one product, find value, and ask us to protect the next part of their development process. This funding gives us the resources to respond faster,” Kurmi added.

articles.title: Google is putting AI chats right on the homepage
articles.text:
Google is updating its homepage to include AI searches. In a post on X, Google’s vice president of product, Robby Stein, shows how you can now open a collapsible sidebar to view and continue your AI chats.
Google is putting AI chats right on the homepage
You can now view your recent AI searches by opening the sidebar on Google’s homepage.
Based on the GIF shared by Stein, it looks like you can open the sidebar by clicking the gray bar that appears on the left side of your screen. From there, Google will show a list of the searches you’ve made using AI Mode, along with the ability to start a new thread, search your threads, or connect a Gemini Notebook.
It’s yet another big change for Google’s homepage, which has long presented you with a single bar to kick off your web search. The company brought its AI Mode button to its search bar last year, which opens up a chatbot-like search experience within Google. In May, Google updated its search box to accommodate longer queries and added AI-powered autocomplete.
Stein says Google is rolling out the option because “people are coming to Search with more questions that aren’t just one and done,” adding that “in testing, this sidebar made a big difference for making progress & continuing to explore the web.” The new homepage is rolling out globally on desktop.

articles.title: Nvidia Reports $115.8B in Quarterly Revenue Under Interim CEO - EE Times
articles.text:
Nvidia reported third-quarter revenue of $115.8 billion on Tuesday, more than twice its revenue in the same period last year. Cloud providers and tech giants kept buying its AI processors at a strong pace.
This was the first financial report under interim CEO Colette Kress, who took over after co-founder Jensen Huang resigned. The results show demand for Nvidia’s enterprise computing systems remains strong, even as the company faces leadership changes, a board investigation, and growing national security questions from Washington.
Rise in data center revenue
Nvidia’s third-quarter revenue rose 20% from the previous quarter and 103% from the $57.0 billion reported in the same period last year.
Most of the growth came from Nvidia’s Data Center business, which brought in $107.6 billion in sales, up 21% from the last quarter and 110% from a year ago. Gross margins stayed high, with a GAAP gross margin of 74.8% and a non-GAAP margin of 74.9%.
Operating income was $77.5 billion on a GAAP basis, up 115% from $36.0 billion a year ago. Net income grew to $65.3 billion, or $2.70 per diluted share, compared to $31.9 billion, or $1.30 per share, a year earlier. On a non-GAAP basis, net income was $64.9 billion, or $2.68 per diluted share. Nvidia generated $43.8 billion in free cash flow for the quarter, up from $22.1 billion in the same period last year.
Nvidia returned $28.1 billion to shareholders through share buybacks and dividends during the quarter. In September, the board had increased the company’s share repurchase authorization by $150 billion. At quarter-end, $227.3 billion remained available under the authorization. The board declared a quarterly cash dividend of $0.25 per share, payable on Dec. 23 to shareholders of record on Dec. 2.
Kress, who has served as Nvidia’s executive VP and CFO since 2013 and became interim CEO last week, said in the earnings release: “Our momentum is real. Nvidia is an exceptional technology leader, powered by the relentless innovation of our people. Vera Rubin is off to an explosive start, our roadmap is on track, and our ambition has never been greater.”
Vera Rubin ready for market adoption
The financial results came as Nvidia began ramping production of its next-generation Vera Rubin NVL72 rack-scale AI computing system and started shipping units to customers.
Nvidia said systems were already running at cloud providers including CoreWeave, Google Cloud, Microsoft Azure, Oracle Cloud Infrastructure, and Nebius. An installation was also underway with SpaceXSI.
Nvidia expanded its product lineup by shipping Vera CPUs, marking its first fully custom CPUs for data centers. Cloud platforms and AI developers such as Meta, OpenAI, Anthropic, AWS, and Verda have been using these custom processors with graphic accelerators to handle inference processing and automated agent tasks. For high-performance computing and complex simulations, Nvidia also introduced the Rubin HPC GPU.
The DSX POD reference design standardized how physical deployments are built, letting partners put together containerized data center modules that need less water cooling.
In networking, Nvidia rolled out more Spectrum-X Ethernet switches and BlueField-4 data processing units. The company also worked with Cisco on a new, higher-density optical transceiver called USFP.
Beyond hardware, Nvidia announced a deal to acquire Hugging Face, an open-source platform popular with AI researchers and software engineers.
Edge computing, PCs, and robotics
Outside of central data centers, Nvidia’s Edge Computing business brought in $8.2 billion in revenue for the quarter, up 14% from the previous quarter and 42% year over year.
RTX Spark laptops began shipping through partners including ASUS, Dell, HP, Lenovo, Microsoft Surface, and MSI.
For desktop software, Nvidia launched DLSS 5 graphics software for games. It also released a 64-GB DGX Spark personal system, supporting local execution of models from Liquid AI, Qwen, and Black Forest Labs locally.
Nvidia’s automotive and robotics segments had more deployments this quarter. Mercedes-Benz and Volvo Cars expanded their partnerships using Nvidia’s automated driving systems, and European logistics companies started testing commercial fleets built on the Hyperion vehicle platform.
The robotics division updated its Isaac platform tools to support human-sized robotic prototypes powered by Jetson Thor chips. It also worked with Nokia and T-Mobile on wireless infrastructure trials that use accelerated computing in cellular networks.
Jensen’s departure and reinstatement campaign
The company reported these results during a major management crisis. Huang resigned suddenly after internal investigations into extramarital relationships with a subordinate and an executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed International, which is under federal investigation for possibly diverting regulated semiconductor hardware.
On Nov. 17, Huang made his first public remarks since stepping down, expressing remorse while leaving the door open to a return as an executive. “I did not live up to the standards expected of everyone at Nvidia, and I have made serious mistakes in my personal life,” Huang said in a published statement. “If the board of directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO.”
A public petition called “Stand with Jensen” has collected over 202,000 signatures, including support from thousands of Nvidia employees. Industry leaders such as Elon Musk and Tim Sweeney have publicly backed Huang’s return, and shareholder groups led by Brad Gerstner of Altimeter Capital and Gavin Baker of Atreides Management sent open letters asking the board to keep all leadership options open.
As of Nov. 19, the Associated Press reported that Nvidia’s board had unanimously rejected Huang’s offer to return as CEO. Board chairman Harvey Jones said the company “unanimously accepted his resignation and does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO.” Jones added, “We want to install the permanent CEO as quickly as possible, but we won’t expedite the CEO before finding exactly the right person.”
Governance and outlook
Governance experts noted that reversing his termination could cause compliance problems with upcoming government proceedings.
Huang has agreed to appear before congressional committees on Dec. 1 to answer inquiries concerning foreign interactions and export compliance, with Nvidia’s general counsel, Tim Teter, scheduled to appear the following day.
In response to the controversy, Nvidia’s board set up a special committee to oversee national security and export rules. The company has also started looking for a new permanent chief executive.
Looking ahead, Nvidia expects revenue of $130.0 billion, plus or minus 3%, for the fourth quarter of fiscal 2027, which includes an extra working week. Gross margins are expected to fall to between 71.0% and 72.0%, and operating expenses should be about $11.0 billion.
Because of current export controls, Nvidia’s guidance assumes no data center revenue from China.

articles.title: Detachable Fiber Connectors Pose New Challenges For Photonics
articles.text:
Multiple designs are emerging for CPO and NPO, but standardization and high-volume manufacturing are still not ready.
Key Takeaways:
As photonics shifts from pluggable optical transceivers toward near- and co-packaged optics (NPO, CPO), engineers are devising new ways to attach fibers to the photonics chips on a board. Several different designs exist today, but so far there is no common interface.
With pluggable photonics, lasers and connections are attached at the server faceplate, with the board itself housing only electronic components. Yet long electrical connections to the faceplate mean higher power and longer latency. Fibers would need to move onto the interior of the board to solve that. That eliminates the need for pluggables, but it requires new solutions.
“With the rapid growth of generative AI, AI data centers are required to process enormous volumes of data faster and more efficiently than ever before,” said Yoshimasa Bando, principal scientist at Mitsubishi Chemical. “To meet this demand, further improvements in communication speed and energy efficiency have become critical challenges.”
The goal of CPO and NPO is to reduce reliance on long electrical connections.
Long lines
One reason for maintaining faceplate pluggables is that lasers are not always reliable. Using a pluggable module makes it easy to replace the laser.
“What we are focused on has the laser on the faceplate, because the laser is the highest reliability risk,” said Vishal Chandrasekar, director of product management at Ayar Labs.
All connections, whether they have a laser or not, happen in pluggable modules today. That means the signals those fibers carry must travel electrically from their origin to the edge of the board. Bandwidth necessitates serial lines driven by serializer/deserializer (SerDes) circuits. Driving those signals over that distance requires high power.
CPO aims to reduce system power by eliminating those long electrical lines and bringing fiber into the processor or switch packages. “CPO unlocks the token economics that everyone cares about,” said Chandrasekar. “The major bottlenecks are compute, memory, and moving data back and forth. If you’re trying to make step changes in hardware every one or two years, the way you make 5× or 10× kinds of improvements is by having new hardware. How do you use that hardware intelligently? How do I ensure that whatever hardware I have, I’m using it for the most important problem so my utilization is good?”
Fig. 1: With co-packaged optics, an optical engine is placed inside a package along with other chiplets. The laser remains outside the package for thermal reasons, and in the near term it will remain pluggable. Source: Bryon Moyer/Semiconductor Engineering
Photonics plays a key role in this effort. “You’re trying to reduce copper, so you’re trying to bring the PIC [photonic integrated circuit] closer to the processor or the switch,” said David Harame, COO at AIM Photonics, which operates with NY Creates (New York Center for Research, Economic Advancement, Technology, Engineering, and Science). “The industry is still very much using pluggables; you plug in the front panel. So there’s a lot of copper going between this [and the processor]. The next step is to move the optical transceiver closer to the switch by putting it on the PCB and reducing the copper line length to the switch. This is called near-packaged optics. Essentially, it moves the optical pluggable connector further inside the box on the PC board, so the optical-to-electrical connection takes place closer to the switch.
CPO is yet another variant of advanced packaging. “And all the challenges in advanced packaging are the same for co-packaged optics, except for fiber coupling and getting the PIC closer to the target chip,” noted Harame.
CPO receives the bulk of the near-term optical development efforts.
Fig. 2: In near-packaged optics, the optical components lie on the board near where their signals originate. Lasers will remain pluggable for now. Source: Bryon Moyer/Semiconductor Engineering
Unknown fiber length
Both CPO and NPO share the need to connect fiber directly to components on the board. One straightforward way is to attach a nominal length of fiber to the chip package and ship it that way, with the system integrator connecting the other end of the fiber directly to the destination.
The challenge there is that chip producers have no way of knowing how long that fiber will need to be. If it’s long enough for designs that require long runs, it will be too long for the many designs that don’t. That said, there are ways of dealing with extra fiber.
“The fiber goes into a fiber management tray, and there are spool points on the board,” said Nick Harris, CEO of Lightmatter. “They’re neatly managed for airflow.”
Others agree. “Usually, you’ll have some kind of excess fiber management,” explained Obie Roy, vice president, strategic commercial development at Senko. “But depending on the system that you’re building, you could cut it to length and terminate it once you know the exact application.”
Some engineers see this as a non-issue, which may be true if one is fusing the fibers or having the integrator attach a connector. “The fiber length is irrelevant,” said Professor Amr Helmy at the University of Toronto. “You connect a strand of fiber to the chip. With the other end, you can connectorize it, cut it, or fuse it with another fiber to make it longer. Fusing is one approach, but each one of these fibers can come with a connector depending on the amount of loss appetite you have.”
For ease of assembly, some means of attaching and detaching a fiber would also be helpful, such as a fixture or clip on the end to which another fiber can attach. But several considerations make this decision about more than simply adding wire connections as shown in the figures above.
Moving beyond the die edge
Today, fibers typically are placed using well-established V-groove technology, where the fibers exit out the side of a photonic chip. This attachment method works at low volumes and low total fiber counts, but it lacks the modularity and convenience needed for high-volume automation.
“The V-groove is a great concept, but the fibers are attached,” explained Gerard John, senior director, chiplets/FCBGA business unit at Amkor. “When being assembled onto a board, if one of them breaks, there’s no rework. People are generally thinking in terms of detachables and moving away from V-grooves.”
In addition, attachment space is bound by shoreline, which is essentially the real estate on the edge of the die. With metal connections, it might include the first few rows of bumps on the package, but fiber footprint is bigger and can chew up a lot of shoreline.
“The fiber diameter is 10 µm, but you have all the cladding around it, making it 125 µm,” John said. “So if you’re putting, let’s say, 16 cables like that, even if it’s staggered you will use a lot of real estate.”
Nevertheless, this is the predominant approach today. For example, Senko has put together a LEGO-like connector, with one part glued to the chip and the other attached to a fiber. This is one of many approaches underway at different companies.
There are three configurations for bringing fiber out (see figure 3, below). One takes the light from a waveguide, reflects it upward 90°, and sends it horizontally to a connector. These connectors would be situated around the periphery of the die.
Another is simply to run the waveguide to the edge of the die and have a connector butt up to the die to capture the light and route it to a fiber. The number of such connections is also determined by the perimeter.
A third approach moves the light vertically but then connects to the top surface rather than going out horizontally. This makes the entire area of the chip available for connections, providing more “shoreline” than the other two schemes.
“You have the waveguide shooting out laterally, and then it hits a mirror at a 45° angle,” said John. “It shoots upward, and once you get it upward, you put a connector with all the fibers on it.”
Fig. 3: The three ways of getting a waveguide signal into a fiber — horizontal-to-vertical-to-horizontal, fully horizontal, and horizontal-to-vertical. Source: Bryon Moyer/Semiconductor Engineering
But vertical approaches must avoid any heat sinks or other elements attached to the top. “When you send it vertically, you may get in the way of your thermal solution,” said Ravi Mahajan, fellow at Intel Foundry. “So if you have a solution that does both vertical and lateral, then you have more flexibility. In cases where thermal is a potential problem, go horizontal. In cases where you don’t worry about it, you can go vertical.”
The problem with pigtails
As depicted above, these connectors could be short pieces of fiber — pigtails — that are affixed firmly to the die and with some sort of clip connector at the end. A matching connector clip could then be plugged in to make the connection. Such a clip would likely cause some insertion loss, but if managed well, it can work. And it can be made to be sturdy.
“We have taken a part with a pigtail and banged it on the desk to convince a VP that it doesn’t come off,” said Mahajan. “We expose it to temperature cycles, to a little bit of moisture, and bake it for a long time, and it doesn’t come off.”
But the greater concerns are the high-volume manufacturing implications. Even without considering how the fiber attaches to the die, a more immediate question is how these chips would be packaged in bulk for test and delivery. The same issue holds for shipping a longer fiber and cutting it to order during integration.
Today, chips go into trays, and automated handling equipment can pick and place them onto boards or into test heads or anywhere else they’re needed. What happens if it’s no longer just a chip in the tray pocket, but potentially a chip wrapped with pigtails?
“If you have a pigtail, it’s very difficult to wrap that pigtail around and put it in a tray, and you probably won’t have many parts on the tray,” said John. “So our choice is to have a detachable connector, and it also makes sense from a manufacturing perspective.”
In addition, it is inconvenient to try to place a chip with pigtails into such a tray in an orderly, repeatable way. And then, when pulling the chip out of the tray, it will have dangling pigtails floating about, potentially interfering with whatever operation the equipment is attempting. Then, presumably, those pigtails would be manually connected.
This arrangement, while suitable at low volumes, may not work in high-volume production.
“I understand people being worried about a pigtail dangling off the edge, so we decided, ‘Why not just bring it to the edge of the die,’” said Mahajan. “Then an integrator just attaches it [to the fiber].”
Fig. 4: A fiber plugs into the side of a package. Source: Intel Foundry
Old habits change slowly, however. “Pigtails are probably still more common because people are trying to make incremental changes,” noted Sanjay Gangadhara, senior architect at Synopsys.
Scaling volumes also must address the assembly of any connector on the package. “Terminating a fiber is complex,” said Badri Gomatam, CTO of STL. “You’ve got to make it low cost, high yield, and repeatable. You’ve got hundreds of connections. No speck of dust can be allowed, and the assembly has to survive high-temperature reflow and all the other growth steps.”
Alignment concerns
One of the unique and challenging characteristics of photonics is that where two conductors meet, as much light as possible must get from one to the other. That applies to assembly and test.
Today, this is done through active alignment, where a tool measures the light exiting a waveguide and positions a fiber to maximize the captured light. This is a six-degree-of-freedom problem, where the aligner must be able to move in three linear dimensions as well as three angles of approach. It can take time.
With the pigtail configuration, presumably the clips would be designed to provide the alignment, but you still need to affix the stationary end of the pigtail during assembly. Given the downsides of pigtails, an alternative is to build the connector into the package itself. That way, nothing is hanging off the package, and it can be handled like other chips.
But alignment is still necessary. One method places a lens over the optical TSV to focus the light into an attached fiber while the other connection hardware aligns.
“One of the advantages when you have a lens is that, even if you do have some misalignment, the lens can correct for some of that because it’s focusing the light into a common region,” said Synopsys’ Gangadhara. “So this idea of using micro-optics, whether in a vertical-coupling or an edge-coupling architecture, is becoming more and more common.”
The Senko technique, for instance, provides passive mechanical fine alignment and restraint when snapped together. Roy explained that the snap-on structure provides the fine alignment, but you need something to hold it down. “We have screws and a structure that pushes it down into the fine alignment. This is the mechanical latching.”
It’s one thing to perform alignment during assembly, but it’s another to require it when attaching system fibers to the chip. Magnetic connectors, such as those used by Apple on iPhones, are being considered. Once the receiver end is built into the package, someone (or an automated handler) attaching the fiber must first align it roughly in place. From there, the magnet pulls it into the necessary precise location.
Unfortunately, some magnetic connectors are easily damaged. Any acceptable CPO fiber connection must be firm.
Stronger magnets could help, and this is an active area of development, possibly along with a mechanical restraint (such as Senko’s screws). What’s unclear, however, is how strong that magnetic field would be and whether it may adversely affect surrounding components such as MRAMs.
“When you design your system board, are you going to put sensitive memory close to these devices?” mused John.
As a result, any mechanical alignment would likely also be supplemented with a latch.
Serviceability and testability are critical
One way to connect fibers, common in long-haul optical applications, is to literally fuse them together. This permanent attachment method does not allow detachment, so it provides poor serviceability if a photonics chip fails.
“People have this concern about any kind of failure,” said Gangadhara. “How do you replace it? That serviceability part of the RAS requirement becomes a challenge.”
Serviceability, reliability, and availability make up the RAS feature that’s in high demand these days. It means components at greater risk of failure must be easy to replace, so you don’t have to throw out an entire expensive module or server.
“Once you attach a pigtail, if it gets damaged during shipment, the whole thing needs to be thrown out,” said John.
Roy agreed. “You need to make it detachable because if you permanently attach it and the fiber breaks, you have to fail the entire module out, which is very expensive,” he said.
Testing is heavily affected by these connector types, especially without standards. “An important aspect is making sure your solution is testable in real life,” noted Roy.
Addressing testability, especially for future high-volume manufacturing, means collaborating with test-equipment manufacturers. “We worked with Advantest and developed a test connector made out of tungsten carbide,” explained Roy. “It has the same bumps [as the LEGO-like connector] on the other side, and so it can come down, align precisely, and test very quickly. And you can scale it to test one at a time or a row of these things.”
Critically, the connection doesn’t require active alignment, saving test time. “We demonstrated 10,000 matings with very little variation in the loss [through the connection],” said Roy.
The connectors themselves must be reliable enough, but only up to a point. “Ideally, you’re not detaching and reattaching frequently,” noted Gangadhara. “If these things are up and running and working, then they’re running for thousands or tens of thousands of hours. Meta published a study last year where they had done serviceability/reliability analysis of some CPO devices, and they showed 10,000 hours of constant usage without any degradation of signal integrity or performance.”
Settling on a common design
Connector attachment is a textbook case of a development that needs standards so that any user can plug into anyone else’s photonics chip. At present, there are numerous pigtail-based designs and no standards. Likewise, no magnetic (or other) pigtail-less approach has been standardized or proven in high volumes. Customer requirements also appear to vary in ways that may make standardization difficult.
Consider the mechanical latching of Senko’s solution, for example. “Each of these parts is custom, depending on the ganging requirements and the mechanical sizes that are important to avoid — cooling plates and thermal elements and such,” Roy said. “Our vision is to take the receptacle part [that gets attached to the package], make that a common interface of the chip, and then sell the cover plate to any FAU manufacturer.”
For that to become an actual standard, however, typical licensing will presumably need to be reasonable and non-discriminatory (RAND). That’s a situation where different connector companies will work closely with photonics companies to find an approach that works functionally and is suited to high-volume manufacturing. That means compatibility with handling equipment.
These efforts will likely continue until standards (or at least multi-source agreements, or MSAs) are put in place, removing one major photonics volume barrier once the solution is established.

Disseqt AI raises $8M to build enterprise AI safeguards
The funds will support the expansion of Disseqt’s enterprise customer base globally. The company is also hiring in India across sales, operations and technology, with plans to expand into London.
Disseqt AI, a Dublin-headquartered AI assurance company with a significant presence in India, has raised $8 million in a round led by Gresham House Ventures, the growth equity arm of investment manager Gresham House.
Other investors include Sure Valley Ventures, an AI-focused venture fund; Delta Partners, an Irish early-stage investor; and Enterprise Ireland, the Irish government’s enterprise development agency. Angel backers include senior leaders from OpenAI, Palo Alto Networks, Salesforce and Meta, alongside cricket legend Rahul Dravid, who invested in his individual capacity.
The funds will support the expansion of Disseqt’s enterprise customer base globally. The company is also hiring in India across sales, operations and technology, with plans to expand into London.
Disseqt helps organisations test and oversee AI agents, software systems that can take actions, access company data and work across business applications. Its platform tests systems before launch, enforces company policies once they are live, monitors behaviour, blocks outputs that breach rules and maintains audit records.
“Every enterprise is handing real work to AI agents, but very few can prove those agents are safe, fair and within policy,” said Apoorva Kumar, chief executive and co-founder.
Disseqt claims it improved the safe-response rate of a global sports league’s fan-engagement agent, used by 80 million fans, from 80% to 99% in tests covering safety, bias and privacy.
Founded in late 2025 by Kumar, Manish Atri and Cyril Treacy, whose backgrounds include senior roles at Microsoft, AWS and Salesforce, Disseqt is entering a market where businesses are increasingly moving from AI chatbots to agents capable of performing tasks within company systems.
McKinsey’s 2026 survey found that 40% of respondents at companies with annual revenue exceeding $1 billion were scaling AI agents in at least one business function, compared with 27% a year earlier.
The risks associated with their deployment are also becoming clearer. OpenAI disclosed in October that two internal coding agents had weakened monitoring safeguards during separate tasks.
Gresham House Ventures partner Rohit Mathur said companies needed “tools that sit apart from the model providers they rely on”.
Investment is also reaching adjacent areas of the sector. Bengaluru-based Karta AI raised $3 million in October to develop voice agents for financial services, while AI infrastructure company Simplismart secured $14 million in a Series B round to expand its technology for running AI models more efficiently.

articles.title: TikTok lance un site pour démasquer les vidéos IA — Frandroid
articles.text:
Sur TikTok, les vidéos générées par IA se comptent en milliards, et l’étiquette qui les signale disparaît souvent dès qu’une vidéo est téléchargée puis republiée ailleurs. TikTok annonce deux nouveaux outils pour y remédier. Le premier permet à n’importe qui, même sans compte TikTok, d’envoyer une image, une vidéo ou un fichier audio sur un site dédié pour savoir si le fichier a été créé ou retouché avec les outils d’IA de TikTok ou des autres applications de ByteDance, sa maison mère (CapCut, Dreamina, Pippit, Hypic). Le second, Likeness Detection, prévient les créateurs quand leur visage apparaît dans un deepfake, ces vidéos truquées par IA qui font dire ou faire n’importe quoi à une vraie personne.
Le vérificateur IA de TikTok
Depuis 2024, TikTok ajoute automatiquement des Content Credentials aux contenus générés avec ses outils. Ce standard, porté par la coalition C2PA, glisse dans le fichier des métadonnées qui disent comment il a été fabriqué, ce qui permet aux autres plateformes de l’étiqueter à leur tour. Sauf que ces informations se perdent quand une vidéo est téléchargée, modifiée puis repartagée. Le nouvel outil cherche donc aussi VeraDura, un filigrane invisible développé par TikTok. Il est caché dans l’image et plus difficile à effacer. L’outil est accessible dès maintenant.
Le site accepte les images, les vidéos et même les fichiers audio, dans la limite de 20 Mo par image et de 100 Mo par vidéo ou fichier audio. TikTok assure que les fichiers envoyés ne sont stockés nulle part.
Du 19 au 30 novembre, le Plaud Note Pro passe à 149 € au lieu de 189 € ! Il enregistre vos réunions, les transcrit et les synthétise pour vous, il suffit d’appuyer sur un bouton. Les Plaud Note, NotePin et NotePin S sont aussi à -20 %. Bref, c’est le moment d’arrêter de perdre du temps au travail !
TikTok affirme avoir étiqueté plus de 5 milliards de vidéos générées par IA sur sa plateforme. Le 10 juillet, l’entreprise en revendiquait encore 3 milliards, soit environ 2 milliards de vidéos de plus en quatre mois. Ces étiquettes viennent des créateurs qui déclarent eux-mêmes l’IA, des Content Credentials et du filigrane maison.
Un vérificateur qui ne reconnaît que les outils de ByteDance
Le vérificateur a une limite importante, que TikTok reconnaît lui-même. Il ne détecte que les signaux ajoutés par TikTok et par les autres outils d’IA de ByteDance, comme CapCut ou Dreamina. Une vidéo produite avec un autre générateur, puis publiée sur TikTok ou ailleurs, sort de son champ.
Un résultat négatif ne prouve donc pas qu’une vidéo est authentique. Pour démasquer une fausse vidéo virale fabriquée avec un outil concurrent, comme Sora d’OpenAI ou Veo de Google, le vérificateur ne servira à rien.
Likeness Detection : TikTok s’inspire de YouTube
La nouvelle fonction Likeness Detection ne s’active que si le créateur s’y inscrit. Il vérifie d’abord son identité auprès d’un prestataire externe, puis TikTok le prévient quand des vidéos ou des comptes semblent utiliser son visage. Le créateur peut les examiner dans l’outil et les signaler aux équipes de modération, qui suppriment les contenus contraires aux règles de la plateforme. TikTok assure ne pas conserver les pièces d’identité.
TikTok testait l’outil depuis juillet avec un petit groupe de créateurs américains, qui passaient par la société de vérification Jumio, rapportait alors Music Business Worldwide. Le déploiement mondial commence maintenant, mais seulement pour les « créateurs éligibles » et les personnalités publiques, y compris les comptes de gouvernements, de responsables politiques et de partis. TikTok n’a pas publié la liste des critères d’éligibilité.
YouTube a pris de l’avance sur ce terrain : son outil, lancé fin 2025 pour les créateurs monétisés, est ouvert à tous les créateurs majeurs depuis mai 2026.

articles.title: Où trouver la maison de GTA San Andreas dans GTA 6 ?
articles.text:
Les théories étaient donc vraies. Dans Grand Theft Auto: The Trilogy – The Definitive Edition, Rockstar Games s’est amusé à ajouter des photos dans GTA San Andreas, photos renvoyant à différents lieux apparus dans ses jeux à l’exception d’une mystérieuse maison au style très floridien. Quand la trilogie est sortie, en novembre 2021, GTA 6 n’avait pas encore été officialisé. Difficile, dès lors, de relier cette demeure au jeu de Rockstar Games sorti ce jeudi 19 novembre 2026 sur PS5, Xbox Series S et Xbox Series X.
La photo en question était accrochée au mur du Lil’ Probe’Inn, le bar de San Andreas consacré aux ovnis. On y voyait un pavillon de banlieue entouré de palmiers, avec une soucoupe volante dans le ciel.
La maison de la photo de GTA San Andreas figure bel et bien dans GTA 6. Numerama a pu se rendre sur le lieu où elle se trouve pour confirmer qu’il s’agit du même design. Les développeurs ont donc glissé un indice sur GTA 6 dès novembre 2021, moins de trois mois avant que Rockstar ne confirme son développement, en février 2022.
Où trouver la maison de GTA San Andreas dans GTA 6
Pour trouver la maison en question, il faut se rendre à Belville, dans le sud de Leonard County, au nord de la maison de Jason (mais assez loin de celle-ci). Elle se trouve dans un quartier résidentiel, avec un voisinage très ressemblant. Vous trouverez ci-dessous le point à marquer sur votre carte pour que le GPS intégré au jeu vous y emmène.
La maison ressemble exactement à la photo de GTA San Andreas, jusque dans les décorations extérieures. Rockstar Games s’est contenté d’ajouter un panneau « à vendre », juste devant. Impossible, d’ailleurs, d’entrer dans la maison. En revanche, le garage renferme quelques secrets.
On peut forcer la porte (via un QTE, une action rapide à réussir au stick) pour entrer dans le garage et découvrir un lieu habité, avec un canapé, un téléviseur, un bureau ou encore un frigo. Le garage est jonché de messages à tendance conspirationniste. Des phrases comme « We don’t die », « We are in a loop », « It’s a simulation » ou encore « Why can’t I leave ? » peuvent être lues. Un clin d’œil savoureux pour une maison qui alimente les théories des fans depuis cinq ans.
Les notes vont plus loin que ces slogans. Leur auteur explique ne pas pouvoir acheter de billet d’avion pour Los Santos ni quitter l’État en voiture, allant jusqu’à songer au bateau. Il désigne aussi deux personnes, J et L, qui échapperaient aux limites de son monde. Difficile de ne pas y voir Jason et Lucia, les deux héros du jeu.
Dans le garage, on trouve aussi deux éléments utiles pour la progression : une carte à collectionner et un magazine, lui aussi à tendance conspirationniste.

articles.title: A hidden limit of space and time could unlock electronics 100,000 times faster
articles.text:
A hidden limit of space and time could unlock electronics 100,000 times faster
- Date:
- November 7, 2026
- Source:
- University of Regensburg
- Summary:
- Scientists have discovered a surprising quantum limit that prevents electrons from being tracked with unlimited precision in both space and time. The breakthrough could pave the way for manipulating chemical reactions and developing electronics hundreds of thousands of times faster than today's technology.
- Share:
Quantum physics places fundamental limits on what scientists can know about the behavior of particles. Werner Heisenberg's famous uncertainty principle states that certain properties, such as a particle's position and momentum, cannot both be measured with unlimited precision. This restriction is not caused by flaws in scientific instruments. It is built into the laws of nature.
But position and time are different. Heisenberg's uncertainty principle does not impose the same restriction on these quantities. Now, researchers have experimentally demonstrated another fundamental limitation: an electron's location and its behavior over time cannot both be determined with arbitrary precision. Known as the "space-time limit," this newly observed relationship could have major implications for the future of quantum technology and ultrafast electronics.
The discovery comes from an international collaboration involving research groups at the Regensburg Center for Ultrafast Nanoscopy (RUN), led by Profs. Jascha Repp, Rupert Huber, Franz Giessibl, and Klaus Richter, along with a team at the Max Planck Institute in Hamburg led by Angel Rubio.
Watching Electrons Move at Incredible Speeds
Understanding how matter behaves at the smallest scales is essential for developing the next generation of technology. Advances in clean energy, quantum computing, and powerful electronics for artificial intelligence all depend on knowing how chemical reactions unfold, how light interacts with materials, and how electrons travel through electronic devices.
However, even the sharpest microscopic photographs cannot reveal the full picture. Scientists also need to observe how these processes change over time, effectively creating slow-motion movies of events occurring at the atomic scale.
At RUN, researchers are developing ultrafast microscopes capable of recording the movements of electrons, atoms, and molecules with extraordinary precision in both space and time. About ten years ago, scientists in Regensburg used ultrafast scanning tunneling microscopy to resolve the movement of a single molecule across space and time for the first time.
Tracking individual electrons presents an even greater challenge. At these microscopic distances, electrons can move roughly a thousand times faster than atoms and molecules, with important changes taking place over just attoseconds.
To appreciate how extreme these scales are, consider that an atom is approximately ten million times smaller than a millimeter. An attosecond is one-billionth of a billionth of a second. The difference between an attosecond and a second is comparable to the difference between one second and the entire age of the universe.
Making these measurements is especially difficult because electrons do not behave like ordinary objects. Their motion follows the unusual laws of quantum mechanics rather than the familiar rules of classical physics.
Ultrafast Lasers Reveal Quantum Tunneling
To observe electron behavior at these extraordinary speeds, the researchers built a new laser system that provides much finer time resolution than earlier experiments. The system allows them to control and study the quantum motion of individual electrons directly.
In the experiments, carefully timed laser pulses drive electrons from an extremely sharp metal tip toward a silver surface. The distance they travel is only a few atomic diameters.
The researchers detect this movement by measuring the resulting electrical current. To determine exactly when the electrons move, they use two pulses of light separated by a precisely controlled interval.
Simon Maier, the lead author of the paper, explains: "By varying the time interval between the two laser pulses, we can directly observe how the electrons respond."
This approach revealed clear evidence of electron motion occurring on attosecond timescales. It showed that the laser pulses could transfer electrons within these incredibly brief intervals while allowing scientists to observe the process as it happened.
What makes the result particularly remarkable is how the electrons travel. Instead of moving like conventional particles, they behave as quantum waves. This allows them to pass through an energy barrier separating the metal tip from the silver surface, even though classical physics predicts they should not have enough energy to cross it.
This phenomenon, known as quantum tunneling, is somewhat like an object passing through a solid wall without breaking or damaging it.
"Our measurement can be understood as a high-speed camera for the electron wave packets, since you can see at what point in time the tunneling process takes place," explains Katharina Glöckl, a doctoral student and co-author of the publication.
A Surprising 500-Attosecond Delay
To understand the measurements more deeply, researchers working with Prof. Angel Rubio performed sophisticated quantum simulations of the electrons' behavior near the "space-time limit."
Their calculations closely reproduced the experimental findings and uncovered another remarkable detail. The electrons did not respond to the light field instantaneously. Instead, their motion lagged behind it by approximately 500 attoseconds.
At such extreme scales, several fundamental features of quantum physics become important simultaneously.
For example, the researchers found that the laser pulses could not be described entirely by treating light as a wave or entirely by treating it as individual particles called photons. Their effects displayed characteristics of both descriptions. This combination was essential for exploring electron behavior so close to the "space-time limit."
The team also discovered that controlling electron motion over extremely short intervals changes how the electrons are distributed in space. Quantum mechanics describes these electrons using wave packets, which represent how their wave properties extend across different locations.
The relationship between the timing of electron motion and the spatial extent of these wave packets revealed the central limitation behind the discovery.
A Hidden Tradeoff Between Space and Time
Raffael Spachtholz, another co-author of the study, explains: "The more precisely we want to pin down the electron's position in time, the more energy we need to provide. And as a result, the electron wave packet spreads out more spatially."
In other words, improving the precision of an electron's timing comes with a cost. The more tightly researchers define when its motion occurs, the more broadly its quantum wave packet spreads through space.
To examine this relationship experimentally, the team placed a single atom on the surface to confine the electron wave packets to an extremely small region immediately before the laser pulses arrived.
This setup allowed the scientists to directly measure the connection between the electrons' spatial distribution and the timing of their motion.
Importantly, even when the electrons received substantial energy from the laser pulses, their wave packets remained sufficiently localized for microscopy with atomic spatial resolution and attosecond time resolution.
The findings provide experimental insight into a fundamental space-time constraint that scientists had previously only suspected. They also make it possible to systematically investigate how changes in electron motion over time affect the spatial structure of quantum wave functions.
Could Quantum Electronics Become Hundreds of Thousands of Times Faster?
Beyond revealing a new aspect of quantum behavior, the discovery could open the door to technologies that operate on timescales far beyond the capabilities of today's electronics.
One especially promising possibility involves using precisely controlled electron wave packets to influence chemical reactions.
Transferring a single electron to a molecule represents the smallest possible transfer of electric charge. But when that electron is concentrated within an exceptionally small region of space and time, the resulting local peak current density can reach as much as 1 trillion amperes per square centimeter.
Such extreme conditions could give scientists new ways to control chemical bonds and observe how molecules change during reactions.
"In the future, we want to use such wave packets to specifically trigger chemical reactions and observe, on the relevant length and time scales, how chemical bonds can be broken or altered," explains Prof. Jascha Repp enthusiastically.
The implications could extend well beyond chemistry. Greater control over electron motion may eventually help engineers develop electronic devices and quantum information systems that operate at speeds approaching the fundamental limits of electron dynamics.
"In the long term, the insights gained could also contribute to operating electronics and quantum information processing at the intrinsic speed limit of electron motion itself -- hundreds of thousands of times faster than the currently dominant CMOS technology," adds Prof. Rupert Huber.
That possibility remains a long term technological goal rather than an achievement demonstrated in the current experiments. Nevertheless, the findings provide a new foundation for exploring how electrons can be manipulated at the smallest distances and shortest timescales.
For Repp and Huber, the results suggest that the range of potential applications is extraordinarily broad. They believe that future advances in controlling electrons at the space-time limit may ultimately depend more on human creativity than on the constraints imposed by nature.
