articles.title: Build Tool-Calling Parsers in Rust with AI Agents | NVIDIA Technical Blog
articles.text:
A tool call can arrive in pieces, an argument can be cut short, or model-specific markup can leak into the answer. A frontend parser turns that output, received as token IDs or decoded text, into visible text, reasoning, and tool calls an application can use.
In this post, you’ll learn how tool-call parsing works and use an AI agent to build a parser for a new model. You’ll start with a weather request and a human-reviewed test set, using frontend-crates, the reusable Rust components behind NVIDIA Dynamo tool-calling parsers.
Suppose you ask for the weather in Paris. The model may generate reasoning followed by a get_weather call with a city argument. The frontend prepares and tokenizes the prompt, then an inference engine runs the LLM to generate tokens. The parser consumes token IDs or decoded text and separates reasoning, visible text, and tool calls in order. A protocol adapter turns those events into an OpenAI-compatible response, using the same parsing path for batch JSON and streaming updates.
The tricky part is recognizing where each piece starts and ends. A call can be malformed or incomplete, a marker can appear inside an argument, or ordinary text can surround the call. The parser has to handle these boundaries without losing data, duplicating calls, or leaking model-specific markup.
Returning to the weather request: the model might stop halfway through a city name or call a tool that wasn’t offered. Either can disrupt the agent’s next action. The following NVIDIA Nemotron examples show these two failures.
Syntax error. The argument and tool-call frame never close, so no complete call can be parsed.
</think><tool_call>
<function=get_weather><parameter=city>Par
Semantic error. The frame is valid, but the named tool is absent from the request.
</think><tool_call>
<function=unknown_tool><parameter=city>Paris</parameter></function>
</tool_call>
These failures require different handling. If the model names an unavailable tool, the parser reports the call it received, and the serving layer validates tool availability, authorization, schema, and call policy. Changing the tool name would hide what the model actually generated.
An incomplete call is harder to judge while the stream is open. The rest of the city name may arrive in the next chunk, and a marker can split across chunks, too. Emit too early and syntax leaks into the answer; wait too long and ordinary text gets delayed. The parser needs consistent rules for what to emit, what to buffer, and how to handle the end of the stream.
A parser can encounter an unbounded range of inputs. With invalid input, it must follow documented recovery rules rather than guess the model’s intent. Even a syntactically valid call that conforms to the schema can be the wrong choice for the user’s request. The parser needs a consistent grammar and recovery policy so it can preserve valid data without inventing calls or leaking model-specific markup.
To check those decisions, frontend-crates pairs model outputs with expected results in a shared Conformance Corpus.
Using the Conformance Corpus
Use the Conformance Corpus to check how applicable parsers handle behavior first observed in one model. Its language-neutral YAML fixtures pair fixed input with expected output, so Rust parsers and Python references can run the same cases. A regression test for leaked markup, duplicate calls, or lost arguments can cover other families when adapted to their grammars.
For a new parser, start with all UNIFIED.* cases across model families. They cover complete, malformed, truncated, multiple, and interleaved calls, plus streaming boundaries and end-of-input behavior. Adapt inputs to your model’s grammar and request settings, add model-specific edge cases, and explain exclusions. You can’t test every possible output, but you can reuse cases from other formats.
Table 1 shows the UNIFIED.1-tool_only case from the Parser Conformance Table. In this example, the GOLDEN test set pairs four model-specific inputs with the same expected result: get_weather with city set to Paris. The markers differ, but each case tests the same behavior. Adapting the input format makes the same behavioral test reusable across models.
| Model | Native input | 
|---|---|
| Beam | <\|start\|>assistant to=get_weather<\|channel\|>analysis <\|constrain\|>xml<\|message\|><rfl:parameter name="city"> Paris </rfl:parameter><\|call\|> | 
| GPT-OSS | <\|start\|>assistant<\|channel\|>commentary to=functions.get_weather <\|constrain\|>json<\|message\|>{"city": "Paris"}<\|call\|> | 
| Muse Spark | <\|start\|>assistant to=get_weather<\|message\|><atem:function_calls> <atem:invoke name="get_weather"> <atem:parameter name="city">Paris</atem:parameter> </atem:invoke> </atem:function_calls><\|eom\|> | 
| NVIDIA Nemotron 3 | </think><tool_call> <function=get_weather> <parameter=city> Paris </parameter> </function> </tool_call> | 
Tutorial: Create a new parser
Now you can create a parser for a model that frontend-crates doesn’t support yet. Ask your AI agent to read this post and work through the tutorial, starting with the prompt in step 1. Your model’s specification defines the grammar; the shared cases provide behaviors to test.
You’ll need a frontend-crates checkout, Rust and Cargo, and the conformance dependencies. The parser exercise runs on a CPU using fixed test fixtures, so you don’t need a GPU. End-to-end testing also requires a working Dynamo runtime, discovery services, and hardware for your model. When you’re ready to test end-to-end, launch the tests with Dynamo runtime on the actual model and GPU(s).
The workflow in Figure 2 starts with the model’s grammar, recovery rules, and reviewed GOLDEN expectations. The agent writes or fixes the parser, runs tests, and uses failures to guide the next change. If it proposes changing the expected behavior, review that decision before accepting it.
Test your parser end to end with real models before claiming deployment support. Plan time to allocate a machine, load the model, initialize the runtime, and run your own test cases. Turn failures into unit tests for the agent, then rerun the end-to-end test to check the fix.
1. Start with a prompt
Give the agent this prompt: In the frontend-crates checkout, follow .agents/skills/tool-parser-generator/SKILL.md to create a v2 Unified parser for [MODEL_NAME]. Research its grammar and prepare the GOLDEN test set, adapting applicable UNIFIED.* cases. Pause for human review. After approval, implement, validate, and provide the local conformance report URL for human inspection.
2. Define the GOLDEN test set
The GOLDEN test set defines the behavior your parser will be tested against. Use the prompt in step 1 to have the agent generate an initial test set in conformance/fixtures-unified-v2/families/<name>/inputs_and_golden.yaml, independently of parser results. Each case pairs an input with its expected output, called GOLDEN. If those expectations are wrong, the parser can pass the tests and still behave incorrectly.
The following example pairs an input with its expected GOLDEN output. It omits request definitions, tools, initialization, and chunk settings; the existing nemotron_v3/inputs_and_golden.yaml shows the full format.
family: nemotron_v3
cases:
  UNIFIED.tool_only.nemotron_v3:
    input: |-
      </think><tool_call>
      <function=get_weather>
      <parameter=city>Paris</parameter>
      </function></tool_call>
    golden:
      - kind: tool_call
        name: get_weather
        arguments: {city: Paris}
Ask the agent for an adversarial review, then go through the set manually, case by case. The initial test set may contain errors because expected behavior depends on context the agent may not have. Review it against the following sources and requirements:
- The model format and API specification.
- The reference implementation.
- Other parsers, including vLLM and SGLang.
- The grammar, tool schema, and request settings.
- Relevant forum discussions and existing tickets.
- Caller needs and recovery costs in latency and complexity.
Where sources disagree, you may need to make a judgment call. Write down the recovery rule and why you chose it, and document the reason for any GOLDEN change. Expectations should follow that decision, not the parser’s output.
3. Implement the parser and inspect the results
After reviewing the GOLDEN test set, ask the agent to continue: build the parser, run all applicable UNIFIED.* cases and shared regression tests, and fix the failures. Have it recapture results, generate conformance/CONFORMANCE_v2.html locally, and provide the local report URL so you can inspect its work.
Open that URL in your browser. The local report uses the published Parser Conformance Table‘s interface with your local results. Inspect each case’s input, request settings, GOLDEN, and recorded output. Investigate regressions and missing captures. Green means the output matches GOLDEN, so the table depends on the expectations you reviewed. Figure 3 shows the report interface.
Guided-decoding support
The agent’s implementation step also covers guided decoding, which can reduce malformed calls by constraining generation to the model’s markers and argument schema. Ask your agent to follow “Add and validate structural tags” in the parser README and “Implement and validate” in the agent skill. These instructions cover builder registration, grammar tests, and backend qualification. Guided decoding can’t ensure that the model chooses the right city or prevent truncation, so keep the parser’s recovery checks.
Common gotchas: speed, streaming, and memory
Passing correctness tests is only a starting point for an agent-generated parser. The implementation may still be slow or use too much memory. Try plain text, tool calls, long arguments, and malformed input with large and tiny chunks. Measure throughput, time to the first event, and memory use on the same build and hardware. Double the input length to spot code that keeps rescanning or copying what it already read.
With streaming, watch what the caller receives as each chunk arrives. A parser can return the right final result and still make the caller wait until the end. Replay short fixtures at every split point, then try one-character and mixed chunks, including splits inside markers, escaped quotes, and arguments. Check that events arrive in order and arguments stay intact. If events are queued, test a slow consumer and cancellation too.
Also try cutting the stream off halfway through a marker or argument. Check that recovery follows the documented rule without leaking markup, duplicating calls, or losing valid text. The parser should handle the input it received without guessing the missing pieces.
Test text containing examples of the model’s format as well as tool calls against the documented grammar and quote-handling policy. The current v2 default treats recognized markers as structural even inside quoted prose, so quotation marks alone do not keep a complete tool-call example in ordinary text. Record the configured policy and test its expected behavior.
Give the agent this prompt to check for common gotchas:
Check this parser for common gotchas. Benchmark speed and memory with short, long, and malformed inputs using different chunk sizes. Look for repeated scanning, copying, or growing buffers. Verify that output arrives incrementally and stays correct across chunk boundaries and truncation. Where queues exist, test a slow consumer, backpressure, and cancellation. Check literal format examples and real tool calls against the documented grammar and configured quote-handling policy. Report measurements, reproducible failures, and anything you could not verify.
How to use the parser crate in your own Rust project
Choose a parser whose grammar matches your model. This example uses the existing NVIDIA Nemotron parser and splits both a marker and the city name across chunks.
This example was tested with Rust 1.96.1 and dynamo-parsers-v2 0.10.3. Run cargo new parser-demo, then cd parser-demo. Add the following entries under [dependencies] in Cargo.toml:
anyhow = "1"
dynamo-parsers-v2 = "=0.10.3"
serde_json = "1"
Replace src/main.rs with:
use dynamo_parsers_v2::{
    Tool, UnifiedParserInit, UnifiedParserOutput, create_unified_parser_for_family,
};
use serde_json::json;
fn main() -> anyhow::Result<()> {
    let tools = [Tool {
        name: "get_weather".into(),
        description: None,
        parameters: json!({"type":"object","properties":{"city":{"type":"string"}},"required":["city"]}),
        strict: None,
    }];
    let mut parser = create_unified_parser_for_family("nemotron_v3", &tools)?;
    parser.initialize_request(UnifiedParserInit::default())?;
    let mut output = UnifiedParserOutput::default();
    for chunk in [
        "Check the forecast.</think><tool_",
        "call><function=get_weather><parameter=city>Par",
        "is</parameter></function></tool_call>",
    ] {
        let mut delta = UnifiedParserOutput::default();
        parser.parse_into(chunk, &mut delta)?;
        output.append(&mut delta);
    }
    output.append(&mut parser.finish()?);
    println!("{}", serde_json::to_string(&output.assembled())?);
    Ok(())
}
Run cargo generate-lockfile, then cargo run --locked. The result contains reasoning followed by a get_weather call with city set to Paris:
[{"kind":"reasoning","text":"Check the forecast."},
 {"kind":"tool_call","name":"get_weather","arguments":{"city":"Paris"}}]
Keep one initialized parser for each request choice.
- create_unified_parser_for_family selects the grammar.
- initialize_request sets the starting state.
- parse_into consumes each chunk.
- Finalize once: use finish() for truncation, cancellation, or the end of the transport stream. Use finish_at_eos() only for a backend-confirmed grammar-ending end-of-sequence (EOS) signal.
- Use assembled() for the ordered results.
In a streaming application, forward the events in delta.events after each parse_into call and the events returned by finish(). This example collects the events to print the final output. Before executing tools, validate completed calls for tool availability, authorization, schema, and call policy.
Get started
To build a parser for your model, start with the source, fixtures, and instructions in frontend-crates and adapt an existing test case. Give your agent the model’s format specification and the repository instructions, then use the Parser Conformance Table to check the parser’s recorded output against GOLDEN. When you open an issue or pull request, include the exact failing input, case identifier, and test results so reviewers can reproduce the behavior.
You can use these parsers in your own Rust project or as part of NVIDIA Dynamo, an inference framework that uses frontend-crates. Before you begin, check the latest repository instructions so you and your agent follow the current steps.
Acknowledgements
Jesse Gu, Alec Flowers, Dong Xu, Qi Wang, and the many partners and proofreaders who helped with this blog and frontend-crates.

articles.title: Kenyan businesses to pay Chinese suppliers in yuan under WapiPay, Alipay deal
articles.text:
WapiPay, a Kenyan cross-border payments fintech, has partnered with Alipay to enable local merchants pay suppliers in mainland China, allowing importers to send shillings while suppliers receive yuan through the Chinese payments app.
The partnership gives WapiPay a second route into China after its earlier work with WeChat Pay. Alipay described the agreement as a first for the company in Africa. The service starts in Kenya, with the two companies looking to serve businesses that buy from suppliers elsewhere in Asia.
Most Kenyan businesses that buy from China pay through their banks, which usually convert the money into dollars on the way. That pushes up transaction costs, a burden for importers working on thin margins. WapiPay is offering a direct shilling-to-yuan route that skips the dollar.
“Our work with WeChat Pay helped lay the groundwork,” Paul Ndichu, WapiPay co-founder, said in a statement. “With Alipay, we’re opening another payment route and positioning WapiPay to serve a market with an estimated $300 billion in annual flows.”
Kenyan importers are heavy buyers of Chinese currency and have little yuan income to offset it, meaning every payment has to be funded by selling shillings, directly or through the dollar. A service that can source yuan cheaply and settle it without a bank in the middle could, in theory, pass on savings.
Kenya’s biggest trading partner
China’s exports to Africa rose almost 26% to $225 billion in 2025, and two-way trade hit a record $348 billion, according to Chinese customs data compiled by Nanyang Technological University’s Centre for African Studies. Machinery, electronics, and clean energy equipment were among the main goods.
China is Kenya’s largest source of goods, and imports from it rose by KES 93.31 billion ($717.4 million) to KES 671.25 billion ($5.1 billion) in 2025, driven by machinery, manufactured goods, and electronics. That was 24.2% of Kenya’s total import bill. Kenya, on the other hand, exported just $130.8 million.
Wapi Pay told TechCabal it has processed more than KES 40 billion ($307.5 million) in cross-border payments across its network, but only Rmb2.5 million ($374,936.25) in transfers from Africa to China. The initial service covers only payments from Kenya to the mainland.
“Trade moves on roads, through ports, and across oceans. Money needs a route of its own,” said Eddie Ndichu, WapiPay co-founder. “For a business owner, that means a simpler way to pay for the next shipment and keep goods moving.”
Nairobi has been moving some of its dealings with Beijing out of dollars. Kenya has been in talks with China, its biggest bilateral lender, to convert dollar-denominated debt into yuan. Chatham House, the London think tank, said the loan conversion also aligns with China’s stated ambition to promote the internationalisation of the yuan.

articles.title: La RTX 5090 alcanza en España los 17.000 euros. Por mucho menos, puedes comprar este PC con esa GPU, 4 TB de SSD y 64 GB de RAM DDR5
articles.text:
La locura de precios que llevamos viviendo desde finales del pasado año en hardware y dispositivos se refleja en dos componentes clave de muchos equipos: la memoria RAM (sobre todo cuando es DDR5) y las tarjetas gráficas de gama alta (como la NVIDIA RTX 5090). Con mención a esta última, que en España llega a alcanzar los 17.000 euros en algunos ensambles.
PC NEO Gaming R7 9800X3D RTX 5090 4TB SSD 64GB
Sin embargo, curiosamente, en el terreno de los PC premontados seguimos encontrando precios mucho más acordes al hardware que encierran. Incluso cuando se trata de equipos de gama alta con algunas de las mejores piezas posibles a día de hoy, a las puertas de 2027. Y este modelo es un buen ejemplo de ello: cuesta 9.999,90 euros, es una bestia y al completo sale más barato que muchas de esas RTX 5090.
Con un Ryzen 7 X3D que, en conjunto, lo convierte en un equipo ideal para videojuegos
Hablamos de uno de los PC Neo que vende Neobyte, tienda especializada en hardware, componentes y equipos. Un ordenador de sobremesa ya ensamblado con un PVP de 11.499,01 ahora rebajado a esos 9.999,90 euros. Un PC caro y no apto para todos los bolsillos, pensado para entusiastas del gaming a quienes les gusta disfrutar de la mejor experiencia jugando sin importar el coste.
Pero a pesar de ese importe que ronda los 10.000 euros, este PC Neo tiene una gran relación calidad precio frente a configurar un ordenador a medida que incluya la NVIDIA RTX 5090, esos 64 GB de RAM DDR5 o los 4 TB de SSD con que viene. Porque, por separado, sólo esos tres componentes nos costarían muchísimo más. Si además comparamos con esas RTX 5090 que rondan los 17.000 euros, el PC sale por casi la mitad.
No es el mejor momento para comprar hardware, eso está claro. Pero si el presupuesto no es problema, no queremos seguir esperando a que el mercado se estabilice y además buscamos un rendimiento de gama alta y gran capacidad de almacenamiento (que evita tener que actualizar a corto plazo), teniendo en cuenta el contexto actual este Neo es una compra inteligente frente a la escalada incansable de precios. Porque quizá, dentro de un tiempo, equipos con este hardware acaben costando mucho más.

articles.title: Científicos argentinos desarrollaron una remera inteligente que mediría las señales del cuerpo en tiempo real
articles.text:
Un equipo de investigadores de la Universidad de Buenos Aires (UBA) trabaja en una remera capaz de registrar en simultáneo la actividad eléctrica y mecánica del corazón, la respiración, la temperatura y el flujo sanguíneo, con el objetivo de transformar el monitoreo cardiovascular ambulatorio. El dispositivo, vestible, portátil y de bajo costo, apunta a reunir en una sola prenda mediciones que hoy se realizan por separado o directamente no se realizan fuera del hospital. Otro de los objetivos del proyecto es acercar ese monitoreo a lugares con escaso equipamiento especializado.
Cuando alguien necesita saber qué ocurre dentro de su cuerpo a lo largo de un día entero, la medicina recurre a un Holter: un aparato que se lleva puesto durante 24 horas y registra, por ejemplo, la actividad eléctrica del corazón o la presión arterial. Es una herramienta valiosa, pero mide pocas variables por vez. El ingeniero Pedro Arini, director del proyecto y del Grupo de Investigación del Sistema Cardiovascular de la UBA, e investigador del Conicet, explicó a Infobae que el objetivo es superar ese límite y ofrecer una visión más completa del organismo en condiciones reales.
La remera registraría señales que el Holter convencional no capta
En primer lugar, el ingeniero explicó cuál es la diferencia principal respecto de los estudios tradicionales. “La principal innovación de esta plataforma es que permite registrar simultáneamente diferentes señales fisiológicas que habitualmente se estudian por separado”, señaló.
La prenda integra mediciones conocidas, como el electrocardiograma, la temperatura corporal y la onda de pulso, que aporta datos sobre la circulación sanguínea. Pero también incorpora sensores para registrar sonidos cardíacos y las pequeñas vibraciones que genera la contracción cardíaca. “El corazón no solamente genera una actividad eléctrica: también se contrae, mueve sangre y produce vibraciones y sonidos”, destacó.
Al tratarse de una prenda vestible, el sistema permite tomar mediciones mientras la persona lleva adelante sus actividades cotidianas, sin necesidad de permanecer en un consultorio. Eso posibilita estudiar cómo responde el organismo en situaciones de la vida diaria.
El dispositivo apunta a detectar alteraciones cardiovasculares antes de que se agraven
Uno de los objetivos centrales del proyecto es la detección temprana de problemas en el sistema cardiovascular. A diferencia del Holter clásico, la plataforma cruza la información eléctrica con la respuesta mecánica del corazón y variables relacionadas con la circulación. A partir de ese procesamiento conjunto, los investigadores buscan identificar patrones asociados a riesgos tempranos.
“Uno de los aspectos centrales de nuestra investigación es estudiar si existen cambios en la sincronización entre la actividad eléctrica y la respuesta mecánica del corazón que puedan funcionar como indicadores tempranos de riesgo”, explicó Arini a Infobae. También trabajan en herramientas para caracterizar alteraciones vasculares.
El director del proyecto fue cuidadoso al referirse a la capacidad predictiva del dispositivo: “Todavía estamos en una etapa de investigación y no contamos con resultados clínicos que permitan establecer una capacidad predictiva concreta. Lo que buscamos es desarrollar y validar nuevos indicadores que, en el futuro, puedan complementar las herramientas de evaluación que utilizan los especialistas”.
El prototipo ya registró señales en laboratorio y avanza hacia pruebas con voluntarios
Actualmente, el equipo cuenta con un prototipo funcional que permitió obtener los primeros registros de múltiples señales en condiciones de laboratorio. Ya se probaron distintos módulos de adquisición, incluyendo sensores para sonidos cardíacos, actividad mecánica, señales ópticas y temperatura.
El desarrollo está a cargo del doctor Pablo Cruces y la ingeniera Andrea Hongn, junto con estudiantes de la carrera de Bioingeniería de la Universidad de Buenos Aires. El investigador subrayó el rol del Laboratorio Abierto de Bioingeniería en colaboración con el Instituto Argentino de Matemática, Alberto P. Calderón del CONICET: “Es una experiencia muy valiosa porque permite que los estudiantes participen activamente y aprendan de todo el proceso: desde el diseño electrónico y la programación hasta las mediciones y el análisis de resultados”.
Los próximos pasos incluyen completar la integración de los sensores en la prenda, mejorar la calidad de las mediciones y desarrollar los algoritmos de procesamiento. Luego vendrán ensayos de seguridad, validación experimental y estudios con voluntarios. “Todavía queda un camino de investigación y desarrollo antes de que pueda utilizarse como una herramienta de monitoreo clínico”, reconoció.
La tecnología podría llegar a zonas rurales, niños y neonatos con acceso limitado a salud
Una de las proyecciones más relevantes del proyecto es su potencial para acercar el monitoreo a lugares donde el equipamiento especializado escasea. En localidades alejadas de los centros urbanos, los centros de atención primaria suelen carecer de tecnología de alta complejidad. Una prenda vestible, no invasiva y económica podría registrar datos fisiológicos durante períodos prolongados y transmitirlos a un profesional sin que el paciente deba trasladarse.
“Esto también podría ser muy valioso para el seguimiento de personas mayores o pacientes que requieren controles frecuentes”, indicó el profesional a Infobae. Además, el sistema tiene una arquitectura adaptable: si bien las primeras etapas de validación están previstas en adultos, una de las líneas que el equipo quiere explorar es su uso en neonatos y niños, donde el seguimiento continuo cobra especial importancia.
El equipo también trabaja en adaptar la tecnología para animales de laboratorio, en particular roedores utilizados en investigación biomédica. Para el director del proyecto, el alcance del desarrollo va más allá del dispositivo en sí. “Se trata de generar tecnología nacional que pueda contribuir a mejorar el acceso a la salud. Y para lograrlo es fundamental fortalecer la ciencia, la educación pública y la formación de profesionales capaces de transformar el conocimiento científico en soluciones concretas para la sociedad”, concluyó.

articles.title: Facebook, la herramienta clave del genocidio contra los rohinyás: “Una cuenta militar los deshumanizaba”
articles.text: Un grupo de refugiados rohinyá ve la retransmisión de la lectura de la sentencia del Tribunal Internacional de Justicia de la ONU en el campo de refugiados de Cox's Bazar, en Bangladesh. El Tribunal Internacional de Justicia de la ONU ha determinado este jueves que el Estado de Myanmar (antes Birmania) cometió un genocidio contra la minoría musulmana rohinyá en 2017. La sentencia menciona explícitamente a la red social Facebook y describe cómo los militares y otras personalidades del país la usaron para difundir contenidos de odio contra los rohinyá, antes y después de que la policía y el ejército del país, así como grupos de civiles, iniciaran la operación de limpieza étnica que dejó al menos 10.000 muertos , miles de violaciones y unos 725.000 desplazados. articles.title: Critical Apache Roller, Axis Vulnerabilities Exploited in Attacks
articles.text:
Two critical vulnerabilities in Apache software are being exploited in attacks, and CISA added one of them to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog on Wednesday.
Apache Axis vulnerability exploited in attacks
CVE-2026-90436, disclosed on November 6, is an unsafe reflection vulnerability in Apache Axis 1.x, an end-of-life Java-based SOAP implementation. The flaw has a CVSS score of 9.8 and can allow unauthenticated attackers to execute arbitrary code on vulnerable systems.
Rapid7 detected exploitation on November 13 in a customer environment running Atlassian Confluence Data Center. The attacker executed hundreds of commands, accessed Confluence’s database using the application’s credentials, and searched for sensitive information.
Within four hours of the initial exploitation, the attacker had obtained a service account credential and was querying a production cloud data warehouse. Roughly twelve hours after the first exploit request, the attacker signed in to Microsoft 365 using an integration service account.
Rapid7 also cited N-able’s report of attacks against N-central involving a vulnerability strongly correlated with CVE-2026-90436. Both Confluence and N-central require non-default configurations to be vulnerable.
Separately, Previdian reported detecting 50 exploitation attempts from 14 IP addresses between November 12 and 19. Its sensor data does not establish whether those attempts succeeded.
Apache does not plan to release a fixed Axis 1.x version and recommends migrating to another SOAP engine or applying its published patch.
Confluence Data Center users can upgrade to version 9.2.28 or an unaffected 10.x release. N-central 2026.4 HF3 disables the Legacy API functionality that exposes the vulnerable Axis component.
CISA has added CVE-2026-90436 to its KEV catalog, instructing federal agencies to address it by November 21.
Apache Roller vulnerability also exploited
Apache has also confirmed active exploitation of CVE-2026-129448, a CVSS 9.8 vulnerability affecting versions 4.0.0 through 6.1.4 of its Java-based blogging platform Roller. The flaw allows unauthenticated remote code execution.
“This issue is being actively exploited,” Apache said in its November 17 advisory, without providing further information about the attacks.
The vulnerability stems from unsafe deserialization in Roller’s XML-RPC interface, which processes malicious data before authentication. Disabling XML-RPC through the application’s administration interface does not prevent exploitation.
Apache initially disclosed the same underlying vulnerability in September as CVE-2026-82384.
“This is the same vulnerability as CVE-2026-82384, which listed only Apache Roller 6.1.5 as affected,” Apache explained.
The flaw was fixed in Roller 6.1.6. Apache recommends upgrading to that version or later. Version 6.1.7, released on November 11, addresses another 15 vulnerabilities.
Related: Apache Patches Critical HTTP Server RCE Found by Anthropic, Google
Related: Java4Shell Exploitation Attempts Begin as Vendors Rush Out Advisories
Related: PHP Readies Critical Security Updates to Patch Another RCE Flaw

articles.title: Can AI Really Engineer Its Way to Superintelligence?
articles.text:
Why a Computer Scientist Thinks Superintelligence Won’t Happen
Yet trying for it may still be disastrous
Many people were caught off guard this past summer when employees of one of the world’s leading AI companies began casually debating whether their products would lead to human extinction. It started when Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon announced his resignation, warning that his employer and OpenAI were “racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives.” Evan Hubinger, Anthropic’s head of alignment science, replied, “Jacob is correct here—we really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans!” And Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei subsequently told CNN, “I agree with Jacob much more than I disagree with him.”
These concerns stem from a belief that has circulated in futurist circles for many decades: Once engineers design an AI system capable of improving itself, it will trigger an accelerating cycle of autonomous upgrades known as recursive self-improvement (RSI). The result will be artificial superintelligence (ASI), a system with cognitive capabilities so vastly exceeding those of humans that it will easily evade our control and perhaps even wipe out our species. Artificial superintelligence is, it should be noted, a far more ambitious goal than artificial general intelligence (AGI), which generally refers to AI that can match human capabilities across a broad range of cognitive tasks.
These ideas have prompted varied reactions. Some argue that the concept of ASI is being used for marketing or to instigate regulation that will help the incumbent labs squash new competitors. Others focus on the plausibility of such systems killing us all, debating the finer points of specific scenarios such as AI-engineered superviruses. Still others claim that aligning ASI to human interests is feasible and so we should rush ahead to usher in this digital utopia.
Amid these conversations, one question has received comparatively little attention: From an engineering perspective, is superintelligence even possible? The answer is important because it can help us calibrate our anxieties and develop the most effective possible responses to this emerging technology.
I recently explored this topic in a computer science doctoral seminar that I taught at Georgetown University, in Washington, D.C., in which my students and I examined the technical and cultural roots of the superintelligence story. (For those who are interested, we published an annotated bibliography of our class readings.) I came away with several key objections to the feasibility of ASI, which I’ll detail below, as well as a deeper fear that even if the promised intelligence explosion never arrives, pursuing it can still create real harm.
Objection #1: Recursive Self-Improvement Is Speculative
RSI is an old concept. In a 1965 paper, statistician I.J. Good speculated that a rapid cycle of AI self-improvement could lead to an “intelligence explosion.” The idea gained traction in the 1990s among the Extropians, a Bay Area futurist group, where it offered a way to discuss ASI without having to address the engineering details of how one would build such a system. The concept was taken up by such notable figures as Eliezer Yudkowsky (who later founded the rationalism movement) and Nick Bostrom (who helped steer effective altruism to focus more on existential risks to humanity).
Recently, however, this topic has shifted from thought experiment to practical engineering within both Anthropic (makers of Claude) and OpenAI (makers of ChatGPT). In a June blog post titled “When AI Builds Itself,” Anthropic described how LLM-powered agents are speeding up the writing, debugging, and optimization of code, and also automating parts of research such as running experiments and logging results. The company’s internal data, the report concluded, “is showing that AI is already accelerating the development of AI systems.” OpenAI has been similarly explicit about its intentions; in a September report, the company announced a goal of developing an automated researcher by March 2028.
But do these efforts put the companies on a trajectory toward uncontrollable RSI? Several obstacles undermine this claim. Consider the availability of the data needed to improve AI systems. Through 2023, major advances in LLMs came from scaling up the size of the models. The original GPT-1 had 117 million parameters (values learned during training that shape how the neural network processes information). This quantity jumped to 1.5 billion for GPT-2, to 175 billion for GPT-3, to (likely) more than a trillion for GPT-4’s release three years ago. After GPT-4, however, continued scaling began yielding diminishing returns. This led engineers to increasingly turn their attention toward “post-training” phases, where techniques from reinforcement learning are applied to improve an already trained model’s performance on specific tasks. This approach rewards a model for producing successful responses, helping it better produce similar answers in the future. It requires, however, lots of examples of relevant inputs paired with correct outputs.
Such datasets are relatively easy to generate in highly structured fields such as computer programming and mathematics, which helps explain why we’ve seen rapid and impressive advances in these narrow domains. Progress in areas that lack easy access to this type of training data has been less dramatic. This might explain why AI can tackle advanced theorems but struggles to empty an email inbox. “What if the jagged frontier is mainly math + code (which you can push arbitrarily far with [reinforcement learning techniques]),” the French AI researcher François Chollet recently hypothesized, “and everything else starts to plateau because it is still bottlenecked by human generated data?” The deployment of automated coding agents and LLM-powered researchers won’t overcome this fundamental limitation.
McKibillo
The Game of Superintelligence
How a decades-old thought experiment became an AI-industry ambition—and where it might lead
Key
• Idea: A concept, argument, or vision
• Technical advance: A scientific or engineering development
• Reality check: A challenge to assumptions about AI progress
1. Alan Turing
1936
Introduces the concept of a universal computing machine. He later proposes that machines could think, laying the foundations for AI.
Shows that some problems can’t be solved by any algorithm.
2. I. J. Good
1965
Proposes that an intelligent machine could design an even smarter one, setting off a potential “intelligence explosion.”
3. Backpropagation
1986
Geoffrey Hinton, David Rumelhart, and Ronald Williams demonstrate how backpropagation can train multilayer neural networks.
4. Vernor Vinge
1993
Proposes that an intelligent machine could design an even smarter one, setting off a potential “intelligence explosion.”
Notes that faster thinking alone isn’t enough for superintelligence: A faster-thinking dog still couldn’t play chess.
5. Nick Bostrom & Eliezer Yudkowsky
1990s–2000s
Bostrom and Yudkowsky discuss superintelligence in Extropian circles, then spread the idea to effective-altruist and rationalist circles, respectively.
6. Deep learning breakthroughs
2010s
Larger models, more data, and greater computing power produce rapid improvements in AI capabilities.
7. The race to self-improving AI
2020s
Dario Amodei and other AI leaders set their sights on superintelligence, with recursive self-improvement proposed as a path toward it.
8. Reality check
2020s
François Chollet questions whether LLMs’ current advances in math and coding will extend to domains where training data and reliable feedback are harder to obtain.
YOU ARE HERE
2026
AI systems are already accelerating AI development, and labs are working on automated researchers. But will this lead to an intelligence explosion?
1. The Intelligence Explosion
AI systems improve themselves at accelerating speed, surpass human intelligence, and potentially escape our control.
2. Danger Without Superintelligence
The intelligence explosion never arrives, but increasingly autonomous AI systems cause real-world harm through misuse, poor design, or loss of human control.
3. A Useful AI Future
Powerful, specialized AI tools bring major benefits, with constraints that make their behavior easier to predict and control.
Claims that RSI is imminent also understate the massive scientific efforts required for major AI advances. Consider the critical role of backpropagation, an algorithm that enables very large neural networks to learn by tuning internal parameters, layer by layer, to reduce errors in their predictions. This algorithm enabled the deep learning revolution, but it didn’t emerge ex nihilo in the minds of its creators. The influential 1986 paper on backpropagation by David Rumelhart, Geoffrey Hinton, and Ronald Williams built on decades of critical breakthroughs in mathematics and computer science.
An intelligence explosion leading to ASI would similarly depend on a long sequence of innovations of comparable importance, which would build on many significant science and engineering advances that haven’t yet happened. This would require AI agents to somehow simulate, organize, and evaluate decades of worldwide scientific effort across numerous fields—an impossibly ambitious task. Indeed, recent research led by computer scientists at Princeton found that current AI tools had difficulty making autonomous progress even on highly constrained research questions. “Our results provide early evidence that today’s agents can do the engineering of AI research,” the researchers conclude, “but struggle with critical parts of the research life cycle.” The leap from this current reality to a future in which these same types of tools are automating science is almost too massive to imagine.
Finally, the RSI narrative downplays resource limitations. Tens of thousands of human brains have worked for decades, aided by increasingly powerful computers, to develop today’s AI systems, which can match human intelligence in some domains. That represents a massive investment in computation of both the biological and digital variety. What if the next intelligence level requires double the resources, and then the next level requires double again? Soon there would be no number of chips or data centers that we could build to provide the necessary compute and keep advancing toward ASI.
Pulling together these threads, I believe that the idea of RSI leading to an intelligence explosion is highly speculative and based on many unproven assumptions. While RSI isn’t definitively impossible, the idea demands more technical skepticism than it’s currently receiving. Carl Sagan’s adage that extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence certainly applies here.
Objection #2: Superintelligence Might Not Be Computable
There’s an implicit claim in the superintelligence discourse that computers are theoretically capable of any calculation that can be imagined, so long as you can find a sufficiently smart algorithm, running on sufficiently powerful digital processors. In this context, RSI is merely a process for rapidly uncovering the special algorithms that can implement unimaginable smarts.
We cannot simply assume that any science fiction scenario we conjure about powerful AI is possible if we give machines enough time to self-improve.
But this is not how computer scientists think about computation. In his canonical 1937 paper, “On Computable Numbers,” Alan Turing proved a surprising and relevant result: Most problems cannot be solved by algorithms. His elegant proof established the space of possible problems to be uncountably infinite (like infinite precision decimal numbers), while the space of possible algorithms is only countably infinite (like whole numbers). Later breakthroughs in computational complexity theory established that of the problems that are technically solvable by computers, many would require an astronomically large amount of time and resources to crack, making them practically impossible to solve. Theoretical computer scientists, in other words, don’t assume that computers will solve everything; we’re instead excited whenever we find something that these machines happen to be able to efficiently handle.
We cannot simply assume, as the futurists often do, that any science fiction scenario we conjure about powerful AI is possible if we give machines enough time to self-improve. There might be some capabilities in which machines can obtain seemingly magical levels of performance, but there will also be many others that no machine, whether computer or human, will ever make much progress.
A relevant counterargument here emphasizes the speed of silicon chips compared to human neurons: Perhaps the sheer speed of digital computation can yield machines that run cognitive circles around our clunky brains, even if they’re not solving vastly more complicated problems than we’re already capable of tackling. But as the computer scientist and science fiction author Vernor Vinge pointed out, rapidity in cognition is not the same as intelligence. Speeding up the mind of a dog, he argued, wouldn’t enable the animal to play chess. Implementing roughly human-level intelligence on a faster machine might be impressive, but it’s not necessarily alarming.
At the moment, there’s a growing list of tasks that AI systems can perform better than humans, including winning complex games, identifying software bugs, and proving certain types of math theorems. It’s tempting to extrapolate from this specific progress to general mastery of every ability you might imagine. But it’s important to remember that the frontier of AI capabilities has always been jagged, with some research directions yielding impressive results and many others proving to be dead ends—a reality that would not have surprised Turing. More likely than a future dominated by an all-powerful superintelligence system is one in which we continue to painstakingly explore the space of problems well suited to AI, creating useful tools but falling well short of the digital deity predicted by the futurists.
Cal Newport, a computer science professor at Georgetown University, is skeptical that AI can achieve superintelligence through recursive self-improvement.
Penny Gray Photography
Objection #3: Alignment Isn’t Hard (Given the Right System Design)
Last fall, the prominent AI doomsday theorist Yudkowsky appeared on “The Ezra Klein Show” to talk about superintelligence. The episode was ominously titled “How Afraid of the A.I. Apocalypse Should We Be?” Klein and Yudkowsky quickly got into the difficulty of “alignment”—training an AI system to act in a manner that aligns with human interests. Yudkowsky argued that we are struggling to control our existing systems, which implies that we’ll have no chance of controlling the much smarter variations of this technology that are soon to follow.
To underscore his point, he referred to a disturbing incident described in the system card for OpenAI’s GPT-o1 model. OpenAI had set up a security challenge that instructed an LLM-powered coding system to break into a server to retrieve the contents of a protected file. But a configuration mistake prevented the server from launching, rendering the task impossible. Instead of giving up, the system exploited a security flaw to start a new instance of the server, adding a command that directly revealed the protected file’s contents. “It jumped out of the system,” explained Yudkowsky, adding: “This is not something that any human particularly programmed into it.”
Explore the Superintelligence Debate
In a Georgetown University doctoral seminar, Cal Newport and his students examined the intellectual history and technical plausibility of superintelligence. Explore their annotated bibliography of key papers.
Though this 2024 incident flew largely under the radar at the time, a more troubling episode made a bigger splash this summer. OpenAI revealed that one of the company’s models circumvented its restricted internet access to hack into Hugging Face servers, seeking information that would help it pass a cybersecurity evaluation—all without the knowledge of its human creators. OpenAI soon admitted that the Hugging Face attack was just one of many examples of its systems going rogue. An opinion article published in The Hill articulated a widely held reaction when it described this behavior as “something straight out of sci-fi.”
These examples seem to support Yudkowsky’s fear that AI will inevitably develop a mind of its own, a key step on the route to uncontrollable ASI. But a closer look reveals a less frightening picture. The systems involved in these hacking incidents were AI agents: programs that continually prompt an LLM to ask what actions to take next in pursuit of a goal. In the hacking incidents, this basic ask/act pattern was repeated in a long-running loop with minimal human supervision.
Using LLMs to suggest actions over long time horizons is a risky proposition. As any frequent chatbot user can attest, LLM outputs can be plausible and logical while still veering off in unexpected directions that violate commonsense human norms about what’s appropriate.
In the GPT-o1 incident, for example, it’s likely that the agent reported the error message caused by the server misconfiguration to the LLM. During its training, the LLM had probably encountered reports of similar error messages accompanied by instructions for how to restart the server in question, so it passed along similar instructions to the agent. This is a perfectly plausible response when considered in isolation, even if it led to actions that a human would immediately reject as violating the spirit of the experiment. Something similar helps explain the hacking attacks over the summer. The LLM suggesting a hack to succeed at a cybersecurity challenge is a perfectly plausible response, even if it’s not what the experimenters had in mind.
I believe that pursuing RSI is an act of clear negligence.
The misaligned behavior that troubles commentators like Yudkowsky, therefore, doesn’t necessarily reveal something fundamental about advanced AI. It’s instead an expected side effect of the particular strategy of letting LLM outputs determine the actions of an autonomous agent without sufficient constraints. An obvious way to address these risks is to consider alternative architectures. Fortunately, there are many examples of AI systems that can complete tasks at human or superhuman levels without relying solely on LLM output to determine their actions.
Consider Tesla’s rapidly improving autonomous driving systems, or DeepMind’s AlphaFold, which helped win its developers a Nobel Prize in Chemistry for its ability to predict protein structures, or the AI game engines that can now beat humans in many popular pastimes, including chess, poker, Go, and the strategy game Diplomacy. None of these systems, impressive as they are, create concerns about going rogue. Their construction prevents such an outcome: Instead of prompting an LLM to generate an open-ended strategy for pursuing a general goal, these AIs consider much more limited spaces of possible actions. AlphaFold never surprises its users because its architecture does only one thing: It maps amino acid sequences to 3D protein structures. Tesla’s cars never unexpectedly form vehicle swarms because they’re asked only to avoid immediate obstacles, not to craft convoluted plans for achieving long-term objectives.
The implication of recent AI hacking attacks, therefore, is not a reflection of the difficulties of alignment. It is instead evidence that autonomous systems powered primarily by LLM prompts are unpredictable and possibly unsafe. More task-specific architectures can produce impressive performance much more safely, if we’re willing to put in the effort to develop them.
The Dangers of Chasing Superintelligence
Even if I’m correct that superintelligence is not a realistic engineering goal, this doesn’t mean we’re safe from harm. Merely pursuing ASI, as both OpenAI and Anthropic seem intent on doing, can create problems. Why, for example, did OpenAI persist in running its problematic hacking experiments over the summer, even after multiple warnings that the agents were likely to act unpredictably? Perhaps the company judged these risks acceptable collateral damage in the race to be the first to bring ASI into the world.
This fascination with superintelligence might also explain why OpenAI and Anthropic have both described RSI as a critical goal. As argued earlier, RSI is a concept from futurism and not computer science, and it isn’t necessary to build useful AI products. But if you believe achieving ASI is your destiny, pursuing recursive self-improvement becomes a primary objective. This matters because even if RSI never produces an intelligence explosion, it will almost certainly lead to systems that are harder for humans to understand and control. Which is why I believe that pursuing RSI is an act of clear negligence.
What’s needed now is for engineers and scientists with no financial or ideological skin in the game to participate in the AI discourse. We cannot let a few AI companies with mixed motives dictate the terms for how we discuss this technology. If superintelligence is a shaky concept, experts need to say so. If agents powered by prompting LLMs aren’t the best path toward safe and productive AI, experts should argue that as well. For the past few years, we’ve let a small group of individuals from the Bay Area who have quirky beliefs and astonishing sums of money tell us how to think about their products. It’s time for those of us able to think for ourselves on these matters to stand up and declare, “We’ve heard what you had to say. Now it’s our turn.”

articles.title: Geekom’s A9 Max is our top Mac mini alternative, and it’s down to $1269
articles.text:
Geekom A9 Max mini PC deal: Black Friday sale drops our favorite Mac mini alternative to $1269
One of our favorite Windows mini PCs gets a major discount for office and creative professionals
We're big fans of Geekom's A9 Max mini PC, which scored 4.5 stars in our review, earning a Highly Recommended award. The combination of AMD’s latest Ryzen AI processor, expandable memory, and extensive connectivity makes ideal for users who need workstation-level power in a compact chassis.
Now, as part of its big Black Friday sale, the Geekom A9 Max is down to $1269 (was $2079) when you use code BFA9M230. That model comes equipped with the AMD Ryzen AI 9 HX 370 chip, 32GB DDR5 RAM, and 2TB SSD. However, you can bump that up to a HX 470 processor $1369.
For my money, this is a clear Mac mini alternative for Windows - it comes with Windows 11 Pro installed, but Geekom notes it's compatible with Linux, too. Not everyone will need a mini PC that delivers this level of performance, but it will easily handle office tasks and content creation without breaking a sweat.
Today's best Geekom A9 Max mini PC deal
We found the A9 Max 2026 Edition a "high-performance mini PC" during our tests. With a focus on AI, it's capable of hitting up to 86 TOPS. Internally, you can expand up to 256GB of DDR5 memory and 8TB storage. Connectivity is excellent, too, equipped with dual 40Gbps USB4 ports, dual HDMI 2.1, dual 2.5GbE, Wi-Fi 7, Bluetooth 5.4, and an SD Card reader. For the full discount, use code BFA9M230.
Why we recommend the GEEKOM A9 Max
In our review, we awarded the A9 Max a lofty 4.5 stars, and we loved its capability in demanding productivity and creative applications. It zoomed through Photoshop, Lightroom, and video editing, and its NPU means it can run local AI models without relying entirely on cloud services.
There are compromises. The integrated graphics aren’t a substitute for a dedicated GPU, so you won’t have as much capability in gaming or creative applications that use a proper GPU - although you can connect an external graphics card via the USB4 port. The standard 32GB of RAM can also feel restrictive for more demanding video production, so we'd recommend upgrading that if you need extra headroom.
Price context and historical value
This is firmly premium mini PC territory, but it's also one of the cheapest prices we've seen on this 2026 Edition of the Geekom A9 Max. That promo code is doing a lot of heavy lifting to make this deal more attractive.
The compact metal chassis, powerful processor, and extensive connectivity make it appealing if desk space or portability matters more than getting maximum value from your next purchase.
Should you buy it?
✅ Buy the Geekom A9 Max if… you need powerful processing in a compact package for creative applications, productivity, and local AI workloads.
❌ Skip the Geekom A9 Max if… You just want a mini PC for general day-to-day tasks like running Microsoft Office and streaming.

articles.title: Superhuman pushes its Go assistant everywhere | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Productivity apps are simultaneously trying to feed more context to their AI tools while also making those AI assistants available in every nook and corner of their products. Superhuman (formerly Grammarly) is going in the same direction with the rollout of features, including a personalized Go assistant, making agents available in Docs, and third-party agent integrations.
While some of the company’s AI features have faced criticism, Superhuman started pushing its Go assistant after its rebranding last year. With the new rollout, it is making Go learn context across different apps and give better personalized suggestions for prompts. Superhuman is revamping its onboarding flow to let users connect their preferred tools and load context about their work upfront.
The assistant works inline with the cursor — just like Grammarly — and also manages other agents. Superhuman is also making the agent proactive, which means it looks for your schedule, keeps an eye on your email, and even drafts responses. The updated Go agent also learns users’ writing styles and responds accordingly in email and Docs.
The productivity company is adding 20 new connected agents, including DeepL, Legora, Amplitude, Databricks, and Blackboard, through its Go SDK.
The company is also thinking about adding AI to different products, including Docs and Superhuman Mail. In Docs, all Go agents work natively, and you can set them off to work on different tasks in the background. Users can also set routines to trigger workflows based on events.
Until now, Mail has used AI as its central tool, which is being replaced by Go. Users can also do enterprise search by using data from the company knowledge base and connected tools. Go also uses this context to form drafts and organize the inbox across Google and Outlook accounts.
Superhuman acquired notetaker Fathom in September to add more context to its suite. The company is now rolling out live collaborative notetaking, which would be shared across the team. Plus, Go can now make decisions post-meeting, like forming an initial draft of a proposal.
The company’s CEO, Shishir Mehrotra, said that Go has had good momentum with over 1 million active users. There are a host of agents now that are vying for users’ attention on both the personal and professional front. Mehrotra thinks that while Go is more work-focused, it can help with personal emails and schedules.
“One of the reasons why these assistants have been popular is that they treat you as a whole person and recognize that we need to cover both extremes. Go is definitely more work-focused than some of the tools coming out of the pure consumer ecosystem. It doesn’t mean we draw the boundary at helping you with your personal tasks or helping you with your calendar or all of your email,” he told TechCrunch over a call.
While Go might not directly compete with the likes of Instinct, Muse, and Fo, Superhuman wants users to choose its assistant over something like OpenAI’s Dots or Claude Duet.

- Para prêmios brutos a partir de R$ 2.428,80: o pagamento é realizado somente nas agências da Caixa. Será necessário apresentar seu comprovante de identidade original com CPF e o recibo de aposta original e premiado.
- Para prêmios de R$ 10.000,00 ou mais: esses valores são pagos em até dois dias úteis. O prazo começa a contar a partir da apresentação em uma Agência da Caixa.
Quais os dias de sorteio da Quina?
Os sorteios da Quina acontecem 6 vezes por semana. Eles ocorrem de segunda a sexta e no domingo.
Qual o horário do sorteio da Quina?
O sorteio ocorre de segunda a sexta, às 21h, e no domingo, às 11h. Todos no horário de Brasília.
Onde assistir ao sorteio ao vivo da Quina?
O sorteio é transmitido online pelo perfil da Caixa no YouTube e Facebook.
Como jogar na Quina?
A aposta simples consiste em marcar 5 números entre os 80 disponíveis.
Até que horas é possível apostar na Quina?
Nos sorteios de segunda a sexta, as apostas poderão ser feitas até as 20h do mesmo dia. Já nos sorteios de domingo, as apostas poderão ser feitas até as 22h do sábado.
Já a venda de bolões nos canais eletrônicos será finalizada 15 minutos antes do início de cada concurso.
Com quantos números se ganha na Quina?
O apostador leva prêmio em dinheiro se acertar a partir de 2 números (duque). Ele também ganha com 3 números (terno), 4 números (quadra) e 5 números sorteados.
Quantos números posso escolher para apostar na Quina?
No volante, seja em papel ou digital, há 80 números disponíveis. A menor aposta possível é escolher 5 números e custa R$ 3. Quanto mais números você escolher, maior será sua chance de ganhar.
Rodrigo Mozelli é jornalista formado pela Universidade Metodista de São Paulo (UMESP) e, atualmente, é redator do Olhar Digital.

articles.title: FCC greenlights rule allowing prisons to jam cellphone signals
articles.text:
The Federal Communications Commission voted unanimously to allow state and local prisons to jam cellphones. In an announcement on Thursday, the FCC argues the rule will help combat an “influx of contraband cellphones” used to carry out crimes from prison.
FCC greenlights rule allowing prisons to jam cellphone signals
The FCC passed the rule despite warnings that jammers could block lawful communications, like 911 calls.
Jammers are generally banned under Section 333 of the Communications Act of 1934, though they’re used at some federal facilities. FCC Chair Brendan Carr claims that giving correctional facilities access to this technology will help prevent prisoners from using phones for illegal activity. “These devices [phones] are being used by inmates to order hits, run drug operations, traffic women and children, and unleash mayhem on our communities from behind bars,” Carr says.
In the months leading up to the vote, trade groups and human rights advocates have raised concerns about the risks of blocking cellphone signals in prisons. The US Chamber of Commerce and the CTIA, a wireless association representing the nation’s biggest carriers, have both warned in letters to the FCC that jamming technology could disrupt lawful communications outside prisons, including 911 calls. Meanwhile, the American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU) has long argued that cellphones can keep prisoners safe by allowing them to document safety and human rights issues that the outside world may not see.
FCC Commissioner Anna Gomez, the sole Democrat on the Commission, voted for the measure despite the risk of “potential unintended consequences,” according to the Associated Press. “I want to make sure that we don’t harm public safety in the name of helping public safety,” Gomez added.
The FCC says prisons that choose to jam cellphone signals will need to obtain a license, adhere to “technical standards and testing requirements,” and ensure that the jamming technology doesn’t interfere with communications outside the facility. Prisons must also notify nearby communities of testing and when the technology is being deployed.

articles.title: Why AI-enabled scientific research is a double-edged sword
articles.text:
OpenAI has sparked a backlash in the mathematics community by apparently using AI to solve more than 700 longstanding maths problems in a short space of time. A recent open letter signed by 28 recipients of the Fields Medal (one of the highest honours in maths) goes some way to explaining why.
Mathematicians who have gone through some of the solutions offered by AI say they are opaque in their reasoning. As the open letter explains: “Solving problems is only a tool and proxy for achieving the primary goal of conceptual understanding and insight.”
As famed mathematician and Fields Medal winner Terence Tao put it: “These companies are dumping carcasses of raw meat onto our communal village table and saying: ‘Here you go, I solved your food problem.‘”
OpenAI said it had consulted with the community prior to announcing the latest three results, one of which was in my own field of computer science.
Nevertheless, mathematicians are having to adapt fast to the disruptive arrival of AI in their field. This challenge extends far beyond mathematics and into all other disciplines of science and research.
The impact AI has had on software development through tools such as Claude and Codex, is undeniable. Industry software teams are now routinely using AI tools in their work.
But now, AI is already having a major impact on the practice of science itself. Academic journals and conferences are dealing with exponential increases in submissions from researchers, in a system largely based on volunteer effort for reviewing and editing.
Breaking peer review?
This year, the International Conference on Learning Representations, a leading academic meeting on AI, received 60,000 submissions. This has increased from 490 in 2017. One researcher, commenting on the figures, said: “AI is breaking traditional academic peer review.”
This doesn’t seem to be a special case. In 2024, Mark A Hanson, from the University of Exeter, and colleagues, published a paper titled: “The strain on scientific publishing”. In it, the authors note that the total number of available academic articles has grown exponentially in recent years.
This is in part the result of a decades-long trend, predating modern generative AI, with many factors playing a role – including pressure on researchers to publish large numbers of academic articles, known as “publish or perish”. In 2022, just before ChatGPT launched, the number of papers published was about 47% higher than in 2016. The increase has occurred while the number of practising scientists has seen little growth. But AI is undoubtedly accelerating the process.
Yet this raises questions about whether the current trajectory is sustainable – and whether the quality of science will suffer. One academic conference has been testing whether AI could be part of the solution as well as the problem. This year, the NeurIPS meeting, which focuses on AI and machine learning, introduced a voluntary AI-assisted review for those submitting conference abstracts.
Afterwards, scientists evaluated the quality of the review and how helpful it was. But some in the field believe this could compound current problems.
Protecting critical thinking
Anecdotal evidence suggests some members of the public who are not professional scientists are using AI to produce and submit their own academic papers and write books on science. Citizen scientists make valuable contributions in areas such as biodiversity monitoring and astronomy.
But AI should not be viewed as a substitute for the formal training, daily research work, critical thinking and expert input from colleagues that academia offers. While AI and related technologies are powerful tools for democratising knowledge, it took me 13 years from my PhD to write my first book (the only one I have written so far), whereas now the same can apparently be done in weeks. But, as with peer review and maths proofs, humans have to check and interpret these.
As this story plays through and repeats, we may need to resort to new modes of scientific dissemination to deal with the new methods of creating research.
This brings me to the critical thinking that research requires. Currently, I provide the ideas, but increasingly rely on my AI assistant to do a lot of the work of thinking for me, or at least appear to. But the results of AI-enabled research can be obtuse, as the Terence Tao quote above illustrates, or even plain wrong. They can only be sorted out with human time and domain expertise.
I increasingly wonder what this means for the role of the researcher and for training the future generation of scientists, mathematicians and engineers. I am finding that a challenging, long term student project that would normally take several months to complete is at risk of being able to be almost completely automated through providing judicious prompts to an AI agent.
If I am guiding the student while they provide the prompts to an AI system, what do they learn from the process? And in my own research, where AI enables me to undertake projects I would not otherwise have the resources to, if I am providing the ideas but the AI is doing a lot of the “thinking” for me, am I even doing my own research anymore?
This could have an impact on the future generation’s ability to generate novel research questions, as well as their capacity for critiquing AI’s attempts to answer them.
One of my favourite sci-fi short stories is Profession, by Isaac Asimov. In it, the author imagines a future where young adults are educated by direct upload into their brains using technology known as magnetic tapes – which could be seen as a stand-in for AI. At one point, the main protagonist, George, tries to convince another character that humans can learn in other ways – by reading books, for example.
The other person is baffled, seeing this only as an unnecessary expense. Through the narrative, Asimov reveals the risks in the “direct upload” approach to learning. He also explores what is needed for society to progress when some forms of knowledge can be gained so easily.
We seem to be arriving at the science fiction future I once looked forward to where, like a science officer on a starship exploring unknown corners of the universe, or a billionaire genius tech superhero, I can just provide the ideas while getting the computer to do the heavy lifting. Like others, I am exhilarated by this, but also concerned about what it means for the practice and future of my discipline.

articles.title: Unbemannter Drogenschmuggel: Wie Kartelle ihre U-Boote mit Starlink und Hardware von Amazon steuern lassen
articles.text:
Keine Crew an Bord: Wie Drogenkartelle mit Standard-Hardware autonome U-Boote bauen
An einem strahlenden Morgen im vergangenen April entdeckte ein Überwachungsflugzeug des kolumbianischen Militärs eine 12 Meter lange, haifischähnliche Silhouette. Sie trieb direkt vor dem Tayrona-Nationalpark im Meer. Es handelte sich zweifellos um ein „Drogen-U-Boot“, ein getarntes Glasfaserboot, dessen Rumpf fast vollständig unter Wasser liegt und das von Drogenkartellen zum Transport von Kokain in Richtung Norden genutzt wird. Die Besatzung des Flugzeugs meldete den Vorfall per Funk, und schließlich erhielten nahegelegene Boote der Küstenwache den Befehl – routinemäßig, aber dringend: Abfangen.
Dieser Text stammt aus der Ausgabe 8/2026 von MIT Technology Review. Darin beschäftigen wir uns mit den Folgen des Klimawandels und wie wir uns an Hitze, Dürre und Überschwemmungen anpassen sollten. Das Heft ist ab sofort im Zeitschriftenhandel erhältlich und in unserem Online-Shop bestellbar.
Kolumbianische Küstenwache fängt U-Boot ab
In Cartagena, etwa 250 Kilometer von diesen Geschehnissen entfernt, setzte sich der Kommandant der regionalen Küstenwache, Kapitän Jaime González Zamudio, an seinen Schreibtisch und verfolgte von dort, was nun passierte. Auf seinem Bildschirm rasten die Symbole für seine Patrouillenboote auf die Koordinaten des U-Boots zu, während er über Funk mit den Besatzungen in Kontakt stand. Ein ganz normaler Tag in kolumbianischen Gewässern.
Kolumbien ist der weltweit größte Kokainproduzent, und seine Marine beschlagnahmt seit Jahrzehnten Schmuggel-U-Boote. Und so war sich der Kapitän ziemlich sicher, wie diese Aktion ausgehen würde: Seine Mannschaft würde das U-Boot einholen, von dem ein kleiner Teil aus dem Wasser ragte. Sie würden es anhalten, entern und die Luke aufbrechen. Im Inneren würden sie zwei, drei, vielleicht auch vier erschöpfte Männer vorfinden, die kurz davor waren, an den feuchten Dieselabgasen zu ersticken. Im Laderaum würden sie mehrere Tonnen Kokain finden.
Der erste Teil verlief wie geplant: Die Boote holten das U-Boot ein. Eine Besatzung der Patrouillenboote enterte es, brach die Luke auf und stellte fest, dass das Schiff sicher war. Doch ab diesem Moment verliefen die Dinge anders.
Starlink, Amazon-Autopilot und Überwachungskamera
Zunächst kam über Funk die unerwartete Info, es befände sich kein Kokain an Bord. Und auch keine Besatzung. Noch nicht einmal ein Steuerrad. Und auch nicht genügend Platz für eine Person, um sich hinzulegen. Stattdessen fanden die Männer der Küstenwache einen Treibstofftank, ein Autopilotsystem und Steuerelektronik sowie eine ferngesteuerte Überwachungskamera. Das Team von González Zamudio schickte Bilder nach Cartagena: Am Rumpf waren eine weitere Kamera sowie zwei rechteckige Kunststoffteile, jedes etwa so groß wie ein Backblech, festgeschraubt – Antennen für die Verbindung zum Starlink-Satelliteninternet.
Die Behörden schleppten das Boot nach Cartagena, wo Militärtechniker es genauer unter die Lupe nahmen. Wochen später lieferten sie die beunruhigenden Ergebnisse: Sie hatten das erste unbemannte Drogen-U-Boot Kolumbiens auseinandergenommen. Es konnte ferngesteuert werden, war aber auch zu einem gewissen Grad in der Lage, autonom zu fahren. Die Techniker schlossen daraus, dass es sich bei dem U-Boot wahrscheinlich um einen Prototyp des „Clan del Golfo“ handelte, einer mächtigen kriminellen Vereinigung, die an der Karibikküste operiert.

articles.title: Las dos oleadas de nerviosismo global por el lanzamiento de GTA VI: así se sufrieron las caídas más importantes de la PlayStation Network
articles.text: Varias personas juegan al Grand Theft Auto VI en dos pantallas suspendidas durante una fiesta de lanzamiento del videojuego en Grails Miami, en Miami (Florida, Estados Unidos), el jueves 19 de noviembre de 2026. Justo a la medianoche, cuando miles de personas estaban frente a su consola contando los minutos para poder jugar GTA VI , la red de PlayStation presentó problemas para concretar la conexión. La caída no se ha dado de manera simultánea en todo el mundo, sino que se ha registrado en momentos diferentes, según ha reportado el portal DownDetector . Ha empezado poco antes de que iniciara oficialmente el 19 de noviembre, fecha de estreno del nuevo videojuego que ha desatado la locura de jóvenes y adultos , y ha acabado horas después, ya durante la madrugada.
