articles.title: Sony’s WH-1000XM5 are cheaper than ever for Black Friday
articles.text:
Back in my day, the only “Doorbuster” sales were at physical retail stores. But now, you can get ultra-low prices before Black Friday whether you want to shop in-store or online. One that stands out is the previous-generation Sony WH-1000XM5 noise-canceling headphones, which are marked down to their lowest price ever, just $169.99 at Best Buy. While their MSRP is $399.99, they’ve been spotted as low as $198 in the last few months.
Sony’s WH-1000XM5 are cheaper than ever for Black Friday
Last-generation noise-cancelling headphones are still a great option for traveling or staying focused.
The WH-1000XM5 launched in 2022, and despite having been succeeded by the WH-1000XM6, they’re still an excellent set of headphones. Their active noise cancellation effect is one of the best out there — competitive with the latest models from Bose and Apple — and the sound profile is tighter and more balanced than the older Sony headphones. There are some minor downsides, like a bulky case and all-plastic design, but those seem easier to overlook at this lower price point.
The newer Sony WH-1000XM6 improve the sound and noise cancellation, with quality of life upgrades not present in the XM5, like a folding design and more comfortable headband. However, they’re significantly more expensive, currently discounted to $348 during Black Friday (Amazon, Best Buy), down from their MSRP of $450.
To make shopping a little more confusing, the newer WH-1000XM4C sit between the XM5 and XM6 in terms of price, and are a slightly updated version of the older XM4 model with its foldable design. Our reviewer John Higgins thinks the XM4C’s noise cancellation lags behind, so I’d opt for the XM5 over them, especially at the sale price.

articles.title: Orange veut remplacer le premier téléphone de vos enfants par une montre à 68 euros
articles.text:
Après Bouygues Telecom et SFR, Orange se lance à son tour sur le marché de la montre connectée pour enfants avec SaferKids, couplée à un forfait bloqué. L'opérateur propose un prix d'appel plus bas que ses concurrents.
Orange a dévoilé ce mercredi 19 novembre l'offre SaferKids, qui est vendue sous la forme d'une montre connectée pour enfants, avec un forfait bloqué sans engagement. L'opérateur historique rejoint ainsi Bouygues Telecom et SFR, qui proposent déjà ce type d'alternative au premier téléphone portable. Avec une montre européenne, un prix cassé à son lancement et une gamme SaferPhone enrichie d’un forfait 100 Go pour les lycéens, la nouvelle offensive familiale d'Orange est plutôt intéressante.
Une montre connectée pour enfants pilotée depuis le téléphone des parents clients d'Orange
Là où Bouygues et SFR ont misé sur les fabricants chinois TCL et Honor, Orange a préféré une marque espagnole, SaveFamily, et son modèle SaveWatch Plus 2. Ici, la montre sert d'abord à appeler ses proches et à être joint par eux. Les parents décident quels contacts sont autorisés, et un bouton SOS permet à l'enfant de joindre un numéro favori en cas de problème.
Tout se gère depuis l'application SaveFamily, sur le téléphone d'un parent. C'est là qu'on consulte la position de la montre, qu'on définit la liste des contacts autorisés et qu'on programme des plages de déconnexion. À l'école, pendant les devoirs ou à l'entraînement, elle se fait oublier. Pour la prise en main, Orange propose des tutoriels et une assistance au 3900, ainsi que des conseils aux parents sur son site Bien vivre le digital.
Concernant les tarifs, Orange marque de gros points, en tout cas pour le moment. Jusqu'au 2 décembre, la montre affichée à 139 euros prix fabricant tombe à 68 euros, avec une formule de 15 % de remise immédiate, puis 50 euros remboursés, à demander soi-même après l'achat. Après le 2 décembre, il faudra compter 89 euros, remboursement déduit. Ces prix supposent de souscrire le forfait SaferKids de 2 Go proposé par Orange, sans engagement. Comme il est bloqué, aucun hors-forfait n'est possible. Il coûte 4,99 euros par mois aux abonnés Internet Orange et 9,99 euros aux autres.
Bouygues, SFR, Orange : quelle montre pour enfants coûte vraiment le moins cher ?
Orange refait son retard sur ses concurrents. Bouygues Telecom a tiré le premier en juin 2025 avec sa Kids Watch signée TCL, remplacée en octobre par le modèle MT48. SFR a suivi le 18 août avec son Pack Kids Protégés, bâti autour de la Honor Choice Kids Watch Plus. Sur le forfait, Orange et Bouygues s’alignent, avec 4,99 euros par mois pour leurs clients box (chez Bouygues, il faut aussi un forfait mobile maison), 9,99 euros pour les autres. SFR facture le sien 11,99 euros, avec une remise pour ses abonnés box qu’il ne chiffre plus sur sa page, mais se montre plus large en data, avec 5 Go contre 2 Go chez ses rivaux.
La principale différence se fait sur le prix de la montre. Orange profite du Black Friday pour être le moins cher avec ses 68 euros, mais d'une courte tête, on va dire. SFR demande 69 euros, payables comptant ou en quatre fois. Bouygues réclame 97 euros pour sa nouvelle MT48 (1 euro, puis 4 euros par mois pendant deux ans). Pour un foyer sans box qui garde le forfait 24 mois, la facture atteint environ 308 euros chez Orange pendant la promotion et 329 euros ensuite, contre 337 euros chez Bouygues et 357 euros chez SFR. Pour les abonnés box, Orange descend à 188 euros pendant le Black Friday, puis 209 euros, contre 217 euros chez Bouygues. Chez SFR, tout dépendra de la remise appliquée au forfait.
Enfin, pour les ados, Orange étoffe sa gamme SaferPhone. Le forfait 5 Go est proposé à 5,99 euros par mois pour les clients Internet. Un nouveau forfait de 100 Go, taillé pour les lycéens, arrive à 13,99 euros par mois pour ces mêmes clients. Les deux donnent droit, sur demande, à un pack Protection Enfant adapté à l'âge, qui comprend le contrôle parental, la géolocalisation du téléphone, l'aide à l'installation et l'alerte anti-cyberharcèlement sur WhatsApp et les réseaux sociaux. Cette alerte, assurée par SafeBear, est offerte un an d'ailleurs. Ensuite, il faudra décider de la garder, pour 10 euros par mois ou 48 euros par an, au choix.

articles.title: Horizon Zero Dawn Remastered sur PS5 tombe à un prix difficile à ignorer
articles.text:
Horizon Zero Dawn Remastered est actuellement proposé à 18,74 € sur PS5 chez Cdiscount. Affiché 49,99 € à sa sortie, il se trouve en général entre 30 et 40 € dans le commerce.
Bienvenue dans un monde dominé par les machines
Dans un futur lointain, l’humanité a régressé à l’état de tribus, et la Terre est peuplée d’immenses machines qui ressemblent à des animaux. C’est dans ce monde qu’on suit Aloy, une jeune chasseuse rejetée par les siens, partie à la recherche de ses origines. Sorti en 2017, le jeu de Guerrilla s’est imposé comme l’une des grandes réussites de PlayStation, avec plus de 24 millions d’exemplaires vendus.
Cette version Remastered, confiée à Nixxes avec Guerrilla, offre une vraie cure de jouvence au jeu original. Végétation plus dense, visages retravaillés, nouvelles animations pour les dialogues et plus de dix heures de répliques réenregistrées, l’ensemble se rapproche beaucoup de ce qu’on a pu voir dans Horizon Forbidden West. La manette DualSense est aussi mieux exploitée, avec des gâchettes adaptatives qui donnent plus de corps au tir à l’arc. Et l’extension The Frozen Wilds est incluse.
Le bon moment pour partir à la chasse ?
Le jeu était sorti à 49,99 € fin octobre 2024. À 18,74 €, il coûte donc près de trois fois moins cher qu’à son lancement. En comparaison, il est actuellement affiché à 33,08 € chez Carrefour.
Avec un 8/10, notre test salue surtout le travail de Nixxes Software, qui donne au jeu l’allure d’une vraie production PS5. Textures, végétation, éclairages, visages, tout a été repris dans la lignée d’Horizon Forbidden West, et le mode Performance assure 60 images par seconde sans sacrifier le rendu. Le gameplay est un peu moins riche que dans la suite, mais il reste efficace, et la beauté du monde d’Aloy donne envie d’explorer chaque recoin. Si vous possédez déjà la version PS4, sachez qu’une mise à niveau vers le Remastered est proposée à 10 €.

articles.title: nginx2root: five new nginx vulnerabilities, and how Cloudflare protects origins from the worst of them
articles.text:
nginx2root: Five new nginx vulnerabilities, and how Cloudflare protects origins from the worst of them
On November 18, 2026, F5 and nginx.org disclosed ten vulnerabilities in nginx. Five of them, detailed by the Xint research team and published under the name nginx2root, are memory corruption flaws that an unauthenticated attacker can use to crash an nginx worker or, per Xint's research, run commands on the server. Xint also found a Linux kernel bug that turns that foothold into root on the host, including from inside a Docker container. Other teams found the two HTTP/2 bugs independently: F5 also credits Rapid7, Wiz Research and Ikotas Labs for CVE-2026-123007, and Metnir, Wiz Research, and Palo Alto Networks Unit 42 for CVE-2026-123633.
nginx is an HTTP web server that also serves as reverse proxy, content cache, load balancer, TCP/UDP proxy server, and mail proxy server. nginx runs a large share of the world's web servers, so this is a patch-now event. But if your nginx server is reachable only through Cloudflare's proxy, attackers cannot reach the vulnerable code paths for the most serious of these bugs, giving you protection while you update your servers.
Here is where Cloudflare stands, what that protection covers, where it stops, and how the bugs work.
The short version
- Cloudflare's edge is not affected. Much of the proxy that handles customer traffic at our edge now runs on FL2, written in Rust. We reviewed the parts still built on our heavily modified nginx fork against all five bugs before disclosure, and an update closing the related code paths finished rolling out globally before the vulnerabilities were published. The same releases fix five other nginx CVEs, including CVE-2026-118899, an infinite loop while reading a request body over TLS 1.3.
- Origins behind Cloudflare's HTTP proxy are shielded from the HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 attacks. For proxied hostnames, Cloudflare terminates every client HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 connection at our edge and opens a separate connection to your origin. The attacker's frames never reach your nginx.
- The resolver and mail proxy vulnerabilities depend on specific configuration. Many configurations of nginx will not be vulnerable, but the safest way to be sure is to update your install or disable features.
- You should still patch. Update to nginx 1.30.7 or 1.31.9 (or your vendor's fixed build) and restart. Some configurations, covered below, are not protected by the proxy.
What was disclosed
nginx2root is five independent bugs. Each one works on its own and each one needs a different configuration.
| CVE | Bug class | Affected configuration | First affected release | 
| CVE-2026-123007 | Integer overflow leading to out-of-bounds heap read/write | HTTP/2 enabled | 1.9.5 (2015) | 
| CVE-2026-123633 | Use-after-free | HTTP/2 with proxy_pass to a backend, worker low on worker_connections | 1.19.7 | 
| CVE-2026-121810 | Use-after-free | HTTP/3 (QUIC) with proxy_pass to a backend | 1.25.0 | 
| CVE-2026-123634 | Use-after-free | resolver + proxy_pass with variables + a subrequest (mirror or SSI) | 0.6.18 | 
| CVE-2026-113425 | Use-after-free | Mail proxy with proxy on and auth_http | 0.5.33 | 
F5 rates each one High (CVSS 3.1: 8.1) and Critical (CVSS 4.0: 9.2), and notes that code execution requires disabling or bypassing ASLR (Address Space Layout Randomization). For CVE-2026-123007, Xint's write-up shows how it leaked memory addresses to do exactly that.
CVE-2026-123007 is the one to worry about most. It only needs HTTP/2 turned on, which is commonly enabled on TLS deployments, and it has been in every nginx release since HTTP/2 support shipped in 1.9.5. Xint ran the exploit over the public Internet against servers on AWS, GCP and Azure. Xint searched Shodan on November 10, before the disclosure, and found 56.7 million hosts matching product:nginx. Of the 11.94 million that reported a version, 98.9% fell in the affected range. As of November 19, Censys's nginx2root exposure tracker counts about 8.8 million services running a potentially affected version with HTTP/2 enabled. Version strings don't prove a host is vulnerable, since distributions backport fixes, but the exposure is large.
The same nginx releases also fix five other bugs. The most serious, CVE-2026-118899, is an infinite loop when reading a request body over TLS 1.3 that lets an unauthenticated attacker stall a worker, in nginx 1.13.0 and later.
The Linux kernel bug is the sixth part of nginx2root. Xint found a use-after-free in the kernel's SCTP send path, present since Linux 4.15 (2018): while a send operation waits, its SCTP association can be moved to another socket, and the waiting send can then free it. An attacker who already runs code as the nginx worker can use it to gain root on the host, and Xint did this from an nginx running inside a Docker container. Many distributions load the SCTP module automatically the first time a program opens an SCTP socket, so hosts that never use SCTP can still be exposed. As of November 18, no kernel fix was available and Xint was withholding the details until there is one.
As of November 19, none of the five nginx2root CVEs is in CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog, and we have not seen reports of exploitation in the wild. Xint and Wiz Research have not released their exploits. Rapid7 has published a proof of concept, which it describes as suitable only for demonstrating the attack against a freshly started local container. Fake 'exploits' are also circulating on GitHub.
Why Cloudflare's proxy protects your origin
nginx2root's most dangerous bugs live in how nginx parses and manages HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 connections. To trigger them, an attacker has to send a carefully ordered stream of protocol frames directly to the nginx process: billions of WINDOW_UPDATE frames, a SETTINGS frame that holds response data back, PING frames that fill the send buffers, partial HEADERS frames, RST_STREAM at exactly the right moment.
When your DNS record is proxied through Cloudflare, that connection ends at our edge.
Cloudflare reads the client's HTTP request, applies your security and caching rules, and then makes its own request to your origin over a connection Cloudflare controls. The flow-control frames, pings, settings, and stream resets that the attacker sends are consumed by our edge. They are not forwarded. Your nginx only ever sees the requests Cloudflare chooses to send, framed the way Cloudflare frames them. This also holds when Cloudflare connects to your origin over HTTP/2: Cloudflare runs its own flow control on that connection and sends WINDOW_UPDATE and RST_STREAM frames only as its own traffic needs, so a client can't make it relay the billions of WINDOW_UPDATE frames the attack requires.
Rapid7 makes the same point in its analysis of CVE-2026-123007: if the HTTP/2 connection is proxied, the attacker's frames "will likely not be retransmitted" in a way that allows exploitation. This breaks each of the HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 attacks.
| CVE | What the attacker needs | Behind Cloudflare's HTTP proxy | 
| CVE-2026-123007 | Direct control over HTTP/2 WINDOW_UPDATE, SETTINGS, PING and RST_STREAM on one connection to nginx | Protected. Control frames terminate at Cloudflare's edge. | 
| CVE-2026-123633 | The first part of a HEADERS frame on a direct HTTP/2 connection, plus the ability to exhaust nginx connection slots and reset the TCP connection | Protected. The client's HTTP/2 connection terminates at Cloudflare. | 
| CVE-2026-121810 | A direct QUIC/HTTP/3 connection to nginx | Protected. HTTP/3 terminates at Cloudflare's edge. We do not communicate to origins over HTTP/3 | 
| CVE-2026-123634 | A request and its mirror or SSI subrequest waiting on the same DNS lookup, and the main request ending while the answer is processed. In Xint's exploit, nginx's resolver had to reach the attacker's DNS server. | Not fully protected. Depends on how your config builds proxy_pass. Patch. | 
| CVE-2026-113425 | A direct IMAP/POP3/SMTP connection to the nginx mail proxy | Not protected. Cloudflare's HTTP proxy does not carry mail traffic. | 
There is one condition to be protected by Cloudflare here: your origin must not be reachable directly. If an attacker can find your origin's IP and connect to it directly (TCP 443 or 80 for HTTP/2, UDP 443 for HTTP/3, or the mail ports), Cloudflare isn't in the path and the protection doesn't apply. You should ensure that your origin servers can only be accessed through Cloudflare’s proxies, using one of the following approaches:
- Cloudflare Tunnel. Your origin makes an outbound-only connection to Cloudflare and exposes no inbound ports.
- Firewall to Cloudflare IP ranges. Accept inbound HTTP/HTTPS only from Cloudflare's published IP ranges. This must be done using an IP firewall, not based on configuration in your nginx server.
- Authenticated Origin Pulls (mTLS). Your origin rejects any TLS connection that doesn't present Cloudflare's client certificate.
Xint's own exposure check makes the same point: "If a CDN or reverse proxy sits in front of nginx, the test only reaches the proxy, so also run it directly against the nginx server."
Where the protection does not apply
There are several situations in which Cloudflare’s HTTP proxy does not provide protection.
- Spectrum TCP/UDP applications. For these configurations, traffic from the Internet is passed unmodified through to your origin. If your origin is running nginx, patch or disable the affected features.
- nginx mail proxy. Cloudflare's HTTP proxy does not carry IMAP, POP3 or SMTP. Restrict mail listeners to trusted networks until patched.
- CVE-2026-123634 (resolver). This depends on how your configuration builds the proxy_pass target from the request, combined with a carefully timed cancellation of an HTTP request. Passing your traffic through Cloudflare’s proxy makes it harder to exploit this, but does not provide full protection. Update regardless.
- DNS-only (grey-cloud), internal or non-proxied nginx. Any nginx server an attacker can reach without going through Cloudflare, including internal services behind a compromised host, needs to be patched.
Cloudflare’s WAF rules are not relevant to these vulnerabilities. These are protocol-level bugs. Because Cloudflare’s proxy handles parsing the HTTP protocol messages, and creates new messages to fetch information from origin servers, origins behind Cloudflare's HTTP proxy are protected from the HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 bugs without needing a rule. We have therefore not released a managed rule. The protection comes from connection termination, not from pattern matching.
What to do now
- Find every nginx server. Include nginx Plus, distribution packages, container images and appliances. Run nginx -V and nginx -T on each and note HTTP/2, HTTP/3/QUIC listeners, proxy_pass with variables plus SSI or mirror, and any mail block.
- Patch. Update nginx Open Source to 1.30.7 or 1.31.9, nginx Plus to 37.0.8.1 or 37.3.0.1, or your distribution's fixed package. F5 lists nginx Plus R34 to R36 as affected with no fixed build, so move those to a fixed 37.x release. Then restart nginx or complete a binary upgrade. A config reload does not replace the running binary.
- Check backport versions carefully. Distributions often patch without changing the version nginx -v reports. Compare the full package version against your distribution's advisory.
- Make sure your origin is only reachable through Cloudflare. Use Tunnel, IP allowlisting or Authenticated Origin Pulls.
- If you can't patch yet, disable what you don't need. http2 off; (nginx 1.25.1 and later; on older versions, remove http2 from the listen directive) blocks CVE-2026-123007 and CVE-2026-123633. Removing QUIC listeners and setting http3 off; blocks CVE-2026-121810. Point proxy_pass at fixed upstream groups for CVE-2026-123634. Don't rely on mirror_request_body alone: Xint's tested setup set it to off, and the default on stopped that exploit, but SSI and other subrequests can still reach the bug. Bind mail listeners to trusted networks for CVE-2026-113425. Restart so old connections close.
- Block SCTP if you don't use it. Add install sctp /bin/false to a file in /etc/modprobe.d/ to stop the kernel module from loading. This doesn't unload an already-loaded module or disable SCTP built into the kernel. When your distribution ships a kernel update for the SCTP bug, install it and reboot. Blocking the module is a stopgap until then.
The Cloudflare Radar Zero Wire entry for nginx2root has the full checklist, a prompt you can give an agent to run a read-only assessment of your fleet, and links to every vendor advisory.
Technical deep dive
Let’s dig into the details of the five bugs by looking through the code. We’re looking at nginx 1.31.8 (commit 140aa94) which was the most recent code published before the fixes, and comparing this to the fixes in 1.31.9 (which were also included in release 1.30.7 on the stable branch).
A note on methodology: we based our analysis on the public advisories, and to verify our reading of the code, we built the public 1.31.8 and 1.31.9 releases with AddressSanitizer and ran tests for four of the five bugs (flow control, HTTP/2 use-after-free, resolver and mail proxy). Each one faults on 1.31.8 and runs clean on 1.31.9. We did not reproduce the HTTP/3 bug; that section is based on the fix commit and the published analysis.
One pattern, in four places
Four of the five bugs are use-after-free bugs. This is a common issue with programs that manually manage memory without language support: one part of the code frees an object that another part is still using.
nginx is event driven. A handler runs, calls other code, and that code returns to the handler. Three of the bugs occur when the called code tears down the connection or request the handler is working on. In the fourth, a second connection still holds a pointer to the object.
- CVE-2026-123633 and CVE-2026-121810. A request needs a connection slot to reach its upstream. nginx is low on slots, so it closes an idle connection to free one. The connection it chooses is the one the request belongs to.
- CVE-2026-123634. A resolver callback ends a request. Cleanup of that request frees a second resolver context that the resolver is about to call next.
- CVE-2026-113425. When a write to a mail client fails, the client connection is closed while the connection to the authentication service still points at its session.
F5 rates all four as potential code execution if address space layout randomization (ASLR) is disabled or bypassed, and in its tests Xint reports code execution with the privileges of the nginx worker.
The fifth bug, CVE-2026-123007, is of a different kind: an accounting error that becomes a length error.
CVE-2026-123007: two flow-control pieces that each look correct
HTTP/2 flow control limits the amount of response data a server may send. nginx tracks a send window for each stream and one for the connection, h2c->send_window. The client enlarges a window with a WINDOW_UPDATE frame, and the protocol caps every window at 2^31 − 1.
nginx enforces that cap when a WINDOW_UPDATE arrives (ngx_http_v2_state_window_update()):
if (window > NGX_HTTP_V2_MAX_WINDOW - h2c->send_window) {
   /* logs "client violated connection flow control" */
   return ngx_http_v2_connection_error(h2c, NGX_HTTP_V2_FLOW_CTRL_ERROR);
}
On its own, this check is correct. But the connection window also grows in a second place. When nginx queues DATA frames for a stream, it subtracts their length from the window. If the stream is canceled before those frames go out, ngx_http_v2_filter_cleanup() takes them off the queue and returns the credit:
h2c->send_window += window;
Nothing caps this line. As the fix commit describes, if the client enlarges the connection window after the frames are queued and before the stream is terminated, the refund pushes the window past 2^31 − 1.
From that point the first check no longer works. h2c->send_window is an unsigned size_t, so NGX_HTTP_V2_MAX_WINDOW - h2c->send_window wraps around to a very large number and every subsequent WINDOW_UPDATE is accepted. The client can then raise the window as far as it wants.
The window is unsigned, but the code that sizes DATA frames compares it as a signed value (ngx_http_v2_send_chain()):
if (limit == 0 || limit > (off_t) h2c->send_window) {
   limit = h2c->send_window;
}
...
if ((off_t) frame_size > limit) {
   frame_size = (size_t) limit;
}
After the window passes 2^63, it is negative as an off_t. The frame size becomes the window value itself, a number between 2^63 and 2^64, and nginx builds a buffer whose last pointer lies before its pos pointer.
Over TLS, that buffer reaches a memcpy() in ngx_ssl_send_chain() with that length. Our TLS test stops at that point under AddressSanitizer. Xint's write-up explains how, with the window pushed close to 2^64, this turns into a controlled out-of-bounds write and an address leak, and Xint, Rapid7, and Wiz each report code execution from it. This post goes no further than the fault.
Over cleartext HTTP/2, the same invalid buffer follows a different output path. Our cleartext test also faults under AddressSanitizer on 1.31.8 and runs clean on 1.31.9. The public write-ups address the TLS case.
How much traffic the known attacks require
The biggest step a WINDOW_UPDATE can take is 2^31 − 1, and a WINDOW_UPDATE frame is 13 bytes. Bringing a 64-bit window near its top therefore requires about 2^33 frames: roughly 8.6 billion frames, or about 112 GB (104 GiB).
Rapid7, which published a proof of concept, gives the same figure and adds that nginx limits control-frame traffic relative to other traffic on the connection, so its run also sends about 15 GiB of other request traffic. Its total comes to approximately 128 GB of HTTP/2 data: about two minutes on a 10 Gbit/s link and about seventeen minutes at 1 Gbit/s. Rapid7 estimates the WINDOW_UPDATE traffic needed to reach 2^63 at about 2^32 frames, or 52 GiB, half of the 104 GiB figure. It also notes that these figures describe its route and are not a proven minimum.
For defenders, this is the useful fact about the bug. At this volume, the known attacks are hard to hide: nginx receives tens of gigabytes from a single client over one long-lived connection and sends little back, much more than the requests in the access log account for.
Why it was difficult to find
The refund line has existed in nginx since HTTP/2 support arrived in 1.9.5 in 2015. Two things made it difficult to notice.
First, each piece looks correct on its own. The check on WINDOW_UPDATE is the right check. The refund is the right refund. The bug is that the check relies on an assumption the refund does not preserve.
Second, testing that waits for a crash is very unlikely to reach it, because a crash requires tens of gigabytes of input. The bad state itself can be reached with very little traffic: Censys published a cleartext test that reaches what it calls the corrupted flow-control state with a 5.69 MB capture. A test that asserts "the send window never exceeds its protocol maximum" after every frame would flag the bad state as soon as a test sequence got there. A test that waits for memory corruption would not.
The fix
The fix (6 lines added) introduces a counter, h2c->send_queued, for DATA that is queued but not yet sent. The WINDOW_UPDATE check now includes those bytes in the window:
if (window > NGX_HTTP_V2_MAX_WINDOW - h2c->send_window - h2c->send_queued) {
From the client's perspective, queued frames still count toward the window, so the client can no longer refill credit that nginx is about to refund. On a fixed version the attempt is rejected with a flow-control error.
CVE-2026-123633: where two protections interact
An nginx worker has a fixed number of connection slots (worker_connections), which the client and upstream connections share. Since 1.19.2, when free slots run low (1/16 of the total or fewer), ngx_get_connection() calls ngx_drain_connections(), which closes connections marked "reusable": connections with nothing in progress, such as idle keep-alive connections.
This works only if a reusable connection truly has nothing in progress. For HTTP/2 that was not always the case. Two commits landed on the same day in February 2021 and were released together in 1.19.7:
- "HTTP/2: fixed reusing connections with active requests" fixed a case in which a cleartext HTTP/2 connection could remain reusable while it had a request.
- "HTTP/2: reuse of connections with incomplete frames" registered a connection as reusable while it waits for the remainder of a partly received frame, so that a client cannot hold slots with partial frames.
The second change is the relevant one here. As the fix commit explains, if the remainder of that frame is a HEADERS frame, a stream is created, but the reusable status was not reset until the connection next went idle. The connection then has a request and remains in the reusable queue.
If that request is proxied, nginx requests a slot for the upstream connection. If slots are short, the drain runs inside that call and can choose this same connection. The drain instructs the connection to close and nginx attempts to send GOAWAY. If that send fails, nginx frees the connection and every stream on it. Control then goes back to the upstream code, which continues to use the request it was called for.
Each change made sense on its own. The interaction between them was subtle and stayed unnoticed until this year. F5's advisory credits Albert Ebb of Metnir, Nir Ohfeld at Wiz Research, Xint.io and memN0ps of Palo Alto Networks Unit 42; nginx.org's changelog credits Albert of Vexera AI.
The fix
Two lines added: ngx_http_v2_create_stream() now calls ngx_reusable_connection(h2c->connection, 0). A connection that has a stream is never reusable, regardless of the state it was in before.
CVE-2026-121810: the same idea, in QUIC
According to the fix commit and Xint's analysis, the HTTP/3 bug reaches the same result by a different route.
In nginx's QUIC code, each QUIC connection uses one connection slot and each stream uses another. A QUIC connection may be drained only when every stream remaining in its tree can be cancelled, and nginx determines this by walking the connection's tree of streams.
ngx_quic_create_stream() removes the QUIC connection from the reusable queue and then requests a slot for the new stream. Before the fix, the new stream was added to the tree only after that. If the slot request triggered a drain that closed another, idle stream of the same QUIC connection, the code handling the closed stream walked the tree, did not find the stream being created, concluded the connection was idle, and made it reusable again. A later drain, for example when the new request connects to its upstream, could then close the QUIC connection while that request was running.
F5's advisory states that exploitation "also depends on conditions beyond the attacker's control". Xint writes that the bug "is triggered by a slightly different mechanism" from the HTTP/2 one.
The fix
Four lines added: the stream goes into the tree before the slot is requested, and is taken out again on the error paths.
CVE-2026-123634: freeing the next item of a list during the walk
When proxy_pass contains a variable, nginx resolves the host name while handling the request. If a lookup for the same name is already in progress, the new request waits on the same resolver node. When the answer arrives, nginx detaches the list of waiting contexts and calls each in turn:
next = rn->waiting;
rn->waiting = NULL;
while (next) {
   ctx = next;
   ...
   next = ctx->next;
   ctx->handler(ctx);
}
The loop stores next before the handler call, so a handler may free its own context. The trouble starts when a handler frees a different context in the same list. This happens when two contexts belong to one request, as with a request and its mirror subrequest resolving the same name (the case Xint tested; F5 also lists SSI subrequests). If the first handler ends the request, the request's cleanup calls ngx_resolve_name_done() for the second context. That function searches the node's waiting list for the context, does not find it because the list has been detached, and frees the context regardless. The loop then advances to the freed context. 
Usually nginx logs this. On vulnerable versions, when the search fails, it writes
could not cancel <name> resolving
to the error log at alert level. This line is worth searching for. It is not proof either way: the fix commit notes that one variant, while following a CNAME, produced no alert.
The fix
A context cancelled while it sits in a detached list is no longer freed immediately. Its handler is swapped for one that frees it when the loop gets to it (31 lines added). The fix also downgrades the alert to a debug message, so the line above shows up at alert level only on unpatched versions.
CVE-2026-113425: two connections, one session
With auth_http, the mail proxy asks an HTTP service to verify each login. During the wait, it holds two connections for one session: the client connection and the connection to the authentication service. The second points at the session and uses the memory pool of the client connection.
Before the fix, the reply the protocol handler had prepared for the client remained queued while the authentication request was in progress, and the client's write handler was still ngx_mail_send(). If that handler ran and the write failed because the client had reset the connection, it closed the client connection and destroyed the session. The authentication connection still pointed at the session, and the next event on that connection used freed memory.
Xint describes two conditions for this: the client's write event must already be registered (for example, because the client stopped reading replies), and the login command and the reset must be handled in the same pass of the event loop. Valid credentials are not needed, because this happens before the login is checked.
The fix
Two added lines discard the queued reply when the authentication request begins. The same release contains three further commits that block client writes while the proxy waits for the authentication response, while it connects to the upstream and reads its greeting, and while it resolves an SMTP client's address and name.
What the fixes share
The five fixes each involve minor corrections to the code. They add between 2 and 31 lines each, and the mail proxy fix came with three further commits. There is no design change needed. Each fix restores an invariant that the rest of the code already depended on:
- a send window never goes above the protocol maximum
- a connection with a request in progress is never reusable
- an object that other code is about to use is not freed out from under it
In every case, one code path failed to keep a rule that the rest of the code relied on, and the fix makes that path keep it. As code is modified over time, it is very easy for these kinds of rules to become broken.
What to watch for
Attempts to exploit this will typically trigger some characteristic log messages. Three of these messages (the two at info and the one at warn) fall below nginx's default error_log level of error and appear only if a lower level is set. The alert messages are logged by default.
| Bug | Log messages or other signals | 
| CVE-2026-123007 | A single long-lived HTTP/2 connection on which nginx receives tens of gigabytes from a client and sends little back, much more than its logged requests account for. On fixed versions a rejected attempt logs client violated connection flow control: received WINDOW_UPDATE frame with window increment ... not allowed for window ... (level info; older versions have the same message for ordinary violations). http2 flood detected (level info) on such a connection can be a failed attempt, but nginx also logs that message for several other limits. | 
| CVE-2026-123633, CVE-2026-121810 | worker process <pid> exited on signal 11 (level alert) on servers that accept HTTP/2 or HTTP/3 and proxy to an upstream, along with worker_connections are not enough, reusing connections (level warn). A use-after-free does not always crash. | 
| CVE-2026-123634 | could not cancel <name> resolving (level alert, unpatched versions only). The absence of this message does not rule the bug out. | 
| CVE-2026-113425 | Worker crashes in a mail proxy using auth_http, with client connections reset during login. | 
| All five | Unexpected programs launched by an nginx worker process, for example from an auditd rule on execve for the worker's user. Xint recommends this check, and it is the strongest sign of a successful attack. | 
Timeline
| Date (UTC) | Event | 
| Oct 11, 2026 | Xint discovers the vulnerabilities | 
| Oct 16, 2026 | Reported to F5 via HackerOne | 
| Oct 27, 2026 | Reports delivered to the nginx development team | 
| Nov 10, 2026 | Xint completes patch validation | 
| Nov 18, 2026 | Public disclosure; nginx 1.30.7 and 1.31.9 released | 
The bugs will keep coming
CVE-2026-123007 sat in nginx for more than ten years. The SCTP bug has been in the Linux kernel since 2018. Xint says one of its researchers found CVE-2026-123007 by hand and an automated Xint scan found the other four nginx bugs. Several other teams found the two HTTP/2 bugs independently. Meanwhile, nginx's advisory list has gone from two entries in 2025 to 36 so far this year. AI-assisted research is finding bugs in heavily reviewed code faster than before, and more disclosures like this one are coming.
That's a large part of why it's worth putting Cloudflare in front of your origin. A protocol bug in your web server becomes much less of a risk when the attacker can't speak that protocol to your server directly. Our edge is not affected, and the HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 attacks against your nginx end at our network. Patch anyway, lock down your origin so Cloudflare is the only way in, and use the Radar Zero Wire page to check your fleet.

articles.title: Can AI Make Its Own Manufacturing Decisions?
articles.text:
AI can optimize processes and find defects, but autonomous decisions require better data and strict process controls.
Key Takeaways:
Semiconductor manufacturing has always depended on engineers making decisions involving complex interactions among process parameters. An etch recipe, for example, may involve combinations of RF power, pressure, gas chemistry, temperature, and timing, each affecting multiple process characteristics. Changing one parameter might improve critical dimension control while creating problems elsewhere. But as devices and manufacturing processes become more complicated, the growing number of variables involved makes those decisions increasingly difficult.
AI-driven manufacturing offers a way to manage some of that complexity, from finding better process conditions to identifying defects and responding to problems on the production line. But how much production responsibility engineers are willing to give those systems remains an open question, and one that drew considerable attention at SEMICON West 2026.
“No matter how good we are as engineers, no matter how disciplined and objective we are, we tend to approach these difficult problems with historical biases,” said David Fried, chief AI officer and corporate vice president of Semiverse Solutions at Lam Research during a conference panel. “A process engineer might look at a set of data and say, ‘I need to move into a lower-pressure, higher-power regime because that’s how we solved this problem 10 years ago.’ But with this massive parameter space, AI can point us in a different direction, into an operating region we might never have considered because we couldn’t see those relationships in the data before.”
Finding a process that keeps working
Finding an unfamiliar operating condition is useful, but determining whether it will hold up in production is another matter. Two recipes may produce similar results during development, yet respond quite differently to changes in incoming materials or equipment conditions. AI can help engineers identify those differences before committing to a particular process.
“It’s not just a question of delivering to a particular performance point. It’s also a question of how stable that particular performance point is, how robust it is,” said Vikas Sharma, senior principal engineer and senior director of pathfinding for Intel Foundry R&D, in a recent presentation. “Minor perturbations in the incoming material or at the tool can lead to a significant drop in performance.”
The scale of the optimization problem helps explain why AI-driven manufacturing is attracting so much interest. Fried described a current Lam Research etcher with a potential recipe space on the order of 10²³ combinations. At Intel, Sharma discussed a process involving 350 parameters and approximately 10⁷⁰⁰ theoretical combinations.
According to Sharma, engineers working with equipment suppliers spent about a year developing a minimally acceptable recipe for that particular tool and process layer, followed by an extended effort to improve it with limited success. After introducing AI-assisted optimization, they began finding better results within a few months, eventually identifying multiple solutions that improved on the original baseline.
The challenge was determining which solutions were worth pursuing. Sharma noted that AI could identify thousands of candidates, but evaluating them still required expensive silicon experiments. Engineers also had to account for nonlinear relationships among parameters, which could change considerably across different operating regions.
“AI is not a magic wand. You can’t use the same AI solution for every problem,” Fried said. “Figuring out whether you’re using full physical simulation, surrogate models, machine learning, deep learning, LLM-based AI, or agentic AI, which of these solutions you’re building in which form to solve which problem and address which workflow, that’s more of what we’re spending our time on than actually building it or implementing it.”
The different approaches serve different purposes, from exploring process conditions to coordinating engineering workflows. Combining them may allow engineers to investigate more possibilities, but it also raises questions about how the results should be validated and whether the assumptions used in one model remain appropriate when its recommendations are passed to another.
When the factory acts on what it sees
Inspection is one of the more established applications of AI in manufacturing, particularly in advanced packaging, where finer pitches and more complicated structures have increased the number of connections that must be examined. Some packages can contain hundreds of thousands of interconnects, each presenting a potential failure point.
Automated optical inspection and X-ray systems collect extensive information about those structures. Machine learning can identify variations that might be difficult to distinguish visually, but manufacturers still need to determine which differences indicate actual defects.
“When we look at X-rays, everybody just sees all shades of gray, but AI can see a thousand shades of gray,” said Ingu Yin Chang, executive vice president at ASE Group. “But the AI only knows if this shade of gray equates to a problem once we say, ‘Hey, this equates to a problem.’ So, you’ve got to have the physical data that says, ‘Okay, that is a problem.’ Then, in the future, they can scan for that shade of gray and that location.”
Once manufacturers determine which image characteristics correspond to actual defects, AI-enabled inspection systems can flag abnormalities during production and trigger predefined equipment responses. At ASE, systems can recognize known abnormalities and trigger equipment responses before additional assemblies are affected.
“We have figured out how to do a lot of automation and use AI to help us identify potential issues, based on the issues that we physically learned through traditional manufacturing methods,” Chang said. “We will know when a wire bond is not bonded correctly, and the machine will immediately stop. There’s constant AI oversight to ask, ‘Are we doing everything correctly? Are we seeing it as we planned to see it?’”
Stopping equipment when a defect is detected can prevent additional losses, but it doesn’t necessarily mean AI is controlling the process independently. The inspection system may identify an abnormal condition while a conventional controller executes a predefined response. Allowing AI to select new bonding parameters and resume production would require considerably more confidence in its decisions.
ASE’s product diversity makes that challenge more difficult. Chang noted that hundreds of package types can pass through the same production lines with different materials, structures, and process sensitivities. A model would have to recognize which product is being manufactured and whether the conditions used during training remain applicable.
An inspection system might correctly identify a defective bond, but changing the process to prevent another failure requires knowing what caused it and whether an adjustment will create problems elsewhere. Manufacturers need considerably more information before allowing AI to make those decisions independently, and much of what’s needed remains difficult to obtain.
Proving the model is right
One of the first obstacles to AI-driven manufacturing is establishing whether an AI recommendation accurately represents the physical process. A model can identify statistical relationships among manufacturing parameters without necessarily capturing the physical mechanisms behind them. That may be sufficient for finding promising operating conditions, but it becomes a greater concern when the system is expected to make decisions that affect production.
Sharma’s Intel example illustrates the problem. Pressure and temperature might dominate the response in one operating region, while voltage or gas flow could become more important elsewhere. A model trained on measurements from one region cannot assume those relationships will hold across another.
“The fundamental principle is that surrogate models are reliable when interpolating within the region represented by their training data and less reliable when extrapolating beyond it,” said Eric Guichard, senior vice president and general manager of AI manufacturing in Silvaco’s TCAD business unit.
Finding an unfamiliar operating region may be exactly what makes AI useful, but it also means engineers have less experimental evidence against which to check its predictions. AI can identify thousands of candidate solutions, leaving engineers to determine which ones justify expensive silicon experiments. Before those recommendations can influence production, manufacturers need to establish where the predictions are reliable and where additional measurements are necessary.
Similar limitations appear in advanced packaging inspection, where a model may distinguish subtle differences in X-ray images without sufficient physical evidence to determine which indicate actual defects. A confident prediction from incomplete information becomes particularly risky when AI is authorized to act on it. An inappropriate adjustment could affect material that continues through several manufacturing steps before the problem is discovered.
When the necessary data doesn’t exist
Semiconductor manufacturers have collected process and equipment data for decades, but much of it remains distributed among separate systems. Equipment logs, inspection records, and engineering databases may contain information about the same product without being connected in ways that make the relationships easy to analyze.
“The growing data challenge was there for us prior to AI,” Fried said. “Five to ten years ago, we really started rolling up our sleeves and building integrated data frameworks for our companies. Those of us who invested earlier and more heavily in building those data frameworks are reaping the benefits of AI now more quickly. Maybe AI has turbocharged this problem, but we’ve had this massive, growing, and complex interwoven web of data for quite some time now.”
Connecting existing data is difficult enough, but manufacturers also face situations where the information needed for a prediction was never measured or isn’t available from the company that generated it. Advanced packaging makes this especially challenging because manufacturing information may originate with several suppliers. A foundry provides the die, another company produces the substrate, and an OSAT performs assembly and test, often without everyone having access to the same manufacturing history.
Some of the most difficult gaps involve physical properties that change during manufacturing. Substrate warpage, thermal stress, and material behavior can affect subsequent operations, particularly as assemblies move through repeated thermal cycles. Those changes aren’t always captured in the available measurements, and a model relying on nominal material properties may miss them entirely.
Manufacturers also need to preserve the assumptions behind the data they exchange. A model developed for one operating range may produce results that appear reasonable when used elsewhere, even though the original calibration no longer applies.
“If the training range, calibration source, or approved use is not carried with the model, it may be good enough for early exploration but not safe for design closure,” said Kenneth Larsen, senior director of product management at Synopsys. “The missing information is not just more data; it is the context that tells the next tool or team how the data should be used.”
As AI systems begin coordinating decisions across multiple process steps, those gaps become more consequential. A recommendation based on one operation may overlook conditions affecting the next, particularly when the model lacks information about the product’s actual physical state. Additional metrology and characterization may help close some of those gaps, but engineers still have to establish whether the available information is sufficient to act on a recommendation.
Who decides what AI can do?
Even with reliable models and better data, manufacturers still have to determine which decisions should be delegated to AI. Existing equipment automation generally operates within established procedures and control limits, but an AI agent capable of evaluating conditions and selecting corrective actions raises questions about who authorizes those decisions and what happens when something goes wrong.
An agent investigating a process problem might need to retrieve inspection results, examine equipment histories, and evaluate possible corrective actions using several engineering tools. Each activity may involve different access permissions, particularly when the information comes from separate facilities or manufacturing partners. Access to those resources also needs to be distinguished from the authority to initiate changes.
“There is a question of data access and data consolidation, and there is also a question of data interpretation,” Sharma said. “But the problem that AI has brought forth as a novel thing, which was not as big an issue before, is governance. When agents are working, how do you ensure that the appropriate privileges for the right data are available to the right agent and accessible to the right person?”
An agent might be authorized to examine process records and recommend an adjustment without having permission to modify a recipe or restart equipment. Those restrictions become harder to enforce when agents coordinate activities across multiple systems, particularly if one tool can initiate actions through another. Access to one system cannot automatically confer authority over every subsequent operation.
Even an authorized adjustment may carry risks. Changing bonding force or temperature, for example, might correct an immediate defect while affecting adjacent connections or downstream reliability. Engineers would have to establish which adjustments can be made within qualified operating ranges, when approval is required, and how the system should respond if a proposed correction falls outside its validated capabilities.
If an AI-directed correction produces an unexpected result, equipment may need to stop while affected material is held for investigation. Manufacturers would also need to establish whether the system should attempt another correction, return control to an engineer, or prevent subsequent operations from proceeding. Those decisions have to be defined before autonomous adjustments are permitted.
Future agentic architectures will likely rely on agents reviewing and verifying one another’s work. That could provide another level of oversight, although the interactions themselves would need to be controlled. Agents relying on the same incomplete information might reinforce one another’s mistakes, and their collective actions could have consequences that none of the individual systems anticipated.
Recent research into agentic AI has demonstrated cases in which systems pursued assigned objectives through actions their operators never intended, including circumventing restrictions or concealing information. [1, 2] Although the research includes controlled experimental scenarios and incidents involving coding agents, it raises questions about how multiple agents might behave when working together.
In manufacturing, a series of individually permitted adjustments could collectively move a process beyond its qualified operating conditions, even if no single action violated its assigned limits. Preventing that would require controls over the combined effects of agent decisions, along with independent verification that the resulting process remains within acceptable limits.
Manufacturing traceability adds another requirement. Engineers investigating a later failure must be able to reconstruct what an agent observed, which alternatives it evaluated, why it selected a particular action, and what material was affected. Those records would need to connect the model’s decisions with equipment settings and manufacturing history.
The amount of authority manufacturers can safely delegate will depend on how reliably AI can operate within those boundaries. A system may be capable of choosing a correction, but it also needs to recognize when the available information is insufficient or when the consequences of an adjustment cannot be predicted with enough confidence.
Maintaining those limits becomes even more complicated when AI models are updated with new production data, potentially changing their behavior after the original operating boundaries have been established.
Qualifying a system that keeps learning
A semiconductor fab may process thousands of wafers between updates to a particular AI model. During that time, equipment conditions change, new material arrives, and engineers collect information that could improve the models’ predictions. Incorporating those results more quickly would be valuable, but manufacturers also need to know whether an updated model will behave as reliably as the one it replaces.
“We are far, far, far away from continuous learning,” Sharma said. “We do episodic learning, once every quarter a model is changed, or once every month a model is changed. But if a factory is running 10,000 wafers, we have 10,000 wafers times whatever number of weeks in between those model changes. How are we using that data in a way that rapidly applies to the learning of that particular model or the agent, or both?”
More frequent updates would introduce additional qualification work. A model might become better at recognizing one process excursion while becoming less reliable under conditions represented in its previous training data. If that model can adjust equipment settings, engineers need to establish what changed and whether the updated behavior remains within qualified limits.
Keeping track of those changes also requires more than identifying which software version was running. Engineers need to preserve the model’s training and validation history, along with the process conditions under which it was qualified. If an AI system changes its behavior during production, investigating a failure weeks later may require reconstructing the model as it existed when a particular lot was processed.
While manufacturers already have procedures for qualifying process changes and software revisions, an AI system that updates itself during production would have to fit within those controls, potentially requiring restrictions on what the model can change and independent checks before revised behavior affects equipment. Changes in manufacturing conditions would also need to be distinguished from changes introduced by retraining the model itself.
The harder question is whether manufacturers can obtain the benefits of continuous learning without having to repeat an extensive qualification process after every update. AI can already help engineers make better manufacturing decisions, but giving it responsibility for those decisions will require evidence that its behavior remains predictable and that its actions can be traced back to validated process conditions.
The path to greater autonomy
Semiconductor manufacturers have spent decades developing processes that can produce consistent results across equipment, materials, and production environments. AI introduces new possibilities for improving those processes, but it also introduces uncertainty about how decisions are made and whether the results can be reproduced. The same standards of process control, qualification, and traceability will have to apply when software begins making decisions that engineers previously handled themselves.
Greater autonomy is likely to emerge gradually, beginning with decisions that can be made within well-characterized operating limits and expanding as manufacturers gain confidence in the systems controlling them. AI may eventually identify a problem, determine an appropriate correction, and verify the result without engineering intervention. Getting there will depend on whether manufacturers can demonstrate that those decisions remain reliable as equipment conditions, materials, and the models themselves change.
