articles.title: When agents go out of bounds: How Lasso is helping enterprises secure the AI agents they build and use
articles.text:
NetApp Excellerator
View Brand Publisher
When agents go out of bounds: How Lasso is helping enterprises secure the AI agents they build and use
Enterprises are deploying AI agents faster than they can track them, and not every agent stays within the boundaries it was given. Lasso, part of NetApp Excellerator, is changing that.
An AI agent handling a refund request starts a funds transfer that no one asked for and no one approved. Would the company notice before the money moved?
This is the problem Lasso is addressing. Part of the NetApp Excellerator program, it protects the AI agents enterprises build and use, wherever they run, by learning what each agent is meant to do and checking every action it takes against that purpose.
Enterprises are putting AI agents to work faster than they can keep track of them. These agents plan their own steps, call tools and MCP servers on their own, and act without a person approving each move. That autonomy is the reason companies deploy them, and it is also how an agent ends up outside the boundaries it was given.
Two challenges make this hard to control.
The challenges of securing AI agents
Agents are everywhere, and each one has its own purpose. AI agents now run in every part of the enterprise. Developers use coding assistants on their endpoints and connect them to MCP servers and skills. Engineering teams build custom agents that run in code and in the cloud, and business teams create their own agent using low-code no-code builder platforms.
Each of these agents are set up for a different purpose, and each one works toward it autonomously. With this many agents running in this many places, it becomes difficult to track what any single agent is meant to do, and without that there is no reliable way to tell when one has gone off task or gone rogue.
Context windows are large, and attacks hide inside them
Each agent gathers the context it needs for a task by calling models, MCP servers, tools, and data sources, and everything it gathers goes into its context window. For a single task, that context can reach hundreds of thousands of tokens. A prompt injection can be one sentence hidden in an email, a web page, or a tool response, and inside a context that large it becomes the needle in the haystack. Most detection models were built for short prompts. On inputs of this size, they slow down or miss the attack, and an agent that reads the injected instruction may act on it as if it came from the user.
How Lasso does it
Lasso’s AI security platform protects the AI agents enterprises build and use, wherever they run, whether that is on an endpoint, in code or in the cloud.
It works from each agent’s intent. Its Intent Security Engine learns what each agent is meant to do from its configuration and its history, and it checks every action the agent takes against that purpose.
An action that does not fit, such as a support agent starting a funds transfer in the middle of a refund conversation, is flagged, masked or blocked inline in under 50 milliseconds, with 98.6% detection accuracy. Because the check is made against the agent’s purpose, it catches an agent that has gone off task even when nothing in the request looks like a known attack.
Lasso’s detection is built for the size of agentic inputs. It holds the same accuracy and latency as the context grows toward a million tokens, so an injection hidden deep in a long input is found before the agent acts on it.
The Lasso platform
The platform covers the full path from finding an agent to protecting it in production.
- Discovery finds every AI agent, model and component in use across SaaS tools, code, cloud and agent builder platforms.
- AI-BOM gives each agent a bill of materials listing the models, MCP servers, tools and components it depends on, so a vulnerable component can be traced to every agent that uses it.
- AI-SPM maps each agent’s connections in a visual graph that shows its blast radius, checks configurations against NIST, OWASP and MITRE, and limits use to approved models and components.
- Automated AI Red Teaming tests agents the way an attacker would. Reconnaissance of each agent shapes static, dynamic and high-agency attacks drawn from more than 300,000 payloads, and the tests run in CI/CD on every deployment.
- Runtime Protection and AI Detection and Response enforce policy per agent at the SDK, API or AI Gateway layer and detect prompt injection and other OWASP and MITRE risks. Each alert explains what happened, which agent was targeted and what to do next.
- Rogue Agent Protection uses the Intent Security Engine to detect goal misalignment, intent drift and behavioral anomalies, and it stops an agent’s action when it moves outside its purpose.
Customer success stories
A European insurance group runs Lasso on the production agents that process its internal claims, where prompt injection attempts arrive embedded inside the claims documents themselves. Lasso blocks them before the agents act. The company has since moved the application to production and is adding hundreds of new agents.
A global hospitality company uses Lasso to secure the agents it built for employee-facing logistics workflows. Intent-based guardrails enforce each agent’s behavior in real time, and the company’s internal MCP-based use cases were secured without code changes.
A global automotive manufacturer runs Lasso’s runtime protection across its customer-facing systems to stop jailbreak attempts and sensitive data exposure. A red teaming engagement on a separate chatbot found more than 15 vulnerabilities that had gone undetected, and all of them were fixed before they could be exploited.
Lasso Security is part of the NetApp Excellerator program. If you’d like to learn more about Lasso, book a demo today.

articles.title: A tiny supercurrent could unlock quantum information without destroying it
articles.text:
A tiny supercurrent could unlock quantum information without destroying it
Scientists have developed a promising new method that could read quantum information with 99.85% accuracy while barely disturbing the qubit itself.
- Date:
- November 4, 2026
- Source:
- Fundação de Amparo à Pesquisa do Estado de São Paulo
- Summary:
- Researchers have proposed a breakthrough technique for reading quantum information without destroying the delicate states that make quantum computers work. By detecting an electrical signal generated by the qubit itself, their method achieved up to 99.85% accuracy in simulations and could make future quantum computers simpler and more efficient.
- Share:
One of the biggest obstacles in quantum computing is surprisingly simple to describe: how do you read information without changing or destroying it? Unlike the bits used in ordinary computers, quantum bits, or qubits, are extraordinarily sensitive to measurement. Trying to determine their state can cause that state to collapse, potentially erasing the very information scientists want to retrieve.
Researchers have now proposed a way to overcome much of this difficulty by using an unusual electrical signal produced by the qubit itself. Their approach focuses on a special type known as an "Andreev qubit," which can generate an oscillating electric supercurrent through its own quantum behavior. By monitoring this current, scientists may be able to determine the qubit's state without directly measuring it or significantly disturbing the information it contains.
The research, supported by FAPESP, was published in Physical Review B Letters. It was led by José Carlos Egues, a full professor at the São Carlos Institute of Physics at the University of São Paulo (IFSC-USP) in Brazil, and Yugui Yao of the School of Physics at the Beijing Institute of Technology in China. If experimentally confirmed, their method could simplify quantum computing by removing the need for extra qubits used in certain measurement techniques.
Why Measuring Quantum Information Is So Difficult
Conventional computers store information in bits that have one of two values, 0 or 1. These values can be checked repeatedly without changing the information. Quantum computers work differently because their qubits can exist in superpositions, meaning they can combine the states 0 and 1 in ways that are not possible with conventional bits.
This unusual ability is central to the potential power of quantum computing. However, it also creates a major vulnerability. Quantum states can be disrupted by interactions with their surroundings, including the instruments scientists use to examine them.
"In the conventional formulation of quantum mechanics, a projective measurement causes the system to assume one of the states associated with the measured quantity. Thus, if a qubit has been prepared in a certain superposition of 0 and 1, its direct measurement tends to destroy that superposition and, consequently, the information it contained," says Egues.
To minimize this problem, physicists developed techniques known as "quantum nondemolition measurements," or QND. Many of these approaches use an additional quantum system called an ancilla. Rather than measuring the original qubit directly, researchers transfer information to the ancilla and measure that auxiliary system instead.
The term "ancilla" comes from a Latin word meaning "slave" or "servant." In modern scientific usage, it describes something that performs a supporting function. Here, the ancilla acts as an intermediary, allowing researchers to obtain information while preserving the original qubit as much as possible.
Although effective, these procedures come with practical disadvantages. Scientists must prepare the auxiliary qubits, connect them to the qubits being studied, transfer information between them, and perform repeated measurements. These additional steps require time and equipment, and the complexity becomes increasingly significant as the number of qubits grows.
"Our strategy is different. Instead of transferring the information to an auxiliary qubit, we seek to obtain it from a signal produced by the qubit under study itself," says the researcher.
A Special Quantum Bit That Produces Its Own Signal
The proposed technique relies on the unusual properties of an Andreev qubit. Its name honors Soviet physicist Alexander Andreev (1939-2023), who identified a distinctive quantum process in 1964 that occurs where normal materials meet superconductors.
Superconductors are materials that can conduct electricity without electrical resistance under appropriate conditions. At the boundaries involving these materials, special quantum states known as "Andreev states" can form. In the system studied by the researchers, these states are confined to an extremely small region between two superconducting materials.
These quantum states can represent the basic values 0 and 1, along with superpositions of those values, making them suitable for storing quantum information.
"In the system under consideration, this region is a quantum dot - that is, a nanoscale structure in which electrons are spatially confined - formed in an indium arsenide [InAs] nanowire connected to superconducting materials on both sides. It's in this environment that the states characterizing the Andreev qubit are formed," Egues explains.
The key to the new approach is an electrical phenomenon called a "supercurrent." Unlike the current flowing through ordinary electrical conductors, a supercurrent moves without resistance.
The researchers found that when the Andreev qubit exists in a superposition, the supercurrent develops a component that oscillates over time. These fluctuations arise from quantum interference between the different states making up the superposition.
Crucially, the oscillations are not random. Their behavior contains information about the qubit's underlying quantum state, potentially allowing scientists to determine what that state is without directly measuring the qubit.
"It's precisely that property that we use to read the qubit. It's that supercurrent that lies at the heart of our proposal," the researcher points out.
How a Tiny Electrical Current Reveals Quantum Information
To understand how the technique works, it helps to consider how physicists describe a qubit's state mathematically.
One common representation is the "Bloch sphere," a geometric model in which every possible pure state of a single qubit corresponds to a point on the surface of a sphere. Two angles determine the location of that point.
The first angle describes how much each of the two basic states contributes to the superposition. The second describes their relative phase, which specifies how the quantum components are aligned with one another. Together, these two measurements provide the information needed to identify the qubit's state.
According to the new research, both pieces of information can be extracted from the supercurrent. Its steady component and the size of its oscillations reveal the relative contributions of the two basic states. Meanwhile, the timing of the oscillations provides information about their phase relationship.
"Our study showed that this information is encoded in the supercurrent itself. The supercurrent has a constant component and a fluctuating component. The value of the constant component and the amplitude of the oscillation reveal the proportion of each state (0 and 1) in the superposition, and the moment when that oscillation begins reveals the phase relationship between them. Thus, by measuring how the current varies over time, it's possible to reconstruct the initial state of the qubit," Egues explains.
This means the electrical current effectively carries a signature of the quantum information stored in the system. By observing how that signature changes over time, researchers could reconstruct the qubit's original state.
A Supercurrent That Oscillates Without Voltage
Another surprising feature of the proposed system is that the electrical current can oscillate without an externally applied voltage.
Ordinarily, producing an oscillating supercurrent in this type of superconducting system requires a voltage. This familiar phenomenon is called the "AC Josephson effect."
The researchers predict something different in their Andreev qubit. Here, the current's oscillations arise naturally from the qubit's own quantum evolution. No outside voltage is required to generate them.
"Our system generates a supercurrent that varies over time like an alternating current but without voltage. It's the very evolution of the qubit's state that produces that oscillation," says Egues.
This behavior is important because it transforms quantum activity occurring on an extraordinarily small scale into a detectable electrical signal. The current provides a connection between the microscopic world of quantum states and the larger physical systems scientists can measure.
That connection is what makes the proposed reading technique possible.
Detecting Quantum States With an Extremely Sensitive Sensor
The researchers envision placing the Andreev qubit inside a closed superconducting circuit, allowing its supercurrent to circulate continuously.
Next to the circuit would sit a SQUID (superconducting quantum interference device), a highly sensitive instrument capable of detecting extremely weak magnetic fields.
Whenever an electric current flows, it produces a magnetic field. Because the supercurrent in this system oscillates, the magnetic field it generates also changes over time.
The nearby SQUID could detect these tiny magnetic variations and use them to determine the behavior of the circulating current. Since the current contains information about the qubit's quantum state, the researchers could then reconstruct that state without measuring the qubit directly.
Egues compares the arrangement to two compasses that interact through a magnetic field.
"We can think of the qubit as one compass and the SQUID as another compass. The current in the circuit produces a magnetic field, and the SQUID 'senses' that field. Since the coupling between the two is very weak, the effect of the measuring instrument on the qubit tends to be very small."
The weak interaction between the sensor and the qubit is especially important. It offers a way to gather information while minimizing the disturbance that normally accompanies quantum measurements.
Reading Quantum Information With Almost No Disturbance
In quantum physics, observing a system is not necessarily a harmless process. A measuring instrument interacts with whatever it is attempting to measure, and that interaction can change the system's behavior.
This fundamental difficulty puzzled the earliest researchers studying quantum mechanics. It remains an unavoidable feature of quantum measurements today.
The proposed technique does not eliminate this effect entirely. The SQUID still interacts with the circuit, creating a small amount of feedback that can influence the qubit. However, the team's simulations suggest that this disturbance can be reduced to a level so small that it becomes effectively negligible.
"Our method doesn't eliminate the fundamental problem of quantum measurement. But it can approach the limit of a non-destructive readout and, at the same time, avoid the use of auxiliary qubits - the ancillas - employed in other non-destructive quantum measurement protocols," Egues notes.
The approach could also remove another complication found in some existing techniques. Because researchers would not need to restore the qubit to its original state after every measurement, they could make repeated observations as the state changes.
This would allow scientists to follow the qubit's quantum evolution over time, rather than obtaining information only through separate measurement and reset cycles.
Simulations Achieve Up to 99.85% Accuracy
To investigate whether the method could work outside ideal theoretical conditions, the researchers performed computer simulations designed to account for imperfections that would arise in real experiments.
These calculations included measurement noise, as well as the small amount of feedback introduced by the detection coil. The goal was to determine whether the qubit's state could still be reconstructed accurately despite these disturbances.
The results were encouraging. Depending on the number of measurements used, the simulations produced accuracies of 99.52%, 99.81%, and 99.85%.
According to the researchers, these values fall within the standard thresholds used in quantum error correction schemes, which are designed to manage errors in quantum information processing.
The findings suggest that the method could provide highly accurate quantum state reconstruction without the additional complexity of auxiliary qubits.
However, the technique has not yet been demonstrated experimentally. The results come entirely from theoretical analysis and computer simulations, so researchers still need to establish whether a physical device can achieve comparable performance.
Could This Make Quantum Computers Simpler?
Despite the lack of experimental confirmation, the researchers emphasize that their proposal does not depend on technologies that have yet to be invented.
The calculations use realistic properties drawn from existing quantum systems, and SQUID sensors are already established tools for detecting exceptionally weak magnetic fields and electric currents.
What remains to be built is the specific arrangement of components required to implement the proposed measurement technique.
"All the numbers we used are realistic. In principle, this can be achieved. In fact, we used parameters from existing systems in our calculations. What doesn't yet exist is that geometry, that setup that we proposed," he argues.
This makes the approach different from theoretical concepts that cannot be realized until scientists develop entirely new materials or manufacturing techniques. In principle, the necessary components already exist, although assembling them into the proposed configuration and demonstrating the predicted behavior remain important challenges.
The research offers two potentially significant advances.
From the standpoint of fundamental physics, it predicts that a qubit can produce an oscillating supercurrent resembling the AC Josephson effect, but without requiring an external voltage. Instead, the oscillations emerge from the qubit's own coherent quantum evolution.
From a technological perspective, the study shows how those oscillations could serve as a measurable signature of the qubit's internal state. By analyzing the electrical current, researchers could recover quantum information while causing very little disturbance to the system.
If future experiments confirm these predictions, the method could make reading Andreev qubits substantially simpler. Eliminating auxiliary qubits and repeated resets could reduce the equipment and procedures needed to retrieve quantum information.
More fundamentally, the work points toward an intriguing possibility: information hidden in the microscopic quantum world may be accessible through an electrical current produced by the quantum system itself, offering a promising new way to observe delicate quantum states without destroying them.
Story Source:
Materials provided by Fundação de Amparo à Pesquisa do Estado de São Paulo. Original written by José Tadeu Arantes. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Xian-Peng Zhang, Chuanchang Zeng, Zhen-Biao Yang, Jose Carlos Egues, Yugui Yao. Andreev qubit readout from dynamic interference supercurrent. Physical Review B, 2026; 114 (8) DOI: 10.1103/6gkt-hghj

articles.title: Inside Helium Health’s difficult year
articles.text:
On November 4, employees at Helium Health, a Lagos-based healthtech startup, received an email from its People & Culture team thanking them for staying with the company through what the company described as “challenging moments.”
That same day, a picture of Dimeji Sofowora, its current CEO, standing beside Babajide Sanwo-Olu, the governor of Lagos State, and Olumide Balogun, Google’s director for West and East Africa, was published as they announced a ₦3.4 billion ($2.5 million) grant from Google.org, tech giant Google’s philanthropic arm. The funding will finance artificial intelligence tools that flag pregnancy risks and improve maternal care in four Nigerian states.
While Sofowora said the timing of both events was “coincidental,” together they signal a return to normalcy for the startup after a turbulent year marked by a leadership change and months of unpaid staff salaries.
“There were delays to salary payments during a period of the year,” he told TechCabal in an emailed response on Friday.
In the email sent to employees, the startup described the delays as “a difficult experience.”
“The November 4 communication was an internal email from our People & Culture team intended to recognise and thank employees for their commitment and to confirm that outstanding allowances had been settled,” Sofowora said.
For nearly a decade, Helium Health worked to digitise the operations of African hospitals. It raised at least $40 million, said it had worked with over 1,000 healthcare facilities, and lent money to hospitals.
Sofowora, who took over as chief executive in August, said the salary delays came from “temporary cash-flow timing” and that the company kept staff informed. Helium Health declined to disclose the number of affected employees or confirm how long the delays lasted. Former employees say they were owed salaries for at least six months.
Nigeria’s difficult healthtech sector
Helium Health’s troubles show the difficulties of running a healthtech startup in Nigeria’s healthtech sector, which saw 40 startups become inactive between 2020 and 2025. Founders and investors point to infrastructure challenges, the difficulty of making money servicing hospitals, and a funding slowdown as reasons why many early healthtech startups struggle to survive.
Spurred by sudden demand for digital health services after COVID-19, funding into Nigerian healthtech startups grew from about $5.5 million in 2019 to nearly $55 million in 2023, and Helium Health’s $30 million Series B round that June was more than half of 2023’s total. Healthtech funding later fell to about $18 million in 2024 and about $3 million in 2025. Helium Health has not announced an equity round since.
Helium Health pitched that round mainly as fuel for HeliumCredit, its lending arm for hospitals, clinics and pharmacies. These healthcare providers were already under pressure from inflation, which drove up the cost of running a hospital sharply in 2023.
After the 2023 currency float, health inflation rose from 20.5% in May 2023 to 24.1% a year later, according to an analysis of the National Bureau of Statistics (NBS) data, and four listed drug makers saw their cost of sales rise 88% between early 2024 and early 2025.
In 2024, the Health Care Providers Association of Nigeria said about one in five small and medium private hospitals had shut down because of operating costs. By 2024, half of all private hospitals had shut down, according to Dr Raymond Kuti, the former president of The Guild of Medical Directors, while existing ones struggled to survive due to operating costs.
Despite this contraction in Nigeria’s health care industry, HeliumCredit’s lending period grew longer, from three to six months in 2020 to 12 to 24 months by 2023, so cash came back more slowly. The currency float also added another layer.
Since its 2023 Series B round, the naira has lost about two-thirds of its value against the dollar. Every naira loan the company facilitated and recovered is worth far fewer dollars than it was when it last raised money. Sofowora did not answer questions about who funds its loans, what Helium Health earns from them, or how they have performed.
“In cases where healthcare facilities default on the payment of loans, we will offer a full cycle of monitoring of the facility and provide support to them, whether it is capacity development through education or financial training,” Olubusi, the former CEO, told TechCabal in 2023.
How Helium Health got here
Founded in 2016 by Adegoke Olubusi, Tito Ovia, and Sofowora, Helium Health launched with an electronic medical records (EMR) system to replace paper records in hospitals. That EMR ended up as the base of everything that followed; the hospital data it collected became the credit-scoring engine for its loan products in 2020.
When Helium Health raised its $10 million Series A in May 2020, it planned to expand beyond digitising hospital records and start lending to healthcare businesses in Nigeria and across Africa. Adegoke Olubusi, then CEO, told TechCabal a week after the round that hospitals struggled to grow because few were run as proper businesses, and most had never raised outside funding.
Helium Credit was meant to fix that with zero-collateral loans, and its 2023 $30 million round used the lending business as the main draw for investors in the second-largest Series B for an African healthtech company.
By 2023, HeliumCredit’s loan book had grown from $250,000 to more than $3.5 million, spread across over 200 Nigerian health facilities. It lent on behalf of financing partners, including banks. In 2023, the US International Development Finance Corporation (DFC), the American government’s development lender, disclosed a $10 million loan to Helium Health to fund new loans to healthcare businesses at a $46,000 average each.
The following year, as inflation rose and hospitals closed, the customers Helium Health earned from through software and lending were squeezed. That likely shaped the startup’s new direction as it focused more on consumer-facing tools, especially in maternal healthcare, and as more of its funding came from donors like Google.
Delayed salaries, leadership change
From January, Helium Health owed salaries, at least seven months before Olubusi stepped down, one employee said.
Three current and former employees told TechCabal that Helium Health owed them salaries, in some cases for six months. One former employee, who asked not to be named to avoid retaliation, said in June they were owed more than ₦2 million ($1,470).
“At this point, I’m unsure if or when I’ll receive the outstanding amount, as my follow-up emails are no longer being responded to,” they said in August.
“Former employees whose final entitlements were still being processed when we responded in August have since completed their exit processes, as well as received those entitlement payments,” Sofowora told TechCabal.
In August 2026, Olubusi stepped down as chief executive after nearly a decade, leaving Sofowora as the only co-founder still running the company.
“A decade of belief, courage, sacrifice, and turning a simple conviction into reality; healthcare in Africa could work better, and technology would play a meaningful role in making that happen,” Olubusi wrote in a public farewell message.
Sofowora declined to discuss the reasons for his exit, calling them “private personnel matters.” He said the transition “is being managed in an orderly manner and does not change the company’s core strategic priorities.”
For the four states rolling out Helium Health’s maternal health tools with Google, Helium Health’s finances now matter as much as its technology. For now, Helium Health says its business remains on track. The company continues to operate across its markets and business lines and says Olubusi’s departure has not disrupted its daily operations or changed its strategic priorities.
“We remain focused on expanding our healthcare technology business,” Sofowora said.

articles.title: The Governance Gap in Open-Weight AI and What to Do About It
articles.text:
Open-weight AI has gone mainstream. As of September 2026, some estimates suggest 42% of enterprises surveyed were running open-weight models in production, up from 31% just two months earlier. But downloading a model also means taking on responsibilities that a provider might otherwise handle, and many organizations have yet to put clear ownership and controls in place.
Renting Capability Vs. Running Your Own Copy
When you use an AI model through a provider’s app or service, you’re essentially renting its capabilities. The provider controls the model and handles the infrastructure, updates, and safety controls. You access it through an app or a software connection.
An open-weight AI model makes its learned parameters, the ‘weights’ that shape its behavior, available to download and run yourself. You can run the model on your own infrastructure and adapt it for a particular use case using your own data. The license may limit how you can use it, and running it still carries infrastructure and staffing costs.
Open-weight models are becoming more capable. One estimate puts the best open-weight models roughly four months behind leading models.
Open-weight does not necessarily mean open-source. Access to the weights does not guarantee access to the training code or details of the training data.
When Benefits Clash with Risks
Zoey is a bank analyst using a provider-hosted model to summarize a loan application. The model does a good job of delivering an actionable summary, but to do so, her request, loan file included, has to go to the provider’s servers. The customer’s data is no longer solely in the bank’s hands. A few quarters later, the provider raises its prices and changes its policies in ways that force workflow changes. Switching providers would take time and effort, so Zoey and her team have little choice but to go along, even though it hurts both their budget and their operations.
Let’s look at the same scenario from the perspective of an open-weight model that is running on the bank’s server. If the model is configured to run entirely within the bank’s system, the loan file can stay there too. The bank can apply its own access controls to the model and the data.
In the above example, an open-weight model does seem like a good option, but there are risks that are easy to overlook:
- Trojan horses: Some model files can execute malicious code when loaded. Others may contain hidden behavior that a particular input can trigger.
- An origin story with missing chapters: A popular model on a public repository may not be the developer’s original. Someone may have modified and reuploaded it without explaining what changed. That version could contain a hidden backdoor or have weak safety rules.
- The upgrade won’t knock on your door: A developer may release improved versions, but your copy is not updated automatically. Your team must track updates, test them, and decide when to switch.
- Attack surface just got bigger: Running your own model creates new targets for attackers. You are essentially adding to your IT infrastructure. This includes the servers and GPUs that keep the model running and the systems that retrain it.
Controls to Address Risks
If an open-weight AI model makes sense for your organization, governance should walk in lockstep with deployment:
- Set a regular review schedule for updates and security notices. Decide who approves a move to a new version.
- Assign an owner for each model, with clear responsibility for approving its use, reviewing updates, and responding when something goes wrong.
- Record each model’s source, version, license, and every fine-tune. Also record its file hash. It’s a unique fingerprint that changes if anyone alters the file.
- Give teams an approved internal repository to fetch models. Before adding a model, verify its source and check its file fingerprint or digital signature against a trusted reference.
- The rule of thumb should be: ‘trust after testing.’ Test the model as an attacker might. Try to bypass its safety rules and look for unexpected behavior, including whether it produces insecure code.
- If you do choose to download a modified version, run the same tests on the developer’s original. This may help reveal weak safeguards or unexpected behavior.
- Higher-risk models need more control. For example, a model that reads source code should also run in isolation, with no access to passwords or keys, and a person assigned to review its output.
- Run the model on a separate server while giving it only the access it needs. Monitor all requests and outputs for unusual behavior, while protecting sensitive information in the logs. If you think a model is misbehaving, have a backup in the form of an earlier version you can switch back to quickly.
Open-weight models need to be scrutinized like any other software brought inhouse. Their benefits are clearly driving their popularity, but there are tradeoffs to be aware of. It’s wise to put ownership and controls in place before putting them into production.

articles.title: NVIDIA and Microsoft Expand Accelerated Computing From Azure to Windows PCs
articles.text:
NVIDIA and Microsoft are extending their full-stack collaboration to help organizations build, customize and deploy intelligent applications — from next-generation infrastructure on Azure to industrial systems and Windows PCs.
At Microsoft Ignite, the companies are expanding access to Azure virtual machines powered by NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 systems, as well as adding customer availability to NVIDIA open models and customization capabilities through Microsoft Foundry, and new options for running AI at the edge, where businesses generate and use their data.
Microsoft is also using NVIDIA technologies to accelerate its own models and services, including NVIDIA Dynamo inference software for post-training and NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell GPUs for Bing search models.
NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 Running in Azure
NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 systems are running in Azure data centers, providing infrastructure designed for demanding reasoning, agentic applications, and large-scale model training and inference.
Microsoft and NVIDIA are also collaborating to extend confidential computing to bare-metal and rack-scale AI infrastructure. The work will help protect sensitive models and data while they are being processed, supporting organizations that need to work with proprietary or regulated information.
NVIDIA Confidential Computing and attestation help customers verify the computing environment before releasing sensitive models, data or keys. As AI workloads span more interconnected accelerators, the companies are working to extend those protections across the AI factory infrastructure.
To help data centers get more performance from available power, NVIDIA and Microsoft are also collaborating on power efficiency using NVIDIA MaxLPS.
Azure’s Vera Rubin preview builds on NVIDIA and Microsoft’s codesign and performance optimization, underscored in the latest NVIDIA Blackwell-based MLPerf results. In MLPerf Training v6.1, Azure scaled to 10,240 NVIDIA GPUs with GB200 NVL72 systems on the DeepSeek-V3 model, the largest scale in the round. In MLPerf Inference v6.1, Azure’s NVIDIA GB300 NVL72 systems led cloud submissions on DeepSeek-R1 interactive throughput by over 10%, per Signal65.
Helping Enterprises Customize and Deploy Open Models
Enterprise AI agents need to reason through complex tasks, find relevant company information and understand business documents. NVIDIA and Microsoft are expanding the models and services available through Microsoft Foundry to help developers bring these capabilities into business applications.
Microsoft’s serverless Programmed Training offering gives developers control over post-training workflows while Foundry manages the underlying infrastructure. Enterprises can focus on their business data, evaluating model responses and improving model behavior.
Foundry Managed Compute adds support for deploying custom model weights, helping connect model customization with deployment through Microsoft’s managed services.
EY used Programmed Training in Microsoft Foundry to adapt NVIDIA Nemotron open models for classifying corporate purchasing records, improving accuracy on its evaluation dataset by 55% and lowering cost by 15x compared with proprietary frontier models. The work demonstrates how enterprises can customize open models for specialized business tasks.
The expanded NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 lineup on Foundry Managed Compute supports different requirements across enterprise applications. Nemotron 3.5 Super is designed for long-running agents working across coding, research and business workflows, while Lightning supports applications that need fast responses and tool use.
Complementary models help agents find relevant information with Nemotron Embed and Rerank, extract structured information from documents with Nemotron Parse and detect harmful content with Nemotron Content Safety. Nemotron 3.5 Bolt — designed for high-throughput, low-latency reasoning — and Transcribe, for speech recognition, are coming soon.
Bringing AI Closer to Enterprise Data
NVIDIA and Microsoft are expanding deployment options beyond the cloud, helping organizations run models and agents closer to their data while maintaining control over their infrastructure and operations.
Expanded support for Nemotron 3.5 in Foundry Local brings capabilities for reasoning, coding and tool-using agents to Azure Local environments. Retrieval models help applications find evidence across text, document images, charts and tables.
Azure Local will also support NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell GPUs from hardware partners, giving organizations additional options for deploying AI on premises.
Azure Local is expanding to NVIDIA Jetson Thor and Jetson Orin edge AI platforms to support industrial applications such as machine vision, robotics and autonomous operations. NVIDIA physical AI models, including Cosmos, are also being brought to Foundry Local.
On Windows PCs powered by NVIDIA RTX Spark, NVIDIA and Microsoft will showcase local large language model experiences at Ignite, demonstrating how developers can run AI applications directly on devices.
For organizations using Cloud PCs, the companies are bringing Direct Stream capabilities to GPU-accelerated Windows 365 Cloud PCs. These capabilities support demanding graphics applications with up to two 4K streams at 60 frames per second and low latency, even over challenging networks. A limited preview is open for sign-ups, with public preview planned for early 2027.
Connecting Scientific AI With Microsoft Discovery
For scientific research, NVIDIA BioNemo Agent Toolkit and NVIDIA ALCHEMI Toolkit are expanding into the Microsoft Discovery catalog, bringing models for life sciences, drug discovery and materials and chemical science into Microsoft’s agentic research platform.
BioNeMo Agent Toolkit helps scientists use natural language to run computational biology workflows in Microsoft Discovery, with agents coordinating the tools and model calls needed to carry out the work.
An initial integration uses the RFD4-Proteina model, developed in collaboration with the University of Washington’s Institute for Protein Design, to generate candidate protein structures and amino acid sequences for further evaluation and laboratory validation.
Accelerating Microsoft’s Models and Services
Alongside expanding customer access to NVIDIA technologies, Microsoft is using NVIDIA software and accelerated computing in its own AI development and services.
Microsoft AI uses NVIDIA Dynamo to support reinforcement learning rollout inference during post-training. This computationally intensive process generates the experiences used to improve models.
Dynamo coordinates inference across a large GPU fleet, optimizing performance, as well as helping manage requests, model updates and recovery from failures. The deployment builds on joint engineering between Microsoft AI and NVIDIA.
Visit NVIDIA at Ignite for demonstrations spanning enterprise applications, robotics, accelerated data processing and local computing, with hardware including an NVIDIA GB300 NVL72 rack and RTX Spark devices. View NVIDIA sessions, hands-on labs and booth theater presentations.

articles.title: Innovation at Speed: New Insights from the 2026 State of Open Source in Financial Services
articles.text:
Innovation at Speed: New Insights from the 2026 State of Open Source in Financial Services
Hilary Carter | 19 November 2026
In financial services, time has always been money. Every millisecond matters on the trading floor, every redundant engineering cycle represents lost opportunity, and duplicated responses to regulatory requirements are costly, time consuming activities that could be shared.
When I joined the Fintech Open Source Foundation (FINOS) community in New York for the Open Source Finance Forum (OSFF), velocity and speed were the defining themes on the mainstage, and in many hallway conversations, and sessions. It was a theme very much supported by evidence from the 2026 State of Open Source in Financial Serivces report, a project I’ve been proud to be part of for the past six years.
This year’s study provides new data combined with first-hand practitioner reflections on this speed, and on a number of other value points relevant to organizational open source engagement within the sector. Together with Scott Logic, a long-standing research partner to FINOS and the Linux Foundation, and BrightQuery, our report sponsor, we have witnessed cautious participation evolving into an industry moving at full throttle. That trendline is among the most inspiring since we first began work on measuring trends at the intersection of open source and financial services.
The report also reveals that the financial sector has officially moved beyond passive consumption into an era of structural mutualization, pooling capital, code, and standards to achieve relevant cost savings and other examples of ROI.
The engine of modern financial velocity
For years, the primary narrative around open source in banking centered on cost reduction. While financial efficiency remains vital—with organizations reporting average annual cost savings of $4.1 million and 15% saving more than $10 million annually—the true story in 2026 is about speed and execution. The report reveals that 88% of respondents agree that open source software delivers faster development time to market and improved productivity, while 88% also agree that it’s valuable to the future of their organization.
This strategic recognition is translating directly into code. Financial services organizations are no longer standing on the sidelines; they are building the tracks as they run on them. Over the past year, GitHub commits by financial services users surged by 63% year over year, reaching more than 1.26 million commits across 67,479 unique public repositories. Furthermore, 93% of institutions now permit open source contribution in some form, and 58% have implemented an Open Source Program Office (OSPO) to formalize their engagement.
Moving from isolated forks to collective resilience
As development velocity accelerates, so too does the complexity of the software supply chain. In a sector governed by strict mandates like the Digital Operational Resilience Act (DORA), knowing what is inside your software estate is non-negotiable. The report shows that 78% of organizations are mostly or fully aware of the open source components running in their systems. Yet, visibility has exposed a massive operational drag: maintenance debt.
According to the report, 35% of respondents spend more than half of their engineering capacity simply maintaining, upgrading, or remediating existing open source dependencies. Even more telling, 71% of organizations maintain private internal forks of open source projects. When hundreds of banks independently patch the exact same vulnerabilities in isolation, they pay a massive single-firm premium for zero competitive differentiation.
With security vulnerabilities (46%) and supply chain attacks (42%) topping the list of industry concerns, institutions are realizing they cannot patch their way out of this challenge alone. Instead, they are turning to neutral foundations to share the load. Initiatives like the Open Source Enterprise Resiliency Alliance (OSERA) allow banks to pool resources and apply secure back-patches collectively at a fraction of the cost. By collaborating on shared infrastructure and industry standards—such as the Common Domain Model (CDM), FDC3, and multi-firm platforms like Fluxnova—institutions eliminate redundant engineering and free up talent to focus on true commercial differentiators.
Governing agentic AI at scale
Nowhere was the theme of speed more palpable at OSFF New York than in discussions around artificial intelligence. The report demonstrates that financial services has rapidly escaped the AI prototype trap: 64% of respondents work at organizations that have already deployed agentic AI in production, either internally (41%) or externally (23%). AI has become a standard fixture in the software development lifecycle, with 87% of respondents reporting productivity gains over the past year.
However, generating code at machine speed introduces new governance bottlenecks. While 65% of respondents use AI tools for code generation, concerns around AI-driven dependency sprawl and code quality are rising, cited by 34% of participants. More broadly, as organizations look to scale autonomous agents across business intelligence (40%) and compliance workflows (38%), the primary roadblocks are not technological—they are institutional.
Looking ahead: The future is open
Reflecting on six years of tracking this ecosystem, the story told by The 2026 State of Open Source in Financial Services is one of an industry coming of age. Financial institutions have proven that fierce competitors can collaborate safely on the foundational layers of technology. The organizations that will lead the next decade are those that treat open source not as a bottom-up developer preference, but as a measured, executive-level discipline.
To build on this momentum, technology leaders should focus on a few core priorities:
- Elevate open source to the boardroom: Quantify the return on investment of open source consumption and contribution, empowering OSPOs to align community engagement with enterprise strategy.
- Mutualize maintenance and security: Shift left by reducing unnecessary dependencies, contributing fixes upstream, and participating in shared remediation alliances like OSERA rather than maintaining costly private forks.
- Standardize on open AI governance: Adopt open protocols, open-weight models, and shared governance frameworks to ensure agentic AI remains explainable, secure, and free from proprietary vendor lock-in.
We extend our deepest gratitude to our research partners, sponsors, survey respondents, and the senior industry leaders who shared their candid insights to make this study possible.
To explore the complete data, benchmark your organization's open source maturity, and discover our full library of insights, download The 2026 State of Open Source in Financial Services and explore our broader collection of reports at https://www.linuxfoundation.org/research.

articles.title: You can now buy a Steam Machine without getting on a waitlist
articles.text:
Valve announced some updates about Steam Machine availability today, including good news if you want to buy one right now and potential bad news about future supply due to RAMaggedon.
You can now buy a Steam Machine without getting on a waitlist
Valve’s 512GB Steam Machine is available to buy now, but the 2TB model is out of stock.
The good news: You can now purchase a 512GB Steam Machine without getting on a waitlist. Initially, interested buyers had to get on Valve’s waitlist if they wanted to purchase one, but the console-like PC is now available in an “add-to-cart” status, according to the company. As I write this, the 512GB versions with and without a bundled controller are showing estimated delivery dates of three to five business days on Valve’s website. If Valve sells through its current inventory, the company says it will indicate that the product is out of stock instead of making another waitlist.
The bad news: If you’re on the waitlist for a 2TB model, you might not get a chance to buy one at all, as Valve says there are more people on the waitlist than there are units available. The company is closing the waitlists for its 2TB models.
Valve says that while it’s still building more Steam machines, “memory and storage costs continue to increase at unprecedented levels” and that it doesn’t know the number it can make or “at what price we’ll be able to offer them.” The 2TB Steam Machine is “especially constrained.” The company anticipates “having more information” to share about additional supply in January.
After delaying the Steam Machine’s expected early 2026 launch due to the memory and storage crisis, Valve launched the product in June with a price starting at $1,049 for the 512GB model without a bundled controller. A 2TB model without a controller costs $1,349.

articles.title: « On choisit la plus difficile » : comment Xiaomi prépare l’arrivée de ses voitures en Europe — Frandroid
articles.text:
Lundi dernier, la veille du lancement mondial des Xiaomi 18 Pro et 18 Pro Max à Paris, une poignée de médias européens se retrouvent autour d’une table près de la gare Montparnasse, sous une pluie battante.
Face à nous, Xu Fei, présentée comme l’employée numéro 14 de Xiaomi, passée par Google avant de rejoindre Lei Jun en 2010. Elle est aujourd’hui vice-présidente et directrice marketing du groupe, et fait partie des dirigeants chargés d’emmener l’automobile hors de Chine. Pas de PowerPoint, un seul graphique, et beaucoup d’histoires. J’ai pu échanger longuement avec elle, et elle a notamment reconnu qu’il serait « vraiment difficile » de faire des smartphones très bon marché.
Sur la voiture, elle commence par raconter un refus. Bien avant de se lancer, Lei Jun, le fondateur de Xiaomi, investissait déjà dans de jeunes constructeurs électriques chinois, mais repoussait l’idée d’en devenir un : « Nos fondations ne sont pas assez solides. Je ne peux pas me lancer dans tout. La voiture, c’est trop sérieux. Je ne suis pas prêt ». Le déclic arrive en 2020, lors des dix ans de l’entreprise, au fil de tables rondes qui duraient parfois de 20 heures à 5 heures du matin.
Selon Xu Fei, Lei Jun en ressort convaincu que la voiture, après être devenue électrique, va devenir intelligente, et donc un appareil connecté comme un autre, « à condition qu’il soit sûr, parce que des vies sont en jeu ». Xiaomi annonce son entrée dans l’automobile l’année suivante.
    Pour aller plus loin
Nous avons testé le Xiaomi 18 Pro Max : il fait le plein de nouveautés
            
    Pour aller plus loin
Xiaomi, roi du petit prix, l’avoue : des smartphones très bon marché ? « Vraiment difficile »
            
En Chine, une gamme qui s’étoffe vite
Depuis, Xiaomi a avancé à un rythme que les constructeurs historiques lui envient. La berline SU7 est lancée en mars 2024, le SUV YU7 suit en juin 2025 avec 200 000 précommandes en quelques minutes, puis la SU7 restylée arrive en mars 2026.
En septembre, la marque a ouvert un nouveau front avec les Sky Nomad N70 et N90, des SUV à prolongateur d’autonomie, c’est-à-dire électriques mais équipés d’un petit moteur thermique qui recharge la batterie. Xu Fei parle de plus de 800 000 voitures livrées, uniquement en Chine continentale, et les chiffres publiés par Xiaomi donnent même 887 966 exemplaires à fin octobre.
Le tableau a pourtant ses zones grises. En octobre, les Sky Nomad ont représenté plus de la moitié des livraisons, alors que la SU7 enchaînait un treizième mois de baisse sur un an et que le YU7 chutait de 70 %. Avec 336 658 voitures livrées de janvier à octobre, l’objectif de 550 000 pour 2026 paraît hors de portée. Autrement dit, la croissance chinoise vient désormais de l’hybride, alors que c’est l’électrique pur qui doit partir en Europe.
L’équipe de Xiaomi nous a surtout beaucoup parlé de son usine de Yizhuang, en banlieue de Pékin, devenue selon elle une attraction qui accueille des centaines de milliers de visiteurs par an.
Xiaomi revendique 91 % de fabrication automatisée et une voiture qui sort de chaîne toutes les 76 secondes, avec plus de 700 robots. Des robots humanoïdes y sont même testés sur la chaîne, que Lu Weibing, président de Xiaomi, qualifie lui-même de « stagiaires ». Xu Fei tempère l’image d’une usine 100 % maison : « On investit beaucoup dans la fabrication intelligente, parce que certaines catégories de produits exigent les lignes les plus avancées. Mais on ne produit pas tout nous-mêmes. »
L’Europe d’abord, et pas par hasard
Pour comprendre le choix européen, Xu Fei revient sur les débuts de Xiaomi hors de Chine, avec pas mal de franchise. « Il y a dix ans, quand on est partis à l’étranger, c’était un peu : on a un tas de téléphones difficiles à vendre en Chine, est-ce qu’il y a un endroit où on pourrait les vendre ? C’est comme ça qu’a commencé le business hors de Chine ».
Pour la voiture, Xiaomi prend le chemin inverse. Là où la plupart des constructeurs chinois testent d’abord l’Asie du Sud-Est, la marque vise directement l’Europe : « Comme l’a dit notre fondateur, c’est une décision très simple. On choisit la plus difficile ». Elle compare ce choix aux essais de la SU7 sur le Nürburgring, « la piste la plus difficile du monde ». Record qui a été depuis battu par Porsche.
Le calendrier, lui, n’est pas une surprise. En septembre, Xiaomi Auto confirmait l’Europe pour 2027, avec l’Allemagne comme porte d’entrée et huit groupes de distribution déjà signés. Xu Fei ne va pas plus loin : « On commencera évidemment par l’Allemagne, mais plusieurs autres pays suivront. On a une feuille de route, mais on ne peut pas la partager, c’est encore en discussion. Désolée ». Pour la France, toujours espérée mais pas datée, il faudra patienter. Elle-même dit avoir passé cinq séjours en Europe l’an dernier et quatre cette année, d’au moins dix jours chacun.
Pas de blitz façon BYD
La méthode tranche aussi avec celle de BYD, très présent en Europe en publicité et en sponsoring.
« Je ne pense pas qu’on suivra le modèle BYD. Pour Xiaomi, l’important est de se faire des amis parmi les utilisateurs », tranche Xu Fei.
Elle veut d’abord convaincre les clients qui comprennent la voiture, puis compter sur leur bouche-à-oreille, car en Europe, la confiance « compte plus que tout, surtout pour une voiture ». Elle n’entend pas non plus miser sur la figure de Lei Jun, star absolue en Chine : « Si on veut une entreprise saine, on ne peut pas trop dépendre d’un seul homme. […] Ici c’est l’Europe, ce n’est pas la Chine. »
En Chine, Xiaomi gère lui-même ses points de vente, à la manière de Tesla. En Europe, il passera par des concessionnaires, et Xu Fei dit en avoir rencontré près d’une centaine, dont certains centenaires qui ont commencé par vendre des vélos.
Le tri reste délicat : « Certains partenaires sont bons. Mais ce n’est pas parce que le gars est bien que je vais l’épouser ». Voir les voitures dans les boutiques Xiaomi, en revanche, « pourrait prendre du temps ».
L’ambition et résumé en une phrase : « Ce Xiaomi n’est pas le Xiaomi que vous connaissiez ». La voiture doit rejoindre l’écosystème « Human x Car x Home », aux côtés du frigo, des aspirateurs et du lave-linge de la marque, de sa machine à laver star, de la Watch S5 en petit format ou du Smart Band 11.
La conduite autonome peut attendre
La discussion a pris un tour inattendu quand l’équipe de Xiaomi a retourné la question aux journalistes : en Europe, faut-il présenter ces voitures comme des autos autonomes, ou d’abord comme des électriques ? « C’est une bonne question. Quelle est votre suggestion ? », nous a-t-on lancé. Autour de la table, les avis ont plutôt convergé. Une électrique très connectée, bien dessinée et dotée de vrais boutons parlera davantage aux Européens qu’une autonomie encore perçue comme de la science-fiction, et un confrère a rappelé que les automobilistes français pensent d’abord à leur pouvoir d’achat, alors qu’une électrique reste chère.
Côté Xiaomi, on a rappelé que la Chine elle-même reste très prudente. La réglementation y plafonne largement au niveau 2, où la voiture gère direction et vitesse mais où le conducteur doit surveiller en permanence, le niveau 3, qui autorise à lâcher la route des yeux dans certaines conditions, restant très encadré.
L’Europe n’est pas plus permissive, et les aides à la conduite de Xiaomi devront de toute façon y être homologuées. Le message qui se dessine est donc celui d’une voiture électrique intelligente, plutôt que d’une promesse d’autonomie.
La SU7 en éclaireur
Xu Fei n’a pas dit quel modèle ouvrirait le bal. Au lancement parisien du lendemain, j’ai pourtant compté trois SU7 exposées et pas un seul YU7.
Selon nos informations, le SUV devrait bien arriver, mais la berline SU7 restylée serait la première à débarquer. Elle passe entièrement sur une architecture 800 volts, qui accélère la recharge sur borne rapide, et reçoit de série un lidar, un capteur laser qui cartographie l’environnement pour les aides à la conduite.
Le changement le plus symbolique concerne les poignées de porte. En octobre 2025, à Chengdu, le conducteur d’une SU7 accidentée est mort dans l’incendie de son véhicule, faute d’avoir pu être extrait par les témoins.
La Chine interdira les poignées affleurantes sur les nouveaux modèles dès janvier 2027, et la nouvelle SU7 adopte une ouverture à triple redondance, avec un secours mécanique qui fonctionne sans courant. En Chine, elle démarre à 219 900 yuans, soit environ 27 000 euros hors taxes, avant les droits de douane européens.
Ce qu’il manque encore
Prix européen, date précise, liste des pays : rien n’est officiel. Pour l’instant, les Européens connaissent surtout chez Xiaomi des smartphones de moins en moins bon marché, un 18 Pro Max, un bracelet, une montre et un lave-linge. Passer de l’électroménager à une berline vendue chez un concessionnaire allemand, c’est un pari autrement plus lourd qu’un lancement de smartphone.

articles.title: Así está el mercado laboral de tecnología: una de cada seis ofertas pide IA, solo uno de cada 60 programadores la pone en su currículum
articles.text: Imagen de una oficina con varias desarrolladoras. El 98% de los programadores españoles usa ya la IA cada día y el 86% dice que así es más productivo. Esa presencia cotidiana inunda inexorablemente el mercado laboral tecnológico: una de cada seis ofertas ya pide IA, pero solo uno de cada sesenta perfiles tiene algo de IA en su currículum. La aparición de la IA es la que más crece en las ofertas, ya aparece en el 15,7%, y las que mencionan agentes de IA se han multiplicado por ocho. La IA también provoca ya la creación de roles propios, como el “ingeniero de IA”, que reúne varios perfiles anteriores y que tiene 20 veces más demanda que en 2023. “Para la gran mayoría de profesionales tech del país, incluir la IA en su currículo va a ser prácticamente una obligación si quieren encontrar oportunidades”, destaca el nuevo informe de Manfred, del que salen los datos citados. articles.title: EEUU busca desesperadamente tarjetas de memoria de los años 90 para su caza furtivo más sofisticado. El problema es que ya nadie las hace
articles.text:
Hay máquinas tan avanzadas que parecen adelantadas a su tiempo. Pero mantenerlas funcionando durante décadas puede convertirse en una batalla contra la obsolescencia, especialmente cuando sus componentes dejan de fabricarse y la tecnología que utilizan desaparece del mercado. Estados Unidos acaba de encontrarse con una de esas paradojas en uno de los aviones más sofisticados de su arsenal.
Un caza de 150 millones buscando tarjetas de los años 90. Sí, la Fuerza Aérea de Estados Unidos está buscando proveedores de tarjetas de memoria similares a las que utilizaban los ordenadores portátiles y las cámaras digitales hace casi tres décadas. Lo extraordinario es su destino: el F-22 Raptor, uno de los cazas furtivos más avanzados del mundo, capaz de superar Mach 2 y diseñado para dominar el combate aéreo.
El 16 de noviembre de 2026, la oficina responsable del programa publicó una solicitud oficial para localizar empresas estadounidenses capaces de suministrar tarjetas con una capacidad mínima de 256 megabytes. Una cantidad diminuta comparada con la memoria de cualquier teléfono actual, pero que sigue siendo necesaria para mantener operativos estos aviones.
La tecnología que sobrevivió a los ordenadores que la utilizaban. La Fuerza Aérea busca dos formatos concretos: tarjetas PC Card de tipo II, también conocidas como PCMCIA, y tarjetas CompactFlash con adaptadores compatibles. Las primeras eran habituales en los portátiles de los años 90 y tenían aproximadamente el tamaño de una tarjeta de crédito. Las segundas se popularizaron en las cámaras digitales de principios de los 2000.
Ambas han quedado prácticamente relegadas a equipos especializados, pero siguen siendo compatibles con los sistemas originales del F-22. El problema no es que Estados Unidos desconozca alternativas modernas, sino que cambiar el formato implicaría modificar equipos militares diseñados y certificados alrededor de una arquitectura informática antigua.
Una tarjeta diminuta con una misión gigantesca. Estos dispositivos forman parte del sistema conocido como Data Transfer Cartridge, una especie de cartucho que conecta la planificación de misiones en tierra con los ordenadores del avión. Antes del despegue, permite introducir rutas de vuelo, frecuencias de radio, coordenadas e información sobre amenazas enemigas.
Después de aterrizar, los técnicos pueden recuperar registros del vuelo y datos de diagnóstico para comprobar el estado del aparato. Es decir, una tecnología que hoy parece propia de un museo informático continúa desempeñando funciones esenciales en la preparación y el mantenimiento de un caza furtivo.
El problema de construir un avión para varias décadas. El F-22 realizó su primer vuelo en septiembre de 1997, entró en servicio en 2005 y su última unidad fue entregada en 2012. Estados Unidos construyó 195 ejemplares de un avión cuyo coste de fabricación rondaba los 143-150 millones de dólares por unidad. Sus prestaciones siguen siendo extraordinarias: alcanza aproximadamente 2.414 kilómetros por hora, puede operar a casi 20.000 metros de altitud y tiene un alcance de unos 2.960 kilómetros con depósitos adicionales.
Sin embargo, buena parte de su electrónica fue concebida cuando las tarjetas PCMCIA eran una tecnología corriente. El resultado es que una aeronave diseñada para seguir volando durante décadas depende de componentes comerciales que dejaron de ser habituales hace mucho tiempo.
Algo peor que quedarse sin tarjetas: comprar falsificaciones. La solicitud estadounidense dedica buena parte de sus requisitos a garantizar la procedencia de los componentes. Los proveedores deberán identificar al fabricante original, especificar el país de fabricación de cada pieza, señalar dónde se realizó el ensamblaje final y documentar toda la cadena de suministro.
También tendrán que presentar medidas para evitar productos falsificados y explicar cuándo dejarán de fabricar las tarjetas, incluyendo posibles oportunidades para realizar una última compra antes de su desaparición. La preocupación es comprensible: un componente aparentemente insignificante puede comprometer la fiabilidad de un sistema militar extraordinariamente caro.
Una flota que envejece, que Washington no quiere jubilar. El suministro de tarjetas es solo una parte de los problemas logísticos del F-22. En 2020, un alto mando estadounidense reconoció que la flota sufría escasez de motores porque los aviones habían acumulado más horas de vuelo de las previstas.
Aun así, el Raptor continúa participando en operaciones y ejercicios internacionales: en octubre de 2026, unidades desplegadas desde Alaska participaron en unas maniobras estadounidenses y japonesas en el sur de Japón. Paralelamente, la Fuerza Aérea está probando nuevos sensores y depósitos de combustible para mantener estos cazas operativos durante la década de 2030.
El futuro de un caza furtivo depende también de su pasado. Por ahora, Estados Unidos no ha comprado ninguna tarjeta: la solicitud publicada en el portal federal SAM.gov es una consulta al mercado, abierta hasta el 1 de diciembre de 2026, para conocer qué empresas pueden suministrarlas, si es que hay alguna. Tampoco se han especificado cantidades ni presupuesto.
Sea como fuere, el caso ilustra una contradicción habitual en la tecnología militar: desarrollar sistemas extraordinariamente avanzados es solo la primera parte del desafío, mantenerlos durante treinta o cuarenta años puede resultar igual de complicado. El F-22 puede volar a más de 2.400 kilómetros por hora y operar con tecnología furtiva de última generación pero, ironías del destino, para seguir haciéndolo necesita que alguien continúe fabricando tarjetas de memoria como las que utilizábamos cuando todavía no existían los smartphones.
