articles.title: Mehr als ein Jahrzehnt unerkannt: Gravierende Sicherheitslücke in Nginx entdeckt
articles.text:
Mehr als ein Jahrzehnt unerkannt: Gravierende Sicherheitslücke in Nginx entdeckt
Eine Reihe von Cybersecurity-Unternehmen hat eine Sicherheitslücke in Nginx entdeckt. Dabei handelt es sich um die Webserver-Software, die von zahlreichen Webseiten genutzt wird. Laut „Built with it“ sind es mittlerweile mehr als 65 Millionen Seiten, darunter die Webauftritte von Mastercard, Morgan Stanley und Logitech.
Wie gravierend ist die Nginx-Sicherheitslücke?
Zu den Sicherheitsforscher:innen, die den Fehler gefunden haben, zählen unter anderem die Expert:innen von Wiz Research, Ikotas Labs und Metnir. Wie Wiz schreibt, handelt es sich im Grunde um zwei kritische Sicherheitslücken, die aber dieselben Auswirkungen haben. Werden sie ausgenutzt, können Server kompromittiert werden. Angreifer:innen haben dann die Möglichkeit, Schadcode aus der Ferne auszuführen, Daten zu stehlen, die betriebenen Webseiten zu verändern oder deren Betrieb zu stören.
Eine der Sicherheitslücken mit der Kennung CVE-2026-123633 soll sich schon mehr als sechs Jahre unbemerkt in Nginx verbergen, die andere sogar zehn Jahre (CVE-2026-123007). Wiz schreibt dazu: „Beide Fehler sind Speichersicherheitsfehler bei Nginx Handhabung von HTTP/2-Traffic. Bei CVE-2026-123633 wird der für eine Verbindung benötigte Speicher schon freigegeben, obwohl er noch genutzt wird, wodurch ein Use-after-Free entsteht. Bei CVE-2026-123007 sorgt eine falsche Flow-Kontrolle für eine ungültige Speicherkopierung.“
Laut Wiz wurden die Fehler in Nginx nicht allein von den Sicherheitsforscher:innen gefunden. Sie haben zunächst ihren eigenen KI-Harness Wiz Atlas genutzt, um die Probleme aufzuspüren. Im Anschluss nutzten sie Gemini 4 Carbon und ChatGPT 5.6 Sol, um die Auswirkungen der beiden Sicherheitslücken zu validieren. Erst im Anschluss wurden die Erkenntnisse an F5, das Unternehmen hinter Nginx, weitergeleitet.
F5 hat eng mit den Sicherheitsforscher:innen zusammengearbeitet, um Lösungen für beide Probleme zu finden. Nicht einmal einen Monat nach der Entdeckung stehen jetzt für beide Lücken Patches bereit. Dementsprechend sollten alle Nginx-Betreiber:innen ein Update der Webserver-Software anstoßen. Andernfalls steigt mit fortlaufender Zeit das Risiko, dass Angreifer:innen die ungepatchten Lücken ausnutzen.

articles.title: Alibaba triplica lucro no trimestre com avanço da IA
articles.text:
O Alibaba, conglomerado chinês de tecnologia e comércio eletrônico, triplicou seu lucro líquido no segundo trimestre fiscal, encerrado em setembro de 2026. O resultado, divulgado nesta quinta-feira (19), chegou a 64,535 bilhões de yuans (US$ 9,626 bilhões), impulsionado pelo crescimento do comércio eletrônico, pela melhora na rentabilidade das operações de inteligência artificial (IA) e por ganhos com investimentos.
O desempenho ficou bem acima das projeções de analistas consultados pela FactSet, que esperavam um lucro de 23,72 bilhões de yuans. A receita do grupo também superou as estimativas de mercado: avançou cerca de 10% em relação ao mesmo período do ano anterior, alcançando 271,52 bilhões de yuans.
Segundo a companhia, o aumento expressivo do lucro foi resultado de ganhos maiores com investimentos e melhora no desempenho operacional. Com sede em Hangzhou, na China, o Alibaba tem direcionado recursos significativos ao desenvolvimento de tecnologias de inteligência artificial, considerada uma das principais frentes de expansão dos negócios.
A empresa se comprometeu a investir mais de US$ 53 bilhões ao longo de três anos em hardware e software voltados para IA. A estratégia, porém, vinha pressionando a rentabilidade nos últimos trimestres, aumentando a expectativa do mercado por resultados concretos dos recursos destinados à área.
O avanço também ocorre em meio a desafios para a indústria chinesa de tecnologia, especialmente diante do aumento do rigor na fiscalização das exportações de chips para o país. A restrição representa um risco para os planos da companhia de ampliar sua atuação no setor de inteligência artificial.
Paralelamente, o Alibaba prepara a abertura de capital de sua unidade de semicondutores, a T-Head, na bolsa de Hong Kong. Para investidores, o movimento representa uma validação importante dos esforços do grupo para desenvolver seus próprios chips. O sucesso nessa frente é considerado relevante para manter a competitividade diante de outras gigantes de tecnologia e startups.
Ana Figueiredo é editora de tecnologia do Olhar Digital. É formada em Jornalismo pela Universidade Federal de Uberlândia (UFU).

articles.title: AI isn’t replacing your job. It’s turning it into low-paid gig work
articles.text:
The gig economy has arrived for cardiologists. Recruiting platform Outlier, run by Scale AI, advertises offers of up to $180 an hour for physicians in the U.S. to design complex cardiac scenarios, review artificial intelligence-generated reports, and rank model outputs. The site offers up to $7.50 an hour for Tagalog work in the Philippines for the same job, and up to $12.50 an hour for Swahili in Tanzania.
Companies like Scale AI first outsourced data work to wherever labor was cheapest. Now, they are recruiting physicians, lawyers, and Ph.D.s to generate and annotate data, rank model answers, and verify outputs. Higher credentials can raise the advertised rate, but the platform still controls payment and working conditions.
I’ve spent the last six years interviewing the people who do this work. Most were in Venezuela, where economic collapse has left a large, educated population online and out of options. One of them, Rogelio, taught computer science until the economic crisis and the pandemic left his family without work. His 13-year-old son discovered they could earn money labeling images of cars and roads on the platforms Hive and Scale AI’s Remotasks, using a laptop the Hugo Chávez government had issued to schoolchildren a decade earlier. The boy made 18 cents for a few hours of work. Rogelio joined him and made just over $2 on his first day.
For a while, the work paid. A task called Beast Mode where workers labeled objects in people’s homes paid more than any other work the family had done. In December 2020, with schools closed and the whole family working, it brought in $20 in a single day. It was the most they would ever make. By early 2021, Beast Mode had disappeared, and their earnings fell below Hive’s $5 weekly payout threshold.
This is how many platforms operate: They begin by paying well to build a workforce, then they cut the rates and move on. Remotasks ended its hourly program in Venezuela in 2021 and made a splash in Kenya the same year. In March 2024, it discontinued operations in Kenya, Nigeria and Pakistan. Scale AI attributed the closures to “enhanced security protocols,” and said notices had gone out three weeks ahead but later acknowledged that Kenyan workers never received them “due to operational errors.” Most workers who spoke to Rest of World at the time said the platform simply froze them out.
The pattern has a name, and it’s older than AI: extractivism. It is a system that takes resources and value from people and places for accumulation elsewhere, on terms set by the buyer rather than the worker. The term also stands for what is taken and what is left behind. The crisis that put Rogelio’s family online was the residue of an oil economy that built little else.
One woman I interviewed in Venezuela drew a pension from the state oil company. By 2021, it was worth about $1 a month, which she said couldn’t buy half a dozen eggs. She was labeling data on Hive to make up the difference, but that income was even less secure. An oil field stays put, while a platform can send the next batch of tasks to workers somewhere else.
AI is usually described as built on extracted data: authors’ books, artists’ works, all used to train models. But the extraction has another layer: the new examples, evaluations, and corrections commissioned to improve those models. That material has to be created by someone, for a fee, which is set by the platform — whether it is $2 for the teacher in Venezuela or up to $180 an hour for a cardiologist in the U.S.
Outlier’s terms let the company delay or suspend payment during an investigation of a worker’s tasks and withhold “some or all amounts accrued” where it finds a violation “in the company’s sole determination.” The company may also deactivate an account “immediately without prior notice for any reason.” The same language appeared word for word in the Remotasks terms that Rogelio’s family worked under in 2021.
Earlier this year, Josh Dzieza reported on the laid-off lawyers, scientists, and screenwriters now filling these platforms. Of the more than 30 workers he interviewed, nearly all described the same arc: Demands increased, target times shrank, and pay fell as a project went on. One designer was tagging videos for Meta at $21 an hour when the project ended for “scope changes.” Days later, the same job reappeared under a new name at $16 an hour — the same sequence that Rogelio’s family went through five years earlier.
Of course, workers can leave, and many do. But the ones who stay are often those who can’t leave. One woman I interviewed was confined to her home during the Covid-19 pandemic by a health condition and couldn’t risk losing the job. “This is my only source of income,” she told me.
None of this is unknown within the industry. In a 2024 meeting convened by the nonprofit Partnership on AI and the Fairwork project which rates platform companies, I sat with representatives of AI companies and the outsourcing firms that supply them. The AI companies said they didn’t employ the data workers; the outsourcing firms said their operations were determined by the prices the AI companies expected. Everyone agreed pay should be better, but when the question of representation came up, the room went quiet as no workers were present.
Workers have still acted. In March 2023, a judge in Kenya temporarily halted the dismissal of 260 Facebook content moderators, prevented Meta from moving their work to another contractor, and barred Meta and contractor Majorel from blacklisting workers. As workers fought in Kenya, Meta moved the work to West Africa.
American courts are also grappling with this issue. Claims by workers on Scale AI’s platforms led to a proposed settlement that has received preliminary approval in San Francisco. The company denies wrongdoing. A separate class action suit alleges Mercor misclassified more than 30,000 lawyers, doctors, and engineers while setting their pay and reviewing their work. Mercor’s clients have included OpenAI, Anthropic, and Meta, but they are not named as defendants. The case is ongoing.
A cardiologist who is offered a three-digit hourly rate is not in the same position as Rogelio and his family. What connects them is the fact that the rate can change suddenly, the task can disappear without warning, and they have no say over any of it.
The work will keep moving, and the rules will continue to be set by the companies that commission it, wherever the next worker logs on, whether in Kenya, Venezuela, or the Philippines.

articles.title: Un mois après le chaos PHP2Shell, que vaut vraiment la nouvelle alerte critique de PHP ?
articles.text:
Les deux alertes sont classées critiques, mais le risque est-il du même ordre ?
Mercredi 18 novembre 2026, l’équipe de sécurité de PHP a annoncé des correctifs pour le lendemain, entre 15h et 15h30 heure française, pour toutes les versions maintenues du langage, de 8.2 à 8.5. Les failles les plus graves sont jugées « critiques », sans autre détail.
Il n’en fallait pas plus pour susciter une vague d’inquiétude. Et pour cause, le 21 octobre, PHP avait corrigé en urgence CVE-2026-109618 et CVE-2026-109619, deux failles notées 9,2 sur 10 qui permettaient d’exécuter du code à distance sans authentification.
Elle avaient rapidement été exploitées par des attaquants, notamment contre des équipements de sécurité de Palo Alto Networks et de Check Point.
La nouvelle faille ne fonctionne que dans une configuration très particulière
L’enjeu reste de taille, puisque PHP fait tourner WordPress et plus des deux tiers des sites dont on connaît le langage côté serveur.
L’une des failles corrigées ce jeudi, CVE-2026-115560, est connue depuis le 23 octobre. Elle touche un mécanisme activé par défaut pour suivre l’avancement d’un envoi de fichier, et peut elle aussi mener à une exécution de code à distance. Mais elle n’est exploitable que si l’application utilise un paramètre spécifique avec une valeur inhabituelle, puis le modifie à la volée avant d’ouvrir la session de l’utilisateur. Les développeurs de PHP parlent eux-mêmes d’un vecteur d’exécution de code « peu probable », et aucune exploitation n’a été confirmée publiquement.
Signe d’une urgence moindre, et contrairement à ceux de PHP2Shell, ces correctifs arrivent dans le cycle habituel de mises à jour, près d’un mois après le premier avertissement, l’équipe s’étant contentée entre-temps d’une mesure temporaire.
Reste que seule CVE-2026-115560 est connue à ce stade, alors que PHP corrige plusieurs failles ce jeudi. Ce sont peut-être les autres, encore tenues secrètes, qui ont valu à l’annonce son classement critique. PHP a seulement précisé que l’exploitation des failles les plus sévères demande une configuration différente des réglages par défaut ou une installation peu courante, ce qui suggère un risque plus limité qu’en octobre.
Les serveurs jamais mis à jour restent le principal danger
Le danger le plus immédiat se trouve sans doute du côté des serveurs qui n’ont toujours pas installé les correctifs de PHP2Shell, des failles déjà exploitées.
Selon le service de mesure W3Techs, près d’un tiers des sites en PHP tournent en outre sur la version 7 ou des versions plus anciennes, que le projet ne maintient plus et qui ne recevront donc pas ces correctifs. PHP 8.2 sera dans la même situation après le 31 décembre 2026, date de fin de son support de sécurité.

articles.title: Six Indian startups selected for Hub71's Immersion Programme in Abu Dhabi
articles.text:
Six Indian startups selected for Hub71's Immersion Programme in Abu Dhabi
The winners were chosen from among ten finalists in the areas of AI, clean energy, advanced manufacturing and digital finance.
Six Indian startups have been selected for Hub71's Immersion Programme in Abu Dhabi, following the UAE-India Start-Up Series 2.0 finale in Bengaluru.
Hub71, Abu Dhabi's global tech ecosystem, is the cross-border partner which will connect the startups with investors, corporate and government partners, regulators, and prospective customers.
Convened by the UAE Embassy in New Delhi, the series drew more than 11,000 applications this year. The winners were chosen from among ten finalists in the areas of artificial intelligence, clean energy, advanced manufacturing and digital finance.
Since the Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement came into force in 2022, bilateral trade between India and the UAE has grown from about $73 billion to more than $101 billion, it added. Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan, President of UAE, and Narendra Modi, Prime Minister of India, have set a target of $200 billion by 2032.
According to a statement, the series seeks to help Indian companies expand globally, with the UAE as their gateway to investment and growth, said a statement.
H.E. Abdulla Saif Al Nuaimi, Ambassador of the UAE to India, announced the winners. Three of them will be shortlisted for Hub71's Access Programme; one startup will join the programme and receive AED 250,000 in in-kind incentives and AED 250,000 in cash through a SAFE note, the statement said.
Al Nuaimi said, “The UAE and India have set themselves the goal of doubling bilateral trade to $200 billion by 2032. Innovative companies like the ones we celebrate tonight will be central to reaching it. The UAE offers Indian founders a gateway to new markets, capital, and partnerships, and we will support these winners as they grow there. I congratulate all ten finalists on the standard they set.”
Ahmad Ali Alwan, CEO of Hub71, said, “India is an important source of technology innovation and entrepreneurial talent, and our collaboration with the UAE-India Start-Up Series is helping more ambitious founders connect with investors, partners, and market opportunities through Hub71.
"Through Hub71's Immersion Programme, startups can deepen their understanding of the market, build meaningful relationships, and access opportunities that support their growth in the UAE and internationally.”
The finale in Bengaluru brought together 10 startups for two days of investor meetings, mentorship and live pitching: CYRAN AI Solutions, Nawgati, KoinX, Onsite, Forthcode, Flo Mobility, Pointo, Econovus, XYMA Analytics, and Sustvest.
The jury comprised Al Nuaimi; Tushar Ved, President of Apparel Group; and members of the UAE-India business community. Al Nuaimi also unveiled a Top 50 Investment Dossier profiling 50 leading applicants.
The six winners will take part in a two-week hybrid programme, comprising a week of virtual preparation, followed by a one-week in-person session at Hub71 in Abu Dhabi from December 7. The programme includes mentorship, curated introductions, and knowledge sessions on Abu Dhabi's business and regulatory environment.
The first edition in 2025 opened a pathway for Indian startups to explore the UAE through Hub71. Endimension, an AI-powered radiology platform, later joined Hub71's Access Programme as part of Cohort 18. BioReform, Docket Run, Data Sutram and SBNRI are the other startups that have completed the Immersion Programme.
Here's a look at the six winning startups this year.
CYRAN AI Solutions (New Delhi, NCR)
The deeptech company uses AI to help aerospace and precision manufacturers catch defects before a part ships, an engine returns to service, or a satellite launches. Founded by IIT Delhi professor Manan Suri, it also builds edge AI for Industry 4.0 and geospatial customers.
Nawgati (Noida, Uttar Pradesh)
The AI and IoT platform helps fuel companies, dealers and governments monitor and run fuel stations from one real-time view. Founded by Aalaap Nair, Vaibhav Kaushik and Aryan Sisodia, the startup raised $2.5 million in a pre-Series A round led by Ajay Upadhyaya, and has deployments in Sri Lanka and the UAE.
KoinX (Bhubaneswar, Odisha)
This crypto tax and accounting platform helps investors and businesses calculate their tax, track their holdings, and keep compliant books. Founded in 2022 by Punit Agarwal, its CEO, the startup raised $1.5 million in seed funding from investors including Polygon founder Sandeep Nailwal, and later attracted investment from CoinDCX Ventures.
KoinX Founder and CEO Punit Agarwal, told YourStory that he has been active in crypto for about 10 years and had previously led the Crypto Relief Fund, a UAE-domiciled fund of close to $500 million. He said India has the most stringent crypto tax regime in the world, and the crypto market would grow in the country with regulations.
Agarwal said KoinX first earned revenue in the June-July 2023 tax season. Revenue grew from about $140,000 in its first year to about $700,000 in the third. He expects about $1.5 million this financial year, aided by B2B contracts.
In the UAE, KoinX sells B2B software to businesses. Agarwal said a local presence, through Hub71's Immersion Programme, would help build trust.
Onsite (New Delhi, NCR)
The AI-powered construction management platform helps contractors and developers control cost and time from site to office. Founded in March 2021 by Sumit Garg, Dheeraj Anand, and Akshansh Agarwal, the startup raised $1.5 million in 2022 in a round led by Foundamental.
Forthcode (Bengaluru, Karnataka)
The aviation technology company helps airlines grow ancillary revenue and automate operations at the airport, on board, and after the flight. Its platform automates inflight retail, services, and catering management. It has partnered with Worldline for inflight payments in India.
Founder and CEO Ajith Balakumar, told YourStory that Forthcode has built an AI model for aviation on Core42's sovereign AI models. Core42 is an Abu Dhabi-based technology company.
On seatback screens in planes, passengers can search for films or ask advanced questions, such as what a city they are flying over looked like 2,000 years ago. He said the software is isolated from avionics and flight controls, and guardrails limit questions to movies, food and the destination.
Balakumar said AI can also answer queries from ground staff on matters such as dangerous goods compliance and support ancillary revenue and disruption management.
Forthcode is a winner of AviationX Labs by Emirates, Thales, Collins, GE and Airbus, has completed a paid pilot with Emirates, and works with Thales as its go-to-market partner.
Flo Mobility (Bengaluru, Karnataka)
Founded by Manesh Jain and Pratik Patel, the construction robotics company helps builders and contractors move materials across large sites using autonomous electric vehicles.
The startup's Flo Hauler robot can carry up to 1.5 tonnes. More than 60 of its robots are deployed across 10 states for developers including L&T and Godrej Properties. Flo Mobility raised $2.5 million in a pre-Series A round co-led by Mela Ventures and Arali Ventures.

articles.title: November 2026 Top500 New Systems Are Few and Far Between
articles.text:
The November 2026 TOP500 list has only 28 new systems, the lowest count in our tracking series going back to June 2018. This dramatic slowdown from previous editions marks a significant shift in how often the list turns over with fresh hardware.
New System Counts Hit a Series Low
Just as a quick note, the official Top500 post says there were 27 new systems, but when we filtered the list on First Appearance 68 (with 68 being the November 2026 list), we got 28 new systems. We will use these new systems for our analysis. The 28 new systems on this November 2026 list mark the lowest count in our series since June 2018, dropping from 43 in June 2026. The previous low was 39 in June 2022, and while November 2024 rebounded to 54, this edition represents a clear step down.
The June 2018 list had 133 new systems, and November 2018 had 153. Those days of roughly a quarter or more of the list turning over with each publication are long gone. Today’s 28 newcomers represent 5.6% of the full Top500.
The 28 new systems together contribute about 1.0 EF/s of Rmax, or roughly 5.1% of the list’s total performance. That is the lowest share since at least November 2021, when new systems contributed over 12%. The prior low was 5.48% in June 2023, so this continues a pattern in which even the systems that do get submitted add little aggregate HPL capability. Part of that is because LineShine was added to the list in June 2026, so a recent new #1 tends to SKU the aggregate addition numbers.
Only five new systems made the Top 100. The highest-ranked newcomer is KISTI’s HANGANG at #12, an HPE Cray EX254n system using NVIDIA Grace CPUs and GH200 Superchips with HPE’s Slingshot 400 interconnect. No new systems made the Top 10. LineShine remains at #1, holding its position from the June 2026 list where it debuted with 2.198 EF/s of HPL performance using custom Arm-based LX2 processors.
With so few new systems and modest newcomer performance, total list Rmax grew from roughly 18.7 EF/s in June 2026 to approximately 19.7 EF/s now. That compares with nearly 25% growth on the previous list, which was driven largely by LineShine’s debut.
The #500 entry point rose from about 2.66 PF/s in June 2026 to roughly 2.87 PF/s now, an increase of around 8%. For context, the November 2021 threshold was just 1.65 PF/s, so the bar has been relatively low to enter the list. Just on a CPU basis, that was when a 64-core AMD EPYC 7003 “Milan” CPU was state of the art. Now, we have 256-core AMD EPYC 9006 “Venice” CPUs. CPU performance has gone up by more than a factor of four (since we get more performance per core), but we have only seen a roughly 74% increase in the “get-in” performance number.
The List Is Aging Rapidly
With only 28 new systems replacing 28 that fell off, the average system on the list has now been there for approximately 3.2 years. That is the highest in our tracking window, up from about 2.2 years in November 2021 and roughly 3.0 years as recently as June 2026.
The systems that dropped off this list had been on it for an average of about 5.4 years, measured as of the current list date. That is a long tenure in terms of list appearances, and it highlights how established these departing clusters were.
There is a stark contrast between what fell off this list and what came on. Of the 28 systems that dropped, 24 were CPU-only, with most using Intel Skylake or Cascade Lake processors from roughly 2017-2019. Seventeen of the departed systems were in the Industry segment, 17 were built by Lenovo, and 14 were located in China.
By contrast, 23 of the 28 new systems are GPU- or other accelerator-accelerated. The churn is slow as well as turning over from old CPU-only commercial clusters to newer GPU-accelerated research and academic systems.
China and Industry Submissions Have Collapsed
Chinese service-provider submissions and commercial Industry clusters have nearly disappeared as sources of new entries. Systems in China fell from 173 on the November 2021 list to just 18 now. China still holds #1 with LineShine, but it has otherwise largely stopped submitting at volume. The country added only one new system this edition: CTyun HPC – shanghai15, an eSurfing Cloud entry using a MetaX C588 accelerator and China Telecom C86 CPUs.
The Industry segment has fallen from 258 systems in November 2021 to 146 now, and only two of the 28 new systems are classified as Industry. The rest break down as 12 Research, 12 Academic, and 2 Government.
This is the same theme we raised in our June 2023 analysis. It feels like the Top500 submissions are not a census of all HPC or AI deployments, and the commercial systems that used to populate the list have largely stopped appearing.
Who Built the New Systems
HPE leads this edition with 8 new systems and by far the most new Rmax at roughly 615 PF/s. That total is dominated by HANGANG at #12 with 342.6 PF/s and ORNL’s Lux at #14 with 220.79 PF/s, an AMD EPYC 9575F system using Instinct MI355X accelerators.
Lenovo has 6 new systems, MEGWARE has 4, and Dell and Fujitsu each have 3. Notably, all three of Fujitsu’s entries are Supermicro-based platforms, including the RIKYU system at RIKEN using GB200 Superchips and Nagoya University’s Flow 2.0 subsystems.
By geography, Europe leads with 11 new systems, followed by Asia with 9 and North America with 8. Germany added 6 new systems, nearly matching the United States’ 7.
South Korea has 3 new systems thanks to HANGANG and its CPU companion system at KISTI, plus a Dell PowerEdge XE9680L with B200 accelerators at Elice Inc. Japan also added 3.
CPUs: Grace Ties Intel as AMD Leads x86
Among the 28 new systems, AMD leads with 13, while NVIDIA Grace and Intel each account for 7. The remaining system uses a China Telecom C86 processor.
All five of the new CPU-only systems are AMD-based, and four of them use Turin Dense (Zen 5c) parts: HANGANG-CPU at KISTI, Manta CPU at Navy DSRC, Nagoya’s Flow 2.0 Type I subsystem, and Lichtenberg NHR-1 CPU at TU Darmstadt. The fifth, ERDC’s Barfoot, uses Genoa.
All seven new Intel systems are GPU hosts. Six use Emerald Rapids and one uses Granite Rapids. There are no new Intel CPU-only systems on this list at all, which is a notable shift for a vendor that has historically dominated the Top500. Maybe more telling is that in the latest (pre-Venice/Vera) generation, Intel has only one Granite Rapids CPU system, while AMD’s Turin has 11 systems.
Across the full list, Intel’s share has fallen to 50.2%, down from 82% in November 2021. AMD sits at 39.8%, and NVIDIA Grace now powers 6.4% of systems with 32 entries.
NVIDIA Grace is the most common CPU among new systems with 7 appearances, all in GPU-host roles. Next comes the AMD EPYC 9655 with 3 systems, followed by several SKUs at 2 each, including the EPYC 9965, EPYC 9654, Xeon Platinum 8568Y+, and Xeon Platinum 8570.
The 28 new systems use 16 different CPU SKUs total. On the full list, however, the story is very different. The AMD EPYC 7763 from 2021 remains the most common SKU with 34 systems, and NVIDIA Grace is close behind at 32.
The EPYC 7742 has 26 systems, and the Xeon Platinum 8480+ has 20. These older models from roughly 2019-2023 still hold significant presence on this list, even as newer SKUs dominate among the latest additions.
Core Counts Split by Role
Most GPU-host CPUs have between 36 and 72 cores per socket. Grace has 72, Emerald Rapids hosts typically run 48-56 cores, and five GPU systems use 96-core EPYC parts.
Every new CPU-only system uses a part with between 96 and 192 cores. That includes the 96-core EPYC 9654 in Barfoot, the 128-core EPYC 9745 in HANGANG-CPU, the 160-core EPYC 9845 in Manta CPU, and two systems using the 192-core EPYC 9965.
The median new system has 72 cores per socket versus 52 for the full list. Five years ago, the full-list median was just 20 cores per socket.
Systems using CPUs with 24 or fewer cores have fallen from 75% of the list in November 2021 to just 19% now. None of the 28 new entries use such low-core-count processors, indicating a distinct shift in the CPU mix appearing on the TOP500.
The shift toward higher core counts reflects a clear division in new system design. GPU hosts typically use moderate-core CPUs, while CPU-only systems leverage high-density EPYC parts to maximize compute throughput per socket.
Accelerators: NVIDIA Blackwell Arrives, but Hopper Is Still the Installed Base
Fourteen of the 28 new systems use NVIDIA Blackwell accelerators, split between 12 with B200 and 2 with GB200 Superchips. Hopper accounts for another 6 systems across H200, GH200, and one remaining H100.
AMD has two new accelerated systems: ORNL’s Lux on MI355X at #14 with 220.8 PF/s, and C-DAC’s PARAM KAVERI in India using MI300X. MetaX has one entry with its C588 accelerator in the CTyun system.
Across the full list, accelerated systems now represent 58.6% of systems and 78.8% of Rmax. That compares with just 30% of systems being accelerated back in November 2021.
Blackwell systems nearly doubled from 18 to 32 since the June 2026 list, while Hopper reached 137 systems. In terms of system count, AMD Instinct across all generations is still roughly at Blackwell’s level.
The installed base story matters here. Even though Blackwell dominates new submissions, the full list still has more Hopper systems than anything else, and 61 Ampere-generation systems from the A100 era remain on the list.
Interconnect: InfiniBand Keeps Taking Share
Among new systems, 19 of 28 use InfiniBand. That breaks down as 14 with NDR, 2 with XDR, 2 with HDR, and one unspecified generation. Five new systems use HPE Slingshot, including the first Slingshot 400 systems on the list: HANGANG and its CPU companion at KISTI.
Four new systems use Ethernet. Two are RoCE-based, one uses NVIDIA Spectrum-X (the MEGARIDE system at CINECA), and ORNL’s Lux uses HPE Juniper with AMD Pensando 400G Ethernet.
Half of the new systems run 400Gb/s per port, and two run 800Gb/s XDR InfiniBand. These are nominal per-port line rates rather than achieved throughput, but they show where high-end cluster networking is heading.
Across the full list, Ethernet has fallen from 45% of systems in November 2021 to just 18% now. The old 10/25/100GbE commercial clusters that drove those numbers have largely aged off the list. InfiniBand now sits at 60% and Slingshot at 15%.
InfiniBand leads new submissions with 19 of 28 systems, while Ethernet accounts for only 4. Across the full list, InfiniBand has grown to 302 systems versus 88 for Ethernet and 73 for Slingshot, showing a clear shift in the reported interconnect mix.
Final Words
The November 2026 TOP500 shows a list with limited turnover, featuring only 28 new systems and roughly 5% performance growth. The average tenure of listed systems has approached 3.2 years, marking the slowest update rate in our tracking window. China’s presence dropped to 18 systems from 173 in November 2021, while the Industry segment fell to 146 from 258. Of the new entries, 23 are accelerators.
New hardware on the list highlights specific architectural trends: Blackwell accelerators appear in 14 systems, all CPU-only newcomers use AMD EPYC processors, and NVIDIA Grace matches Intel’s count among new entrants. The Top500 remains a useful gauge for tracking declared HPL system configurations and platform trends over time. However, it does not capture the full scope of current HPC and AI compute investments, which often prioritize different benchmarks or deployment models.
There’s plenty of new clusters, but none of them will spare even so much as a day of compute time to calculate LINPACK when there are training runs to do.

articles.title: Splunk Patches Nearly 140 Flaws Across Three Core Products
articles.text:
Splunk on Wednesday announced patches for nearly 140 vulnerabilities in its Enterprise, Enterprise Security, and SOAR products.
Enterprise received fixes for 38 security defects, including two critical and 13 high-severity flaws that could allow unauthenticated attackers to bypass authentication, inject arbitrary code, and cause denial-of-service (DoS) conditions.
The critical bugs, tracked as CVE-2026-76536 and CVE-2026-76535, could allow attackers to read and modify clustering configuration using an empty clustering shared secret, or read or modify data and configurations by running arbitrary Search Processing Language (SPL) searches.
Fixes were included in Splunk Enterprise versions 10.6.1, 10.4.5, 10.2.9, 10.0.12, and 9.4.17.
Splunk released Enterprise Security and Splunk App for PCI Compliance version 8.7.0 with patches for 42 vulnerabilities, including a critical flaw (CVE-2026-131202) leading to remote code execution (RCE). It can be exploited by an attacker with the ‘ess_admin’ role by combining lookup file upload and Configuration Checker functionality.
The security updates also resolve 11 high-severity code injection and privilege escalation issues leading to data tampering, service disruption, and command execution with elevated privileges.
Splunk SOAR version 8.8.0 arrived on Wednesday with fixes for 59 security bugs, including two critical flaws leading to remote code execution (CVE-2026-131253 and CVE-2026-131287). Both require authentication.
The SOAR refresh also resolves 27 high-severity information disclosure, missing authorization, RCE, path traversal, XSS, improper authorization, improper access control, and privilege escalation weaknesses.
On Wednesday, Splunk also announced fixes for three vulnerabilities in App for Stream, four flaws in AI Assistant, and nearly 160 bugs in third-party packages for Enterprise, Enterprise Security, and SOAR.
The company makes no mention of any of these security defects being exploited in the wild. More details are available on Splunk’s security advisories page.

articles.title: Into the Omniverse: How Developers Turn Ideas Into Simulations With Frontier AI Agents
articles.text:
Turning a simulation idea into a working application means assembling assets, connecting physics and rendering, and checking that the scene behaves as intended. Developers are combining frontier AI models with NVIDIA Omniverse libraries to help carry out that work — building applications for exploring scenarios, investigating failures and improving designs.
Developers direct AI agents through natural-language instructions, review results and guide changes. Omniverse libraries provide GPU-accelerated physics, rendering and sensor simulation capabilities.
Explore the projects below to see frontier AI models such as GPT-6 Astra at work, and check back for new examples from NVIDIA teams and developers across the ecosystem.
Physical AI Paves the Path to Autonomous Industrial Operations 🔗
AI agents powered by frontier models pave the way to autonomous operations. They use industrial tools and engineering data to help engineers build digital twins that test plans and processes and evaluate operational decisions.
Falkor, a KONGSBERG company, shows how this works in practice. The company’s Falkor Surface platform lets customers turn their computer-aided design and engineering data into facility-scale digital twins using the GPT-6 Astra model. The platform uses NVIDIA Omniverse libraries and NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Server Edition GPUs on Microsoft Azure to enable advanced physics simulation.
AI agents built on Falkor’s agentic engine understand dense technical documentation, spatial relationships and real-world physics. Engineers can create and test plans in simulation before traveling on site, reducing costly delays and mistakes. They can also inspect equipment and check clearances in a shared view.
Read Falkor’s article and watch the livestream for a closer look at how the company builds these tools and checks the agents’ work.
Build a Robot Pick-and-Place Simulation With SimReady Assets 🔗
Getting a robot model into a scene is only the start. Developers also need to assemble its components, add controls and check whether it can complete a task.
NVIDIA developers Dillon Bailey and Rishabh Chadha used 3D assets from the SimReady Central library to build a pick-and-place simulation of a robot moving a can using the NVIDIA Isaac Sim framework. They directed an agent equipped with GPT-6 Sol and Isaac Sim skills to assemble the scene and generate pick-and-place controls.
Testing the assembled scene shows how the assets work together, from joint movement and contact behavior to the gripper’s ability to hold, move and release the can. With that baseline in place, developers can adjust object positions and motion paths and repeat the tests to evaluate how each change affects the task.
Follow the walkthrough to assemble and test a pick-and-place simulation in Isaac Sim, with sample agent prompts and checks for robot movement and grasp behavior.
Build a Voice-Controlled VR Simulation With SimReady Assets 🔗
Bringing 3D assets into virtual reality (VR) requires more than rendering a scene. Objects need to respond to controllers and behave as expected when grabbed, moved or released.
NVIDIA Omniverse community developer Michael Wagner took on this challenge. He directed GPT-6 Astra to use Blender software to model a study environment from two reference images, balancing visual quality with efficient performance in VR.
He then used Claude Code to build an application that lets users find SimReady Central assets by voice and interact with them in an immersive VR scene. The Claude Code agent worked for about eight hours, and Wagner built the application over a weekend using an NVIDIA RTX 6000 Ada workstation and a Meta Quest 3 VR headset.
The application ran on NVIDIA Omniverse libraries: ovstage shared the OpenUSD scene, ovrtx rendered it, ovxr enabled VR and ovphysx ran physics. Wagner later built a second version with ovnewton, which integrates with ovstage, to compare the physics libraries.
The biggest challenge for Wagner was checking what happened inside the headset. Automated tests missed problems he could feel, including objects shaking when grabbed. Wagner reported the symptoms, guided the agent through changes and verified the interaction himself. Updating the grab control once per frame resolved the shaking. His takeaway: Give agents renders and logs to inspect, then check the experience directly.
Explore his open source demo for build instructions, a starting prompt and reusable agent skills.
Send Microducks on Rounds in a Simulated Hospital 🔗
Before adapting a robot to a new environment, developers need to test whether its walking policy — the AI that controls how it moves — can keep it stable in that setting.
AI developer Maziyar Panahi directed Claude Code, using Claude Opus 5.5, to assemble an intensive care unit from 13 NVIDIA SimReady hospital assets and test Microduck robots inside it. The assets came with Newton physics settings, so Panahi didn’t have to model the furniture or create collision geometry from scratch. The Newton physics engine also helped replicate the ward so hundreds of copies could run together on one NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 GPU.
When the cloud containers lacked graphics support, Panahi and the Claude Code agent separated simulation from rendering, recording robot poses in the cloud and rendering them locally. They also treated the furniture as static collision objects, which enabled larger runs within the solver’s limits.
The robots walked using AI they had already been trained on and followed preset points along a route. Panahi checked how many robots remained upright: In a 256-ward run, 766 of 768 Microducks were still standing after 14 simulated seconds. He said the agent’s work took about two hours.
Explore the open source demo for a starter prompt, checks and instructions to begin with one ward on a CPU, then scale to hundreds on an NVIDIA GPU.
Create Editable 3D Assets With Houdini and AI Agents 🔗
Creating animated 3D content requires connecting modeling, simulation, materials and rendering. Nick Scarcella, a senior technical artist on NVIDIA’s BondLab team, directed AI agents — primarily using Claude — to work with CUDA libraries and Isaac Sim to create animations. The BondLab team uses SideFX Houdini and the NVIDIA ovrtx library to develop materials, lighting and the final rendered appearance.
In one experiment, Scarcella guided Astra to recreate an OP-1 portable synthesizer using product images, manuals and technical direction. He exported the model into the OpenUSD framework, tested it in Houdini and Blender, then used Astra and Opus to refine details before adjusting materials and textures for ovrtx rendering.
Scarcella also used a publicly shared robot-hand checkpoint in Isaac Sim, directing the motion and developing materials and lighting in Houdini with Claude’s assistance. Working with team member Steven Dvornik, the team created an “Echos” visualization: translucent versions of the hand overlap and merge into a single hand animation, offering a visual interpretation of robot training.
Figure: An artistic visualization of simulated robot-hand motion, developed with AI assistance and Houdini’s materials and lighting tools.
These workflows bring agent-assisted creation into existing artist tools, giving teams editable content they can inspect, refine and render across applications.
Explore Scarcella’s Houdini MCP tools and agent skill.
Test Robotic Disassembly With Computer-Aided Design and Simulation 🔗
Before a robot can disassemble a product, developers need to know whether its tools can reach and remove the parts. Jens Jebens, a senior product manager for OpenUSD at NVIDIA, directed Astra to model a car suspension in PTC Onshape and configure it in NVIDIA Isaac Sim.
Jebens used simulation feedback to revise the tooling, including a wrench designed to reach the suspension’s bolts, and reported successful removal of a suspension component in simulation.
PTC also connects computer-aided design (CAD) with simulation through Onshape’s SimReady Publisher, built with NVIDIA Omniverse libraries. Robotics startup Sensori uses it to transfer its Yuri robot into Isaac Sim, carrying geometry, joints and configuration data so the team can evaluate design changes without repeatedly rebuilding the simulation model.
Explore the Onshape importer guide.
Create an Editable Building Model From Site Scans 🔗
Planning warehouse automation requires a model of the building itself, but shelving and machinery can obscure its structure in site scans. Omniverse brings together real-to-sim tools and agent skills to help developers turn real-world captures into editable starting environments for physical AI simulation.
David Wehr, from NVIDIA’s simulation technology team, built on that work using Astra to develop a workflow for digitally reconstructing a building without its contents. The goal is an editable, simulation-ready building model where developers can add or reposition shelving and machinery to evaluate warehouse layouts and automation plans before making physical changes.
Wehr guided Astra to interpret panoramic photos, create building geometry and align it with point-cloud measurements. OpenUSD stores the models, while Omniverse’s ovrtx library renders results for inspection.
Explore NVIDIA Omniverse agent skills to help agents build with Omniverse libraries.
Test Gas-Turbine Operating Scenarios With a Digital Twin 🔗
Before changing how industrial equipment operates, engineers need a way to explore the consequences. Pradeep Kaushik, a member of the NVIDIA Omniverse developer relations team, directed Astra to build a what-if analysis application around a simulated gas turbine and generator.
The application lets users adjust conditions such as load, ambient temperature and fuel composition, then compare power, efficiency, fuel consumption and equipment response. Six test procedures explore scenarios including load changes, a stuck fuel valve and an exhaust-sensor error.
The prototype gives engineers an interactive way to investigate how operating changes and faults could affect equipment behavior, supporting decisions about which scenarios warrant further testing.
Astra used tools like Cantera for thermochemistry and SciPy for equipment dynamics. The application maps solver results to rotor animation and color-coded temperature, pressure and flow-velocity indicators in a 3D turbine. NVIDIA Omniverse libraries update the scene (ovstage), render it with RTX (ovrtx) and stream the view to the browser (ovstream). Engineers can rotate and zoom the cutaway, switch between indicators, and pause or scrub through a simulated response alongside charts and virtual instruments.
Build Simulation Scenes With Open Source SimReady Assets 🔗
With SimReady Central Library, announced at GTC Berlin, developers can access more than 2,000 simulation-ready USD assets from equipment manufacturers and asset providers for robotics simulations and AI factory digital twins workflows.
Paul Kind, a member of NVIDIA’s Omniverse documentation team, pointed an AI agent to the library and guided scene assembly through conversation. His kitchen scene included 180 placements drawn from 63 unique library assets, alongside 18 custom geometry pieces. Kind reviewed renders produced with Isaac Sim and guided further adjustments.
For robotics and factory workflows, developers can select SimReady assets with the simulation properties embedded to fit their required task then test in an assembled environment.
Find assets in SimReady Central Library, and learn how to contribute.
Stress-Test a Warehouse Simulation at Scale 🔗
A warehouse simulation needs to keep running smoothly as more robot arms, conveyors and boxes fill the scene.
When it slows down, developers need to identify what’s holding it back. Bhavik Sanganee, principal engineer at NVIDIA, used Astra with NVIDIA Omniverse libraries to build a warehouse simulation, increase its complexity and investigate slowdowns.
Performance first fell below the target when the scene doubled in size. Running physics calculations, image rendering and video preparation concurrently restored performance and enabled further scaling.
With 80 conveyors, 40 arms and 800 boxes, the simulation sustained 30 frames per second at full HD resolution during a two-minute test. The arms completed 640 successful box placements.
Doubling the scene again reduced performance. Testing traced the slowdown to the physics and robot-control pipeline, giving Sanganee a specific area to improve.
Start building with NVIDIA Omniverse libraries.
Test Robot Control for Flexible Cable Routing 🔗
In electronics assembly, a robot may need to position a flexible cable around components before plugging it into a port. The cable bends as the robot moves it, and the connector must line up precisely to fit.
Oyindamola Omotuyi, robotics technical marketing manager at NVIDIA, directed Astra to build a robot simulation using NVIDIA Isaac Lab, Newton physics and Omniverse rendering with a Robotiq gripper handling the cable.
Astra also developed a reinforcement learning system that combined learned cable-routing movements with position-and-orientation feedback and corrective adjustments for USB-C insertion. The simulation gave Omotuyi a way to test cable handling and connector alignment before moving to physical-robot experiments.
The controller used information supplied directly by the simulation. Next steps include testing a friction-held grasp and using information a physical robot could obtain from cameras and sensors.
Get started with robot learning in NVIDIA Isaac Lab.
Turn Robot Computer-Aided Design Into a SimReady Asset 🔗
Before testing whether a robot can pick up and move a box, developers need a simulation model with joints that move correctly and with grippers that can hold the object. A computer-aided design (CAD) model provides the robot’s shape, but it still needs physics properties to perform the task.
Using an ABB Robotics YuMi robot, developers directed Astra with NVIDIA Omniverse content libraries to convert CAD files into OpenUSD, match the robot’s appearance to reference images, and configure joints and collision geometry. They checked the asset against SimReady Foundation requirements before testing it in NVIDIA Isaac Sim.
Both arms and grippers completed four cube pick-and-place cycles, using simulated finger contact and friction. These tests demonstrated behavior under the simulated conditions — estimated physical properties were not calibrated against the real robot.
Follow the five-step SimReady tutorial.
Build a Humanoid Simulator for a Warehouse Environment 🔗
Explore a gamified, physics-based control of a humanoid robot in first- and third-person view.
Before automating warehouse tasks, developers need an interactive simulation environment to explore task behavior and evaluate how the work gets done. Frank DeLise, Omniverse product manager at NVIDIA, used Astra to turn a SimReady warehouse and humanoid robot into an interactive simulator with first- and third-person views.
DeLise directed Astra to connect NVIDIA Omniverse libraries for physics (ovphysx), scene updates (ovstage), rendering (ovrtx) and the user interface (ovui). He also used Astra with SimReady (simready-foundation) to create the physical scene in simulation. Astra then generated animation and application code to bring those capabilities together.
Learn how to prepare and validate SimReady robot assets with frontier AI models and NVIDIA Omniverse libraries.
Connect an Autonomous-Driving Testing Workflow 🔗
Changing a scene, sensor or driving model can significantly affect autonomous-vehicle simulations. Doyub Kim, a manager on the simulation technology team at NVIDIA, asked Astra to build Zero to Alpamayo — a reusable simulation environment based on San Francisco’s Market Street.
Kim directed Astra to map out the workflow, then connect asset creation, traffic, Omniverse RTX sensor simulation and Alpamayo driving in stages, checking each integration. The resulting prototype was a testing ground for comparing models and tracing how scene or sensor changes affect downstream driving behavior. A separate Cosmos3-Nano experiment varied weather and lighting in recorded simulation videos, allowing Kim to compare the driving model’s responses to the same scenario under different conditions.
Use Sensor Differences to Create and Improve Digital Twins 🔗
Comparing recorded and simulated camera and lidar outputs gives developers key performance indicator-based feedback for refining a scene.
To test robots and autonomous vehicles, developers need to know how closely simulated sensors match real ones. Ashley Reid, who works on RTX sensor validation at NVIDIA, directed Astra and Claude Fable 5 agents to compare ovrtx camera and raw LiDAR outputs with recorded data. The agents created two digital twins from scratch and improved two existing ones.
Over about three days, Reid guided an iterative workflow in which agents measured differences, created or modified OpenUSD scenes, and checked the results. Changes addressed missing objects, geometry and materials, with acceptance depending on camera and LiDAR metrics. This gives developers a way to use measured discrepancies to guide scene creation and improvement.
Start by rendering an OpenUSD scene with the ovrtx minimal Python example, then define a sensor measure to compare with recorded data.
Robo Olympics: Test Robot Skills With Simulation 🔗
Teaching robots new movements means checking whether those actions work under physical constraints. Tae Kim, who leads NVIDIA Omniverse engineering and product, used sports videos and natural-language instructions to guide Astra in building Robo Olympics, an experimental project that tests simulated Unitree G1 humanoids performing sports movements.
Under Kim’s direction, Astra built controllers and refined them through physics trials. Newton Physics Engine simulated behavior, the open source NVIDIA Warp framework accelerated calculations and ovrtx rendered scenes and virtual-camera images. In one experiment, the robot cleared a single hurdle in 64 of 100 simulation trials. The trials gave Kim feedback for improving the robot’s timing and control.
Watch Kim explore building simulations with Astra and NVIDIA Omniverse libraries.
Bring the International Space Station Into the Browser 🔗
Turning 3D models into an application requires connecting assets, live data and an interface. Nic Johns, an engineering director at NVIDIA, prompted Astra to assemble NASA assets into an OpenUSD International Space Station model with telemetry. Johns built the application with a single prompt, then used a follow-up prompt to shift the scene to Earth’s daytime side so the planet was visible.
The workflow used Blender for asset preparation and Omniverse libraries for rendering (ovrtx), scene runtime (ovstage) and streaming (ovstream). The application brings 3D models and operational data into the browser, with Johns guiding its development through prompts and corrections.
Try the Omniverse Real-Time Viewer skill.
Turn Captured Rooms Into Testing Environments 🔗
A digitally reconstructed room needs editable objects and accurate physical behavior before developers can test interactions. Chirag Majithia, from the Isaac engineering applications team at NVIDIA, directed Astra to turn stereo camera captures into an editable OpenUSD studio.
The workflow combined PyCuSFM, FoundationStereo and nvblox for reconstruction, with user review guiding object selection and placement. Astra assembled generated and Blender-authored assets and used USD Content Agents to configure how objects move and interact in simulation. Isaac Sim tests guided collision and contact revisions for doors and drawers. The studio connects captured geometry to interaction testing, making gaps and object behavior easier to inspect.
Have a simulation idea? Explore NVIDIA Omniverse libraries to start building with an AI agent.

articles.title: Internet traffic and attacks during the 2026 U.S. midterm elections
articles.text:
Internet traffic and attacks during the 2026 U.S. midterm elections
Visitors to government election websites surged 363% on November 3, the date of the 2026 midterm elections in the United States. Across Cloudflare's election protection programs, we also detected a significant shift in the types and timing of cyberattacks throughout 2026.
Unlike what we saw in other recent elections, attackers focused on gaining access to internal systems and data, rather than knocking websites offline. Government election websites faced website vulnerability attempts 180 times more often than denial-of-service (DDoS) attacks, and at roughly ten times the rate of Cloudflare's broader customer base. We also found evidence of at least one attempt to exploit a recently disclosed critical PHP vulnerability on a state government voting website in the Western United States.
These attacks peaked in late October, several weeks before the election. Vulnerability exploit attempts climbed steadily throughout 2026: from 200,000 per day in January, to 2 million per day in October. However, on Election Day in the U.S., Cloudflare detected no escalation in attack volume and zero major DDoS incidents across protected election sites, marking a sharp contrast to other recent elections, such as in Moldova last year.
Our data regarding cyberattacks on election institutions came from organizations participating in Cloudflare's free cybersecurity programs: the Athenian Project, Cloudflare for Campaigns, and Project Galileo. Together, these initiatives helped protect more than 1,400 election-related websites during the 2026 U.S. midterm elections, including those belonging to state and local governments, candidates, political parties, voting-rights advocates, journalists, and civil society groups.
Cloudflare launched its first election protection program in 2016 after widespread reports of cyberattacks targeting the U.S. elections. A decade later, it is remarkable to see how far governments and campaigns have come in securing their digital infrastructure. We are proud to help protect democratic institutions and are encouraged that cyberattacks were once again not a disruptive factor in 2026.
In this post, we examine traffic and attacks observed against those organizations on Election Day, analyze the most common types of attacks of the 2026 cycle, and provide recommendations based on those findings.
Election Day: significant voter traffic, minimal attacks
Ordinary user traffic to state and local government election websites was higher on Election Day (November 3) than any other day in 2026. Traffic to those sites increased to approximately 602 million requests, up from 130 million on November 1. By comparison, traffic across the rest of Cloudflare’s global network rose by only 12% over the same period.
State and local government election websites provide authoritative information to voters on how to register, where to vote, and who won. Because of their critical role, these platforms are often targeted by those seeking to suppress voter turnout, disrupt the reporting of results, or steal sensitive information.
On Election Day itself, Cloudflare did not record a single significant distributed denial-of-service (DDoS) attack across any of its 1,400 election-related websites. The only significant DDoS attack occurred on November 2, targeting a candidate for the U.S. House of Representatives in California and totaled 520,000 requests. By comparison, the Moldovan Election Commission experienced more than 898 million malicious requests in a single 12-hour period on their Election Day in 2025, with attacks peaking at 324,333 requests per second.
Prior to Election Day: the most common attacks in the 2026 cycle
Website vulnerability scans were by far the most common attack observed by Cloudflare in the 2026 U.S. election cycle. In the 12 months leading up to the election, Cloudflare mitigated 392 million such attacks on government election websites alone.
Website vulnerability attacks exploit outdated or vulnerable website code to gain access to internal systems and data. For example, cross-site scripting attacks inject malicious code into web pages in order to capture administrator credentials or deface site content. SQL injection manipulates database queries allowing attackers to potentially extract voter records or alter data.
Phishing and other malicious emails targeting political campaigns protected by the company occurred at rates consistent with Cloudflare's broader network, but showed signs of sophistication. In the 90 days leading up to the election, 3.9% of emails sent to organizations participating in Cloudflare for Campaigns were identified as malicious, closely tracking the 4.8 percent baseline across other Cloudflare customers. However, nearly 42% of those malicious emails managed to bypass basic email authentication checks, such as verifying sender identity or preventing in-transit tampering. These threats were nonetheless identified by Cloudflare’s advanced phishing detection tools.
Although website vulnerabilities were the most common attack overall, for journalism and election-related civil society organizations, DDoS was the most common. Over the same 12-month period, Cloudflare mitigated over 10.8 billion DDoS requests targeting these groups. The largest single attack occurred on September 10, 2026, hitting a U.S.-based news organization with 3.04 billion requests. This pattern is consistent with Cloudflare research released earlier this year, which found that among all Project Galileo entities in 120 countries, DDoS were by far the most common attack seen, accounting for 81% of all attacks.
PHP vulnerability
On October 21, security researchers disclosed serious vulnerabilities (known as php2shell) in PHP, an open source back-end programming language used by 70% of the world's websites. The flaws reportedly could allow attackers to execute malicious code on vulnerable servers, expose customer data, or disrupt services. Cloudflare deployed Web Application Firewall (WAF) protections for all customers, prior to public disclosure of the vulnerability.
On October 22, Cloudflare's PHP defense was triggered more than 9,000 times on a state government election website in the Western U.S. This attack was only detected on one election-related site and appears to have been an isolated incident rather than part of a broader trend.
Recommendations
Cloudflare research consistently shows that individuals and organizations participating in democratic elections face significant risk of cyberattack. Data gathered during the 2026 U.S. midterm election suggests those attacks continue to evolve, occur throughout an election cycle and not only on Election Day, and can vary depending on the type of organization targeted.
Based on the recent cyberattack trends in the 2026 U.S. midterms and other elections, we make the following recommendations:
- Prepare for surges in user traffic. Legitimate voter interest can create traffic spikes that overwhelm unprepared infrastructure and make essential election websites inaccessible. Organizations should prepare scalable, efficient infrastructure to handle Election Day traffic increases without straining budgets or staff.
- Maintain security protections year-round, not just on Election Day. Cyberattacks targeting democratic institutions occur across the entire election cycle, not just around voting windows. Defensive postures must remain active continuously rather than treated as a short-term, seasonal measure.
- Deploy automated defenses to counter rapid threats. AI has made it easier for attackers to find and exploit new vulnerabilities. Organizations should implement security services that update automatically, like managed rules, to ensure new protections deploy by default.
Ensuring voters have access to reliable information about elections not only helps encourage participation and deliver timely, accurate results, but also protects voter confidence in the democratic process itself. As more officials, more institutions, and the public increasingly rely on the Internet for those services, keeping that digital infrastructure stable, secure, and accessible becomes an essential civic priority.
State and local election offices, political campaigns, party organizations, journalists, and voting rights groups in need of cybersecurity services can access them from Cloudflare at no cost. Visit the Athenian Project (for state and local election websites), Cloudflare for Campaigns (for political campaigns), or Project Galileo (for civil society, democracy, and journalism organizations) to learn more about eligibility and sign up today.

articles.title: Some creators are skeptical of Instagram’s new affiliate program
articles.text:
For years, influencers have come up with workarounds on social media to figure out how to share affiliate links with followers. A new integration between Instagram and Amazon was announced earlier this month as a way to make it easier for influencers to make money from affiliate links — but some content creators are suspicious about who really benefits.
Some creators are skeptical of Instagram’s new affiliate program
Influencers are now able to link their Amazon and Instagram accounts to promote products. Some are concerned about what they’re opting in to.
The new integration allows creators to connect their Instagram and Amazon accounts and automatically tag products with their affiliate links, from which they earn a commission when followers make purchases. Influencers will be able to embed up to 30 product links in a Reel or 20 in a feed post, but a permissions setting has led to concerns about what creators are actually agreeing to.
In connecting an Amazon account, creators must agree to allow the retailer and its brand sellers to create ads from “any public content” that includes a related affiliate link. Influencers must also agree to acknowledge that brands can edit their content and use their “testimonial, caption or media” for ads.
The wide-ranging permissions are giving creators pause. Some have urged peers not to connect their accounts without reviewing the permissions and understanding how the feature would affect earnings. People making money on social media spend years tweaking their content and strategy to maximize reach, engagement, and, by extension, their bottom line. For some, it appeared that they would be giving Amazon and its sellers the ability to use their content under unclear terms. On Instagram head Adam Mosseri’s post announcing the feature, influencers complained about the lack of clarity, questioned whether using the feature would decrease their reach (which some creators say happens when they link to outside products), and demanded answers to whether their commission rate would stay the same when Amazon or brands use their content for ads.
Linking products through the new integration won’t reduce reach, Jimmy O’Keefe, Instagram’s director of product marketing, said in an email to The Verge. O’Keefe also noted that creators will continue to earn commission through affiliate links when Amazon boosts their posts, and that they can stop the boosting in settings or disconnect the integration entirely. There’s also a separate, manual way to add products without linking accounts, if a creator wants to opt out of having their content made into ads.
Amazon has an enormous influencer program that reaches across social media platforms. It is so lucrative that some content creators are able to make a living almost exclusively by hawking products for sale on Amazon, building empires on the shopping habits of their followers. When it comes to putting those links in front of followers, though, social platforms have historically been a roadblock, hence the cottage industry of link-in-bio tools meant to circumvent limits. Slowly but surely, though, platforms like Instagram, Facebook, and YouTube — perhaps chasing the success of TikTok Shop — have added more and more shopping features. The result is that shopping and social media begin to feel more and more like the same thing.

articles.title: GTA 6 : la carte interactive ultime pour découvrir les secrets de Leonida
articles.text:
À chaque nouvel opus, des fans de Rockstar se regroupent sur Discord et GTAForums pour passer chaque image officielle à la loupe. Le site gratuit State of Leonida, développé par Laze, rassemble les relevés de Yanis et de la communauté GTA 6 Mapping.
Plus de 3 800 marqueurs recensés image par image pour GTA 6
Cette carte interactive de GTA 6 est passée par près d’une vingtaine de versions au fil des bandes-annonces et des captures d’écran. Elle repose sur un travail de triangulation minutieux. En croisant les coordonnées issues des fuites de septembre 2022 avec les angles de vue des trois bandes-annonces officielles et des visuels promotionnels ainsi que le contenu final, l’équipe a cartographié les six régions nommées par Rockstar : Vice City, les marécages des Grassrivers, l’archipel des Leonida Keys, Port Gellhorn, Ambrosia et le parc national du Mont Kalaga.
L’outil recense 3854 marqueurs répartis par catégories, accompagnés d’une barre de recherche complète :
- Les infrastructures et commerces : magasins, stations-service, lignes de transports en commun, aéroports, ports et bâtiments officiels.
- La géographie et les points d’intérêt : lacs, parcs naturels, plages et axes routiers principaux.
- Les détails insolites : la communauté a même répertorié des éléments anecdotiques aperçus dans les vidéos, à l’image d’un mystérieux piano abandonné sur une plage.
Comparateur de taille et mini-jeu intégré
Le site propose aussi plusieurs outils annexes. Un outil de superposition permet de comparer l’échelle de Leonida avec les anciennes cartes de Rockstar, de Vice City et San Andreas jusqu’à GTA 4, GTA 5 et Red Dead Redemption 2. Ces superpositions restent une estimation de fans. Côté officiel, Aaron Garbut, codirecteur du studio Rockstar North, a indiqué à Game Informer fin septembre que Leonida fait environ deux fois la taille de la carte de GTA 5.
Le site intègre aussi une base de données de plus de 200 entrées, qui relie chaque lieu à la capture d’écran correspondante. Il propose enfin un mini-jeu baptisé « Find the Marker » : à la manière de GeoGuessr, il faut retrouver sur la carte l’endroit où a été pris un extrait de bande-annonce, avec un classement communautaire à la clé.
Cette reconstitution, menée sans aucun lien avec Rockstar Games ou Take-Two, peut désormais être comparée au jeu. GTA 6 est disponible depuis ce jeudi sur PS5 et Xbox Series X/S.

articles.title: AI can write code, but knowing what to build still matters
articles.text:
AI can write code, but knowing what to build still matters
At TechSparks 2026, Srinivas Chamarthy of Diligent India, Madhusudan N. Murthy of EY GDS, and Arun Kalyanaraman of Target discussed why domain expertise, engineering skills, and human judgement remain important as AI makes software development more accessible.
AI is making it easier to build software. Product managers, designers, and domain experts can now turn ideas into prototypes without necessarily knowing how to code. But turning those prototypes into reliable products that solve real problems remains a challenge.
At TechSparks 2026, Srinivas Chamarthy, Senior Vice President of Engineering, Site Lead and Country Head at Diligent India; Madhusudan N. Murthy, Digital Engineering and Tech Strategy Leader at EY GDS; and Arun Kalyanaraman, VP of Engineering at Target in India, discussed these changes during a panel titled ‘From Who Can Code to Who Can Build’.
The discussion was moderated by Chhavi Mahajan, Chief Content Officer at YourStory.
From prototypes to production
AI-assisted development allows business teams to test ideas, demonstrate concepts, and gather feedback much earlier. However, a prototype that shows an idea can work is not necessarily ready for production. Applications still need to meet security, scalability, and reliability requirements.
Murthy said that AI is making experimentation easier, but companies must distinguish between a proof of concept and a production-ready application. Engineering teams still need to identify vulnerabilities, put safeguards in place, and ensure systems can handle real-world use.
“It's good, it's a very positive development, but it also has to have its guardrails,” he stated.
Kalyanaraman said AI can do more than help developers write code faster. It can also speed up the entire development process, from defining a problem and testing a solution to getting stakeholder approval. However, strong engineering fundamentals, architectural thinking, and technical depth will remain essential, even as AI changes how solutions are built.
He gave the example of a product owner, an engineer, and a UX professional who used AI tools and large language models to prototype a complex concept and present it to leadership within a week. Without these tools, the process could have taken six weeks to two months.
The benefit was not just faster coding, but the ability to test an idea and make a decision sooner.
Chamarthy said coding is becoming a commodity in the generative AI era, shortening the path from prototype to customer feedback to production, with a nine-month cycle potentially coming down to a month or two. As speed increases, he said, knowing what not to build becomes more valuable, so ideas should be tested in a sandbox while experienced engineers harden them for security, scalability, and privacy.
Deciding where human oversight is needed
As companies move from using AI to assist developers to deploying agents that can complete tasks with limited supervision, they must decide how much autonomy to allow.
Chamarthy said this should depend on the risks involved, the potential impact of a decision, and whether its outcome can be reversed.
He suggested organizations consider whether a decision is a two-way-door or a one-way-door call, with significant financial or strategic decisions needing human oversight and contextual judgment.
Chamarthy cautioned that access to AI coding tools cannot replace engineering experience. Experienced engineers understand the architectural decisions that affect security, scalability, and long-term maintenance, including risks that may not be apparent in a prototype.
His advice was to encourage experimentation, but within controlled environments.
“Don't stop the code. Sandbox it.”
This allows more employees to test ideas while giving engineering teams the opportunity to review the applications, address weaknesses, and prepare them for production.
Why domain expertise matters
As AI makes it easier to generate code and find answers, knowing which problems to solve becomes more important.
Kalyanaraman compared using AI to consulting a genie that grants only three wishes. Getting a useful result depends on asking the right questions and understanding the constraints.
“In a world where maybe getting answers are easy, asking the right questions is going to be a really, really critical skill,” he said.
People who understand customers, business processes, and operational requirements are better placed to identify solutions that create value.
Engineering teams will also need systems thinking and platform expertise to help non-engineers develop applications without putting production systems at risk.
The shift also has implications for workforce development.
Murthy said EY GDS is preparing employees for an AI-driven workplace by bringing experienced professionals and younger talent together. Existing employees bring knowledge of customers and systems, while newer team members contribute fresh approaches and develop emerging technical skills.
Chamarthy said teams need a mix of strengths: organizations should upskill existing employees, who understand their products and customers, while bringing in fresh graduates who can work with AI tools.
He also added that engineering performance should be measured by the problems teams solve for customers, rather than only by metrics such as lines of code written or tickets closed.
As AI takes over more routine work, the outcomes delivered by engineering teams become a more useful measure of their contribution.
A workforce of people and AI agents
The panellists expect employees and AI agents to work increasingly closely together.
As agents take on more complex tasks, companies will need to rethink workflows, accountability and performance expectations. They will also need to ensure safeguards keep pace with what the technology can do.
Murthy described a future in which managers will oversee AI agents alongside human employees.
“The future I see is getting used to agents reporting to you and not just humans,” he said.
Kalyanaraman added that The New Tech Order is not just about what AI can do for us. It is about how we evolve our thinking, engineering practices, and decision-making to make the most of it.
While AI is making software easier to build, companies will still need engineering expertise, domain knowledge, and human judgement to decide which ideas are worth pursuing and which prototypes are ready for production.

Points forts
Châssis toujours élégant.
Performances de la puce M5.
Silence complet.
Partie audio irréprochable.
Écran de qualité.
Wifi (presque) 7 et Bluetooth 6.
Clavier de qualité…
Points faibles
…mais toujours propice aux traces de doigts.
Poids qui se fait sentir.
Réflectance de la dalle.

Le MacBook Air M5 (2026) d’Apple est toujours une référence sur son segment tarifaire pour qui cherche un ordinateur performant et endurant sans casser sa tirelire. Si la puce M5 n’offre pas le bond générationnel de son aînée, elle est néanmoins parfaitement capable d’encaisser tous les besoins en bureautique, avec même un peu de création. Mieux encore, Apple se met enfin à la page en proposant d’emblée 512 Go de stockage au même tarif qu'en 2025 !
